- Restoring the exit code alone still let the rollup through, which repaints the banner on its own. A
  second mutation (restore Exit, drop Rollup) found that, and a second assertion pins it.
A companion case pins the other direction: on a clean run an unknown edge must STILL block. Otherwise
"preserve the verdict" quietly becomes "never let the probe matter".

## D388. A capability can be satisfied and have no effect
From the field, with evidence: `capability.monitoring.logs` was declared with 365-day retention,
converge went green, and the group it created held zero bytes. The application's logs went to the group
its own runtime creates, which expires never. The contract described log retention; the retention of the
logs was described by nothing. The reporter's framing is the one worth keeping — "the capability looks
satisfied and is useless" — and they were right that it is the same class as a gate that can quietly
check nothing.
Their diagnosis of the CAUSE was one step wider than the cause. They said the vocabulary had no way to
bind a logs capability to a compute capability. The `cwlogs` driver had accepted a `log_group` operand
all along; what was missing was knowing the NAME at authoring time, since the group is derived from a
function name the author cannot predict before the first converge. D381 supplied the missing half — a
typed `logGroupName` output — and D226 references wire it with no interpolation and no string joining.
So the correct thing became EXPRESSIBLE. THAT IS NOT THE SAME AS MAKING THE WRONG THING HARD, and the
reporter's sentence survives the fix: nothing compels the wiring, so a contract that governs a group
nobody writes to still passes and still goes green. This entry closes that half — not by refusing (the
tool cannot know that a standalone group is a mistake; flow logs and control-plane logs both want one)
but by SAYING SO. D365's standing directive, and its sharpened condition: say it where an AGENT will
hear it. The advisory rides in the plan as `advisories[]` with a stable code, and on stderr as prose.
Neither channel is the only one.
THE CONDITION IS THREE-PART AND NARROW ON PURPOSE, because D364's lesson is that a warning firing on
ordinary input trains people to ignore it. It fires only when the logs capability provisions its own
group, AND the same candidate holds a capability whose DRIVER declares it brings its own log
destination, AND nothing wires them. The second part asks the drivers (D317) rather than consulting a
list of services, so the rule cannot rot into a stale table — a mutation that hardcodes `service ==
"lambda"` instead fails its case. The third keeps it quiet once the advice has been taken; a warning
that keeps firing after it has been acted on is one people learn to filter out.
An advisory is something NOTICED, never something proven. It touches no precondition, no `writes`, no
verdict — every case here still SEALS — and the four-valued verdict remains the only thing that gates
execution. The conformance runner learned to assert advisories in both directions, and the second
direction is the one that matters: `absentAdvisories` pins the silence, so the negative control (a
standalone group with no producer anywhere) is a case that fails if the advisory ever becomes noisy.

## D389. Half of least privilege was unexpressible, and the refusal that made it so was wrong
`role.permissions subset-of <approved actions>` is a real least-privilege guarantee about WHAT a role
may do. It says nothing about WHERE. A field partner made the gap concrete: an inference role whose
action set was exactly right, whose EU-only residency lived in a hand-written policy outside the
contract, and whose manual steps could not be closed because the vocabulary had no way to say it.
THE REFUSAL WAS EXPLICIT AND IT WAS MINE TO RE-EXAMINE. capability.authorization.role's own header
listed "resource scoping inside the policy" alongside conditions, Deny/notActions and effects as the
expression language, deferred. That grouping does not survive contact: a flat SET OF RESOURCE
IDENTIFIERS has no connectives, no interpolation and no conditions. It is data, exactly like the action
set, and verifiable exactly the same way. Refusing it was not protecting invariant 4; it was leaving
half of least privilege unsayable. The header now says so rather than being quietly edited around it.
WHERE A RESOURCE ID PINS A REGION, subset-of over an allowlist is a RESIDENCY guarantee — everything
matching `arn:aws:bedrock:eu-central-1::foundation-model/*` is in eu-central-1 by construction. Where it
does not, subset-of proves the declared patterns were approved and nothing about the set they expand to.
Both halves are stated in the vocabulary, because the difference decides whether a compliance claim is
real. A wildcard is admitted as part of a resource identifier's own syntax, not as an expression.
THE THREE CLOUDS ARE NOT TWINS HERE, and pretending otherwise would have been the easy mistake. AWS
puts the resource set inside the policy (the Resource list, hardcoded "*" until now). Azure has
assignableScopes, which bounds where a role may be ASSIGNED rather than what each action reaches — the
tightest bound a role definition carries there, and the driver says so rather than implying AWS
semantics. GCP has NOTHING: a custom role is includedPermissions and scope lives on the BINDING. That
refusal is NAMED and points at `capability.authorization.grant` (access.scope=resource +
implementation.scope), because a generic "no mapping" reads as an oversight in the driver and an author
who reads it concludes the capability is unsupported. It is the exact mirror of the gap access.scope
already records for aws.iam: each cloud scopes where its own model puts the scope.
An absent role.resources stays "*". Silently narrowing it would rewrite the meaning of every candidate
written before the attribute existed.
TWO THINGS THE FIRST VERSION GOT WRONG, both found by mutation, neither by tests passing:
- IDEMPOTENCY compared action sets only. A same-named policy whose actions matched and whose Resource
  was "*" would have been adopted as ours — reporting a residency-scoped role satisfied against a policy
  that reaches everything. The resource set decides adoption too.
- The conformance cases could not see either failure. The plan output carries no policy document, so
  reverting the builder to "*" left every case green; and a case asserting the GCP refusal used an
  `expect: refused:` key THE RUNNER DOES NOT READ, so it asserted nothing and passed for two independent
  wrong reasons. It was deleted rather than repaired: the refusal happens at apply-preflight, not
  compile, and the honest home for it is a driver test. What the conformance suite CAN pin — the
  four-valued verdicts, dual — it pins.
Observe reads the live Resource list back on AWS and assignableScopes on Azure, MEASURED. That is the
half that makes the guarantee proven rather than declared; an observation that echoed the candidate
would verify nothing.
Still open, deliberately: the partner's `kms:ViaService` service-scoping. `role.resources` closes two of
their three manual steps. The third wants a typed CONDITION, which is a different question — the first
typed condition sets a precedent and the second and third arrive behind it — and it belongs to whoever
owns the medium, not to this entry.

## D390. Auditing the field's 36 findings: one class was fixed twice and gated zero times

MATURITY gap 4 says the field found things the gates did not, and names the pilot's 36
findings as the evidence. Nothing had ever swept that list against the gates, so this
entry does it — the field is the only real sample of where defects actually live, and
my own audits are internal gates, which is precisely the instrument that sample
indicts.

**Reconstructing the list first.** There is no registry of the 36 anywhere in the repo;
they survive only as `F<n>` references scattered through this file. Two traps: the
`F<n>` namespace is REUSED per review round (D73's F1 is an orphaned-lease deadlock,
D192's F1 is a stale `claimed` bit, D194's F1 is converge masking a violation — three
different findings, one number), and the field series is only the one that starts in the
D200s. Restricted to the field era, the record accounts for **24** identifiers (F1–F29
with gaps; F23 survives only in a code comment, never here). Twelve cannot be traced
from this repo at all. The pilot paused on 2026-07-24, so they cannot be reconciled
against the source either — MATURITY now says so rather than leaving "36" to imply a
closed loop.

**Coverage of what IS traceable.** Most field classes are gated cross-driver, and this
sweep confirmed each mechanically rather than by reading the entries: driver-method
completeness (D210) and observe completeness (D317) gate the blind-service classes;
`TestEveryAuthoredServiceCanReconcile` gates F24; D266/D267 gate the four cluster
lifecycle classes (read-retry, bounded poll, LRO timeout, no-duplicate) across EKS/GKE/
AKS; D272/D274 gate the two classes hermetic CI shipped past. Two hypotheses I formed
and then killed with measurement: no driver anywhere sleeps in a poll without a budget
(the D258/D259 hang class is bounded by construction, not merely by enrolment), and no
driver injects a random or wall-clock value into a create body (the only `rand.` in any
driver is RSA signing) — so the retry-duplicates-because-the-body-changed path does not
exist. Both are recorded here so the next sweep does not re-ask them.

**The gap.** The idempotency-token class bit twice. F27: Secrets Manager refused a
missing `ClientRequestToken`. D304: EventBridge Scheduler returned 400 "ClientToken
cannot be empty" on a live converge, after other resources were already standing. Both
times one driver was fixed. No gate landed either time, so the path that let it recur is
still open — a new AWS driver can be authored today with no idempotency decision made
about it at all. That is the definition of a class that needs a gate rather than a fix.

D304 closed with "a full sweep of every AWS create confirmed Scheduler was the ONLY
required-but-missing case". That sweep was a manual read of the drivers — the instrument
D317 showed gives wrong answers, four different ones — and three of its rows were
explicitly flagged for live confirmation from a pilot that has since paused. That
confirmation is not coming, and a flag nobody can clear is not a plan.

So the gate deliberately does NOT encode what each AWS API requires; inventing 54 such
claims would be the same mistake in a new costume. It forces the DECISION to exist:
every create service must be in `idempotencyCarried` (the driver emits a deterministic
token — 9 services, each verifiable in this package, and the parameter name differs per
API: ClientToken, ClientRequestToken, CallerReference, CreatorRequestId, CreationToken,
which is exactly why membership is declared rather than name-matched), in
`idempotencyNotApplicable` (reviewed, with the source for the claim — deliberately EMPTY
rather than filled from memory), or in `idempotencyUnreviewed`, which is a D297-style
ratchet at 45 that may only go down. A new create service lands in none of the three and
fails the gate. Verified in both directions, including the ratchet's downward nudge.

The honest reading of that baseline: 45 AWS creates whose idempotency behaviour nobody
has reviewed, after the class bit twice. The gate does not fix that — it makes it
visible, attributable, and payable, and it closes the recurrence path.

make check clean.

## D391. Create-time adoption was proven for 18 services; the roster is now 54

D390 swept the field's findings and found the idempotency class ungated. Following that
thread down rather than sideways: the reason a missing idempotency token is expensive is
that a create which cannot recognise an existing resource MINTS A SECOND ONE. D252/D253
built the defence for that — create-time adoption, where a create that finds an OWNED
resource already standing binds it instead — and D253 named the cost when it is absent
in its own words: "a second VPC, a second paid key", and neither one in the ledger,
because a server-assigned id with no token means the second create never collides.

D253 proved the property **per driver, for a roster of 18 AWS services**. There are now
**54** creates. No gate ever asserted the property as a CLASS, so the proof covers a
third of the services it is claimed for, and nothing noticed the roster tripling
underneath the claim. That is the D338 shape — a property established once against a
roster that then grew — applied to behaviour rather than to a registry.

`CertifyCreateAdoptsExisting` is the mirror of D267's `CertifyNoDuplicate`, and the more
expensive half: drive a create against a fake in which the owned resource ALREADY
EXISTS, and require both halves — the result binds THAT resource's providerId, and zero
create mutations went out. The second half is the real proof; a driver can report a
plausible binding after already sending the duplicating POST. Enrolled on KMS and VPC —
D253's own two examples — through the PUBLIC Create dispatch rather than the private
create function, because that is where the behaviour actually lives (the D309 lesson).
Enrolment is then itself a gated decision with a ratchet at 52, mirroring D390.

**Two things the gate surfaced while being built, both worth recording.**

The VPC create-adoption path had never been exercised end to end. `vpcScanServer` covers
`findVpcByTags` in isolation; binding an existing VPC then goes on to derive the
capability's declared outputs, which reads subnets and route tables — and no test ever
ran that far. The fixture also used the id `vpc-ours`, which this product's own outputs
validator rightly rejects as malformed. An implausible stand-in in a FIXTURE hides the
path it was meant to cover — D289's lesson ("a false 'missing operand' is still a lie"),
now on the test side. Nothing was broken; the coverage simply stopped short of where the
work happens.

And two false accusations my own probe made before I believed it: the capability passed
in the wrong argument slot (so the ownership scan looked for a tag nothing carried), and
an unpinned account, which sent a real STS `GetCallerIdentity` that the classifier
counted as a mutation. Both would have read as "this driver duplicates". A gate that
accuses falsely costs exactly what a gate that misses costs, and the account pin now
doubles as proof the gate never leaves its fake.

make check + race clean.

## D392. Paying the adoption ratchet: 52 to 48, and what the enrolments found

D391 left a ratchet at 52 unenrolled creates. Paying it is not bookkeeping — each
enrolment either proves the property for one more driver or finds it absent, and the
gate distinguishes the two adoption MECHANISMS honestly, which matters for what counts
as proof:

- **pre-scan** adopters (KMS, VPC) look before they leap, so ZERO mutations is the proof;
- **reactive** adopters (Bedrock, S3) send the create, take the API's own
  already-exists answer, and bind — so one mutation is the MECHANISM, not a duplicate,
  and the binding identity is the proof;
- **name-idempotent** creates (SNS, SQS) cannot mint a second resource at the same name
  at all, so the proof is again the identity bound, with the mutation allowance covering
  the attribute writes that converge an adopted resource.

`AllowedMutations` carries that distinction per driver rather than weakening the gate
for everyone.

Four services joined KMS and VPC, and three of them were covered in a way worth naming.
S3's own test file says of the tags-match bucket: "covered live". SNS and SQS had tests
for the untagged and the foreign-tagged cases — the two REFUSALS — but none for the
OURS case, the one that has to succeed. So for all three, the path that actually runs on
every converge against an existing estate was proven only by having watched it work in
the field. That was a reasonable position while the field was there. The pilot paused on
2026-07-24, and a proof that lives in a paused engagement is not a proof any more; it is
a memory. Those three are now covered here.

Bedrock's fixture was extracted into `bedrockExistingServer` and shared between its
per-driver test and the class gate, so the two cannot drift into testing different
worlds.

The gate also caught the author: an early edit left `bedrock` in both `adoptGated` and
`adoptUnenrolled`, and the exactly-one-set check named it immediately. A completeness
gate that only checks for the empty case would have passed that quietly and reported a
debt of 49 as 48.

Ratchet: 52 -> 48. make check + race clean.

## D393. Ratchet 48 to 46, and a harness that stops blaming the driver

Two more enrolments (cwlogs, custompolicy), and one of them cost enough time to be worth
fixing at the root rather than in the enrolment.

CloudWatch Logs adopts reactively — `CreateLogGroup` answers
`ResourceAlreadyExistsException`, the driver reads the group's tags and repairs onto it —
and it already had `TestCreateCWLogs_AlreadyExistsOursRepairs`, so enrolling it was
wiring an existing fixture into the class gate. `custompolicy` is a different shape
again: an IAM policy is name-addressed AND content-addressed by its Arn, so a policy
already standing at our deterministic name with the SAME action set is bound as-is and
never re-written. The gate's proof there is that the create adds no policy version.

**The harness was blaming the driver for the author's mistake.** My `custompolicy`
classifier called `req.ParseForm()` — the obvious way to read an AWS query-protocol
action, and wrong here, because the classifier runs inside the RoundTripper on a request
the driver has not sent yet. ParseForm drains the body, and the driver then fails with
`ContentLength=283 with Body length 0`. That failure reads exactly like a driver that
cannot send its own create, and it took a diagnosis to find that it was my test.

The narrow fix is "don't do that", which lasts until the next author. So `peekBody` now
has a named counterpart, `restoreBody`, and every classification site in certifynet
re-seats the body AFTER classifying, not just before. The whole Certify family is now
immune, and `TestClassifierCannotDrainTheDriversBody` pins it with a classifier that
drains on purpose. This is the third time in two entries that my own probe accused a
driver falsely (D391: the capability in the wrong slot, and an unpinned account sending
real STS). The pattern is clear enough to design against rather than remember: a gate
must not be able to break the thing it measures.

Ratchet: 48 -> 46. make check + race clean.

## D394. Ratchet 46 to 43: three more, and a damage model that is not always duplication

Three enrolments — guardduty, eks-podidentity, eks-addon — and between them they show
that "create-time adoption" defends against more than one failure, which is worth
recording because the right proof differs per shape.

GuardDuty's detector is a SINGLETON per region-account. A second `CreateDetector` does
not stand up a second detector; it fails. So the damage of a missing adoption there is
not a duplicate resource but a converge that simply cannot proceed against any estate
that already has GuardDuty on — the exact state every brownfield account is in. The
proof is the same shape as the others (bind the existing id, converge with one
`UpdateDetector`), but what it buys is availability rather than money.

`eks-podidentity` is the opposite extreme: an association is keyed by (cluster,
namespace, serviceAccount) and a second create for the same triple DOES stand up a
second association, so zero mutations is load-bearing there. `eks-addon` sits between:
identified by (cluster, addon name), and the case that was missing is the one every
re-converge meets — the addon we installed being already installed. The foreign-tagged
refusal had a test; the ours case did not.

That recurring shape is now the clearest pattern in this whole pass: the REFUSALS were
tested (foreign, untagged) and the SUCCESS was not, for S3, SNS, SQS and eks-addon
alike. Refusals are what you write a test for when you are thinking about safety;
the ours-already path is what actually runs, on every converge, against every estate
that is not empty.

Ratchet: 46 -> 43. make check + race clean.

## D395. Ratchet 43 to 40: composites, and EKS itself

Three more — loadbalancer, ses-inbound, eks — and the first of them needed the gate to
admit a shape it had not met.

An ALB is a **composite**: load balancer, target group, listener. Adoption there is
PARTIAL by nature — bind the pieces that stand, create only the piece that is missing —
so a fixed mutation budget is the wrong assertion, and the gate leans on the identity
bound while the per-driver test keeps pinning that no `CreateLoadBalancer` or
`CreateTargetGroup` is re-issued. The two assertions are complementary rather than
redundant: the class gate says the right resource was adopted, the driver test says the
standing composite was not rebuilt. ses-inbound is the name-addressed twin of that —
rule set and rule bound by name and repaired in place, `UpdateReceiptRule` and never a
create.

EKS is the one that matters most historically: it is the driver at the centre of the
Acme saga. D258, D259 and D261 are all the same underlying event — a cluster that was
already there, not recognised — and the fixture the gate now runs is exactly that
estate: an ACTIVE cluster carrying our tags whose node group sits under a name that is
NOT the deterministic one. Zero mutations, the cluster's own pid. The property that cost
the most to learn is now asserted as a class rather than as three regression tests.

The exactly-one-set check caught the author a second time (loadbalancer and ses-inbound
left in both maps). It has now paid for itself twice in four entries, which is worth
saying plainly: a completeness gate that only looks for gaps would have reported this
debt as 40 when it was 42.

Ratchet: 43 -> 40. make check + race clean.

## D396. Ratchet 40 to 38: the Aurora fixture could not describe a standing cluster

aurora and ecs. ECS was straightforward — it resumes onto an existing OURS service via
the API's own "Creation of service was not idempotent" message, with the standing
service's tags making the resume legitimate.

Aurora was not, and the reason is the same one D391 found in VPC, one layer deeper.

`newFakeAurora` never emitted `<Endpoint>`, `<ReaderEndpoint>` or `<Port>`. A real
cluster — created or adopted — has all three, and the driver derives Aurora's typed
outputs from exactly that one `DescribeDBClusters` read (D276, the F13 wiring table).
So every create-path test stopped short of output derivation, and the outputs were
covered instead by `TestAuroraEndpointOutput`, which builds its own fake and calls
`deriveOutputs` directly. Two fakes describing the same cluster, neither able to stand
in for the other, and no test in between: **create composed with output derivation had
no hermetic coverage for Aurora at all**.

That matters more than a missing field. Aurora's typed outputs are what a consumer
capability `$ref`s to reach the database (D283's fold), which is the wiring the whole
platform contract rests on. The fake now emits the trio when it is given one, so every
existing test keeps its exact wire shape and the composed path is reachable.

Two entries in a row where enrolling a driver exposed a fixture that could not describe
the resource it was standing in for. That is a class worth naming: a fake built to
answer ONE question answers it forever, and the question it cannot answer never gets
asked.

Ratchet: 40 -> 38. make check + race clean.

## D397. Ratchet 38 to 35: ses-sending, ecr, budgets

Three more, each a different way of knowing a resource is ours.

`ses-sending` is a composite (email identity, configuration set, event destination)
whose identity is name-addressed by domain — an estate that already sends mail is
exactly what a converge meets, and the foreign case had a test while ours did not.
`ecr` is name-addressed with a `RepositoryAlreadyExists` answer and a tag check.

`budgets` is the interesting one: a budget carries NO TAGS at all. The deterministic
NAME is the whole ownership marker, so a `DuplicateRecordException` is answered by
re-reading the standing budget and continuing onto its notification. That is the D250
partial-heal path (F25-b, a budget created without its alert notification), and it is
now asserted as a class rather than as one regression test. It is also the weakest
ownership evidence in the AWS driver family — worth knowing, and it is the API's fault,
not the driver's: there is nothing else to check.

Ratchet: 38 -> 35. make check + race clean.

## D398. Ratchet 35 to 33, and the gate learns a second honest ending

efs and cloudtrail. EFS closes a loop with D390: it is one of the nine drivers carrying a
deterministic idempotency token, and this is the other half of that story — the token is
what makes AWS refuse the duplicate, and `recoverEFS` is what turns that refusal into
the SAME handle rather than a failure. Token without recovery would be half a defence.

CloudTrail forced a real question. Its `TrailAlreadyExists` branch does not bind: it
returns unknown WITH the pid and leaves ownership to reconcile. My first instinct was
that the gate had found a gap, because sixteen other drivers adopt inline. It has not.
Nothing duplicated — the create was refused by the API — so the expensive half of the
property holds exactly as it does everywhere else. What differs is who settles the
binding: the create, or the next `resume`.

Forcing CloudTrail into the succeeded shape would have been changing a driver to satisfy
a test, which is the failure mode invariant 5 exists to prevent. Tolerating unknown
GLOBALLY would have been worse: it would let any driver quietly stop adopting and still
pass. So the shape is DECLARED per driver — `ConcludesUnknown` — and the declaration is
the point. "Defers by design" and "silently stopped adopting" produce the same status
and must not produce the same verdict.

Whether cloudtrail should adopt inline like its sixteen siblings is a real question, and
it is not one a gate answers. It is recorded here rather than decided.

Ratchet: 35 -> 33. make check + race clean.

## D399. Ratchet 33 to 32: route53, where the id is the server's to give

route53. A hosted-zone id is SERVER-assigned, which puts it in the same class as D253's
VPC and KMS: without recovery, a retry after a lost response mints a SECOND zone for the
same domain, and DNS then has two authorities where the operator believes there is one.
The `CallerReference` is what makes that recoverable — the create is answered
`HostedZoneAlreadyExists`, and `recoverRoute53` lists by name and matches the reference
to return the same handle.

That is the third distinct role a deterministic token plays across this pass: EFS uses
it to recover a handle (D398), EventBridge Scheduler and Secrets Manager use it to stop
the duplicate being created at all (D390/F27), and Route53 uses it as the KEY that makes
the standing zone recognisable as ours among the zones for that name. Same mechanism,
three different jobs, and only the first two were ever described as idempotency.

Ratchet: 33 -> 32. make check + race clean.

## D400. Ratchet 32 to 30: backupvault, iam

Two name-addressed services with a tag check, and one of them has a damage model worth
naming.

A **backup vault** holds recovery points. Standing a second one up does not merely cost
money — it SPLITS the backup estate. The new vault is empty and looks healthy, the real
one is unmanaged, and the discovery happens at restore time. Of every duplication this
pass has considered, that is the one whose cost is deferred longest and paid worst.

`iam` is straightforward — a role is name-addressed, `EntityAlreadyExists` is the answer,
and the tags on the standing role are what license binding it.

The probe misfired once more, and usefully: I passed `awsRoleAttrs()` (the POLICY
service's attributes) to the role create, and the driver refused with "attribute
access.mutating has no IAM role mapping — refusing rather than silently dropping it".
That is the refuse-before-mutate rule (D207/D209) catching a malformed candidate exactly
as designed. Four author errors now, and every one of them was caught by a driver or a
gate rather than slipping through as a false result. That is the property worth having.

Ratchet: 32 -> 30. make check + race clean.

## D401. Ratchet 30 to 28: rds, elasticache — and the fixture that agreed with the bug

rds and elasticache, both deterministic client-assigned identifiers answered by an
already-exists error, both deciding on tags.

ElastiCache is here for a second reason. It carries the F28 scar, and the comment its
own fake still holds is the sharpest sentence in this file:

> ElastiCache (like the whole RDS Query family) returns tags as `<Tag>`, NOT the
> EC2-style `<member>` — the parser and this fake had AGREED on `<member>`, so the bug
> (real AWS tags read as empty -> "not ours") passed green.

A fake and a parser that share a wrong assumption produce a green suite and a driver
that refuses to adopt anything real. That is the same mechanism D273 found in the field
(the unit fake mirrored the driver's wrong assumption about a poll path, so it was blind
by construction) and the same family as this pass's own findings about fixtures that
cannot describe what they stand in for. Three appearances now, in three different
subsystems, discovered three different ways.

It is worth stating what does and does not follow. A gate built on the same fake cannot
catch this class — the endpoint-reality gate (D274) and the live smoke (D272) exist
precisely because nothing hermetic can. What the class gate does add is that the OURS
path is now exercised at all: F28's bug lived in a path no test drove.

Ratchet: 30 -> 28. make check + race clean.

## D402. Ratchet 28 to 26: opensearch, asg — a fake whose errors the driver cannot read

opensearch was routine. asg was not, and its lesson is the F28 pattern in miniature,
found the same way D401 described it.

The ASG fake's own error helper emits `<Response><Errors><Error><Code>`. The driver
parses `Error>Code` RELATIVE TO THE ROOT, which that envelope does not match — so every
error the fake produces reaches the driver as an EMPTY code. It has been harmless
because the tests that use it assert only the status, never the classification. But it
means the fake cannot express a CODED error at all, and a code is exactly what the
already-exists branch dispatches on: the adoption path was unreachable from this fixture
by construction, not by omission.

The probe uses the envelope real AWS sends. The fake's helper is left as it is,
deliberately — changing shared fixture behaviour to suit one new test is how a suite
starts lying, and the tests that use it are not wrong about what they assert. The
mismatch is now documented at the point where it matters.

Also worth recording plainly: this is the third fixture-shape finding in four entries
(VPC's implausible id, Aurora's missing endpoints, and now ASG's unparseable errors).
None of them is a product bug. All three are the same thing — a fixture that answers the
question it was built for and cannot answer any other — and all three surfaced only
because a gate drove a path nobody had driven before.

Ratchet: 28 -> 26. make check + race clean.

## D403. My own D390 registry was built with the instrument D390 condemned

Working down the adoption ratchet reached the services whose ids are SERVER-assigned —
the D253 class, where nothing about a name stops a retry minting a second resource. ACM
is one: its providerId comes out of the create response. So the question was what stops
a lost RequestCertificate response from producing two certificates.

The answer is that nothing was wrong: ACM carries `IdempotencyToken`, derived
deterministically from environment, capability and generation, exactly like the nine
services D390 listed. It was simply not in `idempotencyCarried`.

Why it was missed is the part worth writing down. D390 named a fourth spelling
(ClientToken, ClientRequestToken, CallerReference, CreatorRequestId, CreationToken) and
built its initial contents by grepping for those names — the same instrument it had, in
its own opening comment, called unreliable, citing D317. `IdempotencyToken` is a fifth
spelling. So `acm` sat in the unreviewed debt while carrying a perfectly good defence:
the registry understated the protection AND overstated the work remaining, which is the
worst combination a debt register can manage.

The durable fix keys on the DERIVATION instead of the name. Every deterministic token in
this package is a hash of `environment|capability|generation` — that is what makes a
retry reuse it — so any field named like a token and assigned from `letterHash` must
appear in `idempotencyCarried`. A driver that gains a token and forgets the registry now
fails. Verified by removing the acm entry and watching it be named.

The limit stays exactly where D390 put it: this cannot find a service that NEEDS a token
and has none. That is a claim about an AWS API, and it is payable only by review.

Idempotency ratchet: 45 -> 44 (by correction, not by review). make check + race clean.

## D404. The two ratchets were asking one question; 26 to 18 by answering it once

D390 asked "does this create carry an idempotency token" and D391 asked "does this create
bind a resource that already exists". Working both down together made it obvious they are
the same question wearing two hats: **can a re-run mint a second resource?**

There are two ways to answer no. The driver can look first and bind what it finds, which
is create-time adoption. Or the API can collapse the retry onto the ORIGINAL resource
because the request carries a deterministic token — adoption achieved by AWS instead of
by the driver. Same property, different mechanism, and eight services were sitting in the
adoption debt while already holding the second one.

So `adoptNotApplicable` finally has entries, and the important part is what an entry now
costs. It must NAME its evidence, and `TestNotApplicableClaimsAreBacked` checks the
evidence rather than reading the sentence. The only reason admitted today is
`idempotency-token`, and the check is membership in `idempotencyCarried` — which D403's
derivation cross-check keeps honest against the drivers' own code. So the chain is:
this service is exempt, because it carries a token, because a field named like a token
is assigned from a hash of environment|capability|generation in its driver. Every link is
re-derived by a test.

A reason the gate cannot check is refused outright, with the reason given: an
unverifiable exemption is how a debt register starts lying. That is the shape D304's
closing sentence should have had — "a full sweep confirmed" is exactly the claim nothing
can re-check, and it is why F27 came back as D304 and why acm was mis-filed for a week.

Verified in both directions: an entry claiming a token that `idempotencyCarried` does not
list is named, and a free-text reason ("reviewed, it is fine") is refused.

Adoption ratchet: 26 -> 18, and this time it moved because eight services were already
safe, not because eight more tests were written.

## D405. Ratchet 18 to 16: kinesis, dynamodb

Two more of the deterministic-name-plus-tag-check shape. DynamoDB is worth a sentence
because its duplication is the data-loss variant of this class: a second table at a
second name is EMPTY, the application writes to it, and the original sits with the real
data until somebody notices the numbers are wrong. Every other duplication in this pass
costs money or availability; this one costs correctness.

Ratchet: 18 -> 16. make check + race clean.

## D406. Ratchet 16 to 14: lambda's pre-read, and app runner's inference

Two enrolments at opposite ends of how confidently a driver can know a resource is
already there.

**Lambda uses the strongest form in the family**: an ownership PRE-READ before any
mutation. `GetFunction` runs first; a function of ours already standing is bound and the
exposure repaired with no `CreateFunction` issued at all. Same shape as KMS and VPC, and
the one where zero create mutations is the entire proof.

**App Runner uses the weakest**, and honestly so. Its own comment says it: a ServiceName
is unique per account and region, so a 4xx on CreateService *may* mean already-exists —
but it may equally be a bad image, a quota, a malformed request. The driver resolves by
name, and only a found-and-ours service turns the failure into an adoption; anything else
surfaces the original error. That is inference over an ambiguous signal, and it is
exactly the kind of path that deserves an assertion rather than a comment, because the
difference between "adopted" and "swallowed a real failure" is one tag check.

The probe caught the author a fifth time: the App Runner fake's default ownership tag is
`app`, and the capability is `capability.workload.container`, so the first run reported
"a service with this name exists but is not ours". Which is the driver being right.

Ratchet: 16 -> 14. make check + race clean.

## D407. Ratchet 14 to 12: rolepolicy, elasticache-serverless

`rolepolicy` is the one service in this whole pass that is safe by the API's own
semantics and says so in its own comment: "AttachRolePolicy is idempotent — attaching an
already-attached policy is a no-op success, so no pre-read is needed". That comment was
the only thing standing behind the claim. It is now an assertion: the create runs against
a role that already carries the policy and must still bind the same pid.

The distinction matters more than it looks. A comment saying an API is idempotent is a
claim about AWS that nothing re-checks — the exact shape D404 refused to admit into
`adoptNotApplicable`. Driving the driver against that state is a claim about OUR code,
and that is checkable. The service ends up in `adoptGated` rather than exempt, which is
the right place: we are not asserting AWS's idempotency, we are asserting that our create
concludes correctly when it meets it.

`elasticache-serverless` is the routine shape — deterministic name, an already-exists
fault, tags off the ARN.

Ratchet: 14 -> 12. make check + race clean.

## D408. Ratchet 12 to 9: the upsert family, and ownership that lives elsewhere

cloudwatch, cloudwatchdash and route53record are all UPSERTs — `PutMetricAlarm`,
`PutDashboard`, `ChangeResourceRecordSets` — keyed by name, so a re-run overwrites
instead of duplicating. They are the cheapest shape in the family and worth asserting
precisely because they look too obvious to test: "it's an upsert" is a sentence about
AWS, and what the gate checks is that OUR create concludes bound rather than, say,
failing on a resource it just found.

route53record has a property no other service in this pass has: **its ownership evidence
lives on a different resource.** A record carries no tags — the gate is the parent
ZONE's tags. So "is this ours" is answered one level up, and a record in a zone we do
not own is refused however the record itself looks. That is the right design (DNS
records have nowhere to carry a marker), and it is now asserted rather than assumed.

Ratchet: 12 -> 9. make check + race clean.

## D409. The ratchet found a real one: vpngateway duplicated, in the class D253 closed

msk and redshiftserverless were routine (redshift is the family's only TWO-STEP adoption:
namespace and workgroup both answer ConflictException, so the property has to hold twice
inside one create). vpngateway was not routine.

**capability.network.vpngateway could stand up a second billed gateway.** Its id is
server-assigned, from the create response. `CreateVpnGateway` takes no idempotency token
— the EC2 API does not offer one for this call, unlike CreateVolume or RunInstances. And
the driver had neither a tag pre-scan nor an already-exists branch, because AWS does not
refuse the second create: it simply makes another gateway. So a converge against a lost
ledger, or a retry after a lost response, minted a duplicate. Two VPN gateways attached
to one VPC is worse than the wasted money: it is a routing question nobody asked.

This is exactly the class D253 addressed, and D253's own words were "the last two — vpc
and kms". They were the last two OF EIGHTEEN. The roster is now 54, and vpngateway landed
into a gap that had been declared closed. That is the same shape as D391 (a property
proven against a roster that then grew) except this time it was not a coverage gap but a
live defect, and the enrolment is what found it.

The fix mirrors D253 exactly: `findVgwByTags` — a tag-filtered `DescribeVpnGateways` that
VERIFIES the tags on what comes back rather than trusting the server filter, skips
deleted/deleting states, binds on exactly one owned gateway, refuses to guess on more
than one, and falls through to a normal create when the scan is empty or unreadable so a
genuine first deploy is never blocked.

Two things the fix had to respect. The `certifynet` honesty harness treats a foreign tag
on an ownership read as "must refuse", which is right for a pre-read of the resource at
our own name and wrong for a DISCOVERY scan, where a foreign tag simply means "not a
match, make our own". D253 had already met this and solved it by having the happy fixture
return an empty set for the tag-filtered query; the vgw fixture now does the same, with
the reasoning written down at both sites rather than only at one.

Proven by removing the scan: the driver issues `CreateVpnGateway` against an account that
already holds our gateway. Ratchet: 9 -> 6.

## D410. A second one: apigateway had the same hole, and had written down the fix

After D409 the remaining candidates were checked for the same shape rather than enrolled
blind — server-assigned id, no idempotency token, no adoption path — and apigateway had
it.

Its own code said so. The unknown branch reads: "server-assigned id and no idempotency
token — a lost create genuinely loses the handle ... reconcile by name via GetApis". The
driver knew the recovery, named the API that performs it, and did it only AFTER the fact.
Doing it only afterwards left BOTH outcomes wrong, and it is worth being precise here
rather than asserting what AWS does: if CreateApi tolerates a duplicate name, a
lost-ledger converge mints a second live endpoint that nothing manages; if it refuses
one, the create hard-fails against an estate that is already correct. The fix is
justified without settling which, because there is no third possibility in which looking
first is wrong.

`apigwByName` lists and matches the deterministic name exactly, the caller verifies the
ownership TAGS before binding, a foreign api at our name is refused rather than adopted
or overwritten, and an unreadable scan falls through to a normal create. Proven by
removing the scan and watching `POST /v2/apis` go out against an account that already
holds our api.

WAF was checked in the same pass and is SOUND — `CreateWebACL` answers `WAFDuplicateItem`,
the driver resolves by name and checks tags. It is enrolled, not fixed. Worth saying,
because "checked and found correct" is the outcome that never gets written down and is
exactly as load-bearing as a fix when the next person asks whether this class was swept.

Two real defects out of the last six services examined. The earlier forty were mostly
already sound — which is the honest shape of this: the ratchet is not finding a broken
codebase, it is finding the tail that was never swept because the sweep predated the
services.

Ratchet: 6 -> 4.

## D411. The AWS create-adoption sweep completes (entry lost in a cross-branch conflict)

As with D358, the prose is missing and the citations are not. What this number is used
for, from the four Go comments that cite it: the completion of the create-time-adoption
sweep across all 54 AWS creates (D391-D411 is cited as the range), the estate a
re-converge meets when a resource is already standing, and the rule that a gate passing
on an unreadable estate rather than on the check it claims to make is a gate passing for
the wrong reason.

The register itself survives in `adoptexisting_gate_test.go` and is the authority on
what was decided; this note exists so the citations resolve.

## D412. The idempotency register was asking a question it could not answer

D390 left 44 AWS creates "unreviewed", and D411 closed with the line that this debt was
"payable only by review — a claim about AWS APIs, not about this code". That framing was
correct about the register as written and wrong about the debt.

The register asked: **does this AWS API require an idempotency token?** Nothing in this
repository can re-derive that. It is a fact about a provider's request validation, and
the only honest ways to establish it are documentation (which drifts) or a live call
(which the paused pilot took away). That is precisely why the number sat at 44 while
every other ratchet moved: it was not hard work, it was unanswerable work.

The question the register EXISTS for is different: **can a re-run mint a second
resource?** A required token matters only because its absence lets a retry duplicate. And
D391-D411 answered that question mechanically, for all 54 creates, by driving each one
against an estate where the resource already stands and requiring it to bind.

So 43 of the 44 are exempt with evidence STRONGER than the one they were waiting for. A
token makes AWS collapse the retry — a property of the provider, taken on trust.
Create-time adoption makes the DRIVER bind the existing resource — a property of this
code, checked here. The 44th is `ami`, which is witness-only and has no create to be
idempotent about.

Both exemption kinds are re-derived by `TestIdempotencyExemptionsAreBacked`:
`adoption-gated` must appear in `adoptGated` (itself gated), `witness-only` drives the
create and requires the witness refusal, and any other reason is refused outright with
the reason given. Verified in all three directions, including a free-text reason ("trust
me") and a claim whose backing was removed.

**What is NOT claimed.** Nothing here says these APIs do not require tokens. Ten drivers
still carry deterministic ones and `TestCarriedTokensMatchTheDrivers` still keeps that
list honest against their derivations (D403). If a create ever starts failing with
"ClientToken cannot be empty" — the D304 symptom — that is still a real bug and the
register does not pretend otherwise. What the register now says is narrower and true: no
create in this driver family can duplicate a resource on a re-run, and here is the test
that shows it for each one.

Both ratchets are at 0. The remaining honest gap is the one MATURITY already names:
internal gates under-sample reality, and the field that would sample it is paused.

## D413. The sweep was one cloud: GCP opens at 44

D391-D412 decided all 54 AWS creates and found two live defects doing it. GCP has 44
creates and Azure 45, and neither had ever been asserted as a class. This opens GCP.

**The damage model differs, and the difference is worth stating rather than assuming.**
GCP resources are name-addressed almost everywhere, so a second create meets a 409 rather
than silently duplicating. The failure it prevents is therefore not a second billed
resource but a converge that HARD-FAILS against an estate that is already correct. Milder
in money, identical in effect: a lost-ledger converge cannot proceed. It is the same
thing D252/D253 built create-time adoption for.

**A scrape lied to me again, on my own measurement.** A first scan reported thirteen GCP
creates with no conflict branch. Several of those were wrong — GCS handles the conflict
thoroughly, including the D82 projectNumber check that labels alone cannot give, but it
spells the status check differently from the pattern I matched. So membership in this
register is not derived from a scan at all: a service is gated when a test DRIVES its
create against an estate where the resource already stands. Third time this instrument
has produced a wrong answer in this series (D317, D403, now here), and the third time is
the one where I did it after writing the warning.

`artifactregistry` is enrolled first. Ratchet opens at 44 and closes this entry at 43.

**The gate caught its own author.** The vacuity guard I wrote first checked
`len(adoptUnenrolled) == 0` — keyed on the DEBT, so it would have fired exactly when the
debt reached zero, turning the moment of success into a failure. It watches the create
dispatch now. D328 said a gate must assert it found its subject; the corollary is that
the subject must not be the thing you are trying to eliminate.

## D414. GCP ratchet 43 to 41: bigquery, secretmanager

Both are the plain GCP shape — a deterministic id, a 409 on the second create, and labels
deciding whether it is ours to bind.

`secretmanager` is worth one note. Adoption here binds the secret CONTAINER and never
touches the payload: the create path does not read or write a version, so an adopted
secret carries whatever value the operator already put there. That is the correct
behaviour and it is a consequence of a design choice made much earlier — the payload was
deliberately kept out of this driver's create path — but nothing had asserted that the
adoption path preserves it. Now something does, by counting the wire.

GCP ratchet: 43 -> 41. make check + race clean.

## D415. Express the difference once: GCP ratchet 41 to 36

The AWS sweep wrote a bespoke already-exists fixture per driver, forty-odd lines each,
and got the wire shape subtly wrong three separate times — an implausible VPC id, an
Aurora fake that could not describe endpoints, an ASG envelope the driver cannot parse.
Every one of those was the same mistake: re-deriving an estate the driver's own tests
already describe correctly.

GCP's fixtures are uniform enough to say it once. `conflictOnCreate` wraps a driver's
OWN happy fixture and answers 409 to the request that creates; everything else — the
reads the adoption path performs, the document shape, the label spellings — stays the
fixture that driver's tests already trust. The estate is real by construction, and only
the create outcome changed, which is exactly the difference being tested.

Five enrolled on that one wrapper: memorystore, filestore, clouddns, cloudkms,
cloudscheduler. `cloudkms` is the interesting one — a key ring AND a key, two creates,
both refused as existing, and the adoption has to survive both.

The lesson is not "write a helper". It is that a fixture should be DERIVED from one the
driver already relies on rather than re-authored, because a re-authored estate is a
second opinion about the provider's wire, and the AWS half of this sweep is three
demonstrations of that opinion being wrong.

GCP ratchet: 41 -> 36. make check + race clean.

## D416. GCP ratchet 36 to 28, and what the two failures were

Eight more on the D415 wrapper. Two failed on the first run and neither was a driver bug,
which is worth writing down because both failures were the driver being RIGHT.

`logmetric` refused with "a log metric with this name exists and is not ours (description
marker does not match)". GCP log metrics carry no labels, so ownership rides in the
DESCRIPTION — and my fixture had been given a plausible human description rather than the
marker the driver writes. The driver correctly declined to adopt something it could not
prove was ours. That is the same shape as route53record on the AWS side: a resource with
nowhere to put a tag needs its ownership evidence somewhere else, and the somewhere else
is easy to get wrong from outside.

`customrole` refused with "exists with a DIFFERENT permission set — refusing to overwrite
(adopt explicitly)". Its fake echoes back the permission set it was given at create time,
and my wrapper had refused the create before the fake ever saw it — so the standing role
described an empty permission set, which is genuinely not the role we asked for. The
driver refusing to silently rewrite a role's permissions is exactly the behaviour you
want from an IAM driver.

That second one made the wrapper better. It now lets the inner fixture SEE the create
before answering 409, discarding the response: a stateful fake only describes a standing
resource once something created it, and in the estate being modelled, something did — the
previous run. Refusing the create without seeding the fake models an estate that cannot
exist.

GCP ratchet: 36 -> 28. Sixteen enrolled, all passing. make check + race clean.

## D417. GCP ratchet 28 to 23, and two adoptions nobody had ever driven

Five more: logbucket, uptime, dashboard, vpc, assetfeed.

I nearly filed two defects here and should not have. `uptime` and `dashboard` both failed
the first run with "create HTTP 409: resource already exists", which reads exactly like a
driver with no adoption path. They have one — D255 gave both a pre-scan by displayName,
because their ids are SERVER-assigned and a 409 branch would come too late to help. The
create is never attempted when the check is already there.

What actually happened is more interesting than a bug. Both drivers' own happy fixtures
create FRESH, so the list they serve is empty, so `findByDisplayName` always finds
nothing — which means **the adoption path D255 added has never been driven by any test**.
The code was written, reviewed and merged; the branch that makes a re-converge work has
sat unexecuted since. Their enrolments serve the list envelope the scan actually reads,
and both now bind with ZERO mutations — no create attempted at all, which is the strongest
form of the property in this whole sweep.

`iambinding` came out of this batch deliberately. Its "create" IS a `setIamPolicy` write,
so refusing it with a 409 models an etag conflict — a concurrent edit — not a binding that
already exists. The driver said so precisely ("setIamPolicy etag conflict (a concurrent
edit) — reconcile and retry"), which is correct behaviour for the estate my fixture
actually built. Modelling the right estate for a policy write is a different fixture, and
it stays on the ratchet until someone writes it rather than being waved through.

GCP ratchet: 28 -> 23. Twenty-one enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D418. GCP ratchet 23 to 21: two services whose ownership proof is not a label

pubsub-topic and gcs, and both are here because their ownership evidence is unusual.

`gcs` is the one GCP service whose proof is NOT labels. Bucket names are a GLOBAL
namespace, so a name collision can be a bucket in someone else's project, and labels are
forgeable cross-project — the authoritative check is the live projectNumber (D82). The
enrolment pins that: the standing bucket reports the project number the driver was given,
and adoption follows.

`pubsub-topic` refused first, correctly: "existing topic storage regions [] do not match
desired residency europe-west1 and pubsub update is not wired". Adoption must not bind a
topic whose message storage policy contradicts the contract's residency — that would be
adopting a lie, which is the rule D52 named. My fixture had given the topic no storage
policy at all. Adding the one the driver checks is what made the case honest.

Both had conflict fixtures already, written for the UNREADABLE and FOREIGN cases. Both
refusals were tested; the ours case — the one every re-converge takes — was not. Fourth
time that exact pattern has appeared in this sweep.

GCP ratchet: 23 -> 21. make check + race clean.

## D419. GCP ratchet 21 to 19, and a defence I chose not to add

billingbudget and backupplan.

`billingbudget` first failed as "create HTTP 409", and the wrapper was modelling an
estate this driver never meets. Its guard is a pre-scan by displayName, with the same
re-list repeated on a lost response and on a 5xx, and its own comment says why: "GCP does
not dedupe on display name — this is the only guard against a duplicate on a retried
create". So the estate is one where the LIST already carries our budget and no create is
attempted at all. The fixture models that, and the enrolment passes at zero mutations.

While there: 409 is the ONE create outcome with no re-list, where `cerr`, 5xx and an
unparseable success all recover. It would be a one-line change to add it, and I did not.
Given the driver's own statement that GCP does not dedupe on this display name, that
branch is likely unreachable for budgets — the API will not 409 a collision it does not
detect. **A defence against an outcome the provider does not produce is a guess dressed
as caution**, and this sweep has spent enough entries on the cost of guesses about other
people's APIs (D412 most of all). It is recorded here so the next person meets the
question rather than the silence.

GCP ratchet: 21 -> 19. make check + race clean.

## D420. GCP ratchet 19 to 18: one enrolled of four attempted, and why that is the entry

`clouddnsrecord` enrolled. Three attempts did not, and the reasons are the substance here
— an enrolment that cannot honestly model the estate is worth less than the debt line it
removes.

`clouddnsrecord` is the GCP twin of route53record: a resource record has nowhere to carry
a marker, so the ownership gate is the parent ZONE's labels, one level up. Both clouds
arrived at the same answer independently, which is mild evidence the answer is right.

`cloudfunctions` failed with a 401 escaping to the real Google IAM endpoint. Its IAM read
goes to a base this probe does not redirect — and a 401 from outside the fake is exactly
what the D391 account-pin rule exists to forbid: a gate that leaves its fixture is
measuring the internet. Left on the ratchet rather than papered over with a second base
URL guessed from the failure.

`loadbalancer` is a composite whose address create the wrapper refuses without the fake
then describing the address, so the driver correctly reported "name conflict, but it was
gone on the follow-up read". The estate my wrapper built cannot exist.

`gke-workloadidentity` joins `iambinding` for the D417 reason: its create IS a
`setIamPolicy` write, so a refusal models an etag CONFLICT — a concurrent edit — not a
binding that already exists. Two services now wait on the same missing fixture shape, and
saying that once is a better description of the debt than two unexplained lines.

GCP ratchet: 19 -> 18. Twenty-six enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D421. The two policy-write services: the estate was never a refused create

D417 and D420 left `iambinding` and `gke-workloadidentity` on the ratchet with a reason
rather than a workaround, and the reason turned out to point straight at the answer.

Their "create" IS a `setIamPolicy` write. Refusing it produces an etag conflict — a
concurrent edit — which is a real condition and not the one being tested. The estate they
actually meet on a re-converge is a POLICY THAT ALREADY CONTAINS the binding, and both
drivers have an explicit branch for exactly that, returning succeeded having written
nothing. `memberInRole(pol, role, member)` — three tokens of code, the whole property.

So both enrol at ZERO mutations with no wrapper involved at all. That is the strongest
form of the property in this sweep: not "the duplicate was refused and we recovered", but
"nothing was sent, because nothing needed to be".

Worth drawing out, because it changes how the remaining ratchet should be read: the
wrapper from D415 was the right tool for services whose create is a create, and the wrong
tool for services whose create is an idempotent write. Leaving those two on the ratchet
WITH THE REASON is what made the second look possible — a debt line that says only
"unenrolled" would have been paid by force with a fixture that lied.

GCP ratchet: 18 -> 16. Twenty-eight enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D422. GCP ratchet 16 to 14, and a predicate that was refusing the wrong request

cloudrun and auditlogs.

`auditlogs` is the third GCP service whose ownership rides in the DESCRIPTION rather than
in labels — sinks take none, like log metrics (D416) and unlike everything else. Its
fixture's own description helper is used rather than a plausible substitute, which is that
entry's whole lesson applied without having to relearn it.

`cloudrun` failed first with "public exposure: setIamPolicy HTTP 409: resource already
exists" — a true statement about an estate that cannot exist. The D415 wrapper's
"is this the create" predicate excluded `:getIamPolicy` and `:testIamPermissions` by name,
which meant `:setIamPolicy` fell through and got refused as if it were the create.

The fix generalises the rule instead of adding a third name: in GCP's API a `:verb`
suffix is a METHOD CALL ON AN EXISTING RESOURCE — getIamPolicy reads it, setIamPolicy
writes its policy, and neither creates anything. A create is a POST to a collection. So
the predicate is now "a POST whose path carries no colon", which is a statement about the
API's shape rather than a list of exceptions that grows by one every time a driver
surprises me.

That distinction is the same one D421 drew from the other direction: a create that IS an
idempotent write needs the estate modelled, not the request refused.

GCP ratchet: 16 -> 14. Thirty enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D423. GCP ratchet 14 to 13: scc, whose create is a settings PATCH

Security Command Center has no create. Its modules exist for a project by definition and
a converge PATCHes their intended state, so the estate a re-converge meets is one where
the modules ALREADY carry what the contract asks for. Same shape as the AWS upsert family
(D408), arrived at from the opposite direction — there the API accepted a re-write, here
there was never anything to create.

Third distinct create-shape this sweep has met on GCP, and worth listing together now
that all three have appeared: a POST to a collection (most services), an idempotent
policy write (D421's iambinding and workload identity), and a settings PATCH on something
that always exists (scc). The one gate covers all three because it asks about the OUTCOME
— did the driver end up bound, and what did it send — rather than about the mechanism.

My first fixture hand-wrote the module keys and got "SCC module container-threat-detection
not found". The fake has a seed helper, `newFakeSCC`, and using it was both shorter and
correct. That is the D415 rule one more time: derive the estate from what the driver's own
tests already build.

GCP ratchet: 14 -> 13. Thirty-one enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D424. Third real defect: vertexai duplicated a model-serving endpoint

A Vertex AI endpoint id is SERVER-assigned, `endpoints.create` takes no idempotency
token, and the driver had no pre-scan. A converge against a lost ledger stood up a SECOND
endpoint — billed, live, serving a model, and absent from the ledger.

The signature is now familiar to the point of being diagnostic. **Every recovery path in
this driver already named the lookup it never performed before creating**: "reconcile by
displayName %q via endpoints.list" appears three times, on the lost-response branch, on
the truncated-body branch, and on the 409 branch. The same sentence, three times, about a
call the create could have made first. apigateway (D410) said "reconcile by name via
GetApis" in exactly the same place for exactly the same reason.

That is worth stating as a rule rather than a coincidence: **when a driver's error
messages tell the operator to recover by a lookup, the create should have done the lookup**.
The knowledge was present; only its position was wrong.

Fixed with `findVertexEndpointByDisplayName`, mirroring D253's `findVpcByTags` and D410's
`apigwByName`: list, match the deterministic displayName, VERIFY the labels rather than
trusting the name, bind exactly one of ours, leave a foreign endpoint alone, fall through
on an unreadable list. Proven by removing the scan and watching the create go out against
a region that already holds our endpoint.

The fake needed teaching too: its `endpoints.list` returned only `name`, so it could not
describe a standing endpoint at all — the fifth fixture in this sweep unable to answer a
question it was never asked before. The real API returns displayName and labels, and it
does now.

GCP ratchet: 13 -> 12. Third live defect of the sweep, first on GCP, all three the same
shape: server-assigned id, no token, no pre-scan.

## D425. GCP ratchet 12 to 10: gke-addon and pd, and a diagnostic that now works

D424 turned a coincidence into a rule: when a driver's error messages tell the operator to
recover by a lookup, the create should have done the lookup. Applied to the remaining
twelve as a targeted scan rather than blind enrolment — grep for "reconcile by X via
Y.list" against the presence of a pre-scan — and it came back CLEAN. vertexai was the last
one carrying that signature.

That is worth as much as a finding. The rule is now a check anyone can run in one command,
and it says the remaining GCP drivers do not have the shape that produced three defects.

Two enrolled on the strength of it:

`gke-addon` is the FOURTH create-shape: an addon is a FIELD on a cluster that already
exists, so "create" is an update and "already there" means already enabled. The driver's
own branch is labelled "idempotent — already enabled" and needs zero writes.

`pd` answers a 409 by reading the standing disk's LABELS, and its comment says exactly why
the check cannot be skipped: "otherwise we would bind a stranger's DATA to this contract,
and put our delete gate over it". Worth quoting because it inverts the usual framing of
this sweep — for a disk, ADOPTING THE WRONG ONE is worse than duplicating, since a
duplicate wastes money while a wrong adoption puts someone else's data under our retire
path.

GCP ratchet: 12 -> 10. Thirty-four enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D426. GCP ratchet 10 to 8: mig and gce, and the sentence three drivers wrote

mig and gce, both the 409-then-check-ownership shape, and both worth quoting because
three drivers independently wrote the same sentence about why the check exists:

- pd: "otherwise we would bind a stranger's DATA to this contract, and put our delete gate
  over it"
- mig: "otherwise we would bind a stranger's FLEET to this contract, and put our delete
  over it"
- gce: "otherwise we would bind a stranger's MACHINE to this contract"

Three authors, three services, one fear — and it is not the fear this sweep started with.
The sweep began from duplication: a second VPC, a second paid key, a second endpoint.
These three are about the opposite error. For a disk, a fleet or a machine, **adopting the
WRONG one is worse than duplicating**, because a duplicate wastes money while a mistaken
adoption puts someone else's running system under our retire path.

That is why every one of these drivers checks ownership on the 409 rather than binding on
the name alone, and why the gate asserts the ownership check by driving a foreign case in
each driver's own tests rather than only the ours case here. mig is also the fourth GCP
service to carry its ownership marker in the DESCRIPTION rather than labels — an instance
group manager takes none.

GCP ratchet: 10 -> 8. Thirty-six enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D427. GCP ratchet 8 to 5: monitoring, vpngateway, pubsub-queue

`monitoring` is the third D255 pre-scan service after uptime and dashboard — server-assigned
id, guarded by a displayName scan, so no create is attempted against a standing policy.
All three were merged with that guard and none of them had a test that reached it (D417);
now all three do.

`vpngateway` was worth checking rather than assuming, because its AWS namesake was the
sweep's first live defect (D409). The symmetry does not hold, and that is the useful part:
GCP's VPN gateway is NAME-addressed, so the 409 arrives and the labels decide, where AWS's
is server-assigned with no token and needed a tag pre-scan built from nothing. Same
capability, same vocabulary, opposite mechanism — which is the D76 parity thesis working:
the contract is the same on both clouds precisely because the drivers are allowed to
differ underneath.

`pubsub-queue` is a topic plus a subscription, both name-addressed, so the wrapper's
refusal lands on each in turn.

GCP ratchet: 8 -> 5. Thirty-nine enrolled. make check + race clean.

## D428. GCP ratchet 5 to 3: the cloud-functions pair, and why waiting was right

D420 left `cloudfunctions` on the ratchet after it failed with a 401 from the REAL Google
IAM endpoint, refusing to guess a second base URL from the error message. The reason it
needed is specific and would not have been guessed correctly: a Cloud Functions gen2
function's public exposure lives on its BACKING CLOUD RUN SERVICE, so the driver reads
`run.googleapis.com` through `RunBaseURL` while the function itself goes through
`CfBaseURL`. A probe redirecting one and not the other abandons its fixture mid-create —
the D391 account-pin failure reached through a different door.

The confirmation that this was a probe gap and not a driver one is that
`cloudfunctions-fn`'s own driver helper sets BOTH bases and always has. The information
was three lines away in a test file; what was missing was the discipline not to patch
past a symptom.

Both enrolled. GCP ratchet: 5 -> 3, and the remainder is gke, loadbalancer and
backupvault — the three composites.

## D429. GCP ratchet 3 to 2: the composite, built the way a real one is

`loadbalancer` was left on the ratchet twice — D417 and D420 — each time because the
wrapper's refusal produced an estate that cannot exist. The root cause was one line in the
fixture: `lbFake` answered every POST by overwriting its store, so "this name is taken"
was not EXPRESSIBLE. A fake that cannot say no cannot describe a standing resource, and
the adoption path had nothing to be tested against.

It answers 409 now, as GCP does. And the estate is built the way a real one is: by a
PREVIOUS CONVERGE. The probe runs the create twice against one fake — the first stands the
composite up, the second is the re-converge under test. That is a better model than any
hand-authored fixture could be, because it is the same code path that made the real estate,
so the two cannot disagree about what a standing composite looks like.

Worth naming as the general form of the D415/D416 lesson: for a stateful driver, the most
faithful "already exists" fixture is the driver's own create, run once. Not a description
of the estate — the estate.

GCP ratchet: 3 -> 2. Forty-two enrolled; gke and backupvault remain.

## D430. The GCP adoption ratchet reaches zero: 44 creates, every one driven

backupvault and gke, and with them all 44 GCP create services are enrolled in
`CertifyCreateAdoptsExisting` — none exempt, none unreviewed. Where AWS finished at 45
gated and 9 exempt-with-evidence, GCP needed no exemptions: every create here could be
driven against an estate where the resource already stands.

`backupvault` is the GCP twin of the AWS one (D400) and carries the same damage model: a
duplicate vault splits the backup estate, the new one is empty and looks healthy, and the
discovery happens at restore.

`gke` is worth the last word, because I predicted it wrong. Its 409 branch returns
unknown-with-pid and says "reconcile ownership", which reads exactly like cloudtrail's
declared deferral (D398), and I enrolled it with `ConcludesUnknown` set. It failed —
because the driver BINDS. A cluster of ours already standing is found before the create is
ever attempted; the 409 branch is the narrower case where the pre-read missed and the API
caught it.

That is the only place in this whole sweep where READING a driver's conflict branch gave a
worse answer than DRIVING it, and it is a fitting last finding: the entire method exists
because reading is not the same as knowing. It failed in the safe direction — I expected
less of the driver than it delivers — but a gate built on that prediction would have
locked in a weaker property than the one the code actually holds.

**Both clouds are now at zero.** AWS: 54 creates, 45 gated, 9 exempt with evidence a test
re-derives. GCP: 44 creates, 44 gated. Three live defects found and fixed on the way
(vpngateway, apigateway, vertexai), all three the same shape — server-assigned id, no
idempotency token, no pre-scan — and all three in a class D253 had declared closed at
eighteen services. Azure's 45 creates remain unswept.

## D431. Azure opens at 45, and needs no conflict wrapper — which is the finding

The third and last cloud. AWS finished at 54 creates decided (D411), GCP at 44 (D430),
three live defects between them. Azure has 45 and none had been asserted as a class.

**Azure needs no already-exists wrapper, and the reason is the whole difference.** An ARM
create is a PUT to a resource PATH, idempotent by construction — a re-run cannot
duplicate, because the path IS the identity. So the question this sweep has asked twice
already has a structural answer here, and D253 said so when it named the cross-cloud
picture. In practice that means a driver's ordinary happy fixture, whose GET already
describes a resource carrying our tags, IS a standing resource of ours: the create runs
against it unchanged, and three enrolments landed on the first attempt with no fixture
work at all.

**What the structure buys in safety it spends elsewhere, and Azure's risk is the subtlest
of the three.** A PUT to an occupied path does not fail — it OVERWRITES. So the danger
here is not a duplicate but a TAKEOVER: a converge finding someone else's resource at our
deterministic path and rewriting it into ours. D254 built the defence, an ownership
pre-read before the PUT, and this ratchet is where that stops being per-driver care and
becomes a class.

The gate therefore asserts a slightly different property with the same instrument: not
"did it avoid duplicating" but "did the pre-read happen and did it bind". The mutation
allowance is not a duplicate budget — the PUT is the converge and is meant to happen.

vnet, cosmos and blob enrolled. Azure ratchet: 45 -> 42.

## D432. Azure ratchet 42 to 34: eight in one pass, none of them fought back

acr, eventhubs, loganalytics, azurefiles, azkafka, rediscache, servicebusqueue,
flexpostgres — eight enrolments, zero fixture work, zero failures on the first run.

That is not a boast about the batch, it is the D431 property showing its consequences.
On AWS the same count took five entries and produced three fixtures that could not
describe the resource they stood in for; on GCP it took four and produced two more. Here
it took one, because there is no "already exists" state to construct: the PUT is the
create AND the update, so a driver's ordinary happy fixture is already the estate.

The honest reading is that Azure's ratchet is CHEAPER to pay, not that its drivers are
better. The gate is asserting less here, because the API guarantees more — and it is
asserting the thing the API does NOT guarantee, which is that the ownership pre-read
happened before the overwrite. Every one of these eight has a driver-level foreign-tag
test for that half (D254's discipline), which is why enrolling them is a completion
rather than a discovery.

Azure ratchet: 42 -> 34. Eleven enrolled.

## D433. Azure ratchet 34 to 21: thirteen more, and a note on what cheap means

apim, aisearch, azurecdn, containerapps, containerappsjob, customroledef, frontdoorwaf,
keyvault, keyvaultkey, metricalert, portaldash, scheduledquery, webtest. Thirteen
enrolments, one pass, no failures.

Twenty-four of Azure's forty-five are now gated and not one has needed a fixture written
for it. The temptation is to read that as Azure being in better shape. It is not what the
evidence says. What it says is that the PROPERTY IS CHEAPER TO ESTABLISH here, because ARM
gives it away: a PUT to a path cannot duplicate, so the only thing left to assert is that
the driver looked before it overwrote — and every one of these drivers already had a
foreign-tag test proving the refusal half (D254).

The gate's value on Azure is therefore different in kind from the other two clouds. On AWS
and GCP it FOUND things: three live defects, five fixtures that could not describe their
own resource, two adoption paths no test had ever executed. Here it is closing a
completeness argument — every create decided, none assumed — and that is worth having for
the same reason a green suite is worth having: not because it discovered something today,
but because it will notice when the next driver arrives without the pre-read.

Azure ratchet: 34 -> 21.

## D434. Azure ratchet 21 to 10: eleven more, and the third backup vault

activitylog, aks-addon, backuppolicy, backupvault, consumptionbudget, dnszone, dnsrecord,
managedidentity, roleassignment, servicebustopic, acsemail.

Azure's backup vault completes a set: the same capability, the same damage model, and now
the same assertion on all three clouds (AWS D400, GCP D430, Azure here). A duplicate vault
splits the backup estate — the new one is empty and looks healthy while the real one goes
unmanaged, and the discovery happens at restore. Three independent driver families, three
independent fixtures, one property, gated identically. That is what the D76 parity thesis
is supposed to deliver, and it is the first time in this sweep a capability has been
closed on all three clouds in the same way.

Two probe slips, both mine and both caught by the compiler rather than by a false pass:
`azDNSRecordServer` takes a capture pointer the call omitted, and ACS Email builds its
fake from a struct rather than a helper function. Neither could have produced a wrong
result — which is the difference between an argument error and the fixture errors this
sweep kept finding, where the code compiled and lied.

Azure ratchet: 21 -> 10. Thirty-five enrolled.

## D435. Azure ratchet 10 to 7: the cluster trio closes

aks, aks-workloadidentity, changefeed.

`aks` completes the cluster trio. EKS (D395), GKE (D430) and AKS now assert the same
property against the estate their own sagas were about — a cluster of ours already
standing. That trio is where this whole line of work started: the Acme findings D258,
D259 and D261 were all one event, a cluster that was already there and not recognised,
and it took until now for all three clouds to have that case asserted rather than fixed.

The exactly-one-set check caught the author for the third time in this sweep, and it is
worth counting: D392, D395, and here. Three occasions on which a completeness gate that
only looked for gaps would have reported a debt smaller than the real one, because a
service can be enrolled and still be sitting in the unenrolled list.

Azure ratchet: 10 -> 7. Thirty-eight enrolled.

## D436. Azure ratchet 7 to 5, and the composite's second resource

azdisk and azvmss.

`azvmss` refused on the first run and the refusal is the most Azure-specific finding of
this cloud's sweep. A scale set is a COMPOSITE — the set itself plus its autoscale
setting — and the stock fixture's autoscale document carries no tags. So the D254
ownership pre-read did exactly its job on the SECOND resource: "a resource already exists
at this name and its ownership tags are not ours — refusing to overwrite a resource
groundhold does not own (an Azure ARM PUT is an unconditional upsert)".

That sentence is the whole Azure risk model in one refusal, and the fact that it fired on
the composite's second member rather than its first is the part worth keeping. A create
that checks ownership on the resource it is named for and then upserts its sub-resources
unchecked would pass every test written about "the resource"; here the driver checks each
one. The fixture, not the driver, was the thing that could not describe an estate where
both members are ours.
