Azure ratchet: 7 -> 5. Forty enrolled.

## D437. Azure ratchet 5 to 2: openai, defender, app gateway

`defender` is the Azure sibling of GCP's `scc` (D423): subscription-scoped PRICING plans,
no resource to create, and "already exists" means the plans already carry the tier the
contract asks for. Two clouds, two security-posture services, the same shape — a converge
that writes settings onto something that exists by definition.

`loadbalancer` used the seed-by-previous-converge pattern D429 arrived at on GCP. This
fake builds its GET document FROM the PUT body, which makes the seeded estate exactly the
gateway our own driver would have made — the most faithful "already exists" a stateful
fixture can offer, and the second time in this sweep that the right fixture turned out to
be the driver's own create run once.

Azure ratchet: 5 -> 2. Forty-three enrolled; azimage and azvm remain.

## D438. Three clouds, 143 creates, every one decided

azvm enrolled; azimage exempt as a witness service, checked the way AWS's ami is (D411) —
by driving the create and requiring the witness refusal, with any reason this gate cannot
re-derive refused outright.

**All three clouds are at zero.**

    AWS     54 creates   45 gated   9 exempt with checked evidence
    GCP     44 creates   44 gated   0 exempt
    Azure   45 creates   44 gated   1 exempt (witness-only)

No create service on any cloud can be added without a decision, no exemption can be
claimed without evidence a test re-derives, and every one of the 133 gated services has
been DRIVEN against an estate where its resource already stands.

**What the sweep cost and what it bought.** Forty-eight decisions (D391–D438). Three live
defects, each able to mint a second billed resource on a re-run, all three in a class D253
had declared closed at eighteen services: `vpngateway` (a second VPN gateway on one VPC),
`apigateway` (a second live endpoint), `vertexai` (a second model-serving endpoint). Two
adoption paths that had been merged and never once executed by a test (uptime, dashboard).
Six fixtures that could not describe the resource they stood in for — an implausible VPC
id, an Aurora fake with no endpoints, an ASG envelope the driver cannot parse, a Vertex
list carrying only names, an lbFake that could not say "taken", a VMSS autoscale doc with
no tags. One harness hardening so a classifier can no longer break the driver it measures.
One register I had built with the very instrument I had just condemned.

**And the shape of the answer differs per cloud, which is the parity thesis working.** On
AWS the risk is duplication, defended by a token or a scan. On GCP it is a hard failure
against a standing estate, defended by a 409 branch that checks ownership. On Azure it is
a TAKEOVER — an ARM PUT is an unconditional upsert — defended by a pre-read before the
write. Same capability contracts on all three, three different mechanisms underneath, one
gate that asks about the outcome rather than the mechanism.

What remains honest to say: this is a hermetic property. Every one of these tests drives a
fake. MATURITY's gap 4 stands unchanged — internal gates under-sample reality, and the
field that would sample it is paused.

## D439. The mirror verb: does a delete refuse a resource that is not ours?

The adoption sweep asked, for all 143 creates on three clouds, "when the resource is
already there and it is OURS, does the driver bind it?". This asks the mirror question of
the mirror verb, and it is the half where being wrong cannot be undone.

**Neither property implies the other.** A create that adopts correctly can still have a
delete that trusts the providerId it was handed — and that id comes from the ledger, which
a mistaken adoption, a hand-authored plan (D47/D48 exist because those are expected) or a
stale binding can populate with a stranger's resource. The asymmetry with create is the
whole reason this register is worth opening: a create that gets ownership wrong duplicates
— wasteful, recoverable, visible on the next bill. A delete that gets it wrong destroys
something that was never ours.

Roughly forty AWS tests already assert a foreign-delete refusal. What has never existed is
the STATEMENT that all fifty-four do. A name-matching scan put the gap at ten services and
I did not believe it — that instrument has now been wrong three times in this series
(D317, D403, D413) — so membership is driven, not scraped.

`CertifyDeleteRefusesForeign` drives the PUBLIC Delete dispatch against a fake whose
resource carries someone else's ownership markers, and requires three things: the result
is not success, ZERO mutations went out, and the refusal carries a reason an operator can
act on. The mutation count is the half a direct per-driver call cannot see — a refusal that
mutates first has already done the damage.

Opened at 54, four enrolled: kms, vpc, s3, dynamodb. Chosen deliberately — a VPC delete
takes its subnets and routes with it, an S3 or DynamoDB delete takes the data.

## D440. Delete ratchet 54 to 38: twelve enrolments off fixtures that already existed

acm, backupplan, cloudfront, cwlogs, ecr, efs, elasticache, kinesis, msk, opensearch,
secretsmanager, waf — twelve in two passes, and not one needed a fixture written for it.

Each of these drivers already HAD a foreign-tagged fixture, authored for its own
per-driver refusal test. Reusing them is the D415 rule applied to the mirror verb: derive
the estate from what the driver's own tests already trust, because a re-authored estate is
a second opinion about the provider's wire and this sweep now has six demonstrations of
that opinion being wrong.

What the class gate adds over the per-driver tests it borrows from is the MUTATION COUNT.
Every one of those tests calls the private delete function directly and asserts the status
and the reason; none of them can see whether a request went out before the refusal. That
is the assertion that matters here — a refusal which mutates first has already done the
damage, and unlike a duplicate it cannot be undone. All sixteen enrolled so far send zero.

Two classifiers had to be written rather than borrowed: CloudFront is REST and Secrets
Manager is X-Amz-Target JSON, and neither fits the shared shapes. Written from the
protocol rather than from the failure — the D422 discipline, which is what stopped the
GCP `:verb` predicate from becoming a list of exceptions.

Delete ratchet: 54 -> 38.

## D441. Delete ratchet 38 to 34: the foreign estate is the adoption estate, one tag over

ecs, sns, sqs, rds.

The adoption sweep left every enrolled driver with a fixture describing a resource of
OURS. The foreign estate is that same fixture with one value changed — the ownership tag.
Two cases differing by exactly the thing under test is as close to a controlled experiment
as a fake gets, and it costs a line rather than a fake.

Where the driver's fixture takes a tag parameter, that is literally one argument. Where it
does not — rds hard-codes ours, sns and sqs build their tag XML inline — a small
substitution wrapper does it, and `foreignTagQueryServer` answers the ownership read with
a foreign owner and nothing else, so anything past that read is a mutation the countRT
will name.

That last detail is the one worth keeping: the foreign fixture does not need to model the
whole resource, because a correct driver never gets past the ownership read. A fixture
that has to describe what happens AFTER the check is a fixture for a driver that fails it.

Delete ratchet: 38 -> 34. Twenty enrolled.

## D442. Delete ratchet 34 to 26: eight more, all zero-mutation refusals

apprunner, aurora, cloudtrail, elasticache-serverless, guardduty, lambda,
opensearch-serverless, route53.

Twenty-eight AWS deletes now assert the property as a class, and every single one refuses
having sent NOTHING. That uniformity is worth stating plainly, because it was not
guaranteed: a driver could legitimately need a write to learn ownership (the ForeignProbe
carries an `AllowedMutations` knob for exactly that), and none of the twenty-eight does.
Every ownership decision in this family is reached by reading.

Two fixtures needed a substitution wrapper rather than a parameter — cloudtrail's tags
come from a separate `ListTags` call and rds hard-codes ours — and both wrappers answer
the ownership read with a foreign owner and nothing beyond it. A correct driver never asks
for more.

Delete ratchet: 34 -> 26.

## D443. Fourth defect, first on the delete side: budgets deleted whatever it was told to

`deleteBudget` performed NO ownership check. It split the providerId, read the budget and
deleted it. So a providerId naming any budget in the account destroyed that budget.

D397 had already established the fact that makes this reachable: **a budget carries no
tags** — AWS offers none on the resource — so its deterministic NAME is the entire
ownership marker, and D397 called it "the weakest ownership evidence in the AWS driver
family". The create path already treats the name as proof: a `DuplicateRecordException` is
resolved as "ours, by name". The delete simply never asked.

Why that is reachable rather than theoretical is the premise this whole register was
opened on (D439): a providerId is not a secret. It comes from the ledger, and a
hand-authored plan is an input the executor is explicitly built to expect and defend
against — D47 and D48 exist for that reason. Every other AWS delete checks a tag before
mutating; this one had nothing to check and checked nothing.

The fix reconstructs what CAN be known. The generation is not passed to delete, so the
full name cannot be rebuilt — but the capability+environment slug can, and that is what
separates our budgets from everyone else's. `budgetNameLooksOurs` requires our prefix, our
slug and an 8-letter tail of the right shape. It cannot prove WHICH generation made the
budget and does not try; it proves the budget belongs to this contract's capability rather
than to somebody else, which is exactly what a tag would have answered.

Proven by removing the check: the delete returns SUCCEEDED having issued DeleteBudget
against `finance-team-quarterly`.

`ami` is exempt and checked the way its create-side twin is (D411): the driver refuses to
delete what it never authored, and says why — "deleting an image groundhold never created
would destroy something a pipeline owns, on the strength of a record we only ever read".

Delete ratchet: 26 -> 24. Twenty-nine gated, one exempt with checked evidence.

## D444. The tag-less three: custompolicy and cwlogfilter had the same hole as budgets

D443 turned the budgets defect into a diagnostic — a delete that performs NO ownership
read at all — and running it over the remaining twenty-four found two more, plus three
that look like it and are not.

**`deleteCustomPolicy` deleted whatever ARN it was handed.** An IAM policy is a permission
set; deleting someone else's detaches it from every principal using it. Its create path
proves ownership by name plus action-set (D407) and the delete checked nothing.

**`deleteCWLogFilter` deleted whatever (log group, filter name) it was handed.** A metric
filter is what turns log lines into an alarm, so removing another team's filter does not
break anything visibly — it silently stops their alerting, which is the failure mode you
find out about during the next incident rather than at the time.

Both are the same shape as budgets: AWS offers no tags on the resource, so the
deterministic NAME is the only ownership evidence, and only the create path was using it.
The fix is now a shared predicate, `nameLooksOurs` — our prefix, our capability slug, a
tail of the right shape and length. It cannot say which generation made the resource; it
says the resource belongs to this contract's capability rather than to somebody else.
Proven for both by disabling the check and watching the delete reach the API.

**Three that the diagnostic flagged and I did not change**, because reading them showed
the scan was matching on shape rather than substance:

- `deleteEKSNodegroup` and the load balancer's `deleteOne` are SUB-RESOURCE helpers,
  called after the composite root has already proven ownership. Adding a second check
  there would be theatre.
- `deleteRolePolicyAttachment` detaches a policy from a role and genuinely has nothing to
  check — an attachment carries no tags and no name of its own, only the pair it joins.
  It is also the one operation in this family that is REVERSIBLE by re-attaching. Left
  alone deliberately, and recorded here so the next reader meets the reasoning rather than
  the silence.

Delete ratchet: 24 -> 22. Thirty-one gated, one exempt.

## D445. The one with "nothing to check" had something to check

D444 recorded `deleteRolePolicyAttachment` as the delete with no ownership surface — an
attachment carries no tags and no name of its own, only the pair it joins — and left it
alone with the reasoning written down. Writing the reasoning down is what made it
obviously wrong on re-reading.

**An attachment has no ownership surface. The ROLE does.** Detaching a policy MODIFIES
that role: it removes a permission the role's workload is currently using. That the change
is reversible by re-attaching is a mitigation, not a licence — and reversibility did not
stop this sweep from treating a duplicate as a defect, so it should not excuse a
modification either.

So the delete reads the role first. An unreadable role is `unknown` rather than a refusal,
because the detach may be perfectly legitimate and we cannot tell — which is what unknown
is for. A role that IS readable and is not ours refuses.

The fixture had to learn the role, which is the sixth time in this sweep that a fake could
not describe the resource the property depends on. It is also the first where the missing
description was of a DIFFERENT resource than the one being operated on — the estate a
correct driver consults is wider than the estate the old test needed.

Worth keeping as a rule: **"nothing to check" is a claim about the whole estate, not about
the resource named in the providerId.** D444's own entry said the attachment "genuinely has
nothing to check", and that sentence was true about the attachment and false about the
operation.

Delete ratchet: 22 -> 21. Thirty-two gated, one exempt.

## D446. The fourth tag-less service, and a gate that passed twice for the wrong reason

`deleteSESInbound` is the fourth service whose only ownership evidence is a name — a SES
receipt rule carries no tags because the API offers none. Its comment already said so:
"the NAME is the ownership marker — the pid carries the name groundhold bound". It never
checked that the name is one we would produce. A rule set is where inbound mail is ROUTED,
so deleting a stranger's rule does not break anything loudly; it silently stops delivering
their mail.

**The enrolment passed before the fix, twice, for two different wrong reasons**, and both
are worth recording because catching them is the difference between a gate and a placebo.

First, the foreign fixture answered every request with an error, so the pre-read failed
and the delete concluded `unknown`. Unknown is not success, so the gate was satisfied — by
an unreadable estate rather than by an ownership check. That is D411's failure mode, met
again.

Second, after making the pre-read succeed, it still passed: my providerId used the prefix
`sesin:` where the parser wants `ses-inbound:`, so the delete refused at PARSING. A
refusal, again for a reason that has nothing to do with the property.

Only with a correct providerId AND a readable foreign rule does removing the check produce
the failure — `DeleteReceiptRule` reaching the API — which is the evidence the entry needed
before claiming a defect. Two false greens in one enrolment is a rate worth remembering:
**a passing ownership gate should be distrusted until you have watched it fail.**

Delete ratchet: 21 -> 20. Thirty-three gated, one exempt.

## D447. Delete ratchet 20 to 16, and a gate verified by watching it fail

bedrock, ebs, ec2, eventbridgescheduler — the stateful-compute batch, where a mistaken
delete destroys a machine, a volume, or the data on one.

Each already had a per-driver refusal test whose fixture describes a READABLE foreign
resource, which D446 established is the only fixture shape that proves anything. Reusing
them meant the enrolments landed first time.

**And this time I checked that they bite before believing them.** Disabling the ownership
check in `deleteEC2Instance` produces:

    aws/ec2: refusing to delete a FOREIGN resource still sent 1 mutation(s) (allowed 0).
    A refusal that mutates first has already done the damage, and unlike a duplicate this
    one cannot be undone.

Note WHICH assertion fired. Without the check the driver still reports a failure — the
terminate call errors out on the fake — so a gate asserting only the status would have
stayed green while `TerminateInstances` went out against a stranger's machine. The
mutation count is what caught it.

That is the strongest argument this register has produced for its own design. Forty AWS
tests already asserted these refusals by status and reason; the property that actually
matters is that nothing was SENT, and it took a wire-counting gate to state it.

Delete ratchet: 20 -> 16. Thirty-seven gated, one exempt.

## D448. Delete ratchet 16 to 12

backupvault, iam, redshiftserverless, vpngateway — all four off their own foreign
fixtures, all four refusing having sent nothing.

`vpngateway` closes a loop. D409 found its CREATE minting a second billed gateway on a
re-run, which was the sweep's first live defect. Its DELETE has always checked ownership;
now the class says so, and the capability is covered on both verbs.

Worth noting what the pattern of this register has become: the create sweep found three
defects in 143 services, and the delete sweep has found five in forty-two. That ratio is
not a statement about delete code being worse — it is a statement about where the
attention went. Create-time adoption was designed as a feature (D252/D253) and reviewed as
one. Delete ownership was implemented per driver, correctly almost everywhere, and never
stated as a rule — so the four services with nothing obvious to check quietly checked
nothing, and each of those was found by asking the same question of every service rather
than by reading the ones that looked interesting.

Delete ratchet: 16 -> 12. Forty-one gated, one exempt.

## D449. The fifth tag-less service, and the ones whose evidence lives a level up

`deleteCWDashboard` had no ownership check. A CloudWatch dashboard carries no tags — the
API offers none — so its deterministic name is the only evidence, making it the fifth
service with the shape budgets started (D443), IAM policies and metric filters continued
(D444) and SES receipt rules completed (D446).

The damage is the quietest yet. Deleting a stranger's dashboard breaks nothing that
alarms, nothing that pages, nothing that appears in a bill. It destroys the VIEW an
on-call rotation works from, and the failure surfaces the next time somebody opens it
during an incident — which is precisely when the cost of not having it is highest.

Enrolled alongside three whose ownership evidence is not on the resource at all:
`route53record` and `route53health` read the parent ZONE's tags, and `apigateway` its own.
That "one level up" pattern has now appeared on both AWS and GCP for DNS records
(D408/D420), reached independently, which is the second time this sweep has found the two
driver families arriving at the same answer without sharing code.

**Five tag-less services, five identical holes, one shared predicate.** Worth stating as
the finding rather than as five findings: whenever AWS offers no tags on a resource, this
codebase used the deterministic name as ownership evidence on CREATE and forgot it on
DELETE. Every single time. That is not five oversights, it is one blind spot with five
instances, and the reason it stayed invisible is that each driver looked correct in
isolation — the missing check is only obvious when you ask the same question of all
fifty-four.

Delete ratchet: 12 -> 8. Forty-five gated, one exempt.

## D450. The AWS delete ratchet reaches zero: 54 deletes, every one decided

asg, changefeed, cloudwatch, eks, eks-addon, eks-podidentity, loadbalancer, ses-sending —
and with them all 54 AWS delete services are decided: 53 gated in
`CertifyDeleteRefusesForeign`, one exempt (ami, witness-only, checked by driving the
refusal).

**What this register cost and found.** Twelve decisions (D439–D450) and FIVE live defects,
against three in the 143-service create sweep:

    budgets          deleted whatever budget the providerId named
    custompolicy     deleted whatever IAM policy ARN it was handed
    cwlogfilter      deleted whatever metric filter, silencing another team's alerting
    ses-inbound      deleted whatever receipt rule, stopping another team's mail
    cloudwatchdash   deleted whatever dashboard, destroying an on-call view
    (+ rolepolicy, which detached from a role it never checked)

**All five are one blind spot, not five oversights.** Every one is a service on which AWS
offers NO TAGS. In each, the deterministic name was already being used as ownership
evidence by the CREATE path — and forgotten by the DELETE path. Every single time. It
stayed invisible because each driver reads correctly in isolation; the gap only appears
when the same question is put to all fifty-four.

**Two things about method that this register proved better than the create sweep did.**

First, the assertion that matters is the WIRE, not the status. Disabling the EC2 ownership
check leaves the driver still reporting a failure — the terminate errors out on the fake —
so forty existing tests asserting status and reason would have stayed green while
`TerminateInstances` went out against a stranger's machine (D447). Only the mutation count
caught it.

Second, a passing ownership gate is worth nothing until you have watched it fail. The
ses-inbound enrolment passed twice before the fix, once because the fixture was unreadable
and once because the providerId did not parse (D446). Both were green, both meaningless.

Remaining: the same register on GCP (44 deletes) and Azure (45).

## D451. The blind spot crosses clouds: two more label-less deletes on GCP

The AWS delete register found five defects, all on services where the provider offers no
tags. Running the same diagnostic over GCP's 44 deletes — which ones perform no ownership
read at all — found the same shape twice.

**`deleteCustomRole`** deleted whatever role id it was handed. A GCP custom role carries no
labels because IAM offers none, so its deterministic id is the only evidence there is.
Deleting a stranger's role revokes every permission it grants, from every principal bound
to it, at once.

**`deleteAssetFeed`** had the reasoning written down and no check behind it: "Ownership is
content-addressed: the feedId lives in groundhold's deterministic namespace (feeds carry
no labels)". True, and never verified. It is the third time in this register that a
driver's own comment named the property it did not enforce (after ses-inbound D446 and the
create-side vertexai D424).

Both proven by disabling the check. `nameLooksOursGCP` mirrors the AWS predicate with the
separator and prefix conventions this package uses, including the `-gN` generation infix
(D48) which the AWS names do not have.

**One case examined and deliberately left alone.** `deleteGKEAddon` reads its cluster but
never checks the cluster's labels — and neither does `createGKEAddon`. Adding the check to
only one verb would make the two disagree about what ownership means, which is its own
defect; adding it to both is a design decision about whether the operator naming a cluster
in `implementation.cluster` is itself the authorisation. That is a real question and not
one to settle inside a delete-ownership sweep, so it stays on the ratchet with the
reasoning recorded — the same discipline D420 used for iambinding, which D421 then
resolved once the right question was visible.

Fixing the two required correcting a test that used `viewer` as a role id — a stand-in the
new check rightly rejects, and one that was never a realistic providerId (the D289 lesson,
on the test side again).

GCP delete ratchet opens at 44, closes this entry at 42.

## D452. GCP delete ratchet 42 to 34

artifactregistry, certmanager, cloudarmor, clouddns, cloudkms, managedkafka, memorystore,
secretmanager — eight off their own foreign fixtures, all refusing having sent nothing.

Nothing surprising in the batch, which is itself the useful result. GCP's labelled
services check labels on delete, consistently, and eight enrolments landing first time
says the discipline held everywhere a label was available to hold it. The two defects this
register found here (D451) were both on services where no label exists — which is now the
same sentence as the AWS half, on a different provider, from a different set of authors.

GCP delete ratchet: 42 -> 34. Ten gated.

## D453. GCP delete ratchet 34 to 26

backupplan, backupvault, bigquery, cloudrunjobs, cloudscheduler, logmetric,
serviceaccount, vpngateway.

`logmetric` deserves the note. It is a service with NO labels, whose ownership rides in
the description — the exact shape that produced five defects on AWS. This driver was
already checking it, and had been since D416 made the description marker explicit. Same
constraint, opposite outcome, and the difference is that GCP's tag-less services were
written after the marker convention existed while AWS's were written alongside it.

That is worth recording because it reframes the AWS findings slightly. Five identical
holes is not five careless authors; it is a convention that arrived mid-way and was
applied to the create paths being written at the time, while the delete paths already
merged kept their original shape. The blind spot has a date.

GCP delete ratchet: 34 -> 26. Eighteen gated.

## D454 — GCP delete ratchet: 26 -> 14, and the pattern holds across a whole cloud

Twelve more GCP deletes driven against a foreign estate through
`CertifyDeleteRefusesForeign`: cloudrun, filestore, clouddnsrecord, monitoring,
dashboard, uptime, pubsub-topic, pubsub-queue, cloudfunctions, cloudfunctions-fn,
vpc, billingbudget. All twelve refuse, all twelve having sent zero mutations, and
every refusal names ownership rather than falling over on a parse — checked
explicitly, because a gate that accepts *any* non-success would happily accept a
driver that crashed before it got as far as looking.

Three of the twelve are the no-tags shape that produced five live defects on AWS
(D444-D449): `dashboard` (ownership rides in displayName), `vpc` (in the
description marker), `clouddnsrecord` (in the parent zone's labels, one level up
— the same answer both clouds reached independently, D408/D420/D449). On GCP all
three were already correct.

That is now eleven no-tags services across two clouds: five broken on AWS, six
right on GCP. The split is not about care, it is about **when the code was
written relative to the convention**. The description-marker convention arrived
mid-way; GCP's tagless services were written after it and inherited it on both
verbs, while AWS's delete paths were merged before it and kept their original
shape while the create paths beside them were being updated. The blind spot has
a date, and this ratchet is how a dated blind spot stops being invisible.

Remaining unreviewed on GCP: 14 (auditlogs, firestore, gce, gcs, gke, gke-addon,
gke-workloadidentity, iambinding, loadbalancer, logbucket, mig, pd, scc,
vertexai). Azure's 45 deletes remain unopened.

## D455 — the gate that asked whether the refusal ever looked

Ten more GCP deletes enrolled (gce, pd, mig, logbucket, gcs, vertexai, gke,
auditlogs, firestore, loadbalancer), taking that ratchet 14 -> 4. But the slice
is named for what happened while enrolling them.

`CertifyDeleteRefusesForeign` accepted any non-success. A driver that refuses at
providerId PARSING — never contacting the estate, never reading a tag — satisfied
it exactly as well as one whose ownership check works. I had already been bitten
by this twice on AWS (a `sesin:` prefix where the driver wanted `ses-inbound:`),
patched both by hand, and left the hole open for everyone else.

So the probe now counts REQUESTS as well as mutations: a refusal that read
nothing fails, unless the driver declares `OwnershipFromIDAlone` — ownership
derivable from a content-addressed providerId, with no estate read possible.

It found four vacuous enrolments immediately, all on AWS, all previously green:

  acm                     providerId certId "abcd1234" is invalid
  elasticache-serverless  providerId "ecsl:..." is not ecserverless:...
  redshiftserverless      providerId name "w" is invalid
  bedrock                 a SYSTEM profile id, so the AWS-managed branch answered
                          before the tag branch was ever reached

Four fixtures serving foreign tags that no driver ever fetched. Four tests
asserting nothing. All four now read the estate and refuse on what they read.

The declared exemptions are the five tagless AWS services from D444-D449
(budgets, custompolicy, cwlogfilter, ses-inbound, cloudwatchdash) plus GCP
customrole, assetfeed and firestore. That the exemption list turned out to be
*precisely* the set of name-derived ownership checks is a good sign: the flag
partitions the register by KIND OF EVIDENCE rather than by driver, and it makes
visible a residual risk worth stating plainly — a name-derived check cannot tell
our resource from a stranger's resource that happens to carry our name. For the
hashed schemes that is implausible; it is not impossible, and it is the price of
an API that offers no tags.

The recurring lesson, third time now (D317, D328, and here): **a gate that
accepts any failure accepts failures for the wrong reason.** Assert what the
refusal was made OF, not merely that one happened.

## D456 — GCP delete register closed at zero, and the two shapes that do not fit

The last four GCP deletes are not "not yet driven". They are two classes the
foreign-delete probe cannot ask its question of, and they deserve different
levels of comfort.

**member-scoped (iambinding, gke-workloadidentity).** The delete removes exactly
ONE member from a shared IAM policy, named by the providerId. There is no
resource to own and nothing to refuse; the safety property is that the blast
radius is one member wide. The exemption is backed by driving both: seed a policy
holding a stranger's member in the SAME role, delete ours, require theirs to
survive. That is a stronger property than the probe's, and both drivers have it.

**settings-flip (scc, gke-addon).** These are honest exemptions and an honest
gap. "Create" means turning a project- or cluster-level FLAG on; retirement means
turning it off. The API offers no per-resource ownership surface — there is
nothing to label, because there is no resource. Worse, both creates treat an
already-on flag as an idempotent success without mutating, which is correct
converge behaviour and is also exactly why the delete cannot tell "we turned this
on" from "it was already on when we arrived". A retirement can therefore disable
a Security Command Center module, or a GKE addon, that someone else enabled.

I looked for the label check and deliberately did not add one. For `gke-addon`
the operand cluster is free-form by design (`implementation.clusterName` — "a
separate capability/operand"), so requiring OUR labels on it would break a
documented use; for `scc` the resource is the project itself. The evidence
these deletes need is not in the estate at all — it is **what the create found**,
and the driver has no channel to carry that across. The fix, when it comes, is to
record found-vs-set at create time so retirement RESTORES rather than disables.
That is a change to resource identity (the providerId is the only channel a
driver controls) and it is larger than this slice; it is not a thing to invent
overnight against a register.

So the exemption gate re-derives the SHAPE rather than claiming safety: it drives
each create against an already-on flag and requires the silent adoption. The day
someone changes that, this exemption is re-examined instead of inherited. The
register is closed at zero on GCP with the gap named in MATURITY, not hidden by
it.

Register: AWS 54 decided, GCP 44 decided, Azure's 45 unopened.

## D457 — the Azure delete register opens at 20 of 45

The third and last delete register. Twenty services driven through the public
Delete dispatch against an estate carrying a stranger's markers; all twenty
refuse having sent nothing, and (since D455) all twenty are shown to have READ
the estate before deciding — or to have declared that they could not.

Two declared: `consumptionbudget` and `backuppolicy`, neither of which carries
ARM tags, both refusing on the name. That is the ninth and tenth instance of the
tagless shape across three clouds. The running tally is worth stating because it
finally says something general: **five broken (all AWS), seven right (GCP and
Azure)**. The convention that a tagless resource's deterministic name IS its
ownership evidence is now something every cloud does — and the only cloud where
it was applied unevenly is the one whose delete paths were written before the
convention existed.

Azure is where the property matters most and where the API helps least. An ARM
DELETE takes a resourceId and nothing else — no if-match, no conditional delete,
no server-side owner. Whatever refuses must refuse in the driver, before the
request goes out. That is the same lesson D254 drew on the create side (a PUT to
an occupied path is an unconditional upsert) applied to the verb where being
wrong is not recoverable.

Twenty-five left, and the shape of what remains is informative: aks and its two
satellites, the compute family (azvm, azvmss, azdisk, azimage), the DNS pair, the
monitoring group, and the identity/role surfaces. Several of those are the ones
where a mistaken delete costs the most.

## D458 — the Azure delete register closes, and finds the four worst holes yet

Twenty-five services decided, and the sweep's whole point arrives at the end.
Four live defects, all on Azure, all the same shape as the five on AWS — the
resource has no tags, the deterministic identity IS the ownership evidence, the
create and update paths knew that and the delete did not:

  activitylog     a subscription-scope diagnostic setting, deleted by name with
                  only a "same subscription?" guard. `discover` deliberately
                  surfaces FOREIGN settings for brownfield onboarding, so a
                  providerId naming a stranger's Activity Log export is a
                  reachable state. Its own UPDATE path refuses on a name
                  mismatch. The delete did not.
  changefeed      identical, on an EventGrid event subscription.
  customroledef   a roleDefinition, deleted by GUID with NO subscription guard,
                  NO read and NO ownership check. Deleting a stranger's custom
                  role revokes every permission it grants from every principal
                  assigned to it, at once.
  roleassignment  a roleAssignment, same: GUID in, DELETE out. Revoking a grant
                  that was never ours removes a principal's access with no record
                  of what it was.

The two authorization ones are the worst the sweep has produced, and they were
the last two doors in the last register on the last cloud.

The fixes are exact rather than heuristic, which is the one nice thing here. All
four identities are content-addressed, so ownership is an EQUALITY, not a
pattern match: `azNameLooksOurs` re-derives `azResourceName` across the D48
generations; the role definition's GUID is `sha256(roledef|scope|roleName)`
recomputed from (subscription, capability, environment); the role assignment's is
`sha256(scope|principal|role)` — which the delete can only check by READING the
assignment and confirming its name is the hash of its own properties. A
stranger's role or grant carries a GUID from Azure's generator and cannot match.

Every fix is pinned by a test that fails without it — verified by reverting each
check and watching the fake's "delete must not DELETE" fire.

Three exemptions, each backed by a driven re-derivation: `azimage` (witness-only,
no create to own anything with) and `defender` + `aks-addon` (settings-flip — the
class D456 named on GCP; the defender backing is the stronger form, reaching the
desired posture with a real create and then requiring the SAME create to be a
no-op against the estate it produced).

**The sweep is complete: 143 creates and 143 deletes decided across three clouds,
nine live defects found.** Every one of the nine is the same sentence: where the
provider offers no tags, the deterministic name was ownership evidence for the
verbs that write and forgotten by the verb that destroys. Not one defect was a
wrong check. All nine were an ABSENT check, in the one place where being wrong
cannot be undone.

## D459 — the update register: the verb between the two we swept

The create sweep asked whether a create binds what is already ours. The delete
sweep asked whether a delete refuses what is not. Nobody had asked the verb in
between, and the delete sweep is the reason to: nine of its defects were a check
the create and update paths carried and the delete did not. The argument runs
the other way just as well.

An update on a foreign resource is not the mild case — it is a TAKEOVER. The
resource keeps running, under someone else's name, with our configuration
written into it: their retention policy replaced by ours, their encryption
flipped, their DNS record repointed. A delete announces itself by the thing that
is gone. This does not.

`CertifyDeleteRefusesForeign` generalised into `certifyForeign`, with
`CertifyUpdateRefusesForeign` as its sibling. Same three demands — no success,
zero mutations, a stated reason — plus the D455 one: the refusal must have READ
something, unless ownership is derivable from a content-addressed id.

AWS: 21 updates decided. Twenty gated, one exempt (`loadbalancer` has no
in-place update at all — every governed attribute is fixed at creation and a
change routes to a replacement, D46/D48; the gate drives it and requires the
categorical refusal).

**One live defect, and it is the most instructive of the whole sweep:**

    // ownership re-check: the name IS the marker (no tags on the object).
    _, found, rerr := d.describeBudget(account, name)

The comment states the property. The code under it checks EXISTENCE. There is no
name check — `budgetNameLooksOurs` was written in D444, is called by the delete
beside it, and was never called here. So `updateBudget` would replace a
stranger's entire budget definition with ours, and read as correct to anyone
reviewing the file, because the comment says what the reader expects to find.

Every previous defect in this sweep was a missing check in a place where nothing
claimed there was one. This is a missing check where a comment claimed there was.
That is worse in the only way that matters: it defeats review. Only driving the
driver found it.

Fixing it broke three existing tests, which is its own small finding — they
addressed the budget as `pv-x`, a name our scheme could never mint (the D289
implausible-stand-in lesson). Repaired with a real derived name at GENERATION 2,
which keeps the "addresses the pid's name, not a re-derived one" assertion
meaningful and exercises the generation branch of the ownership check at the same
time.

GCP (22 updates) and Azure (10) remain.

## D460 — the update register closes on GCP and Azure, and the mirror holds

GCP: 22 updates decided — ten gated, twelve exempt. Ten of those exemptions are a
single categorical refusal ("in-place update is not wired yet") plus loadbalancer
refusing in the same spirit; there is no update to take anything over WITH, and
the gate drives each one to require the refusal is reached before any providerId
or estate is consulted. The other two are `gke-addon` and `scc`, the settings-flip
class from D456 — and the exemption gate now cross-checks the DELETE register, so
a service cannot be settings-flip on one verb and something else on the other
without failing.

Azure: 10 updates decided — eight gated, two settings-flip (`defender`,
`aks-addon`, cross-checked the same way).

**One live defect, and it is D459's exact mirror.** `updateServiceBus` checked
four things — the entity kind, the subscription, that every change is mutable, and
that the rebuilt identity matches the bound providerId — and then PUT the queue
properties. It never read the namespace's tags. `sbDelete`, twenty lines below,
has read them since it was written.

The fourth check is why this survived review: "rebuilt queue identity does not
match the bound providerId — refusing to redirect the mutation" READS like an
ownership check. It is not one. It proves the binding is self-consistent with the
candidate, which says nothing about who owns the namespace standing at that
deterministic path — and on Azure a PUT to an occupied path overwrites (D254).

The fix is not a fifth check in a second place. `refuseForeignSBNamespace` is now
the single ownership boundary both verbs call, because a queue has no tags of its
own — the namespace carries them — so update and delete must ask the same
question of the same resource. They disagreed for exactly as long as each carried
its own copy and only one copy existed.

**The update sweep: 53 updates decided across three clouds, two live defects, and
both were the delete sweep's finding read backwards.** AWS budgets: a comment
claiming a name check with an existence check under it. Azure servicebusqueue: an
identity check standing in for an ownership check. Both are the same failure at a
higher level than a missing line — a check that LOOKS like the one you need.

Three verbs, three registers, 339 decisions, eleven live defects.

## D461 — the meta-gate: which verbs has anyone asked?

Three ownership registers now exist, one per verb, deciding 339 driver paths and
finding eleven live defects. They were built in that order because that is the
order I thought of them, and the update register — the third — found two defects
on a surface nobody had asked about. Not because it was hard. Because "create and
delete" felt like the whole surface until it did not, and **nothing in the repo
would have said otherwise.**

That is the gap this slice closes. `ProviderMethods` derives every method any
provider interface declares, straight from provider.go, and a gate requires each
to be classified: mutating (naming the register that asks whether it writes to a
resource that is OURS) or read-only. A method in neither map fails. It is D338's
shape — a closed set, published once, checked against the source that defines it —
applied to verbs instead of event types.

The classification found two mutating verbs with no register, so a ratchet pins
the count. One is paid down here:

**Probe.** Under `allowIntrusive` a probe stops reading and starts spending: it
creates a scratch resource — a restored database, on the caller's bill — measures
recovery, and destroys it. All four probers gate by hand, each with the reasoning
written by whoever added it; nobody had said they ALL do.
`CertifyIntrusiveProbeRefusesForeign` now drives rds, aurora, cloudsql and
flexpostgres against a foreign estate and requires the refusal BEFORE the spend.
The mutation count is the load-bearing assertion, more than anywhere else in the
sweep: a prober that asks for the restore and then errors reads identically to one
that refused first. The k8s prober takes `allowIntrusive` and never reads it — a
declared exemption the gate re-derives from its source.

**Claim stays unregistered, deliberately, and the entry says why.** Claim exists
to stamp our ownership marker on a resource we did NOT create (D52/D140/D145), so
"is it ours?" is answered no by construction — a foreign-refusal register would
refuse the verb's whole purpose. The question that does apply is `claimLambda`'s,
and its comment states it exactly: *never tag a foreign function the acting
account happens to hold under the same name*. Most other claim paths build the ARN
from the providerId and stamp without reading. Whether that is a gap or the
intended reliance on adoption's own proof is a design question, and settling it
unilaterally would re-litigate D145.

What is not a design question is that it should be visible. **After a claim lands,
every ownership check in this repo says "ours" — it is the one write that makes
its own mistakes invisible to all eleven registers.** So it sits in the ratchet at
1, named, with the argument attached, rather than in a paragraph nobody reads.

## D462 — the registers reach the fourth driver, and create was not looking

D461 asked which VERBS nobody had questioned. It did not ask which DRIVERS, and
that is the gap: every gate in the sweep names three clouds, and the k8s driver —
a full `provider.Provider` with ten mapped services and its own Create/Update/
Delete — was in none of them.

It makes the register cheap and the finding sharp. Every k8s service routes
through one mapped write path, so one gate covers all ten. Two of the three verbs
pre-read ownership. **The create did not look at all** — zero requests before the
server-side apply, confirmed by driving it rather than by reading it.

Why that is a takeover and not a conflict: an SSA with `force=false` conflicts
only on fields another manager OWNS. Our ownership labels are new keys nobody
owns, so on a stranger's object **they apply cleanly**. After that `oursAt`
answers yes, and every ownership check downstream — including the delete's,
including the eleven registers built above — agrees the object is ours. The create
could manufacture its own permission. That is exactly the hazard D461 named for
Claim, arriving on the ordinary path where nobody had to consent to anything.

Worst where the name is operator-supplied: a cluster-scoped object takes
`impl["name"]` verbatim, so a contract naming `kube-system` labelled kube-system,
and the retirement that followed would have issued the DELETE.

`createMapped` now pre-reads like its two siblings: an existing object that is not
ours is refused ("adopt and claim it first" — the message `updateMapped` already
used), an existing object that IS ours is applied onto, since SSA is idempotent
and that apply is the adoption (D252/D253). Both halves are pinned, because a
pre-read that refused its own standing object would be a converge-breaking
regression dressed as a guard.

Fixing it broke one existing test, and the break is its own small finding: the
create fixture answered `200 {"metadata":{}}` to every method, modelling a server
on which nothing distinguishes "creating" from "applying onto whatever is already
there". The create never looked, so nothing noticed. It now answers 404 on GET,
which is what a create's estate actually looks like.

Twelve live defects, four drivers.

## D463 — which drivers exist, asked mechanically

D462 found the k8s create by noticing the driver was in none of the eleven
registers. That was luck: every gate in the sweep names the packages it covers,
and nothing anywhere enumerated the packages that EXIST.

So this gate enumerates them. A package declaring the Provider write verbs must
carry a decision — the registers that ask the ownership question of it, or an
exemption this gate re-derives. Seven drivers, and three of them were never in any
register: `cloudflare`, `hetzner` and `upstash`, each read-only, each write verb a
categorical "not implemented". That is a legitimate exemption and it is now
DRIVEN: the gate calls Create, Update and Delete on all three and requires both
the failure and a reason that says the verb is unwired, so the day one of them is
wired the exemption breaks and the driver owes a register.

The gate found its own bug on the first run, which is the part worth keeping. It
matched both verbs within a single FILE, and gcp declares Create in driver.go and
Delete in update.go — so it silently missed the largest driver in the repo while
reporting success. Fixed by aggregating per package, and pinned by an explicit
floor: aws, gcp, azure and k8s must be found, so a future signature change cannot
quietly shrink the set this gate guards. A detector that under-counts what it
covers is D328 wearing a different hat, and it is the third time that shape has
appeared — a gate that passes because it found nothing to check.

The sweep's shape is now closed in both directions: D461 asks which verbs anyone
questioned, D463 asks which drivers, and both answers are derived from the source
rather than remembered.

## D464 — the sweep's own number, and an honesty pass on MATURITY

The registers marked their defects in comments, in three different phrasings, and
one was not marked at all. So the number of defects the ownership sweep found
depended on which file you counted — the shape this repo has now hit four times
(D329/D330/D338/D463: a closed set published in several places, no two agreeing).
My own running totals inherited it: D459 said eleven, D462 said twelve.

**Counted from one place and checked against the drivers' certified services, it
is sixteen** — aws 9, azure 5, gcp 1, k8s 1. Neither earlier figure was right.
Those DESIGN entries stand as written, because the record is not rewritten; this
is the correction. `internal/provider/sweepdefects_gate_test.go` now holds the
list, refuses an entry naming a service its driver does not certify, refuses a
double count, and pins the total against the figure MATURITY quotes so the two
can only move together.

Three corrections to MATURITY, in both directions (the D287 rule):

**Gap 4 was true and half-told.** It said the field found things the gates did
not, and cited the pilot. It did not say that a systematic internal sweep then
found sixteen live defects that **no field run reported — and most of which could
not have been**. An operator does not notice a delete that would have destroyed
someone else's resource until it does. The honest statement is that the two find
different classes: the field finds what hermetic fakes mirror wrongly, the gates
find what nobody is positioned to observe.

**Two driver rows were missing entirely.** The k8s driver — ten mapped services, a
live takeover-class defect, fixed in D462 — appeared nowhere in a document that
lists AWS, GCP and Azure. Nor did the three read-only drivers. A maturity table
that omits a driver is not conservative, it is wrong.

**Claim is now a named gap** rather than a paragraph in a decision entry. It is
the one write no register questions, for a defensible reason, and the one whose
mistakes are invisible to every register that exists.

## D465 — the gap list aged in the direction nobody challenges

MATURITY entry 3 records the production incident of 2026-07-26 and said the
deeper half — a run's status collapsing per-action outcomes into one bit — was
"NOT yet fixed, and the more important of the two".

It has been fixed since D379 and D387. D379 made the summary lead with what
changed, lifting a per-action `outcomes` map `apply` had been emitting all along
and nothing had read. D387 fixed the rest: converge returned immediately on an
apply failure, skipping the post-apply observe and the reachability probe — the
mechanism built precisely to catch "it applied, but the edge does not answer" —
because evidence collection was conditioned on the run SUCCEEDING rather than on
anything having MUTATED.

I found this by opening `converge.go` to start the work, and finding a test file
named `partial_apply_evidence_test.go` whose header described the fix.

**The direction matters.** D464, one slice earlier, was an honesty pass that
revised three MATURITY entries — and walked straight past this one. A document
that is too hard on itself draws no complaints: nobody writes in to say a project
under-claims. So the optimistic drift gets caught (D287, D324) and the pessimistic
drift sits there, and a reader deciding whether to trust the system is misled
about the one thing the document exists to be honest about.

Staleness is not mechanically decidable. Whether a claim can be CHECKED is. So
the gate demands the anchor: every entry in "the gaps we are NOT hiding" must
cite a decision, and every decision MATURITY cites must be a real heading in
DESIGN.md. That is exactly how this one was caught — follow the reference, read
the code, compare. One gap cited nothing at all (probes, entry 8); it now cites
the decision that built them and the one that gated them.

The gate does not stop the list going stale. It makes each claim followable, so
going stale is something a reader can discover instead of inherit.

## D466 — a convention 39 of 44 drivers followed, and nobody wrote down

Looking for the next thing to ask the drivers, I measured whether GCP's paths
check the PROJECT in a providerId against the one the run pinned. Thirty-nine of
forty-four deletes did. Five did not, and nothing anywhere said which behaviour
was intended.

That is the delete sweep's shape one level up. Those nine defects were a missing
check where nothing claimed there was one. This is a missing check **where every
neighbour had one** — which is harder to see, not easier, because the file reads
like its neighbours until you diff them.

The ownership labels do not cover it, and that is the part worth stating plainly:
a `groundhold-capability` / `groundhold-environment` pair is **identical in every
project we manage**. A providerId naming another project passes the label check
with room to spare. The labels answer "is this the right capability?"; only the
project check answers "is this the right ESTATE?" — the D445 rule again, where
"there is nothing else to check" turned out to be a claim about the whole state
rather than about the resource.

Guarded now: persistent disks, managed instance groups, GCE instances (both verbs
each) and compute images. `sameProject` is a no-op when nothing is pinned, so the
read paths pay nothing and apply/converge gain the check.

Two families are correctly outside it and need no exemption entry, because the
gate is exact rather than curated: `gke-workloadidentity` binds a `poolProject` —
a cross-project pool is the entire point of the feature — and `billingbudget`
splits to a billing ACCOUNT, not a project. Neither binds a variable named
`project` from a providerId splitter, so neither matches the detector. A gate with
no exemption list has no exemption list to rot.

Coverage: 93 project-bearing driver paths, all guarded, and the gate refuses to
run if it finds fewer than thirty — D463's lesson, that a detector which
under-counts what it guards is the vacuity failure wearing a different hat.

## D467/D468 — the same boundary on the other two clouds, and one of them had none

D466 enforced the project boundary on GCP, where 39 of 44 paths already had it.
The same measurement on the other two clouds gives two different answers.

**Azure (D467): 64 of 67, and the three exceptions fail in a way GCP's could not.**
`deleteAzureAlert`, `deleteContainerApp` and `deleteVNet` parsed the subscription
out of the providerId and threw it away with `_ = sub` — a line whose only purpose
is to silence the compiler about an ownership signal.

The discard matters more than the missing check, because `armURL` builds every URL
from `d.Subscription`, never from the bound one. So a foreign-subscription
providerId never reached the other subscription. It **silently retargeted the
delete at the same resource group and name in OURS**. The binding named one
resource and the driver destroyed a different one — and where both exist, the
operator retires the wrong estate believing they retired the other. A gate now
refuses `_ = sub` outright: if the boundary does not apply, say so in a comment
and do not bind it, because a discard reads as an oversight, which is what it was
three times.

**AWS (D468): 0 of 20.** No convention existed, so this establishes one rather
than enforcing one — and the argument was already written in this package, in
`gateIntrusive`, which refuses an intrusive probe whose resource account differs
from the acting identity's because "a forged/stale binding must not redirect a
billed restore off-account". That reasoning does not stop at probes. Unlike Azure,
an AWS ARN names the account directly, so the request goes where the binding says,
and cross-account access to SQS, SNS, S3 and ECR is ordinary and commonly granted
— which makes the aim real rather than theoretical.

No legitimate flow produces a foreign-account providerId: one credential set, a
`discover` that enumerates the acting account, a create that writes what it
resolved. `sameAccount` is a no-op when nothing is resolved, because D29 forbids
turning "we could not find out" into a refusal, and that half is pinned too.

Three clouds, three answers to the same question — near-universal, near-universal
with a discard, and absent — and none of them was written down anywhere before it
was measured.

## D469 — the same compliance hold, refused on one cloud and discovered on the other

Measuring which creates SET a protection flag and which deletes READ one turned up
one gap: S3 can enable Object Lock at create and `deleteS3` never looked at it.
The GCS twin has read `retentionPolicy.isLocked` and refused before trying since
it was written.

The damage here is not destruction — AWS refuses a locked delete too. It is which
sentence reaches the operator. GCS says "bucket retention policy is LOCKED —
deletion is blocked by a compliance hold, never auto-lifted". S3 said "bucket is
not empty", or a raw HTTP error, for the same situation. D47's rule — protection
is never auto-lifted, and a refusal belongs up front — was applied on one cloud
and not on its twin, and only a cross-cloud measurement makes that visible,
because each file reads correctly on its own.

COMPLIANCE mode refuses; GOVERNANCE deliberately does not. It is bypassable by
design and `observeS3` already reverse-maps it to `retention.locked=false`, so
refusing on it would claim a hold that is not there — the same care the verifier
takes not to report a constraint as satisfied by something weaker.

An unreadable or unparseable lock configuration is `unknown`, never "not locked".
The GCS twin says why in a comment I could have written for this one: a truncated
read leaves the flag at its zero value, and deleting on a zero value is the
ambiguity this verb cannot afford. Four branches, four pinned tests — hold,
governance, ambiguity, and no lock at all — because the interesting failures here
are the two that must NOT refuse.

## D470 — the honesty MATURITY claimed, measured: 52 of 53

MATURITY has carried a gap for a long time: "several declared attributes cannot be
read back, so a reconcile reports them unverifiable rather than checked — the
system is honest about it, but honest-about-a-gap is still a gap."

I measured the honesty instead of trusting it. It is real and near-universal:
every AWS service that realises an attribute it cannot observe emits a diagnostic
naming the cause — dynamodb's customer-managed key, msk's, and a long tail
besides. One service did not.

`availability.class` on the VPC is realised — it drives the private-subnet spread,
where regional means at least two subnets in at least two availability zones — and
it appeared nowhere in `observeAWSVPC`. Not as a value, not as a reason. So a
reconcile reported it unverifiable with nothing to say about why it would stay
that way, which is the one thing the surrounding fifty-two services all say.

The convention was 52 of 53, and unwritten — the D466 shape again: a check
everyone had, nothing naming it, one file outside it. Three of those now, in one
session, on three different properties.

I did not derive the value, and the diagnostic says why rather than hiding it: a
zonal VPC creates its subnets with NO availability zone pinned, so AWS may place
the private and public ones in different zones, and counting distinct zones across
all of them would report "regional" for a zonal network. Telling private from
public means reading route-table associations this observe does not fetch. **A
wrong derivation is worse than an absent one** — it would turn an unverifiable
into a false `satisfied`, which is the failure this whole project is built to
refuse.

The gate distinguishes realisation from refusal by whether the case body assigns
to the plan: an attribute the driver never honors has nothing to observe about it,
and `availability.class` on a backup plan or vault — refused outright as "not a
placement" — correctly does not appear.

## D471 — the same measurement on the other two clouds, and the detector's two corrections

Porting D470's attribute-visibility gate to GCP and Azure found one more, and cost
two corrections to the gate itself — which is the part worth recording, because a
gate that reports phantoms is one somebody eventually switches off.

**Correction one: case slicing.** The detector sliced each `case "attr.path":` arm
up to the next ATTRIBUTE case, so a later arm's assignment leaked into an earlier
one. Three attributes that are deliberately accept-and-ignore, each with a comment
saying why — `location.region` on both workload-identity drivers ("scopes a
discover, not a build input"), `sending.productionAccess` on ACS Email ("ACS has
no sandbox gate; accept the type, then ignore") — were reported as realised. Arms
now end at the next arm of ANY shape.

**Correction two: scope.** Function scope missed the drivers that assemble their
observations in a helper (`consBudgetObservations` and friends). Whole-file scope
fixed those and went too far: a path mentioned by the CREATE code in the same file
counted as observed, which a teeth-check found by breaking a mention the gate then
failed to notice. Scope is now the observe's own body plus the bodies of the
same-package functions it CALLS — the set it can actually reach.

Then the real finding. **`retention.maximum` on Azure blob is written and never
read back**, while its S3 twin has always read the lifecycle Expiration rule. Same
capability, same attribute: `satisfied` in one estate, `unverifiable` in the other,
for reasons that are an accident of which driver got written when.

`observeBlobLifecycle` now reads the management policy create writes — and reads
it back by BOTH our rule name and the container prefix it filters on. An
account-level policy can carry rules nobody here wrote, and attributing a
stranger's expiry to this capability would be a measurement of the wrong thing,
which is worse than no measurement. Five branches pinned: ours, a foreign rule
name, our name on another container's prefix, absent, and unreadable.

Three clouds now carry the gate. Every attribute a driver realises is observed, or
says what stops it.

## D472 — the register I built to stop a count drifting, drifted

D464 published the sweep's defect count in one checked place, because the number
had depended on which file you counted. It recorded sixteen: the ownership sweep.

Six slices later the sweep had found nine more — three estate-boundary defects on
GCP, three on Azure, an S3 compliance hold surfaced as an unrelated error, and two
attributes realised but never read back — and **none of them were in the
register**. MATURITY went on quoting sixteen. One slice after building the thing
whose entire purpose was to stop that.

That is the most direct evidence available for the rule this session keeps
rediscovering: a published fact needs a gate, not good intentions, and the author
of the gate is not exempt. The count is now derived across four classes and stands
at **25 — aws 11, azure 9, gcp 4, k8s 1**.

Also worth recording: the register's verb set had to grow. It covered
create/update/delete, because the sweep began at the mutating verbs; two of the
newest findings are on `observe`, where the damage is not a wrong write but a
wrong CLAIM — an attribute reported unverifiable forever, or a value never read
back at all. A register that could not name the verb would have quietly dropped
them, which is how the count would have drifted again with the gate in place.

And the D465 gate caught this entry before it existed: writing "D472" into
MATURITY failed the build until this heading was here. A dangling anchor reads as
evidence and is not.

Four measurements in this family returned nothing after this — region boundaries
(correctly absent: a region is a coordinate, not a boundary), protection-flag
parity, D29 transport honesty, and attributes refused at build yet observed. The
seam is worked out; that is a result too, and cheaper to record than to rediscover.

## D473 — a denied name must be sanitized or absent, checked before publish

The exporter's negative-space audit denies a set of client tokens, and its comment
states the failure mode plainly: "a green `make check` on a tree that names a
client is the failure mode this exists to prevent."

That sentence was not true. Only the build-estate group is checked at `make check`
(D384, added after a runner-pool name reached a published entry through prose).
The client group ran ONLY at export time.

My first attempt at closing it was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the useful
part. I wrote the obvious gate — no published document may name a denied client —
and it failed on 36 lines of DESIGN.md naming `acme`. Those lines are not a leak:
**D340 settled this**. The honest field attribution stays in the private repo and
the name is genericized by an export-time sanitizer, the same stance already taken
for `groundhold` and `a real GCP project`. Enforcing the denylist BEFORE sanitization
contradicts a closed decision and would have forced a scrub the project chose not
to do. A measurement that finds real occurrences is not automatically a finding.

The residual gap is narrower and real: **of the eight denied client tokens, exactly
one has a sanitizer.** For the other seven the export does not genericize — it
REFUSES, at publish time, with the name already written into the tree. So the gate
asserts the export's own outcome early: for every denied token, either the exporter
rewrites it, or it does not appear in the tree that crosses.

The tokens are read from the exporter and never written in the test, because this
file is exported and the exporter is not — the mechanism D384 established after a
first version of that gate was itself the disclosure. Teeth-checked by writing a
denied, unsanitized name into a published doc and watching it fail.

## D474 — the export was believed publishable; now it is proven, and the pin gate caught me

Two findings, and the second is mine.

**The export had no gate.** It is the last step of the roadmap and the only one
nothing checked. It broke once — D340 found a client token across thirty files and
a count gate that hard-read a file the export deliberately omits — and it was
found by a manual readiness audit, not by CI. The script already does the whole
job: whitelist copy, sanitizers, negative-space audit, and a STANDALONE
`make check` proving the public tree has no hidden dependency on the private one.
`make export-check` runs it to a temp directory (always explicit: run with no
argument the script defaults to `../groundhold-public` and wipes it, which is right
for a publish and wrong for a check), and CI runs it as its own job, because
"publishable" is a distinct claim from "the gate is green". It passes today.

**Then I introduced the exact hazard pinning exists to remove.** Adding the CI job
I pinned `setup-python` from memory, to a commit the repo does not use. Two jobs in
one file would have run different commits of the same action. Nothing would have
failed and the pin looked right.

So the pins are gated: every action pinned to a 40-character SHA, and the same
action pinned to the same commit everywhere. It found two more the moment it ran,
and they are worse than mine —
`aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6` and `azure/login@v3`, **mutable tags in
the two workflows that hold cloud credentials**. Those jobs assume a role in a real
AWS account and log into Azure; a moved tag there is not a style issue. Both now
pinned to the commit their tag resolved to.

The lesson is the session's, arriving one more time: the property was already the
repo's convention — every other action pinned, deliberately — and nothing asserted
it, so the two places that mattered most were outside it and read exactly like the
rest.

## D475 — "stdlib + yaml only" is a published claim; now it is a checked one

The README says it, in a sentence that crosses the export boundary: the runtime is
stdlib + yaml only. The instructions file says it twice more, once per implementation.

It is true. The Go module requires exactly one module; the Python reference imports
nothing outside the standard library and PyYAML. That is precisely why it was worth
gating — the property is load-bearing (a verifier with no third-party surface is a
verifier nobody has to audit transitively), it is easy to lose to one convenient
import, and losing it would falsify a public sentence without failing anything.

The Python half asks the interpreter what the standard library IS rather than
carrying a list that would rot, and it REQUIRES python3 rather than skipping
without it: `make check` runs the Python reference through the whole conformance
suite, so an environment lacking it cannot pass anyway — and a gate that skips
itself is how a property stops being checked without anyone deciding to stop.

Both halves teeth-checked by breaking them: a second `require` line, and a
`import requests` at the top of the reference package.

That is the fourth published claim this session turned from prose into a gate — a
defect count (D464/D472), a gap list's anchors (D465), a denied client name
(D473), and now a dependency surface. The pattern underneath all four: **the
project's conventions are real and mostly held; what is missing is the assertion,
and what is missing is exactly where the exceptions live.**

## D476 — the drift was sitting under its own disclaimer

The instructions file said 514 conformance cases, 232 of them dual. The suite holds 521 and
235. Three lines below those numbers the same file says: *"These numbers drift.
Read them from the tools, never from this file."*

It was right, and that is the interesting part. The disclaimer is honest and it is
also what let the number rot: a figure that carries a warning is a figure nobody
has to keep true. The vocabulary count on the very next line has been gated since
D324 and is correct.

So the case counts are gated the same way, and corrected. The file is not exported,
so the gate skips in the public tree and says which other gate still guards the
number there — the pattern D340 established for the vocabulary count beside it.

Nothing was misled into a wrong verdict by this. But the instructions file is the first
document every agent working in this repository reads, its header says the
instructions OVERRIDE default behaviour, and an agent that trusts a stale number
in it reasons from a suite that does not exist. The cost of being wrong here is
not a bad apply; it is a bad decision, taken confidently, somewhere downstream.

## D477 — the threat model did not mention the thing that builds it

`docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` crosses the export boundary and is what a security reviewer
reads first. It covered the ledger, the provider API, the injection boundary and
the authoring boundary — and said nothing at all about the build pipeline.

That omission is not because the pipeline is weak. Reading it end to end, it is
the most carefully built part of the repository's infrastructure: OIDC-only cloud
credentials with `id-token: write` and nothing else, least-privilege permissions in
every workflow, govulncheck/gitleaks/CodeQL each as its own job, a third-party
binary fetched with both a pinned version and a SHA-256 check, and releases that
ship checksums, a CycloneDX SBOM, a BUILDINFO for bit-identical rebuild, a verified
version stamp, and a keyless SLSA provenance attestation.

None of it was written down where a reviewer looks. And an hour before this entry,
two of those workflows — the two holding cloud credentials — were still on mutable
tags (D474). A defence nobody has described is a defence nobody notices the hole in.

So the section states what is enforced BY A GATE rather than by intention, and the
accepted-risks list gains four entries that were true and unsaid:

- provenance is best-effort until the public flip, because GitHub does not serve
  attestations for a private repo (the failure D354 already caught once, when
  release notes promised a `gh attestation verify` that returned 404);
- **a pin is trusted as pinned** — the gate proves the SHAs are SHAs and that they
  agree with each other, never that a hash is the commit its tag pointed at;
- the self-hosted build estate is trusted, and keeping its names out of public
  trees is confidentiality, not integrity;
- reproducibility is **enabled, not verified** — BUILDINFO lets a third party
  rebuild and compare, and no job does it, so "bit-identical" is a claim a reader
  can check and nobody currently does.

The last two are the shape this session keeps producing, one level up: not a
missing defence, a missing sentence about which defence is absent.

## D478 — an invitation to rebuild, now a verified property

D477 wrote down that reproducibility was "enabled, not verified": `BUILDINFO.txt`
records the toolchain and the exact build command so a third party can rebuild
bit-identically, and nothing ever checked that a rebuild produces the same bytes.
The instruction was an invitation, and the first person to accept it would have
been the one to find out whether it was true.

It is true — measured before claiming it. Every release now rebuilds all four
artifacts a second time and fails if any hash differs, so an embedded timestamp,
an absolute path `-trimpath` missed, or a non-deterministic link stops the release
instead of being discovered by a reader. `make repro-check` runs the same
comparison locally on one target.

The claim is deliberately narrower than "reproducible". This proves determinism in
ONE environment. Environment-independence — the same bytes from a different Go
version or a different host — is exactly what BUILDINFO exists to let a stranger
check, and the threat model now says that half is still a reader's check and
nobody performs it.

Which is the distinction worth keeping: a gate that proved "our machine agrees
with itself" and let the document keep saying "reproducible" would have made the
claim WORSE, not better — it would have looked verified.

## D479 — verifying that a pin is the commit its tag claimed

D477 listed it as an accepted risk in as many words: *"a pin is trusted as
pinned. The gate proves every action is a 40-character SHA and that the pins agree
with each other; nothing verifies that a given SHA is the commit its tag pointed
at when it was written down."* D474 had just demonstrated why that matters — I
wrote a hash from memory and it was wrong.

A scheduled job now re-resolves every pinned tag through the API (dereferencing
annotated tag objects to their commit, which is not the same thing and is where a
naive check silently compares the wrong hash) and compares. All twelve pins match
today, including the two D474 added.

**Scheduled, not blocking on pull requests, and deliberately so.** Upstream tags
move — a `v6` retagged onto a new commit is routine maintenance, not a compromise
— so a mismatch is an event somebody must look at rather than a build to stop. A
job that failed every PR on unrelated upstream activity would be trained away
within a week.

Two things the first draft got wrong, both worth keeping:

- **The loop ran in a subshell.** Piping the pin list into `while read` means the
  failure flag cannot escape, so the job would have reported success no matter
  what it found. That is precisely the vacuous-gate shape this session keeps
  finding in code someone else wrote, produced here by me, in a job whose entire
  purpose is to detect a silent substitution. The list goes to a file now, and
  both paths are proven by stubbing the API: a disagreeing stub exits 1, an
  agreeing one exits 0.
- **A pin with no `# vX.Y.Z` comment cannot be verified at all** — there is no tag
  to re-resolve. The `make check` gate now requires the comment, so "pinned and
  unauditable" is not a state this repository can reach.

The threat model's accepted risk is narrowed rather than deleted: the hash is now
checked against the tag, and nobody checks that the tag pointed at code worth
trusting. That remains what a reviewer does, and the document still says so.

## D480 — the cross-host reproducibility check I did not add

D478 verified that a build is deterministic on one machine and said plainly that
environment-independence was the untested half. The obvious next slice was to
close it: both CI portability jobs build the identical `linux/amd64` target with
the same pinned Go, `CGO_ENABLED=0` and `-trimpath`; one runs on Linux and one on
macOS; expose each hash as a job output and compare them.

I wrote it, and then read the job I was depending on:

    portability-darwin:
      if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.repository_owner == 'groundhold'

The only non-Linux runner is gated on the PUBLIC org, which does not exist yet. It
has never executed. A comparison job hanging off it would have been skipped on
every run in this repository — a green pipeline containing a check that never ran,
asserting the strongest reproducibility claim in the document.

That is the vacuous gate this session keeps finding, and it would have been the
worst instance of it: not a gate that passes for the wrong reason, a gate that
passes by never happening, attached to a security property. So it is not added.

What changes instead is the sentence. The threat model said cross-environment
reproducibility was unverified; it now says it is **unmeasurable here**, names the
reason, and says what makes it measurable — the public flip, at which the macOS job
starts running and the comparison becomes a two-line addition. A reader deciding
whether to trust the claim learns it is a structural constraint rather than an
oversight, and whoever performs the flip inherits a concrete follow-up instead of
a forgotten intention.

Reverted before committing, which is the only reason this entry is a design note
rather than a defect.

## D481 — retiring a posture is not obviously the same as switching it off

MATURITY gap 10 records the settings-flip class: for `gcp/scc`, `gcp/gke-addon`,
`azure/defender` and `azure/aks-addon`, create turns a flag on and retirement
turns it off, and because create adopts an already-on flag silently the retirement
cannot tell "we enabled this" from "it was already on when we arrived".

Looking at it again for the fix, the four do not belong together. Two are
capabilities — an addon, disabled on retirement, is defensible. Two are SECURITY
POSTURES, and for those the ownership question is not even the sharpest one.

This repository states a rule and enforces it everywhere it has been noticed:
**a protection is never auto-lifted; lifting it is an explicit prior step** (D47).
It is why a delete refuses while `deletionProtection` is on, why Aurora says "lift
it explicitly first; it is never auto-disabled", and why D469 made S3 refuse a
compliance hold this session. Disabling Security Command Center or Defender as a
