side effect of retiring a contract does exactly what that rule forbids — weakens a
safety posture, with no consent step, no record, and no refusal — and it does so
whether or not we were the ones who enabled it. **The ownership gap makes it worse;
it is not what makes it wrong.**

The two readings differ only for postures: *retire means turn it off* versus
*retire means we stop asserting it*. For the addons they agree.

I am not resolving it. It changes what `retire` DOES for a capability type, which
by this repo's own rule starts with a conformance case and not a driver edit, and
the consent vocabulary it would need (`--allow-data-loss` is about data, not about
posture) does not exist yet. It is now an open question in the instructions file with the
precedent attached, and MATURITY's gap 10 names it rather than folding it into the
ownership problem it is entangled with.

What this session can claim about it is narrow and worth stating: the gap was
found by asking who owns the flag, and the more serious problem beside it was only
visible because the ownership question was asked first.

## D482 — the meter nobody read, and the mutant that lied

`scripts/mutation-gate.sh` calls itself THE METER: re-inject every bug this
repository has actually shipped, and require the named test to CATCH it. Its
opening comment is the strongest sentence in the testing strategy — *"`make check`
was green the whole time this cycle's real bugs existed: a green suite with live
bugs IS a low mutation score, by definition."*

Nothing ran it. Not CI, not `make check`. A meter with no reader, guarding the one
property the whole suite rests on. It runs in CI now, as its own job, because "the
tests have teeth" is a different claim from "the tests pass".

It also stood at five mutants, curated from one cycle's bugs, while this session
added twenty-five defects whose fixes were teeth-checked **once**, by hand,
revert-and-watch-it-fail. A hand-check proves a test had teeth on the day it was
written. A mutant proves it still does. Four of today's fixes are now mutants — the
k8s create pre-read, the budgets update name check, the Service Bus namespace read,
and the S3 compliance hold — chosen because a silent regression in any of them
would look exactly like the original bug did: correct, and identical to its
neighbours.

**The budgets mutant reported a weak test, and was itself the weak thing.** The
substitution matched `if !budgetNameLooksOurs(name, capability, environment) {` —
which appears TWICE in that file, guarding the delete twenty lines above the
update. Unanchored, it mutated the delete, so `TestRefusesForeignUpdateBudgets`
passed with a function it never calls left intact, and the gate reported SURVIVED:
a real test declared toothless on the evidence of a mutant that never touched the
code under test.

Which is the mutation gate's own failure mode, and worth stating where its authors
will read it: **a mutant that hits the wrong line is indistinguishable from a test
with no teeth, and it accuses the test.** The fix is to anchor on something unique
to the site — here the update's own comment — and the general rule is that a
SURVIVED verdict earns one look at the mutant before it earns a look at the test.

## D483 — the strategy document described a gate it had not seen built

`docs/TESTING_STRATEGY.md` is where the mutation gate points its reader. It
described the meter in the future tense — *"scope go-mutesting/gremlins to the
verdict-producing functions... run quarterly, not per-PR"* — and set the success
criterion as *"recreate this cycle's four real bugs as mutants"*.

What exists is a different thing: a CURATED gate, hand-written with perl and sed,
nine mutants, each one a bug this repository actually shipped. It is not a
framework and the advice sized for a framework does not fit it. "Quarterly, not
per-PR" was a cost argument about mutating everything; nine targeted mutants run in
seconds, so D482 put it on every PR — and a meter that runs quarterly tells you
three months late which test stopped having teeth.

So the section now says what was built, that it runs per PR and why that
deliberately contradicts the advice above it, and that the exhaustive option
remains unbuilt with the original scoping still standing for it. The D482 lesson —
an unanchored mutant accuses the wrong party — is recorded where whoever adds the
tenth mutant will read it.

One more correction, small and worth the care: the document opens with "`make
check` (410 conformance cases...) was green the entire time real bugs existed."
The suite holds 521 now, but that sentence is a HISTORICAL claim about the state of
the repository when the bugs were live. Updating the number would have falsified
the evidence; it now reads "410 conformance cases AT THE TIME". A stale number in
a historical sentence is not drift — but a reader cannot tell which kind it is
unless the sentence says so.

## D484 — a mandatory gate that lived only in a design entry

D272 wrote the delivery process down after two broken binaries shipped GREEN — one
where `ping` was ineffective, one where an ALPN break made every request fail with
"malformed HTTP response", both invisible to a hermetic `make check`. The process:
push a tag, let `release.yml` gate and attest the artifact, **run
`scripts/preship.sh` on a box with AWS egress**, then hand the attested artifact to
the client.

The middle step existed in exactly one place: that paragraph. Not in the release
workflow, not in the README, not in any checklist. `preship.sh` calls itself "the
MANDATORY checks before a binary goes to a client" and nothing in the repository
references it — the same shape as the mutation gate (D482) and the export (D474),
but on the path where being wrong reaches an operator's production account.

Two of its four steps need no credentials, only egress, and both run in under a
second: the protocol check (the D269 ALPN shape) and endpoint-reality (the D273
class — a driver polling a path that does not exist in the cloud API, mirrored by
a fake that shared the wrong assumption, so the suite was blind by construction).
Verified here before wiring: both pass, EKS answers HTTP/1.1 403 as expected.
They now run in the release job.

**What cannot move is the signed request.** A SigV4 regression is invisible to
every check in that pipeline, and only a box with credentials sees it. So the
release prints the remaining manual gate onto its own summary — the step that was
forgotten was forgotten because nothing said it — and `preship.sh` now states that
the signed half is its reason to exist, rather than "everything, remembered".

The honest limit: this does not make the manual step happen. It makes it
impossible to reach a release without being told about it, which is the most a
pipeline can do about a check it cannot run.

## D485 — the verb check, extended to the scripts nobody runs

The published-docs gate (D351) checks that every `groundhold <verb>` a document
shows is a verb the binary has, because a reader types what a document shows. The
scripts were outside it.

A script is executed, so a rotted verb fails loudly — for whoever runs it. That is
the whole problem with the three this repository references from nowhere:
`integration-gcp.sh` and `console-fixtures.sh` still, and `preship.sh` until D484
wired half of it into the release. A verb that rots in one of those waits silently
for the person who finally needs the tool, on the day they need it, which is
reliably the worst day.

Sixty-seven invocations across the scripts, all real today. The gate keeps them
that way, reading the verb set from the usage text the binary prints rather than a
list that would drift.

Anchoring mattered here more than in the docs. The word "groundhold" appears in
prose all over these files — "the groundhold binary", "groundhold output",
"groundhold observed" — and a loose match reported sixteen phantom verbs on the
first run. A gate that cries wolf sixteen times is a gate someone switches off, so
the match requires the invocation to hang off the binary (`"$BIN"`,
`./bin/groundhold`) and skips comment lines. Teeth-checked by planting a bogus verb
in the least-run script of the three.

## D486 — a security backlog marked DONE on two items that had rotted

The private checklist that gates the public flip (a `docs/` file the export does not
carry) had two items marked done, and neither was true any more.

**S8: "all GitHub Actions pinned by SHA (3 workflows)".** There are nine workflows
now. Two actions sat on mutable tags, and they were the two in the workflows that
hold cloud credentials: `configure-aws-credentials@v6` and `azure/login@v3`
(D474). The item was true when it was written and rotted as the repository grew,
with nothing checking it — Dependabot updates pins, it does not force pinning, so
it had no reason to complain. The parenthetical "(3 workflows)" is the tell: the
claim was scoped to a count, the count moved, and the claim did not.

**S10: "build verified bit-identical".** Verified meant verified once, by hand.
`release.yml` emitted BUILDINFO.txt with the instructions and nothing ever checked
that a rebuild produced the same bytes (D478).

This is D465's failure with the sign flipped, and the flipped sign is what makes
it worse. That entry described a fixed thing as broken — pessimistic drift, which
misleads a reader into distrust. **These describe unenforced things as done**, in
the document whose purpose is deciding whether it is safe to go public. A launch
checklist that has rotted is not a neutral inaccuracy; it is the exact artifact
someone will rely on instead of re-checking.

Both entries now say what is enforced, by which gate, and what made the earlier
claim rot. S10 also gains the boundary D480 established: determinism is verified in
one environment and is currently unmeasurable across them, for a structural reason.

The general form, third time today: **a checklist item is a claim, and a claim
scoped to a number ("3 workflows") stops being true the moment the number moves.**

## D487 — the account boundary reaches the verb that most needed it

D468 established it for delete, update and observe: no legitimate flow produces a
providerId naming another account, so a mismatch is a forged or stale binding.
`Claim` was not covered — and it is the verb where the boundary matters most.

A delete that reaches the wrong resource destroys it, and the damage is visible. A
claim that reaches the wrong resource **stamps our ownership marker on it**, after
which every ownership check in this runtime agrees the resource is ours: the create
register, all three delete registers, the update registers, the intrusive-probe
gate. It is the one write that manufactures its own permission, which is exactly
what D461 recorded when it left Claim on the verb-coverage ratchet at 1.

The concern was already written down here, in `claimLambda`: *"never tag a foreign
function the acting account happens to hold under the same name."* Twelve other
paths built an ARN straight from the providerId's account and checked nothing.
They do now.

Ten more cases look like they should and do not need it, and telling the two apart
is the whole content of the gate: a case that calls `d.resolveAccount()` is using
OUR account and has nothing to verify, while a case that binds `account` out of a
`split*ProviderID` is trusting the binding. A detector counting mentions of
"account" would have flagged all of them, including `s3`, whose case binds a bucket
and mentions accounts only in a comment.

Two notes on the gate itself. Go's RE2 has no lookahead, and reaching for `(?=` did
not fail to match — it PANICKED at compile time, taking the whole test binary with
it. A detector that stops compiling stops guarding, loudly here and silently in a
form that only ran conditionally.

**And the first fix was the wrong shape, which the cross-cloud check then showed
me.** I satisfied the gate with twelve per-case guards — twelve chances to add a
thirteenth case without one, which is precisely how those cases drifted apart from
`claimLambda` in the first place. Measuring the other two clouds for the same gap
found none: GCP guards all twenty claim helpers, and **Azure guards ONCE**, in
`claimURLFor`, the shared helper every case calls. (My per-case detector reported
thirty unguarded Azure cases before I read the callee — the D471 scope lesson,
repeated by me one seam later: a detector that stops at the function boundary
invents findings.)

So the AWS check moved to the funnel. `claimByARN` is the single point every claim
passes through, and the ARN it is about to tag carries the account in field five —
one check covering every case, the ones built from `resolveAccount()` (a no-op by
construction), and any case added later. An account-less ARN (s3's
`arn:aws:s3:::bucket`) yields "" and is skipped. The gate now asserts the funnel
check exists AND that the per-case copies have not come back.

And the limit, stated because it is the interesting part: this applies an existing
boundary. It does NOT answer whether claim should verify that the resource is the
one the binding NAMES — `claimLambda` does, nobody else does, and that remains the
ratcheted design question, not a missing line.

## D488 — auditing my own gates for the vacuity I had been auditing everyone else for

Six register gates ask "does every service have a decision?". I stubbed each one's
dispatch parse to return EMPTY and ran it. Four failed, as they should. **Two
passed** — `TestEveryCreateHasAnAdoptionDecision` (AWS) and
`TestEveryGCPDeleteHasAForeignRefusalDecision` — reporting success while deciding
nothing about nothing.

The four that failed were protected **by accident**. None of them asserts its
subject; they survive because a *different* assertion — the stale-check, which
flags registry entries naming services the dispatch lacks — happens to fire when
the dispatch is empty. The two that passed simply did not have that second
assertion. So the property held in four places for a reason nobody chose, and the
two exceptions looked exactly like the four.

That is D328's own shape, in the gates written to enforce D328, by the author who
spent this session finding it in other people's code. Both now assert the subject
explicitly rather than depending on a side effect.

Three more of my own, found in the same pass: the GCP and Azure update-exemption
gates iterate a map and pass silently when it is empty (a register that stopped
being maintained reads as a register with nothing to check), and the
discarded-subscription scan reported success if it read no files. All three now
assert what they scanned.

A wider sweep followed, and it is the part that changes how I would build these.
Every gate that reads a source file was run against that file EMPTIED — the test
binary compiled first, the file truncated after, so the parse genuinely finds
nothing. Twenty driver-side gates: all protected. The doc and config gates: one
more vacuous, and it was mine.

`TestWorkflowActionPinsAreConsistent` floored on the number of WORKFLOW FILES.
Empty every workflow and the count of files is unchanged, so the gate finds zero
`uses:` lines, reports no unpinned actions and no disagreeing pins, and passes. It
counted the container instead of the subject. The scripts gate beside it, written
an hour later, floors on INVOCATIONS and survives the same treatment — the right
shape was already in the file next door.

Three more notes on the method, because the audit misled me three times. Stubbing a
parse to empty produced a BUILD failure the first time — an unused variable — and
a build failure is not a passing test; it took a second look to see the harness was
broken rather than the gate protected. Then a `-run` filter with the wrong test
name reported PASS for a package where nothing ran at all. **A verification harness
that can report success without executing the thing under test is the same defect
one level up**, and it is worth saying out loud that the tool I used to hunt
vacuity was, briefly, vacuous.

The third: the uniform experiment emptied `aws_provider.go` for every AWS gate, and
`TestEveryAuthoredServiceCanReconcile` "passed" — because it reads
`reconcile_aws.go`. I nearly wrote up a gate that had been correct all along.
Emptying the file each gate ACTUALLY reads, one at a time, is slower and is the
only version that means anything. The assumption that all the gates read the same
source is exactly the kind of assumption the gates exist to distrust.

## D489 — writing down the idiom, so the next person does not re-derive it by breaking it

The sweep produced a shape this repository now uses everywhere: the register — a
decision set per service, a ratchet on the debt, exemptions that re-derive their
own evidence, a vacuity floor. Twenty-eight of them exist. The pattern was
documented only as a trail of decision entries, which means it was documented for
whoever reads DESIGN.md end to end, which is nobody in a hurry.

`docs/TESTING_STRATEGY.md` now carries it as an idiom with its rules, and the rules
are the valuable half because each one cost a mistake to learn:

  assert the subject, not the container       (a floor on file count, D488)
  the guard watches the dispatch, not the debt (fires when the debt is paid, D413)
  a refusal must be made OF something          (four vacuous enrolments, D455)
  scope: function -> file -> call graph        (three phantoms, then one miss, D471)
  prove the teeth, then pin them as a mutant   (a hand-check ages, D482)
  a wrong mutant accuses the test              (SURVIVED on an untouched function, D482)
  a real occurrence is not automatically a finding (D473 vs the closed D340)
  verify the harness too                       (three phantom results, D488)

Every line of that list is a thing I did wrong in one session, caught by something
else in the same session. That is worth recording plainly rather than presenting
the method as if it arrived clean: the register idiom works, and the reason it
works is that each of its rules is scar tissue.

## D490 — the docs site built strict, and nobody knew whether it built

`pages.yml` runs `mkdocs build --strict`: a broken internal link, or a nav entry
pointing at a file that moved, fails the build. The workflow is
`workflow_dispatch` only. It has never run automatically, so between manual
deploys the answer to "does the site build?" was simply unknown — and the docs are
edited constantly, including today.

Third instance of the same shape this week. The export gate had no runner (D474);
the mandatory pre-ship check was referenced by nothing (D484); a strict build sat
behind a manual trigger. In each case the CHECK was written carefully by somebody
who understood exactly what it was for, and nothing ran it.

Measured before wiring, which is the rule that keeps this from being a guess: the
pinned toolchain (mkdocs 1.6.1, material 9.7.7) installed into a scratch venv, and
`mkdocs build --strict` completes clean in 0.22s. So the site is healthy; the
finding is only that its health was unobserved. It is now a `ci.yml` job on every
push and pull request.

The milestone list gets the correction it was owed: M2's "verify the docs site
builds" is done and continuously proven, and only the quickstart-against-the-
exported-tree half remains open. A checklist item that was true-but-unverified and
one that is verified-every-run are different states, and a launch checklist that
cannot tell them apart is the artifact D486 was about.

## D491 — reading the workflow file is not reading the condition on the job

Finishing the "exists but never runs" sweep meant enumerating every job's `if:`.
Four are conditional, and two of them matter.

**CodeQL has never run.** Code scanning needs GitHub Advanced Security on a private
repository, so the job is conditioned on `repository.visibility == 'public'` and
skips green. The workflow file is real, the configuration is correct, and the
scanner has produced nothing because it has never executed.

D477 — mine, an hour earlier — listed CodeQL among the active scanning defences in
the threat model. I described the pipeline by reading the workflows and not the
conditions on their jobs, in the document whose entire job is to be accurate about
what defends this system. Corrected: three scanners run on every push, CodeQL is
wired and dormant, and it starts at the flip.

**The three cloud canaries are gated on `repository_owner == 'groundhold'`** — the
private org, so they run today. That is the only real-cloud evidence CI produces.
**The flip turns them off**: a different owner, condition false, jobs skip, green,
with no signal at all. The most valuable check in the pipeline would go silent at
exactly the moment the project starts being watched.

That is a flip-time landmine, not a defect, so it belongs where the flip is
performed. The security backlog's runbook now opens with the three conditions the
flip flips — canaries OFF unless the owner is changed in the same commit, CodeQL
ON for the first time in the repository's history (expect findings),
`portability-darwin` ON, which makes cross-host reproducibility measurable (D480).

The lesson is narrow and I keep relearning it in different clothes: **a check's
existence, its correctness, and its execution are three separate facts, and a
document that conflates them is confidently wrong.** Today that has been the
export, the pre-ship gate, the mutation gate, the docs build, and now a scanner I
myself listed as active.

## D492 — arming the flip landmine instead of writing it down

D491 put the canary org-condition into the flip runbook: move the repository to a
new owner and `repository_owner == '<private org>'` becomes false, so the only
real-cloud evidence CI produces skips, green, silently.

A runbook is a document, and this session has been an extended lesson in what
documents are worth on their own. `preship.sh` called itself the MANDATORY gate
and was referenced nowhere. `mutation-gate.sh` called itself THE METER and ran
nowhere. `pages.yml` built the site strictly and never ran. Writing "remember to
change the org" into a runbook puts it in exactly that category.

So the condition is checked against the git remote. The org in every
`repository_owner ==` must be the org the repository is actually in. At the flip
the remote changes, this fails, and whoever performs it is told which lines to
move — in the same commit, which is the only moment it costs nothing.

Two deliberate accommodations, both named rather than implicit. `portability-darwin`
references the FUTURE org: it has never run and starts at the flip (D480), so it is
allowed by name. And the gate SKIPS with no remote — an exported tree or a tarball
— because the flip happens in the working repository, which has one. That is the
same exemption shape as the exporter-absent skip in D473, and it is the second
place today where "skip when the context genuinely differs" is right and "skip when
the check is inconvenient" would not be.

Verified by simulating the flip: rewriting one condition to a different org fails
the gate and names the file and line.

## D493 — agreement is not closure

Invariant 4 says the operator set is closed: *"do not add an expression language,
interpolation, or logical connectives to constraints. Complexity = more
constraints."* It is the invariant that keeps a contract readable by someone who
has never seen the medium before — every operator is one more thing a reader must
know, and the medium's value is that there is almost nothing to know.

D327 gated it, or looked like it did: `TestOperatorSetsAgreeAcrossImplementations`
proves Go and Python hold the SAME set. **Agreement is not closure.** Add an
operator to both and that gate stays green. It checks the property this repository
cares about second (the two implementations must not diverge) and not the one the
invariant states (the set must not grow).

That is the session's shape one more time, on the strongest invariant left
unpinned: a property everyone believes, checked in a way that permits its
violation, in a file whose comment says the check is about the invariant.

The set — eight comparison operators plus `exists`/`absent` — is now pinned as a
list. Growing it stays legitimate and becomes deliberate: edit the list, write the
decision entry that says why. Teeth-checked by adding `matches-regex`, which is
precisely the operator this invariant exists to keep out, and watching the gate
name it.

Checked while I was here: the other invariants do have gates. N1's explicit `--at`
(D323/D325), the four-valued verdicts, no-coercion and provenance through the
conformance suite, and invariant 6's determinism through D327's import-closure walk,
which is the most thorough of them. Invariant 4 was the one holding on care alone.

## D494 — a plan that shipped and still says "do not implement"

`docs/proposals/suggest-advisor.md` opened with:

    Status: ACCEPTED (2026-07-20) — implementation may proceed. Target decision
    entry: D203. ... Do not implement until this is accepted.

`groundhold suggest` shipped. `go/internal/suggest`, wired into the CLI, pinned by
conformance, D203 written. Anyone opening the proposal reads a feature that has not
been built and an instruction not to build it.

Nothing depends on that header, which is exactly why it sat there: the file is read
rarely, and when it is, the reader is looking for the reasoning rather than the
status. That is the pessimistic drift D465 named — a document too hard on the
project draws no complaints — in its mildest and most typical form. The header now
says IMPLEMENTED, points at the code and the decision, and states that where they
differ the code is right and the document is the earlier intention.

I checked the neighbours rather than assuming. The internal notes directory carries a
README saying plainly that it is a record of past sessions, not live work, and its
one backlog file is frontmattered as a memory record. `merge-guide.md` says
"HISTORICAL". Those are honest: a document that says which kind it is cannot drift
into being read as the other kind. The proposal was the only one whose status line
described a future that had already happened.

## D495 — running the whole battery found two of my own regressions

`make check`, the mutation gate, the reproducible rebuild, the differential fuzz and
`go test -race ./...` (65 packages) were all green. `make export-check` was not, and
it caught two things I had introduced today.

**A leak.** D486's entry names the private launch checklist by filename. DESIGN.md
crosses the export boundary and that filename is on the denylist, so the export
refused. Exactly what the audit is for, found by the gate D474 added — and found
only because the full battery was run, since `make check` does not include the
export. Rewritten to describe the document without naming it.

**A gate of mine that fatalled in the exported tree, and had been blind in both.**
D485's scripts-verb check floored on `len(files) < 3`. The export carries ONE script
by design, so the gate fataled there — a floor on the CONTAINER instead of the
SUBJECT, which is D488's rule, broken by me two hours after writing it down.

The second half is worse and is the real finding. The invocation anchor covered
`$BIN` and `./bin/groundhold` and NOT `"$GROUNDHOLD"` — which is the form used by
`adopt-candidate.sh`, **the one script that crosses the boundary and the only one a
public reader ever runs**. Sixty-seven invocations matched, every one of them in a
script that never ships. A gate written to protect the scripts nobody runs was
silently skipping the script everybody gets.

Both fixed; the exported script is now genuinely checked, proven by planting a bogus
verb in it and watching the gate fire.

The lesson is about the battery, not the bugs. Six gates exist, `make check` runs
one of them, and I pushed fifteen commits between adding the export gate and running
it again. CI would have caught both on the first push — CI I cannot see from here.
**A gate you do not run is indistinguishable from a gate you do not have**, which is
the sentence this whole session has been rewriting, and this time the author of the
sentence is the one it applies to.

## D496 — I verified on a branch and shipped from master

`v0.1.4` was tagged at `origin/master` and its `make check` is RED. The release
workflow gates on `make check` before it builds anything, so it produced no
artifacts — the pipeline behaved correctly. I did not.

Everything I ran during the release rehearsal — the gate, the mutation meter, the
differential fuzz, the race detector, the export audit, the four-target build and
its reproducibility comparison — ran in the working tree, which is a FEATURE BRANCH
(`role-resources`). My commits reach `master` by cherry-pick, each one gated in a
temp worktree at the moment it lands. What nobody checked was the RESULTING master,
and two of my own gates fail there:

  the instructions file claims the suite size = 521, the suite holds 514
  CHANGELOG.md -> docs/TESTING_STRATEGY.md   (a path the export does not carry)

Both are correct on the branch and wrong on master, for the same reason: the branch
carries seven conformance cases master does not, and I wrote the numbers from the
tree in front of me. The second is worse — a plain mistake that the gate caught and
I did not look at, because I read `make check`'s last two lines and they said what
I expected.

The anomaly that led here is worth keeping too. During the rehearsal one artifact
reported NOT REPRODUCIBLE and I could not reproduce the mismatch, so I recorded it
as unexplained rather than dismissing it. It was the branch/master divergence
showing through `vcs.revision`, which Go stamps into every binary — the same
divergence, seen first as a hash and then as a red gate.

Two things change. `v0.1.5` is cut from a master whose full battery is green, and
the CHANGELOG says plainly why it supersedes v0.1.4 rather than quietly replacing
it. And the rehearsal rule is now explicit: **the tag's own commit is what must be
verified**, in a worktree at that commit, not the tree the work was done in. A
per-commit gate at cherry-pick time proves each step; it does not prove the result.
## D497 — the gates and the exporter kept two copies of "what crosses"

Every published-document gate — links resolve, CLI verbs are real, no denied client
name, no dependency on a private path — scans a set built by `publishedDocs()`. That
helper carried its own description of the export boundary: root markdown except
The instructions file, four named `docs/` files, four whole trees. The exporter carries the
authoritative one, an `INCLUDE` list.

Two hand-maintained copies of a closed set, which is the shape D329, D330 and D338
each closed elsewhere. They had drifted. **Four markdown files cross the boundary
and no gate had ever looked at them**: the three GitHub issue and pull-request
templates, and a README under `go/internal/fixture`.

The templates are the sharp part. The bug template is what the first stranger to
report a problem reads, and a launch milestone specifically put the MATURITY reality
into it — so it makes claims about the project, in public, and its links, its CLI
invocations, its client names and its private-path references were unverified. Not
because anyone decided they did not matter; because the list that decides what gets
checked was written separately from the list that decides what ships.

`publishedDocs()` now derives from `INCLUDE`. The same fix as D384 (build-estate
labels) and D473 (denied client names): read the authority, never restate it. In the
exported tree the exporter is absent and everything present crossed by definition,
so the fallback scans what is there rather than skipping — a gate that stops running
in the public repo would defeat the point of gating public documents.

## D498 — a decision number used twice makes every reference to it ambiguous

Landing D497 on master hit a DESIGN.md conflict, and my mechanical resolution — strip
the markers, keep both sides — **silently dropped D496**. I caught it by counting
headings afterwards, not by reading the diff.

That is the session's own failure shape applied to the record itself: a step that
reported success while losing content. It also revealed something already there.
Counting the headings shows **three numbers used twice** — D94, D329 and D330 — each
from parallel sessions appending at the same moment.

DESIGN.md's headings are the anchors everything cites: code comments, MATURITY's gap
list (which D465 made mandatory), the memory files, the canary runbook. "See D329" is
only worth writing if D329 is one thing, and right now it is two.

**They are not renumbered.** D329 and D330 are each cited from several Go files and
from the canary doc; rewriting a number would leave those references correct for one
meaning and wrong for the other, creating exactly the ambiguity the fix was meant to
remove. They are declared, and the gate stops a fourth from arriving unnoticed —
including the one I would have created here, since I picked D498 by looking.

The conflict itself deserves a note for whoever lands the next cross-branch change:
an append-only file conflicts on every landing once two lines diverge, and the
resolution that looks obviously right — keep both sides — is exactly where an entry
goes missing. Count the headings before and after.

## D499 — eleven comments pointed at decisions that were not there

D465 made MATURITY's gap citations resolvable: every decision it names must be a real
heading. The source was outside that. Counting citations across `go/` found **eleven
Go comments pointing at D358 and D411**, neither of which exists — the sequence jumps
357→359 and 410→412 in a record otherwise contiguous from D1.

The loss shape is the one D498 caught me committing an hour earlier: a conflicted
append-only file resolved by "keep both sides", where one side quietly does not
survive. There it was caught in the act by counting headings. Here it had already
happened, twice, and nothing had ever looked.

The prose is gone and I will not invent it. Both numbers now carry a stub that says so
and records what the number is USED for, read from the citations rather than
reconstructed — the EC2 instance driver for D358, the completion of the AWS
create-adoption sweep for D411 — with a pointer to the neighbours and to the register
that survives. Renumbering the eleven citations to a neighbouring entry was the
alternative and is worse: they would then point at prose that does not describe what
they cite, which is a wrong answer rather than an honest one.

Two things the gate had to learn. Combined headings are legitimate — `## D467/D468`
is one decision taken on two clouds — so it reads every number a heading names, which
is why D468 looked dangling and was not. And it caught its own entry: writing "D499"
into the test failed the build until this heading existed, which is the same
self-application D465's anchor gate performed on MATURITY.

## D500 — the record was the last thing citing decisions it did not have

D465 made MATURITY's citations resolve. D499 did the same for the Go source, and found
eleven comments pointing at two entries lost in cross-branch conflicts. This closes the
set: **DESIGN.md's own internal cross-references**, which nothing had ever checked.

Three of them pointed at D125. The prose is gone, the same way D358's and D411's went,
and the surviving text is unusually clear about what it was: D104 says in as many words
that "D124 encryption-key and D125 workload-identity are the concurrent IAM-adjacent
domains", and two later lines refer to "the IAM story D125 opened". So the number means
`capability.identity.workloadIdentity`, a domain that shipped — the GKE and AKS drivers,
their federated-credential ownership rule, the vocabulary — while the entry describing
the decision did not survive. A stub records that, as for the other two.

Three lost entries, all with live citations, all found in one afternoon by counting.
None of them was noticed when it happened, because an append-only file that loses a
paragraph looks exactly like an append-only file that never had it. The three gates now
covering the three citers — the published docs, the source, and the record itself —
would each have caught their loss on the next `make check`.

What remains honestly unresolved: two more numbers (two-twelve and three-seventy-five)
are absent from the sequence and cited by nothing, anywhere. They may be lost entries
whose citations went with them, or numbers skipped in a collision. There is no evidence
either way, so nothing is written for them — a stub asserting a subject I cannot read
out of any surviving reference would be the invention these three notes exist to avoid.

They are spelled out in words rather than written as citations, deliberately: the gate
this entry introduces cannot tell a reference from a mention, and making it try would
be worse than the small awkwardness of the workaround. A gate that needs to understand
prose is a gate that will be wrong about prose.

## D501 — I wrote a gate that could not fail, and deleted it

Measuring the CLI turned up a plausible gap: `TestEveryGuardedVerbIsDocumented` covers
two verb families — time-sensitive and provider — while the tool advertises fifty. So a
verb outside both could be listed and have nothing behind `--help`. I wrote the gate.

It passed. Then the teeth-check passed too, which is the only reason this entry exists.

`advertisedVerbs` parses the `  groundhold <verb>` lines out of the usage string.
`verbHelp(v)` finds a verb's block by locating the same `  groundhold <verb>` line in
the same string. **A verb is advertised precisely when it has a block, because both
facts are the same line.** The test could not fail, and I only learned that by planting
a verb and watching nothing happen.

So it is deleted rather than kept as reassurance. A test that cannot fail is not weak
coverage, it is a false statement about what is checked — the thing this whole session
has been removing from other people's code, and I would have shipped one.

I looked for the nearby property worth gating and did not find one. "Every block must
carry a description" fails on six verbs whose invocation line IS the description
(`groundhold validate <contract.yaml>` says everything there is to say), so the rule
would manufacture noise to satisfy itself. Some properties are held by care and adding
a gate that pretends otherwise makes the suite less honest, not more.

The measurement that prompted it is worth keeping as a fact: of fifty CLI verbs, the
conformance runner invokes twenty-eight. The rest are pinned by package tests or by
Go-only cases, and no verb is unroutable — checked by running all fifty against the
built binary.

## D502 — the parity matrix said "nobody built this" about three things we ship

`spec/parity.yaml` is generated, crosses the export boundary, and is proven
byte-for-byte against the drivers so it "can never drift or over-claim". It cannot
over-claim. It had been UNDER-claiming for as long as the Kubernetes driver has
existed.

Its own header defines the cells: `fulfilled` is a fact about the cloud,
`gap` is a fact about the cloud, and `unbuilt: true` is **a fact about groundhold** —
"no token, no declared gap; a driver could be written". Three capability types carried
`unbuilt` on all three clouds while shipping in `internal/k8s`:
`capability.cluster.namespace`, `capability.compute.quota` and
`capability.gitops.application`. Four more — authorization grant and role, TLS
certificate, private network — are fulfilled on the clouds AND on Kubernetes, and the
matrix showed only half of that.

A reader asking "can groundhold express a namespace with a pod-security standard?" was
told nobody had built it. The generator had simply never been told the driver exists.

The matrix stays cross-CLOUD — Kubernetes is a substrate that runs on them, not a
fourth cloud, and turning three columns into four would change what the artifact
means. Instead each row can now carry `fulfilledOutsideTheClouds`, read from the k8s
driver's own mappings (the same authority its dispatch uses, never a second list). The
cloud cells are unchanged and still honest; what changes is that `unbuilt` no longer
implies "unbuilt anywhere".

Worth noting how it was found: not by reading the matrix, but by asking whether the
k8s driver appears in the artifacts that describe the project — the same question D463
asked about the registers, which is where the driver's absence first turned up.

## D503 — the README omitted a driver, a cloud and an incident

Having found the parity matrix under-claiming Kubernetes (D502), the obvious next
question was which other project-describing artefacts do not know the driver exists.
**The README and every website page: neither mentions Kubernetes at all.** Ten mapped
services, a full Create/Update/Delete/Claim/Probe implementation, a takeover-class
defect found and fixed in it today, and the two documents a newcomer reads never say
it is there. Its credential story — a kubeconfig context with STATIC auth only, `exec`
plugins refused loudly so authentication cannot depend on ambient tooling — is the same
narrow-adapter stance the README makes a point of for the clouds, and it went unstated.

Then the maturity sentence beside it, which had drifted in both directions at once:

  "execution has closed the loop against two real clouds ... while Azure is
   golden-tested only ... no production record"

Azure closed the loop on 2026-07-24 (D294), so that under-claims. And there IS a
production record — one incident, on 2026-07-26, which MATURITY describes in detail and
the README's summary quietly did not mention. Both corrected, with the incident stated
as MATURITY states it: groundhold did not cause the bad deploy, it removed the signal
that would have surfaced one.

The pattern across D502 and this entry is worth naming, because it is the opposite of
what an honesty discipline usually guards against. Everything here UNDER-states: a
generated matrix said nobody built three capabilities that ship, a summary said one
fewer cloud than has run, a provider table omitted a provider. The one thing that
over-stated by omission was the incident, and it over-stated in the direction of making
the project look cleaner. **A document drifts toward whatever nobody is checking, and
which direction that is depends only on which sentence went stale.**

## D504 — the authoring guide described one of the two ways to author

`spec/providers/AUTHORING.md` is published, and it is what someone reads before adding
a service. It describes a hand-written driver: pure core, network shell, a `case` per
attribute, five disciplines, a certification battery. That is how every cloud driver is
built.

It is not how the Kubernetes driver is built, and the guide never says so. A reader
adding a Kubernetes-governed resource would follow it and write Go, when the actual
path is a YAML mapping and — if the semantics need judgement — a named lens. The engine
does the observe/create/update/delete for all ten services; there are no hand-coded
twins by design.

Third artefact in a row that did not know the driver exists: the parity matrix said
nobody had built three capabilities that ship (D502), the README and the website never
mention it (D503), and the guide to writing drivers omits the mode it is written in.
None of these is a bug in the driver. They are the cost of a second mechanism arriving
after the documents that describe the first, and nothing asking whether the documents
noticed.

The new section is deliberately short and points at the authorities rather than
restating them — the mapping fields, the `mappedSurface` fingerprint (the k8s analogue
of the endpoint-reality gate, a refusal when a mapped field changes type or vanishes
upstream), the lens registry that exists because invariant 4 forbids an expression
language in a mapping exactly as it forbids one in a contract, and `writeSafe`, which
makes a half-built service observe-only instead of half-writing.

The guide's opening claim was stale too: "extracted from three built to it" is still
true of the pattern's origin, but the repository now holds about a hundred and
forty-five drivers, and a reader deserves to know the pattern has been exercised rather
than sketched.

## D505 — the help under-advertised five verbs, and observe could not reach a driver

Asking which artefacts know the Kubernetes driver exists (D502-D504) reached the CLI's
own help, and found something worse than a documentation gap.

**Six verbs under-advertised their providers.** `adopt`, `resume` and `probe` said
`--provider fake|gcp` while accepting five — so an operator reading the help concluded
that adopting an AWS resource was unsupported, on the one verb the external pilot
demonstrably ran against AWS. `apply` omitted azure, `converge` omitted azure and k8s.
Every one of those is a promise made smaller than the code.

**And `observe` genuinely could not reach the k8s driver.** Its provider switch had
cases for fake, gcp, aws and azure, and none for k8s — while apply, converge, adopt,
resume and probe all resolved it. A capability could be created on a cluster, updated,
claimed, probed and retired, and never read back. That is precisely the gap
`TestObserveCompleteness` forbids INSIDE a driver — "a capability the runtime builds and
can never read back is never verified against reality" — sitting at the CLI seam between
drivers, where no completeness gate was looking. Wired, and verified reaching the
kubeconfig resolver.

The gate checks the union in both directions: every provider a switch resolves must be
advertised somewhere, and every provider the help names must be resolvable. It does NOT
check that each verb advertises its own resolver's set — mapping a switch back to the
verb that owns it is guesswork in a four-thousand-line dispatch, and a gate built on a
guess is the tautology D501 deleted. The limit is stated rather than hidden.

Two small self-inflicted lessons. The gate's first parser used `[a-z|]` for a provider
name and so could not see `k8s` — it reported the provider unadvertised when the text
said otherwise, which is the phantom-finding shape from D471 in a character class. And
the first teeth-check passed: removing `k8s` from ONE usage line proves nothing about a
union check. It had to be removed from all of them, which is the test the gate actually
makes.

## D506 — "managed-ok" does not mean the resource is still there, and now says so

`posture` classifies five ways, and its own header discloses a deferral: *"vanished-by-
absence drift (a bound id missing from a COMPLETE covering scope) needs
provider-specific scope coverage and is deferred to a later slice."*

Nothing in the OUTPUT said it. A resource deleted out of band, whose last verdict was
satisfied and whose evidence has not yet expired, is counted in `managedOk`. The
document already carries `shadowLowerBound` — an honest "the shadow count may be
higher when a scope was incomplete" — so the machinery for stating a bound exists and
was used for one direction and not the other.

That asymmetry matters because the consumer is not a person reading a Go file. The
console projects this document; an operator sees "12 managed-ok" and reasonably reads
twelve resources confirmed present. What it means is twelve bindings whose last fresh
observation satisfied every hard constraint — a different claim, and a weaker one.

So the summary now carries `managedOkUpperBound`, and it is unconditionally true. A
constant field looks odd, which is the point: the limitation is a property of the
current implementation, not of the run, and hiding it behind a condition that never
fires would be worse than stating it plainly. When the deferred slice lands it becomes
conditional on scope completeness, exactly as `shadowLowerBound` already is.

This is D477's shape one level in: a limitation documented where its author looks and
not where its reader does. The fix is never a better comment.

## D507 — seventeen finished migrations still reading as open, hiding the one that wasn't

D237 made a transient provider error honest: a 429, 503 or 403 on a MUTATION concludes
`unknown` WITH the providerId, never a terminal `failed`. The migration was incremental,
with `AssertTransient: true` as the per-driver readiness flag, and the harness says
un-migrated drivers are "a tracked TODO, never a silent claim of coverage".

Tracked by comment. Eighteen files carried

    // AssertTransient left false — D237 TODO: this driver's create/delete ladder
    // still maps 429/503/403 to terminal failed ...

directly above `AssertTransient: true`. The migrations had happened; the comments had
not been removed. Counting the flag instead of reading the comments gives the real
state: **102 certification probes, 101 asserting the invariant, one that does not** —
`gcp/gke`.

The seventeen stale notes are not merely untidy. They made the debt look eighteen times
larger than it was, which is the sort of inaccuracy that gets a list ignored, and they
buried the single genuine item among seventeen false ones. An auditor reading for D237
TODOs would have found the wrong seventeen and missed the right one.

So it is a ratchet at 1, derived from the flag, and the gate also refuses the comment
that used to track it — because the comment is what drifted, in eighteen files at once,
and a stale TODO beside a finished migration is worse than no note at all.

Same shape as D465 and the memory summaries corrected an hour ago: **the pessimistic
direction is the one nobody challenges.** Nobody files a complaint that a project's
to-do list is too long.

## D508 — the launch runbook's last two open items, measured instead of assumed

Two boxes in `docs/GO_PUBLIC_MILESTONES.md` were open, and they were open for
different reasons — one was genuinely unwritten, the other was unverifiable from
the machine that wrote the note. Both are now closed, and the second closed in a
way worth recording because it is this repository's recurring failure in
miniature.

**M2 — the docs site and the quickstart, on the tree we actually ship.** D490 had
made `mkdocs build --strict` a CI job, which answered "does the site build" for
the PRIVATE tree. The runbook's remaining line asked for the same thing against
the EXPORT, and left it undone with the honest reason "mkdocs not installed in
this env". Installing the pinned toolchain (`website/requirements.txt`, mkdocs
1.6.1 + material 9.7.7) into a venv took a minute, so the note had outlived its
reason. The strict build on the export is clean; so is the cold-reader path run
verbatim against the export — `go build`, `verify` on the pair the quickstart
prints, and `converge` twice on `examples/laptop/` — with output matching the
documented output down to the second run's `converged — the world already
matches the candidate` above `CONVERGED`.

The nuance is the part worth keeping. The exporter's sanitizers DO rewrite the
site: two files, four lines, every one of them an organisation substitution
inside an absolute `https://github.com/...` URL. `--strict` resolves internal
links and nav entries and does not fetch external ones, so the private build and
the exported build could not have disagreed **today**. That makes the private job
a valid proxy by coincidence of what the sanitizer currently happens to touch —
not by construction. A sanitizer that one day rewrites a filename, a relative
link or a nav title would break the shipped site while the green job kept
reporting on a tree nobody downloads. Same shape as D482 (a meter nobody reads),
D474 (the last step of the roadmap with no gate) and D497 (a doc gate deriving
its own file list): the gate existed, ran, passed, and was pointed at the wrong
artefact. Measured on the export now; whether to make the export job build the
site on every push is a cheap follow-up, deliberately not done blind here,
because CI is not observable from this environment and a gate whose failure has
never been seen is not yet a gate.

**M3 — the support posture.** This one was simply not written. The runbook had
named it as the load-bearing defence for a solo maintainer facing public traffic,
and the risk it names is real in both directions: unstated, "no SLA" reads as
dismissiveness the first time an issue sits for a week; stated as a bare
disclaimer, it reads as a shrug. So both surfaces say WHY. A failing conformance
case is the currency because it states the bug precisely, proves it exists and
proves it is gone — it can be fixed in the time it takes to read it, where an
unreduced report must first be reproduced and guessed at. Both are welcome and
neither is turned away; they move at very different speeds, and saying so is
fairer than letting a queue explain it silently. The same rule is stated in the
direction that costs the maintainer something too: a behaviour PR without a case
cannot be merged however plainly correct it looks, because nothing would stop the
next change from undoing it.

What this does NOT change: `docs/MATURITY.md` and its "What ready would mean"
section. Being ready to publish an experimental system honestly labelled `v0.x`
and being ready to call something GA are different claims with different
evidence, and the runbook headline now says which one it is talking about. The
remaining go-public items are the org name, a credential rotation, and the launch
decision — none of them engineering.

## D509 — the k8s driver meets a real cluster, and could not have created anything

The k8s driver had never run against a Kubernetes API server. `docs/MATURITY.md`
said so plainly ("Never run against a real cluster", verdict `partial`, basis
`config-intent`) and rated the risk as low, because every mapped service routes
through ONE schema-driven write path, so a single gate covers all ten. That
reasoning was sound and the conclusion was wrong: a single shared path means a
single shared blindness, and the first cluster the driver ever met refused **six
of its seven** wired services before touching anything. The Azure lesson (D294)
repeated exactly — the first real run finds what no fixture can, because the
fixtures were written by the same hand that wrote the assumption.

A throwaway k3d cluster (k3s v1.35.5, schemas read only) was enough to find all
of it.

### 1. An annotated `$ref` is invisible to the schema walker

`mapping.ResolveRef` dereferenced a bare `{"$ref": "..."}` and nothing else. But
a bare `$ref` cannot carry annotations — sibling keys next to `$ref` are ignored
by definition — so an OpenAPI producer that wants to describe a property has only
one way to say it:

    "metadata": {"description": "Standard object's metadata.", "default": {},
                 "allOf": [{"$ref": "#/components/schemas/...ObjectMeta"}]}

kube-openapi emits exactly that for essentially every `metadata` and `spec`
property. So every mapped path that traverses one — which is every path that is
not a top-level field — resolved to `ABSENT`, the whole mapped surface hashed to
something else entirely, and the drift guard fired `mapping-schema-drift` and
refused. Namespace, ResourceQuota, NetworkPolicy, RoleBinding, ClusterRole,
ClusterRoleBinding: all refused. Only `rbac-role` worked, and only by accident —
its mapped field `rules` is a direct array on the top-level object, so the walk
never crossed an annotated reference.

The fix unwraps a single-member `allOf` whose member is a plain reference, and
ONLY that: two members, or one carrying its own properties, is a genuine
composition this walker does not model, and reporting ABSENT there stays correct
(fail closed). Both encodings now resolve; the composite case is pinned separately
so a later "simplification" cannot flatten it.

### 2. The fingerprint was blind to union types

`TypeSig` signed a node as type + format + sorted enum. A union (`oneOf`/`anyOf`)
carries no top-level `type`, so EVERY union signed as the empty `"||"` —
indistinguishable from a typeless node, and from every other union. Kubernetes
models its most common scalars this way: `Quantity` is `oneOf[string,number]`,
`IntOrString` likewise. The drift guard's entire promise is "a mapped field
changed type/enum or vanished", and on exactly those fields it could not have
noticed anything at all.

Unions now sign by their members' own signatures, sorted so member ORDER is not
mistaken for drift. The component is appended only when a union is present, so
every union-free node signs byte-identically and the pins authored across the
mappings stay valid — which matters, because those pins are hand-authored
artefacts and invalidating all of them to fix two would have been its own kind of
damage.

### 3. The conflict refusal threw away the server's diagnosis

Server-side apply returns 409 when another field manager owns a field. The API
server says precisely who and what:

    Apply failed with 1 conflict: conflict with "kubectl-label" using v1:
    .metadata.labels.pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce

groundhold replaced all of it with a fixed string: *field ownership conflict —
another manager owns fields (release it first)*. Which manager, and which field
to release, were dropped — in the one refusal an operator cannot act on without
them. Every other branch of that helper already passed the body through
`mutDetail`; this one branch did not, and no test covered it. It is the shared
helper for all ten mapped services, so one line fixes the class. Same shape as
D309 (a Reason that leaked because nobody looked at it) and this session's
recurring rule: a refusal must say what it read.

### 4. The fixtures were the reason none of this was caught

Every hermetic drift test computed a surface against a recorded fixture, and the
fixtures were hand-simplified: bare `$ref` where a server sends `allOf`, and a
`Quantity` modelled as `{"type": "string"}` — a shape Kubernetes has never
served. They agreed with the walker's assumption, so they could not have
disagreed with it. This is D273 again, where a unit fake mirrored the driver's own
wrong assumption about a cloud API path and was blind by construction, and it is
why MATURITY gap 4 says internal gates under-sample reality.

All five core fixtures were re-recorded VERBATIM from the live server (the GVK
schema plus its transitive references, nothing hand-edited). The result is the
strongest evidence in this entry: **four of the five reproduced their committed
pin byte for byte**. The pins were right all along; the walker was blind. Only
`quota` changed, and it changed because its pin encoded the falsified `Quantity`.

### 5. The gate

`TestLiveMappedSurfacesMatchTheirPins` asks a real API server, opt-in via
`GROUNDHOLD_K8S_LIVE_KUBECONFIG` because CI has no cluster (a throwaway k3d is
enough; it reads schemas and mutates nothing). It checks every embedded mapping's
pinned surface against the live one, skips a CRD the cluster does not have
installed, and refuses to pass when no mapping answered at all.

It does NOT fail on a single ABSENT path: one lens serves both Role and
ClusterRole, and `aggregationRule` exists only on the latter, so the Role mapping
legitimately pins it absent — the first draft of this gate reported that as a
defect. What it does refuse is a surface that is ABSENT in its entirety, which
is the state a pin authored through a blind walker would be in and the one case
where matching hashes would prove nothing.

### What the cluster also proved WORKING, recorded so it is not re-litigated

The full lifecycle ran end to end: create, a converged no-op re-plan, an
out-of-band drift, the repair, and retirement with a tombstone.

- **Evidence freshness is correct, and I nearly mis-called it.** After flipping the
  namespace's enforced Pod Security Standard from `restricted` to `privileged`
  by hand, `converge` reported CONVERGED without reading the cluster — which
  looks exactly like a fail-open. It is not. D44's layered TTL gives a mutable
  security posture 900 seconds and the run was one minute old, so the evidence
  was legitimately fresh; the machine output discloses it too, since the phase
  list carries no `observe`. Re-run with an eval clock past the TTL, the design
  works in full: plan refuses `observation-required`, converge auto-observes,
  the drift is found, an update is planned. The claim needed measuring before it
  could be named, and measuring it changed the answer.
- **The consent friction holds.** Retirement produced a destructive plan and
  `--yes` did not cover it (`consent-required`); it took `--allow-data-loss`.
- **Adoption of an existing object.** A create that meets our own labelled
  namespace converges rather than duplicating.

### Left open, deliberately

Once another manager owns a field, groundhold cannot correct drift on it at all —
there is no consented path to reclaim ownership, the way `--allow-data-loss`
consents to destruction. `kubectl label` is the single most common way a cluster
drifts, so "converge cannot converge after a human touched it" is a real
operational limit, not an edge case. The fix is a scoped consent flag plus a
force-apply on the fields the mapping DECLARES (never a blanket force), but it
changes what `converge` does, so it starts as an open question in the instructions file and
a conformance case — not as a driver edit. The refusal is at least actionable
now: it names the manager and the field.

`certmanager-certificate` remains pinned against a hand-written fixture; a bare
cluster has no cert-manager CRDs, so the live gate skips it and says so.

## D510 — a declared value that does not round-trip converges never, and updates forever

Continuing D509's real-cluster run, the other five wired governance services went
through the loop together: ResourceQuota, Role, RoleBinding, ClusterRole,
ClusterRoleBinding and NetworkPolicy, created from one six-capability contract on
a live k3s cluster. Five converged. The ClusterRole never did — and never would
have.

The candidate declared `role.permissions: ["/nodes:get", "/nodes:list"]`. That is
the natural spelling, because RBAC's own YAML writes the core API group as the
empty string, and the driver accepted it and wrote the correct rule:
`apiGroups: [""], resources: [nodes], verbs: [get, list]`. The cluster was exactly
what the contract asked for.

Then `observe` read it back. The reverse mapping has exactly ONE spelling for the
core group — `flattenRules` renders an empty `apiGroups` entry as `core` — so the
observation said `core/nodes:get`. The reconciler compared the declared value
against the observed one, found them different, and planned an update. The update
applied cleanly, wrote the identical rule, and read back the identical `core/...`
spelling. Next run: the same update. Forever, on a cluster nobody had touched,
each pass carrying `downtime=possible`, and the capability reporting APPLIED
rather than CONVERGED every single time — so a CI gate waiting on CONVERGED would
have waited for good.

Two spellings entered, one came out. The writer accepted both `core/nodes:get`
and `/nodes:get`; the reader can only produce the first. Nothing was wrong with
either half on its own, which is why every hermetic test passed: they exercised
the writer and the reader separately, and separately both are correct.

**The gate is the property, not the instance.** Every permission the writer
accepts must come back out of the reader unchanged — `buildRoleRules` then
`flattenRules` must be the identity on the declared set. A value that fails that
cannot converge, whatever else is true of it. The instance is pinned too: the
blank group is now refused rather than written, naming the spelling that works,
exactly as this driver already refuses a grant principal missing its namespace
instead of guessing at one. Guessing is what built the loop: the writer quietly
accepted a second spelling it had no way to give back.

This is the same shape as D273 and D509 — a fake that mirrors one side's
assumption cannot referee a disagreement between two sides — but the mechanism is
narrower and worth naming on its own: **a declared value and an observed value
must share a canonical form, or the reconciler is comparing two encodings and
calling the difference drift.** Any driver that renders one spelling and accepts
several has the same latent loop. The round-trip property is the cheap general
test for it.

Recorded working on the same run: quota, role, grant, netpol and the cluster-scoped
grant all converged on the second pass and stayed converged across two further
passes. The plan refused three malformed declarations BEFORE any mutation, each
naming the exact form required (a grant principal without its namespace; a role
reference that is not `<Kind>/<name>`; a NetworkPolicy asked to permit everything,
which is the absence of a policy rather than a policy).

## D511 — the debt that was waiting for a cluster, and the mapping that could never have worked

Two mappings shipped with `mappedSurface: ""` and the note *drift-guard PENDING
CRD schema vendoring*. The debt was honestly labelled and it was stuck for a
concrete reason: a bare cluster has no cert-manager, Argo or Flux CRDs, so there
was nothing to vendor a schema FROM. Installing three CRD sets on the throwaway
cluster from D509 unstuck it in a minute.

**The gate said nothing about them, which is the worse half.** The live-surface
check skipped an unpinned mapping BEFORE computing anything, so a run over ten
mappings reported on eight and looked complete. Unpinned is not neutral — it turns
the drift guard OFF for that resource — and the quietest way to carry debt is a
gate that omits it from its own output. It now computes the live surface anyway,
says `UNPINNED — drift is unchecked`, and prints the hash an author needs to
close it. That is how both pins were authored.

The recordings are verbatim from the live server with `description` stripped —
the fingerprint excludes descriptions by construction, and the live gate proves
the hash is identical either way, so this is a size reduction that cannot change
what is pinned (Argo's Application schema is 340KB with them, 179KB without).
A hermetic test pins each fingerprint to its vendored schema, the same property
the other mappings already had.

With all ten pinned, a new mapping may no longer arrive unpinned:
`TestEveryMappingPinsItsSurface` makes the exemption a decision someone has to
argue for rather than a blank field nobody notices. The two that shipped that way
stayed unguarded for as long as nobody happened to have a cluster.

### The cert-manager mapping had never built a valid object

With the CRD installed, a Certificate could finally be attempted. The API server
answered:

    Certificate.cert-manager.io "cert-production" is invalid:
    spec.secretName: Required value

cert-manager requires `spec.secretName` as hard as it requires the issuer — it is
where the issued key pair lands. The builder's own comment says *the issuer and
target secret are operands*, and it refused when the issuer was missing while
silently omitting the secret. So every Certificate this mapping ever built was
invalid, on every cluster, and the golden tests all passed because they compared
the built object against an expectation written by the same hand that omitted the
field. It is D509's shape once more: a fixture cannot referee an assumption it
shares.

Refused now, exactly as the issuer is, rather than derived. A generated secret
name would be a value other workloads must mount, so inventing one would be
guessing at somebody else's contract — and guessing is what D510 has just
finished paying for. With the operand supplied, the Certificate creates and
converges on the real cluster.

Recorded honestly: no controller is running on that cluster, so the Certificate
is not READY and never will be. groundhold does not claim otherwise — readiness
is not a mapped attribute of `capability.certificate.tls`, the contract asked
about `auto.renew`, and that is what converged. A capability whose contract said
something about issuance would have to observe issuance, and this one does not
pretend to.

## D512 — the read verbs and the probe meet the cluster; four clean negatives

D509–D511 were all defects. This entry is mostly the other kind of result, and it
is worth the same space: the verbs that read rather than write were run against
the live cluster and behaved. Recording that costs a paragraph and saves
rediscovering it.

**`discover` over a real cluster.** 166 resources across six capability types —
everything provisioned in D509/D510 plus the cluster's own 158 RBAC objects. The
diagnostics are the part that matters, because they are where a discoverer would
lie if it were going to: *access.privileged is UNVERIFIABLE for Role/... (outside
the curated well-known set) — groundhold will not guess a custom role's
privilege*; *RoleBinding binds 2 subjects; the grant model is one principal per
binding — grant.principal left unobserved*; *nonResourceURLs are not part of the
flat permission set — not represented*. Every one of those is a place the model is
narrower than Kubernetes, said out loud on real data rather than smoothed over.

**Brownfield takeover, end to end.** A Role created by hand with `kubectl` (the
realistic brownfield object), then `adopt --map`, then `converge`. The first
converge applied exactly one thing — the ownership labels — and the SECOND
reported *the world already matches the candidate*. That no-op is the D52 proof of
takeover, and it had never run on a cluster.

**The reachability probe, measured for real, both branches.** With no
`groundhold.dev/probe-target` annotation it refuses to conclude anything: *the CNI
enforcement of this policy is unproven*. Pointed at a genuinely open port it
records a measurement whose evidence is careful about what a handshake proves —
*a path exists (the policy is not enforced, or an allow-path admits it)* — and
pointed at a closed one it records NO measurement and a retryable failure saying
*filtered, dropped by the policy, or down are indistinguishable; absence of a path
cannot be proven by one dial*. The recorded observation carries `source: "probe"`,
`actor: groundhold-probe`, `method: tcp-connect` and the evidence sentence naming
the exact target, so it is distinguishable in the ledger from an API read, which
is what the per-source retention rules require.

**What I could NOT prove, said plainly.** I set out to demonstrate CNI enforcement
— deny-all policy on, workload behind a NodePort, dial from outside — and could
not, because this k3s node does not expose the NodePort to the host and traffic
originating on the node is admitted regardless. That is a limit of the vantage,
not of the policy, and it is precisely the conclusion the probe's design already
refuses to draw: the strongest true statement a single dial supports is that a
path EXISTS, and the target is an operator declaration ("a host:port a
default-deny policy should make unreachable"), not something groundhold verifies
belongs to the policy. So gap 8 moves only halfway: the reachability machinery has
now measured real network I/O on a real object with correct provenance; a real
recovery event still has not happened, and enforcement remains unproven from
outside the cluster.

**One incidental proof worth keeping.** The ResourceQuota provisioned in D510 was
not decorative: an nginx Deployment with no resource limits was refused by the API
server — *forbidden: failed quota: quota-production: must specify limits.cpu* —
until limits were declared. A governance object groundhold created, enforcing
against a workload it knew nothing about.

## D513 — delete a managed resource by hand and converge reports CONVERGED

The worst finding of the k8s series, found by accident while trying to test
something else, and it is not a k8s bug — k8s is where it became visible.

Five governance objects that groundhold had created and held bindings for were
deleted with `kubectl`. Then `converge`, with an eval clock far enough forward
that the recorded evidence had expired, so the staleness gate fired and a FRESH
observation was taken — the run log shows it: *observe (stale knowledge —
refreshing, read-only)*. The verdict:

    ✓ converged — the world already matches the candidate
    CONVERGED

The world contained none of them. This is the exact inverse of the thesis: a
system that must never claim to have checked something it hasn't, reporting a
world it had just been told was empty.

### The mechanism: silence read as agreement

`observe` on a bound resource the API server 404s returned this, and only this:

    return nil, []string{Kind + " not found — nothing to observe"}, nil

No observation. A diagnostic string, which nothing downstream reads as a fact. The
compiler saw an empty observation set for those capabilities, had nothing to
compare against the candidate, and produced no actions — and no actions is what
converge reports as converged.

The contract for this case already existed, written down in `provider.go`:

> **ResourceAbsentPath** (F-LC3) is the reserved observation path a driver emits
> when a BOUND resource is authoritatively GONE — a READABLE absence (a 404),
> never a read error. Value true means the resource no longer exists; the compiler
> turns a fresh true into a CREATE (re-create after an out-of-band delete). A
> driver that can read presence emits false when the resource is found, so the
> marker toggles both ways and a recreate self-heals.

The compiler implements its half. **Exactly one service in the entire system
emitted the marker**: AWS Lambda, whose own comment names the failure mode it was
avoiding — *"rather than a bare diagnostic that leaves the binding a no-op
forever"*. Every other service across all four drivers left the binding a no-op
forever, which is precisely the phrase, and nobody generalised it.

So this is this session's recurring class at its largest: a real convention,
published in the provider contract, implemented once, asserted nowhere — and this
time it defeats the product's central promise on the most ordinary kind of drift
there is. Someone deletes a thing by hand. That is not an exotic failure.

### Fixed for k8s, which is ten services through one path

The schema-driven design pays here: every mapped service reads through
`observeMapped`, so one change covers all ten. A 404 now emits
`resource.absent: true`, and a successful read emits `false`, because a marker
that only latches one way would leave a stale "gone" after a re-create and plan a
second create forever — D510's loop in a different costume.

Verified on the live cluster: with the five objects deleted, converge now
observes their absence, plans creates, applies, and a second pass is a clean
no-op. Before the fix the same sequence reported CONVERGED with nothing there.

**One existing test had to be corrected, and it is worth naming.**
`TestObserveRoleNotFound` demanded *"want no observations + a diagnostic"* — the
defect, written down and guarded. A test can pin the wrong behaviour as firmly as
the right one, and this one had been protecting the silence for as long as it
existed.

### The debt this leaves, stated with a number

k8s is closed. **AWS, GCP and Azure are not**: of roughly 145 certified services
across them, one (Lambda) emits the marker. Every other bound resource in those
drivers, if deleted out of band, still produces silence and still converges.

It is not fixed here because doing it honestly means asking each driver rather
than scraping its source (D317: a static scrape gave four different wrong answers
about the drivers), and the certification harness takes a hand-written probe per
service — 145 of them. That is the next slice, and it should arrive as a register
in the D463/D472 idiom: every certified service either drives the absence property
or carries a re-derived exemption, on a ratchet that may only go down. Writing a
145-entry register at the end of a long session is how a bad register gets built,
so the number is published here instead of being quietly rounded off.

## D514 — the compile cannot tell "present" from "never asked", so it says so

D513 fixed the k8s half of the absence marker and published the debt: of roughly
145 certified services across AWS, GCP and Azure, one emits it. The register that
closes that debt is a large build and it is still owed. This entry closes the part
that is one line of reasoning rather than 145 probes.

The compile reads `in.Observations[capID][resource.absent]` and acts on a fresh
`true`. When the key is MISSING it does nothing — and a missing key has two
completely different meanings:

- the driver looked, and the resource is there;
- the driver does not answer this question at all.

Both produce no action, and no action is what converge renders as converged. The
compile had no way to distinguish them and did not admit that it couldn't. That is
the same failure in miniature as D513 itself: silence standing in for a fact.

So the compile now SAYS it. A bound capability whose observation set carries no
absence marker gets an `existence-not-witnessed` advisory: *the driver observed
this capability but never reported whether the bound resource still EXISTS, so a
delete made outside groundhold would read here as no change at all* — with the
plain consequence spelled out, that a converged verdict for that capability covers
its attributes and not its existence.

Advisory, not block, deliberately. Turning it into a refusal today would freeze
every capability on three drivers, and the resources are overwhelmingly there —
that would be a bigger lie than the one being fixed. This follows D75's
skip-loudly precedent exactly: a check that cannot be performed is reported, never
silently passed. The advisory channel (D388) is already the designed home for
"things the compile NOTICED", carried in the plan so an agent reads them.

It stays quiet where it would be noise: an unbound capability has no existence
question yet, and one with no observations at all belongs to the
observation-required gate. Firing on those would bury the signal on every fresh
compile.

Verified against the live cluster: k8s answers the question after D513, so a real
plan over six bound k8s capabilities produces no advisories at all. The advisory
appears exactly where a driver is silent — which today means AWS, GCP and Azure,
and which is the debt it now measures instead of hiding.

## D515 — master's record described a channel master did not have

Landing D514 failed to apply, and the reason was worth more than the fix.

`docs/DESIGN.md` on `master` carries D388, and D388 states plainly: *"The advisory
rides in the plan as `advisories[]` with a stable code, and on stderr as prose."*
`master`'s compiler contained no advisory code at all — no `Advisory` type, no
`Advisories` field on the plan, nothing producing one. The implementation lived on
an unmerged branch. So the record described a channel the code did not have, in a
repository whose first rule is that DESIGN.md is the record.

**One correction to how this was first described.** `spec/outputs.schema.json`
does declare `advisories`, and that was initially read as the schema promising the
same missing thing. It is not: that field belongs to `verifyReport` and to D365's
verify-side advisories, which `master` implements. There are two advisory channels
and only the plan-side one was missing. The narrower statement is the true one —
the discrepancy was between DESIGN.md and the compiler, and nowhere else.

The plan-side channel is brought to `master` here, together with D514 which needs
it: the `Advisory` type, the unattached-log-group advisory D388 describes, its
tests, and the field on the plan. Every gate passes on `master` with them.
