Why this happened is mechanical and will happen again. Work moves between branches
here by cherry-pick, one commit at a time, and a decision entry and the code that
implements it are frequently different commits. Pick one and not the other and the
record runs ahead of the tree — silently, because nothing compares them. This
session has already paid for the same shape twice at a smaller scale: D498 (a
cherry-pick dropped a DESIGN entry, caught only by counting headings afterwards)
and D499/D500 (source comments citing decisions that did not exist, and decisions
citing nothing).

Those two gates run in the direction that was cheap to check: from a citation to
an entry. The direction that would have caught THIS — from an entry's claim to the
code that must exist for it — is not mechanically checkable in general, because an
entry is prose. What is checkable is narrower and worth having: a decision that
names a Go identifier should find it. That is left as the next slice rather than
half-built here, and named so it is not forgotten.

## D516 — the published output contract, checked against the code that must fill it

D515 named the next slice: a decision that names a Go identifier should find it.
That gate cannot be built honestly, and finding out why is worth more than the
gate would have been. `docs/DESIGN.md` is APPEND-ONLY HISTORY. An entry written at
D100 that names a function deleted at D300 is correct history, not a broken
citation, and a check demanding every named identifier still exist would fail on
hundreds of entries that are telling the truth about their own moment. The
direction is not checkable because the artefact is prose with a timestamp.

The same class IS checkable one artefact over. `spec/outputs.schema.json` is the
other published contract, it names fields rather than describing them, and it is
not history — it describes the CURRENT output. A field it promises that no code
emits is D515's failure with none of the prose: a consumer routes on the name and
gets nothing, and nothing said so.

So every property name in every `$defs` shape must appear as a json tag in the Go
tree, or hold an exemption that re-derives its own evidence. Today there is one
exemption: `explain` (D64) is written into the result map at emission across every
verb, so it belongs to no struct — and the exemption stores the literal assignment
that must still be found in the source, so it cannot outlive its reason.

**The gate found nothing, and its first draft would have found nothing either — for
the wrong reason.** Three things had to be fixed before it measured anything:

1. A first pass flagged `explain` on seven result shapes as missing. It is not
   missing; it is assigned dynamically. A measurement that finds occurrences is
   not automatically a finding — the same correction D473 already cost once.
2. The exemption's evidence was re-derived by scanning the Go tree for its
   literal — and the literal is stored in the test file, which the scan was
   reading. It found its own declaration and passed unconditionally. That is the
   harness reporting success without exercising the thing it measures, and this
   session has now caught it four times.
3. The tag scan included `_test.go` files, so a json tag in a test could have
   satisfied a field the schema publishes to real consumers.

Both directions were driven red before the gate was kept: an invented schema
property fails, and a renamed exemption literal fails. It carries floors on the
property count and the tag count, because a walk that reaches nothing passes
everything (D328).

## D517 — the absence property, asked as a class and paid down on a ratchet

D513 measured the largest known gap in this system and could not close it: of the
services certified across the drivers, ONE emitted `resource.absent`, so every
other bound resource deleted out of band produced silence, and silence is what
`converge` renders as converged. k8s was fixed there because ten services share one
read path. AWS, GCP and Azure have no such choke point — the fix is per service,
and the honest question was how to gate ~145 of them without either writing 145
new probes or writing a declaration nobody drives.

The answer was already in the tree. The honesty harness carries **102 probes**,
each with a driver constructor and ops that encode a working providerId. Asking the
absence question needs nothing new from them: point the SAME driver at a server on
which nothing exists, and require the reserved marker. Every fixture is reused.

`Probe.ObserveAbsent` is the readiness signal, and the shape is deliberately
D237's — a property migrated service by service rather than claimed at once — with
one change learned from how D237 went. That migration used a boolean,
`AssertTransient: true`, and eighteen files ended up carrying a stale TODO above an
already-migrated flag: the debt read as eighteen when it was one, and the single
genuinely open driver was invisible among the seventeen finished ones (D507). So
the signal here is the CLOSURE. A probe asserts the property by handing the harness
something it can actually run; nil means un-migrated and the ratchet counts it.
There is no way to write a flag claiming coverage the harness cannot exercise,
which is the class of lie D507 had to clean up.

`azure/vnet` is the first service migrated — the same three lines k8s needed, in a
driver whose observes all share the shape (`if !found { return nil, diag, nil }`),
which is why the remaining sweep is mechanical rather than investigative. The
marker toggles both ways: a present resource clears it, or a stale "gone" would
survive a re-create and plan a second one forever (D510's loop in another costume).

The ratchet starts at **101 un-migrated** and may only fall. It carries a floor on
the probe count, because a scan that reaches nothing passes everything (D328), and
it fails in BOTH directions — a debt that grew, and a debt that shrank without the
constant being lowered, so the number cannot quietly drift away from the truth. All
three failures were driven red before the gate was kept, including the property
itself: reverting the vnet emit turns the harness red with the sentence that
matters — *the binding stays a no-op forever and converge reports the world as
matching while the resource is gone*.

## D518 — Azure pays the absence debt, and the second driver finds what the first one broke

The first batch of D517's migration: **27 of Azure's 31 certified probes** now
assert the absence property, and the ratchet falls from 101 to 75.

The work itself is mechanical, as predicted — every Azure observe carried the same
silent shape (`if !found` or `if st == http.StatusNotFound`, then a diagnostic
string and no observation), so a script rewrote 37 of them into the marker and
another pass wired the probes. That is the whole point of asking a property as a
class: once the shape is known, the sweep is typing.

**What was NOT mechanical is the part worth recording.**

### Migrating the second driver found a defect the first one had introduced

Azure's discovery gate refused immediately: *D53: unexpected key-vault observation
path "resource.absent" — discovery must be metadata only*. The reverse-mapping code
is shared between `observe` (which reads ONE bound resource) and `discover` (which
enumerates what exists), so putting the marker in the shared reader pushed it into
discovery records, where it is meaningless — everything discovery returns is
present by construction.

D513 had already done exactly this to k8s. k8s discovery calls `observeMapped`, so
the marker had been riding into k8s discovery records since that commit, and
**k8s has no equivalent gate, which is the only reason nobody noticed**. Measured
against the live cluster: 3 of 168 discovered records carried it. The fix is a
shared `provider.WithoutAbsence` applied at the discovery boundary in both drivers,
because the boundary is the thing that differs, not the reader.

The general shape is worth naming: a gate that exists on one driver and not
another does not merely leave that driver unguarded — it makes the FIRST driver's
mistakes invisible until someone touches the second.

### Three tests asserted the silence

`TestObserveAKSWorkloadIdentityNotFound`, `TestObserveAzureImageMissingIsNotAnError`
and `TestAzureOpenAIObserveNotFound` all demanded that an absent bound resource
observe NOTHING. Corrected, with the reason in each: that expectation is the defect
F-LC3 exists to prevent. This is the third time in this series a test was found
guarding the wrong behaviour (k8s's `TestObserveRoleNotFound` was the first). A
test pins whatever it was written against, and "no observations" reads as a
perfectly reasonable thing to assert until you know what silence costs.

### The closure could not lie, twice

Seven probes went red the moment they were wired, because their observes had a
different shape and the script had skipped them. A boolean flag would have said
`true` and passed. Five were then migrated by a second pass; the last two —
`backupvault` and `servicebusqueue`, whose reads genuinely differ — had their
closures REMOVED rather than left asserting a property the driver does not have.
They are counted in the 75.

And the second pass had a bug of its own: `\treturn` is a substring of
`\t\treturn`, so the "present" marker was inserted into the ABSENT branch, and
five services reported `resource.absent = false` for a resource that does not
exist. The harness caught it in the same run. A migration script is code, and a
mechanical sweep is exactly where a silent wrong-but-plausible edit hides.

Remaining: AWS and GCP, 75 probes, same shape.

## D519 — GCP pays the absence debt, and a second failure mode surfaces

The second batch: **25 of GCP's 31 probes** assert the absence property, and the
ratchet falls from 75 to 50. AWS is what remains.

Most of it repeated D518 — the same silent shape, the same script, the same five
tests found asserting that an absent bound resource observes NOTHING (corrected,
with the reason in each). But GCP surfaced a failure mode Azure did not have, and
it is the more interesting one.

### A readable 404 folded into the generic error

Five GCP services never distinguished 404 from any other non-200 status:

    if status != http.StatusOK {
        return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("buckets.get: HTTP %d", status)
    }

So a deleted bucket produced a READ ERROR. The contract is explicit that this is
wrong — *a READABLE absence (a 404), never a read error* — and the two behave
completely differently downstream: an error blocks the binding on `unknown`
forever, where the marker re-creates. It is the safer of the two wrong answers
(it refuses rather than lying, unlike the silence D513 found) but the resource can
never self-heal, and the operator is told the driver could not read when in fact
it read perfectly well and the answer was "gone".

Three were fixed by giving them the explicit branch; the rest have shapes the
sweep could not safely rewrite.

### What was left un-migrated, and why that is the honest outcome

Six GCP probes had their closures REMOVED rather than left asserting a property
their driver does not have: `cloudarmor`, `cloudfunctions`, `pubsub-queue`,
`iambinding`, `customrole`, `monitoring`. Two Azure probes went the same way in
D518. They are counted in the 50.

This is what the closure-instead-of-boolean choice buys (D517). A flag would have
been set to `true` in the same sweep that set the other twenty-five, because
nothing would have run. The closure cannot be written without the harness
executing it against a 404-everything server, so every one of these announced
itself the moment it was wired. The debt that remains is the debt that is real.

### The sweep is code, and code has bugs

D518's second pass inserted the "present" marker into the ABSENT branch because
`\treturn` is a substring of `\t\treturn`. This batch's script anchored every
pattern at line start with an exact tab count, and the same class of error did not
recur — but a first attempt still crashed on a regex group that did not exist, and
an unused-import cleanup had to run three times. A mechanical migration is exactly
where a plausible-looking wrong edit hides, which is why every batch ends with the
harness run rather than a diff read.

## D520 — AWS pays what it can, and the harness learns what a 404 is not

The last batch. **10 of AWS's 37 probes** assert the absence property; the ratchet
lands at **40 un-migrated of 102**, down from 101. Forty-one AWS observe sites got
the marker even where their probe could not be wired, because the driver fix and
the probe wiring are separate things and the first is worth having regardless.

Three findings, each worth more than the sweep that surfaced it.

### S3 described a deleted bucket as a healthy one

`observeS3` never asked whether the bucket EXISTS. It went straight to emitting
`location.region` (parsed out of the providerId string), `service.managed: true`,
`encryption.atRest: true` and `durability.class: regional` — four facts, two of
them marked `Derivation: "measured"`, none of them read from the API. So a bucket
someone had deleted observed as a healthy bucket with every declared attribute
satisfied, and converge would agree.

This is worse than the silence D513 found. Silence plans nothing; **this
fabricates a world**. It fails the project's first rule — never claim to have
checked something you have not — inside the observe path, on the most heavily used
service in the AWS driver. A `HeadBucket` now precedes everything.

Seven fixtures had to learn to answer `HEAD`, which is the smaller half of the
same story: they never modelled the call because the driver never made it.

### A non-200 with no error panicked the process

`describeAlarm` read `if err != nil || st != http.StatusOK` and handed BOTH cases
to `readTransport`, which dereferences `err.Error()`. Every HTTP error response —
`err` is nil, status is not 200 — panicked. It had never been reached because
nothing had ever pointed that driver at a failing status; the absence probe was the
first thing to try.

The harness now RECOVERS from a driver panic and reports it as a finding
(`the driver PANICKED observing a 404`), which is how `aws/waf` was found doing the
same thing. A crashed test binary reports nothing about the other hundred probes,
so a harness that dies on the first panic is a harness that hides the rest.

### What a 404 means is protocol-specific, and the harness assumed otherwise

Twenty-seven AWS probes are un-migrated and most are NOT driver defects. The
harness's "gone" server answers 404 to everything, and AWS's query and JSON
protocols do not signal absence that way — `DescribeVpcs` returns an empty result
set, `DescribeInstances` an `InvalidInstanceID.NotFound` error code with HTTP 400.
`observeAWSVPC` handles its real absence signal correctly and is still counted
un-migrated, because the probe as built cannot exercise it.

That is the honest state and it is why the closures were REMOVED rather than left
in place. A probe that asserts a property its estate cannot express is a green
test that proves nothing — the exact failure this session has caught four times at
the harness level. The next slice for those services is a per-protocol gone-server
(empty result set, error-code body), not another rewrite of the drivers.

### The count, stated plainly

102 probes: 62 assert the property, 40 do not. Of the 40, some are genuine debt
and some are harness limitations, and this entry does not pretend to know the split
for every one. What it does say is that no probe claims a property the harness did
not run — which is the whole reason D517 made the readiness signal a closure.

## D521 — "gone" is not one wire answer, and the harness had assumed it was

D520 ended with 40 un-migrated probes and an honest admission that the number was
a MIX: some real debt, some services the harness simply could not measure, and no
way to say which was which. That is the worst state a count can be in. This entry
fixes the measuring instrument, and the number drops to **23 — all of it real**.

### The estate now speaks the protocol

The gone-server answered 404 to everything. That is how a REST API says a thing is
gone; it is not how anything else does. AWS alone uses three idioms, and the
request itself identifies which:

- an `X-Amz-Target` header — the JSON protocols — say it with **HTTP 400 and a
  `__type` naming a not-found exception**;
- a form-encoded `Action=` — the query protocol — splits again, and the split is
  the interesting part: a **plural enumerator** (`Describe*`, `List*`) answers 200
  with an empty result set, because "no members" is expressible; a **singular
  getter** (`GetQueueAttributes`, `GetRole`) answers an ERROR, because there is no
  empty form of "the attributes of this one thing";
- everything else — REST paths, Google, ARM, Kubernetes — uses 404.

`GoneEstate` dispatches on the shape of the request, so no per-service fixture has
to be written or kept current. Nine probes went green immediately, having been
correct all along: `observeAWSVPC` reads an empty `vpcSet` exactly as it should
and had been counted as debt because the fixture could not say it.

**This is the class this session keeps finding, one level up.** A gate that cannot
express the condition it tests does not report "cannot measure" — it reports
FAILURE, and the failure looks identical to a real defect. D520 recorded the 40 as
a mix precisely because that ambiguity could not be resolved from inside the
harness. It could only be resolved by making the harness able to ask.

### What the sharper instrument then found

With the estate speaking the protocols, thirteen more sites migrated (their
not-found tests carried COMPOUND conditions — `st == 404 || errCode contains
"NonExistentQueue"` — which the earlier pattern had skipped), and the failures that
remained were all real:

- **Two more nil-deref panics.** `describeMSKCluster` and the WAFv2 read had the
  D520 shape exactly: `if err != nil || st != StatusOK` handing both cases to a
  function that dereferences `err.Error()`. Third and fourth instances. Every HTTP
  error response crashed the process, and nothing had ever pointed those drivers at
  a failing status.
- **Discovery started enumerating resources that were not there.** Two posture
  discoverers tested absence INDIRECTLY — `if len(obs) == 0` meant "not
  provisioned" — which was true only while an absent resource produced silence.
  The marker made silence impossible, so the indirect test stopped working and both
  began emitting records for postures that do not exist. A regression I introduced,
  caught by their own tests, fixed with an explicit `provider.IsAbsent`. An
  indirect test for a condition is a test that breaks when the condition learns to
  speak for itself.
- **Eight more tests pinning the silence**, across three drivers. The count for the
  series is now sixteen.

### The 23 that remain are one class

Every one folds a real not-found signal into a read ERROR — `GetRole: HTTP 400
(NotFound)`, `functions.get: HTTP 404`, `backupVaults GET: HTTP 404`. The driver
READ the answer and then reported that it could not read. That blocks the binding
on `unknown` rather than fabricating (the safer of the two wrong answers, D519) but
the resource can never self-heal, and the operator is told a lie about what
happened.

They are named, counted, and on a ratchet that may only fall. The work is a
per-service read-path edit rather than anything structural, and nothing about the
count is ambiguous any more: 79 of 102 assert the property, 23 owe it, and no probe
claims a property the harness did not run.

## D522 — the sharper instrument corrects the previous entry's verdict

D521 ended by saying the remaining 23 were "one class — all of it real". That was
wrong, and finding out why is the substance of this entry. **Eleven of the 23 were
correct drivers the harness still could not hear.** The count is now 12, and the
claim about what they are is narrower and better supported.

### A service's not-found CODE is not a protocol fact

`GoneEstate` had learned each protocol's way of signalling absence (D521) and then
put a generic `NotFound` in the body. A correct driver does not match on that: it
matches on ITS OWN service's code — IAM answers `NoSuchEntity`, EFS
`FileSystemNotFound`, SQS `NonExistentQueue`, ElastiCache
`ReplicationGroupNotFoundFault`. Every one of those drivers was reading exactly
what its API sends, and failed a gate that sent something else.

`Probe.GoneCode` supplies it, a per-probe fact of the same kind as
`OwnerTagValue`. The codes were harvested FROM THE DRIVERS' OWN SOURCE rather than
written from memory (D317: ask the code, do not recall it).

Two further corrections followed from the same root:

- **Per-protocol defaults had to stay.** Collapsing the default to `NotFound` broke
  DynamoDB, Kinesis, ACM, Secrets Manager and Redshift Serverless, which had been
  passing on the JSON protocol's conventional `ResourceNotFoundException`. A
  default is a claim about a convention, and flattening two conventions into one
  broke five correct drivers.
- **The error BODY's shape differs too**, not just the code: EFS reads `ErrorCode`,
  Google and ARM read `error.code`, some AWS REST APIs read `__type`. The REST-ish
  branch now answers in every dialect at once. That is frankly a fixture speaking
  in a way no single server does, and it is the right trade: the alternative is a
  per-service body fixture, which is precisely what this estate exists to avoid.
- The query envelope is now named for the action (`<${Action}Response/>`), because
  a reader may unmarshal into a struct whose root element is exactly that.

### What the corrected instrument then found

With the harness able to hear them, the drivers that still failed were real, and
one of them is the inverse of everything this series has been about:

**`observeCustomPolicy` turned EVERY error into silence** — `return nil,
[]string{"nothing to observe: " + err}, nil`. A transport failure, a 500, an
expired credential: all of them read as an empty world, and converge agrees with
an empty world. D513 found silence standing in for absence; this is silence
standing in for *failure to read*, which is worse, because the read never
happened at all. Now: the authoritative `NoSuchEntity` becomes the marker, and
every other error is returned as an error, which blocks.

Four more were migrated where the absence is structural rather than a status code:
an IAM policy no longer ATTACHED to its role, and a GCP member no longer in the
project's IAM policy, are bound grants that no longer exist — the attachment IS the
resource. Azure's backup vault and GCP's Cloud Functions and project-policy reads
folded a readable 404 into a read error, and now carry sentinels.

### The twelve that remain, honestly split

- **Three AWS list-based reads** (`DescribeReplicationGroups`, `ListClustersV2`,
  `ListWebACLs`) where absence is an EMPTY COLLECTION whose field name is
  service-specific. The estate cannot synthesise that without per-service
  knowledge, and these drivers may well be correct. **Unmeasured, not indicted.**
- **`azure/servicebusqueue`** and eight probes whose `Observe` call could not be
  derived from the probe body at all — genuinely un-migrated, needing hand-wiring.

That split is the point. D521 published a number with a confident label on it and
the label was wrong for eleven of the twenty-three. The number now carries what is
actually known about each part, including "we cannot measure this yet", which is
the verdict this project exists to make sayable.

## D523 — the absence debt closes at zero, and the last of it was the instrument again

**102 of 102 honesty probes now assert F-LC3.** The ratchet that started at 101 in
D517 is at 0. The debt D513 opened — a bound resource deleted out of band produced
silence, and converge reported CONVERGED against a world that no longer contained
it — is paid across every certified service on all four drivers.

The last twelve split the way D522 predicted, and the split held up:

**Three were the instrument, again, and the third time was the same lesson.** MSK's
`ListClustersV2` and WAF's `ListWebACLs` are COLLECTION reads: absence is an empty
list, and both drivers handled it correctly, looping over the returned members and
concluding not-found. They failed a gate that answered 404 to a call whose API
never 404s. `Probe.GoneEmptyList` declares the shape and the estate answers 200
with an empty document, which unmarshals to an empty slice under any field name.
Both passed immediately, having been right all along.

That is the fourth distinct thing the estate had to learn — the protocol (D521),
the service's own error code (D522), the error body's shape (D522), and now
whether the read is a collection at all. Each one was discovered the same way: a
correct driver failing, and the failure looking exactly like a defect. **The
instrument was wrong more often than the drivers were**, which is worth saying
plainly given the series began by publishing a count of "real debt" that was, at
that point, mostly not.

**One WAS a real defect, and a familiar one.** ElastiCache read
`if xml.Unmarshal(resp, &r) != nil || len(r.Groups) == 0 { return readBody(...) }`
— an empty result set and a parse failure, called the same thing. An empty result
IS the API saying the group does not exist; reporting it as unparseable blocked the
binding on unknown instead of re-creating. Same conflation as D522's
`observeCustomPolicy`, in the other direction: there every error became silence,
here an authoritative absence became an error.

**Cloud SQL and Service Bus** folded a readable 404 into a read error and now carry
the marker; the rest were hand-wired, mostly because their probes build a
providerId in a way no sweep could derive. `azure/azureopenai` was last because it
declares `New: newDriver` as a VALUE rather than a function literal, so the
pattern the sweep anchored on did not exist.

**The gate keeps its teeth at zero.** A ratchet whose baseline is 0 is exactly the
kind of gate that can quietly stop measuring (D328), so it was driven red before
being kept: removing one probe's closure fails with *the absence debt GREW: 1
services do not assert F-LC3, baseline is 0*. It still fails in both directions,
and it still floors on the probe count.

What this does NOT claim: that every driver handles every absence correctly in
production. It claims that every certified service was asked, in an estate that
speaks its protocol, its error code, its body shape and its read style — and
answered. The k8s driver's answer was measured against a live cluster (D513); the
rest are hermetic.

## D524 — the same blindness in two more harnesses, one of which passed a driver that did nothing

The F-LC3 series ended on a line worth acting on rather than admiring: **the
instrument was wrong more often than the drivers were**. So the other certification
harnesses were asked the same question — can their estate express the condition
they claim to test? Two could not, and the second failure is the dangerous
direction.

### The foreign-refusal harness: a refusal for the wrong reason

`certifyForeign` requires the driver to REFUSE, to mutate nothing, to state a
reason, and — since D455 — to have READ the estate, because twice on AWS a probe
had passed while the driver refused at providerId parsing, having never looked.

What nothing checked is whether the read FOUND anything. A fixture that 404s every
read still satisfies "the driver looked": it looks, sees nothing, and refuses
because the resource is absent. That is a different code path proving a different
property, while the gate reports the ownership check as verified.

`countRT` now records whether any READ returned a 2xx, and the harness fails when
none did. Every existing fixture passed — a clean negative — and the check was
driven red with an emptied estate to prove it can fail at all.

### The adopt harness: a green test that adopted nothing

`CertifyCreateAdoptsExisting` asserts that a create meeting its own resource
already standing BINDS it instead of making a second. Point a probe at an estate
where the resource does not exist and the driver simply creates one: status
`succeeded`, a providerId returned, mutations within the allowance because a
create is allowed to mutate. **Every assertion passes and nothing was adopted.**

Thirteen probes were in exactly that state. `azDashServer` is the shape: it starts
with `stored == nil`, so the first GET 404s, and a test named
`TestAdoptsExistingPortalDash` exercised the create path from beginning to end.

This is the more dangerous direction of the same defect. D521–D523 kept finding
correct drivers failing a gate that could not speak to them — noisy, but the noise
points at itself. Here the gate was SILENT and green over a property it never
exercised, which is the failure mode this project exists to prevent, sitting
inside the machinery that is supposed to prevent it.

### The register, and why it is not an allowlist

Thirteen fixtures need per-service seeding, so `knownEmptyEstate` names them —
in the D463/D472 idiom, checked BOTH ways. A probe listed there whose estate
starts serving the resource FAILS with *the fixture was fixed and the entry
outlived it*. The list can only shrink; it cannot rot into stale excuses the way a
one-directional skip would, and it cannot be padded, because adding a healthy probe
to it fails immediately.

Both directions were driven red before the register was kept, and one entry was
paid on the spot: `azure/portaldash`'s fixture now starts with the dashboard
already standing under our ownership tags, the gate caught that the entry had
outlived its reason, and the entry came out. **Twelve remain.**

The general lesson has a sharper form than "test your tests". A harness assertion
is a claim about what was EXERCISED, and nothing in a passing assertion says the
scenario it names actually occurred. Both holes here were invisible because every
individual assertion was true — of a scenario nobody had checked was set up.

## D525 — the register was half right, and the half that was wrong was its name

D524 named thirteen adopt probes that certified nothing and put them in
`knownEmptyEstate`. Paying them down showed the register had conflated two
different situations under one name, which is the kind of error that survives
precisely because the list is green.

**Some fixtures were empty. Some drivers never read.** `azDashServer` started with
`stored == nil`, so the first GET 404'd and there was nothing to adopt — that is a
fixture defect. But `aws/cloudwatchdash`'s fixture serves the dashboard perfectly
well; the driver simply issues `PutDashboard` and never looks. The estate could
have held anything. Two causes, one label, and the label described only the first.

Renamed to `knownNoAdoptRead` — *no successful read happened* — which is the thing
actually observed, with both causes spelled out. A register that names a CAUSE it
did not measure is a register that will be wrong the first time the other cause
appears, and it already was.

**The second cause is not automatically a defect, and the harness must be able to
say so.** Azure derives a role assignment's GUID by hashing
`(scope|principal|role)`; a custom role definition hashes `(roledef|scope|name)`;
AWS's `AttachRolePolicy` is idempotent on `(role, policy)`. A write at an identity
derived from the request cannot land on anything the request does not name, so
those creates need no pre-read to be safe. `ExistingProbe.IdentityFromContent`
declares it, and — because a declaration that only ever excuses is worthless — the
gate FAILS a probe that declares it and then reads anyway: a create that reads can
check what it found, and must.

That is a real distinction, not a loophole. A deterministic NAME is not the same
thing: `PutDashboard` writes at a name groundhold chose by convention, and a
stranger's dashboard can occupy that name. Those three AWS services stay in the
register rather than being waved through, even though their delete-side ownership
was already fixed (D446, D449).

**Paid down: thirteen to six.** Three Azure fixtures were seeded with the resource
already standing under our ownership tags (metric alert, scheduled query, web
test — the same `var stored map[string]any` shape as the portal dashboard),
and three creates were reclassified with their evidence read out of the source
rather than asserted. Each removal was forced by the gate itself, which fails an
entry whose probe starts passing, so the list cannot lag behind the truth in
either direction.

Remaining: `aws/cloudwatchdash`, `aws/cwlogfilter`, `aws/cloudtrail`,
`gcp/pubsub-queue`, `azure/activitylog`, `azure/consumptionbudget`.

## D526 — "ours by construction" is a claim about a name, and the name is computable by anyone

Paying the adopt register down from six ran into a question the register could not
settle, and the answer is more interesting than the six entries.

Four drivers write at a deterministic name with no pre-read, and each says why in a
comment: *a setting at our name is ours by construction*, *a dashboard present at
cwDashName is ours by construction*, *deterministic name => ours by construction*.
That reasoning is sound if and only if no other party can compute the name. So:
what goes into it?

`azResourceName` hashes `prefix|environment|capability[|gN]`. The AWS equivalent
hashes `environment|capability`. **Neither carries any estate identity** — no
subscription, no project, no account, no ledger, no deployment id. Two independent
groundhold deployments managing the same subscription, with the same capability id
and the same environment, compute the identical name. Measured, not reasoned:
`azResourceName("pv-al", "prod", "audit", 1)` is `pv-al-audit-prod-407f9735`, and
it is that for everybody.

So the hash is a **collision-avoidance device**, and the comments read it as an
**ownership proof**. Those are different claims and only the first is earned.

The distinction matters because the repository already has the sharp version of it.
D525 accepted `IdentityFromContent` for Azure's role assignment, whose GUID hashes
`(scope|principal|role)` — the resource's own SEMANTICS. A resource at that id
necessarily grants that principal that role; if a stranger created it, it still
means what we need it to mean, so writing there is safe no matter who made it. A
name derived from OUR inputs constrains nothing about what lives there: a
diagnostic setting called `pv-al-audit-prod-407f9735` can point anywhere.

Recorded rather than fixed, and the reason is proportion in both directions. The
exposure is real but bounded — it takes two deployments over one estate, which is
unusual and which the D466–D468 estate-boundary work already treats as a hazard.
The fix is expensive in a way that is not obviously worth it: the name IS the
providerId, so changing its inputs changes every binding ever made and every plan
hash ever recorded. That is a provider-identity change, which by this project's own
rules starts with a conformance case and not with a driver edit, so it is an open
question in the instructions file.

What IS fixed here: the comments no longer claim more than the mechanism delivers,
and `TestResourceNameCarriesNoEstateIdentity` pins the naming inputs, so if an
estate identity is ever added, someone has to come back to this entry and re-read
those claims deliberately rather than inheriting them.

The six adopt-register entries stay. Each is a create that does not read, at a name
of exactly this kind — which is precisely why they should not be waved through as
`IdentityFromContent`. The register's job was to stop a green test standing in for
an unexercised property; here it stopped a comment standing in for a proof.

## D527 — the lesson did not travel, in the harness written the same week

D524 asked one question of two harnesses: can the estate express the condition
they claim to test? This entry asks it of the rest, and the answer says something
about how a defect class actually spreads.

**`CertifyNoDuplicate` never checked that the driver looked.** Its scenario is "the
named cluster does NOT exist, so adopt-by-name must refuse and never create". It
asserted a `failed` status and zero mutations — both of which a driver satisfies by
refusing at VALIDATION, on a malformed operand, without ever asking whether the
cluster is there. Every existing probe passed once the read requirement was added
(a clean negative), and the requirement was driven red with a create that refuses
without looking, to prove it can fail.

**`CertifyIntrusiveProbeRefusesForeign` had BOTH holes**, and it is the one worth
dwelling on. It required an error, zero mutations, and no intrusive measurement —
and nothing more. A driver refusing at providerId parsing passes. An estate that
404s every read makes the probe refuse an ABSENT resource rather than a foreign
one, and it passes too.

That harness was written in D461, in the same series as D455 — the entry whose
entire content is *a refusal that never read is not evidence that the ownership
check works*. The lesson was learned, written down, and applied to delete and
update. Two entries later a new harness was built for the same property on a
different verb and did not carry it.

This is the argument for asking a property of a CLASS rather than of one verb at a
time, made against the author of the class gates. A rule written in prose in one
entry does not propagate; only a shared mechanism does. The four Certify families
now share `countRT`'s `readFound`, so the next family added inherits the check
instead of re-deriving it — or re-forgetting it.

Both new checks were driven red before being kept. The remaining families are
sound as written: `CertifyBoundedPoll` cannot be satisfied by an early refusal
(that returns `failed`, and the gate demands `unknown` with the pid preserved),
and `CertifyReadRetry` and `CertifyDiscoverability` assert over registries rather
than over a single scripted estate.

## D528 — the meter had stopped measuring, and the first thing it measured was a test with no teeth

D482 made the mutation gate a CI job because it existed and nothing ran it. It has
run on every push since. What nobody asked is whether it still covers anything: its
newest mutant was D482, and this session shipped and fixed a dozen more real
defects after that. **A meter that runs on a fixed set of old bugs is a meter that
has stopped measuring**, which is the same shape as D482 itself one turn later —
and the same shape as D527, where a rule was written down and did not travel.

Six mutants added, each a defect this repository actually had:

- the k8s observe dropping the absence marker, so a deleted resource read as
  silence and converge agreed with a world that no longer held it (D513);
- S3 describing a DELETED bucket as a healthy one, four attributes emitted from
  the providerId string without ever asking whether the bucket exists (D520);
- an RBAC permission spelling accepted on write that the read cannot produce, so
  converge planned the identical update forever (D510);
- an empty result set and a parse failure called the same thing (D523);
- every read error turned into "nothing to observe" (D522);
- and the adopt gate's own hole — a harness defect is a defect (D524).

### The meter earned its keep on the first run

One mutant SURVIVED: re-injecting D522's bug broke nothing. Before calling that a
finding it had to be checked that the substitution APPLIED — a mutation that
silently fails to apply looks exactly like a mutant that survived, and this session
has been caught by that class four times. It applied. The survival was real.

The gap was precise. D522's fix separated two things `observeCustomPolicy` had
conflated: an authoritative `NoSuchEntity` (now the absence marker) and any other
error (now returned, which blocks). The tests covered the ABSENCE branch — that is
what the F-LC3 sweep was looking at — and left the FAILURE branch uncovered. So
the half of the fix that matters most, the half about a transport failure not being
reported as an empty world, was protected by nothing.

`TestCustomPolicyReadFailureIsNotAnEmptyWorld` covers it: a 500 from the policy
read must return an error and no observations. The mutant is caught now.

That is the whole argument for a mutation meter, demonstrated rather than asserted:
`make check` was green, the fix was real, the entry describing it was accurate, and
the test protecting it did not exist. Nothing but re-injecting the bug would have
said so.

## D529 — the summary said "nothing was changed" about a world it had not read

From the field, on `master c5f40d6`. A create whose outcome was `unknown` printed:

    0 of 1 actions applied — nothing was changed
    next: groundhold resume ...

The Lambda had been created. The partner checked AWS by hand before retrying — a
habit their own outage taught them — found `pilot-raport-prod-gycaqpde` standing
with the right memory and timeout, and `resume` reconciled it cleanly.

Their sentence is the finding: **"nothing was changed" is a stronger claim than the
evidence the run had.** If the outcome of the action is UNKNOWN then the number of
applied actions is unknown too. They name the rule "three states, not two —
applied / not applied / NOT KNOWN — and the third must not look like the second."

That is D29, which this project states as a non-negotiable invariant and enforces
throughout the machine contract: a transient outcome is `unknown` WITH the
providerId, never a terminal answer. The executor obeyed it perfectly — the status
was `unknown`, the exit code was 4, the `resume` hint was correct and worked. Only
the human-facing summary contradicted it, and the summary is the part a human
reads.

**It is my own line, added one entry earlier for this same partner.** D379 lifted
apply's per-action outcomes into a summary because a partially-applied run reported
only its refusal and an operator could not tell that production had already
changed. That fix leads with what changed — and its `else` branch said "nothing was
changed" without ever looking at whether anything was UNKNOWN. A fix aimed at
honesty about partial application introduced a dishonesty about uncertain
application.

Three states now:

    1 of 2 actions applied before the run stopped — the world HAS changed: a-create-db
    1 further action(s) UNKNOWN — the world MAY have changed beyond that; run `resume` before retrying: a-create-fn

    0 of 1 actions confirmed applied, 1 UNKNOWN — the world MAY have changed; run `resume` before retrying, or a retry may duplicate: a-create-pilot-raport

    0 of 1 actions applied — nothing was changed        (only when every outcome is decided)

The mixed case matters as much as the pure one: a confirmed change leads, because
that is what an operator needs first, but the uncertainty behind it survives on its
own line rather than being swallowed by the headline.

Carried into the mutation meter the same slice (D528's rule: a fix without a mutant
is a fix nobody has confirmed is guarded). Re-injecting the bug — collapsing the
unknown branch — now fails the named test.

The general shape is worth keeping: **a summary is a claim, and it inherits the
evidence bar of everything else.** The four-valued verdict, the transient-honesty
rule and the absence marker all exist because this system refuses to state more
than it knows. A prose line at the end of a run is not exempt, and it is the one
place where nobody had thought to check.

## D530 — the operand guard covered the first second of a resource's life

Two field reports on the same day, which the partner correctly read as one pattern
rather than two incidents: `memory_mb` and then `role_arn` declared in
`implementation:` and silently ignored — `validate` OK, `plan` SEALED, zero
actions, zero warnings. Their Lambda was being killed for running out of the
default 128 MB while the contract said 1024, and the execution role they had just
narrowed stayed the wide one.

They quoted us against ourselves, accurately: for `capability.ai.inference` we
refuse rather than ignore, and the v0.1.4 CHANGELOG says an unknown operand is
*refused at compile instead of silently dropped — the cardinal trust failure this
closes*. So why not here?

**Two different causes, and the pattern the reporter saw is real.**

### The unknown-operand guard walked ACTIONS

`refuseUnknownOperands` iterated the action list. A capability that is bound and
converged has no actions, so its operands were never examined. The guard applied at
the moment a resource is created or updated and at no moment after — which is most
of a deployment's life, and exactly the state a steady-state converge is in.

The claim in the CHANGELOG was true of the case it was written for and not true in
general, which is this repository's recurring failure (D464, D473, D526): a real
convention, published, holding in the situation someone tested. It now iterates
CAPABILITIES; a capability whose only action reads no implementation (delete,
claim) is still skipped.

### `role_arn` was consumed at create and observed nowhere

The other half is not an unknown operand — `role_arn` IS declared consumed by
aws/lambda. It had no OBSERVED twin. Lambda records `implementation.vpcConfig`,
`.environment` and `.package` back for the compiler's operand-drift step; the role
was not among them, so the reconciler had nothing to compare and reported
convergence over a divergence.

The fix is small because the hard part already existed: `updateConfigBody` has
always sent `Role`, so the update path could always repair this. Only the
observation was missing. `implementation.role` is now recorded from the live
`GetFunction`, rendered by a helper shared with `OperandTargets` so declared and
observed compare in the same shape (a shape mismatch would report permanent drift
on a converged function — its own kind of lie), and `ClassifyChange` calls it
mutable, because reading it as immutable would REPLACE a live function to edit a
permission.

**The partner ranked this one first by consequence rather than frequency, and they
were right to.** A divergence between the declared and the actual execution role is
precisely what an infrastructure contract exists to prevent; they had to repair it
with `aws lambda update-function-configuration` by hand.

### What is NOT fixed here

`capability.function.serverless` still has no memory attribute, and that stays a
vocabulary question rather than a driver edit — the partner's own analysis of why
(memory is an AWS concept where `timeout.maximum` and `replicas.minimum` are
portable) is the same reasoning D60 uses. What changes today is that declaring it
as an operand REFUSES instead of being ignored, which is what they asked for and
the cheaper half: they now hear "the contract does not cover this" instead of
discovering it from an OOM kill.

Both halves carry mutants (D528's rule).

## D531 — the plan summary listed everything that was safe and nothing that was not

From the field. A new capability was added to the contract; `plan` sealed, and its
human summary printed twenty-one lines of `no-op (bound, observed==declared)` and
stopped. The capability that would CREATE a resource did not appear at all — not as
a create, not as unbound, not as genesis. The JSON carried `a-create-s3-stan`,
`heads` recorded `"s3-stan": "genesis"`, and `forecast` on the sealed plan
confirmed `willCreate: 1`.

The partner's framing is the entry: reading only the summary — and it is the last
thing on screen, so that is the natural thing to do — the conclusion is *"the plan
does nothing"*, and the opposite was true. **The summary omitted exactly the
category that changes the world.** A bound, converged capability is harmless by
definition; an unbound one is a new resource, a new cost and a new surface.
Attention was distributed inversely to risk.

`renderNoOp` did what its name says and nothing more. Part B (D249) added the
no-op lines to answer "why did converge do nothing to these", which was a real gap
at the time, and the answer was rendered on its own without anyone asking what the
reader would conclude from a summary that contained ONLY it.

Now the actions lead and the no-ops follow as the answer to "why was nothing done
to the rest":

    CREATE: 1 capability(ies) — s3-stan
    api: no-op (bound, observed==declared)
    web: no-op (bound, observed==declared)

A plan with no actions prints exactly what it printed before — inventing a line for
the steady state would be noise on the path every deployment runs, and a warning
that fires on ordinary input trains people to ignore it (D364).

`converge` was checked and already names its actions, so the gap was in `plan`
alone. This is the third field report in three days of the same class, and the
partner said so themselves: *the tool goes silent instead of saying "I don't know"
or "careful, a resource will be created here"* — D529 (an unknown outcome
summarised as "nothing was changed") and D530 (an operand silently ignored) are the
other two. Silence reads as reassurance. That is the class, and it is worth naming
once rather than three times: **every one of these was a place where the machine
contract was correct and the sentence a human reads was not.**

## D532 — a set that was compared as a sequence

From the field, twice in one adoption. The second refusal is the entry:

    declared [eu-central-1 eu-west-1 eu-west-3 eu-north-1 eu-south-1 eu-south-2]
    reality  [eu-central-1 eu-north-1 eu-south-1 eu-south-2 eu-west-1 eu-west-3]
    — fix the candidate or the resource, adoption must not lie

The sets are equal. Only the order differs, and the vocabulary's own description of
`inference.destinationRegions` calls it *"the full set of regions the inference
profile may ROUTE a call to"*. A set has no order, so the comparison was answering
a question nobody asked — and answering it by accusing the operator of lying.

**The comparison was not wrong; the TYPE was under-specified.** `listEqual`
compares positionally and must keep doing so: a `kind: list` is an ordered sequence
and order is part of its identity (D21). Changing `equals` would silently reinterpret
every list in every contract, and the operator set is closed (invariant #4).

So the fix is in the type system, not the operators. `unordered: true` marks a list
whose order carries no meaning, and such a list is CANONICALIZED — sorted — when it
is loaded, where the vocabulary is known. That is D34's answer to "two forms, one
meaning" applied to a type rather than to a document, and it means the set compares
equal EVERYWHERE with no second meaning of equality: verifier, adopt, reconcile,
and the candidate hash, which now cannot differ for two spellings of one set.

Both directions are pinned by conformance cases, written before the implementation
as the rules require: an unordered attribute satisfies a constraint whose value
lists the same elements in another order, and a plain list with the same data still
reports `violated`. The second case is the load-bearing one — the default must not
move.

`inference.destinationRegions` is marked. Nothing else is, deliberately: every
other list attribute stays an ordered sequence until someone shows its order is
meaningless, which is the direction that cannot silently break a contract.

One more thing the meter caught, immediately. The first unit test called
`sortScalarList` directly and passed with the CALL SITE disabled — a test that
exercises the function but not the place it is used proves the function, not the
behaviour. Rewritten to go through `vocabCheck`, which is the wiring the bug would
have lived in.

Two smaller things this cost, both worth noting because they are the gates working:
the embedded vocabulary copy had to be re-synced (the build refuses to let
`spec/vocab/` and the embedded mirror drift), and four documents publishing the
suite size had to move from 514 to 516 — including MATURITY.md, whose gate calls
itself "the honesty document drifted".

Their second request — that the message distinguish "different elements" from
"different order" — is now moot for a marked attribute and still open for the rest;
recorded here rather than half-built, since after canonicalization a surviving
mismatch on an unordered list IS a difference in elements.

## D533 — the validator refused an artefact its own compiler intends to produce

From the field. Converged infrastructure produced `AKCJI: 0, NO-OP: 16`, the
compiler sealed the plan, and apply refused it:

    forecast said: plan error: reads.heads must pin a head per capability
    ⊘ apply
    REFUSED   (exit 2)

Exit 2 is indistinguishable from a real refusal, so "is there anything to deploy"
had to be decided outside the tool.

**This was an internal contradiction, not a missing feature.** The compiler seals a
zero-action plan deliberately — its own comment says so: *"actions == 0 with
blocked/unverified present is NOT nothing to change: a blocked capability is held
back, and an unverified one converged on its observable attrs but has
non-observable ones. Seal a plan carrying both so converge reports them honestly."*
The validator then rejected exactly that plan.

Four checks conflated **"the key is missing or ill-typed"** with **"the key is
present and legitimately empty"**: `plan.actions`, `reads.heads`, `plan.writes` and
`plan.preconditions`. Each was written when a plan always carried at least one
action, and each stayed after that stopped being true. A missing key is still
malformed; an empty one is a converged plan.

The invariant that DOES hold is now checked against the actions rather than
asserted unconditionally: **actions without pinned heads is malformed**, because
heads are pinned per capability WITH an action. Zero actions, zero heads is
complete.

**One check in that group was not the same class and was left alone.**
`report-executable` is mandatory on every plan the compiler emits, converged or not
(D195, the thesis: no plan without the verify gate). The first fixture omitted it
and the validator refused — correctly. The fixture was wrong, so the fixture was
fixed. A sweep that removes checks by pattern would have taken this one too.

Four unit rows pinning the old refusals were removed with the reason recorded; they
were written against a validator whose model of a plan no longer holds. The
sealed-plan spec was checked first and never required non-empty actions — this was
the validator asserting more than the format demands.

Verified on the live cluster: the fully-converged path (no blocked, no unverified)
still refuses at COMPILE with `nothing to change`, which converge translates to
CONVERGED and exit 0, unchanged. The path this fixes is the other one — the sealed
zero-action plan, which now validates and applies to nothing.

## D534 — the observation contradicted the mapping it claimed to implement

From the field, on live production. A Function URL with `AuthType: AWS_IAM` behind
CloudFront/OAC is the CORRECT hardening — anonymous access is cut off deliberately
and only the CDN may sign a request. The reachability probe reported it BLOCKED,
and the partner traced why: `network.publicExposure` observed `true`, because the
driver treated "a Function URL exists" as "publicly exposed" without reading
AuthType. Its comment said so plainly, and gave a reason that sounds right —
AuthType is an implementation operand, not a vocabulary attribute (invariant #4).

The reason does not survive reading the vocabulary. `network.publicExposure` is
defined as *"whether the function is invokable over public HTTPS by ANYONE (an
UNAUTHENTICATED public endpoint), as opposed to reachable only by
authenticated/internal callers"*, and its `aws.lambda` mapping spells out both
gates: *"a Function URL with AuthType NONE plus a resource-based
lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl grant to principal * (BOTH, or the function stays
private)"*.

So the published mapping always said this attribute depends on AuthType. Reading it
is not a vocabulary change and does not touch invariant #4 — the operand stays an
operand; what changed is that the OBSERVATION of a vocabulary attribute now
measures what the mapping says it measures. **The driver was contradicting its own
documented mapping**, which is a sharper thing than a missing feature: the mapping
is the promise, and the code was not keeping it.

### The consequence was a trap, and they found it before stepping in it

Declaring the true value (`false`) would have created a diff against the false
observation, and the repairing action deletes the Function URL — which is the
CloudFront origin. Their note reads: *"That would put the front down. We record
this as: do NOT silence the probe with a declaration."* They disabled the probe
with a flag instead and said why, quoting our own argument back: **a signal that is
always red stops being a signal.** That is the correct move and we said so.

### What the fix measures

Both gates, as the mapping requires. `AWS_IAM` ⇒ private, definitively: no resource
policy can make a signed endpoint anonymous. `NONE` ⇒ read the resource policy and
look for an `Allow` of `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` to principal `*`. A policy that
cannot be read reports private WITH a diagnostic saying the answer rests on the
AuthType alone and is not a measurement of the grant — a read failure must not
invent an exposure in either direction.

The genuinely public shape still reads `true`, and that case is pinned first,
because the dangerous direction of this fix is hiding a real exposure.

### The fixture had the same blind spot as the driver

`TestLambdaCreateObserveDelete` failed on the change with *"AuthType NONE must
observe public"*. Its fake accepted the POST that CREATES the anonymous grant and
modelled no GET for it — because the driver never read it back. The fixture
mirrored the driver's blindness exactly (D520's class, third instance), so it now
answers with what the create put there.

Still open from the same report and NOT fixed here: the probe should measure the
public path (the CDN distribution) rather than the origin when a `cdn.distribution`
points at one, and "not confirmed" and "confirmed failure" should not share an exit
code. Both are real; this entry fixes the observation the other two rest on.

## D535 — a client's name compiled into the binary we hand them

Building a client delivery, a scrub check on the ARTIFACT (not the repo) found one
occurrence of the partner's name in the binary: a comment in
`spec/vocab/capability.function.serverless.yaml`, which is embedded, so its bytes
travel wherever the binary does.

Everything about the existing policy was working. D340 decided the name stays in
the private repo and is genericized on export, and the export is clean — a fresh
`export-public.sh` has zero occurrences, in that file and everywhere else. The
client-name gate is doing its job on the surface it was built for.

The surface it was NOT built for is the compiled artifact. A binary is not the
export: it is built from the private tree, it goes outside this machine, and it can
be forwarded further than intended. Here it goes to the very partner it names, so
nothing leaked — but the same binary handed to a second client would carry the
first one's name, and nobody would look.

Genericized at the source rather than papered over at build time, because a build
step that strips names is a step someone will skip. Go comments naming the partner
(there are several) are NOT affected: comments do not survive compilation, and the
measurement says so — `strings` on the rebuilt binary reports zero.

The general point is narrow and worth keeping: **an export gate proves things about
the export.** Every other artefact that leaves the machine — a binary, a capsule, a
support bundle — is a separate surface, and this one had never been checked. The
check that found it was `strings <binary> | grep -i <client>`, which is cheap
enough to run on every delivery and is now part of how one is prepared.

## D536 — the resilience tool was working against security, quietly

From the field, weight: high, and it opens with a section headed "first the praise,
because it is due". Their `backup`/`restore` was exercised end to end on a live
production ledger — 7.5 MB, 1323 events, 21 bound capabilities. Restore reproduced
a ledger whose plan was byte-identical to the original's, 21/21, empty diff. Their
NEGATIVE control changed one string in one capsule (`eu-central-1` → `eu-west-1`)
and got `CORRUPTED`, the exact broken link named, exit 5, no output file written.

Then they grepped the capsules. Events 66, 67 and 110 of 1323 — recorded before
they migrated to `secretsmanager:` references — carry an Aurora connection string
WITH THE PASSWORD, an OAuth secret and a private key. Current state is clean; the
last `DATABASE_URL` event is a reference. The ledger is append-only, so the capsules
carry the whole chain, faithfully.

Their sentence is the finding: **"the more diligently you back up, the more places
hold live credentials."** A resilience tool working against security, invisibly —
nobody reads a 3 MB capsule.

### What they did NOT ask for, and were right not to

Redaction. It would break the hash chain the whole verification stands on — the
chain their own negative control had just proved works. Immutability is a feature.
They said so themselves and proposed a warning and a manifest instead.

So this warns and COUNTS, and does nothing else. Never a refusal: the finding is a
pattern, a value that LOOKS like a credential sometimes is not one, and the history
cannot be changed anyway. `backup` now reports `credentialWarnings` and
`credentialSites` — capsule, event index, what the pattern recognised, and the
pointer inside the body. **Never the value**: a warning that quotes the secret
defeats itself.

### The same detector, deliberately

`contract.ScanForPlaintextSecrets` already existed (D364) — and it exists because
of THEIR earlier report, on 2026-07-26, about the ledger. This is the same lineage
one step further out: the backup MULTIPLIES that exposure, because a backup is made
precisely to be moved off-host. So the scanner was exposed as `contract.ScanValue`
and reused rather than rewritten. Two detectors would drift, and the one nobody
exercised would be the one that mattered.

### One thing the test caught that reading would not have

The first implementation scanned `event["body"]` and found nothing on a ledger that
demonstrably contains a credential — a capsule event is the ledger envelope
`{apiVersion, kind, event}` and the recorded body is one level in. **A clean result
and a wrong lookup are indistinguishable from the outside**, and this would have
shipped as "warns on nothing, ever" with a green test suite if the test asserting
the warning FIRES had not been written first. That is the whole argument for
case-before-implementation, met in miniature.

Their remaining two suggestions are not built here and are recorded rather than
half-done: a `--manifest` listing capsules and counts, and built-in encryption. The
second carries its own warning from them — their first hand-rolled wrapper had an
`exit` inside a command substitution, so a missing key produced "encryption with an
empty password" and the message "backup complete". Their negative control caught
it. That is an argument FOR shipping it rather than leaving everyone to write it,
and an argument for writing it carefully.

## D537 — a comment asserted a fact about AWS that AWS does not honour

The other half of the field report D534 fixed the observation for. `edgeOutputs`
decided which capabilities the post-apply reachability probe measures, and for
`capability.function.serverless` it said:

> AWS Lambda functionUrl / GCP Cloud Functions gen2 url — both full URLs, both
> PUBLIC-only outputs (present only for a public function), so output-presence is
> the gate.

The parenthesis is false for AWS. A Function URL exists with `AuthType: AWS_IAM`,
which is the CORRECT shape behind CloudFront/OAC — present, and deliberately not
public. So the probe measured the ORIGIN, got a 403 to its anonymous GET, and
reported the run BLOCKED. The 403 was the origin working.

The mechanism for skipping a private edge already existed and is used by
`capability.workload.container`; the serverless case simply opted out of it on a
premise that does not hold. The premise was written down as a justification, which
is the part worth noting: **a comment explaining why a check is unnecessary is a
claim, and this one was never checked against the cloud it names.** Same shape as
D526 (a name asserted to prove ownership) and D534 (an observation contradicting
its own mapping) — three in one week, all of them prose that outranked the code.

Gated on exposure now, which D534 made a true input by teaching the observation to
read AuthType. The partner ranked this fix first and predicted it would come free
from fixing the observation; it did, and it is one line.

The two directions that must not move are pinned: a genuinely public Function URL
is still probed, and a CDN distribution is never gated on a capability's own
exposure flag, because a distribution IS the public path — the one target that
measures what a user actually sees, and the one that was green in their report all
along.

**An operational consequence they will meet on upgrade, worth stating plainly.**
The gate reads the candidate's DECLARED `network.publicExposure`, not the
observation. Before D534, declaring `false` for an IAM-fronted function created a
diff whose repair would have deleted the Function URL. After D534 the observation
IS false, so the declaration is now both true and safe — and it is what turns the
probe off for that origin. A candidate still declaring `true` will keep being
probed and will now also carry a real diff. This is in the delivery note.

Still not built, and still theirs to ask for again: probing the CDN distribution
INSTEAD of an origin it fronts (rather than merely skipping the private origin),
and separating "not confirmed" from "confirmed failure" in the exit code. The
second is a smaller question than it looks — the probe deliberately has no
"denied" verdict, because a 403 to an anonymous request is ambiguous, so today
there is no confirmed-failure state to distinguish. Whether one should exist is a
design question, not a bug.

## D538 — the list that settled a production dispute is 28 entries short

Three findings this week turned on a comment being a claim nobody checked (D526,
D534, D537). Rather than wait for a fourth, the pattern was swept — and the sweep's
best result is a clean negative worth recording before the finding.

`deleteBackupPolicy` skips the data-loss gate on the grounds that *"a policy is a
SCHEDULE, not a store (stateful: false) — deleting it stops future backups but
never deletes recovery points already in the vault"*. That is the same SHAPE as the
three defects: a comment justifying the absence of a check. It is also correct.
`spec/vocab/capability.backup.plan.yaml` makes the identical argument deliberately
and at length, and the code cites the vocabulary rather than asserting on its own
authority. **Citing something checkable is exactly what the three defects did not
do**, and it is the difference between a justification and an assumption.

The same sweep asked whether AWS's `publicExposure` blindness had twins. It does
not: GCP Cloud Run reads ingress AND the IAM invoker binding and refuses to
default-safe when the policy is unreadable — the correct model already existed one
driver over. Azure Container Apps reads `configuration.ingress.external`, which is
faithful to ITS attribute, whose definition is "reachable from the internet" rather
than `function.serverless`'s "invokable by anyone (unauthenticated)". Two
capabilities, two different questions, both answered correctly. AWS was the outlier.

### The finding: the mapping list is incomplete, and it is load-bearing

Checking Azure Container Apps turned up something else. `azure.containerapps`
appears in the `mappings:` of `capability.workload.container` — nowhere. The driver
serves the capability and the vocabulary never names the provider.

Asking the drivers (D317: ask them, never scrape) against the published lists:
**29 (capability, provider) pairs are served by a driver and named by no attribute
mapping at all.** Not one attribute missing a cloud — the provider absent from the
capability entirely: `dns.record` on all three clouds, `network.loadbalancer` on all
three, `observability.changefeed` on all three, `ai.inference` on Azure and GCP,
`cluster.kubernetes` on Azure and GCP.

That matters because of what the list DID this week. D534 was settled by reading
it: an operator said an observation was wrong, and the published mapping — "AuthType
NONE PLUS a resource-based grant to principal *" — is what proved them right and the
driver wrong. **A capability realised on a cloud the vocabulary never mentions has
nothing to appeal to when the next disagreement happens.**

### A ratchet, because a wrong mapping is worse than an absent one

Writing 29 accurate mappings needs per-service knowledge, and inventing one would
be worse than leaving the gap: D534 treated the mapping as authoritative, so a
mapping written from memory would authorise a wrong answer. So the number is
published and may only fall.

One paid immediately, and only one, because it is the only one this session read
the driver for first-hand: `azure.containerapps`, with the distinction that made
it correct written into the entry — the attribute is "reachable from the internet",
so Easy Auth in front of an external ingress does not make it false. **28 remain.**

Both directions were driven red before the gate was kept, and it floors on the
number of capabilities the drivers report, because a probe that returns nothing
would otherwise pass with zero gaps.

## D539 — six mappings written by reading the drivers, not by recalling the clouds

D538 published 28 remaining (capability, provider) pairs the vocabulary never
mentions, and said why paying them down carelessly would be worse than leaving
them: D534 settled a live dispute by treating a mapping as authoritative, so a
mapping written from memory would authorise a wrong answer with the same
authority.

So six were paid the only way that earns that authority: by reading what the
driver's `observe` actually does and writing that down. Two capabilities, three
clouds each — `capability.dns.record` and `capability.observability.changefeed`,
both of which had NO mappings at all for any attribute, which is why each showed
up three times.

The entries say more than a field name, because reading the code turned up limits
that a plausible-sounding mapping would have papered over:

- **`dns.target` is the FIRST value only**, on all three clouds — `ResourceRecords[0].Value`,
  `ARecords[0].ipv4Address`, `rrdatas[0]`. A multi-value record set is not
  represented. Someone contracting a round-robin record would otherwise read the
  mapping and reasonably expect it to be.
- **Azure's changefeed target is a StorageQueue destination or nothing.** The
  driver composes it from `resourceId + queueName` and, for any other
  `endpointType`, emits a diagnostic rather than inventing a target string. That
  refusal is the honest behaviour and now it is documented behaviour.
- **`dns.proxied` is not observable on any of the three clouds**, and the drivers
  each say so in a diagnostic naming it a Cloudflare edge concept. The mapping now
  names the one provider that HAS it, which is more useful than three entries
  saying "not applicable".

That last one is the general shape worth keeping: **a mapping's job includes saying
where an attribute does NOT map.** An attribute with three cloud entries and a
silent fourth cloud reads as an oversight; an attribute that names the provider it
belongs to reads as a decision.

Twenty-two remain. They stay on the ratchet rather than being guessed at, and the
rate is deliberate — six is what could be read carefully in one pass.

## D540 — three more, and a false report the reading caught

`capability.network.loadbalancer` on all three clouds, read the same way as D539:
open each driver's reverse map and write down what it derives the attribute from.
Nineteen pairs remain.

The reading paid for itself again, this time on a distinction that would have been
lost:

**Azure has TWO shapes behind one service token, and they answer
`encryption.inTransit` differently.** The Application Gateway reads a listener
`Protocol=Https` and reports a MEASUREMENT. The L4 load balancer has no protocol to
read at all, so it reports `false` as **config-intent** — a layer-4 balancer
terminates nothing, so the answer is a property of the shape rather than something
observed. A mapping written from the outside would have said "the listener
protocol" and quietly promoted a config-intent to a measurement, which is precisely
the distinction the evidence lattice exists to keep (D44).

**GCP's public-exposure rule has an honest edge the code states and a summary would
drop.** `EXTERNAL`/`EXTERNAL_MANAGED` are internet-facing and `INTERNAL*` are not —
but a classic forwarding rule may omit `loadBalancingScheme` entirely, and the
driver maps an ABSENT scheme to public WITH a diagnostic saying so. Defaulting an
unknown to "exposed" is the safe direction for a security attribute and it is a
choice, not an accident; the mapping now says it is a choice.

**AWS is the plain one** — `Scheme: internet-facing` and "any listener terminates
TLS" — which is worth writing down precisely because it is unremarkable. A reader
comparing the three clouds needs to see which one has no caveat.

The pattern across D539 and D540 is now consistent enough to state: **every mapping
written by reading has come out longer than the one that would have been written
from memory, and the extra length is always a limit or a caveat.** First-value-only
targets, StorageQueue-or-nothing, config-intent-not-measured, absent-means-public.
None of those would have been invented by someone summarising what a load balancer
"obviously" is.

## D541 — the residency attribute, mapped on the two clouds that were missing it

`capability.ai.inference` on Azure and GCP. Seventeen pairs remain.

This one mattered more than its size: `inference.destinationRegions` is the
attribute a partner's EU-residency invariant is asserted against, the one D376
unblocked, and the one D532 marked `unordered` — and its mapping named `aws.bedrock`
alone, while two other drivers observe it.

Reading them showed the same SURFACE reached by different routes, which is what a
mapping is for:

- **Azure** derives it from the deployments' SKU names. A `global*` sku reduces to
  the `["global"]` sentinel — unbounded routing, so `subset-of` an EU allowlist
  yields `violated`, deliberately. A `datazone*` sku reduces to that account's data
  zone. Anything else is the account's own region. **An account with NO deployments
  is regional**, its surface being the account's own region — an edge that reads as
  an oversight until you see the reasoning.
- **GCP** derives it from the endpoint's SERVED location, and the `global` endpoint
  reduces to the same `["global"]` sentinel. The driver's own comment calls it "the
  direct twin of Bedrock's eu-south-2", which is precisely the connection a reader
  of the vocabulary needs and could not have made from three unrelated entries.

That convergence is the entry: **two clouds with unrelated APIs arrive at the same
sentinel because the CONTRACT needs one.** `["global"]` is not an API value on
either — it is what both drivers reduce unbounded routing to, so that one
`subset-of` constraint catches the trap on any cloud. A mapping listing only
`aws.bedrock` hid the fact that this is a cross-cloud convention rather than an AWS
quirk.

`model.access` is now written down as a MANUAL-GATE on every cloud (D55): access is
granted outside the API, so a driver OBSERVES it and never fabricates it — and
GCP's Vertex driver refuses rather than faking a `true` it cannot prove. That is
worth being in the published mapping rather than only in a Go comment, because it
tells an author why the attribute can be `unknown` on a correctly configured system.

## D542 — two capabilities that existed only for AWS on paper

`capability.cluster.kubernetes` and `capability.identity.podidentity`, on Azure and
GCP. Both had mappings for `aws.eks` / `aws.eks-podidentity` and nothing else,
though three drivers serve each. Thirteen pairs remain.

Reading them makes visible what the type system is actually doing, which three
separate AWS-only entries did not:

**`network.apiExposure` folds three unrelated cloud controls onto one three-valued
surface.** Azure reads `apiServerAccessProfile` — a private cluster is `private`,
otherwise non-empty authorized IP ranges make it `mixed`, else `public`. GCP reads
`privateClusterConfig.enablePrivateEndpoint` then
`masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig.enabled` for the same three answers. Different API
shapes, same question, same vocabulary — which is the whole claim of a
capability-typed contract, and it was only legible from the code.

**`encryption.secrets` abstracts over two mechanisms that share a guarantee.**
Azure's is `securityProfile.azureKeyVaultKms.enabled` (etcd encrypted with a CMK);
GCP's is `databaseEncryption.state == ENCRYPTED` (application-layer, CMK-backed).
Neither is the other's field, and an operator contracting "secrets are encrypted
with a key I control" needs to know both count.

**Pod identity is one binding expressed three ways.** Azure parses the namespace
and service account out of the federated credential's `subject`
(`system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>`) — the binding IS that string. GCP carries them
in the providerId and cross-checks the IAM member
`serviceAccount:<pool>.svc.id.goog[<ns>/<sa>]` on the Google service account. Two
totally different identity federations, the same two facts.

The through-line of D539–D542 is now worth stating once. **Every one of these
mappings was AWS-only, and every one of them turned out to describe a convergence
rather than an AWS detail.** A vocabulary that names one cloud reads like a wrapper
around that cloud; the same vocabulary naming three reads like the abstraction it
claims to be — and nothing about the code changed, only what was written down about
it.

## D543 — a sentinel that is a contract convention, and two refusals worth publishing

`capability.security.threatdetection` and `capability.cost.budget`, on Azure and
GCP. Nine pairs remain.

**Both clouds report `location.region` as the literal `"global"`, and neither cloud
has such a region.** Threat detection is a subscription- or project-wide posture,
not a regional resource, and `"global"` is what all three drivers reduce that to so
a residency constraint has something well-typed to compare. It is the same shape as
`inference.destinationRegions`' `["global"]` (D541): **a value the contract needs
that no API returns.** Reading three AWS-only mappings would never have shown that
the sentinel is a convention rather than a field; the entry now says so.

**`protection.malware` on Azure needs TWO things and the driver knows it.** The
Storage Defender plan at Standard is not enough — the malware-scanning extension
must also be enabled, because the plan alone does not scan. That is exactly the
D534 shape (a mapping whose real condition is a conjunction) caught before it could
become a disagreement.

The budget entries publish two refusals that were previously only in Go:

- **Azure does not return a currency on the budget itself.** The driver takes the
