  scope's billing currency and, when it cannot resolve one, states that in a
  diagnostic instead of assuming. An operator reading "budget.limit is
  properties.amount" would not expect the money type to be sourced elsewhere.
- **A `timeGrain` with no vocabulary equivalent is named, never coerced.** Same on
  GCP for `calendarPeriod`. A period the vocabulary cannot express is reported
  missing rather than rounded to the nearest one it can — which is the four-valued
  rule applied to an enum.

GCP's budget adds a third: `amount.specifiedAmount` needs BOTH units and a currency
code, and a partial amount is **not observed at all**. Half a money value is not a
money value.

## D544 — naming where an attribute does NOT map, and one cloud's answer living on another object

`capability.audit.trail`, `capability.messaging.queue` and
`capability.messaging.topic`, on the clouds that were missing. Five pairs remain.

### Three attributes that deliberately do not map, now saying so

Both non-AWS audit drivers OMIT `location.region`, `integrity.logValidation` and
`encryption.customerManagedKeys`, each with a diagnostic. Reading them, the reasons
are not the same reason and the distinction is worth publishing:

- `location.region` is **not observed** because an audit export is global on both
  clouds and residency belongs to the DESTINATION operand — a separate capability
  with its own region.
- `integrity.logValidation` is **unsupported**: neither cloud has any equivalent of
  CloudTrail's log-file validation. The drivers report that rather than `false`,
  because `false` reads as "the feature is off" and the truth is "the feature does
  not exist here".
- `encryption.customerManagedKeys` is again a property of the destination, not of
  the export.

That middle one is the four-valued rule applied to a mapping: **"unsupported" and
"off" are different answers**, and a mapping that lists only AWS lets a reader
assume the silence means the second.

### An attribute whose value lives on a different object

Service Bus made a shape explicit that AWS and GCP do not have. `location.region`
and `network.publicExposure` for a queue or topic are **properties of the
NAMESPACE**, not of the entity — the entity carries neither. So the driver reads a
parent object to answer a question the vocabulary asks of the child, which is
correct and completely invisible from a mapping that says "the queue's region".

Two more Azure specifics that a summariser would have got wrong:
`delivery.guarantee` is expressed through DEDUP (`requiresDuplicateDetection` on
means exactly-once), and `reliability.deadLetter` has **no target to name** because
the DLQ is built in — the posture is `maxDeliveryCount` plus
`deadLetteringOnMessageExpiration`, where SQS names a separate queue.

The topic vocabulary took three of the six, not six: it does not carry
`ordering.enabled`, `encryption.atRest` or `location.region`. The script reported
what it actually applied rather than assuming symmetry — the two vocabularies are
not the same shape and pretending they were would have written entries for
attributes that do not exist.

## D545 — the mapping register closes at zero

The last five, all Azure. **Every provider the drivers serve is now named by the
capability's mappings, and the ratchet is at 0** — driven red at zero before being
kept, by deleting one entry and watching it report the gap.

D538 opened this at 29 with a warning: a mapping written from memory would
authorise a wrong answer, because D534 had just settled a live production dispute
by treating a mapping as authoritative. Twenty-nine were paid across eight entries,
every one by opening the driver and writing down what its `observe` derives the
value from. **Not one was written from recall.**

The last batch keeps the pattern intact — each mapping is longer than a summary
would have been, and the extra length is a limit:

- **A backup policy's `copy.crossRegion` is const FALSE, MEASURED.** Cross-region
  restore is a property of the vault, not the policy, so the policy can never
  report it true. Reporting false is honest rather than an omission — and the
  distinction only exists if someone says it.
- **`location.region` on a policy is the VAULT's**, and on an addon is the
  CLUSTER's. Both are parent objects answering a question the vocabulary asks of
  the child — the third time this shape appeared (Service Bus was the second,
  D544).
- **Log Analytics answers `encryption.customerManagedKeys` by pointing at a
  dedicated cluster.** CMK there is a cluster property, so the workspace's answer
  is a non-empty `clusterResourceId` — a reader expecting a key reference would
  find nothing and conclude the attribute was unmapped.
- **ACS email's `authentication.dkim` is ANY attached domain verified**, not all:
  one verified domain is enough for the service to send signed mail.

### What the whole series changed, and what it did not

Not one line of driver behaviour. Every mapping documents what the code already
did. What changed is that the vocabulary now describes a three-cloud abstraction
instead of an AWS wrapper with two silent partners — and the silences turned out to
be carrying information: `unsupported` versus `off` (D544), a sentinel no API
returns (D541, D543), a conjunction where a summary would have written one field
(D543), first-value-only (D539), measured-versus-config-intent (D540).

**Eight entries, twenty-nine mappings, zero code changes, and every one of them was
a thing the code knew and the contract did not say.** That is the honest summary of
what this register was worth: it did not find bugs, it found a published artefact
that had drifted into being true only about one cloud.

## D546 — measuring which cause each register entry has, and finding a seventh

D525 renamed `knownEmptyEstate` to `knownNoAdoptRead` because it named a CAUSE it
had not measured: some entries were an empty fixture, others a driver that never
reads. The rename was right and the measurement was still not done. Doing it turned
the six remaining entries into five plus one different defect.

**Five are creates that issue no read at all** — activity log, consumption budget,
CloudWatch dashboard, CloudWatch log filter, CloudTrail. Their fixtures serve the
resource perfectly well; the drivers write at a deterministic name without looking.
Seeding cannot fix them, and whether such a create SHOULD read is exactly the open
question D526 raised: the name is computable by anyone, so it does not prove
ownership. **They wait on a decision, not on effort**, and the register now says so
rather than reading as a backlog someone forgot.

**The sixth was a harness defect, not a driver one.** `gcp/pubsub-queue` DOES read —
on a 409 from its create. But every GCP adopt probe shared one predicate for "which
request is the create", `postCreate`, which matches `POST` only. **Pub/Sub creates
its topic with PUT.** So the conflict wrapper never fired, the inner fixture
answered the PUT with a clean 200, the driver took the success branch, and the probe
never reached the code path where adoption lives. A test named
`TestAdoptsExistingPubSubQueue` exercised a first-time create from end to end.

That is D524's defect arriving through a new door: not an empty estate this time,
but a shared assumption about what a create looks like, held by the harness rather
than by any driver. `adoptCase` takes a per-case predicate now, and pubsub-queue
declares that its create is a PUT to `/topics/`.

The general lesson is small and specific: **a harness that recognises "the
interesting request" by a shared rule inherits that rule's blind spots into every
probe using it.** `postCreate` was written for services whose create is a POST, and
was correct for all of them; it silently disarmed the one probe where it was wrong.

## D547 — the honesty document's headline said the opposite of its own tail

A pass over `docs/MATURITY.md` after a week that changed a great deal. Two entries
had accreted corrections at the END while their opening sentence — the bold one, the
only part a skimming reader reads — kept saying what was true when it was written.

**Gap 5 led with "A resource deleted out of band is invisible to every driver but
one"** and "AWS, GCP and Azure are still open — roughly 145 certified services, one
emitter. This is the single largest known gap in the system today." Every clause was
false by then: D523 closed it at 102 of 102 probes with the ratchet at 0. The
closure WAS recorded — appended after the headline, in a sentence that begins "D517
turned the debt into a ratchet". So the entry contained both the claim and its
refutation, in that order.

**Gap 9 led with "Probes have not measured a real failure"** when D512 had measured
reachability for real on both branches, with correct provenance, and the entry's
body already said so.

This is D465's failure exactly, and D465 is an entry in this same document about
this same document: *MATURITY ages in the direction nobody challenges — nobody
writes that the project undersells itself.* Both stale headlines were pessimistic.
A reader deciding whether to trust this system would have read the two loudest
sentences in the gap list and concluded it was in materially worse shape than it is.

**The failure mode is structural, not careless.** Appending is how an append-only
record is supposed to work, and it is right for `DESIGN.md`, which is history. But
`MATURITY.md` is not history — it is a CURRENT-STATE claim, and a current-state
document maintained by appending will always have a stale first sentence. Corrected
by rewriting both headlines to lead with what is true now and keeping the route
there in the body, which is where the useful part actually lives: the D521–D523
detour taught more (the instrument was wrong more often than the drivers were) than
the closure itself.

No mechanical gate is proposed. The gates that exist here check COUNTS
(`TestMaturityCountsMatchReality`) and CITATIONS (`TestMaturityGapsAreAnchoredToDecisions`),
both of which passed the whole time these headlines were false, because a headline
is prose and the numbers under it were right. What would have caught it is the thing
that did: reading the document against a week of work, deliberately, looking for the
direction nobody complains about.

## D548 — the CHANGELOG had no gate, and a client is running a binary it does not describe

The published artefact nobody had checked. `docs/`, the vocabulary, the export, the
error registry and the parity matrix all have gates; `CHANGELOG.md` had none, and it
had drifted about a dozen decision entries behind — the whole absence-marker series,
the seven field findings, the mapping register. **A partner is running a binary
built from a commit the CHANGELOG does not describe**, which is the concrete cost.

Brought current first, and the entries were written to say what a reader needs
rather than what happened: the summary that claimed nothing changed while a Lambda
existed, the operand refused only at create time, S3 describing a deleted bucket, the
execution role never reconciled, the probe blocking on a correctly-private origin,
and the backup that copied credentials forward.

### The checkable property is narrower than "is it complete"

Completeness is not mechanical — not every decision deserves a line, and a gate
demanding one would produce a CHANGELOG written for the gate. What IS mechanical:
**every released tag must appear, or the document must say why it does not.** A tag
is something a person can download; a downloader reading the CHANGELOG has to find
their version or an explicit statement about it.

Four tags have no section and all four are deliberate — three predate the document
entirely (its earliest section is v0.1.3, and its own header scopes them as internal
builds), and v0.1.4 was tagged from a RED commit and superseded. The exemptions carry
the SENTENCE that justifies them and the gate re-derives it, so an exemption cannot
outlive its reason. Both directions were driven red: removing an exemption reports
the tag, and corrupting one reports that the explanation is gone.

That last part matters for v0.1.4 specifically. The instinct when a bad tag ships is
to delete it — and a deleted tag hides the mistake, while CI on it can never be
observed again. It was kept, superseded in prose, and the gate now requires that
prose to stay.

## D549 — the last two k8s mappings meet a real API server

`flux-kustomization` was the only mapped k8s service that had never been pointed at
a live cluster. A Kustomization was created on the k3s cluster, given a real failing
`Ready=False / BuildFailed` condition, and observed: `sync.status: drifted`,
`health.status: degraded` — the same normalisation the ArgoCD twin produced from
`OutOfSync`/`Degraded` in D512. **That agreement is the cross-vendor claim the type
makes**, and it is now measured on both sides rather than asserted from two lenses
that were only ever read separately.

All ten mapped services have now met the real API, each to the extent its verbs go:
seven governance services through the full write loop (create, converged re-plan,
hand-injected drift, repair, retirement with a tombstone), cert-manager through
create and converge, and the two GitOps mappings through observation — which is the
WHOLE of what a witness does, since neither ever writes. MATURITY said seven of ten
and now says ten, with the distinction spelled out rather than flattened.

Two things the exercise turned up, neither a defect:

- **The CRD carries a `status` subresource**, so a plain merge patch silently does
  not set status. The first attempt looked like a lens that ignored its condition —
  the object simply had none. Worth recording because "the driver read nothing" and
  "there was nothing to read" are indistinguishable from the observation alone, and
  this session has now been caught by that shape several times.
- **Flux's `source.repoURL` observes a NAME, not a URL.** A Kustomization references
  a GitRepository by name; the URL lives on that other object. The vocabulary mapping
  already says exactly this — *"spec.sourceRef (the GitRepository name; URL
  resolution is a future lens)"* — so the honest thing was to confirm the mapping
  rather than to "fix" the driver toward it. Worth noting that the mapping being
  right here is the D538–D545 register paying off in its intended way: the first
  question on meeting a surprise was what the published mapping claims, and it had
  an answer.

The attribute's stated PURPOSE — pin which repo governs the cluster — is not served
by a name, since two clusters can each have a `GitRepository` called `platform`
pointing somewhere different. Resolving it means reading the referenced object, which
is a driver change with its own failure modes (the CRD may not be installed), so it
is named here rather than done in passing.

## D550 — a read gated on a write predicate made the k8s driver contradict itself

Adopting a Flux `Kustomization` that exists on a live cluster refused with `k8s
driver: unknown service "flux-kustomization"`. The driver serves ten mapped services.
Two of them — `flux-kustomization` and `argocd-application` — are observe-only: their
mappings have no write lens, deliberately, because groundhold witnesses a GitOps
reconciler and never authors it (author-vs-witness).

Every verb consulted `genericMapping`, which is the registry AND `writeSafe`. So the
two observe-only mappings fell through to `requireService`, a hand-coded list of
seven that predates the registry, and were disowned. Meanwhile `discover` asks
`mappingFor` — the registry alone — and on the same cluster, in the same run,
enumerated `argoproj.io/v1alpha1/Application/default/root-app` with `health.status`
and `service.managed` marked `measured`. The driver reported the object as real and
then denied serving it, depending on which door the question came through.

Reading is not writing. `Observe` and `ClassifyChange` now ask the registry;
`Create`/`Update`/`Delete` keep the write-safety check. The refusal for a write to an
observe-only mapping now says what is true — *observed but not written, its mapping
has no write lens* — because "unknown service" for a service the driver demonstrably
serves sends the reader hunting the wrong bug, which is what it cost here.

`CompetingManagers` was worse than the gate suggested. It is the check that stops
groundhold taking over an object a continuous reconciler already owns, and it was
built entirely on the hand-coded RBAC path: `requireService`, then `kindInfo`, which
knows four kinds. Measured across all ten mapped services, **six failed**, for two
different reasons — three on the gate, three deeper on `kindInfo`. It fails closed,
so nothing unsafe happened; adoption of those six was simply impossible, and the
error named a competing-reconciler check that had never run. It now resolves the
object path through the mapping the way `Claim` already did, and falls back to the
RBAC path only for services with no mapping.

The shape is D505 again: a hard-coded list living next to a registry that already
knows the answer. What is new is that the list had stopped being *reachable* for the
verbs that mattered — every write verb checked the registry first and returned, so
the list was only ever consulted on the paths where it was wrong. A stale constant
that most callers bypass is harder to see than one they all use, because the bypass
looks like coverage.

## D551 — a documented divergence is still a broken contract

With D550 in, the same adopt got far enough to compare, and refused honestly:
`platform.source.repoURL: declared https://github.com/acme/platform.git but reality
says platform`. The Flux mapping copied `spec.sourceRef.name` — the NAME of a
`GitRepository` object — into `source.repoURL`, marked `derivation: measured`.

Both the mapping comment and the vocabulary said so out loud: *"URL resolution is a
future lens"*. That made it honest prose sitting on top of a broken machine contract.
`capability.gitops.application` exists to be controller-neutral, and the attribute's
stated purpose is to pin WHICH repo governs the cluster. ArgoCD emitted a URL, Flux a
local label, under one path — so no portable contract could express the thing the
attribute is for, and the value was not provenance at all, since two clusters can each
hold a `GitRepository/platform` aimed at different repositories. Writing the gap down
does not make the two values comparable.

The fix is a fifth op, `resolve-ref`: a SECOND read, declared in the mapping document
rather than hidden in Go. That keeps the closed-op discipline — invariant #4 is met
with one more named thing, not a richer expression language — and keeps the hop
reviewable. Failure modes are spelled out because a hop has more of them than a copy:
a dangling ref yields a diagnostic NAMING the missing referent and no value (never a
fabricated URL, and never silence — D522's lesson is that a failed read which says
nothing is indistinguishable from a world that is empty), while a transport failure
is a hard error exactly as the primary read is.

The fingerprint had to grow with it. A resolve-ref attribute reads a field on another
kind, in another API group, in a different OpenAPI document; leaving it out would let
the referent's schema drift under a pin that claims to cover the attribute, which is
the precise hole D132 exists to close. `guardDrift` now fetches and merges the
referent's document, and the mapped surface carries both halves — the pin moved from
`7fc563bb` to `d28da26b`, and the `GitRepository` CRD schema is vendored the way D511
vendored the others: recorded verbatim from a live API server, not written from
memory (D317).

Proven on the live k3d cluster: adopt now succeeds and the ledger records
`source.repoURL = https://github.com/acme/platform.git`, `measured` — resolved across
two objects, and true.

## D552 — the mappings block claimed a service that measures nothing, and credited one service's work to its sibling

D551 turned on the vocabulary's `mappings:` block, so the next question was whether
the block is true elsewhere. Two capabilities are served by more than one service on
the SAME cloud — `workload.container` by ECS and App Runner, `gitops.application` by
ArgoCD and Flux — and that is where a wrong line does the most damage, because the
reader finds a plausible mapping and has no way to see it belongs to a different
service.

D538's gate collects provider prefixes per CAPABILITY: "does any attribute name
`aws`?". Naming `aws` once therefore covered every AWS service beneath it. The gate
was green and enforcing something weaker than its name — the fourth time this month
(D323, D325, D328, D464).

Measured by RUNNING the drivers against their own fixtures, not by reading them
(D317), in both directions:

**Understatement.** ECS emits five attribute paths; the vocabulary named `aws.ecs` on
one. On `availability.class`, `network.publicExposure`, `replicas.minimum` and
`tls.enforced` a reader found only `aws.apprunner` — a sibling service with genuinely
different behaviour (App Runner's minimum cannot be zero; ECS's `desiredCount` can,
and the driver then omits the attribute rather than claiming a minimum of zero). Four
mappings written, each derived from the driver source, because D538's own warning is
that a wrong mapping is worse than an absent one.

**Overstatement, which is worse.** `workload.container` named `gcp.gke` on seven
attributes — "HPA minReplicas", "Binary Authorization", "Ingress TLS + redirect".
Nothing measures them. The driver itself says so: `ServiceCapabilities()` reports
`gke -> capability.cluster.kubernetes`, and `observeGKE` emits five paths, all
cluster attributes. Two of the seven also restated, more vaguely, what
`capability.cluster.kubernetes` already says precisely about the same fields.

An absent line reads as absent. An unbacked line is indistinguishable from a backed
one and is trusted for exactly that reason. The seven are removed from `mappings:`
and kept, verbatim and labelled, outside it — the design intent is real and worth
having; it was in the wrong block.

Both gates run the drivers and live in the drivers' own packages, where the
happy-path fixtures are. The GKE one is scoped by the capability the driver reports
serving, not merely by path name: GKE does emit `location.region` and
`availability.class`, but for the cluster capability, so a path-level check would
have passed two of the seven claims. Asking the driver what it serves is what keeps
those apart.

One of the two gates shipped with the flaw it was written to catch. Its vocabulary
reader returned "no mappings" when the document failed to parse, so a malformed file
passed every check — silence read as consent, the same shape as D513 and D522. The
mutation meter found it: an injected duplicate key made the document unparseable and
the gate went green. A parse failure now fails the test.

What these gates do NOT cover, stated rather than implied by a green check: the
general property "every service names every path it measures", for all ~145 services.
That needs happy-path truth for each one. These cover the twin services, which is
where a sibling's mapping gets mistaken for your own.

## D553 — the same class on the two clouds D552 had not looked at

D552 gated where it had measured. That is how a gate ends up covering exactly the
ground already swept, so the remaining implementations of the same capability were
run the same way.

**Azure.** `azure.containerapps` was named on one attribute of nine and measures
four. There is no sibling to confuse it with — Container Apps is Azure's only
implementation of `workload.container` — but the failure is not milder for that. An
attribute documented in detail for AWS and GCP and silent for Azure reads as *not
supported there*, which is a stronger and more wrong claim than *undocumented*. The
four are written from the driver: `location` lower-cased, `zonal` by construction (a
Container Apps environment sits in one zone unless the environment enables zone
redundancy, which this capability does not configure — so Azure's value differs from
the `regional` both other clouds report), `template.scale.minReplicas`, and TLS as
the NEGATION of `configuration.ingress.allowInsecure`.

**Kubernetes.** The GitOps twins were already correct: every attribute names both
`k8s.argocd` and `k8s.flux`. The gate went green on its first run, which is the
condition under which a gate most often turns out to measure nothing (D328), so it
was driven red by deleting one mapping line and confirmed to name the missing pair.
It is a ratchet now, not a discovery — and it is the one that matters most, since
D551's wrong value lived under a correctly-named mapping. Naming the controller is
necessary and not sufficient.

Three gates now, one per driver package, each running its own driver against its own
fixture. The instrument is the same in all three; only the fixtures differ, which is
why it could not be one gate.

## D554 — the same list-beside-a-registry, measured on the three clouds and found clean

D550 was a hand-coded dispatch list that had fallen behind the registry next to it.
The obvious question was whether the cloud drivers carry the same shape, so all three
were measured by running them: every service the driver's own `ServiceCapabilities()`
reports, put through `requireService`.

**Nothing was wrong.** AWS lists 54 tokens and serves 54; GCP and Azure agree with
their registries too, in both directions — no served service is refused, and no token
is accepted that nothing serves. Recorded as a negative result because rediscovering
it costs more than writing it down, and because "we checked and it was fine" is the
part that never survives in memory otherwise.

The first measurement said all 46 GCP services were refused, including three named
literally in the gate. That was the instrument: the probe constructed the driver with
project `"p"`, and the gate validates the project id before it looks at the service
at all. A measurement that condemns everything is nearly always the measurement
(D521).

What was missing is that the agreement was a fact about today's maintenance rather
than a property anything held — the state a gap is in just before it opens, and
exactly the state k8s was in until three services stopped being adoptable. One gate
per driver package now holds it, with a floor so a registry that stops reporting
services cannot pass by emptiness (D328).

k8s is deliberately not given the same gate: two of its mapped services are
observe-only and MUST fail the write gate. The property there is the read/write split
D550 established, which its own tests hold.

## D555 — adopt refused what it could read and stayed silent about what it could not

Chasing D551's new failure mode on the live cluster produced a sharper one. With the
referenced `GitRepository` present, adopting the Flux Kustomization REFUSED
`adoption-mismatch` — it read the URL and it differed from the declaration. With the
same object deleted, the same declaration could not be read at all, and adopt
succeeded, printing `"status": "adopted"` and nothing else.

The weaker evidence bought the friendlier outcome. That is not a bug in the decision:
F-LC3 part 3 settled deliberately that a declared attribute the driver cannot observe
is INTENT, not a lie, and the ledger records it honestly — source
`candidate-declared`, derivation `declared`, never `measured`. Every downstream
consumer sees the truth.

What a human sees is `adopted`. A capability confirmed against reality and one taken
on faith read identically, and an operator binding forty capabilities has no way to
learn which is which. This is the shape the pilot found in D529: the machine contract
right, the sentence a person reads wrong, and wrong toward comfort.

The channel already existed and so did the principle, written in this file's own
comment on `Notes` (D322): *adopt is holding the contradicting observation in its hand
at the one moment designed to confront a declaration with the world; skipping it
silently is the lie of omission the package's own first line forbids.* D322 applied
that to an `assumed` declaration reality contradicts. The attribute that could not be
read AT ALL — a strictly weaker position — got nothing. D527 again: a rule written as
prose in one place does not propagate; only a shared mechanism does, and here the
mechanism was three lines away.

Adopt now notes each intent-recorded attribute, naming the capability, the path and
the basis. The converse is pinned too: a run in which every declared attribute WAS
measured stays silent, because a note on every adoption is a note nobody reads — the
pilot's own argument from D537, that a signal which is always on stops being one.

Not settled here, and deliberately: whether a FRESH reading that cannot measure an
attribute should retire the stale value that is still inside its TTL. Today it does
not — observations are latest-per-path, so a value keeps standing while the newest
reading says "I could not look". That is defensible under the evidence model and it is
the same shape F-LC3 fixed one level up, where "the resource is gone" had to become an
observation because as a diagnostic it left the binding a no-op forever. Doing the
equivalent for an attribute is a contract change, not a missing line.

## D556 — the driver explained itself and adopt threw the sentence away

D555 tells an operator that a declared attribute went unconfirmed. The driver knows
WHY, says so, and adopt was holding that sentence in a discarded return value:

    if _, err := observe.Run(...); err != nil {

`observe.Run` returns diagnostics; `_` dropped them. On the live cluster the k8s
driver said *GitRepository "platform" referenced by spec.sourceRef.name does not
exist — spec.url not represented*, and the operator got *the provider emitted no
value for it*. The gap between those two is the gap between knowing something is
unverified and knowing what would make it verifiable.

They now ride the same `Notes` channel D555 used, so the human-facing print gets them
for free — the one place that formats notes covers every source of them.

Where they deliberately do NOT go: the ledger. D242 settled that an unreadable
capability's reason is *never hashed and never an event*, and a diagnostic is the same
kind of thing — a fact about this run's reading, not about the world. It belongs in
the run's report, which is where it now is. Recording it would also have meant
scanning free text for credentials before hashing it into an immutable chain (D309,
D536), a cost with no matching benefit for text nobody can act on later anyway.

## D557 — two channels answering about the same object, and only one of them checked

D550 had a second half. `discover` asked the mapping registry; `observe` asked the
registry AND a write-safety predicate. On the live cluster one run enumerated
`argoproj.io/v1alpha1/Application/default/root-app` with `health.status` and
`service.managed` marked `measured`, and refused `argocd-application` as an unknown
service. One object, one run, two answers — and each channel was internally
consistent, which is why nothing noticed.

D554 held the dispatch gate to the service registry. That would NOT have caught this:
both k8s registries agreed about which services exist; they disagreed about which
subset each verb serves. The property that catches it is narrower and more useful —
**everything discovery enumerates must be observable** — because discovery is the one
verb that tells an operator a resource is real.

Measured across the three clouds before writing anything: all clean. AWS discovers
50, GCP 44, Azure 42; every one is in its registry and passes its gate. Held now
rather than left to maintenance, with a floor so an empty discovery set cannot pass by
emptiness (D328). The k8s gate — the only one whose subject actually broke — was
driven red by restoring the old predicate and named both observe-only services.

`CertifyDiscoverability` already ran the other direction (every certified service is
discoverable or exempt for a closed-set reason). Both directions now hold. A pair of
one-way checks is not a round trip, and the k8s defect lived exactly in the half that
was missing.

## D558 — the same discarded return value in the two places nobody is watching

D556 fixed one site. The identical `_` sat in two more, and both are worse than the
one that was found first.

`converge` weaves in an `observe` child when knowledge is stale and takes
`c2, _, e2 := o.Run("observe", ...)`. The child's stdout — which carries
`diagnostics` — went to `_`, and its stderr was read ONLY when the child failed. So
the dropped case is precisely the one worth having: observe succeeded, and while
succeeding reported that it could not measure something. The relay pattern sits three
lines below the bug (D202, surfacing the plan child's cost estimate); a child's report
is not noise because the child exited 0.

`refresh` is the sharper one. Its entire job is re-observing proofs before they decay
— keeping the evidence honest is the reason the agent exists — and it recorded a
capability as plain `refreshed` while the driver was saying it could not read part of
it. Of the three sites this is the one that matters most, because refresh runs
unattended on a schedule: nobody is at a terminal when the sentence is dropped.

Both now carry it, `converge` to its human channel and `refresh` in a `notes` field
on its report. Neither goes to the ledger, for D242's reason (an unreadable
capability's reason is never hashed and never an event) — this is a fact about a
reading, not about the world.

The pattern worth naming: `_` on a multi-value return is a decision that something
is not worth knowing, made once and then invisible. Three of them, all on the same
call, all made silently, and the two nobody found first were the two with no human in
the loop.

## D559 — the published schema and the published output, neither checked against the other

D516 walks the output schema and requires the Go tree to carry every property it
promises: a promised field nothing emits. The leak runs the other way too — a field
the CLI PUBLISHES that the schema never describes. Nothing rejects it, because the
schema's shapes are open, so it is invisible from both sides.

Measured: `adoptResult` has published `notes` since D322 and the schema never
mentioned it. Three more kinds of note were added on top of it (D555, D556) before
anyone compared the two. A consumer generating types from the published schema cannot
see a field the tool emits.

This is D552's overstatement in mirror image: two published artefacts describing one
thing, each maintained on its own, neither gated against the other. In D552 the
vocabulary claimed more than the drivers did; here the binary emits more than the
schema admits. Both are only findable by asking one artefact about the other.

D516's comment declined this direction because it needs a def→struct table, "which is
its own thing to rot". The answer is a table that is itself gated: every entry must
resolve to a live def AND a live struct or the gate fails, and the defs not yet pinned
are a ratchet that may only fall — 18 today, a number rather than an implication. That
turns "we did not check the rest" into something a reader can see, which is the whole
argument of D525: a register's own name is a claim, and a gap with a count is honest
where a gap with a green check is not.

## D560 — paying D559's ratchet down the same hour it was created

D559 shipped with 18 unpinned schema shapes. A register created and left at its
opening number is a register that documents the author's stopping point, so it was
worked immediately. Sixteen of twenty shapes now have their producing struct pinned;
four remain, and two of those (`code`, `explain`) are leaf shapes with no struct at
all.

Pinning them found the drift the gate was built for, in the outputs that are consumed
most:

- **`verifyReport`** published `contract`, `contractVersion`, `candidateFor` and
  `code` — the identity of what was verified, undescribed.
- **`applyResult`** published `outputs` (D283 typed outputs — the values a downstream
  capability folds), `outcomes` (D379 per-action results, the field that exists so a
  partially-applied run cannot read as clean), `reachability` and `retryAfterSeconds`.
- **`anchorDocument`** published `manifest`, `baseEvents`, `ledgerId`, `snapshotHash`
  and `trust`. That one is the sharpest: an anchor IS the artefact a receiver checks a
  ledger against, and five of the fields carrying that proof — including the complete
  forest guard D184 added after the chain audit — were not in the document describing
  it.
- **`convergeResult`** published `convergence` and `reachability`. `convergence` is
  D136's whole point: only `verified` earns the CONVERGED banner, and a consumer
  reading the schema could not see the field that says so.

Every description was written from the field's own comment in the source, not from
memory — the D538 rule, because a description invented here would be believed with
exactly the same authority as the accurate ones.

None of this was broken code. It is twenty artefacts and twenty structs maintained
side by side for months with nothing comparing them, which is the same sentence as
D552 and D465 with different nouns. The pattern is now hard to miss: whenever this
project publishes two descriptions of one thing, they have drifted, and the drift is
always in the direction that flatters — the schema omits what exists, the docs claim
what does not.

## D561 — "every provider the drivers serve" meant the three drivers the gate could ask

D545 closed the vocabulary-mapping register at zero and wrote the reason into the
constant: `vocabMappingGapBaseline = 0 // COMPLETE (D545): every provider the drivers
serve is named`. It asked `aws`, `gcp` and `azure`. The k8s driver — ten services
across seven capabilities — was never asked, because it did not implement
`ServiceCapabilities()`, so the gate could not reach it and said nothing about the
fact.

The omission was mechanical and the claim was not. This is D525's rule at the level of
a comment rather than a register name: *a gate's stated scope is a claim, and a scope
that happens to equal "whatever the instrument could reach" is the one nobody
re-derives.* It is also the exact shape of D552 a week later, where a gate compared
provider prefixes per capability and a green result meant less than its name.

Found sideways. Chasing D551's `resolve-ref` into cert-manager showed that
`capability.certificate.tls` names `aws.acm` and `gcp.certificatemanager` and not
`k8s.certmanager`, although the k8s driver serves that capability and measures three
of its attributes. That is not one missing line — it is a whole driver outside the
register.

`ServiceCapabilities()` for k8s is derived from the mapping registry, not written as a
second list (D550's lesson: a list beside a registry falls behind it, and the bypass
looks like coverage). With the fourth driver asked, four capability/provider pairs came
up undocumented, and seven attribute mappings were written from the driver source, per
D538's rule that a mapping invented from memory would carry the same authority as an
accurate one:

- the RBAC role's flat permission set (`<apiGroup>/<resource>:<verb>`, core spelled
  `core`), with `resourceNames` belonging to the GRANT's scope and reported as a
  diagnostic rather than folded in;
- mutating as "any verb outside get/list/watch", and privileged as the full wildcard,
  `bind`/`escalate`/`impersonate`, or any WRITE on an rbac object — a re-grant vector;
- the grant's scope, which in Kubernetes is not read from a field at all: the object
  KIND is the scope (RoleBinding → resource, ClusterRoleBinding → account);
- the certificate's primary domain as `spec.dnsNames[0]`, further SANs being
  implementation detail carried as a diagnostic, and auto-renew as config-intent
  because a cert-manager Certificate renews by design;
- default-deny ingress as `policyTypes` containing Ingress with an EMPTY rule list —
  config-intent, since the policy states an intent and no packet was sent, and a
  non-empty `podSelector` still reports false but says the namespace is not covered.

The mutation meter then refused the first fix. Re-injecting "stop asking the k8s
driver" left the gate GREEN — dropping a driver SHRINKS the set that needs
documenting, so zero gaps is exactly what a missing driver produces. The gate could
not detect its own defect, which is why the defect lasted. It now asserts WHO was
asked, by name, before it believes a zero: a floor on the subject rather than the
container (D328/D488). The first mutant I wrote for this did not even compile, and a
build failure reads as "caught" while proving nothing — the third time that phantom
has shown up.

One more thing, seen first-hand: while writing those entries a broken YAML document
made the gate report MORE undocumented pairs rather than failing, because it read a
parse error as "this file declares no mappings". The same shape D552 shipped with. A
parse failure is now fatal in both gates. Every instrument that reads a document must
distinguish *the document says nothing* from *I could not read the document*, and this
project keeps writing the version that cannot.

## D562 — the fourth driver was missing from the count gate for the same reason

D561 found the k8s driver outside the vocabulary-mappings gate because it did not
implement `ServiceCapabilities()`. The obvious follow-up was whether other "ask all
the drivers" loops meant three as well. One did: `TestMaturityCountsMatchReality`,
the gate written after MATURITY.md — the honesty document — was caught drifting three
ways at once (D352).

It reads AWS, GCP and Azure service counts from the drivers and compares them against
the table. The same table's first row says *k8s driver (10 mapped services)*, and
nothing checked it. Not because anyone decided to skip it: the loop needs a
`CapabilityMapper`, and until D561 the k8s driver was not one. A missing interface
quietly redefined "all the drivers" in every place that phrase appears.

Now gated, and driven red by claiming nine. Two "all the drivers" loops, one cause,
one interface — which is the same conclusion as D527 and D550: what propagates is a
shared mechanism, never a phrase.

## D563 — an exemption written for a test double quietly acquired a production driver

The silent-ignore guard skips any provider that declares no consumed operand set, and
its comment says who that is: *"A driver that declares no consumed set (the Fake
double, which reads no operands) is exempt; the guard binds the real cloud drivers."*

The k8s driver is a real driver. It reads `name`, `namespace`, `issuerRef` and
`secretName`, declares none of them, and therefore qualified for an exemption written
for a test double. Every k8s candidate could carry any misspelled operand and the
guard waved it through — the pilot's D530 failure, reached by a different route.

This is D561 again with different nouns: a capability defined by "whoever implements
the interface" quietly excludes whoever does not, and nothing reports the exclusion,
because from inside the loop there is nothing to see.

The declared set is derived, not restated. `namespace` is only declared for a kind the
mapping registry says is Namespaced, because it is only READ for those — declaring it
for a cluster-scoped service would re-open the hole for exactly the operand most
likely to be meaningful (a `namespace` on a ClusterRole does nothing, and an operator
who wrote one meant something by it). The two lens operands hang off the LENS name, so
a mapping that adopts the lens inherits them and nothing has to be updated twice.

## D564 — the guard was fixed and the wiring was not, and the test could not tell

Proving D563 on the live cluster produced `nothing-to-change` where a refusal was due.
Tracing that found the larger one.

D530 came from the field in these words: a partner declared `memory_mb` on a BOUND,
CONVERGED function; `validate` said OK, `plan` sealed with zero actions and zero
warnings, the operand was ignored, and the function kept dying on the default 128 MB.
The fix made the guard iterate CAPABILITIES rather than ACTIONS, exactly so that a
converged deployment would be covered.

`Compile` returns `nothing-to-change` sixty lines BEFORE it reaches the guard. So a
PARTIALLY converged deployment is covered (a plan is sealed, the guard runs) and a
FULLY converged one is not — and full convergence is the reported case. The remedy was
correct and unreachable for the state that motivated it.

The test could not have caught it. It calls `refuseUnknownOperands(nil, cand, in)`
directly, which proves the function and says nothing about whether anything calls it
in that state. This is the harness rule the D507 series arrived at, in its most
expensive form yet: **a passing assertion is a claim about what was EXERCISED, and a
unit test aimed at the fixed function is aimed away from the bug.** The new test goes
through `Compile` with a fully converged world, and the guard now runs before
convergence is declared rather than after.

Verified on the live k3d cluster: a misspelled `nmaespace` refuses `unknown-operand`
with the edit hint pointing at the candidate, and the clean candidate still reports
convergence.

## D565 — `make check` reported success without re-reading what it was checking

Building a client binary starts with verifying the DELIVERY COMMIT in its own
worktree (D496, written after a red tag). That is what caught this: `make check` was
green in the working tree and RED on the identical commit in a fresh one.

The k8s vocabulary is embedded into the binary, and six spec files had been edited
across D551–D563 without regenerating the embedded copy. `TestEmbeddedMatchesSpec`
exists exactly for that and had been passing — from Go's test CACHE. It reads
`spec/vocab/*.yaml`, which lives OUTSIDE the Go module (`go/` is the module root,
`spec/` its sibling), so the cache never saw its inputs change and replayed a pass for
a gate whose subject had moved underneath it. A fresh worktree has no cache entry, ran
it for real, and failed.

Said plainly: **every commit from D551 to D564 shipped an embedded vocabulary out of
date with its own spec, while I reported "all gates passed" after each one.** The
reports were not lies about what the command printed; the command was wrong, and the
process that catches exactly this is the one I only run before a delivery.

Four test packages read outside the module — `vocab`, `provider`, `state`, `backup` —
and `provider` holds most of the gates written this week: the doc counts, the
vocabulary-mappings register, the published-schema check, the changelog and
decision-number gates. All of them were cacheable and all of them could go stale the
same way. I had in fact hit it twice earlier the same day and worked around it with
`-count=1` without recognising the class, which is its own lesson: a workaround that
makes the symptom go away buries the cause more effectively than the cause hides
itself.

`make check` now runs `go test ./... -count=1`. Twenty-six seconds instead of one and
a half, next to a conformance run that already costs more, and no list of "packages
that need it" to fall behind the packages that do (D550). The inner dev loop can still
use a cached `go test` deliberately.

The general rule this belongs to, now three for three this week (D552's parse-silent
reader, D561's unasked driver, this): **a gate that can report success without
re-reading its subject is not a gate.** Caching is just the version where the subject
is invisible rather than unreadable.

## D566 — one sentence for two states whose remedies are opposite

Exercising the cert-manager write path on the live cluster meant writing a
`capability.certificate.tls` contract from scratch, and I wrote its hard constraints
with `verify: {method: provider-api}` — which blocks the very first plan, because no
observation can exist before the resource does.

The system was right and the record already said so. D290 hit this while preparing the
Azure canary and wrote it down as *"the natural mistake a first-time author makes with
a four-valued verifier"*. Making the same mistake a year later, with the entry in the
repository, is the measurement: **the record is not the channel**. What an author gets
is

    requires provider-api verification; not evaluable from the candidate alone

and that sentence covers two states whose remedies point in opposite directions:

- **bound, not yet observed** → `observe --record` resolves it;
- **not created yet** → observing will NEVER resolve it; the contract is wrong for
  create time.

Take the natural reading in the second case and you run `observe`, get nothing, and
are in the loop D290 describes.

`verify` cannot tell them apart, and should not learn to. It is a pure function of the
two documents — that is why it is dual-implemented and conformance-pinned — and
widening its inputs to improve a message would trade the property for the wording.
`converge` has the ledger, is the verb an author actually runs, and said nothing. It
now names each hard provider-api constraint whose subject is unbound and says why
observing cannot settle it.

Two things kept honest. The hint fires only for an UNBOUND subject: telling an author
their contract is wrong when it is merely unobserved sends them to rewrite a correct
document, which is a worse outcome than silence. And an unreadable ledger yields NO
hints rather than all of them — inferring "unbound" from "could not read" would give
confident wrong advice, and D75's skip-loudly applies to advice as much as to reads.

Checked against the real binary rather than the double: `verify` does publish
`subject` and `verifyMethod` under those names, so the parse that drives this is not a
test-only fiction. Then the advice itself was tested by taking it — the same contract
with `method: static` runs the full loop on the live k3d cluster and CONVERGES,
creating a cert-manager Certificate with its domain, secret name, issuer ref and
ownership labels. Advice nobody has followed is a claim like any other.

## D567 — the CLI absorbed an unknown flag as a positional and answered anyway

Onboarding the live cluster meant running the verbs a new adopter runs. `discover`
found 170 resources across seven capability types. The natural next step is `posture`,
so I ran

    groundhold posture --ledger <l> --at <ts> --discovery discovery.json

and got `"shadow": 0`, a `postureHash`, and `OK` — over a cluster holding 169 objects
under no contract. Posture does not take `--discovery`. The flag switch's `default:`
arm appends anything unrecognised to the POSITIONAL list, so the flag and its value
were absorbed and the run answered a question it had never been asked, with a hash on
it. `--zupelnie-wymyslona-flaga xyz` gets the same treatment and the same hash.

This is D530's class — a declaration nobody reads — one layer out from where the pilot
found it. The compiler now refuses an operand no driver consumes; the command line
accepted a flag no verb consumes. It is also D323's shape: that gate checked `--at` was
PRESENT and not that it PARSED, and this one checked nothing at all.

Two fixes, because there are two failures.

**An unrecognised token starting with `-` is now an operator error.** A lone `-` stays
a positional (stdin, by convention). This is complete and safe: no legitimate
invocation passes a flag no verb defines.

**`--discovery` on posture is refused by name, with the reason.** It is a *recognised*
flag — some verbs take it — that posture ignores, which the first fix cannot catch.
Posture classifies what a CRAWL swept, and the difference is load-bearing rather than
cosmetic: a crawl records whether each scope was listed COMPLETELY, and that is exactly
what `shadowLowerBound` is a claim about. Folding a `discover` output would let posture
report a shadow count with nothing behind it. Worth naming as its own failure because
posture's OWN remediation text tells an operator to run `discover` — the tool set this
trap for itself.

What is NOT fixed, stated rather than implied: **a recognised flag that a given verb
ignores is still silent, everywhere except posture.** Fifty-one verbs and seventy
global flags; a per-verb table is fifty-one entries, and a wrong entry refuses a legal
invocation, which is worse for an operator than the current silence. It needs to be
derived from what each verb reads rather than restated beside it (D550), and that is a
design slice, not a line. The count is here so the gap is a number.

## D568 — the class an operator lands in first was the one with no way out

Walking the onboarding path on the live cluster: pair the provider, crawl (9 resources
in the scope, `complete` — matching `discover` exactly for that namespace), classify.
Posture reported 8 shadow and 1 decayed, each with a recipe, and exit 2. All correct.

Then follow the decayed recipe's first step (`refresh`) and stop. The row moves from
`decayed` — which has a recipe — to `unknown`, which has `{"action": ""}`. Following
half of a two-step instruction leaves an operator with LESS guidance than before they
started. And `unknown` is not an edge case: a binding with no audit verdict is the
normal state the moment an adoption finishes, so it is the first thing a new operator
sees.

Posture's own usage line promises "managed-ok/drifted/shadow/decayed/unknown with
adopt/converge/observe recipes". Three classes had one. `managed-ok` needs none —
advice on a healthy row is noise, and the test pins that it stays bare. Two `unknown`
arms had none, and they need different things:

- **no audit verdict** → run `audit`. Not a judgement call: the decayed recipe names
  that verb as its own second step, two lines away. The note says what the class
  actually means, because "unknown" reads as alarming and the truth is milder —
  *nothing is wrong; nothing has been PROVEN right yet.*
- **unverifiable verdict** → `remodel`. Re-auditing cannot resolve an incomparable
  verdict; advising it would be a loop that never terminates. The steps name the two
  documents and `explain`, not a verb.

The sharper half came from following the fixed advice. `groundhold audit` reported
PROVEN — and re-running posture the way I had been running it still printed
`unknown: 1`, because posture reads verdicts only when given `--contract`. An operator
who takes the advice and re-runs the command they already know concludes the advice
did nothing. Both recipes that end in a re-check now carry the flag. **Advice that
cannot be seen to have worked is indistinguishable from advice that did not.**

Verified end to end on k3d: unknown → audit → PROVEN → `managedOk: 1, unknown: 0`.
Advice nobody has followed is a claim like any other (D566 said the same thing about
a different one, four hours earlier).

One process note. The first fix silently did not apply: a `.replace()` without an
assertion, on an anchor I had guessed from truncated terminal output — the real line
said "not drift" where I had written "not decay". The test caught it, which is the
system working, but the no-op is the same shape as everything else in this series and
I wrote it while writing about it.

## D569 — the recipe's second line could not run, and its first line proved it

Continuing the adopter walk from D568: posture reports a shadow resource with an
`adopt` recipe, so follow it verbatim.

    step 1  groundhold discover --provider k8s --region default --at <ts>   -> 9 resources
    step 2  groundhold adopt <c> <k> --map <cap>=<pid> --discovery ... --ledger ... --at <ts>
            -> adopt requires an explicit --provider ... INVALID

`adopt` is in `providerVerbs`, the CLI's closed set of verbs that must refuse a
defaulted fake driver (F4: fake fabricates reality, so it is never a silent default).
The recipe omits the flag. Step 1 of the SAME recipe carries it — two consecutive
lines disagreeing about the same tool, which is the tell that neither was ever run.

D568 found a recipe whose result was invisible. This one does not execute at all.
Both are the same thing: **advice is a published claim, and these were the only
published claims in the system nobody had ever exercised.**

The gate derives its rule rather than restating it — every `groundhold <verb>` string
in every posture recipe is checked against `providerVerbs` itself, so a verb added to
that set later cannot leave a stale recipe behind (D550's lesson about a list beside a
registry). It skips prose steps ("edit the contract so the two are comparable"), which
are instructions rather than commands, and asserts it examined at least five commands
so an empty walk cannot pass as clean (D328).

Then the whole recipe was run start to finish on the live cluster, from an empty
ledger: discover → adopt → crawl → posture, ending at `managedOk: 1, shadow: 8` for a
namespace holding nine objects. The advice now takes an operator where it says it will.

## D570 — adoption binds; it does not own, and the retirement path never asked

Following posture's shadow note verbatim on the live cluster — *"to remove it, ADOPT
it under a minimal contract, then declare state: retired and converge (the delete
flows through every gate)"* — the delete died:

    action a-delete-prod-quota failed: labels do not match — refusing to delete a
    ResourceQuota that ...

The driver is right. Adoption BINDS a resource; ownership is stamped by a separate
`claim`, and the compiler emitted one only in the create/update loop. The retirement
loop built its delete with no `DependsOn` at all — while the REPLACEMENT delete two
hundred lines below carries `withClaim(...)` under the comment *create BEFORE destroy;
own BEFORE destroy*. The same file states the rule and the retirement path was the one
place that did not follow it.

The measurement corrected itself twice, and both corrections matter more than the fix.

**First reading: "an adopted resource can never be retired."** False. I re-ran the
walk on a resource with no drift, expecting the dead end to be total, and the
retirement SUCCEEDED — because any intervening `converge`, including a no-op one,
emits the claim. The real gap is narrower and matches the note exactly: adopt → retire
with nothing in between. Worth writing down because the wrong version was the more
dramatic one, and I had already started drafting it.

**Second: the safety objection dissolved.** Claiming before a delete looked like it
deserved a design decision — MATURITY gap 12 says a mistaken claim is invisible to
every ownership check, and claim-then-delete is its worst composition. But a plain
no-op converge already claims, and the docs already tell operators to converge. The
claim is not new risk introduced at the delete; it is the claim the system performs
anyway, finally performed where it is needed.

The first attempt then failed on `invalid reversibility` — my claim action omitted
`Risk`, which the plan validator requires and the create/update twin sets. A validator
that refuses an action missing its risk declaration is the system working; it caught a
half-built action before any cloud saw it.

Proven on k3d against an object created with `kubectl` and carrying no groundhold
labels: adopt → retire, no converge in between, `APPLIED`, and the ResourceQuota is
gone from the cluster.

## D571 — two recovery verbs demanded a flag they cannot use

Walking the disaster-recovery path: back up a live ledger, restore it, and check that
operations continue. They do — the restored ledger is line-for-line the original,
answers `plan` identically, accepts new events, and converges. That is the DR promise
kept, verified rather than assumed.

The check itself refused:

    groundhold anchor --ledger <restored>
    anchor requires an explicit --provider (aws|gcp|azure|k8s|fake) ... INVALID

`providerVerbs` states its own membership rule: "the CLOSED set of verbs that OBSERVE
or MUTATE real infrastructure through a provider driver". Two members do neither.
`runAnchor(ledgerPath, checkPath)` and `runRepair(ledgerPath, quarantine,
fingerprint, explain)` take no provider, and neither body names a driver. They are
pure ledger operations.

Nothing unsafe happened — it fails closed. What it costs is a lie about what the verb
does: passing `--provider k8s` to an integrity check tells the reader the check
contacts the cluster. It does not. And of all thirteen members, the two that were
wrong are the RECOVERY verbs, wanted precisely when a ledger is damaged and the
operator may not know or care which cloud it describes.

D567's mirror, four hours later: there a flag that meant nothing was accepted; here a
flag that means nothing was required. Both are the same defect — the set of inputs a
verb declares does not match the set it uses — and they fail in opposite directions,
which is why one was invisible and the other merely annoying.

An existing gate refused the edit until it was justified. `TestProviderVerbsMembership`
pins the exact set precisely so a change here cannot be casual, and it failed the
moment the two were removed — demanding the reason be written down next to the new
list. That is the discipline working on its author, which is the only test of it that
counts (D464).

Removing them is not the fail-open regression that comment warns about. The warning is
about a verb that reaches a driver losing its gate, so `fake` becomes a silent default;
these two have no provider path to fall open onto. The test pins both directions:
these two must work with no `--provider`, and the eleven that do reach a driver must
stay gated.

## D572 — the document explained the mechanism in full and left the scope to be inferred

Continuing the adopter walk into the path a migrating team takes: `hints`, the
terraform/pulumi translator. Fed an ordinary AWS state — an S3 bucket, an RDS
instance, an EC2 instance — it returned an empty `hints` array and three diagnostics:
*no vocabulary mapping for aws_s3_bucket, skipped*, and the same for the other two.

`spec/onboarding.md` describes this verb thoroughly and well: the translation rules,
the allowlist that keeps secrets and implementation noise out, why `expected` carries
no derivation claim, why the document is deliberately not hashed. It never says WHICH
types are translated. The table is one capability, `capability.database.relational`,
from three terraform types and three pulumi URNs — all GCP Cloud SQL.

The runtime is honest at the moment of use: every skip is a named diagnostic, never a
silent drop, exactly as the spec promises. So nobody is misled about a RESULT. What is
missing is the scope in the document, before an operator spends an afternoon
discovering it — and "the tool will tell you" is a poor answer for a page whose job is
to tell you first.

The one mapping that exists is good work, and worth saying so, since the fix here is
documentation rather than code: it emits `availability.class`, `engine.protocol`,
`location.region`, `network.publicExposure` and `service.managed` from a real state
file, and it declines to guess `recovery.rpo` from `point_in_time_recovery_enabled`,
emitting a diagnostic that the value needs a probe. That is the same discipline as an
absent observation — the reason to trust the six types that ARE mapped, and the reason
widening the table is per-service work rather than a loop.

Gated rather than merely written, because a scope in prose is precisely what falls
behind the code (D465, D552): the test reads the `case` arms of both dispatches and
requires every token to appear in the document. A seventh type cannot be added without
the sentence changing with it.

## D573 — "never the resource" is true, and something stays anyway

`unadopt` describes itself honestly: *removes the binding, never the resource*. An
operator reads that as leaving no trace. If groundhold CLAIMED the resource while it
was bound, one stays — the ownership marker — and they meet it a verb later.

Measured on the live cluster. A Role carrying groundhold labels for capability `app`,
adopted as `legacy`, then unadopted; the next converge planned a create and the driver
refused:

    action a-create-legacy failed: a Role already exists at this name and its
    labels are not ours — refusing to adopt it

Every step of that is correct. Ownership is recorded per CAPABILITY, not per tool
(D462), so a marker naming a different capability is foreign and the create fails
closed. The system was right four times in a row, which is worth recording as its own
result — this walk was looking for a defect and mostly found the design holding.

What was missing is the sentence. `unadopt` now says the marker stays, what it will
cause, and what to do instead — and only when the capability was actually CLAIMED,
because warning about a marker groundhold never wrote is the same species of false
statement the note exists to prevent (D555).

Then the note did not appear. It was in the JSON and nowhere else: the `note:`
rendering loop lived inline in the ADOPT branch, and `unadopt` has its own. D322's
comment states the rule it broke — notes go to the human channel *because "JSON alone
would bury it"* — and unadopt buried it. One shared `sayNotes` now, so a verb that
starts producing notes cannot silently omit them.

That is the same shape as D550, D561 and D563 in miniature: a behaviour implemented at
one call site instead of in a shared mechanism serves exactly the callers someone
remembered. Three of today's findings are that sentence with different nouns, and this
one appeared inside the fix for another.

## D574 — the fourth call site, and why the first three were not enough

Running the reachability probe against the cert-manager contract on the live cluster:

    web: probe error: k8s driver: unknown service "certmanager-cert"
         (wired: rbac-role, rbac-grant, rbac-clusterrole, ...)

The driver serves that service. It observes it, creates it, adopts it and retires it —
all proven on this cluster today. What it lacks is a PROBE for it, and `Probe` says so
two lines below its own gate:

    k8s driver: probes for service %q are not wired

That sentence was unreachable. `requireService` ran first and answered a different
question, so an operator reads "unknown service" as *this driver cannot see my
resource at all* and goes looking for a driver bug that does not exist.

**Why D550 missed it.** I found that defect by tracing ONE failing command — an adopt
— and fixed the call sites the trace passed through. The fix covered exactly the
trace. Enumerating the call sites afterwards, rather than following a failure through
them, is what turned this one up: four sites consult the gate, three now ask the
mapping registry first, and the fourth was the one no failing command had walked.

That is a method lesson, not a code one, and it is the more useful half: **a fix
derived from a trace covers the trace.** The same shape as the harness rule from D507
— a passing assertion is a claim about what was EXERCISED — applied to repair instead
of to testing.

The gate now asks the registry first and keeps both refusals distinct: a service the
driver serves gets *no probe is wired for it*, and one it does not serve still gets
*unknown service*, fail-closed. Both directions are pinned, because a friendlier
message that swallows the genuinely-unknown case would trade one wrong answer for
another.

## D575 — a recovery mechanism that works, rated nowhere

Walking the corruption path end to end, on a real ledger from the live cluster with
one event body edited by hand:

    attest   -> CORRUPTED, exit 5, naming the line and the broken link
    repair   -> chain-broken at line 7, validPrefixLines 6, a fingerprint, and the
                exact next command
    repair --quarantine                    -> REFUSED confirmation-required
    repair --quarantine --fingerprint <fp> -> repaired

Everything held. The consent gate refuses without the fingerprint. The quarantine file
keeps the WHOLE original — nineteen lines, not just the removed tail — which is the
right choice for forensics and not what I expected before looking. And the result says
what it cost, unprompted: *quarantined events may have mutated the cloud — re-observe
reality*, and *plans sealed BEFORE this repair are void*. A repaired ledger then
attests clean.

Two corrections to my own measurements along the way, both the same mistake. `echo $?`
after a pipe reports the status of `tail`, so `attest` on a tampered ledger looked
like it exited 0 while printing CORRUPTED — which would have been a serious finding
about the one verb whose job is detecting tampering. It exits 5. I had made the
identical error earlier the same day on a posture run. **A measurement that would be a
major finding deserves one more look before it is written down**, and twice now the
instrument was the thing at fault (D521 said the same about a test estate).

The gap is in the maturity document, not the code. It rates "Capsules, ed25519
signatures, DR restore/merge" as proven and does not mention `repair`, quarantine or
the corruption path at all — a shipped, consent-gated recovery mechanism with no row.
That is the direction D287 warned about and D465 gated for: a self-assessment ages
toward understatement as easily as overstatement, and nobody files a complaint that a
project undersells itself. Now rated, with the limit stated: this was not walked on a
COMPACTED ledger, where the tail continues snapshot heads rather than genesis — unit
tests cover that path and a live walk does not.

## D576 — the chain cannot protect its own tip, and the report did not say so

Closing the limit D575 published one slice earlier — that the recovery walk had not
touched a COMPACTED ledger. It has now: snapshot a real ledger, append a tail, rewrite
a tail line that continues the snapshot heads, and `attest` exits 5. The compacted
path holds.

Rewriting the LAST tail event instead: exit 0, healthy.

That is not a defect and the first reading nearly recorded it as one. A hash chain
protects an event through the link its SUCCESSOR holds; the final event has none, so
rewriting it leaves every remaining link consistent. It is why `snapshot` prints an
anchor and says store it off-host, and why THREAT_MODEL's first row pairs "per-
capability hash chain" with "a positional/manifest tail **anchor** (external)".
Verified rather than reasoned: with an anchor taken before the edit, `anchor --check`
exits 5 on the very file `attest` called clean.

What was missing sits where the reader is. `attest` already reports what it does NOT
establish — `unsigned`, `archivedBase` — and said nothing about the tip. An operator
running it in CI without an anchor concludes "ledger intact" for a ledger whose last
decision was rewritten. The record stated it; the moment of use did not, which is
D566's shape and D568's.

The report now carries a `coverage.tip` note, and only when there IS a tail — a
caveat printed where it cannot apply is the noise D537 warns about.

The test caught me repeating the error I spent the day finding. Its first version
exercised `stampCoverage` directly and passed while nothing called it — precisely
D564's shape, in the same file as its own commentary about D564. It now goes through
`Attest()`. **This one arrived while writing the paragraph explaining it**, which is
the strongest evidence I have that the discipline has to be mechanical: knowing the
rule did not stop me applying it wrongly ten minutes later.

## D577 — the attribute level was right and the headline contradicted it

Exercising `forecast` on a live plan: seal one that changes `pods.max` from 9 to 11,
patch the ResourceQuota to 11 with `kubectl`, re-observe, forecast the sealed plan.

    effect: will-update        rollup: willUpdate 1, noEffect 0
    attributes: [{path: pods.max, desired: 11, current: 11, prediction: "match"}]

The per-attribute prediction is correct and the action-level verdict says the
opposite. A script routes on the rollup and a human skims it; both are told a change
is coming for a plan the world has already overtaken. That is the pilot's shape twice
over — D529's "nothing was changed" while the world HAD changed, D531's summary
omitting capabilities — with the error running the other way: the detail is right and
the summary is wrong.

Reading the effect model, `case af.Operation == "update" && bound` sets `will-update`
unconditionally. The predictions it ignores are computed on the very next line. And
the precedent sits three cases above: a create against a bound capability is called
`no-effect`, with the reason written out — *the executor would 409-continue and change
NOTHING; no-effect is the honest forecast OF THE ACTION*. An update whose every
predicted attribute already matches is that same statement about that same world.

One boundary held deliberately. An update with an EMPTY prediction set is NOT
no-effect: concluding "nothing will change" from "nothing was predicted" is reasoning
from absence, which is D513 and D522 in a third costume. It stays an update, and a
test pins that separately from the two real cases.

Not claimed: that no API call happens. The executor still issues the patch; what the
forecast now predicts honestly is the effect on the WORLD, which is what the verb is
for and what its own create-on-bound case has always meant.

## D578 — the deny entry that looks redundant is the only thing left

Exercising the publication path. `make export-check` passes: the public tree builds,
its standalone `make check` is green, and the client name appears zero times in 37 MB
of output while the private tree contains it in several files — so the check has a
subject and the sanitizer works.

Reading the script, the DENY audit lists the same client name the sanitizer has
already replaced. That looks like dead weight, and it is not.

The sanitizer FINDS case-insensitively (`grep -iE "acme"`) and REPLACES three exact
spellings (`Acme`, `ACME`, `acme`). A fourth — `AcMe` — is found, is not replaced,
and reaches the export. Verified rather than reasoned: put one into an exported file
and the run stops with `LEAK DETECTED in export — do not publish`, exit 1, leaving the
offending file in place to look at. Without that entry it publishes.

So the deny list is not defence in depth against a hypothetical; on that spelling it
is the whole defence. The next reader can reasonably conclude otherwise and tidy it
away, and tidying it fails open, silently, on the one path where output leaves the
building. A test now requires every token the sanitizer genericizes to appear in the
audit, and it goes red on exactly that edit.

Deliberately not "fixed" by making the substitution case-insensitive. Silently
rewriting an unanticipated spelling hides that somebody wrote the name in a form
nobody expected; stopping and making a human look is the safer behaviour and matches
how the rest of the system treats a surprise.

Also checked, since I have written twenty-nine entries about a pilot today: 5143 lines
added across 67 files, zero occurrences of the client's name. The convention held
without the sanitizer needing to catch anything of mine.

The first probe proved nothing and I nearly recorded it as a pass — the file I planted
was not in the export's four-file docs whitelist, so it was never copied. Third time
today that a green result came from a subject that was never exercised (D564, D576).
The tell each time was the same: the result arrived faster and cleaner than the
question deserved.

## D579 — sweeping the suite for the shape I kept finding by accident

Three times today a green result came from a subject that was never exercised (D564's
test aimed at the fixed function, D576's helper nothing called, D578's probe planted
outside the export whitelist). Rather than wait for a fourth, I looked for the shape
mechanically: tests that assert INSIDE a loop over a COMPUTED collection, with no
floor proving the collection was non-empty.

The first count was 695 and meant nothing — most loops walk a literal table of cases
written three lines above, which cannot be empty. Narrowing to computed collections:
53. Excluding anything with a `len()` comparison, a zero-check or a vacuity message:
50. Excluding the `found := false ... if !found` idiom, which is a floor spelled
differently: **15**.

Four looked like gates. One was a false positive (a literal service list), one I
mis-read. Two were real, and they share a subject:

    TestReservedWiringNamespaceIsFree            — scans vocab.Embedded() for a
                                                   reserved attribute namespace
    TestEveryDeclaredEvidenceClassIsInTheClosedSet — validates every embedded vocabulary

Both loop over the embedded vocabulary set and neither checked it had one. An empty
set passes both silently — and D565, earlier the same day, showed that this exact copy
can drift from its source with nothing noticing. "No reserved attribute found" and "no
attribute found at all" read identically, which is D328's rule and the reason it
exists. Both now assert 20+ vocabularies (57 today) and the wiring gate also counts
attributes, because a set of empty vocabularies would clear a count on the set alone.
Both floors driven red.

The mutation meter then taught me something about floors. The obvious injection —
delete the floor — SURVIVED, and correctly: a floor guards a state a healthy tree
never reaches, so removing it changes nothing any test run can observe. The meter is
structurally blind to it. What the meter CAN see is the state the floor exists for, so
the injection now empties the embedded set itself (a glob that matches nothing) and
the floor catches it. **A mutant for a floor must produce the emptiness, not remove
the guard against it** — otherwise the meter reports a hole where there is none, and a
false SURVIVED trains you to distrust the instrument.

The detector is not shipped, and should not be: four rounds of refinement against my
own false positives is a sign it encodes taste rather than a property. What is worth
keeping is the ratio — 695 → 15 → 2 — because it says the suite is in far better
shape than the crude reading suggested, and it says the remaining shape is rare enough
to be worth fixing by hand rather than by rule.

## D580 — I wrote the leak into the gate against the leak

Verifying the day's tip independently, in a fresh worktree at `origin/master` (D496,
after D565 showed a green working tree over a red commit): `make check` passed, the
mutation meter passed 58 of 58, the differential passed — and `make export-check`
FAILED.

    LEAK DETECTED in export — do not publish:
      docs/DESIGN.md:17696                          `AcMe`
      go/internal/provider/exportdeny_gate_test.go:17, :58

All three mine, all from D578 — the entry documenting that the sanitizer misses mixed
casings, and the test protecting against it, both quoting a client name in the exact
casing they describe. The sanitizer rewrote every other spelling on the way out and
left the one I had chosen as the example. **The gate against the leak carried the
leak.**

Then the fix broke it a second way. With the token gone, `export-check` still failed:
the exported tree ran my test, which reads `scripts/export-public.sh` — private
tooling that is correctly NOT exported, because it carries the client list. That is
D340's failure verbatim, quoted in the Makefile four lines above the target I was
running: *"a count gate that hard-read a file the export omits"*. It now skips there,
with the reason stated.

The real finding is the one underneath. `export-check` is thorough and costs minutes,
so it is not part of `make check` — which means **the only gate on the publication
