path is the one nobody runs before committing**, and a leak ships green. That is how
mine shipped, and how D340's shipped before it: both were found by a human running the
export by hand, afterwards.

So the cheap half now lives in the gate everyone runs: grep the files the export ships
for the tokens the deny list forbids, skipping the casings the sanitizer rewrites. No
copy, no sanitize, no standalone build — seconds, not minutes. It does not replace
`export-check`, which proves the public tree BUILDS; it catches the class that has
broken publication twice. The token list is read from the script rather than restated,
so a client added there is guarded here without anyone remembering (D550), and it is
driven red by planting the very leak I had committed.

Worth saying plainly: today's tip was verified by four instruments and only the fourth
found this. `make check`, the mutation meter and the differential were all green over
a tree that could not be published.

## D581 — running the targets nobody runs

D580's lesson was to verify a tip with every instrument rather than the default one,
so I ran the Makefile targets `make check` does not: `race`, `repro-check`, `cover`,
`tidy`, `parity`, `lint`.

Five are clean and that is worth recording, since each is a claim nobody had tested
today: `race` passes under the detector; `repro-check` produces two byte-identical
builds, which is the release's reproducibility claim actually exercised (D477 recorded
it as enabled and unverified); `go mod verify` passes; `parity` regenerates its matrix
without changing it; coverage stands at 74.1%. `lint` cannot run here — golangci-lint
is not installed — which is an environment gap, not a code one, and is stated rather
than counted as a pass.

`make cover` left `go/cover.out` behind: 2.1 MB, untracked, and absent from
`.gitignore`. Nothing is broken by it. It is the kind of thing that becomes permanent
in one careless `git add -A` — a command this project's own notes already record as
having swept up files nobody meant to include — and history does not give it back.

Ignored now, and the rule derived rather than restated: every path the Makefile writes
via `-coverprofile=` or `-o`, outside a temp directory, must be covered by
`.gitignore`. A target added later with a new artifact fails until its output is
declared, which is the shape D550 argued for — a list beside a generator falls behind
the generator, so read the generator.

Two of the last three findings came from running something rather than reading it, and
neither was reachable from the code: one needed the export to actually run, this one
needed a target nobody invokes. The remaining unexercised surface of this project is
mostly not code.

## D582 — the release scripts are read by nobody until the release

Continuing where the unexercised surface actually is. Ten scripts ship in `scripts/`;
four are invoked by neither the Makefile nor CI, and all four are documented
procedures — `adopt-candidate.sh`, `console-fixtures.sh`, `integration-gcp.sh` (an
operator runbook in the canary runbook) and `ansi2svg.py`. The six that ARE invoked
include `export-public.sh`, `preship.sh` and `mutation-gate.sh`: everything standing
between this project and a publish or a release.

All ten parse today. Nothing checked that. A syntax error in `preship.sh` or
`export-public.sh` surfaces at the worst available moment — the release itself — and
`bash -n` costs milliseconds. That is D580's argument again: when the thorough gate is
too slow to run before committing, the cheap half belongs in the gate everyone runs.

Stated rather than implied: this proves the scripts can be READ, not that they WORK. A
green parse over a script whose logic rotted is exactly the false comfort this project
keeps finding, so the test says so in its own words and the skip paths say UNCHECKED
rather than passing quietly when bash or python3 is missing.

The mutation meter then refused it, and was right. Emptying the loop SURVIVED: a
check that iterates over nothing passes silently when the tree is healthy, which is
D579's floor problem in a form that CAN be fixed — the gate now counts what it
actually parsed and fails if that is fewer than it found. **A gate must be able to
fail when it stops doing its work, not only when its subject is bad.**

The gate reproduced D581 on its first run. `py_compile` writes the `.pyc` next to the
SOURCE regardless of working directory, so a check written the day after "make cover
leaves an artifact in the tree" left an artifact in the tree — while checking for that
class. It uses `compile()` now, which parses and writes nothing. Twice in two slices
the instrument has had the defect it was measuring; the pattern is not irony but
proximity — you build the check out of whatever is nearest, and what is nearest shares
the habits that caused the problem.

## D583 — I fixed the instance and left the class, twice, immediately

The final verification of the day found `make export-check` red again, with the two
gates written in the two slices AFTER D580 failing in the exported tree — for D580's
exact reason. `TestMakefileArtifactsAreIgnored` runs `git check-ignore` in a tree that
is a whitelist COPY and not a clone; `TestShippedScriptsParse` globs a `scripts/`
directory the export ships one file of.

D580 fixed the first occurrence by adding a skip to that one test. I then wrote two
more gates that needed the same skip and did not get it, having written the sentence
*only a shared mechanism propagates* three times that same day (D527, D550, D573).
Knowing a rule is not applying it; the rule has to live somewhere a new caller cannot
miss.

So it does now: `skipIfExported(t, wants)`, keyed on the absence of `.git`, because
the export is a copy and never a clone. All four gates that read repo-only material
call it, and the message names the artefact so a future reader can tell a deliberate
skip from a check that quietly stopped running.

The helper has its own gate, and it is the important one: in the SOURCE tree the
detection must report false. A helper that answered "exported" everywhere would
silently disable every gate calling it — the same failure it exists to prevent, one
level up, and the shape of the day's worst near-misses (D579's floor, D582's empty
loop).

The guard test then failed in the exported tree, correctly: there the detection IS
true. Asserting "false in the source tree" cannot be checked against itself without
circularity, so it is checked against a DIFFERENT signal — the presence of the private
export script — and skips, loudly, where that script is absent. A property pinned by
restating its own implementation is not pinned at all.

Four times today the instrument carried the defect it measured: a leak in the
anti-leak gate (D580), an artefact left by the artefact check (D582), an empty loop in
a gate about vacuity (D582), and this. The pattern is proximity, not irony — a check
is built from what is nearest to the problem, and what is nearest shares the habits
that produced it.

## D584 — applying D583's test to my own day: which fixes were mechanisms?

D583 ended with a question worth turning on everything else: *does the next author
have to remember this?* If yes, it is not fixed. Running it over the day's work, most
answers were good — D563's operand set is derived from the registry, D568/D569's
recipes are gated, D573's notes render from one place, D583 is itself the mechanism.

D550 and D574 failed it. Nine dispatch points in the k8s driver each chose
`mappingFor` (any mapped service) or `genericMapping` (mapped AND write-safe) on their
own, and nothing made the choice conscious — `genericMapping` does not say "write"
anywhere in its name. That is exactly how D550 gated a read on a write predicate, and
how D574's fourth call site survived the fix for the other three. A tenth verb would
have repeated it.

`serviceMapping(service, intent)` is now the single place read and write semantics
live. The caller must state which it wants, so the compiler asks the question that was
previously left to memory, and the refusal is worded for the intent — the read-only
service's *observed but not written*, which D550 added at the gate, now belongs to the
one function that can tell the two apart.

The gate is the point of the slice: write-safety may be consulted in exactly one
place. It is a source-level count with a floor on the files it scanned, and it goes
red at two. That is what makes this a mechanism rather than a ninth careful edit — the
next verb cannot repeat D550 by picking the wrong helper, because there is only one.

The refactor then disarmed four mutation-gate entries, and the meter said so. Their
injections were written against the old shapes — `d.genericMapping(service)`,
`d.mappingFor(service)` at particular call sites — and after the change they matched
nothing, so they altered no behaviour and every named test still passed. SURVIVED is
the correct report for that: an injection that changes nothing proves nothing. **A
mutation entry is coupled to the shape of the code it attacks, and a refactor can
disarm it silently — except here, where the meter is the thing that notices.** All
four re-armed against the new shape.

One of them could not simply be re-pointed, and that was informative. The probe
mutant kept surviving because the refactor made its fallback CORRECT for a write-safe
service: `requireService` no longer answers "unknown service" for anything mapped, so
even a broken probe path lands on a truthful message. The protection had become
partly structural. It is still absent for a READ-ONLY mapped service, which falls
through to "observed but not written" — accurate about writing and silent about the
probe the operator asked for. The test now covers both halves, which is what made the
mutant meaningful again and the test stronger than it was.

Verified on the live cluster and in unit-land: a read-only mapped service still
observes, its write verbs still refuse with the wording D550 chose, a service the
driver does not serve still gets *unknown service*, and the probe still names the
missing probe rather than an unknown service (D574).

## D585 — the third kind of sweep, recorded where it belongs

MATURITY's gap 4 carries two directions already: the pilot's 36 field findings, which
hermetic suites could not have caught, and the driver-layer sweep's 25 defects, which
no field run reported because nobody is positioned to notice a delete that would have
hit a stranger's resource until it does.

Today was neither. It was a walk of the OPERATOR'S path — discover, posture, adopt,
converge, retire, refresh, backup, restore, attest, repair, probe, forecast, export —
on a live cluster, doing what the documentation says and reading what came back.
Thirty-five entries, four of them verified-clean.

The recurring shape is worth naming precisely, because it is not the shape either
existing sweep looks for. Almost nothing computed a wrong answer. What failed was
**published claims nobody had executed**: posture's remediation recipes could not run
as written (one omitted a flag its own first line carried); the recipe that did run
left its result invisible, so an operator would read success as failure; the
documented adopt-then-retire sequence dead-ended because adoption binds a resource
without owning it; and a bug the pilot reported was fixed in a way unreachable from
the exact state they reported it in. Two more were in the publication path, which
`make check` does not exercise at all.

So the lesson gap 4 should carry, and now does: hermetic suites test what the code
DOES, cross-driver sweeps test what the DRIVERS do, and neither reads the sentences
the system hands a person. Advice is a published claim like any other, and until this
walk it was the only class of claim in this system that nothing verified.

Recorded in MATURITY rather than left in the decision log, because gap 4 is where a
reader goes to ask "what do your gates miss?" and the honest answer changed today.
This is the direction D287 and D465 warn about: a self-assessment drifts toward
understatement, and nobody files a complaint that a project failed to mention finding
twenty more of its own defects.

## D586 — the help text advertised two invocations that cannot run

D585 named the class the day had found: advice is a published claim, and it was the
only class of claim in this system nothing verified. The usage block is advice — the
first thing anyone reads, and the thing an agent parses.

Two of the eleven verbs that REQUIRE `--provider` did not show it:

    groundhold crawl --at <ts> [--budget <n>] [--out <dir>] [--pairings <f>]
    groundhold react --event <file> --ledger <f> --at <ts> [--crawl <base.json>]

Typed as printed, `crawl` answers `crawl requires an explicit --provider ... INVALID`.
I hit this myself earlier the same day while walking the onboarding path, read it as
my own typo, added the flag and moved on — which is exactly what an operator does, and
why nobody reports it.

The check derives its subject from `providerVerbs`, the CLI's own closed set, so a
verb added there later cannot leave a stale usage line behind; it counts what it
examined so a parse that stops finding entries cannot pass quietly (D582); and it
fails separately when a provider verb has no usage entry at all, because absent and
incomplete are different faults.

The requirement itself is right and stays: `--provider` must be explicit because the
fake driver fabricates reality and must never be a silent default (F4). What was wrong
was the sentence describing it. Both lines now show the flag, and the corrected form
runs verbatim against the live cluster.

## D587 — closing the class D586 opened

D586 fixed `--provider` in two usage lines. D583's test says to ask whether the fix is
a mechanism or an instance, and the honest answer was instance: the gate covered one
flag out of however many a verb can refuse without, leaving the next author to
remember the rest.

The class is "a flag a verb refuses without must be shown in that verb's usage line",
and the subject derives from the refusals themselves — every `"<verb> requires
--<flag>"` message in the CLI source. Measured while writing it: all twenty verbs that
refuse without a flag already advertise it, `--provider` on `crawl` and `react` having
been the only gap. Held anyway, because agreement that nothing enforces is the state a
gap is in just before it opens (D554), and driven red by hiding `--ledger` from
posture's line.

The two gates now share one usage parser rather than each carrying its own, which is
the same reason: a parser fix has to reach both, and a copy would not.

Worth noting what this run did NOT find, since the day has been a long series of
things nobody had executed. The remaining usage text is accurate. Twenty verbs, every
required flag advertised, every provider verb named after D586. The advice layer was
wrong in specific, findable places rather than wrong throughout — which is the more
useful conclusion, and only available by checking all of it rather than the parts that
had already failed.

## D588 — a record that said 1970

Running the last unexercised read-only verbs, `connections` published this for a
pairing registered minutes earlier:

    "pairedAt": "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"

`pair` takes no `--at`, so the CLI handed it the evaluation-time default, which is the
epoch. Nothing READS the field — it is written once and printed — so no decision
turned on it and nothing was unsafe. What it was, is a false statement in a published
record: an auditor reading `connections` is told a credential reference was registered
in 1970.

The project had already decided this case in a different place. D230 echoes the
operator's `--at` into a refusal's suggested command "only when the operator actually
supplied it (never the epoch default)", because a command builder that needs a clock
must omit itself rather than invent one. A stored record deserves the same rule, and
`Validate` never required the field, so omitting it is structurally free.

`StampPairedAt` records a real clock verbatim and records NOTHING for an empty one or
for the epoch. Both are checked, because the epoch is what the default actually
produces and an equality test on "" alone would have passed while the bug stayed.

The first fix was wired only halfway and the live run showed it: `pairedAt: ""`.
Better than 1970 and still wrong — an empty key says the field exists and is blank,
which is a third thing nobody meant. The key is now absent when there is no clock,
which is what D230 means by omitting.

Also worth recording: `deposed` returns an empty set on this ledger, correctly, and
`connections` is otherwise accurate. The remaining read-only verbs are sound.

## D589 — I broke `--version` this morning and found it this evening

Running the last unexercised commands turned up two things, and the second is mine.

`groundhold version` works and the help never mentions it. Fifty verbs are listed and
this is not one, while the drill-down line invites `groundhold <verb> --help` for any
of them. It matters more than its size: this project hands binaries over by hand with
a manifest naming a commit, and the first question anyone holding one asks is which
build they have. The answer existed and was undiscoverable from the tool.

Then `--version` and `-v` exited 1:

    unknown flag "--version" — refusing rather than ignoring it

**That is D567, mine, from this morning.** I made an unrecognised token starting with
`-` an error, which is right; `--version` and `-v` were never in the flag switch —
they were read later from the positional list, where `cmd == "--version"` picked them
up. The new rule closed on them. Confirmed against binaries: the build before D567
answers, the build after refuses, and the binary delivered to the pilot predates D567,
so nobody outside this tree ever saw it.

**A fail-closed rule has to be checked against what it closes ON, not only against
what it is meant to stop.** I tested D567 with invented flags and with the flag that
prompted it, and never with the conventions every user tries first. Both now live in
the flag switch where they belong, and the check runs before the "no command" branch —
the first fix put it after, so `groundhold --version` printed the usage instead, which
is the same defect wearing a politer face.

Found by running the verbs nobody had run, on the last pass of a day spent on exactly
that. The regression was eleven hours old and no gate noticed: it is not a wrong
answer, not a broken build, and not a claim any document makes — it is a convention,
and this project had no test that conventions still work.

## D590 — the conventions, swept once, in one place

D589 ended on a sentence worth acting on: this project had no test that its
CONVENTIONS still work. They are not a wrong answer, not a broken build, and not a
claim any document makes — they are what a person types when the documentation is not
in front of them, and `--version` had been broken for eleven hours behind every green
gate.

So they are swept now, together: `--help`, `-h`, `help`, `help <verb>`, `version`,
`--version`, `-v`, and `--`.

The sweep found a second one D567 had closed on. `groundhold -- version` exited 1 with
*unknown flag "--"*. POSIX `--` means "everything after this is positional", and the
rule refusing an unrecognised `-` token refused the separator too. Nobody here had
typed it, which is exactly the point of the class.

The guard is not weakened by it. After `--` everything is positional, so a bogus VERB
is still a usage error, and an unknown flag WITHOUT a separator still refuses — both
pinned, because a separator that switches the guard off would be a worse bug than the
one it fixes.

One correction to my own words. D567's comment said a lone `-` "stays a positional
(stdin, by convention)". No verb reads stdin. That was a convention this tool does not
implement, asserted in a comment — the precise kind of unearned claim the day was
spent removing, written by me while removing them. The comment now says what is true.

## D591 — a bookmark and a dropped event exited the same

`react` is the real-time path: one change event in, one paced re-list and a
reclassified posture out. Run over a stream by a cron or a watcher, its EXIT CODE is
how the consumer knows what happened.

Measured against the live cluster with three real inputs:

    recognised watch event   exit 2   (posture found drift — correct)
    watch BOOKMARK frame     exit 0
    unparseable envelope     exit 0

The last two are one outcome to a machine and mean opposite things. A BOOKMARK is
routine — there is nothing to react to and nothing is wrong. An envelope nothing can
parse means an event was DROPPED, and a dropped event is the real-time path silently
losing a change, which is the failure this verb exists to prevent.

They collapsed at the source. A BOOKMARK carries no resource coordinate, falls past
every branch of `ParseEvent`, and lands on the same "unrecognised event envelope" as a
garbage document — so the CLI, which has only that one error to look at, returned 0
for both. The package comment says watch BOOKMARK/ERROR frames "are ignored loudly":
loudly on stderr, and indistinguishably on the channel a consumer routes on. Prose in
one place again (D527).

`ErrNothingToReactTo` now marks a well-formed frame with no resource by DEFINITION —
BOOKMARK and ERROR, named explicitly. The first attempt keyed on "the frame has a
type", which the tests refused: `{"type":"MODIFIED"}` with no object has a type and is
malformed, not routine, and calling it benign would drop a real change as if it were a
bookmark. Exactly the wrong direction to be generous in.

Exit codes now separate the three: 0 handled-nothing-to-do, 1 structural error in the
input document (what exit 1 already means in spec/errors.md), 2 the posture verdict.
Still never a crash loop — a malformed event stops that invocation, not the stream.

Found by running the last verb nobody had run, on a walk whose entire yield has been
claims nobody had executed.

## D592 — a splice re-dated every scope it did not read

Following `react` further than its exit code. It re-lists ONE scope — the event's —
and splices that into a base crawl. Measured on the live cluster: base crawl at 20:16
recorded `kube-system` with 14 resources; a fifteenth was then created there; `react`
fired on a `default` event at 20:20. The result:

    at: 2026-07-31T20:20:00Z
      default      status=complete   8 resources
      kube-system  status=complete  14 resources

The document states that AS OF 20:20 the kube-system scope COMPLETELY contained
fourteen resources. It contained fifteen. Nothing recorded when either scope was
listed, so the splice silently re-dated the one it never read.

Not cosmetic, because of what `status: complete` carries. It is the claim
`shadowLowerBound` rests on — the difference between a shadow count that is a real
lower bound and a number with nothing behind it. Posture classifies managed-vs-shadow
from these scopes, so one whose listing has aged was presented with exactly the
authority of one just read.

A scope now records `listedAt`; the splice keeps each carried-over scope's own, and
stamps only the one it re-listed. Verified live: the same run now reads
`default listedAt=20:40` next to `kube-system listedAt=20:30`, and the fifteenth
resource is there because that base was crawled after it appeared.

The mutation meter refused the first test, correctly. It built a `ScopeContext` by
hand and set the field itself — proving the field exists and nothing about whether the
CRAWL fills it — so removing the stamping left it green. That is D564's shape inside
the test written to close this entry, and the fifth time today an instrument carried
the defect it was measuring. It goes through `Run` now, with a floor so a crawl that
produces no scopes cannot pass as clean.

Deliberately NOT in the hashed model, and the existing code said so before I did:
`contentModel` covers content "WITHOUT any timing", because a fingerprint that moves
on every crawl cannot answer whether the WORLD moved. A test pins that the context
hash is unchanged when only the listing time differs — the field had to be added
without weakening the identity it sits beside.

What this does NOT do, stated because the gap is now visible rather than hidden: it
does not decide what posture should DO with a stale scope. That is a semantics
question — how old is too old, and whether `shadowLowerBound` should drop to false —
and it belongs to whoever sets the freshness policy, not to a field that stops the
document lying about its own currency.

## D593 — pinning the set an autonomous agent can reach

The MCP server is the surface an agent talks to, and it had never been exercised here.
It works: six tools, honest descriptions (`observe` says it records to the ledger on
request; `draft` says nothing seals from inline content), and calls behave — `verify`
returns PROVEN, `plan` refuses a stale observation with the reason, `hash` and
`observe` answer against the live cluster.

The boundary around that set is deliberate and documented, including its limit: apply
exists only under `GROUNDHOLD_MCP_ALLOW_APPLY`, behind a hash-pinned two-step, and the
package comment says plainly that the token pins a plan and does NOT authenticate a
human — an autonomous or prompt-injected agent can complete both steps alone.

One test guarded it, by name: `groundhold_apply` must not appear without the env var.
That is one instance. A seventh tool — converge, adopt, retire — is not
`groundhold_apply`, and would have arrived unremarked. D586's shape with
infrastructure mutation at the end of it, on the one surface where the caller may be
an agent following instructions from a document it just read.

The SET is pinned now, as `providerVerbs` is (D571): the default six by name, each
annotated with what it actually touches, so changing it is a deliberate edit a reviewer
sees. A second test pins the escape hatch from both sides — the env gate must add
exactly `groundhold_apply` and must remove nothing — because a hatch that quietly
admitted more, or swapped one tool for another, would satisfy a one-name check.

Driven red by adding a seventh tool, which is the edit the gate exists to stop being
silent.

The first mutant did not do that. It inserted a no-op and the meter reported SURVIVED,
which read as a hole in the gate and was a hole in the injection — the sixth time
today the instrument, not the subject, was at fault. The rule that keeps catching this
is cheap: before believing a SURVIVED, confirm the substitution changed the file and
that the change means what it claims.

## D594 — "never gates", one line above something that gates

`suggest` is the strongest form of advice this system produces: not a command to run
but text to PUT IN YOUR CONTRACT. Its header reads

    # Advisory only — never gates; paste what you want to adopt.

which is true of the suggestion and misleading about the paste.

Measured end to end. A storage contract verifying PROVEN; the three recommended
constraints pasted as hard, which is the default; verify again:

    before  1 satisfied, 0 unknown   PROVEN
    after   1 satisfied, 3 unknown   BLOCKED

The blocking is right — the candidate says nothing about
`encryption.customerManagedKeys`, `network.publicExposure` or `versioning.enabled`, so
those verdicts are unknown, and unknown blocks by design. The four-valued verifier is
working exactly as intended.

What is missing is that the operator was told "never gates" one line before pasting
something that gates, and meets the consequence a verb later with nothing connecting
the two. D566's shape and D568's, on the advice that carries furthest: a snippet lives
in the contract long after the session that produced it.

The escape route already existed and works — `--as soft` on the same three verifies
PROVEN with them still unknown, which is adopting the intent without the block — and
the advice never mentioned it. The header now states both: that a hard constraint over
an undeclared attribute verifies UNKNOWN and blocks, and that `--as soft` is the way
to take the intent now and satisfy it later.

Only in hard mode. In soft the caveat cannot apply, and a caveat printed where it
cannot apply is the noise D537 warns about — pinned by its own test, as is the empty
case, where a contract with nothing to suggest gets one quiet line and no lecture.

Both pasted forms still load: hard gives four hard constraints, soft gives one hard
and three soft. The advice was mechanically correct all along; it was silent about
what it costs.

## D595 — a partial price can only be wrong one way

`costproj` came out of an audit better than most things this week, and that is worth
recording before the change. Verified against real plans: the arithmetic is right; the
weekly figure annualises properly (monthly × 12 ÷ 52, not the naive monthly ÷ 4 that
would read 30.13 instead of 27.81); a second currency is kept SEPARATE with an explicit
"declared in USD - NOT converted" rather than pushed through an invented rate; and the
coverage line states how much of the plan the figure rests on. Its own comment says
the point — a partial figure "can never masquerade as a bill" — and it holds.

What it did not say is the DIRECTION. With "based on 1 of 2 capabilities", the
uncovered capability still costs money, so the true monthly figure is strictly higher.
The number can only be wrong one way, and the headline read "Estimated cost … ~ 120.50
EUR / month" — an estimate with a tilde, which is a central value, the one thing it
cannot be. The error runs toward "cheaper than it is", which is the direction that
gets approved.

The project already owns the word. `shadowLowerBound` exists because a count resting
on partial data is a floor and says so; a price earns it more. Partial coverage now
reads `Estimated cost AT LEAST … ≥ 120.50 EUR / month`, and full coverage is left
alone — hedging a complete answer is the mirror mistake, and a caveat where it cannot
apply is the noise D537 warns about. Both pinned, along with a third test holding the
parts that were already right, so this change cannot quietly cost them.

## D596 — the one payload that leaves the machine, held by nobody

`notify` is the doorbell: on a terminal run it POSTs to an operator-supplied URL. That
makes it the single path where a run's data crosses the network to an address
groundhold does not control, and the package is built for it — the notifier "has no
ledger handle — it is physically incapable of writing truth", delivery is
best-effort-once, a failed webhook is a log line and never a run failure.

The payload is deliberately narrow: schema, handle, kind, state, code, exitCode,
concludedAt, lastEventHash. Every field is an identifier, an enum, a number or a hash.
There is structurally nothing to leak, which is stronger than redacting — and it is
why this path has no redactor, while the receipt's `Reason` needed one (D309).

Nothing held that. `TestBuildPayloadIsExact` pins the exact JSON bytes of one
fully-populated payload, which catches a new REQUIRED field and not a new `omitempty`
one. Measured rather than argued: adding

    Reason string `json:"reason,omitempty"`

to the outbound struct passes every test in the package. The moment any caller sets
it, driver text goes off the machine — and driver text is exactly where D309 found
credentials surfacing.

The field set is pinned by name now, each annotated with what kind of value it is, so
adding one is a deliberate edit that has to state why an external endpoint may see it.
A second test requires every field to be a SCALAR: a map or a nested struct would pass
a name check while carrying unbounded content, which is the same hole wearing a
different shape. Both driven red by the injections they exist for.

Worth saying plainly, because this week has been a long list of things that were
wrong: this one was RIGHT, carefully and deliberately, and had no assertion behind it.
That is the more common state of a good property, and the reason the sweep keeps
finding them.

## D597 — the consent list that was checked, and the one that spends

`autonomy` carries the consent lists, and a dangling capability name in one is a grant
the operator believes they wrote and did not. The loader already refuses that, and a
conformance case is named for it — `autonomy-forbidden-dangling-reference-is-load-error`.
It refuses per key, by name, and it had two keys' worth of coverage for three keys'
worth of lists:

    autonomy: { allow_replace_stateful: [does-not-exist] }  ->  INVALID
    autonomy: { allow_intrusive_probes: [does-not-exist] }  ->  OK, exit 0

The asymmetry runs the wrong way. Intrusive probes are the ones that SPEND — D59's
restore-test restores a backup into a scratch instance and times it to RUNNABLE — and
they carry a DOUBLE consent for that reason: the operator's runtime flag AND the
contract's per-capability grant. That design is sound and `allowsIntrusive` fails
closed on a name it does not recognise. What was missing is that the contract loaded
clean, so the typo survived to the moment of use: a probe refusing "allow_intrusive_
probes was not granted", quite possibly during the incident it was meant to measure.

Checked now from ONE list of consent keys rather than an `if` per key, so a third list
added later is covered without anyone remembering — D583's test applied while writing
the fix rather than after it.

Worth recording what was already right, since the sweep keeps finding good work with
nothing behind it: the consent decision itself lives in exactly one place
(`intrusiveOK := allowIntrusive && allowsIntrusive(c, capID)`), everything downstream
only plumbs the resulting boolean, and no second reader of the autonomy block decides
anything — `canonical` hashes it, which is its job. The defect was in what the loader
would accept, not in how the consent is spent.

## D598 — the fuzzer fuzzed the same 200 documents every time

`make differential` generates random contracts and candidates, pushes each through both
the Go CLI and the Python reference, and requires the two to agree. It is the only
instrument in this project that can find a case nobody wrote — everything else checks a
claim someone thought of. The Makefile pins `SEED ?= 1` and `N ?= 30`, deliberately, so a
local run is reproducible and a reported divergence can be replayed by hand.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` ran bare `make differential`. So it took the default. **Every
CI run since D38 fuzzed the identical ~200 pairs.** A fuzzer pinned to one seed cannot
discover anything it did not discover on its first execution; it is a regression test
wearing a fuzzer's name, and it was reported in delivery manifests as
`differential 200 checks, 0 divergence` — a true sentence that reads as far more coverage
than it bought.

Measured before touching anything, on the tip, seeds the project has never run:

```
seed=2  n=30   202 checks   seed=11 n=120  714 checks
seed=3  n=30   196 checks   seed=29 n=120  720 checks
seed=4  n=30   200 checks   seed=97 n=120  722 checks
seed=5  n=30   196 checks
                              ~2950 checks, 0 divergence
```

Zero divergence at roughly fifteen times the pinned volume. The dual implementation
genuinely agrees well past seed 1 — which is the good news, and exactly why nobody
suspected the instrument: it was never wrong, so it was never examined. The finding is
not a bug in the verifier. It is that the search was not happening.

CI now passes `SEED=${{ github.run_id }} N=60`, so the fleet explores over time and no two
runs cover the same ground. The local default stays fixed, because a divergence has to be
replayable: the run prints its own seed, which is the reproduction recipe
(`make differential SEED=<printed> N=60`).

Two gates, one per direction, because this is a pair of opposing properties and a single
test would let either drift:
`TestCIFuzzesWithAVaryingSeed` fails if the CI step carries no `SEED=` (or pins
`SEED=1` longhand); `TestLocalDifferentialStaysReproducible` fails if the Makefile
stops pinning a default. Both are in the mutation meter's direction of travel — the
mutant restores the bare `make differential` line and the first gate catches it.

The class is D565's, one level out: *a gate that can report success without re-reading
its subject is not a gate.* Here the subject was re-read every time and it was the same
subject every time. Randomness declared in a Makefile variable is not randomness until
something varies it.

## D599 — the two implementations agreed on the alphabet and disagreed on the rule

Immediately after widening the fuzzer's seed (D598) the obvious next question was
whether the fuzzer's *alphabet* was any wider than its seed. It was not. Two
hand-copied lists of event types lived in `conformance/differential.py`: five in
`event()`, eleven in `scenario()`. The published registry holds **21**. Seven types
were generated by neither:

```
converge.started  converge.phase.entered  converge.finished  converge.failed
ownership.claimed  probe.failed  violation.resolved
```

Widening `scenario()` to the full registry, in a scratch copy, on the same seeds the
project has always run:

```
seed=1  n=40   260 checks,  7 divergence(s)
seed=7  n=40   260 checks, 11 divergence(s)
seed=13 n=40   250 checks,  5 divergence(s)
```

Minimized to one step, and to exactly one type out of the twenty-one:

```
- append: {actor: w1, capabilities: [db], type: ownership.claimed}

py: {"results":[{"status":"ok"}]}
go: {"results":[{"reason":"mutation requires a fencing token (D29)","status":"rejected"}]}
```

`go/internal/ledger/ledger.go` carried `ownership.claimed` in `MutationTypes`, so the
runtime demanded an active lease and a matching fencing token. The reference
implementation's `MUTATION_TYPES` did not, and neither does the spec:
`spec/state-model.md` §2 enumerates mutations as `apply.*` and `binding.updated`, and
§1 says in these words that `ownership.claimed` "stamps a takeover's authorship" —
authorship stamps take no lease, which the same section states for
`contract.published` ("a decision event is not a mutation"). Two artefacts against
one: the runtime was the outlier, and it was rejecting a ledger the reference writes.

**This is D338 one layer in.** That entry found four artefacts publishing different
event-type *registries* and gated them into agreement. Nothing gated the *rules*
attached to a member. Agreeing on the alphabet while disagreeing on what a letter
means produces the identical failure — a valid ledger unreadable to the other side —
and the gate that closed the first could not see the second.

An internal tell was sitting there: in the runtime `MutationTypes ⊄ DecisionTypes`
(the claim was a mutation but not a decision), while in the reference
`MUTATION_TYPES ⊂ DECISION_TYPES`. Nothing compared the two, so nothing asked.

Per invariant 5 the fix began with a case, not with code:
`ownership-claim-is-not-a-mutation` failed against the Go CLI (517/518) and passed
against the reference, and `ownership-claim-under-a-lease-still-carries-its-token`
pins the field path — `apply` stamps the claim while holding a lease, and relaxing the
rule must not turn its legitimate token into an error. Both green after moving the
type to `NonMutatingTypes`; the seeds that produced 5–11 divergences produce zero.

Three mechanisms, because one instance is not a fix:

1. `spec/state-model.md` now publishes the mutation set as a **fenced registry block**,
   the way the event registry is published, so a third implementation has something
   other than prose to build against.
2. `TestEventClassificationAgreesAcrossImplementations` compares the runtime's
   `MutationTypes` and `DecisionTypes` against the reference's and against that block
   — driven red from all three directions before it was trusted (runtime re-adds the
   type; spec drops one; the reference's set is renamed so the parser cannot find it,
   which must fail rather than skip, D565).
3. The fuzzer's alphabet is **derived** from `spec/state.schema.json` instead of
   copied, with no fallback: a fuzzer that quietly narrows its alphabet when it cannot
   read the registry is this bug wearing a helpful face. `TestFuzzAlphabetIsTheWholeRegistry`
   *asks the generator* what it will fuzz rather than reading how it is written (D317),
   so re-hardcoding fails even if spelled differently.

The class, stated so the next author can look for it: **a registry can be shared and
still be understood differently.** D338 checked who is in the set. Nothing checked
what being in it obliges you to do — and every per-type rule (fencing, decision heads,
lease arithmetic, head advancement) is a separate opportunity for the same drift.

## D600 — the source of truth passed with zero cases in it

Four read-only audits ran in parallel over surfaces this sweep had not touched: the
gate scripts, the conformance suite, every command published in prose, and the
Go-vs-Python pair outside the differential's three comparisons. Each was told to
return measurements, not suspicions. This entry takes the two findings that sit
highest in the pyramid; the rest are queued behind it.

**The suite had no floor.** `conformance/run.py` collects its work with a glob and
tallies what it collected. Move the directory away:

```
$ mv conformance/cases conformance/cases-moved
$ python3 conformance/run.py; echo EXIT=$?
0/0 conformance cases passed (library)
EXIT=0
```

`make check` runs that three times (library, reference CLI, Go CLI) and, with all
three green over nothing, prints `all gates passed`. This is D328 — a gate that finds
nothing passes — standing at the very top: the suite CI calls the source of truth, and
whose tally every delivery manifest quotes. Two floors now, on files found and cases
collected, both deliberately far below the real counts: this is a guard against the
subject VANISHING, not a second place to maintain the exact totals (docs publish
those, and a gate already checks them).

**A runner dropped its failures on the floor.** `run_show_case_cli` is annotated
`-> list[str]`, accumulates into `fails`, and then the next `def` begins. It returned
`None`, which the harness reads as no failures — so its byte-for-byte golden
comparison and its forbidden-token scan were both dead, and all three `show` cases
were unfalsifiable. Measured with the mutant the case is named for, replacing the
derived plan order with raw input order:

```
before   FAIL none                516/516 conformance cases passed
after    FAIL plan-order-is-derived-not-input-order   516/518
```

The gate covers the shape rather than the function: every `run_*` runner annotated as
returning a failure list must end by returning one, on every terminal path. It is
asked of Python's own parser rather than matched with a regex, because an accumulator
dropped on one branch is invisible to text search.

Worth stating plainly, since it bears on how much the rest of this record is worth:
both defects made a *reported* number meaningless rather than a behaviour wrong. The
"516/516" in three delivery manifests was true as arithmetic and, for three of those
cases, arithmetic over nothing. The class to watch is not "is the gate green" but
"could this gate have been red".

## D601 — forged provenance passed every gate, because four cases asserted nothing

`attest` reports provenance facts — how many signatures self-verify, how many events
are unsigned, whether a present envelope is invalid, where the anchor sits. D139 calls
it the honesty core, and the console reads it. Four conformance cases cover it.

All four wrote their expectations one level too deep:

```yaml
- attest:
    expect:            # child of the verb
      fields: { signatures.selfVerified: 2, anchor.status: verified }
```

The runner reads `step.get("expect")` — a SIBLING of the verb key, which is what every
other case file writes. Nested inside, it is `None`, `expect.get("fields")` is empty,
and the only surviving assertion is "the verb exited 0".

Measured, by forging every fact at the end of `Attest()`:

```go
rep.Signatures.SelfVerified = 999
rep.Signatures.Unsigned = 0
rep.Signatures.EnvelopePresentButInvalid = 0
rep.Anchor = nil
```

```
518/518 conformance cases passed (cli: bin/groundhold-go)
go test ./... -count=1        (no failures)
```

A tampered signature laundered into full coverage, and a ledger with no anchor
reported as anchored, ship green through the entire gate. Un-nested, the same
forgery is caught by name in all four cases: `signatures.selfVerified: expected 2,
got 999`.

**Un-nesting them exposed a second defect the vacuum had been hiding.** With the
assertions live, `attest-reports-full-signature-coverage` failed on
`anchor.status: expected 'verified', got None` — an honest failure. The harness's
`anchorEmit` step wrote the anchor document to its own scratch path, while the runtime
reads the co-located `<ledger>.anchor` (`ledger.AnchorPath`), which is the only place
a verb without a `--check` flag looks. So the step never built the world the case
describes, and `attest` was right to report no anchor. Fixed in the harness, not in
the expectation — the case's intent was correct and the anchor fact is now exercised
end to end.

The mechanism is structural, because the failure is silent by construction: the runner
now walks every case document at collection time and REFUSES the run (exit 2) if any
`expect` sits as the child of a verb key rather than its sibling. Checked across all
55 case files: zero legitimate exceptions, so the rule costs nothing. A Go gate asks
the runner's own walker rather than re-implementing it — two detectors of the same
thing drift, and the unused one is always the one that mattered.

Same family as D530: a run that drops an input answers a question you did not ask.
There the input was a candidate operand; here it is the assertion itself.

## D602 — the third thing D567 closed the door on, and the only one that mattered

D567 made an unrecognised flag a refusal instead of a silent positional. Three things
were reading flags OUT of that positional list. Two were found within a day and fixed
here: `--version`/`-v` (D589) and the POSIX `--` separator (D590). This is the third,
and it was live for both of those days:

```
$ groundhold apireq classify --applied true --deployed true --http-status 200 --json
unknown flag "--applied" — refusing rather than ignoring it: …
exit=1
```

`runAPIReqClassify` parses four flags of its own out of `pos[2:]`, which is exactly how
they used to arrive. The verb has been unreachable from the command line since D567.

**Where that lands.** `scripts/canary-aws.sh` and `scripts/canary-gcp.sh` call
`apireq classify` on a daily schedule to turn a probe result into a verdict, and read
its exit code as `0 | 10 | 20 | *`. Exit 1 fell to `*` → `infra-flake`, with the
refusal on stderr so the message came out as "classify produced no message". A real
provider drift — the one thing those canaries exist to catch, the D329 dual-invoke
class — was being downgraded to a flake on two clouds, every night.

Two fixes, and the second one matters more than the first.

**The flag.** A registry, `verbPrivateFlags`, listing per verb the flags parsed by that
verb's own sub-parser; the global parser passes those through as positionals for that
verb and still refuses them everywhere else (`plan --applied true` refuses). Adding
them to the global switch instead would have been three fewer lines and wrong: a flag
there is accepted by all 51 verbs and read by one, which is the fail-open D567 removed.
Two gates keep the registry exact, both driven red before being trusted: every private
flag a sub-parser reads must be registered (or the next flag dies the same way), and
every registered flag must be read by a sub-parser (or it is silently swallowed).
Plus the first test of the CLI FACE of this verb — `internal/edgecanary` is thoroughly
tested and the four flags carrying its inputs from the command line were covered by
nothing, which is the whole reason this survived.

**The canary.** `*) infra-flake` is the defect that let the first one hide. An exit
code the tool does not define is groundhold failing to answer, not the infrastructure
being unreliable; scoring it as a flake makes a broken instrument look like a bad day
at the provider. Both canaries now classify an unrecognised code as
`groundhold-regression` and print the code and whatever was on stdout.

Same shape as D530 and D601: a run that drops an input answers a question you did not
ask. Here the run refused instead — and the caller's catch-all turned the refusal back
into a quiet answer.

## D603 — the meter scored six mutants it never ran, and an absence gate with no teeth

The mutation meter is what every other claim in this record leans on: each real bug is
re-injected and the named test must catch it. `mutate()` decided that with

```sh
if go test "$pkg" -run "^$run\$" ...; then SURVIVED; else caught; fi
```

`go test` exits non-zero for a BUILD FAILURE exactly as it does for a failing
assertion. Six of the mutants left the tree uncompilable — replacing a variable's only
use gives `declared and not used` — so the named test never ran, its teeth were never
measured, and the gate printed `caught` and signed off with "every re-injected bug was
caught":

```
NO-BUILD  reconcile: skip ownership (elasticache)          TestReconcileElastiCache_ForeignTagsNotClaimed never ran
NO-BUILD  k8s create: drop the ownership pre-read (D462)   TestK8sCreateRefusesForeignObject never ran
NO-BUILD  lambda: call any Function URL public (D534)      TestPublicExposureIsFalseWhenTheURLRequiresIAM never ran
NO-BUILD  adopt: drop the driver's diagnostics again (D556) TestAdoptCarriesTheDriversReasonForNotMeasuring never ran
NO-BUILD  check: stop grepping shipped files (D580)        TestNoDeniedTokenInFilesTheExportShips never ran
NO-BUILD  gates: treat the source tree as an export (D583) TestExportedTreeDetectionDoesNotSkipAPrivateTree never ran
```

This was already a written rule — "go vet the mutated tree and confirm the
substitution changed the file" — held in the head of whoever ran the meter, which is
D583's definition of not fixed. It is now in the meter: a mutant whose substitution
changed nothing reports `NO-OP`, a mutant that does not compile reports `NO-BUILD`,
and both fail the gate. A meter that cannot measure must not report a score.

All six mutants were then rewritten to compile while still carrying the bug
(`ours = true || groundholdTagsMatch(...)`, `if exists && !owned && false`), so the
tests they name are now genuinely measured. Meter after: **83 mutants, 83 caught, 0
no-op, 0 no-build**.

**One of the six then survived honestly, and that is the more useful finding.**
`TestNoDeniedTokenInFilesTheExportShips` scans every file the export ships for a client
name. With the scan disabled it still passed — because the tree is clean, so zero hits
is the answer either way. This is a general property of **absence gates**: a floor
(D328) proves the SUBJECT is non-empty; nothing proved the DETECTOR fires. A regex that
matches nothing, a classifier that returns false for everything, a scanner that is
never reached — all produce a green "no violations found".

The answer is a positive control: run the same detector over a synthetic input that
MUST match, and fail if it does not. Added to four gates:

- deny-token scan — a synthetic line built from the deny list itself, in a casing the
  sanitizer does not rewrite (built at runtime, never written literally: D580 was this
  gate carrying the client's name in its own source).
- hosted-runner classifier — must accept a real GitHub label and reject an unknown one.
- markdown link extractor — must match an ordinary link.
- json-tag extractor — must match an ordinary struct tag.

None writes to disk; each costs a line and turns "we found nothing" into "we looked".
The class for the next author: **for every gate that reports an absence, ask what it
would print if it were switched off — if the answer is the same, it is not a gate.**

## D604 — the pre-ship gate said "safe to ship" without running the check it exists for

`scripts/preship.sh` is what a binary passes before it goes to a client. Its own header
says every other step now runs in `release.yml` and that the script survives for ONE
reason: the SigV4-signed request, the only check anywhere that sees a signing
regression.

The smoke test skips that half when credentials are absent — `t.Log` and `return`,
which `go test` reports as PASS. So on a machine without credentials:

```
    live_aws_smoke_test.go:50: no AWS creds in env — signed DescribeCluster check skipped
--- PASS: TestLiveAWSSmoke
== PRESHIP OK — safe to build + ship ==
exit=0
```

The gate reported success having not run the one thing it exists for. Three delivery
manifests carried that gap as hand-written prose — "the signed half was NOT run, the
building machine has no AWS credentials" — written by a human who knew, while the tool
said OK. That prose is the tell: when a limitation has to be remembered and re-typed
each time, the mechanism is missing (D583).

Two changes, one for each reader.

**For `go test`:** the signed half is now its own test. Behind a `return`, the whole
test reported PASS with the signed half unexecuted; split, the protocol half still
passes on a credential-free box and `TestLiveAWSSignedSmoke` reports SKIP. A check that
did not run should look, to every downstream reader, like a check that did not run.

**For the script:** with no credentials it now refuses.

```
== PRESHIP REFUSED — the signed AWS check did not run ==
   Run it on a box with credentials, or accept the gap explicitly:
     scripts/preship.sh --without-signed-check
```

The escape hatch exists because the gap is sometimes the right call — but it costs a
word on the command line and the verdict changes to `PRESHIP INCOMPLETE`, in the
sentence the manifest should quote. An incomplete run does not get to borrow the clean
verdict's words.

The gate over the gate runs the guard block out of the real script under three
environments (none, `--without-signed-check`, credentials present) and asserts the exit
code and the verdict text of each, so a rewording or a changed exit code fails rather
than quietly ages.

## D605 — three cases that could not fail, and a runner that skipped half the suite

Two findings from the same pull, plus three defects in the meter that surfaced while
proving them.

**The cases.** `conformance/cases/reachability.yaml` defends one property: an apply
that stands up a public edge must not report APPLIED while the edge silently 403s.
Ten of its thirteen cases assert `reachability`. Three — the ones named
`...-has-nothing-to-probe` — asserted `exit` and `status` and nothing else, though
their descriptions say "nothing measured, nothing emitted, no reachability field".
The runner compares the field only when the case mentions it, so:

```go
if len(targets) == 0 {
    r.Reachability = "reachable"   // nothing measured, claim success
    return
}
```

passed all three, and the whole gate stayed green. A private Cloud Run announced as
publicly reachable is the exact inverse of the property the file exists to defend.

The assertion for an absence is `reachability: null` — the key present, the value
absent — which the runner already compares correctly. With it, the mutant fails all
three by name. The mechanism is a suite-level declaration: a case file may state

```yaml
requireExpect: [reachability]
```

and the runner refuses to run (exit 2) if any case in that file says nothing about it.
A suite whose entire subject is one field should not be able to forget the field.

**The runner.** Proving the above needed a mutated binary, and the meter built one at
a temp path — where the suite passed. `is_go` was

```python
any("groundhold-go" in part for part in impl)
```

a guess from the FILE NAME, deciding whether the 282 Go-only cases run at all:

```
$ cp bin/groundhold-go /tmp/renamed-cli
$ python3 conformance/run.py --impl /tmp/renamed-cli
236/236 conformance cases passed (cli: /tmp/renamed-cli, 282 skipped)
```

A green verdict over 45% of the suite. "236/236 passed" is what a reader takes away.
The runner now ASKS the implementation what it is (`--version`), refuses when the
answer is neither, and takes `--impl-kind go|ref` when someone knows better. Renamed,
the same binary now runs 518/518; a stranger exits 2.

**Three defects in the meter, found by using it.**

1. A mutant whose named test does not exist: `go test -run` over a name that matches
   nothing exits 0, which the gate read as SURVIVED — a report that sends the next
   author to fix a test that is not there. The name is now checked against `-list`,
   on the clean tree, before anything is touched.
2. That check was written as `go test -list … | grep -qx …`. `grep -q` closes the pipe
   on its first match, `go test` takes SIGPIPE, and `pipefail` turns a SUCCESSFUL
   lookup into a failed one — so the gate reported tests as missing BECAUSE they were
   found. Rewritten without a pipe. (Third time this session that a pipe's exit status
   made a correct result look wrong; the first two were mine at the terminal.)
3. Some real bugs are covered by the conformance suite and by no Go test — the meter
   could not measure those cases' teeth at all. `mutate_conformance` rebuilds the CLI
   from the mutated tree and requires the suite to go red. The zero-target probe above
   is its first user, and it is caught.

Meter now: **89 mutants, 89 caught**, with no-op, no-build and no-such-test all fatal.

## D606 — two scripts that stayed quiet when they could not find their subject

Both come out of the gate-script audit, and they are the same defect in two shapes:
the check could not ground itself, and said nothing rather than saying so.

**A canary assertion that vanishes.** `scripts/canary-gcp.sh` reads a Cloud Run service
id out of the ledger with a regex, then:

```sh
if [ -n "${SVC:-}" ]; then
  … verdict drift-C …
fi                       # no else
```

When the providerId spelling drifts, `SVC` is empty, the getIamPolicy route is never
asked about, no verdict line is written, no counter moves, and the canary exits all
green. Proven by running the real script against a stubbed provider with the same
injected fault (getIamPolicy → 404) and only the ledger spelling changed: exit 10 with
a `drift-C` verdict under one spelling, exit 0 and six verdicts — no drift-C — under
the other. Every other assertion in the three canaries emits `infra-flake` when it
cannot be grounded. This one was the exception, and the exception is the one that
matters: the drift it watches for is exactly the kind that would also change a
providerId.

**An adoption that confirms nothing.** `scripts/adopt-candidate.sh` builds a contract
from what `discover` OBSERVED, and its header promises that adoption "confirms every
declared attribute against the same reality groundhold measured". With an empty
observation list it produced a contract with zero hard constraints, adopted it, and
printed `adopted`. `discover` appends a resource with whatever the driver returned,
empty included, so the input is reachable by construction, not hypothetical. It now
exits 3 and says what is missing.

Two gates. The canary one is structural, because the defect is an ABSENCE of code: a
guarded block that emits a verdict must have an `else`, across all three canaries.
The adoption one runs the real script against a discovery document with no
observations and requires a refusal — with `GROUNDHOLD=/bin/false`, which also proves
the guard fires before anything is executed.

The class is one this record keeps meeting from different directions: **a check that
cannot reach its subject must say so.** D328 says assert a non-empty subject; D565 says
a gate that does not re-read its subject is not a gate; D605 says a runner must not
pick a subset in silence. Here it is the reporting end — silence read as success by
whoever counts the verdicts.

## D607 — the published CI example could not run, and the gate that should have known was blind

A sweep of every command line the repo publishes — 323 invocations, 62 of them executed
against the built binary — found six broken lines with three root causes. Two are fixed
in D602 (`apireq classify`). These are the other three, all the same shape:

```
examples/ci/github-actions.yml   plan …      -> exit 1, and plan.json written empty
examples/ci/github-actions.yml   forecast …  -> exit 1
Makefile: plan                               -> exit 1, and the target's guard expects 2
```

All three lost `--at`, which those verbs refuse without (N1: a safety clock must not
default to the epoch and make stale observations look fresh). `make plan` and
`make verify` are not in `make check`, and nothing runs the CI example, so all three
sat green — the published GitHub Actions workflow, the one a reader copies, has been
failing at its first groundhold step.

**Why D587 did not catch it, which is the more useful half.** That entry gated the
usage text: every flag a verb refuses without must appear in its usage line, with the
subject "derived from the refusals themselves — every `"<verb> requires --<flag>"`
message in the source". The `--at` refusal is not written that way. It is formatted
from a variable:

```go
if timeSensitiveVerbs[cmd] && !atProvided {
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s requires an explicit --at …", cmd)
```

so a regex over the source finds **none** of the time-sensitive verbs. The derivation
looked authoritative and covered a set that happened to exclude the most widely
required flag in the tool. The new gate reads `timeSensitiveVerbs` — the map the
runtime itself dispatches on — rather than the text of a message about it (D317: ask
the code, do not scrape it). Proven by removing `--at` from the Makefile: the first
version of the gate stayed green, the fixed one names the line.

The gate now checks that every published invocation carries the flags its verb refuses
without, across the Makefile and both CI examples. Its first run produced a false
positive worth recording: a YAML-folded command (`audit` in `gitlab-ci.yml`, with
`--ledger` on the next line) read as truncated. A scanner that mistakes a wrapped
command for an incomplete one accuses correct work, which is how a gate loses its
reader; continuations are now joined for both wrapping styles before matching.

Also fixed in passing, my own: the substitution that added `--at` to the Makefile hit
the `verify` target instead of `plan` — the first occurrence of a shared suffix. The
rule this project already has (every substitution with an assertion) exists precisely
for that, and I applied it only after the fact.

## D608 — the same bytes had two identities, and no case could say so

The dual implementation exists so that two independent readings of a document must
agree. They did not agree on the simplest document there is.

```
$ cat event.yaml            # …LedgerEvent envelope…
  body:
    note:

$ python3 ref/groundhold.py hash event.yaml
sha256:dda3a7d3…
$ bin/groundhold-go hash event.yaml
sha256:f09303ee…
```

An empty scalar is null in YAML 1.2 core, which is what go-yaml resolves and what the
reference's `yamlcompat` loader exists to reproduce. Its null resolver was registered
as

```python
_add("tag:yaml.org,2002:null", r"^(?:~|null|Null|NULL|)$", "~nN\0")
```

The regex allows the empty form. The first-character list does not: PyYAML dispatches
an EMPTY scalar on the key `""`, and this said `"\0"` — NUL, one transcription away.
The resolver never fired, an empty scalar fell through to `str`, and every signature,
anchor, capsule and ledger head over such a document was taken over a different hash on
each side.

**The same slip, one layer up.** `ref/groundhold.py` used plain `yaml.safe_load` — YAML
1.1 — in `hash` and `scenario`, so two of the six document kinds were read by a
different loader than the four around them. `note: yes` hashed as a bool in the
reference and a string in the runtime (11 of 22 ambiguous tokens diverged), and a
scenario step keyed `yes:` resolved to `True` on one side and `"yes"` on the other —
the same file reporting a head as stale to one implementation and fresh to the other,
both exiting 0. Both call sites now go through `yamlcompat`, and the four dead
`import yaml` lines elsewhere in `ref/` are gone.

**Why nothing caught it, which is the part worth keeping.** Every conformance case
carries its document as a YAML mapping, and the harness re-emits it with `safe_dump`
before either implementation sees it. `note:` arrives as `None` and is written back as
`note: null` — so the thing under test, how each side RESOLVES the ambiguous form,
never happens. The parser was unreachable from the suite by construction. The
differential has a raw-document path, but its token list was written by hand and the
empty scalar was not on it.

Three mechanisms, one per instrument:

1. A new case shape, `documentRaw:` — the document as verbatim text, written
   byte-for-byte, hashed by both CLIs. Two cases use it; each fails against its own bug
   re-injected and passes otherwise.
2. The empty scalar joins the differential's raw token list, and the template moved to
   block form so an empty token stays empty. With the fix reverted, the fuzzer now
   reports the divergence at seed 1.
3. An invariant: inside `ref/`, nothing but `yamlcompat.py` may load YAML. A second
   loader is a second answer to "what does this document say", and both must never be
   reachable. The gate carries a positive control (D603).

The audit that found this also measured what AGREES, which belongs in the record:
roughly 340 hand-built inputs — NFC vs NFD, lone surrogates, astral keys, 2^53
boundaries, `-0.0`, BOM, CRLF, UTF-16, 400-deep nesting, every duration and money and
protocol corner — byte-identical on both sides. The divergences are a short list, and
this entry closes the two that change a hash. The rest (duplicate keys, merge keys,
`meta.version` coercion, tracebacks where the error protocol expects a message) are
recorded and not yet fixed.

## D609 — a document one implementation reads and the other rejects

Continuing D608 down the same list. Two more forms where the two implementations did
not agree about what a file SAYS, and one where the reference did not say it in the
shape the protocol defines.

**A duplicate mapping key.** The runtime refuses it —
`mapping key "dup" already defined at line 10` — and the reference silently kept the
last value and hashed the document. Which value the author meant is not knowable, so
neither side may guess; the reference now refuses too. This is the same failure mode as
a hash divergence, one step earlier: a document valid to one implementation and invalid
to the other, with the ambiguous half being the one that answers.

**A merge key.** `<<: *anchor` — go-yaml expands it into the mapping. The reference's
compat loader clears PyYAML's resolver table to get 1.2 scalar resolution and lost
`tag:yaml.org,2002:merge` along with it, so `flatten_mapping` never fired and `<<`
survived as a literal key. Same bytes, two hashes, on a form configuration documents
actually use. The merge tag is registered again, and both sides now produce
`sha256:6fb4c817…`.

**Refusals in the protocol's shape.** A parse failure now leaves `yamlcompat.safe_load`
as a `ContractError`, which every caller already reports as `document error: … / exit 1`.
Before, four classes escaped as Python tracebacks — a duplicate key, a custom tag, a
second `---` document, and nesting deep enough to exhaust the recursion limit. A tool
that crashes has still refused, but it has told a machine reader nothing it can act on,
and `spec/errors.md` defines that line for a reason.

```
before   Traceback (most recent call last): … ConstructorError …
after    document error: mapping key 'dup' already defined at line 11, column 5
         INVALID
```

**Left open, deliberately, with the measurement.** Three forms where the runtime
ACCEPTS what the reference refuses: a file holding two `---` documents (the runtime
hashes the first), an unknown local tag (`!custom x`), and nesting past Python's
recursion limit (1000 deep; 400 agrees). These are questions about what a document IS,
not slips in a loader — silently hashing the first of two documents looks wrong to me,
but changing what the runtime accepts is a spec decision and belongs in a case first,
argued, not in a night's sweep. Recorded here with reproductions so the next person
starts from the measurement rather than from scratch.

## D610 — a contract said version 7 and the tool said v1, with an OK next to it

Last of the loader divergences that is a defect rather than a spec question.

```
$ cat contract.yaml
meta: { id: t1, environment: test, version: "7" }

$ python3 ref/groundhold.py validate contract.yaml
OK  contract t1 v7: 1 capabilities, 1 constraints (1 hard)
$ bin/groundhold-go validate contract.yaml
OK  contract t1 v1: 1 capabilities, 1 constraints (1 hard)
```

The runtime read `meta["version"].(int)` and fell back to 1 when the assertion failed.
So a declared version the loader could not read was DROPPED, the document was accepted,
and the tool printed a confident line naming a version the author never wrote. That is
D530's shape — a run that drops an input answers a question you did not ask — sitting
in the contract loader itself, the first thing every verb touches.

The reference coerced instead: `int("7")` → 7, `int(3.0)` → 3, and a bare `TypeError`
traceback on a list. Three shapes, three disagreements, including the document hash.

Neither guesses now: a present `meta.version` that is not an integer is a load error on
both sides, naming the field. An absent one still means 1, and a plain integer still
loads — both pinned, because the cheap way to satisfy a refusal test is to refuse more
than asked.

Two cases (a quoted integer, a fraction) and a Go test covering all three shapes plus
the two forms that must keep working. The mutant restores the fallback.

That closes the divergence list from the reference-vs-runtime audit except the three
acceptance questions recorded in D609, which need a spec decision rather than a fix.

## D611 — three verbs reported run state from a ledger that does not replay

`spec/errors.md` states the rule without qualification: `ledger-corrupted | 5 | …
nothing proceeds over corruption`. Twelve verbs obey it. Three did not.

The same file — a seventeen-line ledger with line 9 replaced by
`{"this":"is not an event"}`:

```
$ groundhold export --ledger corrupt.ndjson
export error: ledger line 9: event.occurredAt is missing — export refuses what replay refuses
exit=5

$ groundhold runs   --ledger corrupt.ndjson --at 2026-02-01T00:00:00Z
af56b0a5b81a  converge  done  31d  2026-01-01…
exit=0

$ groundhold wait af56b0a5b81a --ledger corrupt.ndjson --timeout 1
converge af56b0a5b81a  done  phase convergence-check
exit=0
```

`runs`, `status` and `wait` printed a handle, a phase and a duration derived from bytes
that do not replay, at exit 0, with an OK banner. `wait` relays a run's exit code to its
caller, so a script would have branched on a number sourced from an unverified file.

**One struct did it.** `runstatus.ReadEvents` unmarshals each line into a shape where
every field is optional, so `{"this":"is not an event"}` parsed cleanly into an event
with no type; and `ledger.ParseTs`'s error was discarded — `clk, _ :=` — so its
timestamp became the epoch. D323 named that pattern exactly ("PRESENT is not the same
as PARSES", every downstream site reading the clock with the error thrown away), and
here it sat in the reader three reporting verbs share. Both halves are now checked: a
line with no `event.type` and an unreadable `occurredAt` are each refused, naming the
line number.

**The rule that had to survive.** These verbs report at exit 0 for a run that FAILED,
deliberately: reporting is not judging, and `status --help` says so. That is untouched.
A file that is not a ledger is not a run that failed — the two rules were never in
tension, and the code had simply never distinguished them.

The gate drives all three verbs over a corrupt line, over an unreadable timestamp, and
over a healthy ledger. The healthy control for `wait` is deliberately weaker (it blocks
for a terminal state and exits 3 on timeout): it asserts only that a readable ledger is
never called corrupt, because building a synthetic run the derivation would call
terminal would pin my model of that derivation rather than the property under test.

Found by an audit of exit codes against `spec/errors.md` — the first of several from
that pass; the others (one condition with two codes, one code at three different exits,
a missing `--ledger` file answered four different ways) are queued behind this one.

## D612 — the security policy stopped at the porcelain boundary, in both directions

`converge` is the verb the README's walkthrough puts in front of operators. It runs
`plan`, `observe`, `forecast` and `apply` as child PROCESSES. `--trust`, `--trust-from`
and `--sign-key` are armed in the parent process, and were never placed on the
children's argv.

**Trust, unenforced.** Same ledger, same flag, four verbs:

```
plan     --trust <foreign key>   exit 5   event signed by a FOREIGN key 8818bb9f…
export   --trust <foreign key>   exit 5
audit    --trust <foreign key>   exit 5
converge --trust <foreign key>   exit 0   ✓ converged — the world already matches
                                          CONVERGED
```

Under an armed trust policy converge read and WROTE a ledger the other three refused.
The chain check still fired (a broken hash chain refuses at 5) — it is the key policy,
the part the operator explicitly asked for, that did not travel.

**Signing, and this one is not recoverable.** A clean, fully signed ledger, then one
`converge --sign-key`:

```
before   attest: selfVerified 10, unsigned 12    export --trust  exit 5, forever
after    attest: selfVerified 22, unsigned  0    export --trust  exit 0
```

The child `observe` wrote unsigned `observation.recorded` events into the middle of a
signed history. History is append-only: `export`, `backup`, `capsule` and `audit` under
`--trust` then refuse that ledger permanently, with no repair. An operator who armed
signing destroyed their own ability to verify, and the run reported success while doing
it. `attest` was honest throughout — `selfVerified 10, unsigned 12` — but nothing put
that in front of the person watching converge print CONVERGED.

The fix is one helper, `policyArgs()`, appended to every child that touches the ledger
(plan, observe ×2, forecast, apply, the convergence-check plan). `verify` is excluded
on purpose: it is a pure document check and takes neither flag.

The gate reads the argv of every child converge spawns and requires the policy on each
one that carries `--ledger`, so a child added later is covered by the rule rather than
by whoever remembers it. Its mirror asserts the opposite: with nothing armed, no child
may carry `--trust` or `--sign-key`, because inventing a policy is its own defect.

The class has a name in this record — a boundary a control does not cross — but this is
the first time it has been a SECURITY control, and the first time the damage was
permanent. Worth stating plainly: every one of the conformance cases that arms `--trust`
invokes a single verb directly. None goes through the porcelain, which is exactly where
the flag stopped.

## D613 — an anchor that pins nothing said "verified", and a foreign one agreed

An anchor's whole job is to detect a rewrite: it pins *this ledger, at this length,
hashed to this*. `CheckAnchor` had two ways to say yes to an anchor that says nothing
about the ledger in front of it.

**Zero events.** An adversarial review had already closed the inflating direction — 0
events with a non-genesis head is a forgery, refused, with the comment *"don't
rubber-stamp any ledger"*. The deflating direction returned `verified`:

```
$ groundhold anchor --ledger tampered.jsonl --check real-anchor.json
exit=5   diverged — "event 19 is sha256:5854b251… but the anchor pinned sha256:ae24f8b2…"

$ echo '{"kind":"LedgerAnchor","events":0,"head":"genesis",…}' > a-zero.json
$ groundhold anchor --ledger tampered.jsonl --check a-zero.json
exit=0   {"status":"verified","anchorEvents":0,"ledgerEvents":19}
```

Replace the sidecar with a document that pins nothing and the tampered ledger passes;
copy it beside the ledger and `attest` republishes `anchor: {"status":"verified"}` to
the console. The status is now `unverifiable`, exit 5, with a reason that says to treat
the document as no anchor rather than as a passed check. **"I could not check" is not
"I checked"** — the same distinction D514 drew for a missing observation, here for a
missing witness. An empty anchor over an empty ledger still verifies; the refusal is
about silence over real history, not about being stricter.

**Foreign identity.** `CheckAnchor` never read `LedgerId`, so an anchor built for
another ledger verified this one. D312 had already found this exact hole, named it —
*a guard conditional on the very field it guards is not a guard* — built
`RequireIdentity()`, and wired it into `restore` and `capsule --verify`. `anchor
--check`, the verb whose entire purpose is this question, did not call it. Identity is
now compared before arithmetic, and the CLI calls `RequireIdentity()` where it uses the
anchor as proof.

Three artefacts, one rule, and the one that needed it most was missed — the same shape
as D584 (write-safety consulted in three places, one of them wrong) and D607 (a
derivation that looked authoritative and excluded the most common case). A fix that
lands in "every place I could think of" is a fix that needs a gate over the places, not
a longer list.

Found by an adversarial audit of the whole evidence chain — capsule, snapshot, anchor,
backup, restore, attest — which attacked interior tampering, tip tampering, truncation,
cross-capability reordering, foreign keys, stripped signatures and forged capsules. All
of those were caught, several with better messages than I would have written. The
findings were concentrated in `restore --documents`, `restore --partial` and the anchor,
which is also where the conformance suite has no cases at all.

## D614 — the surface an agent drives had a default cloud and an impossible schema

The MCP server is the one interface where nobody reads the argv before it runs, so its
defaults and its declared schema ARE the safety boundary. An audit that drove the
server over stdio and then FOLLOWED its advice found three defects.

**A default cloud.** `str(a, "provider", "gcp")` in four places, including the observe
tool's own description, `"fake|gcp (default gcp)"`. The CLI publishes the opposite
invariant, in these words: *the fake driver fabricates reality, so it is chosen
deliberately, never defaulted*. Driving `groundhold_apply` with a candidate that
declares `provider: fake` and no provider argument:

```
step 1  status: confirmation_required   target.provider: gcp    ← nobody chose this
step 2  exit 1  "apply error: plan does not pin reads.provider.project"
```

The confirmation an agent is instructed to show a human named a cloud nobody selected,
and the failure read as a malformed plan rather than as a substituted provider.
`groundhold_observe` carried the same default and would have contacted real GCP.

**A schema whose conformant call cannot succeed.** `inputSchema.required` omitted `at`
on all four time-sensitive tools. A client that reads the schema and sends exactly the
declared-required set gets `requires an explicit --at` from plan, observe and forecast —
