and for apply it is worse than a wasted call, because the single-use confirmation token
is minted and spent before the structural failure. `at` and `provider` are now declared
required AND enforced, with the enforcement placed AFTER each tool's safety gate: a
disabled apply must answer "disabled", not "argument missing", because answering the
smaller question first hides the bigger one.

**A published claim the code contradicts.** `website/pages/mcp.md` said *"The token
proves a human saw THIS sealed decision."* The package doc says the opposite, in
detail: it *"does NOT authenticate a human. It is delivered in-band to the same MCP
client, so an autonomous (or prompt-injected) agent can complete both steps alone — do
not rely on it as SoC/human-approval evidence."* The auditor demonstrated it with a
thirty-line Python driver that completed both steps with no human present. The honest
sentence now lives on the page, where a compliance reader arrives, rather than only in
a source comment they will never open.

Three gates: the declared schema must equal the enforced set (a field declared required
and not checked is documentation, and the reverse is a trap); no tool may default a
provider to any cloud, with a positive control on the detector (D603); and the page may
not carry the stronger claim while the code carries the weaker one.

The same audit ran 104 pieces of published advice end to end and found the rest sound —
`suggest`'s snippets across all 51 capability types paste, validate and verify clean,
and both posture recipes run verbatim. That is worth recording next to the failures: the
advice-is-a-claim work of D568/D569/D594 held.

## D615 — the refusal on one flag read as diligence covering the flag beside it

D567's motivating bug was `posture --discovery discovery.json`: posture takes no such
flag, the value was swallowed as a positional, and the run printed `"shadow": 0` and a
`postureHash` over a cluster holding 169 unmanaged objects. That entry closed it with a
message naming the reason — a crawl records per-scope COMPLETENESS and `discover` does
not, so folding a discovery document would report a shadow count posture has not
earned.

`--crawl`, the flag immediately beside it, took the same file happily:

```
posture … --crawl realcrawl.json   → exit 2   shadow: 1   (fake:existing-db)
posture … --crawl discovery.json   → exit 0   shadow: 0   banner OK
```

`json.Unmarshal` into `crawl.Document` succeeds for a discovery document because every
field there is optional to the decoder — no providers, no scopes, no error. And
`shadowLowerBound: false` is not silence; it is an affirmative claim that the sweep was
complete. Posture's own shadow remediation tells the operator to run `discover`, so the
wrong file is the one they are holding.

Both refusals now exist, plus the emptiness case that neither covered: a document that
is structurally a crawl but names no providers swept nothing, and a posture over an
empty sweep would report zero shadows and mean nothing by it (D328, at the input rather
than at the gate).

The lesson is about the shape of the earlier fix, not about this flag. **A refusal
written for one input reads, to the next author and to the reader of the diff, as a
rule about the class.** D567's message even names the class — "a crawl records
completeness, discover does not" — while the code enforced it in exactly one place.
When a fix states a rule, the gate has to cover the rule, not the instance that
prompted it (D583, again).

## D616 — recovery certified a contract the recovered history had never seen

`restore --documents` is the last step of a disaster recovery. It answers: are the
contract blobs that came back the ones this history was built on? It was handed only
the directory, so it compared each blob to `manifest.json` — a plain file sitting beside
those blobs, written by whoever made the backup.

Replace a contract blob with one where both hard constraints are flipped to `false`,
rename it to its own (different) hash, write a one-entry manifest naming that hash:

```
$ groundhold restore --out sub.jsonl --check anchor.json --documents b_sub/documents …
exit=0
{ "kind": "DocumentVerifyReport", "status": "verified",
  "documents": [ { "hash": "sha256:c623cffc…", "kind": "contract", "status": "verified" } ] }
```

The restored ledger pins `sha256:546690ae…`. The blob just certified is a different
contract, one that permits an unmanaged service. Two weaker variants of the same root:
an empty manifest verified zero documents and reported success, and flipping
`"present": false` left the blob unread and still "verified" — a guard conditional on a
field the attacker sets, which is exactly the shape D312 closed for anchors.

Genuine credit where it is due: a SEMANTIC edit to a blob with the manifest left alone
was caught, exit 5, naming both the recomputed and the pinned hash. The bypass ran
entirely through the manifest, which nothing treated as untrusted input.

The authority is the RESTORED LEDGER — it pins the contract hashes this history was
compiled against, and restore has just replayed them. `VerifyDocumentsAgainst` now
compares three ways: a pinned contract the manifest does not mention is `unaccounted`,
a manifest entry the ledger does not pin is `foreign`, and either refuses the run.
Called without a ledger it degrades to the old manifest-only check AND says so in the
report — an honest weaker answer rather than a silent one.

```
after   exit=5  status refused
        sha256:c623cffc…  foreign      "not pinned anywhere in the restored ledger"
        sha256:546690ae…  unaccounted  "the ledger pins this and the manifest does not"
```

The audit that found this attacked the whole evidence chain and reported the score
honestly: interior tampering, tip tampering, truncation, cross-capability reordering
(interleaving two independent `prev` chains so both stay linked — the subtle one, and
the anchor manifest caught it), snapshot-fold tampering, every capsule attack, foreign
trust keys and forged anchors were all detected, several with better messages than I
would have written. Everything it found was in `restore`, `backup` and the anchor —
which is also where the conformance suite has **zero** cases. Four of six findings sat
in that gap. The suite's step DSL has no verbs for `restore`, `backup`,
`certify-capsule` or `keygen`, so those paths could not be expressed as cases even by
someone who wanted to.

## D617 — "healthy" was the answer to a ledger that did not exist

`ReplayFile` returns an empty ledger for a missing file. That is a deliberate
affordance for WRITERS — the first append creates the file — and six read-only verbs
inherited it:

```
attest  --ledger gone.jsonl   exit 0   a clean IntegrityReport
repair  --ledger gone.jsonl   exit 0   {"status":"healthy"}, fingerprint of the empty string
anchor  --ledger gone.jsonl   exit 0   and it EMITS an events:0 anchor
deposed / posture / refresh   exit 0
export  --ledger gone.jsonl   exit 1
backup  --ledger gone.jsonl   exit 5
```

`repair` is the verb an operator reaches for when they suspect corruption, and it
answered *healthy* about a file that is not there. A typo in a path is the ordinary way
to arrive at that command. And the `anchor` line is worse than it looks: the document
it emits for a missing ledger is exactly the zero-event anchor D613 shows will later
rubber-stamp any ledger it is checked against.

`ReplayExisting` is the reader for a verb that is ASKING ABOUT a ledger rather than
preparing to write one. Six verbs use it; the writer path is untouched.

**The second half is the exit code.** A wrong PATH and bytes that do not REPLAY are
different operator problems, and between them they had four exit codes across sixteen
verbs — including the pair that contradict each other outright: `backup` answered 5
(CORRUPTED), whose published remediation is `groundhold repair`, and `repair` answered
"healthy". A caller could not branch on the status, and an operator following the
published advice got a false all-clear. They are now 1 (fix the path) and 5 (the
history is damaged), separated by a sentinel error rather than by which verb you
happened to run — which also corrected `runs`, where D611's new refusal had swept a
missing file into corruption an hour earlier.

The gate drives all seven verbs at a path that does not exist and requires exit 1 and a
message that says so.

## D618 — a recovery that recovered nothing exited 0 and left an artefact to certify it

`restore --partial` is for the case where some capabilities can be proven from the
capsules you have and others cannot: recover what is provable, and say what is not. It
returned `ExitOK` however much it had failed to recover — including all of it.

```
$ groundhold restore --out none.jsonl --partial --check anchor.json db.capsule.json …
exit=0    status=partial   events=0   ledgerId=None
          none.jsonl         0 bytes
          none.jsonl.anchor  219 bytes   events:0, head:genesis, no ledgerId

$ groundhold anchor --ledger none.jsonl --check none.jsonl.anchor
exit=0    {"status":"verified","anchorEvents":0,"ledgerEvents":0}
$ groundhold attest --ledger none.jsonl --at …
exit=0    anchor: {"status":"verified","events":0,"head":"genesis"}
```

The truth was inside the `partial[]` block of a report nobody re-reads after a green
exit. From the next minute on, the "recovered history" is an empty file that two
integrity verbs certify — and the anchor it left behind is precisely the zero-event
document D613 shows will rubber-stamp whatever it is later checked against. Three
defects composing: the empty restore creates the artefact, the anchor check blesses it,
and the missing-file affordance (D617) means nothing along the way notices there is no
history.

A restore that recovered nothing is a failed restore. It now refuses, and removes the
empty ledger and its anchor — D313 established that rule for `backup` and it belongs
here for the same reason: a refused run must not leave a plausible artefact behind.

**One existing expectation is superseded, deliberately and in writing.**
`TestPartialCouplingDemotes` required `ExitOK` and an empty restored ledger on disk for
exactly this case. That was a considered decision when it was written: `--partial` had
reported honestly per capability, so exiting 0 read as consistent with its contract.
What changed is not the honesty of the report but what happens NEXT to the file it
leaves — D613 and D617 landed hours earlier and turn that empty artefact into something
two integrity verbs certify. The per-capability honesty stays; the run refuses rather
than leaving something to bless. The case now carries that reasoning in its own body,
because a reader who finds a flipped expectation deserves the argument, not a diff.

**This slice also gives `backup` and `restore` their first automated coverage.** The
adversarial audit found four of its six defects in exactly these two verbs, and the
reason is visible in the harness rather than in anyone's attention: the conformance
step DSL has no verbs for `restore`, `backup`, `certify-capsule` or `keygen`, so nobody
could have written a case for them even if they had wanted to. The tests here drive the
real CLI entry point end to end — plan, apply, backup, tamper every capsule, restore —
with an intact-backup control so the refusal is about recovering nothing rather than
about new strictness. (They use plan + apply rather than converge: converge spawns
ITSELF as a child process, and inside a test binary that argv is the test.)

### Meter note (D611–D618)

Eight mutants added, one per fix above; 105 mutants, 105 caught. One of the eight came
back SURVIVED first, and it was a fact about the TEST rather than about the code: the
corrupt-ledger fixture had neither an `event.type` nor a readable `occurredAt`, so
either guard alone refused it and removing one changed nothing. A third fixture — a
line with a perfectly good timestamp and no type — now aims at that guard by itself.
Overlapping guards on one fixture is the same shape as an absence gate with no positive
control (D603): the suite is green either way, and only the meter can tell you which
guard is load-bearing.


## D619 — one code, three exits, and a gate I wrote wrong on the first pass

`spec/errors.md` publishes a code AND an exit for every refusal, and tells callers to
branch on them. The exit lived in exactly two places: that table, and a literal beside
the code at each of 32 call sites. Nothing compared them. An audit that provoked ~244
failures across 54 verbs found:

```
structural-error   emitted at exits 1, 2 AND 3
stale-decision     emitted at 2 and 3
a stale plan       refused as `structural-error` in one arm of apply.go and as
                   `stale-decision` in another, sixty lines apart, same condition
adopt              one helper hardcoded exit 2 for EVERY code it refuses with
```

A caller can map neither direction, which is the whole reason both are published.
D330's registry gate reconciles the code NAMES across four artefacts; the exit column
had no gate, and that is exactly where the drift lived — the same shape as D607, where
a derivation that looked authoritative happened to exclude the most common case.

The exits are now stated once, in `ExitsFor`, and the call sites are held to it. Five
sites moved: the two staleness refusals in `apply` became `stale-decision` (matching the
writer path that already said so), a malformed evaluation time became exit 1 as the
table says, and `adopt`'s two helpers derive the exit from the code instead of writing
2 under all of them.

One conformance case moved with it, and the reasoning belongs here rather than only in
the diff: `adopt-refuses-over-pending-receipts` pinned exit 2 for a refusal whose code
is `reconcile-required`, which the published table gives as `3/4` with a remediation
that names this exact condition — "pending receipts block". The case had encoded
adopt's hardcoded 2, so the same code left `apply` as 3 and `adopt` as 2. The refusal
reason is untouched; only the number that contradicted the spec changed, and the case
now carries that argument in its own body.

**The part worth the entry.** My first version of that registry parsed the exit column
with `\|\s*(\d+)\s*\|` — pure digits — and three rows publish TWO exits by design
(`reconcile-required` is `3/4`: pending receipts block, or an outcome just landed).
Those rows were silently dropped. The gate then compared the dropped map against a
`published` map built by **the same parser**, so it passed with both sides wrong
together; the loss surfaced only when a lookup returned the zero value and `unadopt`
refused with exit 0.

Two artefacts derived by one broken parser are one artefact. It is the same defect as
the vacuous gate (D328) and the absence gate with no positive control (D603), in its
most embarrassing form: I built it while writing the entry that names the class. The
gate now parses `3/4`, treats the exits as a SET, and asserts the runtime knows exactly
as many codes as the table publishes — so a row a parser drops fails loudly instead of
disappearing from both sides of its own comparison.

## D620 — a usage error came back as a verdict about the infrastructure

`apireq classify` turns a probe result into one of four verdicts, and its exit code IS
the class — two daily canaries branch on it. Its two load-bearing inputs were read like
this:

```go
parseBool := func(v string) bool { return v == "true" || v == "1" || v == "yes" }
```

So `--applied yeees` was false, and a missing `--applied` was false, and false is a
FACT ABOUT THE WORLD. With no flags at all:

```
$ groundhold --provider aws apireq classify
groundhold-regression (exit 20)
converge did not stand up the known-good edge (status != applied) — a groundhold-regression
in the edge build path, not a provider change.
```

A confident accusation about the edge build path, derived from inputs nobody supplied.
The rule this breaks is written into the unknown-flag refusal a few entries ago (D567):
*a run that drops an input answers a question you did not ask.* Here the run did not
drop the input — it invented it, which is worse, because the invented value is the one
that reads as failure.

Both halves refuse now, at exit 30 — the flake code, chosen deliberately: nothing was
measured, so the honest answer is "no reading", not a verdict in either direction. A
value that is not a boolean refuses by name; an absent `--applied` or `--deployed`
refuses with what it was used to mean. `--transport` needs no pair (it IS its own
reading), and the canaries pass `true`/`false` explicitly, so their happy path is
unchanged.

Same family as D530 (a candidate operand no driver reads), D601 (an expectation the
harness never reads) and D615 (a sweep document that decoded to nothing): an input that
is missing must not be silently replaced by a value that means something.

## D621 — "the project is empty" and "the cloud was never contacted" had the same exit

```
$ groundhold discover --provider gcp --at 2026-02-01T00:00:00Z
exit=0
{"discovery": {"provider": "gcp", "resources": []},
 "diagnostics": ["locations.list: no usable GCP credentials …", … 43 in total]}

$ groundhold discover --provider aws   …   exit=1  aws discovery requires a region
$ groundhold discover --provider azure …   exit=1  azure discovery requires a subscription GUID
```

The document was honest. The exit code was not, and the exit code is what a script
reads. Worse, the document it wrote is the input `adopt` and `posture` are told to
take — an empty sweep flows straight into "nothing is unmanaged here".

The driver KNEW: every service lister failed identically at one function in `auth.go`,
and each flattened that into a diagnostic string. So the information existed structurally
and was destroyed on the way out. `List` now asks for a token once, before sweeping, and
returns an error the way its two siblings already do for a missing region and a missing
subscription — one refusal, at the point where the fact is still a fact rather than
prose (D317: ask, do not scrape).

The gate holds the RULE rather than the driver: a discoverer that cannot reach its
provider makes `Run` fail, and one that reaches it and finds nothing succeeds WITH its
diagnostics intact. Telling those two apart is the entire value of the verb, and the
second half of the test matters as much as the first — a genuinely empty project must
not become collateral damage of the fix.

## D622 — the capability map that said "every type" listed 51 of 57

`groundhold parity` is published, in the help text and in the bake-off skill, as *"the
capability map: **every type**, and which cloud fulfils it"*. Measured:

```
groundhold parity | grep -c '^capability\.'     51
grep -cE '^  capability\.' spec/parity.yaml     57
groundhold parity | grep -ci k8s                 0
grep -c fulfilledOutsideTheClouds spec/parity.yaml  8
```

Two halves of one cause: the verb derived its world from the three CLOUD drivers, while
the published matrix is generated from the vocabulary plus a `fulfilledOutsideTheClouds`
marker computed **inside the matrix generator's test**. So eight capabilities the k8s
driver ships read as three `unbuilt` rows, and six types nobody builds were not listed
at all — the answers a reader runs `parity` to get. `spec/parity.yaml`'s own header
names that misreading as the reason the marker exists: *"this stops unbuilt from being
read as 'groundhold has not built this' when it has."*

`OutsideTheClouds` now lives in the parity package, derived from the k8s driver's own
mappings, and both the matrix and the verb read it. The type list is the union of the
drivers, the vocabulary and that map — a type nobody builds is three `unbuilt` rows,
which is the truth and is what a reader needs.

**The same data, unread, one verb over.** `example candidate` wrote
`provider: aws` for every capability, including types this same parity data calls a
structural gap on aws:

```
groundhold example candidate jobs.contract.yaml   →   provider: aws
groundhold parity capability.container.job        →   aws  gap (not-capability-shaped)
                                                       gcp  fulfilled: cloudrunjobs
```

and the scaffold's next-step line sends the reader to `verify`, which is a pure document
check and answers PROVEN, while `plan` refuses the same pair as impossible. A default
that reads as a recommendation must not name a driver that cannot do the job: the
scaffold now names the ones that can (`provider: gcp  # or azure — groundhold parity …`),
says so when only one does, and says plainly when nothing does.

The class: **knowledge that exists only in a test is knowledge the product does not
have.** It was correct, it was even published — in an artefact generated by that test —
and every runtime path was blind to it.

## D623 — four nouns the runtime hands you that it could not explain

README publishes `explain` as *"the single place to ask about any noun the runtime
emits — every machine error code and every vocabulary attribute"*. All 33 codes in
`spec/errors.md` answer cleanly. Four others do not:

```
groundhold explain capsule-coupled             exit 1  not an error code and not a vocabulary attribute
groundhold explain capsule-trust-refused       exit 1
groundhold explain existence-not-witnessed     exit 1
groundhold explain logs-group-has-no-producer  exit 1
```

Two are per-capability verdicts `restore --partial` hands a DR operator BY DESIGN —
`restore --help` says it "marks the rest unknown+code", so the code is the product —
and two are compiler advisories. All four were bare string literals in the source,
registered nowhere.

The reason they were missed is worth naming: they are not process-exit codes, so they
have no row in `spec/errors.md`, and the absence of a row was read as "nothing to
register". They are now in `Markers`, deliberately separate from `Explain` (which
carries an exit and appears in the published table), with the same lookup surface and
an honest distinction in the output — "a marker the runtime emits (not a process exit
code)".

The gate closes the class rather than the four: every `Code:` literal the runtime emits
must resolve in one registry or the other, with a positive control on the detector
(D603) and a disjointness check so a code cannot mean two things depending on which
lookup runs first.

## D624 — three verbs refused in JSON without saying what the refusal was

`spec/errors.md` states the coverage rule in one line: *"every JSON-emitting verb
carries `code`"*. It is the whole reason D330 built a four-artefact registry — so a
consumer routes on a code instead of matching prose the same document declares
unparseable. Three verbs did not carry one:

```
audit  … --at …            exit 2   {"status":"violations-found", …}     grep -c '"code"' = 0
backup --ledger corrupt …  exit 5   {"status":"refused","reasons":[…]}   none
repair --ledger corrupt …  exit 5   {"status":"corrupt", …}              none
```

Every one of those conditions already had a published code. `audit` is the interesting
one, because the right answer depends on WHY it blocks: a hard verdict of `unknown`
means the evidence is missing or stale and the next step is `observe --record` — which
is precisely what `observation-required` publishes — while a constraint the world
genuinely fails is `not-executable`. One code for both would have satisfied the letter
of the rule and told the caller nothing.

The gate drives all three refusals and requires the specific code, plus a control that
a HEALTHY run carries none — a code that is always present is a signal that is always
on (D556). Building that control caught me writing a fixture by hand that repair
correctly called corrupt (a hand-rolled event has no `prev`), so the control now
publishes a real ledger first. A control that is wrong in the same direction as the
thing it controls for proves nothing.

The published output schema gained the two fields in the same slice, because the gate
from D559 asks for exactly that and asked immediately.

## D625 — the ratchet said COMPLETE about a smaller number than the one that was published

D513 published a debt with a number: *"of roughly 145 certified services across AWS, GCP
and Azure, one emits the marker"*, and asked for a register in the D463/D472 idiom —
every certified service either drives the absence property or carries an exemption, on
a ratchet that may only go down.

What got built was a ratchet over PROBES. It reads every `certifynet.Probe` in the
driver tests, requires each to carry `ObserveAbsent`, and its baseline constant is
`0 // COMPLETE`. All 102 probes do carry it, so the gate is honest about what it
measures — and what it measures is not what was published. Walking each driver's own
`ServiceCapabilities()` against the probe names:

```
aws    54 certified   17 with no absence probe
gcp    46 certified   13
azure  45 certified   14
                      44 of 145, of which 40 have no test naming the marker at all
```

A service with no probe never answers the question. The word COMPLETE sat above the
smaller number for as long as nobody compared the two.

**Two things I got wrong while measuring this, both worth recording.** First I counted
k8s and got "10 of 10 unprobed" — false: its ten mapped services prove the property
through shared `observeMapped` unit tests rather than through probes, and a
probe-name scan cannot see that. Then a spot check found `aws/bedrock` has a test
naming the marker outside any probe. So the scan lies in both directions, which is why
the ratchet counts the thing it can see honestly (does a probe exist) and the entry
states the rest as measured context rather than folding it into the number.

The emission is broadly implemented — roughly 136 driver files reference the marker —
so this is a PROOF gap rather than a behaviour gap. D317 is why that distinction is
kept: a static scrape of driver sources gave four different wrong answers about those
drivers, so "the code appears to emit it" is exactly the kind of claim this project
does not ratchet on.

`docs/MATURITY.md` carried the softer sentence — "every certified service was ASKED" —
and now carries the number. A ratchet whose subject is smaller than the published claim
is a ratchet that will read as closed while the debt is open.

## D626 — the one event that ships to a user was the one event with no gates

An audit of the release path, running for six hours against last night's tree, came
back with the largest structural finding of the series.

```
ci.yml        on: pull_request, push: branches: [main, master]
security.yml  on: pull_request, push: branches: [main, master], schedule
lint.yml      on: pull_request, push: branches: [main, master]
codeql.yml    on: pull_request, push: branches: [main, master], schedule
release.yml   on: push: tags: ['v*']
```

No `tags:` filter anywhere except the release. **A tag push ran `release.yml` alone** —
no gitleaks, no govulncheck, no golangci-lint, no CodeQL, no race detector, no mutation
meter, no differential fuzz, no export gate. Every one of those exists because
something shipped without it, and the commit that reaches a user was the commit none
of them saw.

It is not hypothetical. `make export-check` was RED for four commits last night — a
gate I wrote failed in the exported tree, the exact D340 class the export gate exists
to catch — and a release cut in that window would have published without noticing.

**The gates run inside the publishing job now**, because a workflow that merely runs in
parallel cannot stop `gh release create`: the release must not be able to publish over
a red gate, and only a step in that job can enforce it. The tag also triggers the other
four workflows so their tools see the released code.

**Three more from the same audit, all in the same file.**

*The version stamp step verified nothing.* It ran `groundhold version` and never looked
at the answer — and `-X` is silently a no-op when the symbol path stops matching:

```
-X main.buildVersion=v9.9.9-TEST         ->  groundhold v9.9.9-TEST
-X main.buildVersionRenamed=v9.9.9-TEST  ->  groundhold dev     (build exits 0)
```

The release notes tell a user to check `groundhold version`, so a rename would ship a
binary reporting `dev` past a green tick. It is compared to the tag now.

*The summary claimed a check that never ran.* The notes said "`make check`, the
differential fuzz, the reproducible rebuild … ran above" and `make check` does not
include the differential; nothing in the workflow ran it. Fixed in the honest direction
— by running the fuzz rather than by weakening the sentence — and a gate now requires
every check the notes NAME to correspond to a step that runs it.

*What the audit found sound, which matters too:* all fifteen third-party actions are
pinned by commit SHA with a scheduled re-resolution against upstream tags, the checksum
is computed over the same bytes that are uploaded, and the export's sanitizers are
asserted rather than assumed. The remaining findings — an unchecked pipe writing
`SHA256SUMS`, nothing binding the artefact to a commit rather than to a mutable tag,
and `repro-check` re-linking without recompiling (verified to still hold on a cold
cache) — are recorded and queued.

## D627 — a contract requiring encryption PROVED a candidate that refuses it

The worst defect found in this series, and the smallest slip behind it.

```yaml
constraints:
  hard:
    encryption:            # a MAPPING where the schema says array
      subject: db
      path: encryption.atRest
      op: equals
      value: true
```

Keying constraints by id instead of listing them reads perfectly well to a human. The
loader did `items, _ := cblock[sev].([]any)`; the assertion failed, `items` was nil, the
loop never ran, and **zero constraints were loaded**. Against a candidate that plainly
declares `encryption.atRest: false`:

```
$ groundhold verify c.yaml k.yaml
  0 satisfied, 0 violated, 0 unknown, 0 unverifiable
  PROVEN                                                exit 0
$ groundhold plan  … ; groundhold apply …               exit 0 — the resource is created
$ groundhold validate c.yaml
  OK  contract t v1: 1 capabilities, 0 constraints (0 hard)   exit 0
```

The product's entire claim — a contract proven against a candidate — evaporated, and
every verb said so cheerfully. `spec/contract.schema.json` says `array`. Nothing at
runtime enforced it. (The Python reference refused, with an uncaught traceback: wrong
in its own way, but it refused.)

**Two siblings from the same seam**, both found in the same audit:

- A candidate whose `attributes:` is a LIST loses every attribute, so an `absent`
  constraint reports `satisfied` — a false pass on a HARD verdict, over a document
  that says the resource is publicly exposed.
- `verify: {method: null}` fell back to the initialised `"static"`. A bogus *string*
  was refused ("unknown verify method"); a bogus *type* was not. So a constraint the
  contract says must be proven against the provider became one proven by reading the
  candidate's own claim, and reported `satisfied`.

The rule, now enforced by two helpers at every load-bearing site: **if a key is
PRESENT, its shape is part of the document's meaning.** A block of the wrong shape is
not an empty block. An absent optional block is still absent — the control test pins
that, because the cheap way to satisfy a refusal test is to refuse more than asked.

The class is `x, _ := doc["k"].(T)` — Go's comma-ok discarded. It is the same shape as
D323 (`clk, _ := ParseTs(...)` making an unreadable timestamp the epoch) and D558 (a
child's diagnostics going to `_`), and it is worth stating as a rule rather than as
three entries: **a discarded ok is a decision to treat "I could not read this" as "this
is empty", and those are never the same thing.**

Found by an audit that ran 993 differential `verify` cases across both implementations.
Its headline result is worth recording next to the failure: **0 divergences in 850
well-formed fuzz cases**, and every attack on the four-valued core — cross-kind
comparison, negation over unknown, empty-set operators, currency mismatch, protocol
majors, canonical equality inside nested lists — behaved correctly. The engine is
sound; the loader in front of it was not.

## D628 — every update reported no data loss and no security exposure, by construction

`updateRisk()` took no arguments:

```go
func updateRisk() Risk {
	return Risk{Reversibility: "R1", DataLoss: "none", Downtime: "possible",
		SecurityExposure: "none", IdentityReplacement: false}
}
```

So one sealed action carrying

```json
"changes": [{"path":"encryption.atRest","from":true,"to":false},
            {"path":"network.publicExposure","from":false,"to":true}]
```

reported `securityExposure: none` — in the plan a human reads before consenting — and
an update cutting a log retention from `3653d` to `7d` reported `dataLoss: none`.
`converge`'s consent gate is exactly `a.Risk.DataLoss == "certain" || a.Risk.IdentityReplacement`,
so the only thing between an operator and a silent encryption-disable under plain
`--yes` was a field hardcoded to the safest value in the vocabulary.

The vector is now derived from the change set the compiler already holds:

- a boolean security attribute weakened (`encryption.*`, `security.*`, `auth.*`, `iam.*`
  going false; `network.public*` going true) → `securityExposure: certain`;
- a provable numeric decrease in a retention/backup/storage/capacity attribute →
  `dataLoss: certain`, compared with the VERIFIER's own scalar comparator rather than
  a second numeric parser — it already knows durations, sizes and the no-coercion rule,
  and a second "is this smaller" would be one more copy to drift;
- **everything else is `possible`, never `none`.** The compiler has established nothing
  about it, and `none` is a claim. That half is the load-bearing one, and the gate pins
  it: an unclassifiable change and an empty change set must both refuse to report
  safety.

What this does NOT do, stated so it is not mistaken for more: the direction of a
non-boolean, non-quantitative change is still unreadable here, and the driver has no
risk channel at all — `ClassifyChange` returns `(class, note)` and nothing else. A
per-attribute risk declaration belongs in the vocabulary, where D311 put evidence
class, and that is a separate build. Until then the honest answer for those is
`possible`, which is what an operator now sees.

Also recorded from the same audit, not yet fixed: the flagship contract's
`autonomy.auto_execute` block (`max_reversibility`, `max_cost_delta`) is read by no Go
code at all — an inert knob in the example every reader starts from.

## D629 — the review of D627 and D628, and what it found in them

Two consultations on the night's work, per the standing practice: a design brainstorm
and an adversarial code review. Both landed on the same shape — my claims were one step
wider than my code.

**"Every load-bearing site" was not every site.** D627 named a class and fixed six
places; three remained with the same unchecked assertion. `capability.requirements`
(constraints the author wrote, silently dropped), `assumptions` and each entry's
`affects` (referential integrity checked against nothing), and the candidate's
per-capability BODY — a capability whose body is a scalar declares nothing while still
counting as implemented. All three refuse now.

**The rule contradicted itself.** `wantList`/`wantMap` treated a present `null` as
absent, while the entry declared "if a key is PRESENT, its shape is part of the
document's meaning". The resolution is a distinction rather than a blanket: **a null
CONTAINER is an empty container** — `constraints:` with nothing under it is idiomatic
YAML for "none here" — **and a null LEAF is unreadable and refuses**, which is why
`verify: {method: null}` is an error. Both directions are pinned, because a rule with
an unstated exception is the exception nobody finds later.

**The release job assumed a dependency its sibling installs.** `make check`,
`make differential` and `make export-check` all run the Python reference. `ci.yml`
installs PyYAML explicitly on the same runner pool; `release.yml` relied on the pool
having it, and the probe recorded in its own comment covered `python3`, not its
packages. The gates I added in D626 would have inherited that assumption. Installed
explicitly now.

**Two findings I am NOT fixing yet, recorded with the reasons.**

*The `securityPaths` prefix list in D628 is a shadow vocabulary.* It decides which
attributes are security-relevant, and it lives in `compiler.go` where no vocabulary
gate looks — the published-registries-drift class (D329/D338), which means the first
attribute added under a namespace it does not know stays `possible` forever, silently.
The recommendation from the design consult is to move `risk:` into the vocabulary
beside `stateful:` and `evidence:` (D311's precedent: declarative in the vocabulary,
the driver does not decide the class), and compose it as `max(derived, declared)` so
an incremental sweep of 57 files can never weaken anything. Explicitly rejected in that
consult: a risk channel on the provider interface — an obligation on ~145 certified
services four days after D625 showed the last such obligation reading "COMPLETE" over
101 of them, and a channel that may LOWER risk is a fail-open pointed at honesty with
145 independent opportunities to fire.

*`converge`'s consent gate still reads only `dataLoss == "certain" || identityReplacement`.*
D628 made `securityExposure: certain` derivable and nothing consumes it, so an update
that flips `network.publicExposure` on still passes plain `--yes`. That is the single
most likely place a user is hurt by the current tree, and it is the next slice rather
than this one — widening a consent gate changes what an operator is asked to confirm,
and that deserves its own case and its own entry.

## D630 — the field that says "this opens something up" reached no gate and no reader

D628 made `securityExposure: certain` derivable. Nothing consumed it. `converge`'s
consent gate was, and had always been:

```go
if a.Risk.DataLoss == "certain" || a.Risk.IdentityReplacement { destructive = true }
```

So an update that flips `network.publicExposure` to true, or turns `encryption.atRest`
off, applied under plain `--yes` — and the per-action line the operator reads before
consenting printed `[R1 dataLoss=none downtime=possible]` and did not mention exposure
at all. Both halves are the same omission: the value existed and no one was shown it.

The line now prints `exposure=`, and a plan with a provable exposure needs
`--allow-exposure` — its own flag, not a fold into `--allow-data-loss`. They are
different harms, and **a consent flag whose name does not describe what it permits is
not consent**; the gate pins that directly, by requiring that `--allow-data-loss` does
NOT cover an exposure.

Two boundaries the gate also pins, because both are ways to get this wrong:

- `possible` does not gate. It is D628's honest default for a change whose direction
  the compiler cannot read, and gating on it would demand consent for every update —
  which trains people to pass the flag by reflex, and a consent everyone types blind is
  worth nothing.
- An unparseable plan is fail-closed on BOTH harms. `describePlan` already treated an
  unreadable plan as destructive; it now treats it as exposing too, because a gate that
  could not read the plan has ruled out neither.

This came from an adversarial review of D628, which named it as "the single most likely
place a real user gets hurt by these three changes" — correctly, and it was a defect I
had already noticed and written down as future work in the D628 entry. Recording that
plainly: I published the derivation and left its only consumer unchanged, which made
the entry's claim ("the vector is now derived") true and its usefulness nearly zero
until this slice.

## D631 — the verb that writes provenance was outside the clock's closed set

`timeSensitiveVerbs` is the set that gets N1's presence gate (an explicit `--at`, never
the epoch) and D323's parse gate (PRESENT is not PARSES). `discover` was not in it, and
`discover` reads the clock:

```
groundhold discover --provider fake --project p1                  exit 0   "at": "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"
groundhold discover --provider fake --project p1 --at not-a-time  exit 0   "at": "not-a-time"
```

Neither is cosmetic. `at` is inside the canonical `discoveryHash`, and
`adopt --discovery` writes that hash into the ledger as the adoption's provenance root
— so an adoption permanently cites an enumeration whose recorded time is the string
`not-a-time`, and a sweep with no clock is stamped 1970 forever.

`pair` is the other verb that reads the clock without being in the set, and it handles
a defaulted one itself, in writing: D588 records "a record saying 1970 is worse than a
record saying nothing". So the pattern was understood; `discover` was simply missed —
which is the whole argument for gating the rule rather than the membership.

The gate asks Go's own parser which dispatch blocks reference the evaluation clock and
requires each to be in the set, with `pair` as a named, documented exception. My first
attempt scanned lines instead and produced two false positives — `--version`, because
the pattern matched a flag, and `apireq`, because a global parse gate sixty lines below
the block was attributed to it. A gate that accuses correct code is worse than none:
the next author learns to ignore it. Rewritten against the AST, where "inside this
block" is a fact rather than an inference.

Two things about the landing, recorded because they are the more useful part.

`TestTimeSensitiveVerbsMembership` pins the set as a literal list and told me exactly
what I had done — "N1 gating changed WITHOUT updating this test; if deliberate, update
`want` and confirm the verb's --at refusal; if not, a safety-clock hole just opened."
That is a membership pin doing its whole job: it does not know whether a change is good,
it insists that a change be deliberate. Updated with the reason and the measured
refusals in the case body.

And I pushed this commit over a RED gate. The command was
`make check 2>&1 | tail -2 && git commit …` — `&&` reads the exit of `tail`, so a
failing suite looked green. It is the same pipe-exit-status trap this record has now
named three times (D605 in the meter, twice at my own terminal), and it is the first
time it let a commit through. The fix in practice is the one already written down:
**measure an exit code as its own statement, never through a pipe.** The tree was green
again within minutes, but the discipline failed before the gate did.

## D632 — apply executed a change justified by a proof that had died four years earlier

`plan` refuses to seal against a decayed observation. `apply` never re-judged it. Its
only freshness check was `foldStaleReason`, which covers folded operands and nothing
else — so the change set's own `from:` value, the assertion about current reality that
justifies the mutation, was trusted from the plan however old the plan was.

```
observation  db.service.managed = true  at 01:00:00Z, ttl 3600  (expires 02:00:00Z)
plan sealed  01:00:01Z, changes: [{path: service.managed, from: true, to: false}]

plan  … --at 2030-01-01T00:00:00Z   exit 2   "observation is stale — re-observe first"
apply … --at 2030-01-01T00:00:00Z   exit 0   APPLIED
```

with a real receipt appended: `operation.receipt 2030-01-01T00:00:00Z {changes:[…]}`.
It fires one second past expiry too. `converge` was never exposed because it re-plans;
the hole is reachable through exactly the seal-now-review-later workflow D36/D89
promote, which is the workflow a cautious operator chooses.

D42/D47/D325 all say the same thing in different words — apply RE-DERIVES rather than
trusts. Freshness was the one thing it still took on the plan's word, and the check that
would have caught it was sitting ten lines away, applied to a different field.

`changeStaleReason` now re-checks, pre-lease, that every attribute a change touches is
still witnessed by a live observation at THIS `--at`, and refuses with `stale-decision`
(exit 3, the re-observe-and-re-seal class) naming the attribute and how long ago its
proof expired. A change whose attribute the ledger has never observed is refused too:
there is no `from` to have been true.

The control matters as much as the refusal and is pinned: an action with no change set
— every create, every delete — is untouched by this check.

**And the first version over-reached, which the conformance suite caught immediately.**
I also refused a change whose attribute the ledger has never observed, reasoning that
there is then no `from` to have been true. That broke
`apply-updates-a-bound-capability`: the compiler derives changes from BINDINGS as well
as observations, and a legitimately seeded binding carries no `observation.recorded` at
all. The suite said so within a minute of the change, in the form of a case that had
been correct for months. This check is about evidence that EXPIRED, not evidence that
was never of this kind — and the distinction is now a control in the test, not a
memory.

**The meter then caught the test twice, and both catches are the point of having one.**

First: the unit test calls `changeStaleReason` DIRECTLY, so a mutant that deleted its
CALL SITE left it green. The helper was proven and nothing proved anything invoked it —
D564 verbatim, second appearance in this record. Replaced with an end-to-end test that
drives the real CLI: publish, plan, apply, observe, seal an update while the evidence is
live, then apply it years later.

Second: the end-to-end version ALSO survived, and the reason is worse than the first.
Applying the plan once mutates the ledger, which moves the decision heads the plan
pinned — so the second apply was refused for a completely different staleness, and the
test passed while proving nothing about freshness. Each apply now runs against its own
copy of the same pristine ledger. A test whose two runs share mutable state is a test
that can pass for a reason it never mentions, and only the meter could tell me which
reason it was.

The first end-to-end attempt also had to be thrown away: it built the ledger by hand,
and a hand-built ledger has no hash chain, so `plan` refused it and the test SKIPPED —
green, and worthless. The fixture is now written by the product itself.

## D633 — two live leases could share a fencing token, and the rule could not tell

The concurrency audit's first finding, and the one that breaks a stated guarantee
rather than a stated intention.

A fencing token is `max(previous tokens for the affected capabilities) + 1` — a
PER-CAPABILITY counter. Two leases over disjoint capability sets therefore both receive
token 1. The mutation rule asked only whether the token matched the active token on
each affected capability, never whether those capabilities were under the SAME lease:

```yaml
- append: {type: lease.acquired, capabilities: [a, b], actor: worker-a, body: {ttlSeconds: 100}}
- append: {type: lease.acquired, capabilities: [c],    actor: worker-b, body: {ttlSeconds: 100}}
- append: {type: binding.updated, capabilities: [b, c], actor: worker-a, fencingToken: 1}
```

Both implementations accepted the third step. `worker-a` wrote into `c`, which is under
`worker-b`'s exclusive lease, and the literal rule in §2 was satisfied throughout. That
is D323/D325's class at its sharpest: **the invariant enforced a weaker property than it
declared.**

**Why not a global counter.** It was the obvious fix and it is wrong for this codebase,
for a reason the design consult found and I had not: token values are NOT stored — they
are recomputed at fold time, and `ReplayFile` re-judges every rule and refuses the file
if any event would now be rejected. Change the arithmetic and every historical lease
folds to a different token than the one its writer honestly obtained and embedded, so
every existing multi-lease ledger becomes unreadable. That is D338's failure inflicted
on our own past, and both escape hatches are crimes this record has already named: an
era-conditional rule is a conditional invariant, and a migration rewrites history.

What landed instead is a fold-time LEASE IDENTITY — a counter incremented on each
`lease.acquired`, recomputed identically on every replay, never on the wire. Token
arithmetic is untouched, so no existing ledger reads differently; the only documents
that now refuse are the ones that actually recorded the violation, which is the correct
answer for a ledger that recorded a broken exclusion.

The control is pinned beside the refusal, because the cheap way to satisfy a refusal
test is to refuse more than asked: a holder of `{a,b}` mutating a strict SUBSET of its
own lease must still pass.

**The snapshot boundary caught the rest of it.** `TestSnapshotEquivalenceFuzz` failed
immediately: lease identity has to survive compaction, or a seeded fold cannot tell two
same-token leases apart and the rule silently relaxes to the old per-capability check
for any ledger that has ever been snapshotted. That is the exact silent-projection-loss
class the fuzz was built for after `ownership.claimed` went missing across the same
boundary, and this time it fired before anything shipped.

**And the other half of the audit's finding is being written down rather than fixed.**
Nothing binds a mutation, renewal, release or break to the lease HOLDER: any writer can
renew someone else's lease with a shorter TTL, release it, or break it. Actor identity
is self-asserted (SECURITY.md says so plainly), so a check keyed on it would be a guard
conditional on a field the adversary writes — D312's shape — while advertising an
identity protection that does not exist. `lease.broken` is a third-party verb BY
DESIGN; §2's reconciliation rule exists precisely because the breaker is not the dead
holder. And the interferences are bounded in the safe direction: a foreign renewal or
release can only DENY, never write under another's fence. `spec/state-model.md` §2 now
says both things where a reader arrives: one mutation, one lease — and leases are
cooperative, not authorising.

## D634 — one line in a vocabulary file turned a forbidden delete into an applied one

`spec/sealed-plan.md` step 3 says apply re-checks the read-set's "toolchain, vocab
versions, provider identity". It checked none of the three. The vocabulary one is the
dangerous one, because `stateful:` in a vocabulary document is what makes a contract's
`autonomy.forbidden: delete_stateful` fire.

Two vocabulary trees, differing by one line — `stateful: true` → `false` in
`capability.monitoring.logs.yaml`, `version:` untouched at `0.1`:

```
plan  --vocab vocabA   exit 2   "retiring applogs destroys a stateful capability and
                                 the contract forbids delete_stateful"
plan  --vocab vocabB   exit 0   a-delete-applogs, dataLoss: none
apply --vocab vocabB   exit 0   APPLIED — the resource is destroyed
```

Byte-identical in everything the plan pins. The same audit showed the rest of the
read-set is equally unguarded: a plan pinning `capability.monitoring.logs: 0.1` applies
cleanly against a vocabulary declaring `version: 9.9`, a rewritten
`reads.toolchain: {compiler: evil-compiler/9.9}` applies, and a rewritten
`reads.provider: {name: gcp, project: victim-prod}` applies with `--provider fake`.

The pin is now `"<version> <canonical-hash-of-the-model>"`, and apply refuses a
mismatch with `read-set-mismatch`. The hash covers what the RUNTIME reads — capability,
version, attributes, stateful — not the file's bytes, so a comment or a reordering does
not invalidate a sealed plan while any change the runtime can act on does. A plan
sealed before this change pins a bare version, and apply compares what that plan
actually pinned rather than inventing a stricter rule for it retroactively.

`HashVocabulary` lives in `canonical`, the one place both the compiler and the executor
can reach without an import cycle (`vocab` cannot import `canonical`, because
`canonical → contract → vocab`). Writing a second canonicaliser inside `vocab` would
have been a copy with no justification — the thing this record spent yesterday
removing.

Still open from the same finding, recorded rather than quietly dropped: `reads.toolchain`
and `reads.provider` are pinned and unchecked. They are the same shape and the same
fix; they are not in this slice because each deserves its own case, and because
`reads.provider` interacts with the `--provider` flag in ways that need arguing before
coding.

The test needed three attempts, and the reason is now a comment in its body: applying a
plan once moves the decision heads it pinned, so a second apply of the same plan refuses
for a different staleness and the test passes while proving nothing. Each apply runs
against its own copy of the pristine ledger. That is the third time this exact
test-design error has appeared here (D632 twice, this once) — it belongs in the
project's habits, not in three separate entries.

## D635 — a capability the contract declares and nobody implements read as success

```
contract: capabilities [db, assets]        candidate: implements db only
$ groundhold verify c.yaml k.yaml
  1 satisfied, 0 violated, 0 unknown, 0 unverifiable
  PROVEN                                             exit 0
$ groundhold converge …   (second pass)
  ✓ converged — the world already matches the candidate
  CONVERGED                                          exit 0
```

`assets` does not exist and never will. `verify` iterates CONSTRAINTS, and the compiler
iterates the CANDIDATE's capabilities, so a declared capability with no hard constraint
and no `requirements` produced no verdict, no action, and no entry in `blocked`,
`unverified`, `noop`, `witnessed` or `advisories`. It fell between two loops.

This is the failure `witnessed` was built to prevent — "an omission-resistant fact, so
no reader mistakes 'witnessed' for 'forgotten'" — reached by the plainer route of a
forgotten line in a candidate, which is the likelier way to get there.

Both implementations now block it, and the reason is in the message: *a capability with
no implementation cannot converge, and silence about it reads as success.*

**The exemption is the interesting part.** A RETIRED capability must not be required to
have an implementation — retirement is precisely how a contract says a thing should NOT
exist (D47), and demanding an implementation for one would make retirement
unexpressible. Both cases are pinned: the block AND the exemption. A rule stated without
its exception is the exception nobody finds later (D629 said this a few hours ago about
`null` containers; it is the same lesson).

Recorded honestly: the whole suite passed with the new refusal on the first run, which
means no case depended on the old permissive behaviour — and also that no case covered
this at all. The Python reference needed the same rule; a fix in one implementation is
half a fix (D25).

## D636 — the method is the durable artefact, so it is written down

Two days of parallel adversarial audits produced roughly seventy confirmed defects,
several of which defeated the product's central promise. The defects are each an entry
above. What is worth more than any of them is the METHOD that produced them, and it now
lives in `docs/BUG_HUNTING.md` rather than in whoever ran it.

Four things in it are load-bearing enough to restate here.

**The strongest predictor of a critical defect is that nobody has looked at that surface
yet.** Stronger than code age, complexity or churn. Every first look at a new surface —
the conformance harness, the release path, the evidence chain, the safety clock, the
lease rules, the document loaders, a live cluster — returned something of critical
class. That is why the find-rate curve has stayed flat at fifty-odd entries a day: it is
not a distribution tail, it is new territory each time.

**Hunt in parallel, fix serially.** Hunting is read-only and parallelises perfectly.
Fixing serialises on this file (one numbered append point), on the mutation meter (one
file), and on a shared working tree. Trying to parallelise the fixing would produce
exactly the conflicts this record spends its time preventing.

**Most of the traps are in the METHOD, not in the code under test.** A pipe eats an exit
code — that one produced false findings and, once, let a red gate be pushed. A test
aimed at a helper proves the helper and not its caller. A control that shares mutable
state with the case passes for a reason it never mentions; that error appeared three
times in two days and is the most seductive of them. A hand-built fixture is refused by
the product and the test SKIPS, green and worthless. Two artefacts derived by one broken
parser agree with each other while both are wrong — I built that one while writing the
entry that names the class.

**Triage by harm to a user, never by novelty.** A silent wrong answer outranks a clever
exploit chain. The order is written out in the document, and it is the order these
entries were fixed in.

The recurring classes are listed there too, and reading that list before a hunt is worth
more than reading the code: a discarded `ok`; a gate that cannot fail; a published set
copied instead of shared; a boundary a control does not cross; silence read as
agreement; a claim wider than the code.

## D637 — resume concluded another driver's operation with a reconciler that never saw it

`apply` pins `reads.provider` from the sealed plan and cross-checks it. `resume` — the
verb an operator types by hand, under pressure, after something died — pinned nothing.

```
ledger: binding.updated  db  provider {name: aws}, providerId arn:aws:rds:…:db:prod
        operation.receipt db  status pending, operation update, changes [backup.retention -> 30d]

$ groundhold resume contract.yaml --ledger aws.jsonl --provider fake --at …
exit=0   status: "resumed"

after:  binding.updated  db  provider {name: FAKE}, generation 2
        operation.receipt db  status SUCCEEDED
```

The fake reconciler answers `succeeded` unconditionally, so the run declared an AWS RDS
patch LANDED, bumped the binding's generation, and rewrote `provider.name` from `aws` to
`fake` — the field a comment fifty lines away in the same function calls identity that
"must survive (F4)". The create shape is worse: it invented a providerId
(`fake:db-real-key`) and bound it over the real one.

The ledger already records who started the work, in two places, and now both are read:
the BINDING for a bound capability, and the pending receipt's `target`
(`"fake.fakedb/db"`) for one that died before its binding landed. The second matters
most — an unbound pending create is exactly the state where a wrong driver invents an
identity — and it is the case my first version of the guard missed, because it only
consulted the binding and an unbound capability has none.

The control is pinned beside the refusal on its own copy of the ledger: the driver that
started the operation still resumes. (Same-copy testing has produced three false passes
in this record; each run gets its own now.)

**Fourteen unit fixtures had to be corrected, and they are the interesting part.** They
seeded receipts with `"target": "gcp.fake/db"` while running `provider.Fake{}` — a
fixture describing a world it was not executing. The guard refused them, correctly. I
changed the FIXTURES, not the expectations: each of those tests is about something else
(a malformed `--at`, a concluded create writing its binding, an `unknown` staying
unknown), and none of them meant to assert that a gcp operation may be concluded by the
fake driver. A fixture that contradicts itself is a defect in the test, and it went
unnoticed because nothing had ever compared those two fields.

**And the meter caught the test, for the fourth time in two days.** The first version
asserted only that the wrong-driver run exited non-zero — and a wrong driver fails for a
dozen unrelated reasons (no credentials, no project), so the test passed with the guard
deleted. It now asserts the REASON. Writing it down as a rule, since it keeps recurring:
*a refusal test must assert WHY, or it is a test that the command failed.*

(The mutant itself took four attempts and now lives in `scripts/mutants/` as a file:
two shell-quoted versions produced a tree that did not compile, one substituted nothing.
The meter reported both honestly — NO-BUILD and NO-OP, the guards added in D603 — which
is the only reason I noticed rather than believing a green line.)

Found by an adversarial audit of the whole recovery path, whose larger half is worth
recording: a real `SIGKILL` two seconds into a 300-action apply left a committed pending
receipt with no outcome, and resume concluded it EXACTLY ONCE — 300 capabilities, 300
distinct providerIds, zero duplicate idempotency keys, and the re-plan afterwards
created 159 rather than 160. Write-ahead receipts, ordering, idempotency across
re-seals, `unknown` never treated as an outcome, six concurrent resumes serialising to
one winner, corruption stopping everything, and compaction preserving reconcile state
all held under attack. The findings are at the edges of that path, not in its middle.

## D638 — the third flag that never reached converge's children, and the gate that ends it

`converge` runs plan, observe, forecast and apply as separate PROCESSES. A flag that is
not on their argv does not exist for them. This is the third time that has produced a
defect, and each was worse than the last:

- **D612**: `--trust` / `--sign-key` — the security policy went unenforced, and a signed
  history was permanently poisoned.
- **D638**: `--kubeconfig` / `--context` — measured on a live k3d cluster, `converge`
  with a kubeconfig pointing at an unreachable endpoint created a Role, carrying
  groundhold's ownership labels, **on the default cluster**, at exit 0 with a CONVERGED
  banner. Every other verb refuses an unknown context; `discover` with the same bogus
  file correctly returns zero resources and seven `connection refused` diagnostics. The
  driver honours the selector; the porcelain seam dropped it.

Patching two more flags would have been the third instance of the same fix. Instead the
rule is now mechanical: **every global flag must carry a written decision about whether
it travels.** A gate reads the CLI's global switch through Go's parser and requires each
flag to appear in exactly one of two sets — `forwarded`, with the reason a child needs
it, or `local`, with the reason it is converge's own. A flag added to the CLI without a
decision fails the build.

**Its first run found nine more.** `--region`, `--bindings`, `--observations`, `--ttl`,
`--budget`, `--require-preflight` all change what a child SEES or DOES and none were
travelling. And three that matter more than they look:

```
$ groundhold converge … --yes --fail-key <key> --retryable-key <key>
exit 0   CONVERGED          # both resources created normally, the flags discarded
```

`--fail-key`, `--unknown-key` and `--retryable-key` drive the fake provider's outcome
injection. Silently dropped, they made converge's own partial-apply behaviour —
D379's "1 of 2 actions applied", D387's post-failure observe and probe, D241's throttle
backoff — **unreachable from the command line entirely**. That is the surface a real
production incident lived on (MATURITY gap 3), and no audit could exercise it. It works
now:

```
$ groundhold converge … --yes --fail-key <key>
exit 4   action a-create-db failed: injected failure   DIED
```

Worth naming plainly: the unknown-flag refusal (D567) does not help here. These flags
are recognised GLOBALLY, so the parser accepts them for any verb and the verb that does
not read them ignores them in silence — the limitation D567's own entry recorded as a
known gap, now shown to have cost three defects.

## D639 — the forecast said nothing would happen, and apply mutated

A forecast is shown to a human immediately before they consent. If it predicts
something other than what apply does, the consent was obtained under a false
description — and this one erred in the dangerous direction.

The no-effect branch (D577's) decided "this changes nothing" from the CANDIDATE's
vocabulary attributes and never looked at the ACTION's own change set — the plan's
authoritative statement of what apply will do, which apply hands to the driver's
`Update` unconditionally. Two measured cases:

```
sealed changes: [{"path":"service.managed","from":false,"to":true}]
forecast  no-effect / target-already-matches   rollup{noEffect:1, willUpdate:0}
apply     applied — receipt changes=[{"path":"service.managed","to":true}],
                    binding generation 1 -> 2
```

and worse, on an operand path:

```
sealed changes: [{"path":"implementation.environment", …}]
forecast  attrs: ['service.managed']   — the changed path is never mentioned at all
          rollup{noEffect:1}
apply     receipt records the operand update
```

The second needs no staging to reach: operands are not vocabulary attributes, so any
Lambda whose only drift is an environment variable compiles inside plain `converge` —
which prints `forecast rollup: noEffect 1` on the line directly above the consent
prompt.

An action carrying a change set is now never no-effect. D577's actual case — an update
whose predictions all match AND which carries no change set — still reports no-effect,
and the control pins it.

**The meter caught the test twice more**, and both are now written rules rather than
memories. The first version called `hasChanges` directly and stayed green when the
mutant deleted its call site — fifth appearance of D564's shape in this record, so the
test now drives `Forecast` itself. The control then failed for a reason that was my
error and not the code's: I gave the candidate no attributes, and an EMPTY prediction
set is deliberately not evidence of no effect (D577's own comment says so), so the
control could not exercise the branch it was controlling for. It now declares an
attribute the ledger observes at the same value.

Landing this also moved D577's mutant anchor, and the meter reported that as NO-OP
rather than passing — the guard added in D603 earning its place a second time.

**Two things this does not fix, stated so the entry is not read as more than it is.**
The forecast still does not PREDICT operand attributes: the effect is now right, the
attribute list is still silent about `implementation.*`. And the same audit found the
mirror defect — a forecast saying `will-update / freshPlan: true` for a plan that both
`plan` and `apply` refuse as decayed (the freshness D632 added to apply). The forecast
computes the age itself and has a `stale-plan` effect in its closed set; it uses
`will-update` anyway. Refusal is the safe direction there, so the harm is a false
description rather than a false mutation — queued, not closed.

## D640 — a capability groundhold can only READ was never compared to reality

A WITNESS capability is one the driver can observe and never author — a Flux
Kustomization, an ArgoCD Application. The compiler correctly emits no mutating action
for it, and records it under `witnessed` so a sealed plan cannot be misread as
"capability forgotten" (D177). Then it `continue`d, before any drift comparison.

Measured on a live k3d cluster:

```
candidate: service flux-kustomization, name does-not-exist-at-all
$ groundhold converge …                     exit 0   ✓ converged — the world already matches
$ kubectl get kustomization does-not-exist-at-all -n gh-audit
Error from server (NotFound)
```

A hard constraint on the capability did not change it. And for a BOUND witness whose
declared `source.repoURL` differed from the measured one:

```
$ groundhold converge …   exit 0   ✓ converged — the world already matches the candidate
$ groundhold plan     …   exit 2   nothing-to-change
$ groundhold adopt    …   exit 2   "gitops.source.repoURL: declared …/other-platform.git
                                    but reality says …/audit-platform.git — fix the
                                    candidate or the resource, adoption must not lie"
```

Same fact, same ledger, two verdicts. And the staleness gate never ran on that ledger's
expired observation, because the loop ended at `plan`.

A capability that CANNOT be written is precisely the one whose drift a human must be
told about, because nothing will fix it automatically. A witness now still gets no
action — the driver would refuse one — and is compared anyway: unbound blocks
("nothing has been observed to match the candidate against, and groundhold cannot
create it"), and a bound witness that has drifted blocks naming the paths ("groundhold
can only READ this service, so nothing here will converge it").

The first version of the test read the compiler's SOURCE for the message text, which
says nothing about whether the branch runs. It drives `Compile` now. That is the sixth
time in this record that the first draft of a test aimed at something other than the
behaviour — it is worth treating as the default failure mode of test-writing rather
than as a series of accidents.

## D641 — two folds of one event disagreed about "I do not know"

`operation.receipt` is folded twice in this repository. The ledger's projection
(`PendingCount`/`PendingReceipts`) is what `resume` acts on; `internal/runstatus`
derives what `status`, `runs` and `wait` report. They answered `unknown` differently:

```go
// internal/ledger/ledger.go
case "pending", "unknown":   // unknown keeps the receipt pending
// internal/runstatus/runstatus.go
case "pending": pending[op] = true
default:        delete(pending, op)   // "succeeded/failed/unknown-with-id conclude"
```

`unknown` is the receipt apply writes when the provider's answer was lost — the
resource MAY exist and MAY be billed, and `apply.go`'s own comment says "`unknown`
must KEEP its pending intent (only a succeeded receipt clears it)". So for the most
dangerous state the system has, `status` printed

```
stalled — the writer's lease lapsed with no outcome — run `groundhold resume`
```

with exit code `run-stalled` while `resume` blocked on the unsettled receipt at
`reconcile-required`. "With no outcome" is a false sentence: there is an outcome,
and its content is that nobody knows. `pendingReceipts` was empty too, so neither a
human nor a dashboard could learn WHICH operation to go looking for.

The fix is not to copy the correct case list into the second fold. The rule now
exists once — `ledger.ReceiptLeavesIntentPending` — and both folds call it. The gate
does not restate the answer either: it folds one receipt of every status in
`ledger.ReceiptStatuses()` through both paths and requires the same verdict, with a
floor on the set size so a collapsed set cannot pass. A control pins `retryable`,
which provably did not land (D241) and must still conclude, because the cheap way to
satisfy the case above is to keep everything pending forever.

Class: a published set copied instead of shared. Fifth occurrence in this record,
and the first where the two copies were both folds of the same event type.

## D642 — three of four drivers could report an unreachable cloud as an empty estate

D621 wrote the rule down: *a sweep that could not happen is not an empty estate.* It
enforced it with one precondition inside one driver. The other three checked
something different and weaker — AWS that a region was given, Azure that the
subscription looked like a GUID, k8s nothing at all — and a dead network passes all
three. Every service sweep failed, every failure became a diagnostic, and `List`
returned a nil error. `discover` then exited 0 with `"resources": []`, which is the
document `adopt` and `posture` are told to take.

The rule now lives once, in `provider.SweepAll`: a service that fails is a
diagnostic (that resilience is the point — one unreadable kind must not hide the
others), and all of them failing is an error. All four drivers route their sweep
loop through it, which also removed four copies of that loop.

The gate is behavioural, not a reading of the rule: it points the four REAL drivers
at a transport that cannot connect and requires each to fail. That matters, because
"the rule exists" was true the whole time three drivers did not follow it.

Writing the gate found the same class two and three levels further down, where no
floor existed at all:

- Five GCP sweeps fanned out over locations with the identical hand-written loop,
  each degrading a failed list to a diagnostic. On a dead network they returned "no
  artifact registries / no backup plans / no certificates / no scheduler jobs / no
  backup vaults" with a nil error — so `List` counted them as SUCCESSFUL sweeps and
  even the new floor could not fire. They share `sweepEachLocation` now.
- `discoverCloudKMS` did the same over key rings, and Azure's load-balancer sweep
  over its two ARM kinds.
- `resolveBillingAccount` returned a single `bool` for five different answers: no
  project pinned, the request could not be made, the API refused, the body was
  unreadable, and "this project has no billing account". Only the last means there
  are no budgets. It returns an error now, and an answered request with no account
  returns `("", nil)` — the one case where zero is a fact.

Class: a published set copied instead of shared, in its most expensive form — the
copies were not of a list but of a LOOP, and each copy quietly weakened the rule the
original was written to hold. The count is what makes it worth recording: one rule,
eleven implementations, one of them correct.

## D643 — the manifest could tell the verifier not to look

D616 made the restored ledger the authority on WHICH documents must be accounted
for. Its entry lists, among the variants it closed, "flipping `"present": false`
left the blob unread and still `verified`". The gate written beside it exercises a
manifest naming a hash the ledger does NOT pin — which refuses on the unaccounted
path, a different mechanism. The named variant was never run, and it still passed:

```
restore --out … --check anchor.json --documents documents  db.capsule.json
exit 0   "status": "verified"
         {"status":"absent","reason":"referenced but not copied into this backup"}
```

with a substituted contract sitting in `documents/<pinned-hash>`. `kind: "candidate"`
does the same through the deferred arm. Both fields are written by whoever made the
backup, and both stop the blob from being read at the last step of a disaster
recovery.

The manifest is the artefact under test, so it cannot be what decides whether to
look. The DIRECTORY says what exists: every blob in the backup is now loaded and
hashed against its own name, whatever the manifest claims about it. An entry may
still say a document is absent — there is no file, nothing to read, and a partial
backup stays honest and passes. It may not say that a blob which is on disk should
be ignored. A blob the manifest does not mention at all is read too, and reported.

The class is one I have written about twice and still walked into: a guard
conditional on a field the attacker sets (D312 for anchors, D616 for manifests).
What is new is how it survived — the entry claiming the fix named this exact
variant, and I believed the entry instead of the test. A gate is what closes a
variant; a sentence in this file is not.

## D644 — the covering-lease rule was decided by list order

D633 requires ONE lease to cover the whole affected set of a mutation. The check
walked the affected capabilities comparing each lease's `seq` against a running
value that started at 0 — and 0 is also a lease seq, so the comparison was skipped
for it:

```
a.seq=0  c.seq=1,  both token 1
caps=[a c] -> accepted        caps=[c a] -> refused
```

Same ledger, same mutation, two verdicts, chosen by the order of a list no caller
thinks about. Both spellings of the sentinel-that-is-also-a-value: `covering` now
has an explicit `have` flag.

Seq 0 reaches a fold exactly one way, and it is worse than the order dependence. A
snapshot written before D633 carries no `seq` field; `omitempty` makes its absence
indistinguishable from zero; every seeded lease reads back as 0; and the rule
relaxes to the per-capability check it replaced — for any ledger an older binary has
ever compacted. D633's own text says "no existing ledger reads differently because
of it", which is false for exactly those ledgers, and this entry does not get to
rewrite that one.

A snapshot cannot say whether two capabilities were held by one lease if it never
recorded lease identity. So seeding does not answer: each seq-less lease gets a
DISTINCT synthetic seq and is marked unprovable, and a multi-capability mutation
over one refuses naming the real reason — the snapshot predates lease identity,
release and re-acquire. A single-capability mutation is trivially covered by one
lease and still works, so an old snapshot does not freeze the ledger.

Two classes in one defect: a gate that cannot fail (the sentinel), and silence read
as agreement (the missing field). Both were introduced by the fix for D633, which is
the ordinary way this happens — a new field is added to a format that already has
readers, and the old shape's meaning is decided by a zero value nobody chose.

## D645 — the forensic window stopped at the compaction boundary

`export --from T1 --to T2` is the 4D disaster-recovery primitive, and step 1 of the
`dr-forensics` skill is to run it. It read only the live ledger file. After a
compaction the live file holds the tail, so a window over events that were folded
away came back empty — at exit 0, with nothing on stderr:

```
before compaction:  export --from … --to …   18 events   exit 0
after  compaction:  export --from … --to …    0 events   exit 0
```

The skill's own rule is "any sentence without an event hash is speculation and comes
out", so the honest conclusion it draws from that stream is *nothing happened in
this window*. The archives holding those events are in the same directory. `--since
<cursor>` had the matching failure: a consumer resuming from before the boundary
silently lost everything between its cursor and the compaction.

D315's comment already names this shape — "a consumer got a short stream with
nothing saying an event was withheld" — one layer up, at the timestamp parser. The
same sentence was true at the compaction boundary the whole time.

`export` now reads the archives back when the request can reach below the boundary,
in chain order, and the stream starts at genesis again: indices stay absolute and
contiguous, and the chain check runs from `genesis` rather than being seeded with
the sidecar's heads — which is strictly stronger, because it also proves those
heads. A cursor already past the boundary asks for none of those events, so a pruned
archive does not block that consumer.

If the archives do not add up to what the snapshot says was compacted, export
refuses and says so. That is the point: the defect was never the missing data, it
was that a short stream looked exactly like a complete one.

## D646 — the field that proved the archive had no readers

`archive.sha256` and `previousSnapshotHash` are written by every compaction, and
`spec/state-model.md` §9 told operators that "a swapped or truncated archive is
detectable, not deniable". Grep found four sites for those two fields across the
whole tree: a struct declaration, a type, and one assignment each. Nothing ever read
them. Truncating an 18-event archive to 3 left `attest`, `anchor --check`, `repair`
and `converge` all at exit 0 — and after D645 that archive is what a forensic window
streams.
