`CheckArchive` is the reader: four-valued (`matched` / `mismatched` / `missing` /
`misnamed` / not-claimed), because "I could not look" and "it does not match" are
different facts. `attest` reports it and still exits 0 — it makes facts, and
changing that would change its contract for every consumer. `repair` turns a
mismatch into a verdict. `export` refuses before emitting a record, since it is
reading those exact bytes.

The snapshot does not get to nominate which file satisfies its own hash: the name
must be the one a compaction at that base would have written. Only the DIRECTORY may
differ, so a backup that was moved still verifies. That is the same shape as D312
(an anchor choosing its own ledgerId) and D643 (a manifest choosing which blobs get
read) — the third time in this record that an artefact was allowed to specify the
terms of its own verification.

§9 also now says what this family of files can and cannot promise. Without a key it
proves CONSISTENCY, not authenticity: the sidecar, the archive and the tail are
checked against each other, which catches truncation, bit rot, a partial copy and
single-field tampering. It does not catch someone who can write the directory — they
re-fold and recompute every co-located hash, because all of those documents are
theirs to author. Authenticity needs a witness they do not hold: an off-host anchor,
or an armed key. The old sentence promised the second thing and delivered neither.

A design consult made two corrections worth recording. The first: I had proposed a
compaction-time "linking event" in the tail pinning the sidecar hash, so the
existing chain check would cover the fold. It is worthless — an unsigned chain is
recomputable by anyone who can write the file, so the linking event is an anchor
stored inside the attacker-writable artefact, strictly weaker than the anchor that
already exists outside it. The second is queued rather than done: a full re-fold of
the archive compared field-by-field against the sidecar would false-alarm on exactly
the D644 leases, whose seqs are synthetic on one side and real on the other. That
comparison needs a per-apiVersion field commitment before it can be written, and an
archive an operator has lawfully pruned must make the claim `unverifiable` rather
than blocking every verb.

## D647 — compaction computed the witness and threw it away

`Rotate` builds an anchor pinning the fold hash, then wrote it only `if _, err :=
os.Stat(AnchorPath(ledgerPath)); err == nil` — that is, only if the operator had
already placed one. Every ledger compacted without that file got no witness at all.

That gate is the whole gap behind the swapped-sidecar finding. D646 says what a
snapshot family can prove without a key: that its parts agree with each other.
Authenticity needs something the directory's writer cannot reach, and the anchor is
the only artefact in this design that can be stored there. Compaction is the moment
the story is weakest — a fold replaces history — so it now always leaves one, and
says at that moment to copy it off-host. Nothing else changes: the anchor stays
opt-in in the sense that matters (it is the operator's copy that does the work), and
a grown tail plus a second compaction both keep verifying, measured.

Deliberately NOT done: an anchor beside the ledger cannot defend against someone who
can write the directory, and pretending otherwise would be the same false promise
D646 removed from the spec. What this buys is that the artefact EXISTS, so copying
it off-host is a decision rather than a prerequisite nobody was told about.

One correction the conformance suite forced, and it is the interesting part of this
entry. The first cut wrote a full anchor, and a full anchor pins the TRUST POLICY
(D135). `trust-from-boundary-survives-compaction` went red: a later replay with a
different `--trust-from` now refused with "the anchor's trust policy and the command
line's disagree" (exit 1) instead of the boundary refusal the case pins (exit 5).
Both refusals are true, but the case was right and I was wrong — pinning a policy is
a deliberate operator act, and a file that appears on its own must not arm one
nobody chose. An anchor compaction creates now carries the fold witness and no
policy; an anchor the operator placed is refreshed exactly as before. The rule
generalises: a side effect that changes what LATER commands are allowed to do is not
a side effect, it is a decision, and decisions belong to the operator.

## D648 — four answers to "is this a credential?", no two the same

Four detectors, each written for its own site, each narrower than its siblings:

| where | what it knew |
|---|---|
| `provider.secretKeyMarks` (the redactor) | 8 key substrings |
| `contract.credentialPatterns` (publish scan, backup's capsule warning) | DSN, PEM, AKIA, SendGrid, Slack, Brevo, GOCSPX |
| `collector.secretKey` (certify-capsule) | 10 key alternatives incl. `pwd`, `access_key` |
| `collector.secretValue` (certify-capsule) | PEM, AKIA, Bearer, JWT |

Measured: a capsule carrying `postgres://app:hunter2@db.internal:5432/orders` in a
receipt reason was CERTIFIED at exit 0 and backed up with `"credentialWarnings": 0`,
while the same capsule carrying a bearer token was refused at exit 5. `admin_pwd`,
`db_pass`, `auth`, `access_key_id` and a DSN under a generic key all passed the
redactor, three of them detectable by another list in this same repository.

Two of these are not "warning gaps". A driver's `Reason` is copied verbatim into a
ledger event, which `export` publishes and `capsule` signs and ships — so a
credential a provider echoes back at us ("Invalid value for
`DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:…@…`") is published, permanently, in an append-only
file. `implementation.environment` is a declared operand on both AWS and GCP, and
`environment` is not a secret-NAMED key, so nothing remembered that value and
nothing scrubbed it.

`internal/secretshape` owns the question now, and the four sites call it. The
alphabet is the union, plus the two shape fixes the union exposed: the
connection-string pattern was anchored at `^`, so a DSN inside a sentence — the only
way one actually arrives — never matched, and its scheme was case-sensitive.
The redactor also remembers a value by SHAPE, not only by the key it sat under.

The key alphabet has two halves, and that distinction is the whole reason a naive
union would have been a regression. `password` is unambiguous anywhere in a name.
`pass`, `pwd` and `auth` are credential names only as standalone TOKENS: as
substrings they match `bypass_cache`, `passthrough_host` and — the one that would
have hurt — `capability.authorization.grant`, which `certify-capsule` feeds through
this same question as an observation PATH. Widening carelessly would have refused
honest evidence. So keys are tokenised on separators and camelCase humps, short
marks match tokens exactly, compound marks match the stripped form, and
key-RESOURCE names (`kms_key`, `key_vault_key`) stay readable — redacting those
blinds the operator to which key was refused while protecting nothing.

The gate is a parity test rather than a restatement: every shape in the table is put
through all three consumers, with a control that ordinary configuration (a region, an
ARN, an instance class, a DSN with no inline credential) is called a credential by
none of them.

Class: a published set copied instead of shared — sixth occurrence, and the most
expensive one, because each copy was individually defensible. The lesson to keep is
in the shape of the harm: four narrow detectors do not add up to one good one, they
add up to four holes each of which some OTHER detector would have caught.

## D649 — the agent that keeps proof fresh reported reads that never happened

`refresh` is the unattended half of the safety clock: it re-observes a capability
before its proof decays, and `posture` prints it as step 1 of the DECAYED recipe.
Pointed at a provider it could not read:

```
$ groundhold refresh --ledger l.jsonl --provider aws --at 2026-07-19T00:00:00Z
exit 0
{"refreshed":["shop-db"],"fresh":[],
 "notes":["shop-db: unreadable: aws driver: unknown service \"sql\" — refusing"]}
$ wc -l < l.jsonl      # unchanged — zero events appended
```

Nothing was read, nothing was recorded, the proof is still decaying, and a `posture`
run immediately afterwards still reports that capability decayed. The operator
following the tool's own instructions is told the step succeeded.

`observe.Run` returns a nil error for a failed read and reports it as
`Partial`/`Unreadable` — that is D242 and it is correct: observe reported reality,
including the part that reads "this capability is currently unreadable". `refresh`
looked only at the error. Three consequences, and the third is the one that would
have hurt longest: the capability landed in `refreshed`; the report had no field
saying otherwise; and the pacer was told the call was `OK`, so the crawl's circuit
breaker could never trip on a provider that was entirely down — refresh would keep
politely asking a dead endpoint every cycle, forever, and reporting success.

The report now carries `unreadable[]` and `partial`, the pacer hears `ServerError`
so the breaker works, and the run exits `observation-required` (2) instead of 0.
That last one matters because refresh runs on a schedule: the exit code is the only
thing watching. It also gained `code`, which `spec/errors.md` says every
JSON-emitting verb carries and which this one did not.

Class: silence read as agreement, in the specific form where one component's honest
four-valued answer is collapsed to two by its caller. D641 was the same shape a week
earlier — `unknown` folded to "concluded" by a second reader of the same event. Worth
stating as a rule: when a function reports "I could not" through a FIELD rather than
an error, every caller that only checks the error is wrong by construction.

## D650 — the completeness flag could not describe a scope that listed nothing

`shadowLowerBound` is posture's whole honesty claim about the shadow count: `false`
means "this number is exact", `true` means "at least this many". It was computed by
walking the discovered RESOURCES and asking each one whether its scope had been
listed completely. A scope cut short before listing anything therefore contributed
no entries, and its incompleteness was unrepresentable:

```
crawl:   scope fake-project-a   status incomplete   resources 0
         reason "crawl request budget exhausted: fake"
posture: {"shadow": 0, "shadowLowerBound": false}    exit 0    OK
```

And an incomplete scope is USUALLY empty. `crawl` emits `status: incomplete,
resources: []` for an auth error, a throttle, an exhausted budget, a tripped breaker
and a failed scope enumeration. So the case the field exists for is precisely the
case it could not see: expired credentials on one project render as "no unmanaged
resources here", at exit 0, under a banner that says OK. The half-truncated shape is
worse, because it looks like work was done — one scope listed cleanly, one never
started, and `shadow: 1` presented as exact.

Completeness is a property of the SCOPE, so it travels as one now: `posture.Input`
carries `Scopes[]`, and the bound is lowered by any incomplete scope — including one
with nothing in it. An input with NO scopes at all lowers it too, which fixes the
published flagless invocation: `posture --ledger l.jsonl` swept nothing and claimed
`shadow: 0` exactly.

The gate is at two levels on purpose. `Classify` is unit-tested, but the defect was
in the WIRING — `classifyPosture` copied completeness onto resources and nowhere
else — so a test aimed only at the classifier would stay green with the builder
deleted. The CLI case drives `run([]string{"posture", …})` with a truncated crawl,
no crawl, and a complete crawl as the control.

Still open, and stated so it is not mistaken for closed: `managedOkUpperBound` is
unconditionally true, and a bound resource that vanished out-of-band is still
counted as managed-ok. That needs the deferred per-provider scope-coverage slice.

## D651 — the export's leak gate read bodies and not names

`export-public.sh` ends with a negative-space audit: a maintained denylist of client
names, internal hosts and private documents, and a refusal if any of them crosses
into the public tree. It ran `grep -r` over the export, which reads file CONTENTS.
A denied term in a PATH walked straight through:

```
examples/<client>-<internal-ip>/notes.md      "A tiny note with no denied words inside."
$ bash scripts/export-public.sh $DST
  … exported to …/expB                        <- the deny audit PASSED
```

A directory named after an engagement discloses the engagement. A repository
listing shows the name before anyone opens a file, and the internal IP range in
that directory name was a second disclosure in the same string.

The audit now checks both, and it moved into `scripts/deny-audit.sh` taking the
denylist as an ARGUMENT. That is not tidying. A gate that reports an ABSENCE looks
identical when it is broken (D603), and this one had no positive control on either
arm — nobody had ever watched it fail. Passing the list in lets a Go test drive both
arms with an invented harmless term, proving they fire, without a private name ever
appearing in a test file. That last part is load-bearing: Go tests ARE exported, so
a gate that spelled out a denied term would itself be the leak. It has been, once
(D606).

A second case pins that `export-public.sh` still calls the audit, because the first
one otherwise proves a script nobody runs.

Writing the mutant for this found a third way the METER can measure nothing, after
the two D603 closed. Mutant target paths are relative to `go/` — the gate cd's there
— so a mutant naming a file outside that tree mutated NOTHING: `cp` and `sed` failed
quietly, `cmp` compared against a backup that did not exist and concluded the file
had changed, the test then passed over healthy code, and the meter printed SURVIVED.
That is the worst possible reading, because SURVIVED sends the next author to fix a
test that is fine. It is `NO-SUCH-FILE` and fatal now, in all three mutate variants. Three of these have been found
by using the meter rather than by inspecting it, which is the argument for keeping
every fix's mutant honest enough to fail once before it passes.

## D652 — posture never read the marker that says the resource is gone

`resource.absent` is the reserved observation a driver writes when it read the
provider and got an authoritative 404. The compiler acts on a fresh one by planning
a re-create (F-LC3) and refuses to seal against a stale one. `posture` did not read
it: grep over the package and over `classifyPosture` returned nothing.

Observations are latest-per-path, so a `service.managed: true` recorded in the same
sweep stands beside the absence marker, the audit computed from it says `satisfied`,
and the row came out **managed-ok** — the one class posture prints with no
remediation at all, the one an operator scrolls past.

Absence is now read, judged for freshness exactly as the compiler judges it (a stale
"it was gone last year" says nothing about now, and the decayed branch already
covers that), and classified `drifted` with a `converge` remediation, which is the
verb that re-creates it. It outranks a violated constraint deliberately: a hard
constraint failing on a resource that does not exist is noise, and the sentence the
operator reads should be the one that explains the rest.

The gate is at two levels for the second time in three entries, and for the same
reason: the classifier is pure and easy to test, but both defects lived in the
BUILDER that feeds it. The CLI case here was worthless in its first form — with no
`--contract` the row is `unknown` either way, so it passed with the wiring deleted.
It needs a contract whose hard constraint reads satisfied from an observation
recorded beside the 404, which is exactly the shape the defect lives in. Measured
both ways before it counted: `managed-ok` without the fix, `drifted` with it.

## D653 — the document the caller asked for was optional

`--out` is how a scheduled run hands its document to whatever reads it next. Both
writers threw every failure away:

```go
if err := os.MkdirAll(crawlOut, 0o755); err == nil {
    _ = os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(crawlOut, "posture.json"), out, 0o600)
}
```

Measured with a plain file sitting where the directory should be: exit 2 — the
findings code, indistinguishable from a normal run — no error, no message, and
nothing written. A read-only directory and a full disk do the same. The consumer
reading `$OUT/posture.json` then keeps consuming the previous run's document
indefinitely, while every run reports success. `react` had the identical shape,
twice, and it writes the crawl document too — so a stale context and a stale
posture stay in lockstep, looking consistent.

Both go through one `writeReport` now: marshal (that error was discarded too),
create, write, and report. The verb prints to stdout first so the information is
never lost, then fails with 1 if it could not deliver. When `--out` is given the
document IS the deliverable, and failing to produce it is not a detail.

Class: a discarded `ok`, in the variant where the discard is written as
`err == nil` around the work rather than `_ =` on the result. Worth naming
separately, because a grep for `_ =` does not find it — the swallow is spelled as a
guard, and it reads like care.

## D654 — repair and attest described the same file in different numbers

`repair` is the verb an operator reaches for when they suspect the history is
damaged, and its output is what they compare against `attest`. It counted the LINES
of the live file and printed them as `events`:

```
repair --ledger l.jsonl   {"events":1,  "status":"healthy", "validPrefixLines":1}
attest --ledger l.jsonl   totalEvents 19   baseEvents 18   tailEvents 1
```

Two wrong answers in one number. It never looked at the compaction, so the whole
archived history was missing; and blank lines counted as events, so `printf '\n\n\n'`
diagnosed as one event. An operator comparing the two verbs concludes one of them
is lying about the same file, and cannot tell which.

The counts are `attest`'s now — `totalEvents`, `tailEvents`, `baseEvents` — so two
verbs describing one file use one vocabulary. The physical line count keeps its own
name, `tailLines`, because it is a different UNIT: `--quarantine` truncates to a
line, and an off-by-one there throws away real history. That distinction is the
whole reason the fields could not simply be renamed.

Two things worth recording about how this went.

The `TestPublishedFieldsAreInTheOutputSchema` gate caught the change immediately —
`spec/outputs.schema.json` describes what the CLI emits, and four new fields were
not in it. That gate did its job without being asked, which is what the fix for a
published-registry drift is supposed to look like (D329/D330/D338).

And my first test asserted `tailLines == 3` for three blank lines. It is 1: trailing
newlines are stripped before splitting, exactly as the quarantine's prefix
arithmetic does it. The expectation was invented rather than measured, and pinning
it would have put an off-by-one into a verb that CUTS files. The test now asserts
what actually matters — zero EVENTS, and the two units separately named — with the
reasoning written down beside it.

## D655 — a lost write into a file that was no longer the ledger

`commitUnderLock` is the linearizable persisted-append, and the comment on `Rotate`
says in those words that a concurrent append cannot interleave a lost write. Both
open the path and THEN take the flock. Those are two steps, and compaction renames
the ledger to its archive in between:

```
( sleep 0.033; groundhold observe … --record ) &
groundhold snapshot --ledger o.jsonl
snapshot exit=0    observe exit=0, stderr empty
snapshot.baseEvents=421    archive lines on disk=422    tail=1
```

The writer opened the file, blocked on the lock, woke up holding a lock on the
ARCHIVED inode, replayed the new path for its heads, and appended to the old one.
The 422nd line is in no fold. Twelve of fifteen trials, and every one of them
reported success — `converge` printed APPLIED.

Then it gets worse, because the snapshot pinned the archive's hash BEFORE that
write. From that moment the ledger is permanently un-exportable: `attest` reports
the archive `mismatched` (D646 gave it that reader an hour earlier), `repair` exits
5, `export` and `backup` refuse. No shipped verb repairs it.

`lockLedger` takes the lock and then checks that the descriptor it holds is still
the file at that path — dev plus inode, which is what "the same file" means to the
kernel. Losing the race is not an error, so it retries against whatever is at the
path now, bounded, and refuses loudly rather than writing into a ghost. `Rotate`
uses it too: two rotations racing would archive the same inode twice, the same
window from the other side. Where inode identity is unavailable the check refuses
rather than guesses, because this decides whether a write lands in the ledger or
nowhere.

One consequence had to be handled: `lockLedger` opens with `O_CREATE`, since naming
a path is how an append creates a ledger. Compaction of a file that does not exist
is a typo, not a rotation, so `Rotate` stats first and returns the same
`ErrNoLedger` every other verb returns (D617).

The class is a boundary a control does not cross, in its physical form: the lock
protects the INODE and the code reasoned about the PATH. Everything above the lock
was correct — the replay, the fencing token, the rules — and none of it mattered,
because the bytes went somewhere else.

## D656 — a handle that did not identify a run, and a fold that preferred good news

Two defects, one shape: a run's identity left out things that distinguish one run
from another.

The converge handle was `sha256("converge:" + sha256(contract) + "|" + at)`. The
CANDIDATE — the file an operator edits to fix an implementation — was not in it, and
neither was `--project`. Editing the candidate and re-running at the same `--at`
reused the handle, so the ledger carried `converge.finished{exitCode:0}` followed by
`converge.failed{exitCode:2}` under one id:

```
status <h> --json   exit 0   "state":"done","code":"run-done","phase":"verify","exitCode":2
wait   <h>          exit 0
```

A CI gate that runs `converge --detach` and then `wait` got a green light for a
deploy that had been refused, and the record contradicted itself in a single line —
`done` beside exit code 2.

The plan file was a fixed path, `.groundhold/converge-plan.yaml`. Two converges in
one directory clobbered it and each applied whichever plan was written last:
measured 8 times out of 8, with one run creating resources in the OTHER run's
project and reporting success. The two plans differed only in `project`, which is
not part of the read-set — so `apply`'s own read-set-mismatch check, the control
that exists for exactly this, was structurally blind to it. It is per-run now.

The fold that turned the first defect into a green CI gate is worth its own line.
`DeriveRunStatus` checked `finished` before `failed`, so given two terminal events
it reported the earlier SUCCESS while carrying the later refusal's exit code. The
last terminal event decides now, in both directions — a retry that succeeded after
a failure reads `done`, and a refusal after a success reads `failed`. The handle is
fixed, so that state is no longer reachable the way it was reached; a fold that
resolves a contradiction by choosing the good news is worth fixing anyway, because
the next way to reach it will not announce itself.

## D657 — four flags read with both return values discarded

```go
_, _ = fmt.Sscanf(args[i+1], "%d", &ttl)
```

`--ttl`, `--window`, `--budget` and `--since` were all read this way. `Sscanf` stops
at the first character it cannot use and reports how many items it converted; both
of those facts were thrown away. Measured:

```
observe … --ttl 1e9 --record    exit 0   ttlSeconds recorded = 1
observe … --ttl abc --record    exit 0   flag ignored, defaults used
refresh … --window 1e9          exit 0   refreshed=[]  fresh=[assets,db]
```

`--ttl 1e9 → 1` writes a one-second freshness window into an APPEND-ONLY ledger:
every later audit blocks on evidence nobody could have kept fresh, and the event
cannot be edited. `--window 1e9 → 1` is the same slip pointed the other way — the
unattended freshness agent reports success while refreshing nothing, which is a
safety control switched off by a flag parse.

`parseIntFlag` refuses what it cannot read, names the flag and the value, and never
substitutes a prefix or a default. Zero stays "unset" where it already meant that;
what changed is that an unreadable value is now an error instead of a guess.

Class: a discarded `ok`, at the outermost layer of the program. Every fix in this
record for that class has been somewhere deep — a fold, a driver, a loader — and
this one sat in the argument parser, in the four flags most likely to be typed by
hand into a cron line.

## D658 — the one block D627 left ungated was the one holding the consent gates

D627 established the rule: a block of the wrong shape is not an empty block, and
reading it as one silently drops everything in it. It gated `constraints`,
`capabilities`, `budget`, `assumptions`, `requirements` and `verify`. `autonomy` was
not in the list, and `autonomy` is where the consent gates live.

```
autonomy:                      autonomy:
  forbidden:                     forbidden:
    - delete_stateful: true        delete_stateful: true      <- a mapping, not a list

plan  →  refused: retiring db destroys a stateful capability   |  DELETE: 1 — db
         and the contract forbids delete_stateful   exit 2     |  SEALED   exit 0
apply →  (not reached)                                         |  x delete db
                                                               |  R4, dataLoss certain
                                                               |  APPLIED  exit 0
```

`validate` said OK for both. A stateful database, bound and observed, destroyed
because a YAML block was indented one way instead of another.

The identity consequence is separate and arguably worse. `autonomy:` written as a
LIST was dropped whole, and the contract then hashed IDENTICALLY to one with no
autonomy block at all — so `contractHash`, which every sealed plan, capsule and
signature pins, could not distinguish "I disarmed the consent gates" from "I never
had any".

`checkAutonomyShape` runs at load over one list of keys, so a knob added later is
covered without anyone remembering to add a branch — D597 drew that conclusion for
reference-checking inside this same block, and the same argument applies to shape.

The lesson I want to keep is about how a rule gets applied. D627 enumerated the
blocks it gated, and the enumeration was of what the audit had found rather than of
what the document has. Six of seven is not a rule, it is a list — and the one that
was missed was, of course, the one that decides whether a destructive action needs a
human.

## D659 — the shipped CI gate could not fail

`examples/ci/github-actions.yml` and `gitlab-ci.yml` are the gate most users will
actually run, and the file's own header calls verify "the PR gate". Both ended the
step with a pipe:

```yaml
bin/groundhold-go verify … --json | tee verify-report.json
```

A pipeline's status is its LAST command. GitHub's default shell is `bash -e {0}`,
GitLab's is `sh -e`; neither sets `pipefail`. Measured with this repository's own
residency pair, which exists to keep failing forever:

```
verify …                       exit 2
bash -e -c 'verify … | tee'    exit 0
```

A pull request violating a hard EU-residency constraint merges green — and
`examples/lifecycle/README.md` says in its own words that "a residency constraint
that quietly stopped biting is the worst regression this project could ship".

`docs/BUG_HUNTING.md` warns hunters about exactly this ("a pipe eats the exit
code"), and this repository shipped it as advice. Writing a trap down is not the
same as not walking into it.

The second half of the same file: the plan step turned every exit 2 into success,
with the comment "exit 2 with nothing to change means converged". Exit 2 is a
FAMILY — `spec/errors.md` gives it to `nothing-to-change`, `not-executable`,
`consent-required`, `adoption-mismatch` and `provider-permission-denied`. It routes
on the `code` field now, which is what that field is for, and re-raises anything
else.

The gate reads the recipes, because the reason nobody noticed is that nobody ran
them. Its first version was itself vacuous: it looked for the tool and the pipe on
ONE line, and the gitlab recipe puts the pipe two continuation lines later — so
reintroducing the bug did not turn it red. It walks the continuation now, and I
watched it fail with the bug back in place before keeping it.

## D660 — a set was canonicalized on one side only

D532 made `unordered: true` mean "this attribute is a SET": the candidate's list is
sorted at load, where the vocabulary is known, "so DECLARED and OBSERVED compare
equal everywhere without a second meaning of equality". The CONSTRAINT's own
operand was never canonicalized, and list equality is positional. So the verdict
depended on the order the contract author happened to type:

```
contract  not-equals [eu-west-1, eu-central-1]   candidate [eu-central-1, eu-west-1]
  → PROVEN,   exit 0        the forbidden set, allowed
contract  not-equals [eu-central-1, eu-west-1]   the same candidate
  → VIOLATED, exit 2
```

and the mirror on `equals`: the same set, opposite verdicts. The candidate HASH is
order-invariant, so the evidence looks canonical while the verdict is not.

The only `unordered` attribute shipped today is
`inference.destinationRegions` — the EU data-residency surface. A contract
forbidding a routing set can seal as satisfied against exactly that set.

The operand is canonicalized at COMPARISON time, not at load, and on a COPY. That
placement is the whole design decision: the contract's identity is hashed from
these values, so sorting them at load would give one contract two hashes depending
on whether `--vocab` was passed — which is a defect the reference-implementation
audit reports for candidates and which must not be extended to contracts. The
shared sorter moved into `internal/scalars` so both sides call one function.

The reference implementation had the identical defect and is fixed identically.
`make differential` could never have caught it: its generator does not produce
unordered attributes, so both implementations were wrong in the same way, in
agreement, at every seed.

## D661 — the export was detected by an absence, and the absence was wrong

Gates that read private-only material call `skipIfExported`, and `isExportedTree`
decided by the absence of `.git`, with the comment "the export is a whitelist COPY,
never a clone". The publication target IS a clone. `export-public.sh` says so five
lines above the copy loop — `# clean previous export content, keep .git` — and
`actions/checkout` makes one on the mirror regardless.

So the same exported bytes behave differently depending on a directory nobody looks
at:

```
export/            make check   exit 0    "all gates passed"     <- what export-check tests
export/ + git init make check   exit 2    six gates fail         <- what the mirror runs
```

The six all fail on files the whitelist deliberately leaves behind — the canary
scripts, `deny-audit.sh`, `export-public.sh` itself. And the exported `ci.yml` runs
`make check`, so the public repository's CI would go red on the next sync. `make
export-check`, whose step in the release workflow is titled "Gate (public export is
publishable)", was asserting a property of a shape that is never published.

The export writes a `PUBLIC_EXPORT` marker now, and the detection reads it. That is
the whole change, and the reason is the recurring class in this record: inferring a
fact from an ABSENCE reads silence as agreement. An export is a positive fact and
can say so. The private tree never carries the marker, which the existing
positive-control test already pins from the other side.

This one was mine, from four hours earlier. D651 added two gates that read
`scripts/`, and the `.git` heuristic had been sitting there since D606 quietly
holding — it only became load-bearing when enough gates depended on it. Worth
recording as a shape: a heuristic that is wrong from the day it is written can stay
green for as long as nothing depends on it, and then fail everything at once.

## D662 — the gate for the advice did not cover the pipeline that builds the artefact

D659 closed `| tee` in the CI recipes this project SHIPS. `release.yml`, which
builds and publishes the binaries, had the identical shape twice:

```yaml
run: sha256sum groundhold_* | tee SHA256SUMS
} | tee BUILDINFO.txt
```

Same reason it does not work — GitHub's default shell is `bash -e {0}` with no
`pipefail`, so the step's status is `tee`'s. Replayed with one artefact unreadable:
the step exits 0, `SHA256SUMS` holds seven entries for eight files, and nothing
downstream re-reads it. The command the release notes and the README hand the user,
`sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing`, then reports OK while passing over the
binary that is not listed.

The checksum step now arms `pipefail`, writes the file, asserts that EVERY artefact
it is about to upload appears in it, and verifies the file it just wrote. An
omission is worse than no checksum file, because it reads as coverage.

`BUILDINFO.txt` also gained the commit. It exists so a third party can rebuild
bit-identically, and it named only the tag — which is mutable, so a rebuild resolves
whatever the tag points at today. That is the wrong direction for a reproducibility
check to fail in.

The gate was extended to `.github/workflows/` and taught two things by being run.
First, the command that must not be piped is not always the binary: `sha256sum`
produces the artefact here. Second, a pipe IS honest when the step arms `pipefail`
— the reproducible-rebuild step does exactly that and computes hashes through
`$(… | cut)`. Refusing those would be an over-reach that teaches people to delete
the gate, so it looks back to the top of the enclosing step for the `set`.

The lesson is about scope rather than about pipes. D659's gate was written for the
directory where the defect was found, and the same defect was two directories away
in the file that publishes the release. A rule aimed at where a bug was seen is not
a rule about the bug.

And one more, caught by the meter rather than by thinking: the first `pipefail`
exemption accepted ANY mention of the word within the enclosing step — so the
comment I had written above the gitlab recipe, explaining that GitLab's shell does
not set pipefail, disarmed the gate on the very line it was explaining. The mutant
survived and said so. Prose about a control is not the control; the exemption now
requires an actual `set … pipefail` command and skips comment lines.

## D663 — the meter could pass by being empty

Ask the diagnostic question of the mutation gate itself: what would it print with
every mutant deleted? Measured — 151 `mutate` invocations stripped:

```
mutation gate — each real bug re-injected; the named test must CATCH it:

mutation gate PASSED — every re-injected bug was caught.
exit 0
```

`FAIL` starts at zero and nothing counted subjects. This is the meter every other
gate in this repository is trusted against, and the argument for trusting the suite
at all runs through it. The sibling gate in `security.yml` has exactly the missing
control — "only $n pins found — this job would be vacuous" — and the meter did not.

It counts now, reports the count in its own success line ("162 mutants ran"), and
refuses below a floor set close to the real number so that deleting a handful is
caught too, not only deleting all of them.

The release's live-endpoint step had the same shape from the other direction:

```yaml
run: go test ./internal/aws -run 'TestLiveAWSSmoke|TestLiveAWSEndpointReality' -count=1 -v
```

`go test -run` over a name that matches nothing exits 0 — measured, with both names
deliberately misspelled. A rename or a move would leave the step green while the two
live checks it exists for never ran. It proves the names EXIST first, with
`go test -list`, which is the control the mutation meter has carried since D605 and
which the workflow that publishes releases did not.

Both floors are pinned by a gate, and the meter's floor was itself measured by
emptying it and watching it exit 1. That measurement also caught me reading an exit
code through `tail` — the trap this record names twice — so the second reading was
taken without a pipe.

No mutant for the floor itself, deliberately. The obvious one edits
`scripts/mutation-gate.sh` while bash is executing it, which is undefined behaviour
and not a measurement — it reported SURVIVED for a change that had plainly been
applied, which is exactly the kind of answer a meter must not produce. The floor is
pinned by the gate test above and by the emptied-meter run recorded here.

## D664 — a consent gate disarmed by a flag, with a comment claiming otherwise

`policy.StatefulOf` reads the vocabulary's `stateful:` flag and nothing else, and
that flag is what arms `autonomy.forbidden: [delete_stateful]`.
`capability.cluster.namespace` was marked `stateful: false`, with this comment beside
it:

> the namespace object holds no data of its own (workloads inside it are separate
> capabilities); deleting an EMPTY governed namespace loses none. (A namespace with
> live workloads is a cascade the delete gate still guards.)

The parenthesis is false. Measured: a contract with `forbidden: [delete_stateful]`
sealed `a-delete-ns` with `"dataLoss": "none"` at exit 0, while the identical
contract over `capability.storage.object` refused with `consent-required`. The
delete is real — `provider.CanAuthor("k8s","namespace")` is true and the driver
issues `DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/<name>`, which the API server cascades to every
namespaced object in it, PVCs included. No emptiness check exists anywhere in the
k8s driver.

The flag is `true` now. The object itself holds no data; what deleting it destroys
belongs to OTHER capabilities, and a static flag cannot know whether the namespace
is empty — so it takes the direction that asks a human.

The mechanism is the second half. `stateful:` is a hand-written claim in 57 files,
and this one was wrong in the most expensive direction while its own comment
asserted the opposite. Capabilities whose deletion destroys other capabilities'
resources are now named once in Go and checked against the shipped vocabulary, so a
new cascading kind has one place to be declared rather than depending on whoever
writes the file knowing what a cascade is. The control beside it requires that
stateless capabilities still exist in numbers — a gate that demanded `stateful: true`
everywhere would fire the consent gate on every retirement and teach operators to
pass `--allow-data-loss` by reflex, which is how a safety control becomes noise.

Writing the mutant found a hazard in the METER, the third this record has collected.
Only the DECLARED file is backed up and restored, so a two-file mutator left an
embedded vocabulary flipped after the gate reported success, and `make check` went
red with no sign of where it came from. Each mutant is now held to what it declared:
the working tree is hashed before and after, and a mutator that touches anything
else fails as `DIRTY`. The first version of that guard compared `git status
--porcelain`, which does not change when an ALREADY-modified file is modified again
— it passed the very case it was written for, so it hashes `git diff` too. A guard
whose positive control does not fire is not a guard, and it took two tries to get
one that does.

## D665 — an empty plan wedged the ledger and blamed a lease that did not exist

The documented quickstart, on the `fake` provider, with no credentials: a candidate
declares an attribute the provider cannot witness. The first converge applies. The
second produces a plan with NO actions — correctly, because D249 isolates the
unobservable attribute as unverifiable and the capability converged on everything
else. `apply` then took that empty write set into `appendLease`, where the ledger's
own document validator refused, and the refusal came back as:

```
exit 3   {"status":"stale-or-conflict","code":"lease-conflict",
          "reasons":["STALE","event.capabilities must be a non-empty list of ids"]}
```

Three things wrong at once. The code is `lease-conflict`, whose published
remediation is "wait for expiry, or break the lease deliberately" — there is no
lease, so the operator waits for nothing. The reason is an internal
document-validator string, which is not a sentence anyone can act on. And the state
is permanent: the same empty plan is produced on every retry, so the ledger is
unusable for that contract from then on. The quickstart calls this scenario "the
observation gate working, not bugs".

`apply` refuses an empty plan as `nothing-to-change` now, before touching the
ledger. And `converge` reads that the way it already reads the plan phase's
`nothing-to-change`: a converged world is the GOAL, not a refusal. The guard alone
would have turned a false exit 3 into a misleading exit 2 — for the porcelain, "the
world already matches on every attribute this run can compare" is the true sentence
and exit 0 is the true code.

The class is a boundary between two components that each behaved reasonably. The
compiler deliberately seals a zero-action plan when a capability has unverified
attributes ("actions == 0 with blocked/unverified present is NOT nothing to
change"), and apply assumed every plan it is handed has something to write. Neither
assumption is wrong on its own; the pair produced a permanently wedged ledger and
accused a lease.

## D666 — six copies of one freshness rule, two of them a second out

`spec/state-model.md`: *"at evaluation time T, an observation is usable iff
`observedAt + ttlSeconds >= T`"* — expired iff its AGE EXCEEDS the ttl. Six places
decide this. Four used `>`; `posture` and `refresh` used `>=`. Measured on one
record (`observedAt` 00:00:10Z, ttl 100):

```
--at 00:01:49Z (age 99)    audit ok      posture managedOk=2 decayed=0
--at 00:01:50Z (age 100)   audit ok      posture managedOk=0 decayed=2   <- disagree
--at 00:01:51Z (age 101)   audit exit 2  posture decayed=2
```

For one second per TTL window, `posture` reported a proof decayed that `audit`,
`plan`, `apply` and `forecast` all still accepted. That matters because posture's
own printed remediation chains `refresh` → `audit` → `posture`: the operator is told
to refresh a proof the auditor accepts, `refresh` (the other `>=` site) agrees it is
stale and re-observes, and if the re-observation lands in the same clock second the
projection keeps the old record (a separate defect, queued) so posture still says
decayed. A loop built out of a one-second disagreement.

The same second was wrong inside my own D652, whose comment says the absence marker
is "judged for freshness the same way the compiler judges it". It was not: posture
honoured it for age < ttl and the compiler for age <= ttl, so for one second per
window posture went green on a resource it was simultaneously planning to re-create.

There is one predicate now, `ledger.ObservationExpired`, and it treats an unreadable
`observedAt` as expired — a freshness decision must not be made against a clock
nobody could read (N1). Two gates: the boundary as arithmetic at ages ttl-1, ttl and
ttl+1, and a source gate that fails when a SEVENTH hand-rolled comparison appears,
with the allow-list naming why each surviving site keeps its own surrounding
conditions. The second gate's positive control was run — reintroducing the `<=` in
`refresh` turns it red.

Class: a published set copied instead of shared — the eighth in this record, and the
first where the copies differed by a single character rather than by membership.

## D667 — a re-observation in the same second was thrown away

`obsNewer` decides which of two readings of one path the projection keeps. At an
equal clock it preferred `measured` over `config-intent` (D45, correct) and
otherwise returned false — so between two `measured` readings of the same second the
INCUMBENT won and the later one was discarded.

Reachable by construction, and reproduced with the product: `converge` runs two
observe phases under one `--at`, and any scheduler pinning a single `--at` per tick
re-observes into the same second. Measured — a second `observe --record` wrote
`service.managed ttl=60` on line 23 while line 19 held `ttl=86400`; `audit` two
minutes later said clean, because it read line 19. The same pair one second apart
blocked as stale. A hand-built variant showed the same for VALUES: a newest record
saying `service.managed=false` at an equal `occurredAt` left `audit` reporting
`satisfied`, `observed: true`.

The ledger is an ordered log, so among equally-timestamped records of equal
derivation the LATER LINE is the later fact — the same reading D656 gave to two
terminal events under one handle. D45's rule is untouched and pinned by its own
case: a measurement outranks a declaration at the same instant whatever order they
arrive in, because the BASIS outranks the order.

This closes the loop D666 describes. `posture` said decayed a second before `audit`
did; its remediation sent the operator to `refresh`; `refresh` re-observed into the
same second the previous reading carried; the projection kept the old record; and
`posture` still said decayed. Three defects, one round trip, each of them individually
a second or a line wide.

## D668 — the refusal existed and nothing called it

`Vocabulary.ValidateEvidence` refuses an unrecognised `evidence:` value, and its own
docstring states the reason: "a closed set that silently tolerates a typo is not
closed — and here the typo's consequence is a reconcile that gates on an observation
which will never arrive."

Its only caller was a gate test, over the EMBEDDED vocabulary. A `--vocab` directory
an operator supplies went unvalidated, so `EvidenceOf` fell back to `resource` for
the misspelled attribute. Measured by an audit on a copy of `spec/vocab` with one
character changed:

```
preflight --vocab <typo'd dir>   exit 2   "cost.monthly has no S3 mapping — refusing"
plan      --vocab <typo'd dir>   exit 0   SEALED
```

The contract sealed and the refusal arrived at `apply` — past the gate, at the
mutation boundary. That sentence is quoted from the gate's own comment describing
the harm it was written to prevent.

`LoadDir` calls it now, naming the file and the value. Class: a control that exists,
is correct, is documented, and is wired to nothing — which is indistinguishable from
not having it, except that the documentation says it is there.

## D669 — the mapping gate read the provider and ignored the service

A `mappings:` key is `<provider>.<service-token>`. The gate that checks them split
on the dot and kept only the PREFIX, so `aws.wafv2`, `azure.portal` and
`gcp.speechtotext` all satisfied it whether or not those tokens exist. The token
half is the part D534 treats as authoritative — it names WHICH driver service
realises the capability, and an operator following it writes that service into a
candidate.

Asked of the drivers themselves: of 155 distinct (capability, cloud key) pairs, 50
named a token that does not serve that capability, and 8 of those named a token that
serves a DIFFERENT one:

```
capability.monitoring.uptime    -> aws.route53          (that token is capability.dns.zone)
capability.monitoring.uptime    -> gcp.monitoring       (that token is capability.monitoring.alert)
capability.monitoring.dashboard -> aws.cloudwatch       (…alert)
capability.monitoring.dashboard -> gcp.monitoring       (…alert)
capability.monitoring.logmetric -> aws.cloudwatch       (…alert)
capability.authorization.grant  -> aws.iam              (…identity.serviceaccount)
capability.authorization.role   -> aws.iam              (…identity.serviceaccount)
capability.function.serverless  -> gcp.cloudfunctions   (…workload.container)
```

Those eight are the sharp ones: they send an operator to a service that EXISTS and
does something else. All eight are corrected — `route53health`, `uptime`,
`cloudwatchdash`, `dashboard`, `cwlogfilter`, `rolepolicy`, `custompolicy`,
`cloudfunctions-fn` — and their baseline is zero and stays there.

The remaining 42 name a token that does not exist at all, which fails loudly at
`preflight` ("attribute check.path has no Route 53 mapping") rather than doing the
wrong thing. They are a ratchet: the count may only fall, and the gate logs it every
run so the number is visible rather than buried in a constant.

An audit reported 48 where I measure 50; the difference is two composite k8s keys
they judged correct. I did not adopt their number — the gate enforces the count MY
parser produces, because a baseline taken from someone else's parser is a
published-registry drift waiting to happen (D619 was exactly that, and I wrote it).

## D670 — the release workflow claimed four gates it does not run

`release.yml` carries a paragraph arguing, correctly, that a parallel workflow
cannot stop `gh release create` — so the gates "run HERE, before anything is built
… the gate has to be in the job that publishes". The list it applies that argument
to names eight things. Four of them — gitleaks, govulncheck, golangci-lint, CodeQL —
appear exactly once in the whole file: in that sentence.

They run in `security.yml` and `lint.yml`, on `pull_request` and on push, which is
precisely the parallel arrangement the same paragraph calls insufficient. And
`codeql.yml` carries `if: github.event.repository.visibility == 'public'`, so on the
private repository it does not run at all. The paragraph is not merely inaccurate:
it uses a true argument to assert a false fact, which is the most convincing shape a
false claim can take.

The comment states what actually runs in the publishing job — `make check` plus the
four `Gate (...)` steps — and says plainly where the other four run and why that is
weaker. Adding them to the job is a real option and deliberately not taken blind:
each needs a network install or a marketplace action and none of it is testable from
this working copy, so doing it unverified would be the same kind of claim in the
other direction.

The gate now reads the workflow's PROSE, not only its release notes: a tool named in
a paragraph that says "run HERE" must have a step that invokes it. Its positive
control fires on all four. This is the second time in two days that a sentence
inside a control was the thing that was wrong (D662: a comment mentioning `pipefail`
disarmed the check on the line it explained), and both were caught by asking what
the artefact says rather than what it does.

## D671 — instructions that cannot be followed literally

The skills are instructions given to an AGENT. A step that cannot be executed as
written is a defect in the same way a broken function is, and an audit that simply
RAN them found five:

- `onboard-existing` step 4 (`adopt`) and step 5 (`converge`) carry no `--at`, and
  step 5 additionally no `--provider` — both exit 1. Step 5 is that skill's own
  "never skip" proof of takeover, and step 1 of the same file carries both flags, so
  the document disagreed with itself. `unadopt` and `adopt-candidate`'s `discover`
  had the same gap.
- `adopt-candidate` step 4 says "trim the contract, then re-publish". The script
  writes that contract into `mktemp -d` under `trap 'rm -rf' EXIT` and never prints
  the path: step 4 asks the operator to edit a file step 3 deleted. The documents
  are kept beside the ledger now, and both paths are printed.
- `spec/errors.md` and the runtime's own `explain` send the operator to `runstatus`
  — an internal package name; the verb is `status`. And `wait --handle` is
  documented while the flag is refused (`wait <handle>` is positional).
- `README.md` runs `ref/groundhold.py hash …`, which exits 126: the file has a
  shebang and no exec bit in git. The claim it demonstrates — two implementations,
  same bytes — is true; the command that demonstrates it could not run.

The gate reads every command in every skill and holds it to the rule the BINARY
enforces, from `timeSensitiveVerbs` rather than a second list that would drift. It
distinguishes a command from a mention: a bare `groundhold adopt` in prose is a
name, and a span carrying any flag purports to be runnable and is held to it. Five
such commands exist today and the gate says so, because a gate that found nothing
would not be a passing gate.

What makes this class worth its own entry: every one of these documents was written
by someone who knew the tool, and each is wrong in a way that only running it can
show. The published-advice audit ran them; that is the whole method.

## D672 — after a compaction, every run had never happened

D645 taught `export` to read the archives. Three verbs still could not: `runs`,
`status` and `wait` all go through `runstatus.ReadEvents`, which read the live file
alone. Measured against the binary:

```
converge …                          exit 0   CONVERGED
status <h> …    → "done"            exit 0
snapshot --ledger …                 exit 0
status <h> …    → "unknown"         exit 0
runs   …        → {"runs":[],"total":0}
wait   <h> --timeout 4              exit 3   after blocking the full 4s
```

Exit 3 is `reconcile-required`, whose published remediation is `groundhold resume`.
So a successful deploy, after the routine compaction this design recommends, tells a
CI gate to go and reconcile it. `ListRuns`'s own doc-comment says a run whose start
event was compacted "reads unknown and sorts last, never dropped" — it was dropped,
and the count was zero.

The archive reader moved from `internal/export` into `internal/ledger`, where the
archive paths already live, and all three verbs read through it. That is the fix
D645 should have been: I put the reader where the defect was rather than where the
knowledge belongs, and the same defect was two packages away.

A short or pruned archive is REPORTED, not refused. `spec/state-model.md` §10 leaves
pruning to the operator, and a reporting verb that becomes permanently unusable
after a lawful prune is a worse answer than "here is what I can see, and here is
what I cannot" — so `runs` and `status` print the shortfall as a note. `export`
keeps refusing it, because a stream a consumer treats as complete is a different
promise from a report a human reads.

## D673 — the loader refused unknown values and accepted unknown keys

`internal/contract`'s package doc has said since D19 that "anything the loader does
not recognize is refused, never silently non-gating". That was true of VALUES —
D627 and D658 gate every block's SHAPE — and false of KEYS. A misspelled top-level
block was dropped without a word:

```
contract with `constraint:` (singular)
  validate typo.yaml     OK  contract t v1: 1 capabilities, 0 constraints   exit 0
  hash typo.yaml   == hash nocons.yaml                     (identical sha256)
  verify typo.yaml cbad.yaml   0 satisfied, 0 violated  PROVEN              exit 0
```

`cbad.yaml` declares `encryption.atRest: false`. The contract requiring encryption
PROVED the candidate refusing it, and `contractHash` — the identity every sealed
plan, capsule and signature pins — could not distinguish that contract from one with
no constraints at all. The candidate side had the same hole with a verdict FLIP:
`attributs:` for `attributes:` made an `op: absent` constraint read as satisfied.

Both loaders refuse an unknown top-level key now, naming it. The escape hatch is an
`x-` prefix: a YAML anchor block or a tool's own metadata lives under `x-defaults`,
and says by its name that the runtime does not read it. Before landing it I checked
every contract and candidate shipped in `spec/`, `examples/` and `conformance/` —
zero used an unknown key, so this refuses nothing that exists.

The reference implementation carries the identical rule; a loader gate that one
implementation enforces and the other does not is a divergence waiting for the first
input that reaches it.

## D674 — a mistyped operand silently built a different resource

The canonical form renders every number as a string (NUMSTR), so `port: 8443` and
`port: "8443"` are ONE canonical value and two candidates differing only in that
have ONE identity. That is tolerable exactly as long as they build the same thing.
They did not:

```
operand port=8443     -> listener Port=8443  TargetPort=8080   err=<nil>
operand port="8443"   -> listener Port=80    TargetPort=8080   err=<nil>
gh hash kA.yaml == gh hash kB.yaml           (sha256:ae58b6cd…, identical)
gh preflight … kA     {"ready": true}
gh preflight … kB     {"ready": true}
```

One sealed identity, two different public front doors, and every gate green. The
cause is small: `implInt` returned `(0, false)` for a value that is PRESENT and
unreadable exactly as for one that is ABSENT, and the caller's default took over —
the discarded-`ok` class, at the operand boundary where the resource is decided.

Absence and unreadability are different answers now. `implIntOperand` leaves the
default alone when the operand is missing and REFUSES when it is present and
mistyped, naming the operand and its type. Four call sites use it: the load
balancer's `port`/`targetPort` and the backup plan's job windows — a backup window
is a recovery guarantee, and it defaulted the same way.

The identity collision itself is not fixed here and should not be fixed quietly:
NUMSTR is the published canonical form, the reference implementation produces the
same hash, and changing it changes every historical identity. What this entry
removes is the reason it MATTERED — with the refusal in place the two documents no
longer behave differently, they behave identically loudly. The collision is recorded
as an open question rather than closed by assertion.

## D675 — a symlink became the archive, and a blocked writer said nothing

Two failures of the same locking path, neither needing concurrency to hurt.

**The symlink.** `os.Rename` acts on the LINK, not its target. Compacting through
one moved the link into `<path>.archive.<N>`, so the "archive" aliased a file that
is still live, a fresh regular file took the operator's path, and the next write
through the real path made the ledger permanently un-exportable — `attest` reporting
the archive mismatched, `repair` exit 5. Measured with no concurrency at all.

Resolving the link instead of refusing would be worse: every reader derives the
snapshot, archive and anchor paths from the path IT was given, so a rotation writing
them beside the resolved file would leave a reader following the link unable to see
any of them, and a tail read as a whole history is exactly the silent answer this
project keeps closing. It refuses, naming the target.

**The silence.** A writer blocked on the flock waited forever without a word.
Measured: a 12-second `observe` against a held lock produced exit 124 — the caller's
own timeout — with an empty stdout and an empty stderr. An operator cannot tell a
held lock from a hang. Worse, the same state made the detach launcher print "run did
not start within 5s" and exit 1 for a process that was alive, blocked, and which
woke up later and mutated infrastructure. The tool said the run had not started; the
run then created the resources.

The lock is taken non-blocking first, so the wait can be announced before it
happens. That does not fix the detach launcher's verdict — it says a run "may have
died" while its PID is alive and its lock wait is now visible on stderr — and that
is recorded here as still open rather than quietly bundled in.

## D676 — one run's lease release killed another run

`DeriveRunStatus` skips events belonging to other handles, with one exception:
`lease.released` and `lease.renewed` are folded whatever run they came from. The
comment explains why — "leases are serialized; a release at/after our acquire ends
ours" — and that is simply not true. A lease covers CAPABILITIES, and two runs over
disjoint capabilities hold live leases at the same time by design.

Measured with the real binary: two converges in one ledger, one over `assets` and
one over `db`, both exit 0, both leases live simultaneously. The moment `assets`
released, the still-running `db` run read:

```
state=stalled  leaseLive=false
remediation: "the writer's lease lapsed with no outcome — run `groundhold resume`"
```

A healthy in-flight run reported dead, with an instruction to reconcile it.

The reason the exception exists at all is worth recording: `apply` writes
`lease.released` with a NIL body, so the event carries no handle to match on. The
capability set is the discriminator that does exist, and the fold now uses it — an
event on `assets` cannot end a lease over `db`.

An event with NO capability list is still treated as ours. The ledger requires a
non-empty list, so an empty one means a reader that could not see it, and for a
LIVENESS signal "cannot tell" must not silently become "not mine" — that is the
direction that reports a dead run as alive, which is worse than the defect being
fixed. Silence stays conservative, and it says so where the code decides it.

## D677 — a candidate could rename the capability it implements

`CandidateModel` built each entry as `{"id": cid, "attributes": …}` and then copied
every extra key over it. `id` was not excluded, so a capability BODY carrying `id:`
overwrote the identity the map key gave it. Two candidates implementing DIFFERENT
capabilities then hashed identically:

```
gh hash candA.yaml   # implements `db`, body carries `id: app`
gh hash candB.yaml   # implements `app`
sha256:c179c26979833bb42c01e7dc17ed0c53d01cfee77e91c5eb72bea352f84641f8   (both)
```

and a measured pair sharing one hash verified PROVEN on one side and BLOCKED on the
other. Every artefact that pins `candidateHash` alone — a capsule, a signature, a
ledger event, an idempotency key — named two documents. The reference implementation
had the identical shape.

Two halves, because either alone is insufficient. The loader REFUSES an `id:` in a
capability body: silently ignoring it would be the D673 shape, a declared field the
loader does not read. And the canonical model writes the identity LAST, so no extra
can overwrite it — an identity a document can rename is not an identity, and the
structural guarantee should not rest on the loader having caught it first.

Both implementations carry both halves, with a conformance case pinning the refusal.

## D678 — the registry dropped exactly what it exists to report

The detach registry's job is to surface a run the LEDGER cannot see. Its own comment
calls "launched but never admitted" the single most attention-worthy condition here.
`ListRegistry` skipped a pointer it could not read, with the reason "a pointer we
cannot read is not truth":

```go
raw, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, name))
if err != nil {
    continue
}
```

So the artefact whose unreadability IS the news vanished. Measured: a truncated
268-byte pointer and one at mode 000 both disappeared with no diagnostic, and two
files naming one handle were listed twice — a caller keying by handle colliding with
itself. Nothing vanishes now: an unreadable pointer, a file that is not an entry,
and a duplicated handle each come back with the reason attached, and `runs` prints
it.

The second half is two verbs disagreeing about one handle at one instant. `runs`
consulted the registry and reported `registry-only` with "launched but no ledger
events — it may have died before admission; check its log"; `status <handle>` never
consulted it at all and reported a bare `unknown` with no source and no remediation.
The PER-RUN verb — the one an operator reaches for when they have a specific handle
— was the blind one. It reads the registry now, for the unknown case only, which is
the only case where the registry can add anything.

Writing the gate caught my own test being weaker than it read. The first version
used a truncated pointer as the "unreadable" case — but a truncated file READS fine
and fails to PARSE, so it exercised the second branch and the mutant on the first
one survived. A dangling symlink is the reliable shape (chmod 000 is not, when the
suite may run as root). The meter said so; I would not have noticed.

Still open and stated rather than bundled: the launcher's verdict. It prints "run
did not start within 5s" and exits 1 for a process that is alive and blocked on the
ledger lock (D675 made that wait visible on stderr, which is not the same as fixing
the verdict), and the registry stores a `pid` that nothing ever checks — so a live
process and a dead one are given the same sentence.

## D679 — "the run did not start", about a process nobody looked at

`converge --detach` waits five seconds for the child to reach admission (its first
ledger event) and then reports. If the wait times out it printed:

```
warning: run did not start within 5s — check the log: …
exit 1
```

Measured with the ledger lock held by another writer: the child was ALIVE and
blocked on that lock, the launcher said it had not started, exited 1 — and the run
woke up 27 seconds later and created the infrastructure. The tool told the operator
nothing had happened, and then it happened.

"Did not start" is a claim about a process, and nothing looked at the process. The
registry has stored a `pid` since it was written and no code ever read it. Signal 0
is precisely the question being asserted — does this process exist — so it is asked
before asserting. A live child that has not reached admission gets a different
sentence, names its pid, says it is most likely waiting for the ledger lock (D675
made that wait visible from the other side), and exits 0: a slow start is not a
failure, and exit 1 tells a caller otherwise.

The verdict is a pure function taking the aliveness as an argument, so both answers
can be driven without forking anything, and one source assertion pins the wiring —
that the launcher hands it `processAlive(e.PID)`.

That shape came from the meter. My first version left the decision inline and the
test asserted only that the source CONTAINS `syscall.Kill(e.PID, 0)`; the mutant
`alive := false && syscall.Kill(e.PID, 0) == nil` kept the substring, so the test
passed with the bug back in. A test that greps for a call proves the call is
written, not that it decides anything — the trap `docs/BUG_HUNTING.md` names, walked
into while fixing a defect of exactly the same kind.

Recorded because it happened in the same commit: I pushed once while the meter was
red. `make check` was green and the composite command gated the push on THAT exit
code alone, so the meter's failure — a mutant that did not compile — went past. The
second time this session; the fix is the same as the first, and the lesson is that a
gate you run is not a gate you check.

## D680 — three claims about what a user downloads

**One binary of eight was ever executed.** The cross-build writes four versioned
artefacts and four version-less copies, and the only execution in the workflow was
`./dist/groundhold_<tag>_linux_amd64 version`. `groundhold_linux_amd64` — the asset
the README's install line fetches — was never run anywhere. Every artefact this
runner can execute is now executed, and the ones it cannot are NAMED in the log,
because a cross-built target that was never run is a coverage gap and should read as
one rather than as silence.

**The checksums could not cover half the published assets.** `Checksums` ran before
`Record build info` and `Generate SBOM`, with the glob `groundhold_*` — so
`BUILDINFO.txt` and `sbom.cdx.json` were published unlisted by construction. The
file the rebuild instructions live in was the one nobody could verify. The step is
last now and names all three kinds.

**The install snippet verified a file it did not download.** `gh release download …
--pattern 'groundhold_linux_amd64'`, then "verify a download with `sha256sum -c
SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing`" — measured in that exact state: `sha256sum:
SHA256SUMS: No such file or directory`, exit 1. The snippet fetches the sums file
and runs the check.

The three share a shape worth naming. Each is a claim about an artefact rather than
about code, and each was true of something adjacent: one binary WAS executed, the
checksums DID cover the binaries, the verification line IS correct given the file.
A claim that is nearly true is the hardest kind to notice, and the only way any of
these surfaced was someone running the published steps in order.

## D681 — one document, two identities, each belonging to a different document

Every string-typed field was read as `x, _ := raw["k"].(string)`. A non-string value
became `""` and the field was omitted from the canonical model — while the reference
implementation canonicalized the RAW value instead (NUMSTR renders `7` as `"7"`).
Three contracts differing only in one constraint field:

```
A: path: 7      ref sha256:0707a8e8…   go sha256:147f3436…
B: path: "7"    ref sha256:0707a8e8…   go sha256:0707a8e8…
C: no path      ref sha256:147f3436…   go sha256:147f3436…
```

The reference gives A the identity of **B**. The runtime gives A the identity of
**C**. So a plan sealed on B's `contractHash` is satisfied by A under the reference,
and a plan sealed on C's is satisfied by A under the runtime — in both cases by a
document its author never wrote. `spec/contract.schema.json` types these as strings
and neither implementation refused. The same shape existed on a candidate's
`source:` and on `subject`, `op` and `id`.

Both implementations refuse a wrong-typed value now, with the same rule the shape
gates use: a value of the wrong type is not an absent one. A conformance case pins
it on both sides.

This is the same root as D674 (`port: "8443"` building a listener on 80) seen from
the identity end rather than the behaviour end. There the two documents shared a
hash and did different things; here they shared a hash with documents they had
nothing to do with. Both come from one habit — reading a typed field with the `ok`
discarded — and the sweep for the remaining instances of it is worth doing on its
own rather than one defect at a time.

## D682 — enum values no driver can honour, and a probe that nearly lied

An enum value that NO serving driver accepts is a promise the vocabulary makes and
cannot keep: a contract can hard-constrain it and no candidate can ever satisfy it.
The drivers are asked directly, through the refuse-before-mutate hook they already
implement, and twelve values are dead today:

```
capability.cache.keyvalue     availability.class = multi-regional
capability.cluster.kubernetes availability.class = multi-regional
capability.database.nosql     availability.class = multi-regional
capability.compute.instance   availability.class = regional
capability.apigateway.http    protocol           = websocket
capability.authorization.grant access.scope      = account | resource
capability.cdn.distribution   viewer.protocol    = redirect-to-https
capability.cost.budget        budget.period      = daily
capability.monitoring.uptime  check.protocol     = tcp
…
```

They are not deleted here. Each is a spec decision — unbuilt-but-intended, or a
mistake — and removing an enum member changes what a published vocabulary means. The
ratchet makes the number visible on every run and stops it growing.

The interesting half is the probe. My first version simply called `Validate` with
the one attribute and counted every refusal as evidence: it reported **76** dead
values, including all three members of enums that plainly work. The driver was
refusing something else entirely — a missing operand, an unsupported service — and
reading that as "this value is dead" turns an incomplete probe into a finding.

A refusal only counts as evidence when it DIFFERS from what the same service says
with no attributes at all. With that baseline diff the count is 12, and the twelve
survive an independent check: an audit reached `multi-regional` on two of the three
capabilities I find it on. Two measurements, two numbers, and the gate enforces the
one whose method I can state.

That is the entry's real content. A gate built on a probe that conflates two
questions does not become trustworthy by being green — it becomes a machine for
manufacturing findings, which is worse than having no gate, because the findings
look measured.

## D683 — the sweep D681 asked for

D681 ended by saying the remaining instances of one habit — reading a typed field
with the `ok` discarded — were worth sweeping as their own job rather than one
defect at a time. This is that sweep, across both loaders.

Seven sites: `meta.id`, `meta.environment`, a capability's `id` and `type`, a budget
constraint's `severity`, a soft constraint's `objective`, and the `outcomes` block.
Each read `x, _ := m["k"].(T)`, so a wrong-typed value became the zero value, the
field vanished from the canonical model, and the document hashed identically to one
that never declared it.

`meta.environment` is the sharpest. D610 refused a non-integer `meta.version` and
left the sibling untouched — and `environment` reaches resource TAGS and NAMES, so
the estate gets stamped with an empty one while `validate` prints OK. `outcomes` is
the sibling of `assumptions`, which was shape-gated by D627; the one beside it was
not.

Both implementations carry all of it, and the gate drives four of the seven through
the loader with a control that a well-formed document keeps every field.

Writing the gate corrected one of my own assumptions: I aimed a case at `severity:`
inside a `constraints.hard` entry, where the severity comes from the BLOCK NAME and
the key is simply unread. The `severity` read that exists is in the `budget` block.
A test aimed at a site that does not exist proves nothing and passes — which is the
same failure as a gate with no subject, arrived at from the other direction.

## D684 — an integer past int64 fell through every arm of the load gate

`spec/canonicalization.md` says, in these words: *"Both implementations refuse such
a value at LOAD … as a structural error."* `CheckSafeNumbers` had arms for `int`,
`int64` and `float64`. yaml.v3 decodes an integer larger than int64 as **uint64**,
which matched none of them:

```
validate u.yaml   OK  contract t v1: 1 capabilities, 0 constraints    exit 0
hash u.yaml       document error: cannot canonicalize value of type uint64
ref  (python)     REFUSED: integer 18446744073709551615 exceeds the JSON-safe range
```

Nothing unsafe shipped — it failed closed one layer down — but with the wrong error,
from the wrong layer, naming a Go type instead of the operator's number, and without
the remediation this gate's message carries. The reference refused it correctly all
along, so the two implementations disagreed about WHERE a document is rejected while
agreeing that it is.

`uint64` and `uint` have arms now, and `validate` refuses with the same sentence as
every other out-of-range number.

Class: a closed set with a member nobody enumerated. The switch was written against
the types a JSON decoder produces; the YAML decoder in front of it produces one
more, and the arm that was missing is the one for the values furthest outside the
safe range.

## D685 — the reference gave two documents one identity, and one it refuses another's

Two defects in `ref/`, both of the same shape: a document the RUNTIME refuses took
the identity of a different, valid one.

**Non-string mapping keys.** `canon` rendered every key with `_quote(str(k))`, so
`{8: v}`, `{"8": v}` and `{010: v}` — three distinct documents — produced one hash,
while the runtime refuses the first and third outright ("cannot canonicalize map
with non-string key of type int"). Seventeen of twenty-seven key-position tokens
diverged this way. That is exactly the injectivity argument `_num_str`'s own two
refusals (>2^53, <1e-17) are built on, one level up and unguarded. The reference
refuses a non-string key now, in the runtime's words.

**Unquoted YAML timestamps.** `yamlcompat`'s resolver table had no timestamp
resolver, so a bare `occurredAt: 2026-07-11T12:00:00Z` stayed a STRING and hashed
identically to the correctly quoted document — while go-yaml v3 resolves it to
`time.Time` and the runtime refuses it, as `spec/canonicalization.md` says it must
("YAML timestamps are not canonicalizable in v1"). Two consequences beyond the
identity: `state.py`'s own `occurredAt must be a quoted RFC3339 string` guard was
UNREACHABLE code, because its loader could never produce a non-string; and the
module's docstring claims the table mirrors go-yaml "EXACTLY (verified
token-by-token against the runtime)", which was not true of this token.

Measured after the fix, on the same file:

```
unquoted   go exit 1 "must be a quoted RFC3339 string"   ref exit 1 (same sentence)
quoted     go sha256:bc4e32bc…                            ref sha256:bc4e32bc…
```

The differential harness could not have found either. Its generator writes documents
through `yaml.safe_dump`, so the parser only ever sees what PyYAML produced — never
a bare date, never a non-string key. Both implementations were wrong about the same
inputs in different directions, and every seed agreed.

## D686 — a rule I could not state, and did not ship

D682 measured enum values no serving driver accepts. The obvious next rule is the
same question one level up: an ATTRIBUTE every serving driver refuses for every
value it can take. An audit had already named one — `dns.proxied`, refused by all
three DNS-record drivers for BOTH `true` and `false`, the only attribute in 340
where no value at all is acceptable to anyone.

I built it, with D682's baseline-diff discipline, and it flagged **78 attributes**:
`service.managed` on nearly every capability, `encryption.atRest` on eight,
`security.scanOnPush`, `auto.renew`. Those are not dead. They are attributes a
driver MEASURES rather than authors, or ones it accepts only alongside operands the
probe does not supply — and the message differs from the baseline because it names
the attribute in a "requires …" sentence, not because the value is unsupported.

The premise is what is wrong: "every declared attribute must be acceptable to
`Validate`" is false, because the vocabulary contains observation-only attributes
and nothing in it distinguishes authored from observed. `evidence:` classifies
projections and probes, not this.

So the gate is not shipped. A gate whose subject I cannot define would manufacture
findings, and 78 of them would bury the one that is real. What would make the rule
statable: a driver-side signal for "this attribute is authorable by this service" —
the same shape as `provider.CanAuthor` but per attribute. That is a real piece of
work and it is not this slice's.

Recorded because the alternative is that the next person measures it, gets 78, and
either ships it or spends the afternoon I just spent. D682's lesson generalises: a
probe is only as good as the question it can isolate, and an unshipped gate with a
written reason is worth more than a green one nobody trusts.

## D687 — a mapping named a provider that cannot build anything

`explain <attribute>` prints the attribute's `mappings:`, and a reader takes a
provider named there as support. `dns.proxied` lists exactly one —
`cloudflare.dnsrecord` — and the cloudflare driver is read-only discovery. No
candidate can carry the attribute; a contract requiring it cannot be satisfied by
