anything; and all three cloud DNS drivers refuse it for BOTH values, which is how an
audit found it: the only attribute in 340 where no value at all is acceptable to
anyone.

The vocabulary is honest about this — in a COMMENT above the mapping, which
`explain` does not print. It printed the mapping and stopped.

`explain` now says `NOT AUTHORABLE` when no mapping names a service that can CREATE
the capability, and says what it costs the reader. Writing the predicate found a
second thing: `provider.CanAuthor` answers a NARROWER question than its name
suggests — "is this service witness-only within a driver that has registered a
predicate" — and it defaults to TRUE for a provider it has never heard of. So it
said cloudflare can author. The check requires the provider to be one whose driver
authors AND the service not to be a witness within it.

This is the rule D686 could not state, narrowed to where it IS statable: the
question is about the PROVIDER and the SERVICE, which the drivers answer, not about
whether an attribute is authorable, which nothing currently records.

## D688 — the tool's own help contradicted the tool, twice per verb

`--help` states which verbs REQUIRE an explicit `--at`. It named nine.
`timeSensitiveVerbs` — the set the binary actually enforces — holds twenty. So
nineteen verbs were absent from the sentence that documents them, including every
verb added to the set after the sentence was written.

The per-verb usage lines were wrong in the same direction and in the help's own
notation: `[--at <ts>]` means optional, and twelve time-sensitive verbs showed it
bracketed. Measured on the one an audit walked into:

```
groundhold discover --provider fake --region eu-central-1 > discover.json
  discover requires an explicit --at (RFC3339 timestamp)      exit 1
groundhold --help
  groundhold discover … [--at <ts>]                <- optional
  Time-sensitive verbs (plan/apply/…/resume) …     <- discover absent
```

Two published statements about one verb, both false, in the text the tool prints
about itself.

The gate reads `timeSensitiveVerbs` rather than a second list, so the sentence
cannot drift from the enforcement again: every verb in the set must appear in the
paragraph, and no usage block for one may bracket `--at`.

Its first version read only the words BEFORE the phrase "REQUIRE an explicit --at",
so when I moved the list to the other side of that phrase it reported all nineteen
verbs missing. A gate that reads a sentence's SHAPE rather than its content is
measuring the author's habits — it takes the whole paragraph now.

## D689 — the quickstart's only real-cloud instruction could not work

`website/pages/quickstart.md` told a newcomer that GCP "credentials come from
Application Default Credentials — `gcloud auth application-default login`". The
driver does not read ADC. `README.md` says so in those words — "In order:
`GROUNDHOLD_GCP_ACCESS_TOKEN` → `GROUNDHOLD_GCP_KEY_FILE` → the GCE metadata server.
**Not ADC**" — so two published documents contradicted each other about a
credential boundary, and the one a newcomer reads first was the wrong one.

Measured on a host that HAS an ADC file:

```
env -u GROUNDHOLD_GCP_ACCESS_TOKEN -u GROUNDHOLD_GCP_KEY_FILE \
  groundhold discover --provider gcp --project my-project --at …
discover error: gcp discovery cannot reach the provider: no usable GCP credentials
  (set GROUNDHOLD_GCP_ACCESS_TOKEN or GROUNDHOLD_GCP_KEY_FILE, or run on GCE)
exit 1
```

The quickstart names the real chain now and shows the one line that makes the
example run, `export GROUNDHOLD_GCP_ACCESS_TOKEN="$(gcloud auth print-access-token)"`.

The gate reads `internal/gcp/auth.go` for the environment variables the auth path
actually consults, and requires every document that explains GCP credentials to name
them. ADC may be mentioned — saying it is NOT used is exactly what the README does —
but it may not be offered as the way in. Positive control run: restoring the old
sentence turns the gate red on both counts.

Class: a published claim that is false, in the document with the highest ratio of
readers to authors. The runtime had been refusing this setup with a precise message
the whole time; nobody had put the message and the instruction side by side.

The gate took three attempts and the meter caught each one. Reading LINES missed a
claim that wraps across a newline — the shape D659's first gate had. Matching
"not application default" missed the negation because it is written `**not**` and
the asterisks sit between the words. And accepting a nearby `print-access-token` as
proof the document is honest was plainly wrong: the corrected example sits inside
the same window as the sentence it corrects, so its presence says nothing about
whether that sentence is true. Only an explicit negation excuses the mention now.

## D690 — one attribute, three closed sets, none of them published

`addon.name` declares no `enum`, and the three drivers each enforce a closed set of
canonical names:

```
gcp    backup-agent, config-connector, dns-cache, filestore-csi-driver,
       gce-pd-csi-driver, horizontal-pod-autoscaling, http-load-balancing,
       network-policy
azure  azure-policy, http-application-routing, ingress-appgw,
       keyvault-secrets-provider, monitoring, open-service-mesh
aws    free-form EKS addon names (vpc-cni, coredns, …)
```

Pairwise intersection: empty. An EKS addon is a versioned package, a GKE addon is a
cluster flag, an AKS addon is an addonProfile key — the same word names three
different kinds of thing. The vocabulary's description listed only the AWS examples,
so a capability attribute that reads as portable is portable to exactly one cloud,
and `AUTHORING.md` §3's promise — "the loader rejects a candidate value outside it" —
bought nothing here, because there was nothing to reject against.

**No enum is added, and that is the decision.** The union of three disjoint sets is
not a set any single candidate can draw from: declaring it would make the loader
accept a name the chosen cloud refuses, while implying the name is portable. The
honest artefact is three published sets, one per provider, which is what the
mappings carry now — and `explain` prints mappings, so an author sees their cloud's
list before writing the candidate.

The gate checks the publication against the DRIVERS' own tables, so the vocabulary
cannot fall behind the code that enforces them, and it fails if an `enum` ever
appears — the decision is pinned, not just taken.

## D691 — three capability types nothing can build, and the ladder said nothing

`capability.ai.speech` (5 attributes), `capability.identity.sso` (6) and
`capability.identity.oauth-client` (15) are declared in the vocabulary and realised
by no shipped driver. The last carries no `mappings:` anywhere at all — it is the
one capability type with no published implementation story. Two of the three are
`stateful: true`, so they also arm a consent gate for a delete that can never be
planned.

A contract can declare any of them, and nothing can ever implement it. `parity`
already knew — it prints `unbuilt` for exactly these, per cloud. `explain <type>`,
the rung of the discovery ladder an author reads BEFORE writing the contract,
printed the attribute list and said nothing, so the author learned at the bottom
(`verify` reporting the capability unimplemented, `plan` blocking) what the top
could have said.

`explain` asks the drivers which services realise the type — the same question D687
asks one level down about an attribute's mappings — and says `UNBUILT` when the
answer is none.

The gate pins both directions and, deliberately, the LIST: if one of the three ever
gains a driver, the test fails and says to remove it from this entry's claim rather
than leaving the record wrong. An entry that quietly becomes false is the failure
mode this whole record exists to avoid.

## D692 — the teardown that could not run, on the one example that spends money

`examples/canary-azure/README.md` is the live-cloud canary: a stranger runs it
against their own Azure subscription. Its teardown section is headed *"run it — an
unowned canary is how bills start"*, and it read:

```
sed -i 's/^  - id: net/  - id: net\n    state: retired/' examples/canary-azure/canary.contract.yaml
bin/groundhold-go converge ... --allow-data-loss --yes
```

Neither line works. The `sed -i` mutates a repo-tracked contract in place and
produces a document the loader REFUSES — `constraint targets retired capability`,
the very rule the same README explains two sections further down. The converge has
no operands to copy. And the README knew: *"the retirement pair used here lives in
the session notes rather than the repo"*. A reader who followed the loop to the end
was left with a resource they could not retire through the contract, on the example
whose entire point is that leaving one running costs money.

The retirement pair now SHIPS — `canary-retired.contract.yaml` (version 2, `net`
marked `state: retired`, constraints dropped) and `canary-retired.candidate.yaml`,
which does not mention the capability at all, because an empty attribute map is
still a declaration and the delete acts on the providerId pinned in the binding.
Both are the documents the README names.

That is the instance. The mechanism is that a document which SHIPS is a document
`examples/check.sh` loads, while one a README synthesizes at read time is checked by
nobody — so a published procedure may not conjure its own input. Gated in
`TestPublishedProceduresNameDocumentsThatShip` over `examples/*/README.md`, the
files a reader copies against their own cloud: inside a fenced block, a groundhold
invocation may not elide operands with `...`, may not rewrite a shipped document in
place, and every `*.contract.yaml` / `*.candidate.yaml` it names must exist. D607
gated the FLAGS of a published invocation; this gates the DOCUMENTS. Website and
docs prose stays out, where a partial illustration is legitimate — the same boundary
D607 drew.

The second half is `examples/check.sh` itself. Its validate list was ten paths typed
by hand, and the first shipped contract to test that list was this entry's own
retirement contract: added in the same commit, missed by the list, validated by
nobody. The scope is now discovered per document kind, with a floor so an empty
discovery cannot pass as a clean run (D328), and every shipped candidate must be
named somewhere in the script. Expectations stay declared — the script still refuses
to guess whether an example is meant to compile or to be refused — but WHICH
examples get checked is no longer a question of what an author remembered (D583).

One note for the next author, from this entry's own negative control: the vacuity
floor was written ABOVE the findings, and the historical defect DELETED two
invocations, so restoring it tripped the floor and the run reported a broken scan
while the three real violations went unprinted. A guard that fires before the check
it guards hides exactly what it was written to surface. Findings first, floor after.

## D693 — the advice a refusal prints, and whether it can be followed

Nine remediations printed by the runtime named a verb the reader could not run:

```
run `groundhold resume`     -> resume requires an explicit --at … (also --ledger, --provider)
run `groundhold discover`   -> discover requires an explicit --at …   (x5, in four drivers)
Run `groundhold repair`     -> repair requires --ledger
Run `groundhold crawl`      -> crawl requires an explicit --at …
run `groundhold suggest`    -> usage: groundhold suggest <contract.yaml> …
```

Every one of them appears inside a refusal — the ledger is corrupted, a foreign
cluster sits at our deterministic name, an in-flight receipt is unsettled — so it is
read by someone already stuck, who pastes it and is refused a second time by the tool
that just told them what to do. N1 is exactly why: a time-sensitive verb refuses a
defaulted clock, and none of this advice carried a clock.

Each now names what the verb needs, using the values the caller already holds — the
AWS drivers know their region, GCP knows project and location, Azure knows the
subscription — and `perr.AtNow` for the clock: `--at "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)"`, a shell
substitution the reader pastes verbatim rather than a `<placeholder>` they must fill.
It lives in `perr`, the package with no dependencies, so twenty verbs' advice cannot
drift into twenty spellings of one operand. It also holds `%F` and `%T`, so it must be
passed as an argument and never concatenated into a format string — `go vet` refuses
that, and caught all six call sites on the first draft.

The gate asks the CLI rather than reading it. A verb advised with no operands is RUN
with no operands through the same `run()` main uses, and must not refuse. That matters
more than it sounds: D607's derivation reads `"<verb> requires --<flag>"` out of
main.go's source, and `resume`'s `--provider` refusal is formatted from a variable, so
that map never knew about it. A gate built on the same scrape would have blessed a
remediation still missing a required flag. Ask the code, do not read its text (D317).

Scope is deliberately the IMPERATIVE mention — "run `groundhold x`". A verb named as
a noun ("the id column of `groundhold export`") is a reference, not advice, and
demanding flags of it would manufacture findings out of correct prose. Two gates now
stand either side of the same claim: D607 for the invocations the project publishes in
files, this one for the advice the binary prints at the moment of failure.

One boundary, stated rather than implied: the gate judges the BARE mention — a verb
advised with no operands at all. It does not render a format string and judge the
result, so advice that names operands badly (a `%s` landing in the wrong place) still
passes. That is where the first version of this entry's own mutant survived, and the
honest reading is that this gate closes the class it was built for and no more. What
it did close on the way there: a scanner that read Go's concatenated strings line by
line saw no verb in either half of a wrapped message — two of the nine defects had
exactly that shape, and a mutant proved the blindness before a reader did.

## D694 — a publicly reachable function, observed as private, on a route AWS does not have

Reported from the field, on the binary this project had just delivered:

| capability | AuthType | anonymous call | observed |
|---|---|---|---|
| api | NONE | 200 — answers | `publicExposure = false` |
| web | AWS_IAM | 403 — refuses | `publicExposure = false` |

The second row is right. The first is a live function answering an unauthenticated
caller, recorded as not exposed — with no diagnostic — while the contract that
declares it exposed reads as satisfied. The reporter named the class before we did:
*a gate that can quietly check nothing is not a gate.*

D534 made this observation a two-gate reading, correctly: a Function URL is public
only with AuthType NONE **and** a resource policy granting `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl`
to `*`. The second gate read the policy at

```
GET /2021-10-31/functions/<name>/policy
```

`/2021-10-31` is the Function URL API version. Lambda has no policy route there. The
two write sites either side of it — AddPermission and RemovePermission — used
`/2015-03-31`, the correct one. Measured against the live endpoint, no credentials:

```
GET /2015-03-31/functions/x/policy -> {"message":"Missing Authentication Token"}    route exists
GET /2021-10-31/functions/x/policy -> "Unable to determine service/operation name"  route does not
```

So AWS answered OUR bad URL with a 404, and the reader took that 404 for an answer
about the WORLD: "this function has no resource policy" — therefore private. Every
Function URL with AuthType NONE reported private. The 404 was ours, not the account's.

Three things follow, and the path fix is the least of them.

**One spelling.** `lambdaPolicyPath()` is now the only place that route is written, so
the read and the two writes cannot drift apart again. Two spellings of one route, with
only one of them exercised against reality, is what made this possible.

**The fixture could not see it.** `lambdaExposureServer` matched with
`strings.HasSuffix(path, "/policy")` — it answered whatever API version the driver
asked for. Every test in this package passed with the wrong route, because none of
them was testing the route; they were testing the shape of the request. It matches by
EXACT path now, and an unknown path fails the test by name. A fixture that answers a
request the cloud would reject is not a double for the cloud.

**The live gate covered one service.** `TestLiveAWSEndpointReality` (D274) asks the
real API whether every path a driver constructs is a real route — for EKS. That is
where this belonged, and it was never extended when Lambda grew a second API version.
It now covers ten Lambda routes across both versions, with the D694 wrong path as the
negative control: if that path ever reads as real, the gate has stopped working.

The reporter also flagged the consequence for their next converge: with `publicExposure`
misread as false and a candidate declaring true, the plan wants to switch it ON — which
for the IAM-protected function would be a security regression introduced by "bringing
things into agreement". Two answers. The immediate one is that this reading was wrong
and the observation is now measured. The structural one already landed in the same
release: `securityExposure: certain` is derived from the change set (D628) and reaches
a gate that plain `--yes` does not satisfy (D630) — a plan that opens something up
refuses without `--allow-exposure`. The tool would not have opened it silently. It
should never have needed that backstop here.

## D695 — an alarm that cannot fire, and the four values that decide whether it can

Reported from the field, as a capability gap rather than a bug — and argued better
than the code deserved. Eight alarms on a live payment path could not be brought into
a contract, because `aws/cloudwatch` reads exactly one operand
(`notification_channel`) and refused the rest:

```
alarm-checkout.dimensions          is not an operand the aws/cloudwatch driver reads
alarm-checkout.evaluation_periods  is not an operand ...
alarm-checkout.period_seconds      is not an operand ...
alarm-checkout.statistic           is not an operand ...
alarm-checkout.treat_missing_data  is not an operand ...
```

The refusal was right — D530 exists so an operand no driver reads never passes
silently — and the reporter said so. What was wrong was that the driver had nothing
to read them into. Their metrics carry a categorical dimension, and **an alarm with no
dimension watches the dimensionless variant of the metric, which their exporter never
emits**: the alarm is created, `notify=true` is satisfied, the contract reads as
covered, and it can never fire. Their words, and this project's own phrase back at it:
a gate that can quietly check nothing is not a gate.

This file used to say those values were "fixed defaults (tuning, not capability
semantics)". That judgment was wrong twice over. With `Average` over 300 seconds and
one evaluation period, "three failures in a quarter of an hour" cannot be stated at
all — the threshold means something else than the author wrote. Without
`treat_missing_data`, a failure counter alarms all night at zero traffic, because a
differential metric only appears when something was measured. These are not tuning.
They decide whether the alarm's claim is true or vacuous.

**Operands, not vocabulary attributes.** They are CloudWatch's own evaluation
vocabulary, and the contract keeps saying WHAT is watched (`alert.metric`,
`alert.threshold`, `alert.comparison`) rather than how the watching is configured —
the same line `log_group` and `subnet_ids` already sit on. Inventing cross-cloud
attributes would have meant inventing GCP and Azure mappings for them in the same
breath, and the reporter explicitly said reading the four keys from `implementation:`
was enough.

Each is validated against CloudWatch's closed set at build time, so a typo refuses at
compile rather than mid-apply: the five statistics, the four missing-data treatments,
a period of 10/20/30 or a multiple of 60, a positive evaluation count, and dimensions
as a map of at most 30 printable name/value pairs. An EMPTY dimension map refuses
rather than defaulting: omitting the key already says "alarm on the metric as a
whole", so an empty map states nothing, and guessing which was meant would rebuild the
dimensionless alarm the author was trying to avoid.

**The other half is what makes it real.** Reading an operand into the create request
is not enough: a candidate that ADDS dimensions to an alarm that already exists would
produce no action at all, converge would report converged, and the alarm would stay
dimensionless — the same pretense one level down. So the driver now implements
`OperandDrifter` for `cloudwatch` and observe records the live evaluation state under
the reserved `implementation.*` paths. Both sides go through ONE canonicalizer, never
one through it and one around it; CloudWatch returns dimensions in no particular
order, so the live side is sorted before rendering. Defaults are exactly what this
driver sent before (`Average` / 300 / 1, and `missing`, which is what the API reports
for an alarm that never set it), so an alarm built before any of this existed does not
read as drifted the moment it is observed.

Two boundaries, stated rather than discovered later. There is no in-place update path
wired for `cloudwatch`, so changing an evaluation operand on an existing alarm is a
REPLACEMENT under a new deterministic name — create-before-destroy, and consent-free
because `capability.monitoring.alert` is `stateful: false`. And the GCP and Azure alert
drivers are untouched: their twins have their own spellings for the same four
questions, and inventing them here without a live account to check against would be
the kind of claim this record exists to prevent.

One thing fell out of the shared helper on the way. `implIntPresent` truncated a
fractional operand: `period_seconds: 60.5` became 60 and passed a "must be a multiple
of 60" check the author's own value fails — the D674 shape exactly, a value the loader
could not honestly read, silently built as a different one. A fractional operand is
unreadable now, not rounded, for every caller of that helper; and `int64`, which
yaml.v3 produces once a literal exceeds int's range, is accepted instead of refused.

## D696 — three states, because two of them were the same bucket

The field asked for this and answered the design question that had been left open
since 2026-07-30. Their argument, and the incident behind it, are better evidence than
anything this repo could have produced on its own:

> A deployment gate probed an anti-bot control through an endpoint rate-limited to
> 5/min. Several runs in a row it took a **429**, whose body did not contain the phrase
> it looked for, so the control fell through to "skipping". The gate **changed its mind
> between runs** and let through an image built without the key — a site where every
> user write would bounce off a 403. The probe did not fail. Collapsing a third state
> into a second did.

The reachability prober had two verdicts: `reachable`, and `unknown` for everything
else. So "the edge answered 5xx" and "I could not establish anything" arrived in the
same bucket, with only prose to tell them apart. Their hard ask was not for a new exit
code — it was for the DATUM: three disjoint, machine-readable states, so the policy
stays on their side. *The probe measures; we decide.*

`failing` is now the third state, and it is deliberately narrow: an answer with no
alternative explanation. A **5xx** — the edge answered and what it answered is a
failure; no policy reads that way and no vantage point produces it. A **TLS layer that
did not complete** — a certificate that does not verify is not a policy and not a
propagation delay. A 403 stays `unknown`, as it was: anonymous denial is genuinely
ambiguous, and they explicitly agreed.

**Where this stops short of what was asked, and why.** They also proposed NXDOMAIN for
a declared-published name, and a refused connection, as confirmed failures. Both stay
`unknown`. Minutes after a create, NXDOMAIN is propagation and a refused connection is
an edge still provisioning — and this probe runs *right after apply*. Turning those
into confirmed failures would manufacture confident accusations, which is the same
error this package refuses in the other direction, wearing the opposite sign. Bounding
propagation is a policy decision (how long is too long), and policy belongs in a
declared constraint, not compiled into a prober. Said to them plainly rather than
quietly not done.

A confirmed failure is a MEASUREMENT, so it enters the observation stream as
`network.reachable = false` with its evidence, where a declared constraint can be
violated by it. `unknown` still records nothing: absence of knowledge is not a reading,
and writing one would be the collapse this entry undoes, from the other end. In the
run verdict `failing` outranks `unknown` — "this is broken" carries strictly more
knowledge than "I could not tell" — and the banner is VIOLATED rather than BLOCKED,
which the presentation order already had right.

**Their third point cost nothing and closes a real hole.** A function that would not
start answered HTTP 200 carrying `{"errorType":"Runtime.InvalidEntrypoint"}`, and a
smoke gate keyed on the status class passed it as clean. They did not ask us to read
bodies — the content contract belongs to whoever owns the service, and they want that
boundary kept. They asked for the probe to say what it CHECKED. So every result now
carries `checked`: *reachability and HTTP status class only — the response body was not
inspected, so a 2xx carrying an error payload reads here as reachable.* The principle
is the one `--no-reachability` already followed ("the edge was NOT probed"), extended
to a probe that DID run and measured less than a reader assumes.

Two things fell out on the way, both of the same family this record keeps naming.

**The published closed set was wrong in both directions.** `spec/outputs.schema.json`
enumerated `reachable | denied | unknown | skipped` in two places. `denied` was removed
from the runtime when a 403 became ambiguous and no code path has produced it since;
`failing` did not exist. A consumer generating types from that schema got a value that
never arrives and missed one that does — in the exact field they asked to key their
policy on. The set has one home in `reach.ReportedVerdicts` now, the assignment sites
use the constants rather than string literals, and a gate holds both schema locations
to it (D329/D330/D338, again).

**The classification lived in two renderers.** `converge`'s phase output and the
`probe` verb each had their own copy of which verdict means what, and adding a third
state meant editing both — which is how a third state gets collapsed again in one of
them. `reach.Fold` owns the meaning; the prose stays per-verb.

The 5xx conformance case is REPLACED, not edited: `server-error-is-unknown-not-success`
pinned the old model faithfully and is superseded by name, per the rule that a semantic
change starts with a case and history is never quietly rewritten.

## D697 — the probe verb had the same two-state collapse, one verb over

D696 landed because the field reported a gate that could not tell "I did not confirm
this" from "this is broken". Asking the same question of `probe` — the verb whose whole
purpose is to MEASURE, and which is allowed to spend money and restore backups to do
it — gave the same answer:

```
$ groundhold probe … --fail-key probe:db --json
{ "status": "probed", "measurements": [], "failures": [ … ], "runId": "f6399820f478" }
$ echo $?
0
```

Every attempted measurement failed, nothing was recorded, and the verb reported
`probed` with exit 0. `res.Status, res.Exit = "probed", 0` was set BEFORE the loop and
never revisited: the status described the fact that a run had started, not anything it
established. A script keyed on the exit code — which is the reason the machine field
exists — reads that as a successful probe.

The downstream core was never fooled: no observation was written, so a constraint
resting on probe evidence stays `unknown` and blocks, and `probe.failed` is recorded
rather than an observation (D59, and correct). But the verb's own answer was wrong, and
the field's incident is precisely a gate keyed on a probe's own answer.

Three disjoint statuses now, computed from what the run actually produced:

- `probed` — every attempted measurement produced a reading. Exit 0.
- `partial` — some measured, some failed. Exit 2. The failed paths stay unknown and no
  observation was written for them; the successful half does not get to speak for the
  run.
- `unmeasured` — nothing was measured: every attempt failed, or the driver returned
  none at all. Exit 2, with the reason stated in the result.

Exit 2 for the latter two is the point rather than a side effect. A probe is expensive
and sometimes intrusive; it is run in order to learn something, so a run that learned
nothing is not a success and a run that learned half is not a complete one. The banner
follows the same reading: BLOCKED (missing knowledge), naming each unmeasured path —
not REFUSED, because the run was not refused, it happened.

`probeResult.status` published `probed | refused`, so the published closed set had no
word for either new state — the same drift D696 found in `reachability`, in the
neighbouring field. Both are now gated by ONE test over a table of (schema location →
the closed set the owning package exports). The first version of that gate was
reachability-only; adding the probe field to it would have meant copying it, which is
how the two reachability locations drifted from the runtime to begin with.

Two conformance cases carry this. `probe-crash-is-not-an-observation` is superseded by
name — its claim about observations was right and is kept, its status expectation was
the collapse — and a new case pins `partial` across two capabilities where one probe
crashes, because a third state that only ever appears in the all-or-nothing cases is a
state nobody has tested.

## D698 — retiring a protection is not the same as switching it off

Answers: D481.

D481 raised this and deliberately did not resolve it. Resolved now, in the direction
D47 already points, and generalized past the two drivers that raised it.

`capability.security.threatdetection` is `stateful: false`. That is CORRECT — a
detector holds no data a delete would lose — and its vocabulary reasoned from there
that retirement needs no friction at all: no deletion-protection, no consent. So a
plain `converge --yes` on a contract that marks it `state: retired` switched threat
detection OFF for the region. **The absence of DATA loss is not the absence of harm**,
and statefulness was the only question anything asked.

This repository states the rule and enforces it everywhere it has been noticed: *a
protection is never auto-lifted; lifting it is an explicit prior step* (D47). It is why
a delete refuses while `deletionProtection` is on, why Aurora says "lift it explicitly
first", why D469 made S3 refuse a compliance hold. Disabling Security Command Center or
Defender as a side effect of retiring a contract does precisely what that rule forbids.

The blast radius also depends on state nobody recorded. Create adopts an already-on
control silently (MATURITY gap 10), so the retirement cannot tell "we enabled this" from
"it was on before groundhold arrived" — an operation whose reach depends on unknown
prior state must not be implicit.

**The resolution is a data marker, not a driver judgement.** `protection: true` in the
vocabulary says: deleting this removes a CONTROL rather than a resource. Two types carry
it — `capability.security.threatdetection` and `capability.security.waf`. The addons
(`gke-addon`, `aks-addon`) do not: D481 was right that for those the two readings agree.

Retiring a marked capability REFUSES, with `consent-required`, and the message names
both ways forward:

- `autonomy.allow_protection_lift: [<cap>]` — scoped to the capability, the D48 shape
  where consent names what it covers rather than being a blanket. It rides the D597
  one-list-of-keys check, so a typo in it is a load error rather than a silent
  no-grant — verified, because that check covered the new key without an edit.
- or drop the capability from the contract entirely. groundhold stops asserting it and
  the control stays ON; `posture` then reports it as unmanaged, which is TRUE. This is
  the "we stop asserting it" reading, and it needs no new machinery — it is what
  removing a capability already does.

**One predicate deliberately does not fail closed, and the reason matters.**
`StatefulOf` fails closed because statefulness only gates when a contract opts in
(`forbidden: delete_stateful`), so guessing costs nothing where nobody asked. This gate
always binds, so guessing "protection" would refuse EVERY retirement compiled without
vocabularies, under a message that would be false — we would not know. It reads the
declared value and nothing else. The premise that makes that safe is checked rather
than believed: every capability type in the closed v0.1 set has a vocabulary (all 56),
the set is compiled into the binary, and a new gate holds that true — a type with no
vocabulary is typed by nothing and would skip this check in silence.

Adding the key found a dual divergence that had been sitting since D597. The runtime
learned then to check EVERY consent list that names capabilities from one list of keys;
the reference never did — it checked `allow_replace_stateful` alone. So a typo in
`allow_intrusive_probes`, the list that SPENDS (an intrusive probe restores a backup
into a scratch instance), loaded CLEAN in the reference and REFUSED in the runtime.
Nothing caught it because no case exercised that key dually. Both are fixed and both
keys now carry a dual case: a document one implementation accepts and the other rejects
breaks the dual guarantee as surely as a hash divergence does.

One thing this cost, worth recording because it will happen again: the machine `code`
for a plan refusal is derived by SUBSTRING-MATCHING the refusal prose in
`planRefusalCode`. A new refusal therefore carries NO code until someone adds a clause,
and nothing says so — the conformance case asserting `code: consent-required` is what
caught it here. That is the case doing its job, and it is also a shape worth replacing
with typed refusals: a machine contract derived from a human sentence is one rewording
away from silence.

## D699 — the repair that could never run again after one `kubectl label`

Answers: D509.

D509 raised this from a live cluster and left it open. Kubernetes server-side apply
refuses with 409 when another field manager holds a field we declare, and groundhold
fails closed. That is right by default — forcing would let it stomp a legitimate
controller, which is the whole reason SSA refuses. But `kubectl label` is the most
common way a real cluster drifts, and after one, converge could never correct that
field again: the repair was permanently blocked, and the refusal told the operator to
"release it first" with no supported way to do so.

Resolved along D48's line: consent that names what it covers. `autonomy.allow_field_reclaim:
[<cap>]` permits ONE thing — when an apply is refused for field ownership, re-send the
SAME patch with `force=true`. What that takes is narrow by construction rather than by
promise: an apply patch carries exactly the fields the mapping declares, so forcing it
takes those and nothing else. There is no call in this driver that forces a broader
object, and `ssaApplyAt` still sends `force=false` always, so a conflict always comes
back as a 409 for someone to decide about.

**The reclaim records whose fields it took.** The 409 body names the manager and every
path it holds ("conflict with \"kubectl-label\" using v1: .metadata.labels.pod-security")
— D509 already made that detail survive into the refusal, and it is now the record of
what was reclaimed, carried in the succeeded result's reason. A reclaim nobody can audit
would be worse than the block it replaces.

**The consent is SEALED, not re-derived at apply.** The compiler stamps
`fieldReclaim` on the update action, so it enters the plan hash: granting the consent
after sealing produces a DIFFERENT plan rather than quietly changing what an existing
one does. The executor sets it on the driver per action through a new optional
interface (`provider.FieldReclaimer`, the same shape as `Claimer` and
`ProgressReporter`) and CLEARS it afterwards, so a grant can never leak onto the next
action. The driver's field is unexported: the only way to arm it is the setter, so
there is no field a caller can set at construction and forget.

The test carries both halves, and the second one earned its keep immediately: the first
draft of the fixture used the wrong ownership label, so the no-consent case refused at
the ownership pre-read, never reached the conflict, and PASSED. It now asserts that an
apply patch was actually sent and that the refusal names the conflict — a refusal for
the wrong reason is not the refusal under test.

## D700 — the first of the "ours by construction" writes now reads

Answers: D526.

D526 measured a claim four drivers make in comments — *a resource at our name is ours
by construction* — and found it unearned: the deterministic name hashes environment and
capability and carries no estate identity, so two groundhold deployments over one
account compute the SAME name. The claim is about a name, and the name is computable by
anyone. D526 recorded it rather than fixing it, because changing the name's inputs
changes every providerId and every recorded plan hash.

The name stays. What changes is the reasoning that rested on it: `aws/cloudwatchdash`
READS before writing.

A dashboard carries no tags, so ownership cannot be read from one — which is why this
was the hard case and why it stayed unfixed. But the dashboard itself can be read, and
that answers the only question that matters at a create: if what stands at that name is
byte-identical to what we would write, overwriting changes nothing and binding it is
safe. That is D525's identity-from-content reasoning applied to content actually read
rather than asserted. Three outcomes, all of them measured:

- absent → create, as before;
- present and identical → bind it, mutate NOTHING;
- present and different → `unknown`, refusing to overwrite a dashboard this contract did
  not author, and saying why the collision is possible at all.

An unreadable estate is `unknown` too: a write at a computable name cannot be shown to
be safe when the read gave no answer.

**Three fixtures were lying, and each lie flattered the code.**

The shared dashboard fixture answered `GetDashboard` with HTTP 200 and an EMPTY body
before anything had been put — a dashboard that exists and is empty, which is a
different world from an absent one. Nothing had noticed because nothing read.

The adopt probe's fixture served `{"widgets":[{},{}]}` — a STRANGER's dashboard — while
the probe's own doc comment says it is "a fake in which the resource this create targets
already exists AND carries this runtime's ownership markers". The probe passed anyway,
because the create never looked. It serves the body this contract would write now, and
the allowance dropped from one mutation to ZERO: a dashboard that already is what the
contract describes is bound without a single write, which is the property in its
strongest form.

The request classifier counted `GetDashboard` as a MUTATION — it knew `Describe` and
`List` and not `Get` — so the first honest run reported both "no read of the estate" and
"sent 1 mutation" about a create that had read once and written nothing. A classifier
that mislabels a read accuses the driver of the opposite of what it did.

`aws/cloudwatchdash` leaves the `knownNoAdoptRead` register by the register's own rule:
the debt list must shrink when the debt does. Four entries remain — `aws/cwlogfilter`,
`aws/cloudtrail`, `azure/activitylog`, `azure/consumptionbudget` — each a create that
writes at a name of exactly this kind without reading. They are named here rather than
waved through: the shape of the fix is now demonstrated, and what is left is work, not
an open question.

## D701 — the vocabulary had no closed key set, and the best prose in it was invisible

Twelve attributes across nine vocabularies carry a `note:` — and it holds the sharpest
writing in the whole vocabulary set:

```
network.publicExposure:
  note: static verification proves configuration intent; an outcome probe
        (anonymous GET attempt) proves the actual absence of public reads.
```

That is the distinction this project exists to make, written down at the exact place an
author needs it, and **no reader has ever seen a word of it.** The vocabulary loader
took the keys it knew and dropped the rest in silence. `explain` prints kind, enum,
description, verification and mappings; `note` was not on the list, so it loaded and
did nothing.

This repository refuses exactly this shape everywhere else — an operand no driver reads
is refused rather than dropped (D530), an unknown top-level key in a contract or
candidate is a load error (D673) — for the reason that applies here word for word: a
key that loads and does nothing is indistinguishable, to its author, from one that
works.

So the vocabulary document gets a closed key set too, in BOTH implementations, at the
document level (`capability`, `version`, `stateful`, `protection`, `attributes`) and per
attribute (`kind`, `description`, `mappings`, `evidence`, `verification`, `enum`,
`recommended`, `note`, `unordered`). The entry condition for a key is that something
consumes it: `kind`/`enum` type candidate values, `description`/`verification`/`note`/
`mappings` are published by `explain`, `evidence` classifies at the boundary (D311),
`recommended` drives `suggest`, `unordered` makes a list a set, `stateful` and
`protection` gate deletes (D47/D698). `note` is on that list because it now HAS a
consumer — `explain` prints it — not because it was grandfathered.

Nine of 340 shipped attributes carried no `description`, so `explain` answered with a
kind, a mapping list, and nothing that said what the attribute MEANS. All nine are
written, and a gate holds the set at zero.

One boundary drawn deliberately. The closed KEY SET is enforced at load, for anyone's
document: a dropped key is a defect whoever wrote it. "Every attribute is documented" is
a gate over `spec/vocab` only, because `--vocab` extends the built-in set with a
reader's own types, and refusing to LOAD someone's undocumented-but-valid file would be
a much heavier claim than the one being made. The first draft put both in the loader and
a fixture caught it immediately — a minimal test vocabulary is a legitimate document,
and a rule about what THIS project publishes had no business refusing it.

## D702 — the published mapping said which service realises the attribute, and 42 of them named nothing

`mappings:` is the line an operator follows. It says WHICH driver service realises an
attribute on a cloud, and D534 treats that as authoritative: read
`aws.backup: recovery point retention`, write `service: backup` into a candidate. D669
measured the token half against the drivers and found 42 keys naming a service token
that does not exist — the gate it added is a RATCHET, because the harm is a wasted
round trip rather than a wrong action (following one gives `preflight exit 2`, loud
rather than silent).

Paid down to 11, by asking the drivers what each capability's token actually is
(D317 — `ServiceCapabilities()`, never a guess) and renaming the key to it. Thirty-one
distinct pairs, 130 keys across 24 vocabularies:

```
aws.backup           -> aws.backupplan / aws.backupvault
gcp.pubsub           -> gcp.pubsub-queue / gcp.pubsub-topic
azure.monitor        -> azure.metricalert / azure.scheduledquery
gcp.logging          -> gcp.logbucket / gcp.logmetric
azure.vm/vmss/image  -> azure.azvm / azure.azvmss / azure.azimage
aws.wafv2            -> aws.waf
azure.portal         -> azure.portaldash
gcp.computeengine    -> gcp.gce
…
```

A rename was made only where the driver serves that capability under exactly ONE token,
so nothing was guessed at and no ambiguous case was touched. No collisions: not one
renamed key already existed on its attribute.

**The 11 that remain are a different thing, and the number stops there rather than at
zero for a stated reason.** They sit on two capability types NO driver builds —
`capability.ai.speech`, where all three clouds are `unbuilt`, and
`capability.identity.sso` on GCP and Azure. There is no real token to rename them to,
because there is no service. `explain` already answers UNBUILT for such a type (D691),
which is the honest reading of those lines: a recorded design intent, not a route an
operator can take today. They come down when a driver does.

## D703 — the index that tells the next author what is open was itself out of date

Three of the instructions file's open questions were answered in one session — D481 by D698, D509
by D699, D526 by D700 — and the file went on listing all three as open, under the
heading *"do not resolve unilaterally — flag them"*.

The decision record was correct and complete the whole time. The record is append-only
and 700 entries long; the INDEX is what a reader consults first, and nothing connected
the two. So the next author to open this repository would have been told not to resolve
three questions that had been resolved that morning, and to treat as live a hazard
already gated — which is the same failure this project keeps paying down in its
published material, aimed at itself.

MATURITY gap 11 had the sharper version of it. It said the posture problem was "raised
as an open question in the instructions file rather than settled in a driver" — no longer true —
while the OWNERSHIP half beside it (a create cannot tell "we enabled this" from "it was
already on") is genuinely still open. One paragraph carrying one true half and one
false half is worse than either, because a reader who checks one sentence trusts the
next.

Both are corrected, and the correction is now checkable. An entry that resolves an open
question writes `Answers: Dxxx.` on its own line — a link machine-findable in the
direction it is needed, from the answer back to the question — and
`TestAnsweredQuestionsAreNotStillListedAsOpen` walks it: if the instructions file still presents
that question as open, it must say ANSWERED in the same breath. The gate deliberately
does not check the reverse (an open question with no answer is just an open question),
and it says nothing about whether the answer is any good.

## D704 — the agent-facing surface answered over the top of the verb

Two defects on the MCP server, which is the boundary an autonomous agent reads. Both
are the same shape: a second opinion published beside a first-hand answer.

**A verdict reported as a refusal.** Every tool result carried

```go
payload["status"] = map[int]string{0: "ok", 1: "structural-error", 2: "refused", …}[code]
```

`verify` exits 2 when a hard constraint is violated or unknown. That is a VERDICT — the
tool ran, measured, and reported — and the agent was told `status: "refused"`, which
says the tool declined to act. The two call for different next moves: a refusal is
fixed by changing the invocation, a violated constraint by changing the candidate. The
tool's own description tells the agent *"unknown/unverifiable on hard constraints
blocks — that is the system working, never route around it"*, and then the status field
contradicted it.

The verbs answer this themselves. They emit a machine `status` (`applied`, `converged`,
`probed`, `partial`, `unmeasured`, `adopted`, `refused`…) and a `code` when they refuse;
`verify` emits `executable`, a boolean saying whether its verdicts let execution
proceed. `execStatus` reads those and falls back to the exit code only when there is no
JSON to read — so a probe that measured nothing now reaches an agent as `unmeasured`
(D697) instead of "refused", and a not-proven candidate as `not-proven`.

**And a map lookup with no default.** An exit code outside 0..5 produced the empty
string, because that is what a Go map returns for a missing key — the discarded-`ok`
shape wearing a different hat, in a machine field. Latent for the currently exposed
verbs, and now impossible: an unrecognised code is reported AS unrecognised.

**The second defect is a closed set kept in two copies.** `groundhold_observe`
published `fake|aws|gcp|azure|k8s`. `groundhold_apply`, twenty lines below it in the
same file, published `fake|gcp` — so an agent reading the schema for the verb that
MUTATES believed AWS, Azure and Kubernetes were out of reach, on a surface whose reader
is a machine that cannot ask. One constant now, and a gate requiring every
provider-taking schema to name every driver.

That makes three closed sets in one day published in a shape that did not match the
runtime — `reachability` (D696), `probeResult.status` (D697), and this one. The
pattern is not that any of them was written carelessly; it is that a set with two
homes has no home.

## D705 — the refusals the agent surface raised itself had nothing to route on

`website/pages/mcp.md` promises *"refusals pass through structurally, never
summarized"*, and the project's machine contract is *"route on the process exit code
and the JSON `code` field, never on banner text"* (D64: the code IS the contract;
reasons are prose and are never parsed).

Both hold for refusals FORWARDED from the CLI — the verb's own result carries its own
code, and D704 just made the server report that answer rather than a guess. Neither
held for the five refusals the server raises ITSELF:

```
apply is disabled: set GROUNDHOLD_MCP_ALLOW_APPLY=1 to enable
unknown confirm_token — request a fresh confirmation
confirm_token expired — the human must see the decision again
plan changed since confirmation (sha256:… != sha256:…) — re-confirm
the apply target changed since confirmation — re-confirm for this target
```

Every one of them, `{"status": "refused", "reasons": [...]}` and nothing else. An agent
deciding between *ask for a fresh confirmation*, *show the changed plan to a human* and
*this server does not offer apply at all* had only English to route on — on the one
surface whose reader is a machine that cannot ask a follow-up question.

No new codes were needed, which is itself the check on the reading. The four token
refusals are `confirmation-required`, whose registry remediation already says
"Confirm interactively, pass --yes, or **complete the MCP two-step**" — written for
exactly this. A server started without the apply tool answers `unsupported-operation`:
this server genuinely does not offer that operation, and the reason line says how to
enable it.

Gated by a scan over the server's own source: a `"status": "refused"` literal must
carry a `"code":` before the composite ends. Static rather than behavioural because two
of the five need a server state a unit test cannot reach cheaply, and the shape is
uniform and small — with a floor so a broken scan cannot pass, and a positive control
proving the detector can see a bare refusal.

## D706 — twelve ways to say something went wrong, on the surface that cannot ask

D705 gave the server's refusals a machine code. Looking at the neighbours of those five
showed why the gate had found so few: TWELVE other sites answered `status: "error"`,
and none of them called itself a refusal, so nothing was looking at them.

`error` appears in no published set — not in the CLI's status vocabulary, not in the
output schema, nowhere. And it covered three different things at once:

- **refusals**: a missing required argument, a path escaping the workspace, an operand
  that looks like a flag, an unknown tool name, an empty draft;
- **the server's own environment failing**: it could not create the drafts directory,
  could not write the file, could not read entropy for a confirmation token.

Half of them carried `error: "<string>"` and half `reasons: [...]` — two payload shapes
for one thing, which is two things to a machine reader.

Refusals now say `refused` and carry a code, which puts them under D705's gate rather
than beside it. The three that are NOT refusals say `failed`, and carry **no** code
deliberately: no registry code describes the tool's own environment failing, and
inventing one to satisfy a gate would be the worse mistake — the field would be filled
with something untrue. That boundary is written into the gate and onto the published
page, so the next reader meets it as a decision rather than an omission.

The MCP page now states what an agent routes on, which it never did: `status` is the
verb's own answer when there is one, `refused` always carries a code, `failed` never
does and says why not.

## D707 — one witness, two capabilities, and a report that said nothing about it

`survey` compares a code survey against a contract, and `--complete` is the mode where
an operator asserts "these surveys are the whole system" so that a capability nobody
witnesses hardens into drift. That is the mode you run to find the database nobody uses
anymore — cost, and attack surface.

A finding names a capability TYPE. So with two capabilities of one type:

```go
case len(capsByType[f.CapabilityHint]) > 0:
    row.Capability = capsByType[f.CapabilityHint][0]   // the first, alphabetically
    for _, id := range capsByType[f.CapabilityHint] {
        witnessed[id] = true                            // …but ALL of them
    }
```

one repo witnessing one database silences BOTH `db-orders` and `db-billing`, and the
report says nothing about either. The operator asks "does anything still use
db-billing?" and gets, in effect, yes-by-association.

**This was deliberate and pinned by a test**, and the reason it was right is worth
keeping: marking only the alphabetically-first capability witnessed would invent a
distinction the evidence does not carry, and hardening the others into drift would
accuse every contract with two capabilities of one type and a single witnessing repo —
a confident accusation, which this project refuses everywhere else. So the verdict is
UNCHANGED: still witnessed, still no drift.

What changes is that the report stops being silent about the one case its evidence
cannot settle. Each such capability is reported **witnessed-by-type** — information,
sitting beside `unwitnessed` and `orphaned` — so an operator running `--complete`
sees "nothing sighted this one individually; a sibling of its type was" instead of
seeing nothing. A single capability of its type is unambiguous and is not reported,
so the new row cannot become noise on every contract; a test pins that silence too.

Smaller than its neighbours in this run, and named as such: nothing here was lying.
The report was answering a question it had not been asked ("is this type used?") in
place of the one it was ("is this capability used?"), and the difference was invisible.

## D708 — six callers, one three-valued answer, three of them counting to two

`LoadSnapshotFile` has always answered three ways: absent is `(nil, nil)`, unreadable
is `(nil, err)`, present is `(snap, nil)`. Three of its six callers wrote

```go
if snap, err := LoadSnapshotFile(SnapshotPath(p)); err == nil && snap != nil { … }
```

**One of the three is live, and the correction matters more than the finding.** My
first reading of this code claimed all three were reachable harms. Measuring each one
said otherwise:

- **`runstatus` — LIVE.** `runs`, `status` and `wait` read through `ReadEventsFull`
  WITHOUT replaying first, so the fold was reached: an unreadable sidecar meant the
  archived pre-compaction events were simply not read, and a run recorded before the
  compaction answered "no such run" — an absence manufactured from a file nobody could
  open.
- **`backup` — LATENT.** It refuses a compacted ledger because capsule DR and
  compaction are mutually exclusive (D313), and that refusal did not fire on an
  unreadable sidecar. But `ReplayFile` runs FIRST and fails closed on exactly this, so
  the capsules were never emitted. The fold was real; the harm was already caught by a
  neighbour.
- **`attest` — LATENT**, for the same reason: `ReplayExisting` refuses before the
  snapshot facts are assembled. Had it not, an attestation whose entire job is to be
  evidence would have silently omitted a compaction it could not parse.

Both latent sites are fixed anyway — defence in depth, the shape D188 already uses —
and both are now honest about which guard is holding. Writing "three live defects"
would have been the easier sentence and the false one.

The other three callers (`replay`, `capsule`, `repair`) refuse on the error and always
did. Same predicate, six readings, split three to three — which is the shape this
record keeps naming: a meaning with more than one home has none.

`SnapshotStateOf` returns `absent | present | unreadable` so the third answer has a
name a caller must look at, and each of the three sites now says what it found:
`backup` refuses while the file is unreadable, `attest` records
`unreadable: true` with the reason, `runstatus` returns the error instead of a
shortened history.

**The gate bans the idiom, not the outcome**, because the idiom is what travels: a
regex over every `LoadSnapshotFile` call site rejecting `err == nil &&`. And it earned
its own lesson immediately. The first pattern was `LoadSnapshotFile\([^)]*\)…`, which
cannot cross the nested paren every real call has — `LoadSnapshotFile(SnapshotPath(p))`
— so it matched NOTHING, while its positive control passed, because the example the
control fed it was `LoadSnapshotFile(p)`: simpler than any line in the tree. **A
positive control that is easier than reality proves only that the detector can match
its own example.** The control now uses the shape the code actually has, and the
negative control — reintroducing the fold in `backup` — fails the gate by file and
line.

## D709 — a damaged anchor disarmed the trust it exists to carry

The twin of D708, on the neighbouring loader, and the consequence is not visibility but
trust.

D135 put a trust policy inside the anchor so that *the receiver's held artifact brings
the policy — forgetting `--trust` no longer downgrades anything*. Every verb that takes
a `--ledger` loads the anchor beside it and applies that policy:

```go
if a, err := ledger.LoadAnchorFile(ledger.AnchorPath(ledgerPath)); err == nil && a != nil {
    ledger.ApplyAnchorPolicy(a)
}
```

`LoadAnchorFile` returns an error for a MISSING file and for a CORRUPT one alike, so
`err == nil` reads them identically. A damaged anchor therefore took the absent path:
no trusted keys added, no `trustFrom` cutoff set, signature verification never armed —
**events the policy required to be signed accepted unsigned, on every verb, silently.**
The exact downgrade D135 was written to prevent, triggered by a damaged file instead of
a forgotten flag.

`AnchorStateOf` answers `absent | present | unreadable`, the same shape D708 gave the
snapshot, and the call site refuses on the third: running under a policy we cannot read
is not something to do quietly.

`attest` also records `status: "unreadable"` with the reason instead of leaving the
anchor facts empty — but measured through the CLI, that branch does not run: `attest`
takes `--ledger`, so the global guard above refuses first and no report is produced at
all. Defence in depth, and stated as such rather than advertised as a feature. The
correction came from testing the advice: a draft delivery note told the operator to run
`groundhold attest` and read `anchor.status`, and running it showed a refusal instead.
**Advice is a claim too** — this one was checked before it went out, unlike the class
D692 exists for.

Both halves are pinned, and the second matters as much as the first: **an absent anchor
must still be fine.** A ledger with no anchor carries no policy to lose, and turning
that into a refusal would break every ordinary run to fix a rare damaged file. Absent
and unreadable are different answers — that is the whole entry, twice over.

## D710 — the pin that omits itself, twenty lines from the one that refuses

`CheckAnchor` compares the snapshot pin **only when it is non-empty**:

```go
if a.SnapshotHash != "" && led.snapshotHash != a.SnapshotHash { … diverged … }
```

So an anchor written without that pin is not a weaker anchor with a warning — it is an
anchor whose swapped-fold detection silently does not run. It still catches a rewritten
tail; it says nothing at all about a fold replaced underneath it, which is the specific
attack the pin exists for (D137).

Compaction wrote exactly that anchor whenever hashing failed:

```go
anchor := BuildAnchor(led)
if h, err := HashSnapshot(doc); err == nil {
    anchor.SnapshotHash = h
}
```

two lines under a comment promising *"pinning the fold hash so a swapped snapshot is
detectable"* — and **twenty lines under `previousSnapshotHash`**, which does the same
kind of work and reads:

```go
h, err := HashSnapshot(prevDoc)
if err != nil {
    return nil, nil, err   // never swallow: previousSnapshotHash must be honest
}
```

One file, one kind of pin, two opposite readings, and the honest one had already
written down why. Both refuse now.

The ledger side of the same pin (`replay`) had the milder version: a hash failure left
`led.snapshotHash` empty, which makes `CheckAnchor` report DIVERGED against any anchor
that HAS a pin. Fail-closed, but with a reason that accuses a swap when the truth is
that the fold could not be hashed — an alarm naming the wrong cause is a bad alarm. It
returns the error instead.

The gate holds the SHAPE — no `HashSnapshot` call may sit behind `err == nil` — because
that shape is what travelled between the two sites, and the next integrity pin will be
written by someone who read one of them.

## D711 — the recovery verb had a window where the ledger did not exist

`repair --quarantine` is the verb that runs AFTER corruption: it cuts the bad tail,
preserves the whole file aside, and puts the valid prefix back. It did that with two
renames:

```go
os.WriteFile(tmp, prefix, 0o600)
os.Rename(path, qpath)   // history aside — the ledger path is now EMPTY
os.Rename(tmp, path)     // prefix in
```

Between those two lines there is no file at the ledger path. And a missing ledger
replays as an EMPTY one — deliberately, so a first converge can create one
(`ReplayFile` treats `IsNotExist` as a fresh ledger). So a crash in that window hands
the next converge an empty history for a full estate: every capability unbound, every
action a create. That is D253's named cost — *"a second VPC, a second paid key, and
neither one in the ledger"* — reached through the verb whose entire job is to recover
from corruption.

The window closes by LINKING rather than renaming: the preserved copy appears while
the original stays in place, so the path never lacks a file, and the rename that
follows swaps the prefix over it atomically. The temp file is written with `fsync` and
the directory synced after each step, which is what compaction already does one file
over — the helpers existed; this path simply never used them.

**The test earned the entry's real lesson.** The first one asserted the end state:
after a quarantine, both files exist and the preserved copy holds the cut lines. It
passed against the very `os.Rename` it was written to forbid, because with either
ordering everything is in place once the function RETURNS. The property lives in the
window, and a window is not observable without a fault hook. So the shape that creates
it is banned instead: the ledger path may never be the source of a rename in this file.
The end-state test stays — it proves the history is preserved rather than destroyed —
but it is no longer asked to prove the thing it cannot see.

## D712 — two builds agreed with each other, and both were wrong

The delivery discipline for a client binary includes: build twice, compare, ship only
if the bytes are identical. That check has an unstated premise — **from a clean tree** —
and nothing enforced it.

Preparing v0.1.9 I started the mutation meter in a worktree and then, in that same
worktree, ran the two release builds. The meter injects a mutant, runs a test, restores
the file, and moves to the next; both builds landed inside the same mutant window. They
were byte-identical to each other, the check passed, and the artifact carried an
injected bug. The manifest was already written with its sha256.

It was caught by accident. A docs-only correction moved the delivery commit, I rebuilt
in a fresh worktree to show the binary was unchanged, and the hash did not match. Three
builds settled it: a clean tree at the old commit and a clean tree at the new one both
produce `80b5a8ba…`; the contaminated pair produced `73b7e5d8…`.

**"Two independent builds agree" is a claim about independence, and two builds from one
mutated tree are not independent.** The agreement was real and meaningless — the same
shape as a gate whose subject is empty, or a positive control easier than the code.

`scripts/release-build.sh` now produces the claim and checks the premise in one place:
it REFUSES on a dirty working tree, naming the files — the first thing it refused was
itself, untracked — then builds twice, compares, and runs the client-name check the
manifest asserts rather than leaving it to be remembered. A manifest line saying the
build is byte-reproducible is now the output of a tool that cannot produce it unless
the premise holds.

Nothing shipped: the contaminated binary never left the scratch directory. But it was
one rebuild away from going out, and that rebuild happened for an unrelated reason.

## D713 — every workflow a stranger can trigger ran on our own machine

`ci.yml`, `lint.yml` and `security.yml` trigger on `pull_request`, and all fourteen of
their Linux jobs ran on the self-hosted pool — a persistent runner with our network and our disk. On a PUBLIC repository that means a stranger's pull request
executes their code there.

Nothing was exposed: the repository is private, so only collaborators can open a PR.
The point is the distance to exposure. **Opening the repo is a settings flip** — no
line of code changes, no gate fires, nothing says a word — and the machinery for
accepting outside contributions (CONTRIBUTING, DCO, issue and PR templates, a
governance promise) is already written and inviting.

D383 moved this pool to self-hosted deliberately, when the organisation's Actions
budget hit 100% and the release path went down with it. That is the right answer for a
private repository. It is the wrong one for a public repository, and the reason the fix
costs nothing is the same fact from the other side: **GitHub-hosted runners are free
for public repositories**, so the case that needs them is exactly the case that gets
them free.

Every fork-triggerable job now selects its runner:

```yaml
runs-on: ${{ (github.event_name == 'pull_request' &&
  github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository)
  && 'ubuntu-latest' || '<the self-hosted label>' }}
```

A fork PR goes to a hosted runner; a push, or a PR from a branch in this repository,
keeps the fleet. `pull_request_target` is not used and must not be — it runs untrusted
code in the base repository's context, which is the same hole with the safety label on.

The expression is repeated in fourteen jobs rather than shared through a `needs` edge
on every one of them, and that repetition is only safe because a gate holds it: in a
workflow reachable by `pull_request`, every `runs-on` must be a hosted label or carry
the guard. This is the same trade as every other repeated closed set in this record —
copies are allowed exactly when something checks them.

**The change walked past two mechanisms built for exactly it, and a third accused the
wrong entry.** All three were found in the ten minutes after the fix, and they are the
more useful half of this decision.

The exporter rewrites a self-hosted `runs-on:` to the hosted default before publishing,
because a public tree asking for a pool that does not exist there queues forever — "a
permanently pending check says nothing while looking like it is about to". Its pattern
anchored the label at END of line. My jobs now say
`runs-on: ${{ … || '<label>' }}`, so the rewrite silently did nothing, and the
assertion beside it — anchored the same way — passed. The public tree would have
carried fourteen jobs waiting on a runner nobody offers. **A guard matches a SHAPE, and
the fix changed the shape.** Both now match the label anywhere in the value.

The new gate spelled the pool's label in its own source. Go tests are exported and the
exporter is not, so the gate would have been the disclosure it exists to prevent — a
sentence the neighbouring estate gate already carries, having been that leak once. The
export audit refused, by file and line, on the first run. The label is now read from
the exporter's denylist, which is also why the two ends cannot drift.

And the estate gate that caught it had been checking the wrong subject for months: its
heading pattern was `^## D\d+\.` — with a DOT — while entries have been written
`## D123 — title` for hundreds of decisions. Everything since that style change was one
undivided blob attributed to the last dot-style heading, so the first entry to trip it
accused a decision 260 entries earlier. **A per-entry gate whose entries are wrong is
not a per-entry gate**, and it produced a false accusation before it produced a true
one.

What this does NOT do, stated so it is not mistaken for done: it does not make the
repository ready to accept community pull requests. Two things are still missing —
the return path (a change merged on the public repo has no documented way back into the
private tree the export is generated FROM), and branch protection with CODEOWNERS,
which cannot be applied until the repository is public. Those are the next two slices.

## D714 — the publish path had no way back, and nothing noticed

`D345` fixed the direction that mattered first: change and validate in the private
tree, scrub through the exporter, push a BRANCH to the public repository, merge by PR,
never push public `main`. Fourteen syncs have gone that way.

It says nothing about a change that originates on the PUBLIC side — which is the only
kind that exists once anyone else contributes. The private tree is the source of truth
and the export is GENERATED from it, so the next sync overwrites the public tree
wholesale. A merged community pull request would have been erased by the following
sync, silently, with the contributor's commit still visible in the history and its
content gone.

Nothing could have detected it either. The only record of where a public tree came from
was the commit SUBJECT — "Sync from upstream: …" — and this project routes on prose
nowhere else.

Two pieces, and the small one carries the weight:

**The export writes `.github/sync-source`**, naming the private commit it came from.
That makes the question mechanical: the commit that last wrote that file is the last
sync, and everything after it on the public side came from someone else. (Not under
`.groundhold/` — that path is gitignored, so the marker would have existed on disk and
never in the history, which is not a record.)

**`scripts/sync-public.sh` refuses rather than resolves.** It stops on a dirty private
tree (D712), then lists the public commits after the marker and REFUSES if there are
any, naming them: *replay each one in the private tree first — they touch exported
paths by construction — then run this again, and the diff disappears because the
private tree already contains the change.* Automating the merge would be the wrong
answer; a refusal that names what it would have destroyed is the right one.

It does not push. Pushing is outward-facing and stays a human act, as it already was.

This does not open the repository to contributions — it removes the reason not to. What
remains before that is branch protection with CODEOWNERS, dormant until the repository
is public, and a reviewer's checklist that does not repeat what the gates already
check.

## D715 — the one contributor obligation that rested on memory

`CONTRIBUTING.md` tells every prospective contributor: *"A PR whose commits are not
signed off cannot be merged."* Nothing read a commit trailer. No workflow, no gate —
the only thing between an unsigned commit and `main` was a maintainer remembering, on
a repository that has never had an outside pull request to forget about.

The DCO is not paperwork here. It stands in for a CLA under the never-relicense promise
in `GOVERNANCE.md`: no copyright assignment, and in exchange each contributor certifies
they wrote what they sent. A promise of that shape, enforced by memory, is enforced by
nobody on the day it matters.

`.github/workflows/dco.yml` checks every non-merge commit in a pull request for a
well-formed `Signed-off-by`, and — the part a trailer-grep usually misses — that the
sign-off is the AUTHOR's own. A sign-off typed in someone else's name is not a
certification, it is a claim about a third party. The remediation is printed with the
exact command (`git rebase --signoff`), because a rule that stops a contribution
without saying how to satisfy it is a wall, not a standard.

Its runner selection is the same expression as every other fork-triggerable job (D713),
and that reconciliation is worth recording: the D383 gate refuses to spend hosted
minutes on an ordinary run, while D713 requires a fork's PR to stay off the fleet. Both
hold — a fork goes hosted (free on a public repository), a branch in this repository
stays on the fleet. The first draft picked a side, and the older gate caught it.

**`docs/REVIEWING.md`** is the other half. CONTRIBUTING says what a contributor does;
nothing said what a reviewer looks at — so a review would have re-run, by hand, what
seven workflows already prove. The page names those explicitly and tells the reviewer
NOT to repeat them, then lists what only a person can decide: whether the conformance
case pins the intended behaviour rather than some behaviour, whether the fix is at the
mechanism or the instance, whether the change widens a published claim without a gate,
whether the DESIGN entry argues instead of re-litigating, and whether missing knowledge
is answered with `unknown` rather than a default that reads as success.

It also carries the settings to apply when the repository becomes public — branch
protection, required checks, outside-collaborator approval, the dormant integrations —
as a list to flip rather than a thing to remember. Written where the reviewer is, not
in a maintainer's head.

Two links in that page pointed at files the export does not carry, and the doc gate
refused: the hunting method and the sync script are private. The fix was to say the
thing rather than link it — a published page that depends on a private path is a page
that is only true where nobody needs it.

## D716 — what a code freeze admits, decided before the first thing tests it

The runtime enters a code freeze. The rule, agreed rather than improvised, is that the
freeze admits exactly one class of change:

**A defect where the tool says something FALSE about reality, in the dangerous
direction.** D694 is the shape: a publicly reachable function reported as private, so a
contract reads as satisfied while the door stands open. D709 is the other: a corrupt
anchor silently arming no trust policy, so events the policy required to be signed were
accepted unsigned. In both, acting on the tool's answer is worse than having no tool.

Everything else waits and is recorded: missing visibility (D707), published debt
(D702), an ungated claim (D715), a latent fold nobody can reach (the `attest` halves of
D708 and D709). These are real and none of them makes the runtime lie about a live
estate.

The rule is written down now, before the first finding tests it, because a freeze
decided case-by-case is not a freeze — the first interesting defect argues its own way
in, and the second one cites the first. The distinction to apply is not severity and
not effort: it is whether a person acting on what the tool said would be worse off than
if the tool had said nothing.

Field work continues through the freeze and is the reason it can hold. Adoption against
a real estate reads and binds; it does not require the runtime to change. What it
produces is evidence, which is the input the next unfreeze should be spent on — and the
measurement that argued for this order is in the week's own numbers: the days with the
most contact with a live account produced the sharpest defects, and the day with none
produced the most entries about my own instruments.

## D717 — a delete addressed to a route AWS does not have, and the two services the gate was watching

D694 was a driver reading a Lambda route that does not exist: AWS answered our bad URL
with a 404, the reader took the 404 for an answer about the account, and a publicly
invokable function was observed as private. The mechanism put in against the class was
`TestLiveAWSEndpointReality` — ask real AWS, with no credentials, whether every path a
driver constructs is a path AWS actually routes. Its own comment said the pattern
"extends to every service/cloud."

It did not extend. Both of its route lists were typed by hand, so it covered EKS and
Lambda: **29 routes across 2 services** of the 40 the AWS drivers speak to. Under the
freeze the missing coverage is only debt, so the question asked was the admitted one —
is there a route out there that is actually wrong?

Asking it meant getting the routes from the drivers rather than from their source
(D317: a static scrape of these drivers gave four different wrong answers). Every AWS
request passes one funnel, `doSignedH`. A recorder on that funnel, plus one run of the
package's tests, yields what the drivers actually build: **191 routes across 39
services**. Replaying each against real AWS, unauthenticated, on the signal that
separates an unmatched route from a real one:

```
DELETE /api/v2/clusters/<arn>  ->  "Unable to determine service/operation name"
```

MSK carries two API versions and they do not cover the same verbs. Create, List and
Describe have V2 forms; **DeleteCluster has only the V1 form**. Measured, with the
controls that make the reading mean something:

| route | AWS |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/v2/clusters/<arn>` | real |
| `DELETE /v1/clusters/<arn>` | real |
| `DELETE /api/v2/clusters/<arn>` | does not exist |

The same shape as D694, one service over: two API versions, the read on the right one,
the write on a route that version does not have.

**Why this is the dangerous direction and not merely broken.** An unmatched route
answers **403**, not 404. `Classify` reads 403 as `ClassDenied`, so `deleteMSK` returns
`unknown` with the reason *"permission denied — grant the permission, then reconcile"*.
Every MSK retire fails, and the tool names a cause that is false about the account: it
says the acting identity lacks an IAM grant. A person acting on that widens IAM on a
production account to fix a URL we got wrong — and the retire still does not complete.
That is worse than saying nothing, which is the freeze's admission test.

**Why nothing saw it.** The fixture matched `r.Method == "DELETE"` and nothing else, so
