it answered 200 to a delete addressed anywhere. This is D694's second finding verbatim,
in a package that had already been taught it: a fixture that answers a request the cloud
would reject is not a double for the cloud. It matches the exact path now, and an
unexpected one fails the test by name — which is how the defect proved itself before the
route was touched.

**The mechanism, this time not a list.** `TestLiveAWSEndpointReality` no longer carries
routes. Its subject is `internal/aws/testdata/aws-routes.txt`, recorded from the funnel,
and the checked-in file is compared against a fresh recording on every unfiltered run —
so a driver that starts calling a new route cannot do it invisibly; it arrives as a
reviewable diff saying the route is unverified, not wrong. Coverage went from 29 routes
across 2 services to **191 across 40**, and a driver added tomorrow is covered without
anyone remembering this entry exists.

Three things hold that up, because each could fail silently:

- `TestTheRouteRecorderSeesWhatTheDriversBuild` — the positive control. Unwire the
  recorder and the file freezes, the comparison finds nothing to report, and the live
  gate asks about routes no driver builds. All three failures are quiet.
- `TestEveryRecordedServiceHasAHost` — the replay resolves a host per signing name, and
  an unmapped service would simply not be asked. That refusal belongs where `make check`
  can see it, not on the pre-ship box.
- The three known-wrong routes (D273, D694, D717) stay written down as negative
  controls. The drivers no longer construct them, so the recording cannot produce them,
  and without them a green run would not show the classifier still works.

The comparison is skipped for a filtered or `-short` run, where the recording is a
subset by construction and a mismatch would mean nothing.

**What this does not cover.** GCP's `TestLiveGCPEndpointReality` is still hand-listed,
and Azure has no equivalent. Both are recorded here and wait: neither is a claim that
is currently false, and the freeze admits the false ones only.

## D718 — two GCP services whose exposure could never be read, on a method Google does not route

D717 derived the AWS route-reality gate from what the drivers actually build. The same
question, asked of GCP, needed one more thing first: whether an unauthenticated probe
can even tell a missing route from a missing resource. Measured:

| cloud | signal | usable |
|---|---|---|
| AWS | an unmatched route answers "Unable to determine service/operation name" | yes |
| GCP | a real route answers 401/403; the frontend answers an unmatched one with HTML | yes |
| Azure | ARM resolves the SUBSCRIPTION before it routes | **no** |

Azure is worth stating rather than leaving as a silence. A well-formed but nonexistent
subscription short-circuits to `SubscriptionNotFound` for a real provider path and a
made-up one alike, and a made-up `api-version` changes nothing. Without an account,
this class cannot be measured on Azure at all.

On GCP the recorded set was 694 routes. Twelve existed nowhere, and after triage the
real one was a family:

```
GET  /v1/projects/p/secrets/x:getIamPolicy   -> 401   route
POST /v1/projects/p/secrets/x:getIamPolicy   -> 404   no route
```

Secret Manager and Artifact Registry were both reading — and writing — their IAM policy
under **POST**, where Google routes only GET. Five call sites. Against real GCP,
`network.publicExposure` on those two services was unreadable 100% of the time, and
`setSecretPublic`/`setSecretPrivate` and the public-grant half of an Artifact Registry
create could never succeed.

**It is not the D694 class, and that is the good news.** Both observers guard on
`err == nil` and emit a diagnostic instead of a value, so the tool never claimed a
secret was private. The absence-marker discipline held exactly where it was supposed
to. What the tool did instead was refuse to answer, forever, on a question it appeared
to support.

**Why nothing saw it.** The fixture matched `r.Method == "POST"` for `:getIamPolicy`,
so it encoded the wrong method as the truth. This is the D694 and D717 finding for the
third time in one day, and the shape is always the same: a fixture that answers a
request the cloud would reject is not a double for the cloud. It matches the method now
and an unexpected route fails the test by name.

**The gate, and an honest weakening.** `TestLiveGCPEndpointReality` carried eight GKE
paths by hand. It reads the recorded set now, like the AWS one. But GCP's test harness
points several base-URL overrides at ONE fixture server, so a recorded URL's origin
often cannot say which service it belonged to: 344 of 732 lines are ambiguous. Rather
than guess, such a line carries its candidate set and the gate accuses only when a
route exists under NONE of them. That still catches "the driver builds a path this
cloud does not have anywhere" and never accuses a driver because the harness was
vague. The predicate is weaker than the AWS one and the entry says so.

Four things had to be fixed before that gate told the truth, and all four are the same
mistake — a gate manufacturing its own evidence:

- **It accused two dozen healthy routes.** Asked naively, thousands of requests
  produced transport errors, and the classifier could not tell one from "route absent".
  Distinct requests are asked once now, and a transport failure is reported as
  unmeasured rather than counted against a driver.
- **It read every 404 as "no such route."** Cloud Storage and IAM answer an anonymous
  caller about a RESOURCE rather than demanding credentials, so every GCS path in the
  set was accused. Only a 404 carrying the frontend's HTML is an absent route.
- **The resolver was blind to package-level overrides.** Service Usage keeps its base
  in a package variable, not a Driver field, so reflection missed it and its calls were
  attributed to Artifact Registry — which the gate then accused of building Service
  Usage paths.
- **Two fixtures returned an operation name in a shape GCP never emits** (`operations/op1`
  where the API returns the full resource name). The driver polls `base + "/" + name`,
  so the recorded path was one no API routes. Same lesson as the method above.

After those, 732 routes across 4715 distinct requests: every one real, and the three
negative controls (D273's nested path, D694's Lambda policy route, D718's POST
`:getIamPolicy`) still flagged.

## D719 — a refusal that names one mistake at a time, over a vocabulary it is holding

The second tester's first report. A contract using 21 capability types was refused:

```
contract error: unknown capability type: capability.security.detection
```

Two of the 21 were wrong, and the reporter found the second one themselves, by reading
the vocabulary. Two things are wrong with that sentence.

**It stops at the first.** A contract with two mistakes costs two runs to discover, and
for the machine-first medium this project argues for, an agent pays the same round
trips a person does.

**It names what is wrong without naming what is right.** The vocabulary is CLOSED —
57 types — and the loader is holding it at the moment it refuses. Sending the reader
away to find a list the tool has in its hand is the D693 shape: advice that cannot be
acted on.

Both halves are local. The type check accumulates instead of returning, and the refusal
names every unknown type with the known types nearest to it by edit distance:

```
contract error: 2 unknown capability types
  capability.network.firewall
    closest known types: capability.network.private, capability.network.loadbalancer, capability.audit.trail
  capability.security.detection
    closest known types: capability.security.threatdetection, capability.security.waf, capability.audit.trail
  the vocabulary is closed and has 57 types; `groundhold explain <capability.type>` describes one
```

It says "closest known types", not "did you mean". For `security.detection` the right
answer is first; for `network.firewall` the right answer is `security.waf`, which no
string metric could find — and the list still tells the reader that
`capability.network.*` has no firewall in it, which is the fact they needed.

**Both implementations, byte for byte.** A refusal whose advice differs between the Go
runtime and the Python reference is two tools, so the edit distance and the tie-break
(lowest distance, then lexicographic) are the same in both.

**And the case can now see what a refusal SAYS.** `expect: {error: contract}` proves an
exit code, which is all the suite could assert about a refusal — so two implementations
could refuse for the same reason with different words and pass. Cases opt into
`errorContains`, checked on both the library and CLI paths.

This is not the frozen class: nothing here says anything false about a real estate. It
is admitted because the freeze exists to protect people from acting on false readings,
and this defect meets a different bar that matters just as much for going public —
every outside contributor's first contact runs through this refusal, and until today it
made them do the tool's work.

## D720 — a permission check that asked a different question than the one apply would ask

The second pilot, on a live account, with a hard EU-residency requirement enforced by an
SCP that allows only EU regions:

```
apply → refused: provider-permission-denied
        the acting identity lacks required permissions   (~65 actions)
```

The identity lacked none of them. Their measurement, the same action and the same role,
differing only in context:

```
simulate-principal-policy --action-names ec2:CreateVpc                      → deny
simulate-principal-policy --action-names ec2:CreateVpc \
  --context-entries ...aws:RequestedRegion=eu-central-1                     → allowed
real ec2:CreateVpc in eu-central-1                                          → succeeds
```

`internal/aws/preflight.go` sent `PolicySourceArn`, `ActionNames` and `ResourceArns`,
and **no `ContextEntries` at all**. An account whose guardrail is written in a condition
key therefore simulates as denied for everything that guardrail touches. The tool was
not measuring the caller's permissions; it was measuring its own incomplete question.

**What it cost, which is the part that decides this is admitted.** Their workaround is
to detach the regional statement from the SCP for the duration of each apply — about
four minutes per deployment, logged, in a project whose whole point is EU residency.
*Our security tool made them switch a security control off so that our security tool
would agree the control was satisfied.* By the freeze's test, a person acting on what
we said is worse off than if we had said nothing.

Two fixes, and the second is the one that generalizes.

**The region, because we always know it.** The simulation now carries
`aws:RequestedRegion` — the driver's region for the account-level check, and the region
out of the resource's own ARN for the resource-level one. Keys are sent in sorted
order: a check whose request depends on map iteration is not a check.

**AWS's own report of what it needed, because we cannot enumerate the rest.** Every
`EvaluationResult` carries `MissingContextValues` — the condition keys the evaluated
policies asked for and the request did not supply. A verdict resting on a key we did not
send is not an answer about the caller. Such an action is now **unattested**, never
denied, in both checks. This covers `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, tag conditions,
`aws:SourceIp` and every guardrail we have not thought of, without a list anyone has to
maintain — the reporter asked for the region and for the general case, and the general
case is the one the provider will answer for us.

**The interface had to widen.** `ResourcePreflighter.CheckResourcePermissions` returned
only `denied`. An in-context deny there is AUTHORITATIVE and blocks, so a
context-incomplete verdict is most damaging exactly there — and without an unattested
channel the only choices were to drop the action (silently "granted", so
`--require-preflight` would report a certainty it does not have) or to fail the whole
group (discarding real denials found alongside). It returns `(denied, unattested, err)`
now; GCP, Azure and the Fake return nil for the new channel and behave as before.

**Two mutants, because the two halves fail differently.** Removing the context entries
is caught by the region tests; making `trustworthy()` return true unconditionally is
caught by the missing-context tests. Verified by injecting each: they fail the right
tests and no others.

**An audit of this fix found it re-creating its own bug, plus two more.** Five agents
swept the generalizations of the two field reports; the one aimed at this file came back
with three defects in the code above, written the same hour:

- **The fix asserted a region for services that do not run in one.** Route 53,
  CloudFront, IAM and Budgets are signed for us-east-1 and have no regional endpoint;
  `cloudwatch` is worse than either, since alarms are regional and the dashboards driver
  signs us-east-1. Claiming `eu-central-1` over `iam:*` against a guardrail written as
  "deny iam:* outside us-east-1" yields an explicitDeny with the key PRESENT — so
  `trustworthy()` is true, the deny is authoritative, and the apply is refused with no
  way around it. **The reported bug, re-created by its fix.** The asymmetry that decides
  the direction: OMITTING a key is safe because `MissingContextValues` catches it;
  ASSERTING a wrong one is not. Anything not plainly regional is now omitted, and the
  simulation runs as two batches.
- **An action the simulator never answered was a denial.** `dec[p] != "allowed"` on the
  resource path cannot tell "answered deny" from "not in the response" — a map miss is
  the zero value. Absent and denied are two answers (the D708 shape again, one file
  over).
- **The simulator paginates and this code did not follow the marker**, while the driver
  follows markers everywhere else. A truncated page left later actions unanswered, which
  the previous point then turned into a refusal.

Three more tests, each verified against its own mutant. The first one is the reason this
entry exists in the form it does: a fix reviewed only by its author would have shipped a
refusal for `iam:*` to the same pilot who reported the refusal for `ec2:*`.

**What is NOT verified, stated rather than implied.** This project has no AWS account,
and an unauthenticated call cannot reach parameter validation, so the Query-protocol
encoding of `ContextEntries.member.N.{ContextKeyName,ContextKeyType,ContextKeyValues.member.1}`
is pinned by a fixture that asserts what the driver sends — not by AWS accepting it.
The pilot has the account and has already run the simulation both ways from the CLI;
the delivery note asks them to confirm the refusal disappears. Until they do, this is a
fix believed, not a fix proven.

## D721 — the plan carried the reason and the verb never said it

From the first pilot, on v0.1.8, and the sentence that matters is theirs:

> `plan` NIE POWIEDZIAŁ NIC. […] 24 zdolności z 27 zadeklarowanych, bez słowa o
> brakujących. […] plan wyglądał na kompletny i wykonywalny, a po cichu pomijał połowę
> wdrożenia.

They report the capability as absent from `actions`, `noop`, `unverified` and
`advisories`. Reproduced against the compiler — a driver whose `OperandTargets` refuses,
which is exactly their `url_auth=iam` + `publicExposure: false` shape:

```
actions=0 blocked=[{fn  fn: implementation.url_auth=iam requires network.publicExposure: true}]
```

**The capability did not vanish.** It is in `plan.blocked`, with the same sentence they
would later read out of converge, and it has been since D249. The four keys they checked
did not include the fifth.

That is worth stating precisely, because it moves the defect rather than dissolving it.
The tool held the answer and **never spoke it**:

- `plan` prints the JSON document on stdout and returns **0**.
- Its prose channel on stderr names the cost projection, the hardening hint, and every
  converged **no-op** — capabilities deliberately left alone, the harmless case.
- Nothing names the capabilities that fell OUT of the deployment, which is the dangerous
  case. Attention was distributed inversely to risk, the same finding as D531, one
  channel over.
- `converge` reads the same field and says it out loud, and refuses the clean
  "converged" verdict while it stands.

So one state had two verbs and two answers, and the verb people run first was the one
that said fine. That is the defect, and by the freeze's test it is admitted: a person
acting on `plan` — exit 0, a sealed plan, no word — applies a deployment they believe is
complete.

**The fix is the missing sentence, plus agreement between the two verbs.** `plan` now
names every blocked capability with its reason on the prose channel, prints how many
capabilities the contract declares against how many this plan covers (the reporter's
third point: "różnicę potrafi zauważyć tylko ktoś, kto liczy"), and **exits 2** — the
code this codebase already uses for "a human has to look". Nothing was printed on the
complete path, where a line every deployment sees is how a real warning stops being read.

Per-capability isolation (D249) is untouched: the document still carries the other 24
actions and they remain applicable. What changed is that the tool now says so.

**The conformance suite corrected the first version of this fix**, which exited 2 for
any blocked capability and broke two decided cases. An unbound WITNESS capability is
blocked and also recorded in `witnessed` with its own reason — D177 put it there so "a
signed/capsuled plan cannot be misread as capability forgotten" — and the suite decides
that such a plan is a success. So the refusal keys on a narrower and truer set: a
blocked capability named in NO other channel. That distinction was already in the code;
I had flattened it. The suite is the source of truth and the code moved, not the case.

**Not fixed here, and it is the reporter's second point:** `network.publicExposure` is
MEASURED as "callable anonymously" and VALIDATED as "has a Function URL", so a
CloudFront-fronted function with `AuthType: AWS_IAM` has no declaration that converges —
`true` makes the plan want to open it, `false` makes the builder refuse. Their reading is
the better one and I agree with it: exposure is a fact about risk, and `url_auth: iam`
describes precisely the URL that is NOT public, so requiring public exposure to
authenticate a URL is self-contradictory. Changing it moves a vocabulary boundary and
touches the D628/D630 exposure gate, so it is its own entry with its own conformance
case, not a rider on this one.

## D722 — the tool carried the marker and threw it away at the one moment it decided anything

From the second pilot, on a live account, product handling special-category data under a
declared EU-residency requirement. Their contract carries a HARD constraint,
`egress.restricted == true`. It read SATISFIED. What `discover` reported:

```json
{"path": "egress.internet",       "value": "none", "derivation": "measured"}
{"path": "egress.restricted",     "value": true,   "derivation": "config-intent"}   <- the only one
{"path": "serviceAccess.private", "value": true,   "derivation": "measured"}
```

What their account actually held — both security groups in that network, including the
one this driver created:

```json
{"IpProtocol": "-1", "IpRanges": [{"CidrIp": "0.0.0.0/0"}]}
```

Every protocol, every destination. Default-allow, which is the exact opposite of the
vocabulary's own definition ("a default-deny egress allow-list"). The attribute is not
unmeasurable; it is measurable in one call, and the measurement says false.

Their sentence is the entry:

> **Narzędzie ma znacznik `derivation` i go nie używa przy ocenie ograniczeń.**

`Derivation` exists precisely to record this difference (D45): `config-intent` means the
resource STORES the value and does not itself enforce it. `audit` reads it, copies it
into the verdict for display, and judges `satisfied` without it. The evidence ladder
that already refuses to let a provider-api read satisfy a probe-method constraint —
`latestSufficient`, D190/D191 — keyed on **source alone**, so a config-intent reading and
a real measurement both ranked 1.

**The fix is one rung.** `evidenceRank(source, derivation)` places a config-intent
reading at the STATIC bar and no higher. An author who wrote `verify: {method: static}`
accepted the document's own word and still gets `satisfied`; an author who asked for
`provider-api` or `probe` asked for something this reading is not, and gets `unknown` —
which on a hard constraint blocks. That is what the reporter asked for, in their words:
*"Wolimy REFUSED observation-required niż SEALED na deklaracji. Ograniczenie spełnione
deklaracją jest gorsze niż ograniczenie niesprawdzone, bo wygląda na sprawdzone."*

The change is small and its reach is not: 72 emission sites across four drivers carry
`config-intent`, and every hard constraint standing on one of them now blocks instead of
passing. That is the correct direction and it will surface work — each one is either an
attribute that can be measured (and should be) or a constraint whose author meant
`static`. Neither was visible while the two ranked the same.

**What this does NOT fix, and the reporter is right about both.** `egress.restricted` on
AWS should be MEASURED — an outbound rule of `-1` to `0.0.0.0/0` in any security group
attached to the workload means false, and that is one call. And the VPC endpoints this
driver creates carry the provider's default policy, `{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":"*",
"Action":"*","Resource":"*"}`: measured on their estate, nine of ten endpoints, the only
narrowed one being the endpoint they built by hand. A private route says which way the
traffic goes, not where to — so with that policy a principal inside the network reaches
a bucket, a key or a secret in someone else's account, by a path every architecture
diagram calls private. Both are separate entries with their own tests; this one is the
mechanism that stops the tool from calling any of it verified.

## D723 — the replacement that adopts the resource it is about to delete

Not reported. Found by sweeping the generalization of a field report about an endless
replacement loop (ACME-007), and it is worse than the loop it was found under.

A replacement is create-before-destroy: create at generation N+1, then delete the
generation-N resource, pinned by providerId. Several drivers scan for an existing
resource carrying our ownership tags and BIND it rather than create — D253, so a
converge against a lost ledger does not mint a duplicate. Those tags are
`groundhold-capability` and `groundhold-environment`. **The generation is not among
them**; for the VPC driver it lives only in the `Name` tag, which the scan never read.

Reproduced:

```
the generation-2 create ADOPTED the generation-1 network (vpc:eu-central-1:vpc-generation-one)
```

What follows is mechanical. The binding is written to that id. The delete then acts on
the PINNED identity — "delete acts on the pinned identity, never on the binding
projection" — which is the same id. The network is destroyed, the capability is left
unbound, **both actions report `succeeded`**, and apply exits 0. The next converge sees
nothing bound, creates a fresh network, and the estate has silently lost a generation
plus everything composed into it — for a VPC that is the subnets, the NAT, and in the
reporting pilot's case eight interface endpoints.

It also explains their loop better than the loop's own diagnosis did: generations 2, 3
and 4 "coming back identical" is what adopt-then-destroy looks like from outside.

**Two layers, and the important one is not the driver fix.**

*The backstop, provider-independent.* A create carrying `replaces` that returns the
identity it is replacing did not create anything, and writing that binding hands the
following delete a resource this run just claimed. The executor refuses there, before
the binding is written, naming what happened. Whatever any driver's scan does now or
later, this cannot recur — and it covers the two other drivers with the same scan whose
resources carry no generation-bearing name at all (`kms`, `vpngateway`). For those, a
replacement now REFUSES instead of destroying, which is the safe direction and is worth
saying plainly rather than filing as fixed: giving them a generation-bearing name changes
what is written to resources that already exist, and that is its own decision.

*The driver fix.* The VPC scan keys on the deterministic `Name` too, so a generation-2
create can still adopt a generation-2 resource (the lost-ledger case D253 exists for)
and can never adopt the one it replaces. `apigatewayv2` had this shape all along — it
scans by name and then verifies tags — so the fix is a driver catching up with its
sibling, not a new idea. The server-side filter is a narrowing hint and the match is
re-verified on the response, because a double that answers what the cloud would reject
is not a double (D694).

**Why nothing caught it, measured.** `CertifyCreateAdoptsExisting` is the class gate for
exactly this behaviour and **75 enrolled creates all drive it at generation 1**. The
replacement case — the only case where adopting is wrong — is unexercised across the
entire roster. Extending the probe means teaching 75 fixtures to stand up a
generation-1 resource, so it is recorded here as measured debt rather than claimed:
the backstop is what makes the class safe today, and the gate that would have caught it
is still blind.

## D724 — the WORM lock we built backwards, and the read that could not tell either way

Not reported by anyone. Found sweeping the "a control that exists and does nothing"
class that ACME-003 and ACME-007 belong to, and it is the worst thing in this series
because it is entirely ours: no cloud misled us, no field report was misread. We wrote
it inverted and pinned the inversion with a test.

AWS Backup Vault Lock has two modes and one parameter chooses between them. The vendor's
own contract, quoted rather than remembered (`PutBackupVaultLockConfiguration`):

> Before the lock date, you can delete Vault Lock from the vault … **On and after the
> lock date, the Vault Lock becomes immutable and cannot be changed or deleted.**
> **If this parameter is not specified**, you can delete Vault Lock from the vault …
> **at any time.**

So `ChangeableForDays` is what MAKES a lock immutable. The driver had:

```go
if p.LockMode == "governance" {
    p.ChangeableForDays = 3
}
...
body["ChangeableForDays"] = p.ChangeableForDays  // "omitted => compliance (immutable)"
```

Exactly backwards, comment included. Two consequences, in opposite directions:

- A contract asking for **`governance`** — the deliberately reversible mode — got a lock
  that becomes **immutable after three days and can never be removed by anyone,
  including the account root.** Permanent, unrecoverable, from a declaration that asked
  for the recoverable option.
- A contract asking for **`compliance`** got a lock deletable at any time. The WORM claim
  was false, which is the D694 class on the control people buy backups for.

**And the read could not tell the difference in the first place.** `Locked` is a Boolean
that AWS documents as "whether Vault Lock is currently protecting the vault" — true in
BOTH modes. The driver mapped `Locked: true` straight to `compliance`. `LockDate` is the
only field that separates them and it was in the same response, unparsed:

> If you applied Vault Lock to your vault **without specifying a lock date**, you can
> change any of your Vault Lock settings, or delete Vault Lock from the vault entirely,
> **at any time**.

Three answers now, not one: no lock date is `governance` (measured), a lock date in the
past is `compliance` (measured), and a lock date in the FUTURE — configured for
compliance, still inside the cooling-off window — **withholds the value with a
diagnostic naming the date**, because the WORM guarantee is not in force yet and saying
it is would be the same lie one step smaller.

**Two tests encoded the defect and were superseded by name, not edited.** One asserted
`if _, has := lb["ChangeableForDays"]; has { t.Fatal("compliance lock must be immutable
(no ChangeableForDays)") }` — it *required* the inversion. The other,
`TestBuildBackupVaultGovernanceGrace`, required a governance lock to carry the lock date
that makes it irreversible; its successor is
`TestBuildBackupVaultGovernanceStaysChangeable`. A third asserted `compliance` from a
fixture that set `Locked: true` and no lock date — the exact estate AWS calls deletable
at any time. Each carries the quote it was measured against, so the next reader can
check the claim instead of trusting this entry.

**How it was verified without an account.** This project touches no client environment,
and the class the defect belongs to (create-side, irreversible) is one where guessing is
the failure mode. The vendor's published API contract is a legitimate and checkable
source: two documents fetched, the deciding sentences quoted here verbatim. What remains
unverified is the same thing as always — that AWS behaves as AWS documents. A tester with
an account can settle it in one call: create a vault with `retention.lockMode: governance`
and check that `DescribeBackupVault` returns no `LockDate`.

## D725 — two controls that were on and delivering nothing

Same class as D724, two more sites, both with the answer already on the wire and
discarded. Both verified against the vendor's published contract rather than recalled.

**The audit trail.** `capability.audit.trail`'s `delivery.assured` is documented in our
own vocabulary as *"whether the trail is actually LOGGING (delivering events), not merely
configured"*. The driver read `IsLogging`, which AWS defines as "Whether the CloudTrail
trail is currently logging AWS API calls" — that is, `StartLogging` was called. A trail
whose destination bucket policy denies `s3:PutObject`, or whose bucket was deleted, or
whose SSE-KMS key policy refuses `kms:GenerateDataKey`, keeps `IsLogging: true`
indefinitely and writes not one object.

`LatestDeliveryError` is the field that knows, and it is in the same response:

> Displays any Amazon S3 error that CloudTrail encountered when attempting to deliver
> log files to the designated bucket. **This error occurs only when there is a problem
> with the destination S3 bucket**, and does not occur for requests that time out.

Worth recording: the audit that surfaced this proposed `LatestDeliveryAttemptSucceeded`,
which looks exactly right and which AWS marks **"This field is no longer in use."**
Fetching the contract rather than trusting the suggestion is what caught that.

Four answers now: not logging → false; logging with a delivery error → false, with the
error named; logging, no error, and a log file has reached the bucket → true; logging,
no error, nothing delivered yet → **withheld with a diagnostic**, because a trail that
has never delivered has not earned the word "assured".

**The flow log**, which is the second half of a field report (ACME-007). `flowLogs.enabled`
was `len(flowLogId) > 0` — a row exists. The reporter created a flow log with a role
carrying no permissions and no service trust; AWS accepted it, reported `ACTIVE`, and it
delivered zero records. Had they left it in place, we would have called that security
control enabled — and it satisfies a CIS-3.9-shaped constraint. AWS says it plainly in
the response the driver already reads:

> `deliverLogsStatus` — The status of the logs delivery (`SUCCESS` | `FAILED`).
> `deliverLogsErrorMessage` — … **`Access error` indicates that the IAM role associated
> with the flow log does not have sufficient permissions to publish to CloudWatch Logs.**

So a flow log AWS reports as FAILED no longer counts as enabled, and the error message
is carried into the diagnostics.

**What this does NOT close, said plainly because the reporter measured it.** They saw
`Deliver: SUCCESS` on their broken flow log — a fresh flow log has not tried yet, so
SUCCESS at creation time is not proof. This fix catches the state after AWS has tried and
failed, which is strictly better than existence and still not the same as proving the
role can do the job. The half that would have saved them is a pre-create read of the
role's trust policy for `vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com`, refusing before writing rather
than measuring afterwards. That is its own slice, and it is the one their point 2 asked
for.

**The mutation meter caught my own toothless test.** The first version of the CloudTrail
test asserted that the driver READ `LatestDeliveryError` — plumbing. Re-injecting the
bug left it green, so the meter reported SURVIVED. It asserts the OBSERVATION now, which
is what a contract is judged against. A test that checks a field was parsed is not a
test that the answer changed.

**Three fixtures had to become truthful**, the same pattern as D724: two CloudTrail
doubles returned `{"IsLogging": true}` and nothing else, which is a trail that has never
delivered, while asserting `delivery.assured: true`. They carry a delivery time now. A
double that describes an estate the assertion does not hold for is not a double.

## D726 — an alarm that names a pager and will never ring it

Three clouds, the same omission made independently in each, which is what makes it a
class rather than three bugs.

An alarm has two separate facts: WHO to notify, and whether the alarm is armed. All
three creates set the arming switch — AWS `ActionsEnabled: true`, GCP `enabled: true`,
Azure `properties.enabled` — and **no observe read any of them back**. `alert.notify` was
computed as "the action list is non-empty", so it answered *"this alarm names somewhere
to send a notification"* when the attribute claims *"this alarm will send one"*.

An alarm switched off enters its alarm state and invokes nothing. The contract reads
satisfied. Nobody is paged. This is the same shape as D724 and D725: the field that
decides was in the response the driver already had.

All three now AND the action list with the switch, treating an absent switch as armed
(which is what each provider documents as the default).

**The gate is over the SOURCE, and that is a deliberate choice with a stated cost.** The
defect was three drivers omitting the same thing independently; the thing worth
preventing is a fourth. `TestAlertNotifyConsultsTheArmingSwitch` extracts whatever
expression each driver uses to produce `alert.notify` and requires it to mention the
arming field — so a new alarm driver that computes it from the action list alone fails
before it ships. What a source gate cannot see is whether the logic is RIGHT, only that
the identifier appears, so it is backed by a behavioural test that drives the real
observe path against a fixture whose alarm is switched off. Both were checked against
their own mutants.

**One test was written and deleted rather than kept.** The first behavioural attempt
re-computed the same boolean expression the driver uses and asserted it equalled itself
— circular, and green by construction no matter what the driver does. A test that cannot
fail is worse than no test, because it is counted.

## D727 — refusing before we build a control that collects nothing, and the create that never reported success

The half of ACME-007 that a measurement afterwards cannot cover. Their words: *"`create-flow-logs` zwracające `Unsuccessful: []` **nie jest** dowodem działania."*

**The handoff check.** The VPC create takes `flow_log_role_arn` as an operand and hands it
work on faith — a non-empty string check and nothing else. The reporter's role was
trusted only by the account root, so `vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com` could never assume it;
AWS accepted the flow log, reported it ACTIVE with delivery SUCCESS, and it wrote nothing.
D725 catches that state only *after* AWS has tried and failed. The create now READS the
role's trust policy first and refuses, naming the missing principal, before building a
security control that collects nothing.

The direction of the refusal is deliberate. A policy this driver can read and that
plainly lacks the principal is an authoritative negative and blocks. A policy it cannot
read does NOT block — an account may withhold `iam:GetRole` — and the D725 delivery
reading is the second line there. `iam:GetRole` joins the declared permissions for a
flow-logs create, so the preflight asks for it up front rather than surprising anyone
mid-apply.

**And on the way, a defect nobody was looking for: the create could not report success at
all.** The batch outcome was decided by two substring tests:

```go
strings.Contains(body, "<unsuccessful>") || !strings.Contains(body, "<flowLogId>")
```

AWS's own documented sample of a SUCCESSFUL create:

```xml
<unsuccessful/>
<flowLogIdSet>
    <item>fl-1a2b3c4d</item>
</flowLogIdSet>
```

Neither substring occurs. The empty element is self-closing, so `<unsuccessful>` never
appears; the element is `flowLogIdSet`, and `<flowLogIdSet>` does not contain
`<flowLogId>`. **Every successful flow-log create was reported as a failure** — on a
composite that had already built the VPC, the subnets, the NAT road and the endpoints.

That is D717's lesson one file over: a check written against a response shape the cloud
does not produce. It parses the XML now, like every other batch response in this driver,
and the unsuccessful item's own code and message reach the operator instead of an empty
`()`. Both directions are pinned — the vendor's sample must not read as failure, and a
batch that created nothing must still fail.

It also plausibly explains why the reporting pilot's `vpc` capability never converged and
kept planning a replacement, though I cannot prove that from here: their flow-log create
would have returned `failed` every time, on a network that had in fact been built. Their
decision to leave that capability unsealed was better founded than they knew.

## D728 — two evidence bars, because verify and audit ask different questions

The second pilot took D722 seriously, mapped **all 131 of their hard constraints** onto
whether the driver actually measures the attribute each one stands on, and set out to
write `verify: {method: provider-api}` wherever it does. Then they measured what that
costs:

```
verify · every constraint without `verify`      →  146 satisfied,   0 unknown   PROVEN
verify · ONE constraint with provider-api       →  145 satisfied,   1 unknown   BLOCKED
verify · 127 constraints with provider-api      →   16 satisfied, 130 unknown   BLOCKED
```

The cause is structural, not configuration. **`verify` compares the contract with the
CANDIDATE, before anything exists**, so it can never hold an observation from a provider;
demanding provider evidence there is unsatisfiable always, whatever the cloud looks like.
The same constraints behave exactly as intended in `audit`, which they had already
verified themselves.

So the advice in my own answer to ACME-009 — "each case is either an attribute to
measure or a constraint whose author meant `static`" — was wrong, and their measurement
is what showed it. There is a third category and it is larger than both: **127 of 131**
constraints want to say *declaration before deployment, measurement after it*. There was
no way to say it, so they chose `static` and went back to the state before the fix,
deliberately and with the debt written down.

**The chosen shape is two bars in one field**, of the three they offered:

```yaml
verify: { design: static, runtime: provider-api }
```

Their first option — make the bar depend on which command is running — is the smallest
change and it is the one I refused. `verify` blocking on an unmeetable bar is not an
accident of implementation; it is this project's founding case. A hard `recovery.rto`
with `verify.method: probe` MUST NOT deploy, the plan refuses, and only a real restore
test resolves it: `probe-closes-the-thesis-loop`. A rule that made `verify` judge every
constraint against the candidate's declaration would delete that. The two-bar form keeps
it — the thesis case simply writes the same bar twice, and `verify: {method: probe}`
still means what it always did.

Four refusals came with it, each closing a way for the feature to become the defect it
fixes:

- **`method` together with `design`/`runtime`** is one thing spelled twice, and a set
  with two homes has no home (D311, D696, D697). Refused rather than letting one win.
- **Half the two-bar form** is refused: writing only `design` would leave the other bar
  to a default nobody wrote, which is the original defect wearing new clothes.
- **A non-string bar** is refused, for the reason D627 established: a bar the loader
  cannot read must not fall back to `static`, the weakest evidence there is.
- **A design bar stronger than the runtime bar** is refused. A constraint that demands
  probe evidence before shipping and accepts a config read forever after abandons the
  guarantee at the moment it starts mattering — the same principle the two bars exist to
  serve, applied to their own relationship.

**Hashes.** The canonical form keeps the scalar spelling when the two bars agree, so a
contract that never writes the new form is the same document it always was and its
pinned hash is unchanged; a contract that does write it hashes differently, because it
IS different. Adding a key unconditionally would have rewritten every pinned hash in the
suite for contracts nobody touched.

Three dual conformance cases, both implementations, and an audit-side test proving the
runtime bar is the one consulted there — checked against a mutant that swaps it back.

**The default is NOT changed here, and that is a separate decision they also asked for.**
Their argument is my own from D722 turned on its last unguarded place: a hard constraint
written in the simplest syntax is today satisfied by the document's own word, and an
author who does not know `verify.method` exists gets green without learning they never
asked. They propose that `severity: hard` default to the strongest bar available for the
attribute and make `static` deliberate. It is a good argument. It also flips the meaning
of every existing contract that relies on the default, so it belongs in its own entry
with its own migration, not as a rider on this one.

## D729 — the attribute that was measured for the couriers and declared for the vaults

D722 ended by saying that each `config-intent` site is either an attribute that can be
measured, and should be, or a constraint whose author meant `static`. The second pilot
did that mapping across all 131 of their hard constraints and sent back the sharpest
instance of the first kind:

```
✓ measured      encryption.atRest = True   sqs:…, sns:…, asm:…
⚠ config-intent encryption.atRest = True   s3:…media…, s3:…state…, s3:…audit…
```

Their sentence: *"To jest najgorsze możliwe rozłożenie"* — measured for the resources that
only carry data, declared for the three that hold it. And the reading was already on the
wire: the S3 observer calls `GetBucketEncryption` for `encryption.customerManagedKeys`
and threw the rest of the answer away.

`encryption.atRest` was asserted unconditionally as `config-intent` with the comment "S3
always encrypts". That is TRUE — S3 encrypts every object as a platform guarantee — but
it is a statement about the SERVICE, not a reading of this bucket. After D722 that meant
a hard constraint demanding provider evidence for data-at-rest on a media store, an
application-state store and an audit store could never be satisfied.

Three answers now, from the call already made: a bucket with a default-encryption rule
is **measured**, because the rule is this bucket's own configuration; a bucket with no
rule keeps `config-intent` with a diagnostic saying the value rests on the platform
guarantee rather than on anything read here; and a read that FAILED withholds the
attribute entirely, because nothing was witnessed.

**One of their two observations is not a defect, and saying so is part of the answer.**
They also reported `key.exportable` emitted for IAM roles and never for the KMS key,
concluding that *"a role is not exportable" is a sentence without content*. It is not:
`key.exportable` belongs to `capability.identity.serviceaccount`, whose AWS fulfilment IS
an IAM role, and D53 made it the one honest boundary of that vocabulary — groundhold
never manages a downloadable key. Emitting `false` on a role is exactly the meaningful
statement. They read it as belonging to `capability.key.encryption`; whether KMS key
material can be exported is a real and separate question that no vocabulary asks today,
and that is worth recording as a gap rather than as this defect.

**ACME-010 is recorded, not built.** The S3 driver writes no bucket policies at all, so
a CloudTrail trail bound to one of our buckets by `$ref` cannot be created
(`InsufficientS3BucketPolicyException`) and no bucket denies `aws:SecureTransport: false`.
Their consequence is zero audit trail on a product with a 72-hour breach-notification
duty, which is serious — and the tool refuses honestly rather than claiming a trail it
does not have, so it is a missing capability and not the class this freeze admits. The
object-storage vocabulary has no `encryption.inTransit` attribute either, so the TLS half
cannot even be declared. Both belong to the unfreeze, and the decision is the user's, not
this entry's.

## D730 — advice that named a verb the binary does not have, and hid the one thing that works

The second pilot wanted to remove a DNS zone the tool had created and that turned out to
be unnecessary. Every road was closed:

```
$ groundhold unadopt <contract> dns-zone
REFUSED binding-conflict
  dns-zone: bound but NOT adopted (groundhold created it) — unadopt reverses an
  adoption; retire or delete a created resource, never abandon it

$ groundhold explain binding-conflict
  next: Unadopt or retire the existing binding first.
```

**There is no `retire` verb.** They searched a fifty-item verb list for a quarter of an
hour, assuming they had missed it rather than that the tool was pointing at nothing.

The thing they needed **exists**, and is the second of the three options they proposed
themselves: retirement is a CONTRACT state, not a verb. `state: retired` on a capability
has compiled a pinned delete since D47, with the delete-stateful consent gate in front of
it. Measured before writing this: a contract with `state: retired` loads clean.

So the defect is exactly their third point — which they called a detail, and which is
not one. **Teaching the caller what to do next is a founding requirement of this CLI**,
not a courtesy: the whole thesis is that a probabilistic author is steered by
deterministic refusals, so a refusal that routes at nothing does not merely waste a
reader's time — it steers an agent into a loop or into the wrong action, which is the
failure mode this project exists to prevent. Recorded as CRITICAL for that reason, not
for the fifteen minutes.

**The remediation named a thing that does not exist and never named the thing that
does** — D693's class, advice that cannot be acted on, and here it also concealed the
answer.
The text now says what to do for each of the two cases and adds the fact that made their
measurement confusing: removing a capability from the contract deliberately does NOT
delete anything.

**The sentence the pilot actually saw was not in the table.** It was inline in
`internal/adopt`: *"unadopt reverses an adoption; retire or delete a created resource,
never abandon it"*. Same defect, second place, and the second place is the one a caller
hits first. Both now name `state: retired` and both add the fact that made their
measurement confusing: removing a capability from the contract deliberately deletes
nothing.

**Two gates, and the second one needed a convention before it could exist.** The first
reads the CLI's verb set out of `main.go` and checks the remediation table against it.
The second sweeps every non-comment string in `go/internal` and `go/cmd` — 478 files —
for the same thing, because the table is not where the damage was.

That second gate forced an honest limit into the open. Free prose cannot be checked: the
offending sentence names `retire` with no marker of any kind, and no regex separates it
from "groundhold created it". So the gate enforces a CONVENTION instead — **routing
advice names the action in backticks** — and judges backticked tokens against a closed
set of words that WOULD be read as commands (the real verbs plus the plausible ones this
project has been asked for and does not have: `retire`, `delete`, `destroy`, `rollback`,
`import`, `diff`, `drift`). A word outside that set is prose and is not judged. The
convention is what makes the class machine-visible; the gate is what makes the
convention real. Both assert a non-empty subject first (D328) — the verb set, the file
count, and the citation count — so a refactor breaks them loudly instead of letting them
sweep nothing. 35 routing citations across the tree today.

Each gate was checked against its own mutant restoring the old wording, and each names
the file and the token.

**Two things the mutation meter said about this entry that I would not have noticed.**
The first mutant for the inline gate wrote its replacement through a double-quoted bash
string containing backticks — which bash ran as command substitution, deleting the very
word `retire` the mutant was supposed to inject. The file changed, so the NO-OP guard was
silent and correct; the meter reported SURVIVED, which was also correct, because what got
injected was not the bug. Written with `\x60` instead, it is caught. A mutator that
mutates the wrong thing is invisible to every guard except the result being wrong.

The second is the honest limit, and it is worth more than the fix. The sentence the pilot
hit — *"retire or delete a created resource"* — carries no backticks, and injecting THAT
form survives both gates by construction. So this mechanism covers the convention and not
the class: prose advice can still name a door that does not exist. The real answer is that
routing should be structured data rather than a sentence — an error carrying the next
ACTION as a field the CLI resolves, so an unresolvable one cannot be written. That is a
bigger change than this entry, and until it exists the convention plus these two gates is
what there is. Saying so is the point; a mechanism whose reach is overstated is the thing
this project keeps finding in other people's code.

**What is recorded and not built**, because it is capability and not falsehood: they also
ask for a `retire` verb, so a one-off withdrawal does not require editing the contract.
Their own framing is the reason it is worth doing later — today there are two states,
"managed" and "abandoned, which is forbidden", and the missing third is "withdrawn
deliberately, resource deleted, ledger entry closed". Their refusal to work around it is
the right instinct and they said why better than I would have: *"Wolimy płacić pół dolara
miesięcznie niż mieć rejestr, któremu nie można wierzyć."*

## D731 — a true sentence that was false about the operator's situation

The second pilot, hardening toward zero long-lived keys:

```
AWS_PROFILE=acme-iac       groundhold discover  →  "no AWS credentials in the environment"
AWS_PROFILE=jpdevops-admin  groundhold discover  →  "no AWS credentials in the environment"
```

All three profiles work in `aws` CLI at the same moment. The third is an ordinary static
key in `~/.aws/credentials` with no role assumption and no MFA — so this is not an
unhandled assume-role chain, it is **not reading the credentials file at all**.

**The narrowness is not the defect and is not being changed here.** D346 documented it
deliberately: this driver reads the three standard variables, and `~/.aws/config` /
`~/.aws/credentials` / `AWS_PROFILE` are not consulted. A cloud engineer who assumes the
SDK credential chain will be surprised, so the surprise was put on the front page. That
was the right call and the request to widen it is a capability, not a falsehood.

**The sentence is the defect.** "No AWS credentials in the environment" is true and
teaches nothing — and in the case an operator is most likely to be in, it is *false about
their situation*: they have credentials, configured the way AWS recommends, in a place
this adapter does not look. `AWS_PROFILE` is sitting right there in the environment and
the message does not mention it. This is D730's class, one entry old: a refusal whose job
is to teach the next action, teaching none.

The cost was measured. They created a **separate MFA-less role**, pinned to one source
address, purely so the driver would have something it could authenticate with — a
security posture built downward to satisfy a message that could have named the bridge.

The refusal now names what it reads, says plainly that profiles, MFA and Identity Center
are invisible to it, and gives the vendor's own one-liner:

```
eval "$(aws configure export-credentials --profile <p> --format env)"
```

which turns any profile — static, assume-role, MFA, SSO — into the three variables this
driver does read. Verified against the AWS CLI reference before it was written into a
refusal, because naming a command that does not exist is precisely the defect D730 was
about, and doing it in the fix for D730 would have been remarkable.

**What stays open**, recorded and not built: reading the credential chain itself. Their
third argument is the one that will decide it, and it is not about convenience — the
environment is the most exposed place a secret can sit. It is visible in
`/proc/<pid>/environ` to every process of that user, **inherited by every child process**,
and it lands in crash dumps. A tool this careful about evidence and about destructive
operations currently forces the weakest available form of secret storage. That is a
coherent argument for widening the adapter, and it belongs to the unfreeze.

## D732 — three read-only drivers the compiler believed could write

Found while answering a request for a Cloudflare authoring driver (ACME-014), which is
outside the freeze. The answer turned out to be more interesting than the request: the
driver already exists, discovers DNS records and MEASURES `dns.proxied` — the exact
attribute their hard constraint is about — so their four security records (null MX, SPF
`-all`, DMARC `p=reject`, CAA) are not "outside infrastructure as code forever". They can
be observed and audited today; only authoring is missing.

Checking that claim before making it exposed the defect. `provider.CanAuthor`:

```
CanAuthor(cloudflare, dnsrecord) = true
CanAuthor(upstash,    redis)     = true
CanAuthor(hetzner,    server)    = true
CanAuthor(aws,        ami)       = false
```

All three of those drivers refuse **every** write verb — `Create`, `Update`, `Delete` and
`Validate` return not-implemented. None had registered a witness predicate, so
`CanAuthor` returned its permissive default. The consequence is stated in D177's own
comment, which built the witness concept for precisely this: a witness "gets NO mutating
action: emitting a create would lie (the driver refuses it at apply)". For these three
the compiler emitted a create, the plan **sealed**, and only apply discovered there was
nothing to write. The capability was also absent from `witnessed`, whose stated purpose
is that "a signed/capsuled plan cannot be misread as capability forgotten".

**The gate derives its subject.** A driver package whose `Create` body is an
unconditional failure is read-only by construction, so the gate finds them by shape and
requires each to declare itself a witness — a fourth read-only driver cannot join without
either authoring or saying it does not. It asserts a non-empty subject first (D328).

**Its first version had the defect it hunts.** The pattern matched one exact spelling,
`Reason: notImplemented`, and silently skipped `hetzner`, which writes its reason inline —
so the gate reported two of three and passed. A gate that recognises one dialect of the
thing it is looking for is the thing it is looking for. Widened to any unconditional
failure, it finds all three; checked against a mutant that un-declares one.

**What this does NOT do**, so the entry is not read as more than it is: these capabilities
are now WITNESSED, which means groundhold observes them, verifies their constraints and
refuses to author them. It does not create a Cloudflare record. ACME-014 asks for
authoring and remains open — but the honest answer to "our security records are outside
IaC forever" is that observation and audit are available now, and that is most of what a
control needs.

## D733 — the recovery control whose cadence applied to nothing

Same class as D724–D726, and the last of the family with the answer already in the driver's
own file. `capability.backup.plan` reports `schedule.frequency`, `retention.duration` and
`copy.*` from the plan document alone. The vocabulary is explicit about what the first of
those means:

> HOW OFTEN a backup is taken (`schedule.frequency`) — **this is what determines the
> Recovery Point Objective**.

A plan's cadence is a promise about the resources its SELECTIONS name. The driver knows
this and says so in its own header — *"A plan without a selection backs up nothing, so
create is composite: CreateBackupPlan then CreateBackupSelection"* — and the create refuses
a selection-less plan for exactly that reason. **Observe never asked.** An adopted or
drifted plan attached to zero resources reported a cadence and a retention as `measured`,
so a hard RPO constraint read satisfied on a plan backing up nothing at all.

`listBackupSelectionIDs` was already in the file, called from the delete path and nowhere
else. Observe calls it now, and withholds the cadence, the retention and the copy posture
with a diagnostic saying why.

**An unreadable selection list withholds too**, which is the choice worth stating. The
alternative — assert the cadence when we could not establish that the plan protects
anything — is fail-open on a recovery control, and this project's rule is that `unknown`
blocks. "We could not tell whether this protects anything" is not a reason to say it does.

**A fixture error worth recording, because it looked like a bug and was not.** The first
version of the test used `cron(0 5 * * ? *)` and the positive case failed with
`schedule.frequency` absent. The cause was the driver being right: that cron is not one of
the five canonical cadences, so it emits nothing and says *"bespoke cron with no canonical
cadence — RPO not derivable"*. Correct behaviour, wrong fixture. Chasing it cost a few
minutes and would have cost far more if I had "fixed" the driver to satisfy my own test.

**GCP and Azure are worse and are NOT fixed here.** Neither cloud's backup driver reads any
association at all — GCP sends a `resourceType` and Azure a `datasourceTypes`, both of
which are CLASSES rather than instances, and neither `backupPlanAssociations.list` nor
`backupVaults/{v}/backupInstances` appears anywhere in this tree. So on those two clouds a
plan protecting nothing is the DEFAULT path, not a drifted state. The vocabulary even
argues the gap into existence: *"WHICH resources are backed up is placement/operand, not a
verifiable promise about the plan's DR posture"* — which is the same sentence as the WAF
gap a tester reported, written by us, in advance. Closing it needs an attribute the
vocabulary does not have (`protection.subjects` or its equivalent), so it belongs to the
same decision as ACME-003 and is recorded here rather than half-built.

## D734 — `--provider cloudflare` was accepted and answered with fabricated reality

Reported within an hour of my telling them to run it, which makes this entry partly about
my own advice.

```
$ groundhold discover --provider cloudflare --at …
{"discovery": {"resources": [{"providerId": "fake:existing-db",
                              "resourceType": "capability.database.relational", …}]}}
```

A DNS sweep answered with a fabricated relational database. Not a refusal, not a warning.
And the name is RECOGNISED — `--provider xyzzy` is rejected with *"unknown provider (want
aws|gcp|azure|k8s|fake)"*, while `cloudflare` passes the validator and lands on the fake.
They ruled out misuse first: five credential variable spellings, four `--project` /
`--region` combinations, eight attempts, one result.

**It broke the rule printed a few lines above the validator, in this binary's own words:**

> `observe` requires an explicit `--provider` … fake fabricates reality, so it must be
> chosen deliberately (`--provider fake`) rather than defaulted

Nobody chose the fake. They chose `cloudflare`.

**The cause is D311's shape at its worst: four copies of one mapping.** `knownProviders`
lists eight names; `discover`, `adopt` and `observe` each carried their own
provider→driver chain, and `crawlProvider` a fourth. Three of the four ended in
`else { prov = &provider.Fake{} }`, so any name present in the validator and absent from
that particular chain silently became the fake. A set with two homes has no home; this
one had four.

There is now ONE dispatch. `driverFor` is the only place a name becomes a driver, it
returns an ERROR for a name this binary cannot construct, and the callers refuse on it.
A gate drives every name the validator accepts through that dispatch and requires a real
driver whose own `Name()` matches what the user typed — the fake only when it was asked
for by name — plus its twin, that an unaccepted name has no driver, so the two spellings
of "which providers exist" cannot drift apart again.

**What they were one step from.** Their plan was the one I recommended: `discover
--provider cloudflare` → `adopt` → `audit`. The second step would have written
`fake:existing-db` into their ledger as the resource fulfilling a capability — a binding
pointing at something that does not exist, in a ledger describing 39 real ones, with
their own reading rule (*resource present + capability bound = fine*) unable to see it.
They caught it because they read the discover output before adopting, and by accident:
they were looking for their four DNS records and saw a database.

**An older gate caught the second half.** Wiring the three names into one dispatch made
`TestAdvertisedProvidersMatchTheResolvers` (D505) fire: *"providers the CLI resolves but
never advertises: [cloudflare hetzner upstash] — an operator reads the help and concludes
the provider is unsupported"*. It had been passing only because the fall-through meant
nothing resolved those names in the first place — the inconsistency was hidden by the
defect. They are advertised now, with their read-only nature stated in the usage text
rather than discovered by trying to create something. The reporter had noticed the same
thing from the outside: `discover --help` said `fake|gcp|aws|azure|k8s` and `parity`
listed no `cloudflare`.

**Their note on my positive control is the part worth keeping.** I wrote that I had
checked `Observe` really emits those paths rather than inferring it from the code. Their
reply:

> sprawdziliście, że komponent emituje ścieżki, a nie że `--provider cloudflare` do tego
> komponentu dociera. Kontrola trafiła o warstwę za nisko.

Exactly right, and it is a sharper statement of the D717 lesson than I had: a positive
control has a LAYER, and verifying the component does not verify the path to it. I checked
that the driver was registered in one dispatch and that its observer emits the attributes;
I never ran the verb. The rule I take from it: **when advice tells someone to run a
command, the control is running that command.**

## D735 — the security capability that could never be created, and the reads that hid it

From the field, with a differential control the reporter built because they had no
payload to send:

```
driver:  CreateDetector HTTP 400: The request is rejected because the JSON could not be processed.
manual:  aws guardduty create-detector --enable --finding-publishing-frequency SIX_HOURS
         → 8307a606287c453ba13f953d7730065e
```

Same role, same region, same moment. That control is what makes this diagnosable at all:
it puts the fault in the REQUEST and rules out the account, the permissions and the
region without anyone needing to guess.

GuardDuty's REST-JSON body is **camelCase**, per its own request syntax:

```json
{ "enable": bool, "features": [{"name": "…", "status": "…"}],
  "findingPublishingFrequency": "…", "tags": {…} }
```

The driver sent `Enable`, `Features`, `FindingPublishingFrequency`, `Tags`, and
`Name`/`Status` inside each feature. AWS drops unknown keys and then finds the REQUIRED
`enable` missing — hence "the JSON could not be processed". **`capability.security.threatdetection`
has never been creatable on a real AWS account.** Same for the update path, which carried
the same three keys.

**Why nothing here looked wrong, and this is the part worth keeping.** The RESPONSE
structs are PascalCase too — `json:"Status"`, `json:"Features"`, `json:"DetectorId"` — and
they work, because `encoding/json` matches field names **case-insensitively when
decoding**. So every read succeeded, `observe` reported the real posture, and `adopt` even
caught a genuine drift on this capability for the reporter (`protection.kubernetes:
declared false but reality says true`). The driver looked healthy from every direction
except the one that writes. Marshalling has no such forgiveness: the key goes out exactly
as spelled.

That asymmetry is the general lesson and it is not GuardDuty's alone: **a REST-JSON driver
whose reads work proves nothing about its writes**, because Go's decoder is lenient and
its encoder is not. Anywhere else this project pins a request body, the fixture is the
only thing standing between a wrong key and a dead capability.

**And here the fixture was standing on the wrong side.** `TestGuardDuty_CreateFresh`
asserted `cb["Enable"] == true`, `cb["Tags"]`, `cb["Features"]`, `m["Name"]` — so it
passed on a body AWS rejects. Superseded in place, with the corrected names AND an
assertion that the PascalCase spellings are ABSENT, so the defect cannot return wearing
both spellings at once. Fourth time today a test encoded the bug it was meant to catch.

**What is not fixed here.** Which services use which casing is a per-service fact that
lives in the vendor's contract, not in any rule this repo can derive — GuardDuty and API
Gateway v2 are camelCase, Lambda and Backup are PascalCase. A gate would need the request
shapes checked against real endpoints, the way D717 checks routes. That is the natural
next step for the live pre-ship gate and is recorded rather than claimed.

## D736 — resume said OK about three cost controls that were not under management

From the field, one of three defects out of a single `apply`. Three budgets were created,
their receipts came back `unknown`, and the operator did what the error code told them:

```
$ groundhold resume … --provider aws --at …
{"status": "resumed"}
OK                                   ← exit 0
```

After it, the ledger still knew none of them. `discover` saw all three standing in the
account, named with this tool's own prefix.

**The mechanism, traced rather than guessed.** Every receipt reached a TERMINAL state, so
the `still-unknown` path (exit 3) did not fire. The terminal state was `failed`, for a
reason the reconciler documents deliberately: a budget whose alert notification never
landed is a PARTIAL create, reconcile cannot rebuild the notification (it has no access to
the candidate's threshold and topic), so it concludes `failed` **on purpose** — clearing
pending, so that a re-apply re-runs the create, whose duplicate-record path heals the
budget. That design is coherent and I did not change it.

What was missing is that nobody said so. `resume` answered `resumed`, exit 0, and the
three `failed` entries sat inside the JSON's `resolved` array. This is D721's shape in a
second verb: **the document carried the answer and the headline said success.** The
consequence here is not academic — a budget without its notification never alerts, so
three cost controls stood in the account doing nothing while the tool reported OK.

`resume` now names every operation that concluded as a failure, says plainly that those
resources are NOT under management, and gives the next action (re-apply to heal).

**The exit code is NOT changed, and that is deliberate.** The reporter asked for it —
*"żeby `resume` albo uzgadniał, albo odmawiał"* — and an existing test pins `resumed`/0
for exactly this case. There is a coherent argument on each side: concluding a pending
receipt is what this verb is FOR, and it did that, so the failure belongs to the original
apply; against that, a script reads only the exit code, and exit 0 means "nothing more to
do" when there is. Overturning a decided semantic while nobody is awake to weigh the
second-order effects on the heal path is not a call I should make alone, so it is written
down as an open question rather than answered by whoever happened to be typing.

**Open question (do not resolve unilaterally):** should `resume` exit non-zero when a
receipt concludes as a failure? Raised D736 by the second pilot; the loud reporting above
is in place either way.

## D737 — two mutation meters at once, and the mutant one of them left behind

Found by running the meter twice concurrently — once in the background, once in the
foreground — while working through the entries above.

The meter mutates the working tree IN PLACE: inject a bug into a file, keep a backup
beside it, run the named test, restore. Two runs interleave those steps. The immediate
symptom is loud and correct — the D664 guard reports `DIRTY … the mutator changed a file
it did not declare`, because each run sees the other's injection. The real damage is
quieter: each restores from a backup the other took **while a mutation was in place**, so
an injected bug can survive the run.

It did. After the race, two source files still carried their mutants:

```
-		if n, _ := attrs["note"].(string); strings.TrimSpace(n) != "" {
+		if n, _ := attrs["note"].(string); false && strings.TrimSpace(n) != "" {
-		if _, has := body["id"]; has {
+		if false {
```

`go build` passed. `make check` passed. The tree looked like working code and was not.
This is D712 one layer down — there, two "independent" release builds run inside a
mutating worktree agreed byte-for-byte on a binary containing an injected mutant, and it
was caught by accident. Here it would have been committed.

A lock directory, taken at startup and released on exit, refuses the second run with the
reason. Verified by racing two runs: the second is refused, and the first finishes with
the tree clean.

**The first lock had the failure mode locks have.** The racing test left it behind when
the backgrounded run was killed, and the next invocation refused — permanently. A gate
that cannot run is not a gate, which is the D328 shape wearing a different hat. The lock
names its holder's pid, and a run whose holder is gone is taken over with a note rather
than obeyed. Verified by planting a lock owned by a pid that does not exist.

The meter is a measuring instrument, and this is the third defect found in it during this
series — after the mutator whose bash backticks deleted the word it was injecting, and
the mutators that left the tree uncompilable so their tests never ran. **An instrument
this project trusts to certify everything else deserves the same suspicion as the code it
measures**, and it has now earned it three times over.

## D738 — the audit sink whose delivery nobody had granted

The GCP half of D725, found in the same sweep and left until the AWS side was closed.

`capability.audit.trail` on GCP reported `delivery.assured` as `!doc.Disabled` with
derivation **measured**. That reads the sink's own configuration flag. It is not a
measurement that anything arrives — and this driver knows it, in its own create:

```go
// uniqueWriterIdentity=true so the sink gets its own writer SA (the operator grants
// it write access on the destination — a separate capability, D26).
```

The sink is created with an identity that must be granted write access on the
destination, that grant is somebody else's job, and **nothing ever checks it happened**.
Until it does the sink exists, reports `disabled: false`, and writes zero entries
forever. Groundhold's own create is the most likely way to reach that state.

**There is no reading to upgrade to.** GCP publishes no delivery status for a sink, the
way CloudTrail publishes `LatestDeliveryError`. So unlike D725 the fix is not a better
measurement; it is a correct CLAIM. `delivery.assured` is `config-intent` now, with a
diagnostic naming the unverified grant — and after D722 that means a hard constraint
asking for provider-api evidence gets `unknown` and blocks, instead of `satisfied` on an
audit trail that may deliver nothing.

**Two assertions had to be superseded, and the second is the more interesting.** The test
required EVERY observation to be `measured`, which is how the over-claim got pinned rather
than caught — a blanket assertion cannot distinguish a fact from a flag. The other
required exactly three honesty diagnostics; a count is a weak assertion, since it cannot
say WHICH diagnostic, so the substance is now checked as well: the one a reader most needs
is the one about the grant nobody verified.

**Recorded, not built:** verifying the grant needs a read of the DESTINATION's IAM policy
from the sink's observer — a cross-service, cross-capability read whose permission cost
lands on every audit-trail observe. It is the same decision as the WAF association and the
GCP/Azure backup-plan subjects, and belongs with them.

## D739 — the firewall in blocking mode that blocks nothing

The Azure half of D726, and the third control in this family whose arming switch the
create sets and the observer never read back.

`azure/frontdoorwaf` creates its policy with `policySettings.enabledState: "Enabled"`.
The read struct carried `policySettings.mode` and nothing else, so a policy someone
switched OFF still reported `policy.mode: prevention` — which the vocabulary defines as
*"matched requests are BLOCKED"*. A firewall in blocking mode, blocking nothing, read as
satisfied. The field was in the same response body.

A disabled policy now reports `detection` regardless of its mode, and an absent
`enabledState` is treated as enabled, which is Azure's documented default.

**I wrote the circular test again.** The first version of the test re-computed the
driver's own boolean expression and asserted it equalled itself — green by construction,
exactly the shape D726 recorded and deleted, written again by the same author on the same
night. It is now driven through `observeFrontDoorWAF` against a fixture whose policy is
switched off, and checked against a mutant.

That recurrence is the argument for writing such entries down at all. The lesson did not
transfer on its own; the record is what caught it, on re-reading D726 while looking for
the next site in the family.

## D740 — the tool built a role it would then refuse to use

D727 taught the VPC create to read a flow-log delivery role's trust policy and refuse one
`vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com` cannot assume. The second pilot accepted that refusal and
then named its consequence exactly:

> Dziś jest tak, że narzędzie tworzy rolę, której samo potem odmawia użyć. Odmowa jest
> słuszna, ale zamyka drogę, którą samo otworzyło.

Their flow-log role IS a capability in their contract, so groundhold created it — with the
same-account default trust, because that is what the IAM role builder writes when no
`assume_role_policy` operand is supplied. A road closed by a refusal I added, with no
other road opened.

Two things were wrong, and the first is worse than the missing feature.

**A trust policy the builder could not read vanished.** The line was
`p.TrustPolicy, _ = impl["assume_role_policy"].(string)`. A policy written as a YAML
MAPPING — the natural shape, legal everywhere else in `implementation:` — failed the type
assertion, left the field empty, and the account-root default was written instead. The
author sees a role they believe they scoped to a service; the service cannot assume it;
nothing anywhere says so. That is D627 and D674's class on the field that decides **who
may assume an identity**, which is the whole content of one. It refuses now, and the
refusal names the operand for the common case.

**And that operand now exists.** `trust_service: vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com` builds the
policy, with the principal bounded by a pattern before it is interpolated into a policy
document (D73). Writing the JSON by hand is how the reporting estate got its unusable
role in the first place, so the fix for a refusal about hand-written JSON should not be
more hand-written JSON.

**And the meter's lock earned its keep the same hour it was written.** Two background runs
were killed by the harness mid-flight; the takeover found each stale lock, said whose it
was, and proceeded. It also exposed the gap that a lock cannot close: a SIGKILL runs no
trap, so a killed run leaves whatever it had injected. The restore now also fires on INT,
TERM and HUP, and the takeover prints a warning telling the next run to check `git status`
before trusting the tree — because a killed run is exactly when a leftover is possible,
and that leftover looks like working code (D737).

**The two halves are tested against each other.** A role built from `trust_service` is
fed to `trustsService` — the check D727 added — and must satisfy it. Without that, the
builder and the refusal could drift and the tool would go on refusing roles it built
itself, which is the whole defect this entry is about. Both spellings at once refuse, an
unbounded principal refuses, and the minimal default survives when no operand is given.

## D741 — a refusal that named a cause nobody had established

The Azure backup vault rewrote **every** failed delete into one sentence:

```go
r.Reason = "vault still holds backup instances — recovery points are data; " +
    "they must age out or be deleted first (never forced): " + r.Reason
```

That is a specific, data-safety claim about the estate, asserted whatever the provider
actually said. A missing `backupVaults/delete` permission, a throttle, a wrong
subscription, an Azure Policy denial — all of them told the operator to wait for recovery
points to age out. The implied action is wrong for every cause but one, and the one it
describes may not be there at all. It is D730's class turned inward: not advice pointing
at a door that does not exist, but a diagnosis of a condition nobody measured.

**So ask.** A vault's own `backupInstances` collection is one call, on a path that has
already failed, and it turns an invented reason into a measured one — or into an honest
admission:

- instances read, count > 0 → the stateful reason, **with the count**;
- instances read, count == 0 → "this refusal is NOT about stored data", followed by the
  provider's own reason;
- instances unreadable → "the cause was not established", followed by the provider's own
  reason. An unreadable list must never become "empty", which is how a refusal starts
  asserting a cause nobody measured — the same rule as D725's withheld attributes.

**And the reason the invention was tempting in the first place.** `deleteAndConfirm`, the
shared Azure delete helper, discarded the response body and reported `HTTP 409` and
nothing else. A caller wanting to explain a refusal had only a number, so it supplied
