derived from it now instead of chosen — the D745 rule (compute the claim from the field
that decides it) applied to advice rather than to an observation.

Measured before changing anything: all 12 recommended attributes are resource state, and
every one of them is emitted by at least one driver. The stronger bar is not aspirational;
it is meetable today, which is why this is a fix and not a wish.

**A pasted constraint now BLOCKS until an observation exists.** That is the intended
consequence and the direction D722 chose deliberately: `unknown` on a hard constraint
blocks. A hardening control that goes green before anyone looked is worth less than one
that refuses to go green until someone did.

The golden test that pinned the old snippet was updated, and the new test asserts the
DERIVATION rather than the three strings — so a fourth evidence class fails here instead of
quietly taking the default.

## D774 — a create requirement is not a drift requirement

From the field, marked BLOKADA, and the reporter's accounting the same day put it in
context: their whole ingress and event layer stands outside the contract, and this is one
of the three reasons why.

**Four ZIP-packaged functions — bound, converged, untouched by the plan — blocked the plan
of 43 capabilities**, 39 of which have nothing to do with Lambda:

```
4 capability(ies) COULD NOT BE PLANNED and are not covered by this plan:
  api:    lambda requires implementation.image_uri (the container image; PackageType=Image)
  …
the contract declares 43 capability(ies); this plan covers 29
REFUSED
```

The operand-drift step derives the DESIRED operand shape so a reconcile can compare it
against what was observed. For Lambda it derived that shape by calling `BuildLambda` —
which refuses without `image_uri`, because a CREATE needs one. **The question being asked
was "has this drifted", and the answer came back "you have not told me how to build it".**

Without an image the driver cannot state a desired PACKAGE, and it says so by omitting that
target. It can still state the environment, the role and the VPC config, and those keep
drift detection alive for the parts it does govern.

**The same principle, twice more, in the same report.**

`observe` recorded outputs all-or-nothing: one declared output missing from the driver read
discarded EVERY readable one. The driver had just adopted the function BY ITS ARN and then
recorded no outputs at all — including that ARN — because a second output was absent. Every
`$ref` to the function then refused, blocking the plan by a route with nothing to do with
the missing value. In the reporter's words: *"nie umiem jednego, więc nie zapisuję nic"
zamienia lukę w blokadę.* Outputs are partial now: what was read is recorded, what was not
is NAMED, and a consumer that needs the missing one refuses at the point of use — which is
where the refusal belongs.

And the output that was missing was `functionUrl`, on functions declaring
`network.publicExposure: false`. **Its existence would have violated the reporter's own
security constraint.** The registry described those outputs as conditional IN PROSE —
"present ONLY when the function has a URL" — while the loop treated every declared output
as mandatory. `Conditional` is a field now, so an absence that is the contract being
honoured stops being reported as a driver that cannot read itself.

One thread runs through all three: **a missing piece should refuse where it is used, not
everywhere.** The create operand blocked reconciliation; the unreadable output blocked the
readable ones; the conditional output was reported as a fault. Each collapsed a local gap
into a global refusal.

Two things worth recording about the work rather than the defect. The reporter also wrote
that our `unknown-operand` refusal caught an operand they had invented (`zip_key`) and
saved them from a silent divergence — they report what works, which is why their reports
can be trusted about what does not. And the first version of the outputs test RE-COMPUTED
the loop beside the code instead of driving `outputDocs`; I caught it myself this time,
which is the only reason D726 is written down.

**And the meter caught the second-order damage again.** Refactoring `OperandTargets` moved
the line D530's mutant patches, so that mutant's substitution stopped compiling — NO-BUILD,
which is fatal here for exactly this reason. Twice in one day a change of mine silently
disarmed an existing mutant (the D722 pair earlier, this one now), and both times nothing
but the meter said so. **A refactor is a change to every mutant anchored in the lines it
touches**, and the only mechanism that knows is the one that re-injects them.

## D775 — a probe that dialled nothing said it had

`probe` exists to measure an OUTCOME rather than trust a configuration. That is the entire
reason the verb is separate from `observe`, why it is allowed to be expensive, and why an
intrusive one needs double consent. So `Method` on a measurement is not decoration: it
says what was DONE to learn the value.

All three probers stamped `tcp-connect` on a value obtained by reading a config flag and
dialling nothing:

```go
if address == "" || !publiclyAccessible {
    out.Measurements = append(out.Measurements, provider.ProbeMeasurement{
        Path: "network.publicExposure", Value: false,
        Method:   "tcp-connect",
        Evidence: "not publicly accessible — no public endpoint to reach"})
```

That is D766's defect one layer down: a field whose job is to say how we know, saying
something we did not do. The evidence line beside it was honest, exactly as `Basis` was
honest beside `observed` — and a footnote does not correct a headline.

**Two of the three also folded an UNKNOWN into a proven negative.** `PubliclyAccessible:
true` with an empty endpoint address is an instance whose address is not readable yet, not
one without a public endpoint; Azure's twin is `publicNetworkAccess` not Disabled with an
empty FQDN. Both reported `network.publicExposure: false` as MEASURED. A proven negative
invented out of missing data is what D306 and D513 exist for — absent is not no — and here
it is the safest-sounding possible answer about a public database.

Split three ways now:

```
provider says there is NO public endpoint  -> measured false, method `provider-config`,
                                              evidence saying nothing was dialled
configured public, address not readable    -> RETRYABLE FAILURE, no measurement
configured public, address known           -> dial it; handshake proves, silence fails
```

GCP was the third prober and needed only the method: for Cloud SQL the allocated-address
list IS the answer, so there is no unknown-versus-absent fold to split. Saying which of the
three was different is the point — the same words would have made a fix look bigger than
it was.

The gate holds the narrow, checkable half: a measurement whose own evidence says nothing
was dialled must not claim a method that dials. It cannot judge whether a method is
otherwise apt, and says so.

**The D775 mutant SURVIVED first**, and the reason is worth keeping. Flipping
`address == ""` to `address != ""` makes the branch fall through and DIAL the empty
address — which fails, and produces a retryable failure too. The test asserted "one
retryable failure" and could not tell the two apart. It asserts the REASON now. **A test
that checks the SHAPE of an outcome and not its content passes for the wrong reason
whenever the wrong path produces the same shape.**

## D776 — two operands that were not two spellings of the same thing

From the field, and found the only way it could be: by checking reality instead of
trusting our advice.

D751's refusal routes an author at the operand to use, and said `trust_service` was "the
common case". The reporter then measured their own six roles:

```
pv-api-role         lambda.amazonaws.com          | condition: YES
pv-web-role         lambda.amazonaws.com          | condition: YES
pv-match-role       lambda.amazonaws.com          | condition: YES
pv-scheduler-role   scheduler.amazonaws.com       | condition: YES
pv-scheduler-safety scheduler.amazonaws.com       | condition: YES
pv-flowlog-role     vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com   | condition: YES + ArnLike on the VPC
```

**All six.** `trust_service` writes a bare Service principal and NOTHING else, so
declaring any of them with it would have recorded trust WEAKER than the trust that stands.
And because `trust.principals` is not an attribute (ACME-025 pt 1, frozen), that
divergence is UNDETECTABLE — it would surface at the next re-create, as a silent
weakening of a role that had been hardened by hand.

Their sentence for it: *dziś czyta się to jako dwie równorzędne pisownie.* It did, and the
refusal that says so is the defect: **advice that routes at the operand which would quietly
downgrade you is worse than no advice**, because it carries the tool's authority into the
weaker choice.

Both refusals and the operand's own documentation now say it: `trust_service` is the
shortcut for an UNCONDITIONED role, and any `aws:SourceAccount`/`ArnLike` guard belongs in
`assume_role_policy`, written from the role as it stands.

What this does not fix is the reason the divergence would be invisible, and that stays
frozen and named: with no `trust.principals` attribute, nothing compares a role's trust to
a declaration at all.

## D777 — an exact count of what we never looked for (FLAGGED, not resolved)

`posture` publishes `shadow: N` — resources on the estate that no contract binds — with
`shadowLowerBound: false` whenever every crawled scope completed. That flag's published
meaning is *this count is exact*.

**A crawl can only enumerate what it has a discoverer for.** Measured by asking the
drivers: 54 / 46 / 45 services certified across AWS / GCP / Azure, and 50 / 44 / 42 with a
discoverer — **nine certified services that discovery never sweeps** (`route53record`,
`rolepolicy`, `cwlogfilter`, `changefeed`, `clouddnsrecord`, `assetfeed`, `dnsrecord`,
`keyvaultkey`, `changefeed` again on Azure). Most are child resources whose parent is
swept, which is a defensible design; none of them is the point.

The point is what lies OUTSIDE the certified set entirely. A tester's accounting the same
day: nine functions on the account against four in the contract, fourteen IAM roles against
six, four event-bus rules against zero, fifteen log groups against two, five alarms against
zero. Their whole ingress and event layer is invisible to `discover`, because groundhold
has no types for it — and `shadowLowerBound: false` says the count of unmanaged resources
is exact.

**The file already contains the answer to this class, chosen deliberately for its twin.**
`ManagedOKUpperBound` is a CONSTANT `true`, and its comment explains why:

> A constant field looks odd and is the point: a consumer — the console projects this —
> must not read "managedOk: 12" as twelve resources confirmed present.

By that reasoning `shadowLowerBound` should be constant `true` as well: a shadow count is
ALWAYS a lower bound, because discovery sees only what it knows to look for, and the
provider's catalogue is always larger than ours.

**Flagged, not changed, and the reason is a conflict I should not resolve alone.** Making
the flag constant would make D650's gate — *an incomplete scope lowers the bound* —
vacuous, and a gate that cannot fail is the thing this repo spends its days removing
(D328). The alternatives each cost something a published schema owner should weigh:
constant flag plus a separate scope-truncation field; a `sweptServices` / `certified`
pair so the qualification is machine-readable; or leaving the flag and correcting only its
documented meaning. Each changes what an existing consumer reads.

Recorded with the numbers so the decision can be made from measurement rather than from
memory of a conversation.

## D778 — the reference that could not resolve, to a value already in the identifier

From the field, open since 2026-08-03 with no answer — which is its own debt, and the
reason this sweep went looking at what the reporter still counts as unanswered rather than
at what I found interesting.

A `$ref` to a QUEUE or a LOG GROUP was refused, because neither service declared any
output at all:

```
plan refused: harmonogram-retencji.target_arn: bound producer "kolejka" has no
              outputs.queueArn observation
```

So a scheduler targeting a queue, or a trail naming its group, had to be written as a
LITERAL ARN. The reporter named the cost without being asked: a candidate bound to one
deployment, which a re-create silently invalidates — the same workaround class they had
already paid for once.

**Both values are entirely in the providerId.** `sqs:region:account:name` is the queue ARN
and URL; `cwlogs:region:/group` is the name, and the ARN is that plus the account. No API
call, no read, nothing server-assigned — exactly the property the registry's own comment
cites for `sns.topicArn` and `lambda.functionArn`: *"fully in the pid (no read)"*.
**Declaring what costs nothing to know is not a feature; withholding it was an accident.**

One detail is a judgement rather than a derivation, and it belongs in the record: the log
group ARN ends `:*`. Every AWS policy statement and subscription filter names a group's
STREAMS, so a bare group ARN is not what a consumer references — a reference that resolves
to the wrong shape is worse than one that refuses, and the test asserts the suffix rather
than the whole string for exactly that reason.

A test that used `sqs` as its example of "a service with no declared outputs" moved to one
that still has none. That was a fixture choice, not the property under test, and saying
which it was is the difference between updating an example and editing an expectation.

## D779 — two tests for one consent gate, both driving the same half

Continuing D767's list of gates no mutant had ever exercised, taken in order of what their
failure costs. After the foreign-DELETE registers (D768), the next is the consent gate on
an INTRUSIVE probe — a restore test is a WRITE, and doing one against someone else's data
is the second most unrecoverable thing this tool can do.

`gateIntrusive` has two guards:

```go
if resourceAccount == "" || resourceAccount != acct { … }   // not our account
if tags["groundhold-capability"] != sanitizeTag(capability) { … }   // not our resource
```

The register named two tests — `…ForeignRDS` and `…ForeignAurora` — and **both fixtures
serve the ACTING account with a foreign capability tag.** So the tag guard refuses in both,
and the account guard has never decided anything in any test. A mutant that disabled the
account branch entirely passed them both, which is how this was found: writing the mutant
first and watching it survive.

**Two named tests are not two covered branches.** They read as thorough — different
services, different fixtures, a register listing both — and they exercise one guard twice.
The new case gives the account branch the only shape that isolates it: a FOREIGN account
with a MATCHING tag, so nothing else can refuse.

With the mutant applied it now fails, and the message is the one that matters:

> refusing an intrusive probe on a FOREIGN resource still sent 2 mutation(s). The refusal
> came after the spend, which makes it a report rather than a guard.

That sentence is the harness's, written for D461, and it is exactly right: a consent check
that fires after the write is not consent.

**Only AWS, and the reason is structural.** The GCP and Azure intrusive-probe gates have
the same two-guard shape and the same single-tag fixture, so the same question applies —
but their boundary half delegates to `sameProject` / `sameAccount`, shared helpers with
their own direct tests and their own boundary gates (D779's neighbours in the unmutated
list). Disabling either fails somewhere else immediately. AWS was the outlier because
`gateIntrusive` INLINES its account comparison, and an inlined check is covered by exactly
the tests that drive it — here, none.

Worth generalising: **a guard extracted into a named helper inherits that helper's
coverage; a guard written inline inherits only its own callers' tests.** Both are correct
code. Only one of them tells you when it stops being tested.

## D780 — the update registers, and a finding I almost invented

The UPDATE twin of D768, taken by the same rule: work the unmutated list in order of what
failure costs. Patching a stranger's resource is recoverable where deleting one is not, so
it comes second — and the registers that promise every update carries a foreign-refusal
decision had never been re-injected either. All three now have a mutant, and all three
caught it.

**The part worth recording is the near-miss.** Testing by hand, the AWS mutant appeared to
SURVIVE while GCP's was caught — which reads exactly like D779's finding one entry earlier,
and I was one sentence from writing it up as another coverage gap. It was not. The
substitution had never applied: my pattern did not match the file's actual bytes, and
`go test` answered from its CACHE, so the "pass" was a replay of a run against unmutated
source.

Two instruments wrong at once, both silent. What caught it was measuring the LINE COUNT
before and after rather than reading the exit code — the substitution removed zero lines.

The mutation meter checks exactly this automatically and calls it NO-OP, fatally. Testing
by hand, I skipped the check the tool exists to make. **Every mutant is two claims — "the
code changed" and "the test noticed" — and only the second one is interesting, which is why
the first is the one that gets assumed.** Patterns here are now verified against the exact
bytes before they enter the script, and hand-runs use `-count=1`.

## D781 — the adoption registers, and the pattern that kept missing

Third on D767's consequence-ordered list, after foreign delete (D768) and foreign update
(D780). Create-time adoption is where being wrong makes a DUPLICATE: the new resource is
empty and looks healthy while the real one goes unmanaged, and the discovery happens at
restore. All three registers now carry a mutant; all three caught it.

**The patterns are tail-tolerant on purpose**, and that is the entry's whole technical
content. Two attempts here matched nothing — the first because a trailing comment ran past
where the pattern ended:

```
	"s3":                     "TestAdoptsExistingS3",  // the ours-tagged path …
```

An exact-bytes pattern written from a TRUNCATED view of the line is a pattern written from
a guess. The fix is to anchor on what identifies the entry — the key and its test name —
and let `.*` absorb whatever follows.

Which is the same lesson as D780's near-miss, one turn later and cheaper because the line
count was checked first: **when a mutant appears to survive, the first question is whether
it was ever applied.** Two entries in a row, and both times the answer was no.

## D782 — the boundary twins, and the write that manufactures its own permission

D779 mutated AWS's account-boundary sweep and left its twins unmutated in the other two
clouds — the same class gated in one cloud and unproven in two, which is the inconsistency
D461 was written about. Both now carry the same mutant, and both caught it.

The third is sharper and the gate says why itself:

> Claim stamps our ownership marker, so a claim that reaches the wrong resource makes every
> later ownership check agree it is ours — **the one write that manufactures its own
> permission.**

`claimByARN` must compare the ARN's OWN account against the acting one, not the acting
account against itself. The mutant substitutes exactly that — `d.sameAccount(d.Account)`,
a comparison that is true by construction — and the gate names it.

Three mutants, all verified by hand against the file's actual bytes before entering the
script, and each hand-run with `-count=1`. That is now the routine rather than a reaction
to D780: **the mutant is written first, its APPLICATION is measured, and only then does its
survival mean anything.**

Backlog after this entry: 27 gate files with no mutant, down from 43 when D767 counted
them. The remainder is mostly document gates and count ratchets, and it stays a list rather
than a claim.

## D783 — the other two consent gates, and a file I corrupted getting there

D779 gave AWS's intrusive-probe consent gate its first mutants and established that its
account half had never been tested. The GCP and Azure gates had no mutant at all; both
ownership halves now carry one, and both caught it.

**The entry exists mostly for what went wrong on the way.** Chaining two hand-runs in one
shell command produced this shape:

```
cd go && cp file /tmp/g.bak && perl … ; cp /tmp/g.bak file
```

The `cd` failed — the shell was already there — so the `&&` chain never ran and `/tmp/g.bak`
was never written. The `;` after it does not care: it restored a STALE backup, left over
from an unrelated command, on top of `internal/gcp/probe.go`. The Go package then contained
a file declaring `package azure`, and the build said so immediately.

Nothing was lost — `git checkout --` put both files back at HEAD, and the tree was verified
clean and rebuilt before continuing. But the failure mode is worth naming: **`&&` guards the
setup and `;` does not guard the teardown, so a broken chain restores whatever the backup
path happens to hold.** Unique backup names per mutant, absolute paths, and one mutant per
command are the routine now — not because the discipline is elegant, but because this took
four minutes to notice and could as easily have been committed.

That is three consecutive entries whose real content is about the instrument rather than
the code: a pattern that never matched (D780), a pattern truncated by a comment (D781), and
a teardown that restored the wrong file (this one). The gates found nothing wrong in any of
the three. **The tooling around a measurement fails more often than the thing measured, and
it fails silently unless something counts.**

## D784 — a gate whose subject set is empty cannot be mutated through it

Working D767's list produced a case that does not fit the pattern of the four entries
before it. The attribute-visibility sweep asks whether any driver REALISES an attribute its
observe never mentions. Disabling its assertion outright — `if false && !strings.Contains(…)`
— changes nothing, and no mutant aimed at the sweep can bite.

**That is not D328 vacuity.** A vacuous gate has no subject; this one has a subject and an
empty violation set, because the violations were all fixed. It will fire on the day a
driver adds one. What was never proved is that the MACHINERY still works — the detector
gets its input by parsing switch arms and by walking an observe function's callees, and its
comment records two earlier corrections where it reported phantom findings and where it
missed a real one.

So the detector is driven against a SYNTHETIC pair: a builder body realising two
attributes, an observe body mentioning one. A mutant that inverts the realisation test
makes it report nothing, and the self-test fails with `map[]` while the real sweep stays
silent — which is exactly the split that was missing.

**The general rule this adds to D767's backlog:** a gate that sweeps for violations can be
mutated through its subject only while a violation exists. Once the subject set is empty —
which is the goal — the gate must be proved through a synthetic case or not at all. Some of
the 27 remaining unmutated gates are that shape, and calling them all debt was wrong; they
need a different instrument, not more of the same one.

The idempotency register beside it is the ordinary shape and got the ordinary mutant: a
create retried without its token makes a duplicate, and the register that promises every
create carries a decision now notices when one goes missing.

## D785 — the two gates that guard invariants, not drivers

The remaining unmutated gates were classified rather than worked through in file order: 23
files, of which 9 assert a fixed expectation, 3 sweep for violations, and 11 read a
document. That classification is the useful output of D767's list — **"no mutant" was one
label over three different problems**, and only the first shape takes an ordinary mutant.

Two of the nine guard INVARIANTS rather than any driver's behaviour, which makes them the
most consequential in the set:

**The closed operator set** (invariant 4). The gate's own words: *an expression language is
what the medium exists NOT to be, and every operator is one more thing a reader of a
contract must know.* The mutant adds one operator. It fails, naming both sets.

**The deterministic verification core** (invariant 6). The gate walks the core's import
graph and forbids network, subprocesses, randomness and the wall clock — *the evaluation
clock is an INPUT (N1), never read here.*

Its mutant needed the D784 lesson applied immediately: **trimming the forbidden LIST would
change nothing**, because nothing in the core violates it today — the same empty-subject
shape, and the same trap of mutating a gate's configuration instead of its subject. The
mutant introduces a REAL violation instead, a blank `_ "math/rand"` in a core package,
which compiles and is exactly what the graph walk exists to find. The gate names the
package, the import and the reason.

Two entries apart, the same mistake was available twice and avoided the second time only
because the first one was written down.

## D786 — the two gates that decide whether the tool acts on evidence it no longer has

Next from the expectation-shaped nine, chosen because both answer the same question at
different layers: may this run act on a reading that has expired?

**apply's change-level re-check.** A sealed plan asserts a `from` value; if the
observation justifying it expired between sealing and applying, the plan asserts something
nothing currently witnesses. The mutant doubles the window — `rec.TTLSeconds*2` — and the
gate catches it on the past-the-ttl case while the inside-the-ttl case still passes, which
is the pair that makes it a boundary test rather than a direction test.

**The freshness predicate having ONE home.** Five sites are grandfathered by name, each
with a reason; anywhere else, comparing an age against a TTL by hand is the drift D311's
"a set with two homes has no home" warns about — and freshness is the set that decides
whether every other verdict is allowed to speak.

Its mutant follows D784/D785's rule and ADDS a violation rather than shrinking the
allowlist: a hand-rolled comparison appended to `internal/refresh`, a package outside the
five. The gate names the file, the expression and the line.

Third time in three entries that the right mutant was the one introducing a violation
rather than relaxing a register. **A gate over a rule that nothing currently breaks can
only be proved by breaking it** — and reaching for the register first is the natural move,
which is why it keeps needing to be written down.

## D787 — a flag that does not travel, and a validator nothing tested

**Flag forwarding.** converge runs plan, observe, forecast and apply as separate
PROCESSES; a flag that is not on their argv does not exist for them. The gate's header
records three occasions when one failed to travel, each worse than the last — `--trust`
and `--sign-key` leaving a signed history permanently poisoned, and `--kubeconfig`
sending WRITES to the default cluster while the operator had named another, measured on a
live k3d cluster where a Role appeared with groundhold's labels at an endpoint nobody
asked for.

The rule is not "remember the important ones": EVERY global flag needs a written decision
about whether it travels. The mutant adds one that has none, and the gate names it.

**The evidence-class validator** was the fourth empty-subject case in as many entries, and
this time the missing piece was more basic: `ValidateEvidence` had NO test of its own. The
gate that runs it over every embedded vocabulary cannot fail while no vocabulary violates
it, so `return nil` as the entire body passed everything.

It has a direct test now, against a synthetic vocabulary and — deliberately — against
NEAR-MISSES: `projections`, `Probe`, and `measured`. That last one is the interesting
case: `measured` is a DERIVATION, not an evidence class, and a set that accepted it would
be conflating the two vocabularies D759 spent an entry separating. D311's warning is the
test's own comment: *a closed set that silently tolerates a typo is not closed, and here
the typo's consequence is a reconcile that gates on an observation which will never
arrive.*

## D788 — the gate that keeps a password out of a signed history

The last of the expectation-shaped nine worth taking before the remainder changes
character. Its subject is the sharpest of the batch and D309 wrote it down: a driver
diagnostic may never carry a provider response body wholesale, because

> the Reason is persisted in the ledger and SIGNED into capsules

and provider error bodies echo request fields back — `MasterUserPassword`,
`administratorLoginPassword`. A leak there is not a log line that scrolls away; it is a
secret written into a hash chain that is then handed to someone else as evidence.

The mutant appends a function that pastes `string(body)` into a `Sprintf` inside a driver,
which is the exact shape the detector hunts, and the gate names the file, the line and the
remedy (`mutDetail` — a bounded message plus the provider's error CODE).

**This one needed the violation introduced too**, for the same reason as the four before
it: nothing in the tree leaks a body today, so relaxing the detector would have changed
nothing. Five consecutive gates where the only working mutant was an added violation. That
is now less an observation than a property of a codebase whose defects have been fixed:
**once a rule holds everywhere, the only way left to test its enforcement is to break it on
purpose.**

## D789 — a gate with an expiry date nobody set

Two document gates caught me in person today: one refused a release tag missing from
`CHANGELOG.md`, the other refused a source comment citing D766 before D766 was written.
Their teeth were demonstrated, not merely asserted — but neither had a standing mutant, so
both got one.

The changelog mutant works. The citation mutant did NOT: appending
a comment citing a four-digit decision number to a driver changed nothing.

The pattern was `\bD(\d{1,3})\b`. **One to three digits.** There are 787 entries today and
forty were written in the last day, so at four digits the gate would have stopped seeing
citations entirely — every reference to a decision beyond the boundary invisible, the
check still green, and nothing to indicate the moment it stopped meaning anything.

The bound is now unbounded, and the widened gate immediately caught this entry TWICE: once
for a comment naming the four-digit threshold as a decision number, and once for quoting
the mutant's own text here. Both were citations of something that does not exist, which is
exactly its job — and being caught by it while writing the entry that widens it is the
strongest evidence it works that I could have produced deliberately.

**A gate that measures a growing quantity through a fixed-width pattern has an expiry date,
and nobody writes it down.** Worth looking for elsewhere: any counter, id or version this
repo matches with `\d{1,N}` inherits the same silent horizon. Recorded rather than swept —
this one was found because a mutant that should have been caught was not, which is the only
signal such a bound ever produces.

## D790 — the same bound, in a second file, found after committing the first fix

D789 widened a three-digit pattern that was weeks from going blind, and closed with a note
to look for siblings. Looking took one grep and found one: `docrefs_test.go` carried the
SAME pattern twice — `\bD([0-9]{1,3})\b` for citations and `^## D([0-9]{1,3})` for
headings — with the same horizon and the same silence.

So the citation set had two homes, and I fixed one and shipped it. That is D757's sentence
verbatim — *a fix is aimed at the copy that failed, and the others are not looked for* —
committed two entries after writing it down, in the file family I had just been editing.

Both are widened now. The rest of the fixed-width patterns in the tree were checked and
are correctly bounded: Azure resource-name validators and an OIDC issuer length, all
enforcing limits the PROVIDER imposes, where the bound is the specification rather than an
assumption about growth.

**The distinction is the useful part.** A fixed width over a value someone else limits is a
rule. A fixed width over a value that grows on its own is an expiry date. The two look
identical in a regex, and only the second one lies as it ages.

## D791 — three copies of one detector, one of them proved

D784 gave the AWS attribute-visibility detector a synthetic self-test, because its sweep
has an empty violation set and cannot be mutated through its subject. The same sweep exists
in GCP and Azure — and each package carries its OWN copy of `realisedAttrs` and
`assignsToPlan`, so proving one proved nothing about the other two.

That is the D782 argument again, and it keeps arising because the codebase deliberately
duplicates these detectors per driver package rather than sharing them. The duplication is
defensible — each cloud's builder shape differs — but it means a self-test is not a
statement about the class, only about one copy.

Both twins now carry the same synthetic pair and the same mutant. All three fail when the
realisation test is inverted, and all three stay silent on the real sweep, which is the
split the whole shape needs.

Backlog: 13 gate files without a mutant, from 43 when D767 first counted them. What remains
is the three sweeps whose detectors are shared rather than duplicated, and the document
gates over registries and schemas.

## D792 — an event written, hashed, signed, and read by nothing

A different question of a list, on a surface untouched today: which event kinds does the
ledger WRITE that no projection READS?

Six kinds are written. Five are consumed in several places each. One is not consumed
anywhere:

```
probe.failed   written by internal/probe
               declared in the ledger's "knowledge, never a change" set
               declared in the state model's valid-kind set
               read by: nothing — not a projection, not a verb, not the console
```

The event is appended to the ledger, linked into the hash chain, and signed into capsules
alongside everything else. Its cost is real and its consumers are zero.

**This is not a false statement, and it is worth being precise about why.** A probe that
failed produces no observation, so an audit demanding probe-grade evidence blocks on the
ABSENCE — correctly, and without ever consulting the recorded failure. The four-valued
verdict is not weakened by nobody reading this event.

What is lost is a distinction an operator would want and cannot get: **"nothing was
measured yet" and "measurement has been failing for three days" are the same silence
today.** `posture` can say `decayed` when a proof outlives its ttl; it cannot say that the
thing meant to renew that proof keeps failing, even though the ledger has been recording
exactly that.

Recorded, not built — it is missing visibility, which the freeze defers, and building it
means deciding what posture should SAY, which is a vocabulary question. Written down
because an event kind that costs storage, hashing and a signature while nothing reads it
looks like coverage from the outside: *"we record probe failures"* is true, and does no
work.

## D793 — asking the provider what its fields are called

A decoder that reads a field the API does not return does not fail. It writes the zero
value, returns no error, and hands the result to the same road every real measurement
travels: derivation `measured`, into an observation, into a verdict. A misspelled tag is
therefore not a broken driver — it is a **confident false statement about someone's
estate**, in the dangerous direction, because the zero value of a security flag is `false`
and the zero value of a name is empty.

```
`json:"isZoneRedundant"`  vs  the API's zoneRedundant           -> "not zone redundant"
`json:"effectiveState"`   vs  the API's effectiveEnablementState -> "not enabled"
```

**Fixtures cannot catch this, and it is worth saying why precisely.** The fixture-coverage
gate (D756) proves every decoded field is exercised by SOME fixture — but we wrote the
fixture. A typo repeated on both sides agrees with itself perfectly. That is D317 in a new
place: *a scrape of our own material proves nothing about reality.* Only the provider can
say what the provider returns.

Google publishes exactly that, and publishes it **without credentials**: a
machine-readable description of every field of every API. So the question could simply be
asked. 619 tag occurrences, 256 distinct names, against 67 discovery documents covering 30
of the 31 API hosts the drivers call:

```
confirmed present in the real API   256
service-account key-file fields       4   (auth.go — a credential format, not an API)
unconfirmable                         2   (securitycentermanagement serves its own
                                           discovery document only to an authenticated
                                           caller: 403 without credentials)
misspelled                            0
```

No defect. The value is in keeping the zero.

**The gate runs offline, deliberately.** The convention for network checks here is opt-in
plus `t.Skip`, and a gate that skips is not a gate (D328). So the network step is a
refresh (`scripts/refresh-gcp-fieldnames.sh`) and the gate is a comparison against the
checked-in answer. A name absent from the verified list has never been confronted with the
real API, and the gate fails rather than assume it — which is the right direction, because
a NEW name is exactly when a typo enters.

Three things are load-bearing and each has a mutant: a misspelled tag fails; an emptied
verified list fails as a gate without a subject rather than passing vacuously; a scan that
reads no files fails the same way. The two unconfirmable names are listed as exceptions
carrying the reason, not omitted — **"checked, and here is why the check cannot apply" is
a different statement from "not checked"**, and only the first belongs in a repository.
A stale exception fails too: an exemption for a field nobody reads is a claim about
nothing, and it silently catches the next name that lands on it.

Not extended to AWS and Azure: neither publishes a comparable credential-free description
of its wire shapes (AWS ships them inside SDK packages, Azure inside its Swagger repo).
That is a real gap in coverage and is recorded as one rather than papered over — the class
is proven live on one cloud, not on three.

## D794 — correcting D793: AWS publishes its field names too

D793 closed with a sentence about coverage:

> Not extended to AWS and Azure: neither publishes a comparable credential-free
> description of its wire shapes (AWS ships them inside SDK packages, Azure inside its
> Swagger repo).

For AWS that is **false**, and it is the kind of false that matters here: it converts a
thing not done into a thing that cannot be done, and nobody re-checks the second. AWS's
models ARE inside an SDK package — and that package is a public git repository, so every
`service-2.json` is one credential-free HTTP GET away. "Shipped inside an SDK" described
where the file lives and was allowed to answer whether it could be read.

So the question was asked of AWS as well. 508 tag occurrences, 299 distinct names, against
43 botocore service models covering all 40 signing names in `aws-routes.txt`:

```
confirmed present in the real API   290
documents carried inside an API       8   (see below)
protocol envelope                     1   (__type)
misspelled                            0
```

**The exceptions are one shape, not a list of oddities.** An IAM policy, a CloudWatch
dashboard body, an SQS redrive policy, an OpenSearch Serverless network policy: each is
JSON we compose or parse, carried inside a field the API models as an opaque **string**.
The model cannot confirm those names because to the API they are not names at all. That is
a real limit of this check and the table says so per name, rather than letting them sit in
the verified list as if a model had vouched for them.

**The first sweep produced nine phantoms, and the reason is worth keeping.** A signing name
is not a model name — and worse, two APIs can SHARE one signing name, because the v2 API
kept the v1 credential scope. Fetching only `ses` reports every SES v2 field as unknown;
same for `apigateway`/`apigatewayv2` and `es`/`opensearch`. The finding looked exactly like
a defect and was an incomplete fetch — the third time in two entries that a gap in my own
measurement dressed up as a discovery (D793's SCC names, D780's unapplied substitution).
The refresh script now names those pairs explicitly and REFUSES to write a list when a
model is missing, so the failure mode is a stopped script rather than a quiet phantom.

Azure stays out, and for the reason D793 should have given: not that its specs are
unpublished — `azure-rest-api-specs` is public — but that resolving which spec version
describes a given request needs the api-version we send, per resource type, and that
mapping is work rather than a fetch. Recorded as work not done, which is what D793 should
have said about AWS.

## D795 — the third cloud, and a listing that lies by truncating

D794 left Azure out with a reason: its specs are public, but resolving which one describes
a given request is "work rather than a fetch". The work turned out to be two obstacles,
and both are worth recording because both first appeared as FINDINGS.

**One: the listing truncates, and says so where nobody looks.** The GitHub tree API caps
its response and sets `truncated: true` in the body while returning a plausible-looking
39422 entries. Read as data, that listing says twenty-five namespaces have specs and the
rest have none — and the ones it kept were alphabetical, so everything from B onward
looked absent. A gate built on it would have been confidently wrong about most of Azure.
The fix is to stop asking for a listing that can be silently short: a blobless shallow
clone gives every path (326959) in 45 KB, and files are fetched only after selection.

**Two: "newest api-version" is not a property of a namespace.** Within one namespace,
different resource types ship on different api-versions, so the newest directory under
`Microsoft.Compute` holds the disk spec and nothing else. Selecting per directory reported
twelve real Azure fields — `osDisk`, `managedDisk`, `virtualMachineProfile` — as names the
API does not have. Selection is per FILE: for each (namespace, group, filename), the
newest stable version that has that file. Twelve phantoms went to one.

```
confirmed present in the real API   205
document carried inside an API        1   (chart — a dashboard tile's body, which the
                                           Portal spec types as a generic object)
misspelled                            0
```

Three clouds now, 750 distinct names, **zero misspellings** — and that is the honest
headline: this class was not costing us anything. What it was costing was the ability to
say so.

**The recurring lesson is not about clouds.** Four times in three entries, an incomplete
measurement of MINE dressed itself as a discovery: the SCC document I never fetched, the
v1/v2 models sharing a signing name, the truncated tree, the per-directory selection. In
each case the tool reported a finding, the finding was shaped exactly like a defect, and
it was my own gap. The habit that caught all four was cheap and always the same — *before
believing a finding, check whether the thing that produced it actually looked at
everything it claims to have looked at.* Every refresh script now refuses to write a list
when its own coverage is thin, so the failure mode is a stopped script rather than a
quiet phantom, and the exceptions carry per-name reasons rather than a silent allowlist.

## D796 — asking for a tighter RPO shortened the backups

Two durations sit next to each other in every backup API and mean opposite things:

```
retention  — how far BACK a restore can reach
RPO        — how much a failure LOSES
```

Both are days, both are about backups, and one reads as the other until somebody asks
which. The Azure PostgreSQL driver did not ask. It divided the requested `recovery.rpo`
into DAYS and wrote it to `backupRetentionDays`:

```
contract: recovery.rpo <= 15m
          -> days = 0 -> clamped to 1 -> backupRetentionDays = 1
```

**A contract asking for a fifteen-minute data-loss window set the estate's backup
retention to its floor of one day.** Asking for better recovery made recoverability worse,
silently, on a real server. And observe echoed those same retention days back as the RPO,
so the loop closed: the metamorphic round-trip wrote "7d", read "7d", and passed. It was
proof the loop was closed, not that either end meant a data-loss window. *A round trip can
only ever prove the loop.*

The other two clouds were already honest about this and disagreed with Azure in the same
way. Neither writes the requested VALUE anywhere — both read an RPO as *"automated backups
must be on"*, and GCP goes further, refusing to emit a value at all when PITR is on
because *"the value is a measurement — a probe's job, not a config reader's."* One driver
was disagreeing with two, and with the world.

The fix follows the clouds that were right. Flexible Server restores to any point inside
its window, so:

- **create refuses** `recovery.rpo`, and the refusal says WHERE the two properties live
  and why writing one into the other is backwards;
- **observe withholds** it and emits a diagnostic naming the retention days it read and
  why they are not the answer — silence alone would be the D513 mistake;
- the vocabulary's `azure.flexpostgres` mapping, which published the conflation as the
  intended design, now says `none` and gives the reason. The line was the source of the
  bug, not a description of it.

The gate is deliberately NOT another entry in the curated D748 table. It asks one general
question of every driver file: when a file emits an attribute naming a LOSS window, is
that attribute's VALUE computed from something named for RETENTION? It reads the value
EXPRESSION rather than the file, because using retention as a GUARD is correct and common
— AWS emits an RPO only when retention > 0, since retention > 0 is what turns PITR on. The
distinction between a guard and a derivation is the whole content of the rule.

What this cost to find: nothing but a question nobody had asked — *which driver
observations carry a unit, and does each one convert?* Thirty-five emissions, thirty-four
converting correctly, one that was not converting at all because it was reading the wrong
noun. The unit sweep found a meaning bug, which is the usual way: you go looking for
arithmetic and find vocabulary.

## D797 — the privileged grant was in the statement nobody read

`discover` enumerates EVERY customer-managed IAM policy in an account and reverse-maps
each one into `role.permissions`, `access.mutating` and `access.privileged`. The function
doing the reverse-mapping read `Statement[0]` and stopped.

```
{"Statement":[
  {"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject"]},     <- read
  {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"iam:PassRole"}        <- not read
]}
                     -> access.privileged: false
```

A policy is privileged here if it grants `iam:`, `sts:` or a wildcard. Put that grant in
the second statement and the tool reported the policy as unprivileged, as a **measured**
observation, for every policy in a real account. Under-reporting privilege is the most
dangerous single direction this tool has: the operator reads a clean list and stops
looking.

The comment above the function said what it assumed — *"extracts the Action set from a
single-statement policy"* — and the assumption was true of the policies this driver
WRITES. It was never true of the policies it READS. That gap is the whole defect: an
authoring assumption that survived into a reading path, where the input is somebody
else's.

Azure had the same shape one cloud over (`Permissions[0].Actions`, one block of several).
GCP did not, and could not: its custom roles carry a flat `includedPermissions` list with
no structure to pick the first of.

**The contrast that should have caught this lives in the same package.** The policy
ATTACHMENT reader classifies only AWS-managed policies it knows, and for a custom policy
it withholds the attribute with a diagnostic saying *"a custom policy's privilege is not
guessed"*. Two readers, one security question, opposite answers — one refusing to guess,
the other guessing from a fragment and calling the guess measured.

Fixed on both clouds by reading everything and being explicit about what cannot be read:

- every `Allow` statement / permission block is unioned, not just the first;
- `Statement` is accepted as an object as well as a list — IAM allows both, and the old
  struct simply failed to parse the object form, so those policies errored out entirely;
- `Deny` grants nothing and is excluded. Its NARROWING effect on other statements is
  deliberately not modelled: ignoring it over-reports privilege, which is the safe side;
- `NotAction` ("everything except") cannot be enumerated into an action list at all, so
  `role.permissions` is withheld and the two booleans are reported true, with a
  diagnostic. A complement grant is not a narrow one, and silence would repeat D513;
- Azure's `NotActions` can only narrow, so they are not subtracted; their presence is
  said in a diagnostic rather than folded away.

The gate is narrow on purpose, because a general one is not formulable. "Never index
element zero" is false — `parts[0]` from splitting a providerId is fine. What is not fine
is picking one grant out of a list somebody else wrote, so the gate flags exactly that
shape: a file that emits a privilege attribute, indexing `[0]` of a FIELD (a selector
expression) rather than of a local slice. That distinction — between chopping up a string
we made and choosing one item from a document we received — is the whole rule.

Two entries in a row now have the same root, and it is not carelessness about lists. It
is an assumption formed while WRITING that survived into READING: single statement,
retention equals loss window. The tool's own output is the only place such an assumption
is visible, and it looks correct there, because we produced the input as well. The
question that finds them is the same each time: *whose document is this, and did we write
it?*

## D798 — the alert that watched a prediction

`alert.threshold` on `capability.cost.budget` is defined as *"percent of the limit at
which a notification fires"*. Every cloud lets a budget carry several threshold rules, and
each rule declares WHAT it watches:

```
AWS      ThresholdType   PERCENTAGE / ABSOLUTE_VALUE, ACTUAL / FORECASTED
Azure    thresholdType   Actual / Forecasted
GCP      spendBasis      CURRENT_SPEND / FORECASTED_SPEND
```

The AWS driver filtered on it. The Azure driver filtered on it. The GCP driver took
`thresholdRules[0]` and multiplied by 100.

So a budget whose first rule fires on a FORECAST reported a spend threshold that does not
exist. The direction is false assurance: a contract asserting *"warn me at 80% of spend"*
verified SATISFIED against a budget that only warns when a projection says it expects to
get there. Nothing in the estate does what the tool said was configured. And with several
rules, the wrong one was reported even ignoring the basis — `[0]` is not `the one that
matters`, which is the same sentence as D797, one attribute over.

Two clouds drawing a distinction and the third not drawing it is the most useful smell in
this codebase, because the disagreement is visible without any access to a real estate:
three drivers implement one attribute, and if their answers to *"what does this field
mean"* differ, at least one is wrong. That is how this was found — not by suspecting the
GCP driver, but by asking what every driver DOES with the discriminators next to the value
it reads.

Fixed by reading the first rule that watches actual spend, and withholding the attribute
with a diagnostic when every rule is a forecast — a budget that only predicts is a real
configuration, and it is not the one the vocabulary describes. An ABSENT `spendBasis` is
current spend, which is the API's own statement (*"Behavior defaults to CURRENT_SPEND if
not set"*), so absence is read as the default rather than as an unknown; reading it the
other way would withhold thresholds that are really there.

The rule went into the curated table next to D748's, for all THREE clouds rather than for
the one that was broken. An attribute means the same thing on every cloud or it means
nothing, and the two drivers that were already right are exactly the ones a later change
could quietly make wrong.

## D799 — the derivation that says "it cannot be otherwise"

Three derivations, and only one of them is a claim about the SERVICE rather than about
the resource:

```
measured            we read this value on this resource
config-intent       somebody asked for this value
platform-invariant  the platform cannot be otherwise — nothing to read, nothing to drift
```

That makes `platform-invariant` the only derivation which can be **false while the code
is working perfectly**. There is no field to misread, because the point of the label is
that no field was consulted.

Forty-eight such claims were in the drivers. Forty-six hold. Two did not:

```
aws/dynamodb   availability.class "regional"   — until the table is a Global Table
gcp/firestore  availability.class "regional"   — until the location is nam5 or eur3
```

Both are claims about **where the data is**, which is what residency means. A Global Table
replicates rows into every replica region; a Firestore multi-region stores them across
several. Each was reported as `regional`, with `location.region` naming ONE place — so an
EU-only contract verified SATISFIED against an estate holding copies of its rows
elsewhere. That is the residency thesis failing quietly on the two services where it is
easiest to get wrong.

DynamoDB's comment said the quiet part: *"a single-region DynamoDB table is
zonally-redundant within the region"* — true, and about a table nobody had checked was
single-region. `Replicas` was never decoded at all.

Both now read the field that decides and report `measured`, and both say the residency
part out loud rather than leaving it implicit: the replica regions are named in a
diagnostic, and a Firestore location that is not a region says so, because a residency
constraint comparing `nam5` against a list of regions is not comparing what it appears to.

**The gate cannot check these claims, and that is the interesting part.** Whether a
platform permits something is a fact about the platform, and our code is not its author —
so no amount of reading our source settles it. What a gate CAN do is make the claim
reviewable: every `platform-invariant` in the drivers must appear in a checked-in list of
claims that were confronted with the provider's own description. A new one fails the gate,
and the failure is the review request. A line in the list that no driver makes any more
fails too, so the list stays a description of the code rather than a memory of it.

Found by a question that needed no cloud account: **for one attribute, do the drivers
agree on what KIND of evidence it is?** Seventeen attributes are emitted with more than
one derivation across the clouds. Most of those disagreements are honest — services
genuinely differ. But sorting by derivation put all forty-eight invariant claims on one
page, and a page of sentences that all begin "this cannot be otherwise" is a page that
asks to be checked.

The meter itself was fixed in the same slice, because the night was being spent inside
it. Two things:

**A lock released by nobody.** Three `trap ... EXIT` handlers were installed at file
scope, and bash keeps only the last one. The second replaced the first (losing the lock
removal), the third replaced the second (losing it again), so every run ended without
releasing the lock and the next one began by announcing a stale lock and taking it over.
A lock that always looks abandoned is not a lock: two meters could run at once, mutating
and restoring each other's files. One handler now, naming everything that must be cleaned
up — the same shape as D328, a guard that could not guard.

**Three compiles per mutant.** `go test -list` to check the test exists, `go test -c -o
/dev/null` to check the mutated tree builds, then `go test -run` to run it — each one
compiling the same package. The list is a property of the package on the clean tree, so
it is computed once per package and cached (the lookup still happens before the mutation,
so D605's meaning is unchanged); and the build check now compiles to a real binary that
is then RUN, instead of compiling to /dev/null and compiling again. Same two checks, one
compile.

## D800 — a key id is not a key owner

Every encrypted AWS resource reports a KMS key. When the customer brings none, the service
uses the account-default `aws/<service>` key and reports THAT — so the presence of a key
id says a resource is encrypted, and says nothing at all about who manages the key.

`encryption.customerManagedKeys` is the attribute an organization writes BYOK policy
against. Six drivers emit it. Three of them read the field that decides:

```
backupvault           excludes the aws/backup key by name
kinesis               isAWSManagedKMSKey(keyId, "kinesis")
opensearchserverless  excludes the "auto" sentinel
```

and three inferred it from presence alone:

```
efs           if fs.KmsKeyId != ""                       -> true
elasticache   if rg.KmsKeyID != ""                       -> true
opensearch    if dom.EncryptionAtRestOptions.KmsKeyId != "" -> true
```

On a default-encrypted file system, cache or domain — which is what you get by ticking
"encrypt at rest" and not naming a key — those three certified BYOK. At adoption, on
someone else's estate, against a compliance attribute.

**The correct implementation was already in the same package.** RDS refuses this exact
inference, in a comment that describes the bug precisely: *"an encrypted instance always
reports a KmsKeyId ARN, whether it is a customer key or the account-default aws/rds key.
Trace it to KMS (DescribeKey -> KeyManager) so a real CMK is measured rather than punted;
an unreadable trace stays a diagnostic, never a false."* DynamoDB refuses it too, with a
diagnostic. Two drivers had thought it through, three had not, and nothing connected them.

Note what an alias check would NOT have fixed: `isAWSManagedKMSKey` matches alias forms,
and these APIs return a key ARN. Only KMS can say who manages a key, so the fix is the
trace, not a better string match.

The three now call `kmsKeyIsCustomerManaged` and report what it says; an unreadable trace
is a diagnostic and no observation, never a false true. The curated gate carries a row per
driver, because the next service to grow this attribute will look exactly like these did.

## D801 — the addon that was on, encoded as nothing

GKE reports cluster addons like this:

```json
"addonsConfig": {
  "httpLoadBalancing": {},                       <- ENABLED
  "networkPolicyConfig": {"disabled": true}      <- disabled
}
```

The empty object is not a mistake. Google serializes JSON the proto3 way, which OMITS a
field holding its default value — so `disabled: false`, which is how an addon says it is
ON, is not in the response at all.

The driver read that as "not present":

```go
v, ok := sub[s.toggle].(bool)
if !ok { return false, false }        // "absent or not a bool"
```

and three of the eight registered addons toggle on `disabled` — including
`http-load-balancing`, which is on by default in every GKE cluster.

Two things followed, and the second is the defect the freeze admits:

- `discover` skipped the addon silently, so an enabled control was invisible in the
  estate listing;
- `delete` treated it as *"never enabled — idempotent"* and returned **succeeded**. The
  tool reported that it had removed a control which was, and remained, switched on.

The function's own doc-comment warned about this: *"present=false means the field is
absent or not a bool — the caller must NOT treat that as 'disabled' blindly."* Every
caller did. A comment is not a mechanism, which is the same lesson as the gates: if the
only thing standing between the code and the mistake is a sentence, the mistake is
already there, waiting.

The pair of booleans is replaced by a state with four values, because false/false was
carrying three different meanings:

```
absent      no config block — the addon is not configured
on / off    a block we read, polarity applied; a MISSING toggle is false, which is
            what proto3 means, so `disabled` absent is ON
unreadable  a block we cannot parse — neither on, nor off, nor absent
```

`unreadable` blocks rather than resolving: observe refuses, delete answers `unknown`
rather than claiming a removal, and discover names it in a diagnostic instead of dropping
it. That is D306's distinction — absent, unreadable and denied are three answers — applied
to a case where the API's own encoding made "absent" the easiest wrong one to reach for.

The Azure twin (`aksAddonReadEnabled`) collapses the same three cases into false/false.
ARM serializes `false` explicitly, so the proto3 trap does not apply there — but the
unreadable-becomes-absent half does, and it is fixed in the same shape.

## D802 — the fourth ending

An observer has three honest endings: observations, an error, or the absence marker.
There is a fourth that looks like the first and means nothing:

```go
return nil, []string{"load balancer not found — nothing to observe"}, nil
```

No observations. No error. The ledger keeps observations latest-per-path, so the last
good reading of a resource that has since been DELETED stays the freshest word about it:
`service.managed: true`, every hard verdict `satisfied`, `posture` **managed-ok**,
`converge` with nothing to do. The tool reports a compliant, managed resource that does
not exist — and the operator, reading a clean list, stops looking.

This class has a name here and a marker to say it with (`resource.absent`, D513/D518/D522),
and 135 of 143 observers already emitted it. The stragglers were exactly where silence
costs the most: **load balancers on all three clouds**, two budgets, a backup policy, a
workload-identity binding.

**Then the gate found six more that the search had not.** They emit the marker somewhere
in the function and ALSO have an empty-success path, so grepping for "observers without
the marker" missed them — the question had to be asked of the RETURN, not of the file.
And answering it forced a distinction that the single silent shape had been hiding, three
different truths wearing one sentence:

```
gone         an addon that is off, an association that is not there   -> absent: true
present      a change feed that exists with no destination            -> absent: false
unreadable   a federated credential whose subject cannot be mapped    -> an error
```

The third is the one worth pausing on. "The credential exists but its subject is shaped in
a way this driver cannot map" had been returning the same empty world as "the resource is
gone", which is the D306 collapse again — absent, unreadable and denied are three answers.

**The gate needs no exception list**, which is the strongest form it can take. A facet
observer — blob immutability, an egress road — returns observations or an error, never an
empty success, because its subject's absence belongs to its OWNER to report. So the rule
is flat: no observer may return "nothing, and nothing went wrong".

## D803 — the first page, called the whole estate

Cloud list APIs answer in PAGES. Of the 140 discovery sweeps in this repository, **139
read the first page and stopped.**

On its own that is a missing feature. What makes it a false statement is what sits
downstream. `posture` reports how many resources are outside the contract, and marks that
count `shadowLowerBound` only when a SCOPE was incomplete (D650). A truncated page is not
an error — the request succeeded — so the scope was recorded **complete**, and the number
went out as exact:

```
shadow: 12, shadowLowerBound: false     <- an affirmative claim of exactness
```

on an account that had ninety. That is the D650 lesson exactly, in the case D650 did not
cover: it taught the crawl to admit that a scope it could not READ was incomplete, and
said nothing about a scope it read only part of. Both end with a number nobody should
trust; only one of them said so.

The direction is the one that matters. Under-counting shadow resources tells an operator
their estate is more thoroughly under contract than it is, and the whole point of the
number is to decide where to look next.

**The signal is a property of the RESPONSE**, so it is read where responses arrive — one
place per driver, at the transport chokepoint — rather than in 139 sweeps that would each
have to remember. Each driver records the calls whose answers said "there is more"; the
crawl asks for that record through an optional interface shaped like `Enumerator`, and a
truncated sweep becomes an **incomplete scope with a reason naming the calls**. The
resources found are kept, because they are real; what changes is the claim made about the
count.

The detector is deliberately conservative, and the asymmetry is the reason: a false
positive costs an honest "at least N" where the count happened to be exact, while a false
negative restores the lie. So it fires on `NextToken`, `nextPageToken`, `NextMarker`,
`nextLink` and `IsTruncated: true` — and never on a bare `Marker` or `ContinuationToken`,
which several AWS APIs echo back from the REQUEST.

**What this does NOT do is follow the pages.** A sweep still returns one page; it now says
so. That ordering is deliberate: pagination in 139 sweeps is a long piece of work, and
until it is done the honest report is a lower bound. Recorded as the next work, not as
done.

The fixture-coverage allowlist was cleaned in the same slice, because this work walked
into it. Adding a fixture that returns a continuation token made `aws:NextMarker` served,
and the mutant that had been guarding the allowlist SURVIVED — the entry it removed no
longer mattered, so removing it broke nothing. The meter caught its own guard going
blunt.

Reading the whole list then found twelve of thirty-four entries in one of two rotten
states: eight naming a field a fixture had since started serving (debt paid, permission
left standing) and four naming a field no driver decodes any more (an exemption for
nothing). Both now fail the gate rather than sit there — the same rule as the API
field-name exceptions one entry over. An allowlist is debt, and debt that nobody rereads
turns into permission.

## D804 — emptying the register of creates that never looked

D700 answered the question D526 raised: *"a resource at our name is ours by construction"*
is a claim about a name **anyone can compute**, so a create that writes at a deterministic
name must READ first. It fixed one driver and left a register naming four more —
"each one work rather than an open question". This is that work.

Three were the case the register described. `PutMetricFilter`, and an ARM PUT of a
diagnostic setting or a consumption budget, are all **upserts** sent blind at a name
derived from environment and capability alone. A second groundhold deployment over the
same account computes the same name; so does anyone following the same convention. The
blind upsert replaces whatever stands there and reports `succeeded` — which says *"I made
this"* about a resource somebody else authored and has just lost.

None of the three carries tags, so ownership cannot be read from one. What can be read is
the resource, which answers the only question that matters: identical content means the
write changes nothing and binding is safe; different content means someone else authored
it, and the create refuses rather than replacing it.

Two details of the comparison are load-bearing, and both were found by the tests refusing
our own resources:

- **Recurse into list ELEMENTS.** ARM echoes fields inside a list entry that no contract
  sets — a diagnostic setting's `logs` come back carrying a `retentionPolicy` this driver
  never wrote. Comparing lists whole called every resource foreign, including ours, which
  is precisely what makes a lost-ledger converge unsafe (D252/D253).
- **Compare the contract's terms, not the run's facts.** A budget's `timePeriod.startDate`
  is stamped from the clock. Comparing it would make the driver refuse its OWN budget
  after every period boundary, so the pre-read compares amount, grain and notifications
  and nothing else.

**The fourth entry was not the case the register described at all.** `aws/cloudtrail` has
read the trail and checked its tags since D391. It sat in a register whose stated cause is
*"their creates issue no read at all"* because its adopt probe served a fixture modelling
a RACE — GetTrail finds nothing, CreateTrail answers TrailAlreadyExists — which is a real
and interesting case, and a different one. That is the register naming a cause it never
measured: the error its own comment records having been made here once before, made again
in the same file. The probe now asks the ownership question, and the race keeps its own
test rather than being lost.

Two fixtures had to be corrected, and the correction is itself the finding: both served a
resource that had never been created. A fake that answers a GET before anything is PUT
makes every create look like an overwrite of a stranger's resource — which is why the
blind writes had gone unnoticed for so long. The estate a test invents is as much a claim
as the code, and neither was being checked against the other.

The register is now **empty**, and stays in the tree. It is the shape of a check rather
than a list: an entry can only be added deliberately, and its two-way rule means it can
only ever shrink again.

## D805 — an invariant that lived in a comment

Two drivers say this, and nothing checked it:

> every mutable path here is wired in updateConsumptionBudget
> (invariant: mutable-with-an-updater, never a false claim)

It matters because of what `mutable` MEANS to the compiler. A classifier answering
`mutable` promises the change can be honoured in place, so the plan carries an UPDATE
action instead of a replacement. If the updater then has nothing to do with that
attribute, apply reports a change it did not make: the receipt says applied, the estate is
untouched, and the next observe reads the old value — a drift the tool created by claiming
to have removed one.

**No violation exists today**, and the gate says why in the shape of the rule. An updater
keeps the promise in one of two legitimate ways: it REBUILDS from the new attrs and sends
the whole desired state (so every attribute lands without a per-path branch), or it NAMES
the path and does something specific with it. A third shape — neither — is the false
claim, and now cannot appear quietly.

**Measuring it wrongly was easy, and I did it twice before getting a true answer.** A
regex over case bodies read `"immutable"` as containing `"mutable"`, and reported nine
paths as unwired that were nothing of the kind. A second regex assumed two tabs of
indentation where these files use one, so every case merged into a single block and every
path inherited every verdict — a different confident list, equally wrong. Both looked
exactly like findings. The AST answers the question that was actually asked, and the
difference between the two is the difference between measuring the code and measuring a
guess about its formatting.

That makes five times in one night that a measurement of mine dressed up as a discovery
(D793's unfetched document, D794's shared signing names, D795's truncated listing and
per-directory selection, and these two). The habit that caught every one is cheap and
always the same: **before believing a finding, check whether the thing that produced it
looked at what it claims to have looked at.**

## D806 — "immutable" is a claim about the provider, not about us

Three drivers implement `capability.cost.budget`. Two called `budget.period` **mutable**;
AWS called it **immutable**, with a reason that sounds like knowledge:

> the budget period (TimeUnit) is its fundamental recurrence — a change is a replacement

AWS's own documentation of `UpdateBudget` answers it in one sentence: *"You can change
every part of a budget except for the `budgetName` and the `calculatedSpend`."* `TimeUnit`
is part of the budget and is not excepted.

**`immutable` is not an opinion about how fundamental something feels.** It tells the
compiler an in-place change is impossible, so the plan carries a REPLACEMENT: delete the
budget, create a new one. The estate loses the budget's identity and its history to make a
change one call could have made, and the reason given is a fact about an API that the API
contradicts.

The fix was one word plus one case label — the updater already re-sends the whole budget
definition, TimeUnit included, so the machinery to honour it was there all along. That is
the shape of this class: the capability existed, and a sentence in a comment stood in
front of it.

**Found by the lens that found D798**, applied to a different field: for one attribute,
where do the drivers disagree? Mutability disagreement is USUALLY correct and expected —
it is a property of the service, not of the attribute, so S3's region being immutable
while a DNS record's target is mutable says nothing at all. The signal is narrower: a
single-cloud outlier on a **directly comparable** service. That is one row of a
twenty-two-row table, and the other twenty-one are honest.

What this leaves open, and states rather than fixes: **every `immutable` verdict in the
drivers is a claim about a provider's API, and nothing checks any of them.** There are
about ninety. The D799 registry is the shape the answer should take — a checked-in list of
claims confronted with the provider's own description, failing the gate when a new one
appears unreviewed — and auditing ninety API claims is its own piece of work, not a
footnote to this one. Recorded as the next work on this surface.

## D807 — a ratchet for the claims that destroy things

D806 fixed one false `immutable` and named the rest as work: there are **129 of them**,
and nothing checked any.

The number matters because of what the verdict does. `immutable` tells the compiler an
in-place change is impossible, so the plan carries a **destroy and recreate**. Each of
these 129 lines is therefore a claim about a provider's API with a deletion attached, and
only the provider can settle it.

Auditing 129 API claims is not a footnote to a fix, so this slice builds the thing that
makes the audit possible incrementally and honestly:

```
aws/S3|location.region|checked: no Update*/Modify*/Put*/Set* operation in any of the 43
                                botocore models this repo calls accepts a region
aws/ASG|availability.class|unchecked
```

Every claim in the code must appear in the registry, and **the number of `unchecked`
lines may only fall**. A new `immutable` cannot arrive unnoticed, and the debt cannot grow
while looking like progress. The ceiling is a constant in the gate, and lowering it is the
work; the gate fails BOTH ways — if the debt grows, and if the ceiling trails an audit
that already happened, because a ratchet that lags stops being one.

Nineteen were audited on the spot, and by a mechanical argument rather than a plausible
one: **no `Update*`, `Modify*`, `Put*` or `Set*` operation in any of the 43 AWS service
models this repository calls accepts a region.** (Four look like they do; all four are
GuardDuty's `Location`, which is the URI of a threat-list file.) A resource's region is
part of its ARN, and the provider's own models say so across the whole surface.

110 remain. That is the honest number, it is in the tree, and it can only go down.

Both shapes this could have taken instead are already known to fail here. A list with no
ceiling rots into permission — the fixture-coverage allowlist did exactly that, and twelve
of its thirty-four entries had quietly become excuses (D803). A demand that all 129 be
settled at once turns a ratchet into a blocked branch. The debt-list idiom that works is
`knownNoAdoptRead`'s: a two-way check on a number that only shrinks.

## D808 — eight of the hundred and ten, and the instrument that could not answer

The first eight lines came off D807's ratchet: 110 unchecked, now 102.

They are the GCP services whose driver addresses the resource **by its location**:

```
/projects/{p}/locations/{region}/repositories/{id}      artifact registry
/projects/{p}/locations/{region}/clusters/{id}          GKE
/projects/{p}/zones/{zone}/instances/{id}               GCE instance
/projects/{p}/regions/{region}/disks/{id}               persistent disk
```

A patch addressed at another location is not a move — it is a request about a different
resource. That argument is checkable in our own source (the URL the driver builds) and
needs nothing from a network.

**Most of this entry is about the instrument, because the instrument cost more than the
answer.** I tried five ways to settle these mechanically before one worked, and each of
the four failures produced a confident number:

```
"location in the request body"        184 methods — but 156 are Output-only, and the
                                      marker is [Output Only] in brackets, which my
                                      filter did not match
"location in the flatPath"            0 for every API — the paths say {locationsId},
                                      my pattern said {location}
"percentage of an API's methods"      the wrong question: what matters is the ONE method
                                      the driver calls, not the API's average
"attribute the recorded routes"       impossible: most rows are AMBIGUOUS across two
                                      dozen base-URL fields, so every field inherits
                                      every ambiguous route
```

The recorded-route file is the interesting failure, because it is a good instrument for
the question it was built for (D717: does the driver believe in a route AWS has?) and
cannot answer this one at all. A row marked `AMBIGUOUS` names every base URL the fixture
could have used; grouping by field therefore gives each service every other service's
routes. Nothing about it is broken — it simply does not carry the fact I wanted, and the
shape of the data says so if you read it before using it.

What did work was the plainest thing available: read the URL the driver builds. Twelve
greps.

So the honest note for whoever lowers this ceiling next: **the four remaining GCP region
claims (Cloud SQL, GCS, Secret Manager, the audit sink) are not path-addressed**, and each
needs its own source — a bucket's location and a secret's replication policy are
create-time properties documented as such, not facts derivable from an address. That is
