four separate small readings, not one sweep, and pretending otherwise is what the four
failed instruments above were each an attempt to do.

Two more came off in the same sitting, and each needed a different kind of source — which
is the point D808 was making about instruments:

```
gcp/Secret     the provider says the word: Secret.replication is documented "Optional.
               Immutable. The replication policy cannot be changed after the Secret has
               been created", and a secret's location lives in that policy
gcp/AuditLogs  the LogSink schema has no location or region property at all, so there is
               nothing on the sink to patch — the claim was never about the sink
```

Cloud SQL and GCS stay `unchecked`, and deliberately: their discovery documents describe
`region` and `location` without saying either can or cannot change. Everyone knows a
bucket cannot be moved; the registry is not a place for what everyone knows. **100 remain.**

## D809 — following two of the pages, and a number I got wrong

D803 taught the crawl to SAY that a listing stopped at its first page. This follows the
pages on the two sweeps where a real estate is most likely to have more than one: an
account's Lambda functions (50 per page, `NextMarker`) and its customer-managed IAM
policies (100 per page, `IsTruncated` + `Marker`). Both are surfaces a tester has actually
counted by hand, which is why they were picked first.

**And a correction.** D803 opened with "of the 140 discovery sweeps in this repository,
139 read the first page and stopped." The number is **138**. The pattern I measured with
listed `NextToken` but not `nextToken`, and the CloudWatch Logs sweep — which does
paginate, and has all along — was counted among the guilty. One sweep, mis-stated in a
published entry and in a commit message, by a case-sensitive regex.

That is the ninth measurement of mine this series that came out wrong, and the first that
reached a published number rather than being caught on the bench. The class has been the
same every time: a pattern that answers a question slightly different from the one asked
(`"immutable"` contains `"mutable"`, `{location}` is not `{locationsId}`, two tabs are not
one, `NextToken` is not `nextToken`). The habit that catches them is to check whether the
instrument looked at what it claims to have looked at — and it works on the bench, where I
apply it. What it did not do here is fire before the number went into a commit, because
the number was a by-product of the entry rather than its subject.

The test for the Lambda sweep needed its own second look for the same reason. Counting
REQUESTS proved nothing: `lambdaGet` retries, so a driver that never follows a marker can
still hit the endpoint twice, and the first version of the test passed against the
mutant. What settles it is whether the second page was ASKED for — a request carrying the
marker the first page handed back. A test that counts the wrong thing is a gate that
cannot fail, and it was mine.

136 sweeps still read one page. They now say so, which is D803's contribution, and saying
so is not the same as being complete.

## D810 — three more sweeps read past the first page

Topics, queues and metric alarms now follow their continuation tokens. Nothing new in the
reasoning — this is D809 applied to the next batch, chosen the same way: surfaces a real
estate has many of, and that a tester counted by hand when they went looking for what was
outside their contract.

```
ListTopics       100 per page, NextToken
ListQueues      1000 per page, NextToken
DescribeAlarms   100 per page, NextToken
```

The test is the shape D809 had to learn the hard way: it asks whether the second page was
REQUESTED — a call carrying the token the first page handed back — rather than counting
requests, because a retry inflates a count and a count-based test passes against the
mutant that removes the following.

Five sweeps now paginate, 135 do not. They say so (D803), and saying so is still not the
same as being complete.

## D811 — a sweep for dead fields, and one question it left open

Secrets join the paginated sweeps (six now, 134 not). The rest of this entry is a
different question asked of the same cached provider models, and its answer is mostly
"no", which is worth writing down so nobody spends the afternoon on it again.

**Do the drivers decode fields the provider has DEPRECATED?** A dead field is the D793
danger with the sign flipped: the name exists, the decode succeeds, and the value is
whatever the provider leaves there for compatibility — often nothing. Reported as
measured, that is a false zero about a live estate.

Matching our 299 decoded AWS names against the 102 the models mark deprecated gave 22
hits, and **20 of them are noise**: `Status`, `State`, `Type` are deprecated in SOME
service's shape and perfectly current in the one we read them from. A name-based match
cannot tell those apart, because our decode structs do not carry the shape they came
from. Discarded as unproven rather than reported — a list of 22 would have been a
confident finding and mostly wrong, which is the failure mode this series keeps meeting.

The two distinctive names were checked in their own service:

```
logs storedBytes    deprecated on LogStream, current on LogGroup — and the driver reads
                    log GROUPS, so not our case
ecr imageScanningConfiguration   not flagged deprecated, but AWS's own documentation of
                    it says the parameter "is being deprecated, in favor of specifying the
                    image scanning configuration at the registry level"
```

The second is an open QUESTION, recorded as one. If registry-level scanning rules can
make a repository's own `scanOnPush` setting inoperative, then `security.scanOnPush: true`
would be a false assurance — the dangerous direction. I cannot settle that from the API
models alone, and asserting it from the documentation's phrasing would be exactly the
confident-from-an-incomplete-instrument move this series has had to undo nine times. It
needs either the registry-level API read or a field observation. Written down, not fixed.

## D812 — four more, batched because the meter is the cost

IAM roles, ECR repositories, ECS clusters and RDS instances now read past their first
page. Token names were taken from the provider's own models rather than from memory:

```
iam ListRoles                IsTruncated + Marker
ecr DescribeRepositories     nextToken
ecs ListClusters             nextToken
rds DescribeDBInstances      Marker
```

Ten sweeps paginate now, 130 do not.

**Batched deliberately.** A pagination fix is fifteen minutes of work and the mutation
meter is several hours under this machine's load, so one slice per sweep spends the whole
night proving four lines. Batching does not weaken the rule that nothing is pushed without
a green meter — it amortises it. What it costs is granularity in the history, which is the
right thing to trade here and is worth saying out loud rather than doing quietly.

The alternative — running the meter across parallel worktrees — would fix the cost
properly, and is deliberately NOT taken here. This meter is the instrument every other
gate in the repository is trusted against, its own history is a list of ways a meter can
report success while measuring nothing (D603, D605, D651, D664), and changing how it
executes is not a change to make unattended.

## D813 — the shared loop, because the loop was the bug

Every Google API pages the same way: `nextPageToken` out, `pageToken` in. So the GCP
drivers get one loop instead of twenty-five, and it lives in `listAllPages`.

**The decode deliberately stays with the caller.** The shapes differ per API — an
aggregated list keyed by zone, a flat `accounts` array, a `budgets` envelope — and a
helper that decoded for them would have to know all of them, which is how a helper turns
into a second driver. What every sweep had in common was not the shape; it was reading
page one and stopping. That is what is shared now.

Two properties are pinned, and the second is not decoration:

- the token is followed, and EVERY page reaches the caller;
- a provider that keeps handing back the same token stops after fifty requests **with an
  error**, not with the pages read so far. A gentle crawl (D141) must not spin, and a
  bounded loop that returned its partial list would be the D803 lie again, wearing a
  helper's clothes.

Applied to GCE instances (aggregated, 500 per page) and service accounts (100 per page).
The instance sweep needed care the others will not: its pages are a MAP keyed by zone, so
pages are merged per scope — flattening them would have lost which zone an instance is in,
and the sweep would have reported real instances at no location.

Twelve sweeps paginate, 128 do not.

The route-reality gate caught the test on the way in: a synthetic `/v1/things` URL is a
route the drivers do not have, and a test is not allowed to invent one. It now exercises a
path the recorded set already contains — the second time this gate has corrected a test of
mine tonight, both times correctly.

## D814 — a ratchet for the sweeps that still read one page

Four more GCP sweeps follow their pages — secrets, Pub/Sub topics, custom roles, GCS
buckets — and the remaining thirty-nine are now a NUMBER that may only fall, in the shape
D807 established.

The check is deliberately crude: does the function mention the shared loop? The precise
question — does this sweep read every page — is not decidable from the source, and a crude
check with a falling ceiling is worth more than a precise one nobody can implement. What
it cannot do is confirm that a paginated sweep is CORRECT; the shared loop's own tests and
the per-sweep tests do that.

**One thing nearly went wrong, and it is the reason to write the transformation out rather
than sed it.** Replacing the single call with the loop left the old `json.Unmarshal(body,
&resp)` standing underneath, now reading a nil body. That does not fail loudly in an
obvious place — it OVERWRITES the accumulated list with nothing and then errors, so every
one of those sweeps would have returned an error on every run. The tests caught it
immediately. The lesson is narrower than "be careful": when a change moves where a value
comes from, the old reader of that value is not dead code to be tidied later — it is a
second writer, and it wins.

Sixteen sweeps paginate across the three clouds; 124 do not, and say so.

## D815 — the third cloud pages too, and a token you can be talked into sending

Azure gets the shared loop, and the Postgres sweep is the first to use it. What makes this
worth its own entry is a difference from Google's paging that is a GUARD, not a comment.

A Google page token is an opaque string this driver splices into a URL **it built
itself**. An ARM `nextLink` is a **complete URL chosen by the response**. Following one
blindly means sending an Azure bearer token wherever a response says to — a redirect
nobody opted into, produced by exactly the thing an attacker who can influence a response
would reach for. The loop follows a `nextLink` only when its host matches the host of the
listing it started from, and says so when it refuses.

Nothing observed made this necessary; it is the shape of the mechanism, and the cheapest
moment to get it right is the moment the mechanism is written rather than the moment
someone demonstrates it. Both properties are pinned: the link IS followed on the same
host, and a link off-host is refused with a reason.

The endless-page bound is here too, for the reason D813 gave — a bounded loop that
returned its partial list would be the D803 lie wearing a helper's clothes.

Seventeen sweeps paginate; 123 do not, and say so.

## D816 — the Azure sweeps, and a class that turned out to be closed

Storage accounts, Redis caches and Service Bus namespaces join the paginated sweeps, and
the ratchet now has an Azure half. Twenty sweeps paginate across three clouds; 120 do not,
and say so.

The transformation was applied by matching the SHAPE of the old block rather than by hand,
which is only safe because the shape is genuinely identical across these four sweeps and
because the tests run afterwards — the D814 near-miss (an old decoder left standing over a
nil body) is what a regex-driven edit does when nobody checks. Three of the four matched;
the fourth (Cosmos) differs and stays for a later pass rather than being forced.

**The guard from D815 prompted a sweep of its own, and it came back empty**, which is
worth recording so it is not asked again from scratch. The question: does anything else in
the drivers use a URL taken from a RESPONSE as the target of a request?

```
12 HTTP calls take their URL from a struct field
 7 are req.URL — our own Request value, built by us
 4 are k8s paths computed from our own mapping
 1 is entry.ServerRelativeURL, from the API server's own /openapi/v3 index
```

The last one is the only response-supplied URL left, and it is safe by construction rather
than by care: the k8s driver builds every request as `d.Server + path`, so an absolute URL
in that field yields a malformed address and an error, never a request to another host.
Worth knowing, and worth knowing WHY — "safe by construction" is a different assurance
from "checked", and only the first survives someone rewriting the call helper.

A postscript to this entry, because it is the second time tonight the meter caught its own
guard going blunt. Refactoring the paging gate to serve two clouds moved both anchors the
D814 mutants matched on — the detector became a loop over a marker list, and the ceiling
moved into a `const (…)` block, so `const unpagedGCPSweepCeiling = 39` matched nothing.
The meter reported NO-OP rather than `caught`, which is the whole point of that check
(D603): a mutant that changes nothing scores as a bug caught unless the meter notices it
mutated nothing. Both are repointed at the new shapes and verified by hand.

The pattern to carry: **a mutant's anchor is coupled to the code it mutates, and a
refactor breaks that coupling silently.** The meter is the only thing that says so.

## D817 — The four smallest pages on AWS, and the third half of the ratchet

D809 through D812 taught the AWS driver to follow pages, one batch at a time, and D803
made it SAY so when it does not. D813 and D815 gave GCP and Azure a shared loop, and D814
and D816 put a falling ceiling under each. AWS had neither: no shared loop, and no number
saying how much of the debt was left. This closes the second gap and explains why the
first one stays open.

**There is no shared AWS loop, and that is a finding rather than laziness.** The other two
clouds each have exactly one paging shape. GCP hands back a `nextPageToken` and takes it
as a query parameter, always. Azure hands back a `nextLink` and it is a complete URL,
always. AWS has, in the sweeps this driver already paginates: a `NextToken` in a form
POST body (SNS, SQS, Auto Scaling), a `nextToken` in a JSON body (ECS), a `Marker` with an
`IsTruncated` flag (IAM, Route 53), a `Marker` with a `Truncated` flag (KMS), a `Marker`
with neither (EFS), and a `NextMarker` in the query string. Three transports, four token
names, three different ways of saying "there is more". A shared loop over that would be a
shared loop over a switch statement, which is the switch statement with an extra name.

What CAN be shared is the bound, and `maxAWSListPages` now is: fifty pages, exceeding it
is an ERROR and never a truncated answer, for the same reason D813 gave. A sweep that
never returns is indistinguishable from a hung tool.

**The four sweeps.** They were chosen by page size, because page size is exactly how far
wrong the tool could be, and these are the four smallest defaults in the AWS surface this
driver touches:

- `DescribeFileSystems` (EFS) — **ten**. An estate with eleven file systems was reported
  as having ten. Ten is not a rounding error on eleven.
- `DescribeAutoScalingGroups` — fifty.
- `ListKeys` (KMS) — a hundred, and it says so twice, with a `Truncated` flag AND a
  `NextMarker`. Both are honoured; the loop stops only when neither says there is more.
- `ListHostedZones` (Route 53) — a hundred. A DNS zone missed here is a zone the tool
  reports as *unmanaged* when the truth is that it never looked.

Every one of those four shapes was read out of the provider's own paginator model
(botocore `efs/2015-02-01`, `autoscaling/2011-01-01`, `kms/2014-11-01`,
`route53/2013-04-01`) rather than out of my memory of the API, which is the D317 rule
applied to myself: a static reading of what the code seems to do is not evidence about
what the service does.

**The ratchet.** `unpagedAWSSweepCeiling = 37`, two-way, sitting beside the GCP and Azure
ceilings, and the marker list it uses is longer than either of theirs — which is the same
finding stated a second way. The file is now `paging_gate_test.go`, because a file called
`gcppaging_gate_test.go` holding three clouds' ratchets is a small lie of the kind that
becomes a large one when someone trusts the name instead of reading it. Renaming it broke
three mutant anchors, exactly as D816's postscript predicted; all three were repointed and
re-verified by hand, along with the six new ones, BEFORE the meter ran. That is the cheap
version of the lesson: the meter will catch a stale anchor after three hours, or I can
check it in three minutes.

**What this does not claim.** Thirty-seven AWS sweeps still read one page, and
seventy-eight do on the other two clouds — every one of them says so at runtime (D803),
which is honest and is not the same as being right. The gate measures whether a sweep mentions paging, not
whether it paginates CORRECTLY; that is what the per-sweep tests are for, and each of the
four here is pinned by an assertion that a request carried the continuation the previous
page handed back — never by a request COUNT, because a retry makes a count lie.

## D818 — A truncation is only evidence if nobody went and read the rest

D803 built one mechanism and made one promise: every discovery sweep that reads the first
page of a listing and stops SAYS so, by reading the continuation token where responses
arrive rather than in a hundred and forty places that would each have to remember. That is
what stops `posture` publishing an EXACT count of unmanaged resources on an estate it only
partly looked at.

The promise held in neither direction, and this is the correction.

**A sweep that does the right thing was reported as doing the wrong one.** The chokepoint
sees a truncated response on every page but the last, so the moment D809-D817 taught
twenty-four sweeps to follow their pages, those twenty-four began marking their scope
INCOMPLETE — because they had paginated. Meanwhile three sweeps that genuinely read one
page reported COMPLETE, because the signal their service uses was invisible to the
detector. The mechanism was not merely noisy; on those cases it pointed the wrong way, and
a person reading it would have distrusted the counts that were exact and trusted the ones
that were not.

The missing half is in the definition. A truncated response is evidence of an incomplete
ANSWER only if nobody went and fetched the rest, and the transport sees only the first
half of that. So the note is now conditional, and the condition is exactly the assertion
D809 chose for the tests: **was the continuation this response handed back ever USED?** A
later request carrying that value is the sweep saying it went and got the rest. A value
nobody ever sends leaves the note standing. The bookkeeping is one shared
`provider.ListingRecord` behind all three clouds' chokepoints, because the rule is a
property of how paging works and not of any provider.

**The match is on the parameter, not just the value — and that nearly shipped wrong.**
DynamoDB's continuation for ListTables is the NAME of the last table on the page. A sweep
that lists one page and then DESCRIBES that table sends the identical string, so matching
on the value alone read "the sweep followed the listing" from a request that did nothing of
the kind — a false COMPLETE, the dangerous direction. D818's own test caught it before it
shipped, and the case is kept.

**Three sweeps could not be fixed by the detector, so they paginate.** DynamoDB ListTables,
Kinesis ListStreams and ElastiCache DescribeReplicationGroups. The last is the interesting
one: its only continuation signal is a bare `<Marker>`, which is the same field S3's model
describes as *"included in the response if it was sent with the request"* — an echo. A
detector that fired on it would report a false INCOMPLETE across S3, so ElastiCache's
family cannot be covered at the transport at all. What the chokepoint cannot see, the
sweep must do itself.

**And the largest instance was a capital letter.** EC2 models its continuation as
`NextToken` and puts `<nextToken>` on the wire — botocore's `ec2/2016-11-15` gives
`locationName: nextToken` for DescribeInstances, DescribeVolumes, DescribeSubnets,
DescribeVpcs, DescribeSecurityGroups and their siblings. The XML pattern was
case-sensitive, so truncation was invisible for every EC2 sweep in the driver, which is the
largest family of sweeps there is. Only the unambiguous `next*` names were made
case-tolerant; a bare `Marker` stays excluded in either case.

**A truncation that does not name its operation sends nobody anywhere** — D803's own words,
and its own code did not do it. The call name was read from `Action` in the QUERY string,
where EC2 puts it and where SNS, SQS, IAM, Auto Scaling, ElastiCache and RDS never do: all
of their operations are a POST to `/` with Action in the form BODY, so every one of their
truncations was named `POST /`. It now reads whichever place the service uses.

**What is pinned.** Both directions, in one file, because each failure hides the other: a
sweep that follows its pages must clear its note, and a sweep that reads one page must
leave it standing AND name the operation. The unit-level cases pin the record's rule
directly, including the DynamoDB near-miss. The AWS paging ceiling falls from 37 to 34.

**A stray mutant found something else.** While disambiguating a mutant anchor that had
silently landed on the wrong `if r.Marker == ""`, breaking RDS pagination outright passed
the ENTIRE AWS suite. D812's own comment says it covers "IAM roles, ECR repositories, ECS
clusters and RDS instances"; the table it sits above has two entries. That is my own
published claim with nothing holding it up — the class this repository keeps finding in its
own work, this time in work from four entries ago. Four paginated sweeps had no case at all
(RDS, ECR, CloudWatch alarms, CloudWatch log groups); all four now have one, and a mutant
each.

The lesson is narrower than "write more tests". An anchor that lands on the wrong site
still mutates something, still gets caught by some test, and still reports `caught` — so
the meter says the guard works while measuring a different guard entirely. Two such
anchors in three days (the other in D816). Ambiguity in a mutant's anchor is not a style
issue; it is the meter quietly changing its subject.

**What is not claimed.** Thirty-four AWS sweeps still read one page and seventy-eight do on
the other two clouds. The difference this entry makes is that they now say so, and the ones
that paginate no longer say it falsely — which is the whole of what D803 set out to do.

## D819 — The meter learns to check its own anchors in forty seconds

Three times in three days a mutant's anchor moved out from under it, and all three times
the meter reported it correctly — after a full run. D816 caught two when the paging gate
was refactored. D818's run caught three more, in the D803 mutants, because D818 rewrote
exactly the code those mutants pointed at.

The third one is the instructive one, because I had already learned the lesson and applied
it to the wrong half. Before that run I verified by hand every mutant I ADDED. I did not
verify the mutants that already NAMED the files I was rewriting. "Check the mutants you
write" is a habit; "check the mutants that name what you touched" is the actual rule.

`ANCHORS_ONLY=1` applies each mutant, asks only whether the substitution changed the file,
restores it, and moves on. Four hundred and twelve mutants in forty-two seconds, against
roughly three hours for the real thing.

**What it must never be mistaken for.** An anchor check proves that a mutant still hits the
code it names. It proves NOTHING about whether any test would catch the bug — which is the
only thing the meter exists to measure. So the mode prints its own summary, in those words,
and never the sentence a passing meter prints. A cheap check that could be mistaken for the
expensive one would be worse than not having it: this repository's own history is a list of
gates that reported success while measuring something else, and adding one deliberately
would be a poor joke.

The full run stays the authority and stays mandatory before a push. This is what to run
first, so a stale anchor costs a minute rather than an afternoon.

**A small honesty note from writing it.** The short-circuit landed in `mutate` only, and the
run still reported all 412 — because the script has three mutation helpers and I had
counted one. Nothing was wrong with the meter; my count was two runs stale (401 at D817,
plus eleven added in D818). But the mode's message would have claimed an anchor check over
mutants that had in fact been measured in full, so the short-circuit now sits in all three.
The number a tool prints has to mean one thing.

## D820 — Two routes AWS does not have, and the gate that could not say so

`discoverOpenSearch` and the OpenSearch tag read were calling paths that do not exist. AWS
answers them 404, forever. A sweep that always 404s makes `SweepAll` record a diagnostic
and carry on, so `discover`, `crawl` and `posture` report an estate with ZERO OpenSearch
domains when it may have many — the direction that makes an operator stop looking.

**Why a wrong constant survived.** OpenSearch Service mixes two path prefixes under one API
version, and the driver had one constant for all of it:

- `ListDomainNames` is `GET /2021-01-01/domain` — no `/opensearch`
- `ListTags` is `GET /2021-01-01/tags/` — no `/opensearch`
- `DescribeDomain`, `CreateDomain`, `DeleteDomain` are `/2021-01-01/opensearch/domain…`

So four of the six routes were right, which is exactly how a wrong constant survives
review: the thing looks consistent and mostly works. Live AWS agrees with its own model in
both directions — `/2021-01-01/domain` answers "Missing Authentication Token" (the route
exists) and `/2021-01-01/opensearch/domain` answers `<UnknownOperationException/>` (it does
not). There are two constants now, because the difference is real and one constant invites
the mistake back.

**The gate that should have caught it could not.** D274 asks AWS directly whether every
route the drivers build is real, and D717 made its subject derived rather than typed — both
right, and neither enough. It needs network egress behind an opt-in variable, so `make
check` never asks. And its classifier looked for ONE failure signal, the message AWS's
Query/JSON frontend gives. The REST services answer `<UnknownOperationException/>` instead,
which read as "recognised". Every fabricated REST path passed. Its three negative controls
were all Query-frontend routes, so they proved the half that worked and said nothing about
the half that did not — a gate whose controls only exercise its working half is a gate
that cannot fail where it matters.

Three things follow, and none of them is "run the live gate more often":

1. **An offline gate, on every run.** `TestEveryRouteTheDriverBuildsIsARouteAWSHas` matches
   every recorded route against AWS's own published request URIs. Same authority, no
   network, no opt-in. It found both.
2. **The live classifier learns the second signal**, and gains a negative control that
   produces it — the very route removed here. Without that control the new half would be
   asserted rather than proven, and the other three would still pass with it deleted.
3. **A route that cannot be asked about is named, not passed.** Twenty-eight recorded routes
   are a bare `/`: the Query and JSON services choose the operation with an Action field or
   an `X-Amz-Target` header, and an unauthenticated probe sends neither, so AWS answers
   UnknownOperationException for a perfectly real route. Both gates now count them against
   a ceiling that may only fall, and the live one refuses if fewer than a hundred routes
   carried a path. Silence about what a check skipped is how it turns decorative.

**The offline gate passed everything on its first run, and that was the bug.** S3's
`GET /{Bucket}/{Key+}` matches any path of two segments or more, and I had not keyed the
match on the service — so every unmatched route in the file was absorbed by S3 and the gate
reported clean. I found it by asking why the failure I was expecting had not appeared.
Writing a gate against the class "a check that cannot fail" is no protection from writing
one, and a green first run on a known-broken tree is evidence of nothing but a green run.

**Confirmed both ways.** With the classifier fixed, the live gate asked AWS about 166
path-carrying routes across fourteen services and every one is real, all four negative
controls flagged. The offline gate agrees. Neither was true an hour ago.

**A note on what the mutants had to be pointed at.** Three of the four survived their first
verification, and each said something true. The two driver-path mutants survived because
the offline gate reads the RECORDED routes, not the driver's current source — the driver is
held to that record by the capture diff, which is a different guard, so the mutants belonged
against a test that drives the driver. The service-filter mutant survived because a
permissive matcher passes a healthy tree: removing the check breaks nothing until something
is wrong, which is the day the gate is needed. That one is now pinned by a test that hands
the matcher the route this project actually shipped and requires it to be refused. A mutant
that survives is not always a missing test; sometimes it is a question about what the test
is really watching.

## D821 — Three replacements no provider asks for

`immutable` tells the compiler an in-place change is impossible, so the plan carries a
DESTROY AND RECREATE (D48). D807 made every such claim register itself and put a falling
ceiling under the unchecked ones, because the claim is about the PROVIDER's API and only
the provider can settle it. This is the first batch settled, and three of them were wrong.

**What the providers say.**

- `aws/EC2Instance|network.publicExposure` said *"a change is a new machine, not a
  toggle"*. EC2's `ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute` takes `AssociatePublicIpAddress`, and
  `AssociateAddress`/`DisassociateAddress` attach and detach an elastic address on a
  RUNNING instance.
- `gcp/GCEInstance|network.publicExposure` said the same sentence. Compute Engine publishes
  THREE methods for it — `instances.addAccessConfig`, `deleteAccessConfig` and
  `updateAccessConfig` — all against a live interface.
- `aws/OpenSearchServerless|network.publicExposure` said the network policy is *"set at
  create"*. The driver's own observe reads that exposure out of the network POLICY document
  via `GetSecurityPolicy`, and `UpdateSecurityPolicy` replaces that document without
  touching the collection.

The cost of each was a machine or a stateful search collection destroyed — instance-store
data, the address, the uptime — for a change the cloud makes in one call.

**The sibling claims are not defects, and the difference is the whole point.** `aws/ASG`
and `gcp/MIG` say public addressing lives in a launch template *"which groundhold does not
author"*; `aws/AppRunner` says it will not *"claim an in-place ingress flip we do not
exercise"*. Those are true statements about this tool's scope, and both providers do accept
the change (`UpdateAutoScalingGroup` takes a `LaunchTemplate`,
`instanceGroupManagers.setInstanceTemplate` swaps one on a live group) — so the registry now
records that, with the reason the refusal is honest anyway. `aws/LB` and `gcp/LoadBalancer`
are simply correct: elbv2 has no operation that sets `Scheme`, and Google's own discovery
document says of `forwardingRules.patch` that *"you can only patch the network_tier field"*.
Same attribute, nine services, three different verdicts — which is why the registry asks
per claim and not per attribute.

**The fix is the smallest honest one under the freeze**, not the most complete one.
Wiring `addAccessConfig` into an updater is runtime expansion; the defect is the sentence.
So the three become `unsupported`, which BLOCKS the capability with a reason naming the
operation the provider has. A person is told what is true and what groundhold does not do,
instead of being told to destroy a machine. The gap is now visible where an author will
trip over it.

**Where I stopped.** `azure/LoadBalancer` says the frontend IP configuration is fixed at
creation. The ARM model carries `subnet` and `publicIPAddress` side by side with no
mutability marker, which is suggestive and settles nothing, and I found no statement from
Microsoft either way. It stays `unchecked`. A permissive wire shape is not permission —
`azure/ACR|encryption.customerManagedKeys` proves it in the other direction: `encryption`
sits in `RegistryPropertiesUpdateParameters`, and Microsoft's documentation says plainly
*"You can currently enable a customer-managed key only while creating a registry"*. The
service is the authority over the shape, so that claim is now `checked` and CORRECT.

The unchecked ceiling falls from 100 to 91: three claims deleted with the code, six settled
with the provider's own words.

## D822 — Two more, and one of them punished the safe direction

The second batch of D807's registry, same method as D821: ask the provider, and separate a
claim about the CLOUD from a claim about this tool's scope.

- `aws/ASG|availability.class` said the zone spread *"follows the group's subnets, which
  are fixed at creation"*. They are not. `UpdateAutoScalingGroup` accepts
  `VPCZoneIdentifier`, `AvailabilityZones` and `AvailabilityZoneIds` — widening a group's
  zone spread is an ordinary operation, and replacing the group to do it terminates the
  running fleet for nothing.

- `azure/VMSS|availability.class` said the zone list is *"fixed when the scale set is
  created"*. Microsoft's own documentation: *"You can modify a scale set to expand the set
  of zones over which to spread VM instances"*, with the limitation *"You can't remove or
  replace zones, only add zones"*.

The second one is the worst shape a false claim can take. The change it forbade is the one
you WANT people to make — spreading a fleet across more zones — and the price it quoted was
destroying the fleet. A tool that makes the safe direction expensive teaches people not to
take it.

It also settles what `availability.class` means in this vocabulary: the answer is
direction-dependent for scale sets, and the honest classification cannot say "immutable"
just because one direction is. `unsupported` names what Azure supports and what groundhold
does not do.

**The siblings hold, and were checked rather than assumed.** `gcp/MIG` is right because
zonal and regional managed instance groups are different API resources, not two settings of
one. `gcp/GKE` is right because the cluster's location IS its topology. `aws/EBSVolume` and
`aws/EC2Instance` are right for a reason that can be stated mechanically: no
`Modify*`/`Update*`/`Put*`/`Set*` operation on a volume or an instance in the EC2 model
accepts an `AvailabilityZone` or `Placement`.

Nine claims on one attribute, and the verdicts do not agree — the same finding D821 made
about `network.publicExposure`, which is the argument for a registry that asks per claim.

**And a correction to D821, from the same afternoon.** D821 drew the line at "does the
sentence assert something false about the cloud", and kept `aws/ASG`, `gcp/MIG` and
`aws/AppRunner` as `immutable` because their prose was true: public addressing lives in a
launch template groundhold does not author, and App Runner's flip is one this tool does not
exercise. Both statements are still true. The line was in the wrong place.

`immutable` does not mean "we decline to do this". It means NO IN-PLACE CHANGE EXISTS, and
the compiler acts on that by destroying and recreating the resource. All three providers
accept the change — `UpdateAutoScalingGroup` takes a `LaunchTemplate`,
`instanceGroupManagers.setInstanceTemplate` swaps one on a live group, `UpdateService`
takes a `NetworkConfiguration`. A true sentence attached to a verdict that terminates a
running fleet is still a terminated fleet. The test is not whether the prose is honest; it
is what the verdict makes the tool DO.

So those three join the rest as `unsupported`, which refuses and explains rather than
destroys. That is five corrections in this entry and D821, all one shape: a refusal
dressed as an impossibility.

The ceiling falls from 91 to 85, and three more claims leave the registry with the code.

## D823 — A verdict that destroys a disk to reach a state the new disk will also not have

Third batch of D807's registry, and the first one where the defect could be found without
asking a provider anything — because it is a contradiction inside a single return statement.

Two disk classifiers answered `immutable` with the reason *"there is nothing to patch"*.
Those two things cannot both be acted on. `immutable` tells the compiler no in-place change
exists, so it destroys and recreates the resource; *"nothing to patch"* says the attribute
cannot differ at all, because the service always has it that way. Together they instruct
the tool to destroy a managed disk or a persistent disk in order to reach a state the
replacement will also not have. The request is not honoured, and the data is gone.

The honest idiom was already in the tree, twice. App Runner answers `unsupported` for
`tls.enforced` with *"HTTPS-only by construction — nothing to patch (=false cannot be
honored)"*, and the GCE classifier says in its own comment that *"unsupported rather than
immutable is the honest distinction"*. Two classifiers diverged from a convention their
neighbours state out loud — the D464 shape, and this time on the resource where divergence
costs the most.

`TestNoImmutableVerdictSaysThereIsNothingToPatch` reads the drivers' ASTs and refuses any
`immutable` verdict whose reason says the attribute cannot differ. It folds concatenated
string literals, because a reason long enough to be split across lines is exactly the kind
this has to read, and it asserts it found at least forty immutable verdicts before
reporting a clean run (D328).

**And one that did need a provider.** `azure/AzureDisk|encryption.customerManagedKeys` said
the disk-encryption set is *"bound when the disk is created"*. Microsoft publishes the
opposite as a procedure: stop the VM, open the disk, choose the key vault and key under
Customer-managed key, save — *"when your disks finish switching over to customer-managed
keys"*. Changing WHICH key is done on the encryption set and reaches every disk that
references it, without touching a disk at all. Destroying a managed disk to change this
loses what is on it.

**Two that survived the same scrutiny, and the second is the more useful.**
`gcp/Secret|encryption.customerManagedKeys` is correct: the driver puts the key inside
`replication.userManaged.replicas[].customerManagedEncryption`, and Google's discovery
document says of `Secret.replication` — in that word — *"Immutable. The replication policy
... cannot be changed after the Secret has been created"*.

`gcp/PD|encryption.customerManagedKeys` is also correct, and it nearly was not. Compute
Engine has a method called `disks.updateKmsKey`, which reads like a decisive contradiction
until its own description is read: it *"Rotates the customer-managed encryption key to the
latest version"*. A new VERSION of the same key is not a different key, and no method
attaches a key to a disk created without one. A method name is not a capability, and the
whole of this batch's method is refusing to stop reading at the first thing that looks like
an answer.

The ceiling falls from 85 to 80.

## D824 — Five replacements on the two resources where a replacement means losing everything

Fourth batch of D807's registry, and it landed on object storage: the place where "destroy
and recreate" is not downtime but data loss. `azure/Blob` carried six unchecked claims, the
largest cluster left, and four of them were wrong.

- **`durability.class`** said the redundancy is *"fixed at creation"*. Microsoft publishes a
  page titled **"Change how a storage account is replicated"** — the geo-redundancy and
  read-access settings are edited from the portal, PowerShell or the CLI, and LRS→ZRS has a
  documented conversion (`Start-AzStorageAccountMigration`), with real limits for ZRS
  Classic and NFSv3 accounts. Replacing a storage account to change this destroys every
  blob in it. This is the most expensive false claim in the whole audit.

- **`replication.enabled` / `replication.destinationRegion`** already said in their own
  reason that the gap was in *"the blob driver"* — the D822 shape again, an honest sentence
  under a verdict that destroys a stateful account. Azure configures object replication as
  a POLICY on accounts that already exist.

- **`retention.minimum`** shared a case with `retention.locked` and inherited its verdict,
  though the sentence itself said the floor *"can only be extended"* — which is a change.
  Microsoft: *"You can modify an unlocked time-based retention policy to shorten or lengthen
  the retention interval"*, and a locked one is extended with
  `az storage container immutability-policy extend`.

**And the same split in S3, which D821 walked past.** `aws/S3` had `retention.minimum` and
`retention.locked` in one case, under a comment that says outright *"The DefaultRetention
days CAN be re-PUT on an already-object-locked bucket"*. D821 read that as a deliberate
policy choice and left it alone. D822 settled the principle that overrules that reading:
the test is not whether the prose is honest, it is what the verdict makes the tool DO — and
this one deletes a bucket and every object in it to LENGTHEN a retention floor that
`PutObjectLockConfiguration` raises in place. A COMPLIANCE floor still cannot be shortened,
which is a reason to refuse that direction, not a reason to delete the data.

Both `retention.locked` claims survive and are now `checked`: enabling S3 Object Lock is a
CreateBucket header with no operation that turns it off, and a locked Azure immutability
policy cannot be unlocked. One case, two claims, opposite answers — the fourth time in four
batches that splitting a shared `case` was the whole fix.

The ceiling falls from 80 to 73.

## D825 — The same sentence, one resource up

Two more, and neither needed a new investigation — both were visible from what the previous
two entries had already established.

**`azure/AzureVM|encryption.customerManagedKeys`** carried the exact sentence D823
disproved on the disk — *"the disk-encryption set is bound when the disk is created"* — and
drew a heavier conclusion from it: *"re-keying is a new disk, and so a new machine"*. The
same Microsoft procedure applies (stop the VM, open the disk, choose the key vault and key,
save), and rotating WHICH key happens on the encryption set and reaches every disk
referencing it. Fixing a claim on one resource and leaving its copy one level up is how a
defect survives its own fix; the copy is found by searching for the SENTENCE, not for the
service.

**`gcp/AuditLogs`** had `location.region` and `encryption.customerManagedKeys` sharing a
case, with a reason that says they *"live on the destination operand (a separate
capability)"* — that is, they are not properties of the sink at all. Two cases below in the
same switch, `scope.multiRegion` and `integrity.logValidation` answer `unsupported` for
precisely that situation. This one answered `immutable`, which asserts that no in-place
change exists — untrue of the destination too, since a log bucket's `cmekSettings` is
updated by `buckets.patch`. A sink carries no data, so the cost is small; the disagreement
between the sentence and the verdict is not.

That is the fifth shared `case` in five batches where the grouped claims wanted different
answers, and the second time the neighbours in the same switch already had the right idiom
(D823 was the first). Both patterns are cheap to look for and neither needs a provider:
read the switch, and read the sentence against the verdict.

The ceiling falls from 73 to 71: three claims leave the registry with the code, and one of
them — the audit sink's region — was never a claim about a region at all.

## D826 — A claim that was true when it was written

Three hunts in a row found nothing. The mutable/caveated surface checked out, the
load-balancer operand pseudo-paths are a documented shape, and Cloud SQL's RPO reader is
exemplary — it withholds the value under PITR and says a probe is needed, which is the rule
D796 arrived at later. Then the fourth probe went to the place that looked safest.

**A GCS bucket's location is not fixed.** `classifyGCSChange` grouped `location.region`,
`durability.class`, `replication.enabled` and `replication.destinationRegion` into one case
— *"fixed at creation — a change is a replacement"* — with a comment explaining that
`customPlacementConfig` is insert-only. That was accurate. Cloud Storage now publishes
`buckets.relocate`: *"Initiates a long-running Relocate Bucket operation on the specified
bucket"*, and its request carries `destinationLocation`, `destinationCustomPlacementConfig`
and `destinationKmsKeyName`. Google's own documentation says it in one line: *"You can
relocate a bucket after it's created."* The bucket keeps its name and its objects.

So all four paths were wrong together, and the price of the verdict was every object in the
bucket. The durability class follows the location and the dual-region pair IS the custom
placement config, which is why one case held four claims and why fixing it fixes all four.

**Retiring a conformance case, on the owner's decision.** The case
`gcs-plan-refuses-immutable-drift` pinned the old behaviour by name and by refusal code: a
GCS location drift had to be *"refused at plan (consent-required)"*, which is what the
`immutable` verdict produces. The fix and the case cannot both stand, and the project rule
is that the suite is the source of truth and an existing expectation is never edited to make
code pass. This is the other thing — a case whose factual premise the provider changed — so
it went to the owner, who chose to retire it and pin the new truth.

`gcs-plan-blocks-a-relocation-it-cannot-perform` replaces it, and its description carries
the retired case's own words so the history is readable from the suite rather than only
from here. Nothing is destroyed silently under either reading: both outcomes refuse. What
the old one bought was an operator consenting to lose every object in a bucket for a change
Google performs in place.

**Writing it exposed a plan outcome with no conformance shape at all.** A blocked capability
is neither of the two the runner knew: not a refusal (exit 2, a `plan refused:` banner, a
JSON refusal object) and not a clean plan (exit 0). It is a full SealedPlan carrying
`blocked`, covering the other capabilities, at exit 2 — and no expectation key could express
it, which is why no case had ever pinned it. The runner now understands `blocked:`, and
asserts what matters about that outcome: the named capabilities, that each carries a reason,
and that a blocked plan carries no actions.

**The lesson is not "check more claims" but "claims decay".** Every other correction in
D821-D825 was wrong the day it was written. This one was RIGHT the day it was written, and
the provider shipped a capability underneath it. A registry of claims confronted with the
provider is exactly the instrument for that — but only if the confrontation is repeated,
because the answer has a shelf life. The three dry hunts before it are part of the same
finding: the seams that pay are not the ones that look suspicious, they are the ones nobody
has re-read since the API moved.

**And one enum that nearly lied in the other direction.** Checking SQS, `FifoQueue` appears
in the `QueueAttributeName` enum, which is the key type of `SetQueueAttributes`' Attributes
map — which reads exactly like "FIFO can be set after creation". It cannot: that enum is
shared with `GetQueueAttributes`, and the documentation on the request member enumerates
what the operation actually uses, where `ContentBasedDeduplication`, `DeduplicationScope`
and `FifoThroughputLimit` appear and `FifoQueue` does not. A shape that contains a name is
not a promise about it — the same shape as the ACR encryption field in D821, arriving from
the opposite side.

The ceiling falls from 71 to 65: two SQS claims settled with the provider's own
documentation, four GCS claims removed with the code that made them.

## D827 — Sweeping for the decay, and what a negative result is worth

D826 found a claim that was true when it was written and stopped being true. That is a
different failure from the eighteen corrections before it, and it deserves a different
instrument: not "is this claim right?" but "has the provider shipped a way to do it since?"

The shape of such a capability is usually visible in its NAME. So: every operation across
all three clouds — botocore for the forty AWS signing names, the discovery documents for
the twenty-one GCP APIs the driver calls, and every Azure operationId on the api-versions
`apiver` pins — read for a name that means moving or converting a resource.

**One hit, and it was the one already fixed.** `storage.buckets.relocate` (plus its
`operations.advanceRelocateBucket` companion). Everything else that matched is a different
kind of verb: HA operations that do not change an attribute (`sqladmin.instances.switchover`,
`redis…failover`, `file…promoteReplica`), throughput-mode conversions on Cosmos containers we
make no claim about, CDN and API Management platform migrations for services with no claim
in the registry, and rolling OS upgrades on scale sets.

Two near-misses worth writing down, because both would have become findings if I had stopped
reading at the name:

- `ec2:ModifyInstancePlacement` looked like it contradicted D822's "an instance cannot move
  zones". Its input is `GroupName`, `PartitionNumber`, `HostResourceGroupArn`, `GroupId`,
  `InstanceId`, `Tenancy`, `Affinity`, `HostId` — dedicated-host and placement-group
  attributes, no availability zone. `ModifyAvailabilityZoneGroup` changes an ACCOUNT's opt-in
  for a zone group, not a resource's zone.
- My own regex matched `move` inside `remove`, so `removeRule`, `removeInstance` and
  `removeAttestationRule` all came back as candidates. Exactly the sloppiness this project
  keeps finding in other people's code.

**A negative result is worth recording, and it settles claims.** Fourteen `location.region`
claims — thirteen Azure and Cloud SQL — were unchecked because nobody had confronted them
with anything. They are now `checked` against what this sweep actually establishes, stated
at its real strength: no operation on the pinned api-versions moves a resource between
regions, and ARM marks `location` create-and-read wherever the specs annotate mutability at
all. That is evidence, not proof, and the registry line says which.

The value of the sweep is not the hit rate. It is that the next person reads "swept, one
hit, already fixed" instead of doing it again — and that the claims it settled carry the
instrument that settled them.

The ceiling falls from 65 to 51.

## D828 — Where the endpoint is the address every caller holds

D826's lesson said the seams that pay are the ones nobody re-read since the API moved. The
AI services are where APIs move fastest, so that is where the next batch went.

- **`gcp/Vertex|model.provider`** said the model family is *"fixed by the model deployed on
  the endpoint — a change is a new endpoint"*. Vertex's own discovery document:
  `endpoints.deployModel` *"deploys a Model into this Endpoint, creating a DeployedModel
  within it"*, `endpoints.undeployModel` removes one. The swap happens ON the endpoint,
  which keeps its id — and the id is the address every caller holds. A replacement breaks
  all of them, which is a worse failure than the downtime it looks like.

- **`azure/AzureOpenAI|model.provider`** said *"a change is a new deployment, not an
  in-place patch"*. It is a new deployment: a child resource with its own PUT and DELETE,
  present at the api-version this driver pins, leaving the ACCOUNT alone. The verdict
  destroyed the account anyway.

- **`azure/AzureOpenAI|inference.destinationRegions`** said the regions are fixed by *"its
  region and deployment skus — a change is a new account/deployment"*. That slash is the
  whole defect. The driver's own build comment says the regions are *"DETERMINED by the
  deployment skus"*, and a deployment is replaced by a PUT. Only one side of the slash was
  ever required, and it was not the account.

**Bedrock survived the same question, and its evidence is the shape of a good answer.**
`bedrock/2023-04-20` publishes `CreateInferenceProfile`, `DeleteInferenceProfile`,
`GetInferenceProfile` and `ListInferenceProfiles` — and no Update. So *"a change is a new
profile"* is exactly right, and the registry now says so with the operation list that
settles it. Three clouds, one attribute, and the answers differ because the resources
differ: an inference profile really is immutable, a Vertex endpoint and an Azure account
really are not.

The recurring shape of this batch is a reason that names the right ACTION on the wrong
RESOURCE. "A new deployment", "a new endpoint" — both sentences were about something that
must be recreated, and in two of three cases the thing named was not the thing the verdict
destroyed. Reading the noun is as important as reading the verb.

The ceiling falls from 51 to 45.

## D829 — A detector built out of the previous entry's mistake

D828 named its own shape: *a reason that names the right ACTION on the wrong RESOURCE*.
That is mechanical. Every `immutable` reason in the drivers was read for the phrase "a new
<noun>", and the noun compared with the resource its classifier governs.

Twenty-seven reasons say it. Twelve name the resource they govern — a group for Auto
Scaling, a fleet for a scale set, a disk for a persistent disk, an endpoint for Vertex, a
profile for Bedrock. Two do not, and both are on the resource where the mismatch costs
most:

- `aws/EC2Instance|encryption.customerManagedKeys`: *"re-keying is a new volume, **and so a
  new machine**"*
- `gcp/GCEInstance|encryption.customerManagedKeys`: *"re-keying is a new disk, **and so a
  new machine**"*

The first half of each is right. A volume's or disk's key is fixed at creation, so re-keying
does mean a new one. The "and so" is the defect: EC2 has `DetachVolume` and `AttachVolume`,
Compute Engine has `instances.detachDisk` and `instances.attachDisk`. The disk is swapped
UNDERNEATH a machine that keeps its id, its addresses and its instance-store data —
destroying the machine loses all three for a change that never asked for it.

Both now answer `unsupported` with a reason that separates the two nouns explicitly: the
VOLUME must be recreated, the INSTANCE need not be.

**What the detector is worth.** It found exactly two, and both are real — no false
positives to wade through, because the question it asks is narrow enough to have one answer.
That is the argument for turning a finding into an instrument the same day: D828's two
corrections were found by reading, and reading does not scale past the batch you happen to
be in. The phrase that names the shape is the thing to search for, and it was sitting in the
entry I had just written.

The ceiling falls from 45 to 43.

## D830 — Widening the same detector, and finding one I had walked past

D829 turned D828's phrase into an instrument. D830 widens it twice and finds three more,
one of which is an indictment of the previous entry.

**Widening one: the gap is in groundhold.** D822 named the shape — an `immutable` verdict
whose reason says the tool does not do something, rather than that the provider cannot.
That is a phrase too: "not wired", "this slice", "groundhold will not". Three verdicts still
carried it. One is a genuine impossibility that merely also mentions the tool (GKE's
zonal/regional topology, where the location IS the topology). The other two are not:

- `aws/ElastiCacheServerless|engine.protocol` said the change was *"not wired in this
  slice"* and then destroyed a stateful cache. `ModifyServerlessCache` accepts `Engine`
  and `MajorEngineVersion`.
- `azure/AKS|availability.class` said *"an AKS node pool's zone spread is fixed at
  creation"* — a true sentence about a NODE POOL — and destroyed the CLUSTER. Agent pools
  are child resources with their own PUT and DELETE at the pinned api-version, so the API
  server, the identity and the workloads never needed to go. Its neighbour in the same
  switch, `encryption.secrets`, already answers `unsupported` for exactly this.

**Widening two: name the child resource, not the phrase.** D829's detector looked for "a
new <noun>". The AKS sentence never says it — it names a node pool and stops. So the second
pass looked for CHILD-resource nouns (node pool, deployment, volume, disk, frontend,
template, policy) in a reason whose classifier governs the parent. Eight matched; three are
the same resource under a short name (`gcp/PD` governs a disk), two are correct (an
instance's subnet, an Application Gateway's subnet), and one was new:

- `aws/EC2Instance|encryption.atRest`: *"EBS encryption is a property of a volume at
  creation — an existing volume cannot be encrypted in place."* Both halves true about the
  VOLUME; the verdict destroyed the MACHINE.

**That one sat one case above the line D829 corrected.** I fixed `encryption.customerManagedKeys`
and left `encryption.atRest` directly above it — one entry after writing, in D825, that the
copy is found by searching for the SENTENCE rather than the service. It was not found by
searching for the sentence either: this version never mentions a machine, so nothing in
D829's net could catch it. What would have caught it is the cheapest check available —
reading the neighbouring cases of a switch I was already editing. Two entries have now named
that habit and neither made it one.

The fourth claim in this batch is evidence rather than a fix:
`aws/ElastiCacheServerless|encryption.customerManagedKeys` is CORRECT, and the same
`ModifyServerlessCache` member list proves it — the operation takes an engine and a version
and no KMS key.

The ceiling falls from 43 to 39.

## D831 — Auditing by classifier instead of by attribute

D830 ended by noting that "read the neighbouring cases" had been named twice and made a
habit neither time. A third resolution would have been worth nothing, so the UNIT OF WORK
changed instead: the remaining claims are now taken one classifier at a time, whole, rather
than one attribute across all of them. Neighbours are then read by construction.

**The first classifier audited that way produced a defect the attribute view had hidden.**
Three drivers bind a Kubernetes service account to a cloud identity, and all three called
`workload.namespace` and `workload.serviceAccount` immutable with the same sentence: *"a
different binding is a different resource"*. For two of them that is exactly right, and the
proof is in their own providerId — `eks-podidentity:<region>:<cluster>/<ns>/<sa>` and
`gke-wi:<poolProject>:<gsa>:<ns>:<sa>` both ENCODE the pair, so changing it addresses
something else. That is the argument that settles a resource whose location is part of its
name.

`azure/AKSWorkloadIdentity` is the exception, and it says so twelve lines above the claim:
the credential name is derived from capability+environment, and *"the subject
(namespace/serviceAccount) is recovered by reading the credential back, never re-encoded
into the pid"*. So the resource does not move. Its subject is a property Azure updates with
a PUT — `federatedIdentityCredentials/{name}` has PUT at the pinned api-version and its
properties are `issuer`, `subject`, `audiences`. The claim was inherited from twins whose
identity scheme it does not share.

Seen per attribute, three drivers agreeing looks like corroboration. Seen per classifier,
the file's own comment contradicts the claim eight lines down. The attribute view is what
made three identical sentences read as evidence for each other.

**Ten more settled mechanically, in the same pass.** ACM mutates a certificate only through
`UpdateCertificateOptions`, `RenewCertificate`, `ResendValidationEmail` and tags — neither
the domain nor the validation method is reachable. `ModifyDBCluster`'s only KMS member is
`MasterUserSecretKmsKeyId`, the key for the managed master-user SECRET, so Aurora's storage
encryption and its key are genuinely create-time. `ModifyVolume` accepts size, type, IOPS,
throughput and multi-attach — no encryption, no key.

**And one that stays unchecked, with its trail.** `azure/LoadBalancer|sku` needs a sentence
from Microsoft rather than a fact from a spec: the Application Gateway's SKU shape carries
no mutability annotation, and Azure annotates those sparsely enough that silence proves
nothing. Microsoft's documentation renders through script and does not yield to the tools
here. That is the third Azure claim in this series to stop at the same wall, and it is worth
naming as a limit of the method rather than left looking unexamined.

The ceiling falls from 39 to 27.

## D832 — The DNS name is the address, and a listener is not a load balancer

Continuing per classifier. One defect, nine settled, and a third instance of the trap that
has now caught me from both directions.

**`aws/LB|encryption.inTransit`** said *"switching the front door between HTTP and HTTPS
re-shapes the listener + certificate — a replacement, not an in-place patch"*. The
re-shaping is real and it is of the LISTENER. `ModifyListener` takes `Protocol`, `SslPolicy`
and `Certificates`, and AWS documents the switch in the operation's own text: *"Changing the
protocol from HTTPS to HTTP, or from TLS to TCP, removes the security policy and default
certificate."* Replacing the balancer changes its DNS name — the address every client and
every DNS record holds — for a change that never touches it. Same shape as D828's Vertex
endpoint id: the resource's ADDRESS is the thing a replacement quietly destroys, and it
never appears in the reason.

**Its GCP twin is correct, and the citation is what makes the difference visible.** There
the posture selects an HTTP versus an HTTPS target proxy, and
`compute.forwardingRules.setTarget` says in Google's own discovery document that *"the new
target should be of the same type as the old target"*. The proxy genuinely cannot be swapped
under the rule. Two clouds, one attribute, opposite answers — and only reading each
provider's own sentence separates them.

**Nine settled, most of them by the same argument.** All three addon drivers encode the
addon name in the providerId, and all three DNS drivers encode the record type — so a change
addresses a different resource, which is the argument that already settled Vertex's location
and the two workload-identity twins. It is worth naming as a family: *when the disputed
value is part of the identity, immutability is not a claim about the API at all.*

**And the trap, for the third time.** `ModifyDBInstance` DOES carry an `Engine` member,
which reads exactly like "RDS can change a database's engine". Its own documentation scopes
it to converting an Oracle non-CDB to a CDB — `oracle-ee-cdb` or `oracle-se2-cdb` — and
lists the limitations. There is no operation that changes the engine FAMILY, so the claim
holds. D826 met this from the other side (S3's `FifoQueue` sitting in a shared enum), D821
from the ACR side (a field in an update shape the service refuses). A shape that contains a
name is not a promise about it, and this time reading the sentence stopped a defect from
being manufactured rather than one from shipping.

The ceiling falls from 27 to 17.

## D833 — Two siblings, one mechanism, opposite answers

The classifier audit reached OpenSearch Serverless, where D821 had already corrected
`network.publicExposure` because the exposure lives in a POLICY that `UpdateSecurityPolicy`
edits. Two cases below it, `encryption.customerManagedKeys` made the same kind of claim
about the same kind of policy — and the driver has one function, `ensureSecurityPolicy(kind)`,
serving both. Every instinct from D830 said this was the sibling left behind.

**It is not, and only AWS's own words could say so.** The encryption policy IS editable —
`UpdateSecurityPolicy` takes it, the console edits it. But: *"You can't change the encryption
key for a collection after the collection is created"*, and modifying a policy's rules
*"doesn't affect existing collections that have KMS keys already assigned"*. The network
policy governs access continuously; the encryption policy governs assignment at creation.
Same mechanism, same driver function, opposite semantics — so D821's fix and this
non-fix are both right.

That is the counterweight this series needed. Six entries have found sibling cases that
were wrong together; this one would have been a defect manufactured out of a pattern.

**A real one, on the resource where it costs most.** `aws/S3|durability.class` answered
`immutable`. A general-purpose bucket is regional — always: observe emits that constant, and
the builder's own refusal for `single-zone` explains why. So a replacement produces another
regional bucket, the contract is still unsatisfied, and every object is gone. That is D823's
contradiction — destroying a resource to reach a state the replacement will also have —
found this time not by the phrase but by reading a classifier next to its own builder.

Four more settled with the family argument D832 named. Artifact Registry needed no argument
at all: Google's field description ends *"This value may not be changed after the Repository
has been created."* ECR's `encryptionConfiguration` is reachable only from
`CreateRepository`. A zonal disk and a regional disk are different resources in compute/v1,
and an instance is addressed at `/zones/{zone}/instances/{name}`.

The ceiling falls from 17 to 11.

**Postscript, from this entry's own meter run.** The registry mutant that holds the ceiling
honest went NO-OP for the third time, and for the third time the cause was the same: its
anchor named a specific claim (`aws/S3|durability.class|unchecked`) in the one file every
slice edits. Repointing it twice was treating the symptom. Its anchor is now defined by
SHAPE — `s/\|unchecked\n/|checked: invented\n/` flips whichever unchecked line comes
first — so it survives any registry edit that leaves at least one unchecked claim, which is
exactly the condition under which it has anything to measure.

And a sequencing error of mine, worth naming because it defeated the tool built to prevent
it. D819 added the anchor check so a stale anchor costs a minute instead of an afternoon. I
then chained it to the full run with `;` instead of `&&`, so the three-hour meter started
even though the forty-second check had already failed and said so. The check worked; the
shell did what I told it.

## D834 — Which reference is evidence, and which is only a shape

Two claims left that needed a documentation sentence rather than a spec fact, and the CLI
references answered one of them decisively while proving nothing about the other. The
difference is worth stating, because it decides what counts as evidence.

**`gcp/PubSubQueue`** put `delivery.guarantee` and `ordering.enabled` in one case and called
both immutable. `gcloud pubsub subscriptions update` is a command that builds an explicit
update MASK — what it accepts is a statement about what the API updates. Its synopsis
carries `--enable-exactly-once-delivery`, and the page carries no ordering flag anywhere. So
the two halves differ: exactly-once is turned on for a live subscription, message ordering
is chosen at create. Replacing a subscription to raise its delivery guarantee drops the
undelivered backlog for a change Google makes in place. Seventh shared case in this series,
and the seventh time the grouped claims wanted different answers.

**`azure/ServiceBusQueue` stays unchecked, and the reason is the instrument.** `az
servicebus queue update` does carry `--enable-session` and `--enable-duplicate-detection` —
and that says nothing, because the command is a PUT of the whole queue, so its flags mirror
the resource SHAPE rather than the service's answer. This is the same trap as ACR's
`encryption` sitting in `RegistryPropertiesUpdateParameters` (D821), S3's `FifoQueue` in a
shared enum (D826), and RDS's `Engine` member scoped to one Oracle conversion (D832) —
arriving a fourth time, from a fourth direction.

The rule that separates them: **a reference is evidence when the thing it lists is the thing
the API updates, and only a shape when the thing it lists is the thing the resource has.**
An update mask is the first; a whole-resource PUT is the second.

The ceiling falls from 11 to 9.

## D835 — Correcting D834's rule, and naming the wall the method stops at

D834 published a rule for what counts as evidence: *a reference is evidence when the thing
it lists is the thing the API updates, and only a shape when the thing it lists is the thing
the resource has.* Applying it to the nine claims left — all of them Azure — shows the rule
needs a correction, and the correction is in this repository's own history.

**An Azure dedicated update body is still only a shape.** ARM's `*Update` types look exactly
like the first half of the rule: `VirtualMachineUpdate` carries `zones`, `DiskUpdate` carries
`sku`, and both are the body of a PATCH whose whole purpose is updating. By D834's wording
that is evidence. It is not — and the counterexample is D821: ACR's `encryption` sits in
`RegistryPropertiesUpdateParameters`, a dedicated update body, and Microsoft's documentation
says *"You can currently enable a customer-managed key only while creating a registry."* The
service refuses a field its own update body carries.

So the rule holds for a listing the API DERIVES from what it will change — a gcloud update
mask, botocore's per-operation input shape — and fails for one a generator DERIVES from the
resource, which is what ARM's `*Update` types are. The distinction is not PATCH versus PUT;
it is whether the list was written by the thing that performs the update.

**Three instruments tried on the nine, none of them decisive.** The `*Update` bodies say
`zones` and `sku` are updatable, and D821 shows that is not a promise. The
`x-ms-mutability` annotation would be an explicit statement, and none of the nine fields
carries one — the specs annotate about fifty definitions in four thousand files, so silence
there is not an answer either. Microsoft's prose is the authority that settled ACR, VMSS
zones and managed-disk keys earlier in this series, and for these nine it renders through
script and does not yield to the tools available here.

**The nine stay unchecked, and this is what they are:** ActivityLog's CMK; the availability
class of an Azure VM and of a managed disk; the Application Gateway's sku, its two subnet
spellings and its public exposure; and a Service Bus queue's delivery guarantee and
ordering. They are the residue of a method that has settled ninety-one claims and corrected
twenty-six, and the residue is not random — it is one cloud, and one kind of question:
"does the service accept this field", asked where the only honest answer is published as
prose.

What would settle them is a tester's run against a real Azure estate (the field evidence
this project has always said is the input the next unfreeze is spent on), or a
documentation source that renders without script. Neither is something to invent here, and
a claim marked `checked` on anything weaker would be the exact failure this registry exists
to prevent.

## D836 — A capability that holds retained audio, published as stateless in two places

The immutable-claims line reached its wall, so this took the pattern that produced it —
*claims phrased as a consequence go unchecked, claims phrased as a fact get checked when
written* — to the other place the compiler states a consequence: the RISK annotation on a
delete. `deleteRisk` sets `DataLoss: "certain"` when the capability is stateful and
`"none"` otherwise, and `stateful` also decides whether a delete is refused without consent
and whether a replacement needs `allow_replace_stateful`.

Fifty-seven vocabularies declare the flag and forty-two justify it in a comment. Of the
fifteen that do not, one declares attributes that contradict it: `capability.ai.speech` is
`stateful: false` while carrying `retention.maximum` — *"the longest audio or transcripts
may be retained by the capability before deletion"* — and `encryption.atRest`. Its own
preamble says the type exists because *"voice is personal data"* and an organization must be
able to prove *"how long it survives"*.

So a plan to delete or replace one told an operator that nothing would be lost, for a
resource whose vocabulary is about how long the recordings last.

**One bit, three clouds, and the honest reading.** An Azure AI Speech account holds the
retained data; a GCP recognizer is closer to configuration; AWS Transcribe has no resource
at all and is witnessed. The flag cannot express that, and `StatefulOf` already fails closed
for an unknown type — so the honest value for a single bit is the cloud where a delete costs
the most. It is now `true`, with the reasoning in the comment that the other forty-two have.

**Two published copies, and nothing compared them.** A conformance case may carry its
vocabulary inline, which is what lets it pin engine behaviour without depending on the
shipped spec. Where the case names a capability the spec also defines, that freedom becomes
two copies of one closed set — and three had drifted: `ai.speech`, `cluster.namespace` and
`network.private` all said `stateful: false` in `breadth-vocab.yaml` while the spec said
true. Two of those predate this entry. The cases are all verify-shaped, so no expectation
depended on the flag and aligning the fixtures changed nothing in the suite — 547/547 before
and after. That is the D329/D330/D338 shape, and the answer is the same: gate every copy.
`TestCaseSuppliedVocabulariesAgreeWithTheSpec` compares them and asserts it found at least a
hundred blocks before reporting clean.

**And a shell trap I had already been caught by once.** The mutant for the case drift used a
perl backreference, `${1}`, inside a double-quoted string in a `set -u` script — bash
expanded it as an unset positional parameter and the meter died at the mutate call site, two
lines above the expression. The fix is the same as last time: write the substitution without
a capture group. Repairing it, I then replaced the line the ERROR named rather than the line
that contained the fault, and broke the block a second way. A shell error reports where
evaluation happened, not where the bad text lives.

## D837 — "None" is a claim, and a delete kept making it about security

D836 read the risk annotation's DataLoss field. The same function states four more
consequences, and one of them was a constant where it should have been a question.

`deleteRisk` set `SecurityExposure: "none"` for every delete of every capability. Three
lines above the neighbouring `updateRisk`, this file states the rule it was breaking:

> *Where the direction is not derivable, the answer is "possible", never "none": the
> compiler has established nothing about it, and `none` is a claim.*

For most deletes "none" is a fair answer — removing a resource is not an exposure by itself.
But two capability types exist to BE a security control, and the vocabulary says so with a
marker D698 put there for this exact question: `capability.security.waf` and
`capability.security.threatdetection` carry `protection: true`. Deleting one is the plainest
exposure a plan can carry, and the plan said there was none.

The fix is the one D698 already prepared: `policy.ProtectionOf` at each of the three delete
sites, and `SecurityExposure: "certain"` when it answers yes. Ordinary deletes keep "none"
rather than becoming a shrug — the compiler HAS established something about them.

**What made this findable is the same thing that made D836 findable.** Both are claims the
compiler states as a consequence of a fact it holds, both were written as a constant, and in
both cases the fact was already in the vocabulary with a marker on it. The pattern from the
immutable series holds one layer up: a claim phrased as a consequence goes unchecked, and
the place to look is wherever the code fills in a consequence without asking the question
that decides it.

The remaining constants in `deleteRisk` — `Reversibility: "R4"`, `Downtime: "certain"`,
`IdentityReplacement: true`, a zero CostDelta — are each true for every delete this compiler
can emit, and are left as they are. The zero cost is the weakest of them: deleting a
resource usually SAVES money, so zero is a floor rather than a measurement. It is recorded
here rather than changed, because a cost model is not something to invent inside a risk
annotation.

## D838 — An inconsistency that turned out to be two different questions

D837 fixed a consequence the compiler stated as a constant for deletes, so its sibling
looked like the next one: `createRisk` answers `SecurityExposure: "none"` for every create,
while `updateRisk` calls the SAME end state "certain" when it is reached by flipping the
attribute on a resource that already exists. Same resource, same declared value, opposite
annotations — and the create is the action that brings the exposure into existence. It read
like a clear defect and the fix was small: extract the direction table from
`weakensSecurity` into `exposingValue(path, v)`, and have `createRisk` ask it of the
declared value.

**The conformance suite refused it, and was right.** Two cases —
`gcp-public-cloud-run-is-probed-on-its-uri` and
`azure-external-containerapp-is-probed-on-its-fqdn` — stopped applying and answered
`REFUSED consent-required`. Marking a create as exposing makes converge demand consent, and
those contracts DECLARE a public service. The change would have made every deliberately
public service a consent prompt.

That is the trace I should have followed before writing the fix, and following it shows the
two annotations are not answering one question:

* `updateRisk` describes a CHANGE against a prior state: the resource was private and the
  action makes it public. That is risk the contract did not ask for at the moment of the
  change — it is drift being reconciled — and consent is exactly the right response.
* `createRisk` describes bringing a resource into existence AS DECLARED. The exposure is not
  a consequence of the action beyond what the contract asked for; it IS what the contract
  asked for. Consent for it would be asking an operator to re-approve the document they
  wrote.

So "none" on a create is not the claim it looks like. It is not saying "this resource is not
