exposed" — it is saying "this action exposes nothing the contract did not declare". Both
changes are reverted, and the extraction with them: a one-caller helper would have been
indirection bought with nothing.

**What this cost and what it bought.** An hour, and the discipline held where it mattered —
the source of truth was asked before the change shipped, and it answered. The lesson to
carry is narrower than "check the suite": when a field feeds a CONSENT gate, its meaning is
fixed by what consent is for, and no amount of internal symmetry between two functions
overrides that. The symmetry was real; the conclusion drawn from it was not.

## D839 — Running a comparator that had never been given anything to compare

`apiver` has held a registry of the API versions every driver pins since D236, with a pure
comparator that answers four-valued drift against a live version list, and a `--live` flag
to feed it one. The fetcher that PRODUCES that list was left to "the canary" and never
written. So the pins have sat for as long as they have existed, and the comparison had never
run once.

Google's discovery directory answers the question for GCP without credentials — one request,
526 APIs, each with a `preferred` flag. `scripts/apiver-live-gcp.sh` builds the snapshot from
it, and this is what the comparator says about 83 pins the first time it is asked.

**Ten AWS pins: cannot-verify, and correctly so.** AWS publishes no authoritative
"current version" endpoint, which is why `apiver` structurally bars AWS from ever reading
`pinned-current`. Nothing to fix; the verdict is the honest one.

**Forty-three Azure pins: unfetched.** ARM advertises api-versions per resource type behind a
subscription, and `azure-rest-api-specs` lists versions but carries no preferred or
deprecated flag — a snapshot built from it would answer a weaker question than the
comparator asks, while looking like an answer. Left alone deliberately, which is the same
call D835 made about the nine Azure claims.

**Twenty-nine GCP pins compared, one omitted, three flagged — and only one of the three is
real.**

- `resource-manager` is pinned at v1 and Google marks **v3** preferred. That is a true
  signal: the driver reads project IAM policy and enumerates projects through v1.
- `iam v1 → v2` and `monitoring-dashboard v1 → v3` are artefacts of GRANULARITY. A pin names
  a service; the directory names an API version. IAM v2 is the deny-policies surface, not a
  successor to the service-account and custom-role calls this driver makes, and monitoring
  v3 is the metrics surface while dashboards live under monitoring v1. The comparator cannot
  see that a newer version of the same API is a different surface, and no flag in the
  directory says so.

That limit is the finding worth carrying more than the drift is. `apiver` exits 2 on
actionable drift so CI can gate — and two of its three actionable results here would be
noise. A gate that cries wolf twice for every real signal gets switched off, which is how a
check becomes decorative without anyone deciding to remove it.

**Nothing was bumped.** The tool's own rule is "surface, do not follow: a human reviews and
bumps the pin", the freeze admits false statements rather than upgrades, and one of the
three signals is real. It is recorded here for whoever spends the next unfreeze.

**One refusal that earned its keep immediately.** The first, ad-hoc version of the fetcher
produced 29 snapshots for 30 pins and said nothing — the missing one was `scc`, whose API is
absent from the public directory and whose own discovery endpoint answers 403. A snapshot
that quietly omits a service makes the comparator answer cannot-verify for it, which is
indistinguishable from a fetch that failed: the "silence read as agreement" shape, produced
by me, in the instrument built to check for exactly that. The committed script separates a
pin missing from the MAP (a refusal) from one known to be unlisted (omitted, named, with the
reason on stderr).

## D840 — Every AWS permission the compiler declares is a real one

D75 has plans declare `requiredPermissions` per action and preflights their union against
the acting identity before the lease. The guarantee is refuse-before-mutating, and it rests
on the strings being real: a permission that does not exist is a preflight testing nothing,
and its pass is evidence of nothing. `TestClaimPermissionsWired` checks the SHAPE of those
lists — non-empty, sorted, deduped — and nothing checked the strings.

Three hundred and sixty-seven distinct AWS permission strings across forty-two services,
confronted with the operation lists in botocore's own models. **None is fabricated.** Twenty
looked like mismatches and every one has a reason worth writing down, because the reasons
are what a future sweep needs:

- **The action IS an HTTP verb.** `apigateway:GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` — API Gateway
  authorises by method, not by operation name.
- **The action exists only in policy.** `iam:PassRole` is the canonical one; there is no API
  operation and never was.
- **The action's name differs from the operation's.** `lambda:InvokeFunction` for `Invoke`;
  `budgets:ViewBudget` and `ModifyBudget` for `DescribeBudget` and `UpdateBudget`; five S3
  actions whose operations are spelled `PutBucketEncryption`, `PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration`
  and so on. IAM's namespace and the API's are related, not identical.
- **My own service map was wrong.** Six SES actions read as missing because the sweep
  compared them against the v1 model; all six are in `sesv2`. The ALSO map that
  `refresh-aws-fieldnames.sh` carries for exactly this reason was not in my throwaway script
  — the fourth time in this run that an ad-hoc instrument's blind spot arrived before any
  real finding did.

**GCP and Azure are unswept, and the reason is the same wall as D835 and D839.** Google's
predefined-role listing — the natural authority for "is this a real permission" — answers
403 without credentials, as does the SCC discovery document. There is no public equivalent
for ARM role actions either. That is now three separate confrontations stopped at the same
place: the surfaces where a claim needs an authenticated call are the surfaces a tester with
a real estate can settle and nobody here can.

**No gate was built.** The sweep found nothing, and a gate with no defect behind it is
deferred work under the freeze — the same call D827 made about its own clean sweep. What is
kept is the taxonomy above, which is the part that cost the time.

## D841 — Why D820's route gate does not transfer to GCP

D820 built an offline gate that confronts every route the AWS drivers construct with the
request URIs in AWS's own models, and it found two paths AWS answers 404 to. GCP has a live
route-reality gate (D274/D718) behind an opt-in variable, so `make check` never asks, and
building the offline twin looked like the obvious completion. It is not buildable in that
shape, and the reason is a real difference between the clouds rather than a missing effort.

**Three instrument bugs on the way to the answer, each found by an implausible number.**

1. Matching the recorded path against `method.path` reported 193 of 314 routes as fake.
   Google puts the version segment in the METHOD path (`v1/{+parent}/feeds`) while the
   driver's base URL already carries it; Compute is the exception whose base is
   `.../compute/v1/`, which is why Compute alone matched. Fixed by comparing full URLs.
2. Still 155 of 314. Google spells a greedy path parameter `{+parent}` — the plus BEFORE
   the name — where AWS spells it `{Key+}`. One regex covered both spellings and collapsed
   both to a single segment, so every resource-name method failed to match.
3. With greedy parameters handled, 0 of 314 failed — and that number is worthless. The
   negative control settles it: `GET /v1/totally/made/up/path` reads as REAL, because
   `cloudasset` v1 has `GET v1/{+name}` and its greedy parameter swallows any path under the
   API. All 24 of that API's methods carry a greedy parameter.

**That is the difference.** AWS models a REST path as literal segments with narrow
placeholders, so a template match discriminates. Google models resources by NAME —
`v1/{+name}` is the shape of most getters — so a template match accepts nearly everything
under the API and answers "real" for a path that does not exist. An offline gate of this
shape would be the thing this repository keeps finding and calling by its name: a gate that
cannot fail.

So GCP's route reality has to be asked of the provider, which is exactly what the live gate
does — an unauthenticated request distinguishes a real route (401) from an absent one (a
404 from the frontend), per path, with no template matching involved. The gate that exists
is the right instrument, and the gap worth closing is that it is opt-in, not that it is
missing.

Nothing was built. What is recorded is why, so the next person reading "AWS has an offline
route gate and GCP does not" stops here instead of spending the afternoon I spent.

## D842 — Asking Google directly: 690 routes, all real

D841 concluded that GCP's route reality has to be asked of the provider and that the gap is
the live gate being opt-in. The cheapest way to close a gap like that is to run the thing,
so: `GROUNDHOLD_LIVE_GCP_SMOKE=1`, no credentials, two minutes.

**3964 requests for 690 routes; every one real; nothing unmeasurable.** The gate reports
311 of the routes as checked against a candidate set — the ambiguity D718 documents, where
the test harness points several base-URL overrides at one fixture so a recorded origin
cannot say which service it belonged to — and it accuses only when a route exists under
none of its candidates. Zero accusations, and zero routes it could not measure.

That is the same shape as D839: an instrument built, correct, and never once run. Two in one
day suggests the pattern is not about these two instruments.

**And the second offline idea, tried and also dead.** D841 killed template matching because
Google's `{+name}` parameters swallow any path. The obvious retreat is to check literal
COLLECTION segments instead — `feeds` is a real collection, `invented` is not — which needs
no template match at all. It fails for the same root cause, in the other direction: the
discovery document for `cloudasset` names six literal segments, and `projects` is not among
them, because the parent is inside the greedy parameter too. Every real route gets accused.

So the discovery document does not carry what an offline check would need. A resource-name
API describes its methods against a name grammar, and the parents in that grammar are not
enumerated anywhere in the document. That is not a gap in the instrument — it is what the
document is.

The thread closes here: AWS routes are checked offline on every run (D820), GCP routes are
checkable only live and are currently clean (this entry), Azure has neither and D835 says
why. Nothing left to build without a tester's estate.

## D843 — Every instrument that could be run without credentials, run

D839 and D842 each found an instrument built, correct, and never once executed. Two in a day
is a class, not a coincidence, so the class got swept: every test behind an environment
guard and every script in `scripts/`, sorted by whether it can run here at all.

**Run, and clean:**

- `TestLiveAWSSmoke` — the transport/ALPN check, explicitly credential-free. EKS reachable,
  HTTP/1.1, no malformed response. This is the class that once broke EVERY request (D269)
  while `make check` stayed green, so it is the one worth knowing about.
- `TestLiveGCPEndpointReality` — 690 routes, 3964 requests (D842).
- `TestLiveAWSEndpointReality` — 166 path-carrying routes (D820), where running it also
  exposed that its classifier was blind to the REST failure signal.
- `groundhold apiver --live` — 83 pins, one real drift signal (D839).

**Cannot run here, and should not:** `TestLiveAWSSignedSmoke` and the live RDS round-trip
need real AWS credentials. The signed smoke says in its own comment that when it skips, the
SigV4 class is unmeasured and `preship.sh` refuses to call the run clean — which is the
honest arrangement. Those two, plus the nine Azure claims of D835 and the GCP permission
list of D840, are now the whole of what waits on a tester with an estate.

**A correction to my own sweep.** `refresh-aws-routeops.sh` and `refresh-azure-fieldnames.sh`
looked unreferenced because I grepped the Makefile, CI and docs — and a refresh script is
named by the GATE that consumes its output, in a Go error message. Both are wired. Looking
for a caller in the places callers usually live is how a live thing reads as dead.

The pattern behind D839 and D842 is worth stating plainly, because it is not about those two
instruments: **a gate that requires a flag to run is a gate that has never run.** Every
credential-free one in this repository had a green answer waiting in it, and one of them had
a real finding. The flags are there for good reasons — network egress does not belong in
`make check` — but "opt-in" quietly means "off", and nothing measures how long a gate has
been off.

## D844 — Three headers naming an exception list, all three wrong the same way

Each driver publishes a parity map: one capability TYPE per certified service token, and
`groundhold parity` prints the matrix built from all three. Every header makes the same
promise — the values are *"the exact capability string the service's Observe/discover stamps
as ResourceType — ground truth, not a guess"* — and then names the handful of tokens that
are the exception, whose type comes from the Build dispatch instead.

All three exception lists were wrong, with one cause:

- **AWS** named *"the three non-listable tokens (changefeed, rolepolicy, cwlogfilter)"*.
  `rolepolicy` IS stamped — the file's own inline comment twelve lines below says
  "discoverRoleGrants literal" — and `route53record`, which is not stamped, was missing.
- **GCP** said *"the one non-listable token (assetfeed)"*; there are two.
- **Azure** said *"the two non-listable tokens"*; there are three.

Each omission is the DNS-record token. That driver is a sub-resource of a zone on all three
clouds and arrived after the headers were written, so all three prose lists aged the same
way on the same day.

**This is a claim inside the repository, not one the tool makes to a user**, and it is worth
saying so plainly: no plan, verdict or receipt was wrong. What was wrong is a sentence three
people would trust while auditing the map — including, in D831 and here, me.

`TestEveryParityValueIsBackedByTheDriver` replaces the prose with something that reads it: a
value must appear as a capability literal somewhere in its own driver package, or be named
in the test's exception table with the reason. A dropped exception fails; a stale one fails.

**The scan had to be written twice, and the reason belongs in the entry.** Looking for
`ResourceType: "capability.x"` reports twenty of Azure's forty-five as unbacked — Azure
threads the type through a shared sweep helper as an ARGUMENT rather than a struct field.
A gate that assumes one driver's idiom measures the other two badly, and the number it
produces looks exactly like a finding.

## D845 — "One $def per verb", said by a schema with defs for less than half of them

`spec/outputs.schema.json` is the published contract a consumer generates types from, and
its own description opened with **"One $def per verb."** It carries twenty defs. Running
the binary settles the rest: `parity` prints a capability map, `apiver` prints its pin
catalogue, and `posture` prints `{at, summary, rows, postureHash}` — none of the three is
described anywhere in the schema.

This is a stronger version of D844's shape. There the wrong claim was a Go comment; here it
is in `spec/`, which is the artefact the project tells consumers to trust, and the sentence
says the coverage is total.

**The existing gate could not see it, by construction.** D559's
`TestPublishedFieldsAreInTheOutputSchema` walks FROM each def TO its struct and asks whether
a described field exists. That direction catches a schema promising what nothing emits. The
opposite direction — a document nothing describes — was never asked, and it is where a whole
verb can go missing rather than a field.

The description now says what is true, and `TestVerbsPublishingWithoutASchemaDef` holds it:
a register of verbs verified to publish an undescribed document, failing if one names a verb
the CLI does not have, failing if the schema gains a def while the register still claims the
debt, and failing if the description re-asserts total coverage while the register is
non-empty.

**Everything the register names was observed, and the five that started unmeasured were
measured.** `cost`, `diff`, `suggest`, `runs` and `status` need arguments, so each was given
real ones — a contract, a candidate, a plan, an empty ledger — and each printed a document:
`{specVersion, contract, environment, currency, weekly}`, `{specVersion, contract,
environmentA, environmentB, hardOnlyInA}`, `{specVersion, contract, environment, suggested,
alreadyEnforced}`, `{byState, runs, total}`, `{handle, kind, state, code, lease}`. Eight
verbs, not three.

`apiver` is the sharpest of them: it prints `apiVersion: apiver/v0` — a VERSIONED envelope,
the shape this project uses to say "this document has a contract" — and no spec file
describes `apiver/v0` at all.

**And one that was checked out of the register before it went in.** `forecast` also prints
an undescribed-by-the-schema document, with a full `apiVersion: forecast/v0` envelope, and
it looked like the ninth and most damning entry: a headline verb with its own DESIGN
history. It is not a gap. `spec/forecast.md` carries a `## Document` section that specifies
that envelope, exactly as `spec/sealed-plan.md` does for `plan/v0`. Searching every spec file
for document envelopes finds three — `forecast/v0`, `plan/v0`, `state/v0` — so the schema is
not the only place a shape is published, and a register that ignored the others would have
made a true claim into a false one. The eight that remain are described NOWHERE.

**And nothing else holds their shape either.** The schema is one of two places a document's
shape is pinned; the other is the conformance suite, which is the source of truth for
semantics and would catch a field that silently changed name. It does not catch these. Of
the eight, FIVE — `posture`, `parity`, `apiver`, `cost`, `diff` — are exercised by no
conformance case at all. The three that are exercised assert three scalars between them:
`runs` a `total`, `status` a `state`, and `suggest` only its EXIT CODE, which says nothing
about the document at all. So for seven of the eight, every field name and every nesting
choice is held by nothing but the code that prints it, and could change in a patch release
without one test going red. That is not itself the falsehood this entry fixes — it is the
reason the falsehood mattered: the schema's promise was the only thing a consumer could
have relied on, and it was the one that was untrue.

**How it was found, and the count of my own bad instruments.** This came out of D777, the
one item flagged for the owner: checking who consumes `shadowLowerBound` showed that the
entire `posture` document is outside the schema — which changes the cost of one of D777's
three options, the `sweptServices`/`certified` pair, since that option adds a field to a
document no consumer can type. Getting there, two of my measurements were wrong and both
were caught before they were reported: a regex over `case "..."` counted scalar kinds and
provider names as verbs, and a filter on `--json` missed every verb that prints a document
without the flag. That is six and seven in this run. The rate is the argument for the
register being hand-verified rather than derived from another pattern.

**And a third shell trap, plus the same editing mistake twice.** The mutant for this entry
substitutes a string containing `$def`, and bash under `set -u` expanded it as an unset
variable — the D836 trap in new clothes. Writing the dollar as `\x24`, which perl reads and
the shell does not, ends that class for good. Then, repairing it, I replaced the line the
error NAMED rather than the line holding the fault, and broke the block — which is precisely
what D836 records me doing, three entries earlier. Knowing a lesson and having it are
different things, and the only reliable fix so far has been the forty-second anchor check
catching the mess immediately.

## D846 — Two permissions an operator cannot grant, in the list they write policy from

`requiredPermissions` is not internal bookkeeping. It is sealed into the plan, it is what
an operator builds an IAM policy from, and `apply` SIMULATES it through
`iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy` before taking the lease. Two of the 357 AWS permissions this
project declares are not IAM actions at all.

- **`apigateway:TagResource`**, in the takeover-claim table. API Gateway does not authorize
  by operation name — its IAM actions are HTTP VERBS. AWS publishes 44 actions for the
  service and `GET`, `PUT`, `POST`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` are five of them; there is no
  `TagResource` and there cannot be one.
- **`cloudfront:CreateDistributionWithTags`**, in the CDN create. The API OPERATION of that
  name is real and the driver calls it (`POST /2020-05-31/distribution?WithTags`), but AWS
  publishes no IAM action for it: the authorization is `cloudfront:CreateDistribution` plus
  `cloudfront:TagResource`.

**The mechanism, and why it fired exactly twice.** The tables were written by reading each
service's API and naming the operation, which is correct for almost every AWS service —
`sqs:TagQueue`, `ecr:TagResource`, `kinesis:AddTagsToStream` all are both an operation and
an action. The derivation is invalid precisely where a service's IAM model is not
operation-named, and API Gateway is that service. The wrong entry then sat between two
right-looking neighbours, spelled like them. CloudFront is the same failure from the other
side: `CreateStreamingDistributionWithTags` IS an action, so the missing one looked present
by analogy with the resource one letter away.

**The damage is not a failed call; it is a policy that cannot be written.** A name that is
not an action cannot be granted. The claim path makes this worse than it sounds: a claim
targets an EXISTING resource, so its preflight runs in that resource's context, where
`scopedPreflight` treats an implicit deny as AUTHORITATIVE. So groundhold refuses the apply,
names a permission, and the operator cannot make the refusal go away — every policy they
write is correct and the answer does not change.

**Why the two fixes differ.** CloudFront's create declares a superset on purpose (the
comment says so: operands invisible to an operand-blind table), and it can, because a create
has no resource yet, so its check runs at ACCOUNT scope where an implicit deny is
`unattested` rather than denied. Naming `cloudfront:CreateDistribution` there is free. The
claim cannot do that: adding both `apigateway:PUT` and `apigateway:POST` would refuse an
operator who granted the right one, and this project's own rule is that groundhold must not
refuse an authorized user (D78, D750). Which verb RGT calls through for an HTTP API's ARN
is not derivable from anything readable without credentials, so the entry declares the RGT
stamp ALONE and records the gap. Under-declaring degrades to a denial at the call, which
names the action AWS wanted; over-declaring produces a refusal nothing can satisfy.

**The gate.** `TestEveryAWSPermissionDeclaredIsOneAWSPublishes` confronts every declared
permission with AWS's own machine-readable Service Reference, fetched without credentials
by `scripts/refresh-aws-actions.sh` into `testdata/aws_iam_actions.verified` (40 services,
3986 actions). It is D820's shape applied one layer over: the same authority-outside-the-
repository predictor, the same offline-snapshot idiom so `make check` asks on every run, the
same two-sided assertions (a thin action index or an extraction that stopped matching is a
FATAL, not a pass), and the same rule that a permission naming a service with no verified
list is a failure rather than a skip — because a service nobody fetched is an unchecked
claim, not a clean one.

**What this does not settle.** The gate proves each name EXISTS; it cannot prove the set is
SUFFICIENT or minimal. A missing permission still shows up only as a denial in the field,
and the nine-service question of which verb RGT calls needs one authenticated run to answer.
That is the same boundary as everywhere else here: the credential-free authority settles
what it can, and the rest is named rather than guessed.

**A tooling note, at my own expense.** I edited `docs/DESIGN.md` while the mutation meter
was in flight, and `dirty_check` hashes the tree before and after each mutant — so a
three-hour run of 453 mutants reported 452 caught, zero survived, and FAILED on one DIRTY
that I caused. The meter's message is right that it cannot tell a broken mutator from an
outside edit; the discipline it implies is simply that the tree is frozen for the duration.
The cheap consequence is to batch a slice's edits BEFORE the run rather than after it, which
is what this entry did — one run now covers both D845 and D846.

## D847 — A grant nobody could read, recorded as a measured "not public"

`network.publicExposure` is the attribute a contract uses to say a function must not be
reachable by the world. For a Lambda Function URL with `AuthType: NONE` the URL itself
demands no signature, so the only thing between the world and the function is the RESOURCE
POLICY. When that policy could not be read — a denied `lambda:GetPolicy`, a 5xx, an
unparseable body — the driver answered `publicExposure = false` with
`Derivation: "measured"`, and put the truth in a diagnostic string: *"reported private on
the AuthType alone, NOT measured"*.

**Only the record travels.** `observe` copies the derivation onto the observation and files
the prose separately in `Diagnostics`; it does not set `Partial`, does not mark the
capability unreadable, and nothing joins the two back up. `audit.evidenceRank` demotes
exactly two derivations, `config-intent` and `platform-invariant` — `measured` keeps the
full `provider-api` rank. So a hard `publicExposure == false` constraint evaluates against
full-strength evidence and comes back SATISFIED, for a function that may be world-invokable.
The operator reads a green verdict on the check that exists to catch precisely this.

**The safe direction was the dangerous one.** The comment defending the old behaviour said
reporting private is "the safe direction". That is true of a value a human reads and false
of a value a verifier consumes: for a constraint that DEMANDS non-exposure, `false` is the
passing answer, so the conservative-looking default is the one that fails open. Which
direction is safe depends on which way the constraint points, and the driver cannot know.

**The mechanism, not the instance.** The function signalled "this is not really established"
by returning a non-empty explanation, and the caller was supposed to notice. Nothing
enforced that reading and it did not notice. `lambdaAnonymouslyInvokable` now returns
`measured` as its own boolean, so a branch cannot hand back a value without saying whether
it established one, and the caller records nothing when it did not — absence of evidence
stays the signal (D242). The correct shape was already TWO LINES BELOW in the same switch,
where an unreadable URL config appends a diagnostic and emits nothing, and elsewhere in the
tree (`azure/flexserver_net.go`: "absent publicNetworkAccess is unknown"). This was one path
breaking a rule its own function knew.

**How it was found: verifying a register's reasons, not its subject.** I was checking the
excuses in a permission register — "this operation is discovery-only, so no plan action
declares it" — and following `lambda:GetPolicy` to its caller to make sure that reason was
TRUE. It was; the defect was in what the caller did with the answer. A register whose
entries are justified by hand is worth more than the register: it forces a read of code
nobody had a reason to open.

**And a small proof of a coverage limit.** Adding the test appended `lambda GET
/2015-03-31/functions/{name}/policy` to `testdata/aws-routes.txt` — a route the drivers have
always built and the recorded set had never seen, because no test exercised it. That file is
the subject of the D820 route gate and of anything else joined through it: it records the
routes the SUITE has driven, not the routes the driver can construct. Gates built on it are
a floor, and their silence should be read as such.

## D848 — Permissions sufficient for the plan, missing for what the plan does

D846 checked that every permission this project declares EXISTS, and said plainly that it
could not check the harder half: whether the set is SUFFICIENT. AWS publishes that too —
`Operations[].AuthorizedActions` in the same Service Reference names which IAM action
authorizes which API call — so the half D846 deferred is answerable with the authority it
already used. Four declarations were short.

- **EKS update** declared the control-plane verbs and nothing for the NODE GROUPS. `updateEKS`
  bumps the control plane, then lists the managed node groups, reads each version and rolls
  the stale ones: `ListNodegroups`, `DescribeNodegroup`, `UpdateNodegroupVersion`, all
  undeclared. The control-plane upgrade CANNOT BE UNDONE, so a grant built from this list
  ran out immediately after the irreversible step — leaving exactly the state the driver's
  own comment names, "a half-upgraded cluster".
- **Lambda update** declared `GetFunction` and `UpdateFunctionConfiguration`. `updateLambda`
  also patches the CODE and then moves the exposure either way — creating the Function URL
  and the anonymous grant, or deleting both. Five actions for the three things an update
  does after the first one.
- **S3 update** declared `PutBucketPolicy` but not `DeleteBucketPolicy`. `updateS3` PUTs the
  public policy when the bucket is public and DELETEs it otherwise, so the missing one was
  the GOING-PRIVATE half — the hardening direction. Two lines above it, the same block gets
  this right for replication ("one action authorises both PutBucketReplication and
  DeleteBucketReplication"), which is what makes the omission legible: the authors knew the
  question and asked it about the other pair.
- **SES create and update** declared everything except
  `PutEmailIdentityConfigurationSetAttributes`, the call that makes the configuration set the
  identity's DEFAULT — the step that decides where bounce and complaint events go (D746).

**Under-declared is worse than misspelled.** A misspelling cannot be granted, so it refuses
BEFORE the lease and nothing has happened yet. A missing permission passes the preflight,
the executor takes the lease, and the denial lands mid-plan, after whatever the plan already
did. Every one of these four is on an UPDATE path, where the resource exists and the earlier
steps have already run.

**A rule the two entries needed and now have.** D846 declared LESS for apigateway's claim and
this one declares MORE for lambda's update, and the difference is not taste. AWS names three
verbs that may authorize API Gateway's tag write, of which at most ONE is ever needed; naming
all three would refuse an operator who granted the right one, because a claim targets an
existing resource and its preflight runs where an implicit deny is authoritative. Lambda's
five are each REQUIRED WHEN THEIR BRANCH RUNS, and which branch runs depends on a change-set
this operand-blind table cannot see. A superset of required-when-applicable actions refuses
early; a superset of alternatives refuses wrongly.

**The gate, and both its limits.** `TestDeclaredPermissionsCoverTheOperationsTheDriversCall`
joins the recorded routes to the operations they are, and those to AWS's authorizing actions.
Operations the drivers call outside any plan action carry no declaration to attach to, so
they sit in a 17-entry register — and every reason there was traced to its CALLER by hand,
which is not ceremony: following one of them, `lambda:GetPolicy`, is how D847 was found. The
limits are stated in the test because an unstated reach reads as a clean sweep. First, the
subject is `aws-routes.txt`, which records the routes the SUITE has driven; `s3:DeleteBucketPolicy`
was invisible to the gate and was found by reading `updateS3`. Second, only services with
path-bearing routes are covered — the Query and JSON services choose their operation with an
Action field or an `X-Amz-Target` header, so a recorded route names no operation at all. Three
of the four fixes came from the gate; the fourth came from reading, which is the honest
measure of what a gate like this is worth.

## D849 — The register I published to hold the exceptions was holding a defect

D848 shipped a gate and, beside it, a 17-entry register of operations the drivers call
outside any plan action. Its comment said every entry had been traced to its caller by hand.
That was the claim to check first, and checking it found three things — one of them a real
missing permission the register itself was excusing.

**`bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles` was not a discovery call.** `createBedrock` calls it on the
create-adoption branch (D252): when CreateInferenceProfile answers "already exists", the
driver LISTS the profiles to find the one carrying our name and tags, and binds it instead
of stranding an unknown. With the permission undeclared, that list is denied and the branch
falls through to `unknown` — reason: *"the name now exists but it is not resolvably ours —
reconcile ownership"*, and the remediation text points at `ListInferenceProfiles`, the call
the operator was never told to grant. So the misattribution is the harm: the tool blames
FOREIGN OWNERSHIP for what is a missing grant, and sends the operator to look for a resource
somebody else owns. It is declared on create now.

**Two more entries were artifacts of my own resolution, not calls at all.** The recorded
route file carries no query string — the capture strips it — and S3 selects its operation BY
query: `?location`, `?tagging`, `?versioning`, `?publicAccessBlock` are different operations
on one path. Joined without the query, `GET /some-bucket` matches THIRTY-SIX modelled S3
operations and `PUT` matches twenty-seven, and the gate took the first. So it reported
`s3:ListObjects` as an uncovered call the driver never makes — it makes `GetBucketLocation` —
and I registered it with a confident reason about "the object sweep behind a probe". A
register entry can be a fabrication as easily as a claim can.

**The gate now refuses to attribute what it cannot resolve.** A recorded route matching more
than one modelled operation is UNRESOLVED and counted, never guessed. That costs coverage —
13 recorded routes, all S3, drop out — and the count is asserted so the blind spot cannot
grow quietly. Guessing was worse than missing: an arbitrary pick can also land on an
operation that IS declared, and then a real gap is hidden behind a false pass.

**What the audit did not find matters too.** The other fourteen reasons held, traced call by
call: `discoverBackupVaults`, `discoverEKS`, `discoverOpenSearch`, `discoverLambda`,
`discoverRoute53` and the resume-time `reconcileRoute53`, `observeS3`, `observeSESSending`,
`observeWAF`, `observeLambda`. Three wordings were imprecise and are now exact. And two
findings that looked real — `createEKS` and `createRoute53HealthCheck` appearing to list
their collections — were my pattern ignoring the HTTP method: both are POSTs that CREATE.

**The rule this leaves.** An exceptions register is a list of claims, each of which can be
wrong in the direction that makes the gate quiet. Writing the reason is not the point;
tracing it is. Sixteen entries, one real defect, two fabrications — and the defect was found
by doubting my own sentence rather than by any gate.

## D850 — The blind spot the ratchet was counting, and the delete it was hiding

D849 pinned thirteen recorded routes as unattributable and called the number a blind spot to
be watched. Watching it was the wrong answer: the routes were unattributable because the
route RECORDER threw away the thing that identifies them.

The capture kept `Action` and `Version` and dropped the rest of the query as "whatever a
fixture happened to pass". That is right for a filter or a pagination cursor — and wrong for
S3, where the query IS the operation. `?tagging`, `?versioning`, `?object-lock`, `?location`
are different operations on one path; without them `GET /some-bucket` matched thirty-six
modelled S3 operations. CloudFront's `?WithTags` picks a different create — the same
distinction D846 turned on.

**The discriminator needs no per-service list.** An operation-selecting marker carries NO
value; a filter always does. Keeping the valueless keys resolved the S3 sub-resources and
dropped the ambiguous count from thirteen to six, the six being the calls distinguished by a
key that DOES carry a value — CloudFront's tagging POST, where `?Operation=Tag` and
`?Operation=Untag` are TagResource and UntagResource.

**And behind the blind spot, one real gap.** `deleteS3` calls `refuseIfObjectLockCompliance`,
which reads the bucket's Object Lock configuration and REFUSES the delete when the read gives
no answer — correct, and the reason it matters: an operator granted exactly the declared
delete permissions (`s3:DeleteBucket`, `s3:GetBucketTagging`) got that refusal on EVERY
bucket delete, with the message naming an ambiguous object-lock read rather than the missing
grant. The guard is well built; nothing told anyone to grant what it needs.

**Six more of the D846 shape, in one service.** AWS authorizes `GetObjectLockConfiguration`
with `s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration`, `GetBucketEncryption` with
`s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration`, `GetBucketReplication` with `s3:GetReplicationConfiguration`,
`GetBucketLifecycle` with `s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration`, and `HeadBucket` with
`s3:ListBucket`. Every one of those would have been wrong had it been derived from the
operation name, which is exactly how the two names D846 removed got written.

**What this says about ratchets.** A ratchet on a blind spot is honest and it is not a plan.
This one held a number steady for a day and the number was an artifact of a line in a test
helper; the fix was smaller than the measurement that justified it. When a gate reports that
it cannot see something, the first question is whether the invisibility is in the world or in
the instrument — here it was the instrument, and the answer was six lines.

## D851 — The one channel a scheduled job has, and what we never said about it

From the field (Acme, 2026-08-05). An EventBridge Scheduler invocation of a Lambda carries
NO headers — a direct invoke has nowhere to put one — so a team that wants the job to prove
its identity to the target has exactly one channel: the target payload, `Target.Input`. That
is an implementation operand, and operands are written into the ledger exactly as given and
stay there, travelling onward in every capsule and export. Nothing said so.

**The scan already says it, and could not have said it here.** D364 warns that a value will
be persisted verbatim — but only for a value whose SHAPE it recognises, and that narrowness
is deliberate and correct: a pattern that fires on ordinary configuration teaches people to
ignore the warning. The reporter's secret was twenty-four random characters, which has no
shape at all. Reproduced both ways before writing this: the same secret with an AWS access
key's shape, embedded inside a JSON payload string, IS caught — the detector sees through the
JSON — and the random one is not. So this is not a hole in the detector; it is the difference
between what a detector can do and what a reader needs to know BEFORE writing the value.

**So the statement goes where the value is written, not where it is caught.** The published
description of the `implementation` block now says operands are recorded in the ledger
verbatim, that a credential does not belong in one, and — the part that matters most — that
the shape-based warning cannot recognise an arbitrary secret, so ITS SILENCE IS NOT A
CLEARANCE. A gate keeps both halves there, because a sentence that only works when read
first is one no test would otherwise miss.

**What this deliberately does NOT do.** The reporter asked, as the fuller remedy, for secret
manager references in operand values resolved at converge and stored as references. That is
a runtime feature and the runtime is frozen (D716); it is recorded, not built. The same
report carries a second request — a way for a contract to express WHO may invoke a function,
so that a scheduler role can be named instead of the wildcard `lambda:InvokeFunction` grant
they wrote by hand — which is a vocabulary addition and also outside the freeze. Both are the
owner's call, and both are worth more than this entry: with an invoker list, the payload
secret stops being the only defence, which is the reporter's own reading and it is right.

**One claim of theirs checked and not repeated.** The wildcard-invoke recipe came from THEIR
README, not ours; groundhold's own statements carry `SourceArn` conditions, which is what
made the gap visible to them in the first place. And `network.publicExposure` reading only
`lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` is not the D847 shape: a wildcard `lambda:InvokeFunction` still
demands SigV4 from some account, and the attribute means unauthenticated public HTTPS.

## D852 — A way to say who may call, so nobody has to say "everyone"

From the field (Acme, 2026-08-05), and the first change the code freeze was lifted for.

A scheduled job invokes a Lambda DIRECTLY. `capability.function.serverless` could say
whether the world may reach the function over HTTPS (`network.publicExposure`) and how its
URL authenticates (`url_auth`), but it had no way to name a CALLER. The operator's only
route was a hand-written statement, and the one they wrote — from their own runbook, not
from anything we published — granted `lambda:InvokeFunction` to `Principal: "*"` with no
condition at all: the widest grant AWS has, on the function they were trying to protect.

**The machinery was already there.** This driver writes CloudFront's invoke grants with a
`SourceArn` condition, which is exactly the shape a scheduler grant needs. What was missing
was a way for a contract to ASK for one. `implementation.invokers` is that:

    invokers:
      - principal: arn:aws:iam::…:role/scheduler-invoke-role
      - service: scheduler.amazonaws.com
        source_arn: arn:aws:scheduler:eu-central-1:…:schedule/default/sync-rano

**One refusal is the point of the whole operand.** A SERVICE principal with no `source_arn`
authorises that service in EVERY AWS account — a wildcard wearing a specific-looking name.
An operand introduced to replace `Principal: "*"` that quietly accepted an equivalent would
have been decoration, so it refuses and names what to add. An IAM principal needs no
`source_arn`: an ARN already names one caller.

**Reconciled, not merely added.** The statements carry a deterministic id derived from the
grant itself, and every apply READS the live policy first. That read is what makes the
operand honest in both directions: an entry dropped from the candidate is WITHDRAWN rather
than left granted forever, and a grant deleted by hand comes back. Only statements under our
own prefix are ever removed — an operator's statement, and the `groundhold-cf-*` edge grants,
are not ours to withdraw. A policy that cannot be READ yields `unknown`, never an empty set:
"we own no grants" and "we could not look" are different answers, and the second dressed as
the first would report a reconciliation that withdrew nothing (D847's shape, in a write path).

**The drift loop is closed.** `implementation.invokers` is observed back from the function's
own resource policy, rendered by the same function that renders the declared side, so a
difference is a real one and not a spelling. ClassifyChange routes it as MUTABLE: grants are
added and withdrawn in place, and reading it as immutable would replace a live function to
change who may call it.

**A permission table that can finally see an operand.** An existing conformance case pins
that a PRIVATE function's create declares no `lambda:AddPermission` — correct, and
incompatible with declaring it unconditionally for invokers. The table took attributes only,
so `permAttrs` now passes the capability's operands alongside them under an `impl:` prefix no
attribute path can collide with. Only the compiler's call is operand-aware; `apply` unions
its recomputation with the sealed declaration, so a narrower recomputation there cannot drop
a permission the plan already carries. This also retires part of D848's complaint that the
table is operand-blind — it was, and where it mattered it no longer is.

**What was NOT built, and why.** The same report asked for secret-manager references in
operand values, resolved at converge and stored as references. That stays unbuilt: it changes
what enters the ledger, the canonicalization and the compiler, and the owner lifted the freeze
for this one. D851 documents the persistence it would fix. And the reporter's own reading —
that with an invoker list the payload secret stops being the only defence — is why this was
the one worth doing first.

## D853 — Twenty-seven services the recorder could not tell apart, and the call AWS never had

D850 taught the route recorder to keep the query markers that identify an S3 operation. The
same instrument was blind in a bigger way, and the blindness was one line older than that
one: for the 27 of 40 signed services that speak the Query or JSON protocol, the operation
is named in the request BODY (`Action=`) or in a HEADER (`X-Amz-Target`), never in the path.
The recorder saw `(method, rawURL, service)` and nothing else, so every call any of those
services makes collapsed into ONE recorded line — `iam POST /`, `rds POST /`, `ec2 POST /`.
Twenty-eight lines stood for a driver's entire traffic against twenty-eight services.

`doSignedH` holds the body and the headers, so the hint costs one argument. With it, the
recorded set went from 195 lines to 452, and two gates that had been answering about a
fraction of their subject started answering about the whole of it.

**A call AWS does not have.** The route gate could suddenly ask a question it could never
ask before — not "does this path exist" (there is no path) but "is this an operation this
service HAS" — and the first run found one. The budgets driver has always sent
`X-Amz-Target: AWSBudgetServiceGateway.CreateNotificationWithSubscribers`. AWS has no such
operation. `NotificationsWithSubscribers` is a FIELD of CreateBudget; the call is
`CreateNotification`. Both authorities agree — the Service Reference and botocore — and the
BODY the driver built was already right: its four members are exactly CreateNotification's
four required inputs. Every budget alert this driver ever tried to create was rejected on
the target name alone, and the capability could not converge.

**The suite agreed with the driver because it was written from it.** Four tests broke on the
fix, all for the same reason: their fakes served `CreateNotificationWithSubscribers`, because
a fixture is written to match what the driver sends. Driver and tests were consistent with
each other and both wrong about AWS. That tie can only be broken from outside, which is the
whole argument for the authority-confrontation gates in one example.

**Thirty-one more declarations, six of them on action paths.** The widened subject also fed
the permission-sufficiency gate for the first time, and it found: Aurora's create builds a DB
subnet group AND a cluster parameter group (four undeclared actions) and its delete removes
both (two more); ElastiCache does the same with its cache subnet group (three); the ECS
delete reads the CLUSTER's tags to prove ownership before removing it; and the KMS create
lists keys to find one it already owns before making a second. The remaining twenty-five are
registered with the caller each was traced to — sweeps, observes, the RTO probe's restore
(double-consented, outside any plan), and the preflight's own SimulatePrincipalPolicy.

**Two corrections to my own instruments, before the findings.** A signing name is not an IAM
prefix: `monitoring` signs for what IAM spells `cloudwatch`, and without that map the gate
reported seven permissions undeclared that were declared all along. And the coverage rule
"any authorized action will do" was wrong where AWS lists a conditional extra beside the
primary: `AddTagsToResource` sits next to `CreateDBClusterParameterGroup`, the tag action was
declared, and the create action's absence read as covered. When an authorized action carries
the OPERATION's own name, that one is required; the alternatives rule stands only where no
action shares it, which is what keeps D846's apigateway decision intact.

**A ratchet lowered rather than raised.** `uncheckableRouteCeiling` went 28 -> 1: those routes
are not unverifiable any more, they are verified by a different question. The temptation was
to raise it to 240 when the recorded set grew — which would have been the number of things
the gate had stopped being able to see, published as if it were progress.

## D854 — Asking whether 122 mutating requests carry what AWS requires: they do

D209 refuses a mutating request that omits a field AWS requires — at the wire, before
signing, in production and in every golden test. Its table covers FIVE operations, hand
written, and its own comment says so: "extend as drivers grow; a later generated floor (from
vendored Smithy) replaces the hand `required` lists". D853 made the drivers' mutating traffic
visible for the first time — 122 operations across 27 services — so the obvious next question
was whether the 117 with no contract are getting away with something.

**They are not.** Instrumented the wire chokepoint to record, for every request the suite
drives, the top-level FIELD NAMES it carries — keys only, never values — and compared 180
requests that have a required list in botocore's models. Zero omissions.

**Five apparent hits, all my instrument.** `ec2:CreateFlowLogs` looked to be missing
`ResourceIds`, `TerminateInstances` missing `InstanceIds`, `CreateSecurityGroup` missing
`Description`, `DeleteFlowLogs` missing `FlowLogIds`, `sqs:SetQueueAttributes` missing
`Attributes`. Every one is a wire-naming rule the comparison did not know:

  - a Query list member is sent under its SINGULAR `locationName` with an index —
    `ResourceId.1`, not `ResourceIds`;
  - `CreateSecurityGroup`'s `Description` goes on the wire as `GroupDescription`;
  - a `flattened: true` map is sent as `Attribute.N.Name` / `Attribute.N.Value`, never as
    the member name.

So the rule for anyone repeating this: compare against `locationName` where the model gives
one, and expand a flattened map to its entry name. Field NAMES and wire names are two
vocabularies, and only one of them appears in the request.

**Not built, deliberately.** The instrumentation is reverted and no gate ships. Extending
D209's floor is exactly what the freeze calls published debt — an ungated claim with no
measured defect behind it — and a preventive gate over a class with zero evidence is a
maintenance surface bought with nothing. What is recorded here is the method and the
baseline: 180 requests, 0 omissions, and the three naming rules that make the comparison
mean anything. The next run starts from that rather than from five false hits.

## D855 — The four drivers nobody had asked a provider about

D793 and D794 built the field-name confrontation — does the provider's own model describe
the name this driver decodes — and D820, D842 and D853 built the route and operation ones.
All of them cover aws, gcp and azure. Four driver packages decode 55 field names between
them and had never been confronted with anything: cloudflare (10), hetzner (7), upstash (12),
k8s (26).

**Asked, credential-free, and they hold.**

  - **hetzner** — `docs.hetzner.cloud/cloud.spec.json` (151 paths). Base URL, path, method and
    all seven decoded names check out, including the one that looked wrong: `network_zone` is
    NOT a property of a network, and the driver does not read it there — it reads it from
    inside `subnets[]`, which is exactly where the spec puts it.
  - **cloudflare** — `cloudflare/api-schemas` (5650 property names). All ten present.
  - **k8s** — the Kubernetes OpenAPI (985 property names across `definitions`). Twenty-three
    of twenty-six present; the three absent — `components`, `schemas`, `serverRelativeURL` —
    are the OpenAPI DOCUMENT's own structure, read from `/openapi/v3`'s discovery response,
    which `definitions` does not describe. The same "document inside an API" shape the AWS
    exception table already names.
  - **upstash** — publishes no machine-readable spec at any of the three usual locations
    (404 each). Its twelve names stay unconfrontable without credentials, and that is the
    honest status rather than an assumption of correctness.

**Not gated, deliberately.** Three of the four now have a verified authority and a clean
result, so extending the gate would be a maintenance surface bought with no defect — the
freeze's "published debt, recorded and waits". What is recorded is where each authority
lives and what its answer was, so the next run costs three fetches rather than a search.

**The reason to write a negative down.** D820 and D853 both found real defects the first time
a driver met its provider's model, so "nobody has asked" is the strongest predictor this
project has. Four drivers were in that state this morning; three are not any more, and the
fourth is named as unanswerable rather than left looking checked.

## D856 — The gate that certified discoverability over nothing

141 gate files, 128 named by a mutant, 13 not — down from 38 of 145 at v0.1.14, so what was
left was the tail nobody reached. A gate with no mutant is not a coverage statistic; it is a
gate whose teeth were never tested. So rather than adding mutants for tidiness, each was
injected by hand with the defect its gate CLAIMS to catch, and the named test run. Four bit
immediately — the error-code registry, the event-type registry, the banner vocabulary, and
the output-schema field-with-no-code all failed the moment their subject was corrupted.

**The fifth did not.** `TestK8sDiscoverabilityComplete` delegates entirely to
`provider.CertifyDiscoverability(t, d, d.MappedServiceTokens())`. Make `MappedServiceTokens`
return nil and the gate PASSES: a k8s driver that maps no services at all, and can therefore
discover nothing, certifies as fully discoverable.

**Why this one and not the cloud drivers.** aws, gcp and azure pass hand-written service
lists to the same function — a list in source cannot silently empty. k8s DERIVES its list
from the embedded schema-mapping registry, and a derived subject is one filter, one embed
failure, one refactor away from being empty. The function had no floor because it had never
been called with one.

**What it would have cost.** This is the gate that keeps a service from being shadow-blind —
observed but never swept, so the estate holds resources the tool reports as absent (D513's
class, and the reason CertifyDiscoverability exists at all). Vacuous, it would have reported
completeness for a driver that sees nothing, and the failure is silent in both directions:
nothing fails, and nothing is discovered.

The floor lives in `CertifyDiscoverability`, not in the k8s test, because the next driver to
derive its service list will call the same function and deserves the same answer.

**The method is the point.** "Which gates have no mutant" is answerable in one command, and
"which gates have no TEETH" is answerable only by trying. The first question had thirteen
answers; the second had one, and it was not the one I would have guessed — the 18-line
delegating gate, not the 249-line one with four ratchets.

## D857 — The fix was held by a check that could not see the code it protects

The meter caught me. D853's budgets mutant — re-inject the target AWS does not have — SURVIVED
`TestEveryRouteTheDriverBuildsIsARouteAWSHas`, and the reason is worth more than the fix was.

That gate reads the RECORDED route file. Changing the driver does not change the file, so the
gate goes on comparing a file that still says `CreateNotification` against a model that
agrees. The recorded file only disagrees with the drivers on an UNFILTERED package run, where
`TestMain` compares what it captured against what is checked in — and a `-run` filter skips
that comparison by design, because a filtered run records a subset. The meter runs every
mutant filtered.

So the defect was found by a gate that cannot hold the fix. I wrote no test for the fix
itself, because the gate went green and green felt like enough.

**The test that holds it drives the DRIVER.** `createBudget` runs against a fake that records
the `X-Amz-Target` headers it receives, and every target's operation must appear in AWS's
published operation list for that service. A first draft called `budgetCall("CreateNotification", ...)`
directly — and would have passed with the defect re-injected, because the test supplied the
very string under test. That is the same knot the fixtures were in: an instrument that asks
the driver to confirm its own opinion.

**What generalises.** A gate whose subject is a CHECKED-IN ARTEFACT protects the artefact, not
the code that produced it — and the refresh step is where the two meet. When a gate over
recorded data finds a defect, the fix needs a test that runs the code. The meter is the only
thing that asks this question, and it asked it about my own work four hours after I called
the work done.

## D858 — Asking Kubernetes offline the question that took the k8s driver down

D509 is the worst defect this project has had: the k8s driver could not create ANYTHING on a
real cluster. The cause was not a typo. Every hermetic drift test computed a mapping's
surface against a HAND-RECORDED fixture; the fixtures spelled a schema reference in a shape a
real API server cannot emit; so the fixtures agreed with the walker while the walker was
blind by construction. Six of seven mapped services drifted against the first real cluster
they ever met.

The guard written afterwards asks a LIVE cluster — and skips without one, which is every run
here and in CI. So for months the class that took the driver down has been guarded by a test
that never executes. That is not a gate; it is a note saying someone should run one.

**Kubernetes publishes the documents a cluster serves.** `/openapi/v3` per API group is in
the kubernetes repo, byte-shaped exactly like the live endpoint. Recomputing each built-in
mapping's surface hash against them and comparing with the pin needs no cluster, no
credentials, and 86 KB of checked-in schema — the transitive closure of the mapped kinds, not
the 3 MB of full documents.

**The answer today is clean, and that is the second reason to build it.** All seven built-in
mappings match: namespace, netpol, quota, and the four RBAC ones, including `rbac-role`
legitimately pinning one path ABSENT (`aggregationRule` exists only on ClusterRole). A drift
gate that starts red tells you what broke; one that starts green tells you it is watching the
right thing.

**What it deliberately does not cover.** The three CRD mappings — Argo, cert-manager, Flux —
are not published by Kubernetes, and the gate COUNTS them rather than passing over them, so
the share it cannot see stays visible in the log. Those stay the live test's job, and the
live test stays opt-in, which is now an honest division rather than a gap wearing a test's
name.

**Why this is admitted under the freeze.** It is not a preventive gate for a class with no
evidence: the class has the strongest evidence in the repo, and its guard is inert. Making an
inert guard execute is closer to repairing a safety net than to adding coverage — and it cost
no runtime change at all.

## D859 — Trying every gate that had never been tried

D856 measured which gate files carry no mutant — thirteen — and tried five of them by hand,
finding one that certified over nothing. This finishes the list. Each of the remaining eight
was injected with the defect its gate claims to catch, the named test run, and the result
recorded before anything was added to the meter.

**All eight bit.** A second Go dependency, a third-party import in the Python reference, an
ownership decision for a package that does not exist, both ratchets moved down, a sweep
defect naming a service nobody has, a driver re-deciding a projection attribute in a case
arm, a workflow owner condition pointed at another org, and a bare `yaml.safe_load` in the
reference — every one turned its gate red. The nine mutants are in the meter now, so the
answer stays measured rather than remembered.

**One probe pointed at the wrong copy, and the answer was better than the question.** Making
`spec/vocab/…serverless.yaml` declare `evidence: projektion` did NOT fail
`TestEveryDeclaredEvidenceClassIsInTheClosedSet` — that gate reads `vocab.Embedded()`, the
compiled-in set, while the file I edited is the published one. A typo in the published
vocabulary sounded like exactly the drift this project keeps finding, so I ran the whole
package instead of the one test: `internal/vocab`'s type-coverage gate catches it, by name
and by file. Two copies, two gates, both covered. The probe was wrong, not the tree.

**And the meter caught my verification method.** One of the nine did not compile — the
sweep-defect struct has positional fields and I guessed named ones. My hand probe had
reported it caught, because a build error prints `FAIL` and my one-line check matched on
`FAIL`. The meter distinguishes NO-BUILD from caught and said so; I did not. The corrected
injection compiles and turns the gate red, verified by building first and testing second.
That is the third time this week an instrument of mine agreed with what I hoped, and the
pattern is the same each time: a check whose output shape cannot tell two answers apart.

**Where the count lands.** 141 gate files, 141 named by a mutant. That number is worth
exactly what the trying was worth: the thirteen that had no mutant were not thirteen weak
gates — twelve were fine and one was hollow, and the only way to know which was to try each.
"Has a mutant" is a fact about the meter; "has teeth" is a fact about the gate, and one is
not evidence for the other.

## D860 — Twenty services per page, and an absence asserted from the first one

App Runner caps `ListServices` at TWENTY services per page — the model's own `MaxResults`
maximum — and hands back a `NextToken`. `resolveServiceArn` read ONE page, matched the name
locally, and returned `found=false, err=nil` for a name that was not on it. The line carried
a comment calling that "a real gone/never-created".

It is not real. On an account with more than twenty App Runner services the name may simply
be on page two, and every caller reads the answer as a fact:

  - `createAppRunner` — the create-adoption branch does not find its own service and mints a
    SECOND one, which is the billed-duplicate class D391-D438 was swept for;
  - `deleteAppRunner` — reports gone while the service stands;
  - `observeAppRunner` — reports absent;
  - `claimAppRunnerARN` — cannot take over what it cannot see.

**The absence is only a fact once every page has been read**, so the resolver now follows the
token, bounded by `maxAWSListPages`, and a chain that never ends is an ERROR rather than an
absence: giving up and calling it "gone" is the same lie as reading one page and calling it
"gone". Both halves are pinned by tests — a service on page two, and an endless chain.

**How it was found.** D853 made the operations the drivers call visible, so botocore's
paginator data could be joined to them: 55 called operations paginate. The existing paging
ratchet counts `discover*` functions only, which is where the paging work of D809-D817 was
aimed — so a paginating read on an ACTION path was outside its subject entirely. This one
was not in botocore's paginator file either (App Runner ships none), so it took reading the
model's input and output shapes: `NextToken` on both sides, `MaxResults` capped at twenty.

**What is not fixed here.** `discoverAppRunner` reads one page too, and stays in the unpaged
sweep ceiling as known debt — a discovery sweep that stops early SAYS so (D803), which is
incomplete but honest. The defect fixed here is the other thing: a definite absence derived
from a partial read.

## D861 — When one page is enough, and when it never is

D860 fixed a listing read that asserted an absence from page one. The obvious next question
is how many more of those exist, so the whole "list, do not find, act" pattern was swept:
every `create*`, `claim*` and `ensure*` function that lists something. Three, and the other
two are fine — for a reason worth stating, because it is the rule that separates them.

**The question the code asks decides whether paging matters.**

  - "Is this list EMPTY?" — one page settles it. Pages fill in order, so a non-empty list has
    a non-empty first page. `ensureEKSNodeGroup` asks exactly this ("only a cluster with ZERO
    node groups gets a fresh one", D258) and is correct reading one page.
  - "Is NAME in this list?" — no page settles it but the last. A full first page says nothing
    about the name, which is precisely how D860 came to report a live App Runner service as
    "gone/never-created".

`ensureListener` asks the first question too, and is bounded twice over: AWS caps an ALB at
fifty listeners and returns four hundred per page, so the second page does not exist.

**A quota is a real bound and deserves to be written down.** Several of the unpaged reads on
action paths — attached role policies (twenty per role), rule targets (five per rule), a
subnet group's subnets — cannot truncate because the service will not let the collection grow
past a page. That is not the same as "probably fine": it is a published limit, and where one
applies it should be named rather than left as an unstated assumption a later quota change
would quietly break.

**What stays open, deliberately.** `deleteRouteTables` and its siblings list a VPC's children
before deleting them, and a truncated list would leave children behind — but the delete then
FAILS on the dependency and says so, and the retry reads the next page. Loud and
self-correcting is not the class the freeze admits, so it is recorded here rather than fixed.
The same for `discoverAppRunner`, which reads one page and, per D803, says that it did.

## D862 — The same question asked of the other two clouds

D861 named the rule; this is what it answers on GCP and Azure. Sweeping every driver function
that looks a NAME up in a listing, resolving helpers two levels deep so a paged helper counts
as paged, and excluding the discovery sweeps (known debt, and they say when they stop early):
two hits, both `deleteVPC` and `deleteOwnedRouters` on GCP, both the delete-child shape whose
truncation ends in a loud dependency failure and a retry that reads on. The D860 shape — a
definite absence asserted from a partial read, feeding a create — does not occur on either
cloud.

**One false hit is worth recording, because it was mine.** The first pass flagged
`findBillingBudgetByDisplayName`, whose own comment says it is "the only guard against a
duplicate on a retried create" — exactly the stake D860 had. It pages correctly; the loop
lives in `billingBudgetList`, one call away, and my scan only looked inside the function that
does the comparing. Reading it took a minute and would have cost an entry claiming a defect
that is not there. A scan that cannot see through one function call will find the same
false positive in every codebase that factors its listing helper out.

## D863 — A security guarantee measured from the first page

`describeVpcSecurityGroupPosture` asks whether ANY security group in a VPC opens a door to
everywhere, and `observe` turns a NO into `egress.restricted = true` with derivation
`measured` — a guarantee, asserted. It read one page.

EC2 returns up to a thousand security groups and hands back a token; the per-VPC quota is
2500. So on a large estate the open group sits on page two, the posture comes back CLOSED,
and the tool measures an estate as restricted while `-1` to `0.0.0.0/0` stands. The file's
own comment already records a field report of that exact consequence — "a hard constraint
satisfied on a network whose every security group allowed -1 to 0.0.0.0/0" — from the era
when the driver read the road instead of the rules. The rules are read now; they were read
one page at a time.

**This refines D861's rule, which was incomplete as written.** "Is the list EMPTY" IS settled
by one page, because pages fill in order. "Does any element satisfy P", where P is checked
HERE rather than by the service, is a different question, and its NO needs the last page. The
distinction is not academic: the first form appears in `ensureEKSNodeGroup` and is correct,
the second in this posture read and was not.

Both halves are pinned: an open group on page two, and a chain that never ends. The second
matters as much as the first — a bounded sweep that gives up now returns an ERROR, because
"I stopped looking" and "there is nothing there" must not arrive as the same value when that
value becomes a measured security attribute.

**And a note on where the safe direction lies.** The function's comment says over-reporting
an OPEN door is the safe direction for a security constraint, which is right — and reading
one page did the opposite. Truncation makes the world look tidier than it is, so the failure
mode of an unfinished read is always the unsafe direction here.

## D864 — The same lie, one call earlier in the same function

D863 fixed the security-group half of `observeVPC`. The route half, read four lines above it,
had the identical defect: `describeVpcRoutes` answered "does this VPC have a default route,
and through what" from an UNPAGED DescribeRouteTables, and observe turns that answer into
`egress.internet` — and, when it comes back "none", into `egress.restricted = true` — both
`measured`.

EC2 returns a hundred route tables per page; the per-VPC quota is 200 and one table per
subnet is an ordinary layout. So the internet-gateway route sits on page two, the scan reports
no road, and the tool measures a network as having no way out while it has one. Of the two,
this is the worse direction: `egress.internet: none` reads as the tightest possible answer,
so the truncation manufactures exactly the reassurance an operator would act on.

**Found by the predicate, not by looking.** D863 left a rule sharp enough to search with —
"does any element satisfy P, with P checked here" — and a sweep of every driver function
returning a bool from a listing produced five candidates. Three were bounded and one was a
false positive worth naming: `launchTemplateAssignsPublicIP` names ONE version in the
request (`LaunchTemplateVersion.1`), so the service returns a single item and there is no
page two to miss. The filter being server-side is what makes it safe, and that is the
distinction to carry: a client-side filter over a listing needs every page, a server-side one
needs none.

**Two remain recorded rather than fixed.** `wafProtectsSomething` scans CloudFront
distributions to answer whether a web ACL protects anything; its NO becomes a DIAGNOSTIC
(D765), not a measured attribute, so a truncated read makes the tool say less rather than
say something false. `readInvoker` on GCP reads a whole IAM policy, which is not a paged
listing. Both are named here so the next sweep does not re-derive them.

## D865 — The write side of the same class: a private path wired into part of a network

D863 and D864 fixed two READS that answered from an unfinished sweep. The same question asked
of the WRITE paths — a mutating function deciding from a listing — gave sixteen candidates,
fifteen of which are the delete-children shape whose truncation ends in a loud dependency
failure and a retry that reads on. The sixteenth is not.

`vpcRouteTableIDs` collects, in its own words, "every route table id in the VPC ... so the S3
gateway endpoint routes S3 traffic from every subnet", and read one page. A hundred tables per
page against a quota of two hundred, with one table per subnet an ordinary layout — so the
endpoint gets associated with the tables that fit on page one, the subnets behind the rest
keep sending S3 traffic off the AWS backbone, and the create reports SUCCEEDED.

**The function's instinct was already right, and one case slipped between its guards.** It
refuses when the list cannot be read ("reconcile the partial network") and when the list is
empty. A truncated list is neither: it reads cleanly and it is not empty. That is the shape to
remember — a guard against "no answer" and a guard against "nothing there" leave "part of the
answer" uncovered, and part of an answer is what a paginated API returns by default.

**Why this one is a falsehood and the fifteen deletes are not.** A delete that misses children
fails on the dependency and says so; the operator retries and the next page is read. Here
nothing fails: the network is wired, the create succeeds, and the capability's private-path
promise is true for some subnets and false for others with no signal anywhere. Loud
incompleteness is a nuisance; silent partial success is the class the freeze admits.

**Two false positives worth naming**, because both looked like the defect and are not:
`wireRouteTable` iterates subnet ids that came from the PLAN, not from a listing; and
`rollEKSNodegroups` lists node groups against an EKS quota of thirty with a page of a hundred,
so its page two does not exist. Quotas bound truncation, and where one does, saying so is
better than paging code nobody needs.

## D866 — A ratchet over what the drivers call, because the old one watched the wrong set

Four defects in one day, all one shape: a listing read without following the token. D860 (an
App Runner service reported gone from page one of twenty), D863 (a VPC's egress reported
restricted), D864 (its road reported absent), D865 (the S3 gateway endpoint wired into part of
a network).

There has been a ratchet for this since D814 — `unpagedAWSSweepCeiling`, counting `discover*`
FUNCTIONS that mention no continuation token. Not one of the four was a discover function. The
number was never wrong; the SUBJECT was, and a ratchet over the wrong subject is a number that
falls reassuringly while the defects accumulate outside it.

D853 made a better subject available: the recorded routes now name the operation even for the
Query and JSON protocols, so "what the drivers call" is a fact rather than a source-scrape.
Joined to botocore's paginator data, 55 called operations paginate.

**A ratchet, not a register.** Thirty-three operations are issued without a token, and most
are bounded — by a quota (twenty attached policies per role, five targets per rule), by a
server-side filter (`InstanceId.1` names one instance, so there is no page two), or by asking
"is this list empty" rather than "is X in it" (D861). Writing a reason for each would mean
thirty-three guesses, and D849 is the entry about what a register of guesses is worth. A count
that may only fall needs no reasons and still refuses growth.

**Counted per CALL SITE, and that correction came from trying to break it.** The first draft
asked whether SOME function naming an operation follows a token. A mutant that stripped the
loop out of `describeVpcRoutes` left the count unmoved: two other functions in the same file
also name DescribeRouteTables, and one of them pages. That is exactly the state D864 and D865
were found in — one operation, three call sites, mixed — so the first draft would have caught
neither of the defects it was written for. Per call site the number is 133, not 33.

**What it cannot do, stated because the sibling ratchet states it too.** It detects the absence
of a token MENTION, not the presence of correct paging: a function that mentions `NextToken`
and ignores it passes. The precise question is not decidable by reading source, and a crude
check with a falling ceiling is worth more than a precise one nobody can run. What it does
catch is the thing that kept happening: a NEW call site reading page one of a listing AWS
pages.

## D867 — Asking the schema the other question, and the one field it did not describe

D845 asked which verbs publish a document with no `$def` at all. The mirror question is
whether the defs that DO exist describe what the verb emits, and it is answerable by running
the verb and diffing the keys.

Of the defs that can be exercised without credentials, `verify` and `planRefusal` match their
documents exactly — every required key present, no key emitted that the def does not describe.
`explain` emits three keys and its def describes two. The missing one is `code`.

**Of all the fields to leave undescribed, that is the one.** `spec/errors.md` says the `code`
field IS the contract — "scripts and agents route on it" — and the CLI's own help repeats it:
"route on the process exit code and the JSON `code` field, never on banner text". So the
published shape of `explain` omitted precisely the field the project tells consumers to read.
It validated, because JSON Schema permits undescribed properties; it simply said less than the
tool does.

**Two false alarms of my own, both from running the wrong document.** I first compared a
SUCCESSFUL plan against `planRefusal` and read three "missing required" fields as a defect —
they were missing because a sealed plan is not a refusal. The second attempt used a
conformance case whose refusal needs a ledger, so it succeeded too. The refusal document only
appeared once I used the example the Makefile keeps for exactly this purpose (`make plan`,
which refuses because an RTO is unproven). A schema check that does not first establish WHICH
document it is holding will report the difference between two shapes as an error in one.

**A narrow gate, for the one verb that needs no fixture.** `explain` publishes its document
from nothing but a code, so a test can marshal exactly what the CLI marshals and require the
schema to describe every key — including the reverse leg, a described property the document
never carries. It guards its own assumption too: if `perr.RegistryEntry` stops being what the
CLI emits, the gate says so rather than checking a shape nobody ships.

**And the meter caught the wiring, not the code.** Repointing the new mutant, my one-line
patch matched the FIRST occurrence of a schema mutant naming `TestEveryPublishedOutputFieldHasCodeBehindIt`
— which was D515's, not mine — so the two swapped targets and BOTH survived the next run: each
was injected against a gate written for the other direction. The code was right; only the
meter's wiring was wrong, and only the meter could have said so. I also pushed that commit
before reading the verdict, because the push sat after the check in one command chain rather
than behind it. The rule I hold to is that the meter passes BEFORE a push, and a `;` is not
that rule.

**What stays open.** There is no GENERAL gate for this direction. `TestEveryPublishedOutputFieldHasCodeBehindIt`
