(D515) walks the schema and asks whether the code emits each field; nothing walks the OUTPUT
and asks whether the schema describes each key. Building it means running every verb with
fixtures — several of them need a ledger, a provider, or both — so the general form is recorded
rather than half-built, and the one verb that needs none of it is gated now.

## D868 — Who may assume the identity, which nothing compared

The first change the unfreeze bought, and it is the one the project had already named as
frozen and consequential. D776 fixed the ADVICE about AWS trust operands and closed with a
sentence about what it could not fix: *"with no `trust.principals` attribute to compare
against, the divergence would surface only at the next re-create, as a silent weakening."*
D751 said the same from the other side: the trust policy is the first property of a role —
"a set of permissions plus who may take them" — and the vocabulary had no attribute for it,
so a contract could not ask.

So a role's permissions could be pinned exactly while the answer to WHO MAY PICK IT UP
changed underneath, and every attribute the tool looked at was unchanged, because everything
it looked at WAS unchanged.

**Where it belongs, which is not where I first put it.** My first draft added the attribute
to `capability.authorization.role` — and on AWS that capability is fulfilled by a managed
POLICY, which has no trust at all. The IAM role is the resource behind
`capability.identity.serviceaccount` (`aws.iam`, alongside `gcp.serviceaccount` and
`azure.managedidentity`). An identity is the thing that can be assumed; a policy is a list of
permissions. The vocabulary gate caught the mistake by refusing mapping keys that name no
real service token, which is exactly what that gate is for.

**The condition rides with the principal, and that is the design.** A bare
`service:events.amazonaws.com` and the same principal guarded by
`aws:SourceAccount=000000000000` are not two spellings of one trust. A set of bare principals
would compare them EQUAL — and D776 is the entry recording a field estate where all six roles
carried that guard, so declaring them the bare way would have recorded trust weaker than the
trust that stands. An attribute built to detect that divergence must not be blind to it. The
condition OPERATOR is dropped on purpose: `StringEquals` and `ArnLike` on one key narrow the
same axis, and carrying the operator would make two spellings of one guard compare unequal —
the mirror mistake.

**Three refusals inside the renderer.** Only `sts:AssumeRole*` statements count, because a
trust document also carries `sts:TagSession` and `sts:SetSourceIdentity`, whose principals
cannot assume anything. Only `Allow` counts. And a document that does not decode yields
`ok=false`, never an empty set — an empty set is the safest-looking possible answer about who
can assume a role, and inventing it from missing data is D847's shape in a security
attribute.

**Scope, stated.** This slice makes the tool SEE. AWS observes the set; GCP and Azure declare
in the vocabulary that they do not yet, naming the read each would need (a service account's
own IAM policy; an identity's federated credentials) rather than leaving a silent gap. There
is no update path for a role's trust here — the driver has none for roles at all — so a
declared divergence blocks rather than being patched, which for a security property is the
honest answer and not a placeholder for one.

### D868b — the GCP half: a role in place of an action, and the sweep that must not pay for it

GCP fits the same attribute without translating AWS's shape into it. There the trust document
names an ACTION (`sts:AssumeRole`); here the account's own IAM policy names a ROLE, and three
of them end with a principal acting as the identity: `serviceAccountTokenCreator` (mints a
token), `workloadIdentityUser` (a Kubernetes workload picks it up), and the one an audit
forgets — `serviceAccountUser`, which mints nothing and instead lets a principal ATTACH the
account to a resource they create, after which the resource runs AS the account. Leaving it
out would under-report who ends up acting as this identity, and for a trust attribute the
safe direction is to over-report. So the role rides with the member for the same reason the
condition does: a set of bare members would compare a token-minter equal to someone who may
merely attach the account to a VM.

**What the sweep may not do.** `discoverServiceAccounts` reuses the observe function, so
adding the read there would have put a second call on EVERY account in the project — a crawl
doubling its calls to answer a question discovery does not ask (D141's pace). The read is now
opt-in: `observe` makes it, the sweep does not. But silence would have been the worse defect,
because an ABSENT `trust.principals` reads exactly like an empty one (D847) — so the sweep
emits ONE diagnostic saying the trust was not read and where to get it. Once for the sweep,
not once per account: a diagnostic nobody can read through is not a disclosure.

**The permission followed the call.** `adopt` observes before it binds, so
`iam.serviceAccounts.getIamPolicy` joins its declared set. A read the code makes and the
preflight does not name is a permission the operator learns about from a 403 — the
under-declaration class this session already paid down.

Azure stays declared-not-observed, naming the read it needs (the identity's federated
credentials, a separate ARM collection).

## D869 — the disclosure had one consumer, and two claims were made where it does not reach

Azure already knew about pages. The transport notes any response that said there was more
(D803), a shared loop follows a nextLink and refuses to follow one off-host (D815), and a
falling ceiling counts the sweeps that still read one page (D816). What none of that
covered is a question nobody had asked: **who reads the note?**

One caller does — `crawlProvider`, which turns it into an incomplete scope with a reason.
Every other read in the driver leaves the same note in the same place and nobody collects
it. So the honest question is not "does this read page" but "does the claim this read
supports have a consumer for the truncation". Two did not, and both were reading a
collection ARM's own specification marks pageable.

**The first is the preflight, and it lies in an unusual direction.**
`CheckResourcePermissions` is documented as the AUTHORITATIVE half: "the permissions list
at the resource's own scope includes every inherited assignment, so an ungranted action IS
a real denial", and `internal/apply` refuses the whole apply on it. It read one page of
`Permissions_ListForResource`, which the spec (pinned version 2022-04-01, the one the
driver sends) marks `x-ms-pageable` with a nextLink. Truncation can only REMOVE grants, so
this is never a false permit — it is a false DENIAL: the tool tells an operator they lack a
permission they hold and blocks work that would have succeeded. Under the freeze's test
that still qualifies, and squarely: with no preflight at all the apply would have gone
through, so a person acting on what the tool said is worse off than if it had said nothing.

The other two clouds are why this is an instance and not a class. AWS's simulator follows
its `Marker` and refuses past fifty pages; GCP's `testIamPermissions` is a server-side
query with no pages at all. Azure was the odd one out.

**The second is sharper, and its own comment names the harm.**
`inference.destinationRegions` is measured by reducing an Azure OpenAI account's
deployments to a union of destination surfaces, and the point of it is written above the
function: "a Global sku reduces to ["global"] ... NOT bounded EU regions, so the trap
becomes a `violated` verdict DETERMINISTICALLY". `Deployments_List` pages. A GlobalStandard
deployment on page two drops out of the union, the surface comes back as the account's own
region, and a contract saying inference must not leave the EU is reported SATISFIED on an
account routing inference anywhere on earth.

The read directly above it already refuses when the list is UNREADABLE, with a comment
naming this exact consequence — "never a fabricated absence that would understate the
residency surface and let the trap slip through". That is D865's triad for the third time:
guards written for "no answer" and "nothing there", with PART of an answer left uncovered,
and part of an answer is what a paginated API returns by default.

**What the authority was.** `x-ms-pageable` in `Azure/azure-rest-api-specs` is the ARM
twin of botocore's paginator files: per operation, machine-readable, and answerable without
a credential. It also said NO twice, which is why it is worth using rather than reasoning
from shape. `ObjectReplicationPolicies_List` carries `nextLinkName: null` — a list with no
second page — so `observeBlobReplication` is correct as written and was left alone.
`countBackupInstances` asks whether the vault holds ANY instances before explaining a
failed delete; one page settles that, because pages fill in order (D861), and the exact
count in the sentence is not what the sentence turns on.

**The gate.** A second ratchet, over ARM list decodes OUTSIDE the sweeps — the ones the
crawl's disclosure never reaches. Per decode site rather than per function, which is
D866's lesson from AWS: a function that decodes two envelopes and pages one of them is one
unfollowed read, not zero. Eight left, and the count may only fall. The detector requires
the envelope's element type to be a named or struct type, because an ARM listing's elements
are resources — that keeps a DNS record's `Value []string` out of a count about pages.

Recorded, not fixed: `listACSDomains` reduces to `authentication.dkim` by asking whether
ANY domain is verified, and `Domains_ListByEmailServiceResource` pages. Truncation there
can only turn a true into a false — the tool would report mail as less authenticated than
it is, which over-warns rather than under-warns. It is in the ceiling, and it is the next
one to fall.

## D870 — the third cloud, and the first page-one defect that MUTATES

D869 asked ARM's specification which of the Azure driver's listings page. The same question
put to Google's discovery documents — public, credential-free, and per method — found three
reads in the GCP driver, and the third is a different kind of wrong from anything in this
series.

**`egress.internet`, measured from page one of the routers.** The observer asks whether ANY
router in the region carries a Cloud NAT, and Compute lists 500 per page with a
`nextPageToken`. A NO becomes `egress.internet = "none"`, which the vocabulary defines as
"no road (isolated by construction)". So a network whose NAT router sits on page two is
published as ISOLATED, and a contract asserting isolation passes on an estate whose
workloads reach the internet.

**`ingress.public`, measured from page one of the firewalls.** Same shape, and the harm is
the one this freeze was written around: a NO becomes "not publicly exposed" while a rule
allowing `0.0.0.0/0` sits on the next page — a reachable network reported private, which is
D694. The `network=` filter in the query narrows the listing to one network and is not a
bound; Compute still pages at 500 and hands back a token. Its sibling `egress.restricted`
truncates in the safe direction (GCP expresses restriction by the PRESENCE of a deny-all
rule, so a missed page can only under-report protection), which is worth noticing rather
than assuming: the same page boundary lies in opposite directions depending on whether the
attribute is proven by presence or by absence.

**The Vertex adoption scan, and why it is not like the others.** Every create in this
runtime reads before it writes (D700, closed in D804 with an empty `knownNoAdoptRead`
register). The Vertex create's read is `endpoints.list` filtered client-side by displayName,
and its caller states the stake in its own words: "a blind create on a lost ledger mints a
SECOND model-serving endpoint — billed, live, and absent from the ledger". Vertex pages that
listing. Past the first page the guard was not weak, it was ABSENT — and this defect does
not merely say something false, it MUTATES: it creates a second live billed endpoint that
nothing manages. Every other entry in this run is a wrong sentence; this one is a wrong
resource.

That is worth stating as a rule rather than an anecdote. **A read-before-write guard that
scans a paginated listing is not a guard past its first page.** The rest of this series has
been about claims; a guard is a claim the runtime acts on itself, which makes truncation
there strictly worse than truncation in an observation.

**AWS had one too, and it is why a gate built today already has a blind spot.**
`wafListByName` searches a page of `ListWebACLs` for a deterministic name, and both callers
turn a miss into a fact: `observeWAF` publishes resource-absent with derivation "measured"
for a live firewall, and `deleteWAF` reports SUCCEEDED as idempotent while the WebACL stands
and keeps filtering traffic. The listing pages — `NextMarker` sits in both the request and
the response shape of the service model.

Botocore ships NO paginator entry for `ListWebACLs`. The D866 ratchet is built from paginator
data, so it could not see this operation at all, and the same is true of every operation AWS
pages without a modelled paginator (App Runner's `ListServices`, the D860 defect, was the
first). **Paginator data is a LOWER BOUND on what paginates; the service model is the fuller
authority.** Rebuilding `aws_paginating_operations.verified` from `service-2.json` would move
the ceiling and deserves its own pass — recorded, not smuggled into this one.

**What the sweep found that needed nothing.** Ten adoption guards scan a listing; four were
already correct, and four more are bounded in a way that can be established rather than
assumed, which is the D861 discipline and the reason to look rather than to fix on sight:

	findVpcByTags          three server-side tag filters — the filtered set is one VPC
	resolvePodIdentityID   server-side namespace= and serviceAccount= — at most one match
	listDetectorIDs        asks "is it empty" and takes any one; pages fill in order
	findVgwByTags          DescribeVpnGateways does not paginate at all

**Where the authority came from, and what it could not settle.** Google's discovery
documents answer per method — `pageToken` in the parameters, `nextPageToken` in the response
schema, `maxResults` defaulting to 500 for Compute — with no credential and one request. The
question they do NOT answer is the one D861 cares about: whether a QUOTA bounds the
collection below a page. Cloud Router and firewall-rule limits are published as rendered
tables that are not in the page source, and there is no credential-free API for a project's
quotas. So the position taken here is the one the ratchets already state: the API pages, the
code read one page, and nobody has established that the collection is smaller. Where a bound
IS establishable the answer stays no-change — that is why `observeBlobReplication` and
`countBackupInstances` were left alone in D869.

Deferred with its reason: GCP has no route-to-paging join like the one D866 built for AWS
from botocore. The materials exist — `gcp-routes.txt` records every route the drivers call,
and the discovery documents say which methods page — so the gate is a script and a ceiling
away. It is named here rather than half-built (D849).

## D871 — the ratchet was counting a different quantity

D866 built a ceiling over "called operations AWS paginates that no function following a
token issues". It found real things and it stopped new ones, and its number was never
right — not too high or too low, but a different quantity from the one its name claimed.

Two faults, both visible only once something forced a look.

**The authority was a lower bound.** It asked botocore's paginator data. D870 found
`ListWebACLs` paging — `NextMarker` in both the request and the response shape of the
service model — with no paginator entry at all, so the gate built to catch that class could
not see the instance. App Runner's `ListServices` (D860) was the same and had been written
off as "a service with no paginator file", which is a narrower excuse than the truth:
**paginator data is what botocore chose to model, and the service model is what AWS
implements.** Rebuilt from `service-2.json` — a continuation in the input shape AND one in
the output shape — the count of called paginating operations goes 55 → 59, and the four
additions are exactly the ones no paginator names.

**The join was by operation NAME.** `ListTagsForResource` paginates for wafv2, and that
literal appears at twenty-three call sites across thirteen OTHER services. `ListServices`
belongs to App Runner and to ECS. `ListClusters` to ECS and to EKS. So the old ceiling
counted sites that issue an unrelated service's operation, and — the direction that
matters — could call a genuinely unpaged read "followed" because a namesake elsewhere
mentioned a token.

**The fix is to ask the recorder instead of the source.** D853 taught the route sink to name
the OPERATION; it now also names the CHAIN of driver functions that led to the request
(`wafListByName>wafListPage>wafCall>doSigned`), captured into
`go/internal/aws/testdata/aws-callsites.txt` beside the routes. That is D317's rule applied
to the join itself: a static scrape of these drivers gave four different wrong answers, so
the question "who called this?" is asked of the drivers at the funnel they all pass through.

Three choices inside it, each with a reason rather than a default:

  - **A chain, not one frame.** "The call site" is genuinely ambiguous — a read may follow
    its pages in the reader, in a per-page helper, or in a shared loop — and paging is
    followed if ANY function in the chain handles the continuation.
  - **The TAIL of the chain is the key** (reader, per-service helper, transport). The head
    names who wanted the read; the tail names the read. `Delete>deleteASG>describeASG` and
    `Observe>observeASG>describeASG` are one unpaged `describeASG`, and keying on the whole
    chain would let a new test move a defect count. Two DIFFERENT readers of one operation
    stay two entries — that is the D864 case (one operation, three call sites, mixed) that
    the previous subject could not represent at all.
  - **Test frames are dropped.** They would make the chain per-fixture instead of per read.

The new number is 61, and it is not comparable to the old 133: one counted name matches in
source text, the other counts reads the drivers actually make. What IS comparable is the
property both were built for, and only the new one has it — a service-attributed, reachable
read that ignores its token raises the count.

**The trade, stated because it is real.** The recorder sees what the suite EXERCISES; the
scrape saw every literal. A read no fixture reaches is invisible here, where it was counted
before. That is the D756 concern pointed at a gate rather than at a branch, and the guard
against it is the coverage assertion: the capture must carry at least a hundred distinct
(service, operation) pairs or the gate refuses to report anything. It carries far more today
because the driver suite is the thing that produced the 452 recorded routes.

The old gate is deleted rather than kept beside the new one. Two ceilings over one property,
one of them measuring something nobody can state, is how a register of guesses starts
(D849).

## D872 — the read cap that made every Azure subscription's roles unreadable

The first defect found by running the tool against a real cloud account. `discover
--provider azure` against our own subscription returned, among its diagnostics:

	roleDefinitions.list: HTTP 200 but the body did not parse

The cause was the read cap, not the estate. `doARM` read `io.LimitReader(resp.Body,
1<<20)` — 1 MB. A real subscription's `roleDefinitions.list` returns EVERY built-in Azure
role in a single body: 1.14 MB across ~922 roles, with no `nextLink`. So it was truncated
mid-JSON on every real subscription that has ever existed (built-in roles are not optional),
the parse failed, and `capability.authorization.role` could never be enumerated. Confirmed
against live ARM: the body is 1,193,585 bytes.

**Why nothing caught it.** Three guards that should have and didn't, each for a precise
reason:
- The D803 truncation disclosure fires on a response that SAYS there is more — a `nextLink`.
  This response said nothing; the loss was entirely client-side, imposed by our own cap.
  A continuation-based disclosure cannot see a continuation that was never sent.
- `SweepAll` turns a single failed sweep into a DIAGNOSTIC and returns `err=nil` (it only
  fails hard when ALL sweeps fail). So the failure was one line among eight, and the
  `authorization.role` scope was not marked incomplete — which means on a subscription WITH
  custom roles, `posture` would count zero of them as EXACT (`shadowLowerBound=false`), the
  D803/D650 shape: an affirmative claim of completeness on a read that wholly failed.
- Every fixture was under 1 MB. The cap was invisible until a real estate's built-in roles
  crossed it, which is the whole argument for field validation (D716): the fixtures agreed
  with each other and none agreed with reality.

**The fix is two-part, because raising the number alone would only move the cliff.** The cap
becomes `maxARMResponseBytes = 16 << 20` — the floor is set by the largest UNPAGINATED ARM
list, and roleDefinitions is that list. But a bigger cap that still silently truncates is
the same defect one estate later, so the read now takes ONE byte past the cap and, if the
body fills it, returns an ERROR naming the cap rather than handing a possibly-truncated list
to a decision-gating parse. That is the D87 discipline (a short body must not read as the
whole answer) applied to the client-side cap, not just to a mid-body transport drop.

Confirmed end to end: the test stands a >1 MB roleDefinitions body with the one custom role
past the old cap and asserts it is surfaced; with the cap reverted to 1<<20 the test fails.
Re-running `discover` against the real subscription with the fix, the parse-failure
diagnostic is gone.

**Recorded, not fixed here.** AWS's read is capped at the same 1 MB (`aws.go`), but AWS list
responses paginate — individual responses are bounded by a page size — so no confirmed
over-cap body exists there; the same cap-hit-as-error hardening is a parallel candidate.
GCP already reads at 4 MB. The `SweepAll` fail-open (a failed sweep not marking its scope
incomplete) is the deeper of the two findings and is its own candidate: it is what turns a
read failure into a false claim of completeness, and it is not Azure-specific.

## D873 — a failed sweep was tolerated, but never disclosed

D872 fixed the read cap that made Azure's roles unreadable and noted a deeper thing in
passing: when that sweep failed, nothing marked the scope incomplete. This is that entry,
and it is not Azure's — it is the shared `SweepAll` every cloud and k8s discover through.

`SweepAll` was built for RESILIENCE (D621/D642): one unreadable service must not hide the
others, so a failed sweep becomes a diagnostic and the crawl keeps the resources the other
sweeps found. That half is right and stays. The missing half is HONESTY about what the
failure cost. A partial failure returned `err=nil` with the failures buried in diagnostic
strings, and the only channel that marks a scope incomplete — `ListingCompleteness`,
fed by page-truncation notes — never heard about it. So the scope was recorded COMPLETE,
and `posture` set `shadowLowerBound=false`: an affirmative claim that it had counted every
shadow resource exactly, on a capability whose sweep it never read a byte of.

That is precisely the D650/D803 shape, in the case those two did not cover. D650 taught the
crawl to admit a scope it could not START (no crawl at all). D803 taught it to admit a page
it did not FINISH (a truncation). Neither covered a sweep that RAN and ERRORED — and a real
Azure subscription hit exactly that, every time, until D872, because its roleDefinitions
sweep failed on the read cap and posture would have called the custom-role shadow count
exact.

**The fix routes a failed sweep through the same channel a truncation uses**, because the
consequence is identical: the count is a lower bound. `SweepAll` takes the driver's
`ListingRecord` and, on a failed sweep, notes it — the note carries the sweep's token, not
the error text, so it stays deterministic (the error detail is already in the diagnostics).
`TruncatedListings()` then surfaces it, the crawl marks `Incomplete`, and posture flips to
`shadowLowerBound=true`. No new interface, no change to the resilience: the resources found
are still returned, the run still succeeds, and now it also says the estate was read only
in part.

**k8s gained the channel it never had.** The three cloud drivers each had a `ListingRecord`
(D818); k8s had none — it reads full lists (no `limit`), so it had no page-truncation to
note, and the absence was taken for "nothing to say." But a FAILED sweep is incompleteness
regardless of paging, and k8s could not say even that. It now carries the recorder and
implements `ListingCompleteness`, so a discovery sweep that fails against a real cluster
marks the scope a lower bound like everywhere else. This surfaced from the field run against
the Talos cluster, where absent CRDs (ArgoCD, Flux) make sweeps 404 — tolerated, and now
disclosed.

## D874 — Cloudflare WAF, built from the schema because the field could not answer

The DNS-only Cloudflare driver gained `capability.security.waf` — the vocabulary AWS,
Azure and GCP already fulfil. This entry is as much about HOW it was built as what it maps,
because it is the first capability added without a field read to check it against.

**The mapping.** A zone's WAF posture is one `capability.security.waf`, read from two zone
endpoints:
- `managed.ruleset`: an ENABLED rule in the `http_request_firewall_managed` phase entrypoint
  whose action is `execute` and whose target is one of Cloudflare's own managed rulesets
  (the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset or the OWASP Core Ruleset — a customer's custom ruleset is
  not a managed baseline and does not count).
- `policy.mode`: that rule's override action — `log` is detection, the default block/
  challenge is prevention. The same axis `aws.waf` reads off OverrideAction Count-vs-None.
- `bot.protection`: the zone `bot_management` config, true if Bot Fight Mode is on, any
  Super Bot Fight Mode action is not `allow`, or Enterprise `enable_js` is set. Over-report
  is the safe side of a security flag.

**The honesty problem, stated plainly.** The token available was DNS-scoped and 403s on
both endpoints, so this mapping was NOT confirmed against a live response. It was built from
Cloudflare's public api-schemas — which pin the SHAPES (the entrypoint's `rules[]`, the
bot_management fields) but not the BEHAVIOUR: what a free-tier zone returns when no managed
phase exists, whether a plan without bot management 404s or answers with defaults. Those are
exactly where D872 found the fixture-reality gap. So the field-validation-pending status is
recorded here and in the vocab mapping, not buried — and the driver's four-valued honesty
does the load-bearing work: a 404 is an authoritative absence (`managed.ruleset=false`,
`bot.protection=false`, measured), a 403 or 5xx is UNKNOWN (the attribute is omitted with a
diagnostic, never a fabricated "off"). The distinction matters most for the security
attribute a contract would gate on: "we could not read your bot posture" must never render
as "you have none".

**What is NOT here.** Turnstile — a new capability, deferred (no vocab yet). And the field
proof itself: a WAF-scoped Cloudflare token is the one thing that closes the gap this entry
is careful to leave open. The DNS half of the driver IS field-validated (a real account,
36 records); the WAF half waits for a token that can read it.

### D874b — the field token that proved it, and the coupling it exposed

The WAF-scoped Cloudflare token arrived, and running `discover` against it turned D874 from
schema-derived to field-checked for the paths this estate exercises. Nine zones, every one
returning an authoritative 404 on the firewall-managed entrypoint (no managed ruleset
deployed) and a real 403 on bot_management. So the two honesty branches D874 built were
confirmed against LIVE responses: `managed.ruleset=false` from a real 404, and
`bot.protection` OMITTED with a diagnostic from a real 403 — never a fabricated "off". The
`managed.ruleset=true` / `policy.mode` paths stay fixture-only, honestly, because no zone
on this account deploys a managed ruleset.

The run also caught a real defect in the day-old D874 code, which is the whole point of a
field token with an unusual scope. This token can LIST zones but cannot READ dns_records
(403). The discovery loop treated a DNS-record failure with `continue` — and the WAF
emission sat AFTER the records loop, so `continue` skipped it. Every zone's WAF posture went
invisible whenever its records could not be read. DNS records and the WAF posture are
independent reads; coupling them meant a token scoped for WAF-but-not-DNS — exactly this one
— discovered nothing. The fix falls through instead of continuing: a record failure is a
diagnostic, and the WAF read happens regardless. Fixtures never caught it because every
fixture served both reads; the field token served one and not the other.

## D875 — the transfer gate that a name can slip past, and the class backstop under it

The publication path scrubs client names and then audits the result against a denylist
(deny-audit.sh, D578/D651). This session shipped the proof that the whole approach has a
floor: `acme` — the second field tester — rode into the export as an example AWS profile
`acme-iac`, in a test and its DESIGN entry, and the export gate PASSED. The scrub missed
it (no `acme` substitution) and the denylist missed it (no `acme` entry). A maintained
list of names has one failure mode, and it is structural: a name nobody added is a name
nobody catches. The immediate fix was the entry and the scrub; this is the backstop that
does not depend on the list being complete.

`scripts/class-leak-scan.sh` detects a CLASS by SHAPE rather than a name from a list: a real
AWS account id in ARN position (`arn:part:svc:region:ACCOUNT:...`), minus the reserved test
placeholders. A denylist could never carry this — an account id is a number, not a name, so
there is nothing to list. It is the one class where shape-detection is both high-signal and
low-noise, and getting to "low-noise" is the whole of the work:

- A bare 12-digit run flagged a GCS `retentionPeriod` (a ten-year duration) and a 12-digit
  slice of a sha256. Matching the ARN SHAPE, not a bare run, drops both — the `\b…\b` a
  naive scan would use does not, because the hash digits are word characters on both sides.
- A generic e-mail address flagged `git@github.com`, `o@e.test`, `name@project.iam.
  gserviceaccount.com`, `a@b.com` — test placeholders are pervasive, and a REAL address is
  at one of OUR domains, which the denylist already carries. The allowlist to make e-mail
  quiet would grow into the same maintained list this backstop exists to not need, so the
  class was dropped. LAN/RFC1918 addresses are the denylist's job too (our LAN prefix is a
  listed term) and fire on legitimate examples (a test's private-range host, k8s's own
  CIDR doc strings), so they are left out on purpose. One class, narrowly, is worth more
  than three that people learn to ignore.

The backstop runs in TWO places. In `export-public.sh` it is an arm beside deny-audit, so
the full export refuses on a real account id (ci.yml already runs `make export-check` on
every push, so this is CI-gated the moment it lands). And a make-check gate
(`classleak_gate_test.go`) drives it with an INVENTED account id to prove the control fires
— assembled from fragments so no ARN literal sits in the test's own source to trip its live
arm — and then runs it over the working tree, so a real account id committed in an ARN fails
`make check` at the desk, months before an export would have caught it. The pins that keep
it honest: a placeholder-account ARN must PASS (or every driver fixture breaks the export),
and the duration/hash shapes must NOT read as accounts (the false positives, frozen so a
future widening reintroduces them).

The transfer procedure is now layered: whitelist → scrubs → name denylist → class backstop
→ standalone `make check` on the export → gitleaks → reproducible build. The lesson `acme`
taught is the one that generalises past this account-id class: a control that depends on a
human remembering to add an entry needs a second control that depends on nothing being
remembered.

## D876 — the coverage matrix, machine-derived so it cannot flatter itself

The launch consult (Codex + Fable, both independently) named the same signature move: publish
a coverage matrix labelled with our OWN values — `measured` vs `config-intent` — instead of a
marketing "N services." It turns the project's biggest weakness (breadth is proven-in-plan,
not applied) into the sharpest demonstration of its thesis: a medium that never claims to
have checked what it hasn't, applied to itself. `docs/COVERAGE.md` is that table, one row per
driver service.

The table is only worth its ink if it cannot lie, and a hand-kept table lies three ways: it
omits a service (breadth overstated by absence), it names a service the drivers do not have
(a phantom), or it calls a service `measured` with no citation (the overclaim). The gate
(`coverage_gate_test.go`) closes all three. Crucially, the SERVICE LIST is not the table's to
assert — it is read from the drivers' own `ServiceCapabilities()` (D317: ask the drivers,
never scrape), so a driver that gains or drops a service forces the table to match or the
gate fails. That is what makes completeness real rather than aspirational: the subject
generates itself, and the annotation must keep up. `measured` must carry evidence in its own
column, or the row does not stand — the same discipline the whole system applies to a
verdict, turned on the maturity claim.

The number it prints today is the honest one and the uncomfortable one: **23 of 145 services
field-tested** — AWS 16 (the pilot), GCP 4, Azure 3 — the rest `config-intent`, passing
`make check` against golden fixtures and having never touched a real account. Saying so, in a
gated table a reader can trust, is the product. The count is derived conservatively: a
service is `measured` only where a real-cloud run is cited, so the matrix under-claims by
construction rather than over-claims — the safe direction for a trust artifact, and the only
one this project's thesis permits.

## D877 — the registry the driver could not create, found by the e2e climb

The coverage matrix (D876) turned "e2e everything before publication" into a walk down the
service list, and the walk immediately earned its keep. An own-account e2e of `azure/acr` —
a plain registry, no exposure declared — failed at apply: Azure 400, "Disabling public
network access is not supported for the SKU Standard." The driver could not create a
container registry on a real account, and no fixture had ever said so.

The bug was a default meeting a SKU rule. `createBody` always sent `publicNetworkAccess`,
and its value came from `p.Public`, whose zero value is `false` — so a registry with no
exposure attribute got `publicNetworkAccess=Disabled`. But that field is PREMIUM-only on
ACR (the driver's own observe comment already knew this), and the default SKU is Standard,
which rejects it. Every test set `network.publicExposure` explicitly, so none hit the
zero-value default; the field, which does not, hit it on the first try.

Two changes, both consistent with what the driver already did for CMK. A registry is now
PUBLIC by default (`Public: true`) — public is the honest default for a registry, and
private is the opt-in. And a private registry (`publicExposure=false`) FORCES Premium, the
same SKU upgrade CMK already triggers, because that is the only SKU where disabling public
access is legal. `createBody` then emits `publicNetworkAccess` only on Premium; on
Standard/Basic it is omitted, matching a registry that is public by construction. Verified
in the field: with the fix, `azure/acr` creates, converges and retires on a real
subscription, cleanly.

The wider point is D876's thesis paying out. The matrix is not just a scoreboard — driving
its number up is what runs each driver against reality, and reality is where the fixtures'
agreement with each other stops mattering. `measured` costs a real run, and a real run finds
what golden tests cannot.

## D878 — the API the driver could not create, hidden by a PascalCase golden

The e2e climb reached `capability.apigateway.http` on AWS and the create came back
`HTTP 400 (Invalid protocol specified. Must be one of [HTTP, WEBSOCKET])` — with a plan
that provably built `ProtocolType: "HTTP"`. The body was right; the KEY was wrong.
apigatewayv2 is restJson1, and every member carries a camelCase `locationName`
(`name`, `protocolType`, `tags` on the request; `apiId`, `name`, `protocolType`,
`apiEndpoint`, `tags` on the response; `items` on the list). The driver spoke
PascalCase throughout. AWS ignored the unknown `ProtocolType` field, saw `protocolType`
empty, and refused — the create was dead for every input on a real account, and had it
somehow landed the response would have parsed to a zero-value `ApiId` ("create returned
no api id") and never bound.

The golden httptest hid all of it because the fake server echoed PascalCase too: the
request writer and the response reader agreed with each other and disagreed with AWS.
That is the D390/D876 lesson in one file — two halves of a golden can be
self-consistently wrong, and only a real run tells them apart. The fix corrects the
wire on both sides (request body keys, `apigwAPI` json tags, the `items` list wrapper),
rewrites the fixtures to the real camelCase shape (so the golden now models reality),
and pins the exact request key set against the botocore locationNames — a mutation back
to `Name`/`ProtocolType`/`Tags` now fails at the desk. Proven on our account:
create → converge → retire, endpoint provisioned and torn down.

This is the code-freeze admitted class (D716): the tool could not do what it said for
valid input, in the direction that leaves a person worse off than if it had said
nothing. It rhymes with D877 (ACR) — the e2e climb keeps finding the same shape, a
create path golden-green and field-dead, because a fake API validates nothing.

### D878b — the same casing in the discovery path, and the gate that let both through

Fixing the create surfaced two more things. First, `discoverAPIGateway` decoded the
GetApis list with `Items`/`ApiId` (PascalCase) too — on a real account the list is
`items`/`apiId`, so every entry parsed to an empty ApiId and the loop skipped it:
discovery would report ZERO apis on an estate that has them, the false-absence
direction. Fixed to camelCase alongside the create.

Second, and the reason both escaped: the D794 field-name gate confirms each decoded name
against botocore, but it accepts the SHAPE MEMBER name (`ApiId`, PascalCase) as readily
as the wire `locationName` (`apiId`, camelCase) — it adds both to the confirmed set. For
a `json`/`query`/`ec2` protocol service the member name IS the wire name, so that union
is correct. For a `rest-json` or `rest-xml` service the wire name is the locationName and
the member name is wire-DEAD — so the gate green-lit apigatewayv2's PascalCase as
"confirmed to exist in the provider's models," which was true and useless. The gate
cannot tell wire-correct from wire-dead for the eleven rest-json/rest-xml services in the
route table (apigateway, backup, bedrock, efs, eks, opensearch, msk, lambda, scheduler,
sesv2, and the rest-xml cloudfront/route53/s3). That blind spot is now the next sweep:
each of those drivers is checked that its decoded/sent names are the camelCase
locationNames, not the PascalCase members, and the gate is taught the protocol so it can
enforce it. Until then the D878 unit pin — not this gate — is what holds apigateway.

## D879 — MSK, the second driver the sweep found dead on the same wire

D878b named the next sweep: the eleven rest-json/rest-xml AWS drivers, checked that they
decode and send the camelCase `locationName`, not the PascalCase shape member. The sweep
confronted each driver's json tags with botocore's own locationNames and cleared ten of
them — lambda, backup, scheduler, opensearch, sesv2 keep PascalCase because their
`locationName` IS the member name (botocore set no camelCase alias), and efs was already
proven by a real e2e run. One driver did not clear: MSK.

`kafka` (MSK) is restJson1 and every CreateClusterV2 / ListClustersV2 member carries a
camelCase locationName (`clusterName`, `provisioned`, `encryptionInfo`, `clusterArn`,
`state`, `clusterInfoList`, ...). The driver spoke PascalCase in all three places
apigateway did: the create body (AWS drops the unknown fields, then 400s the request for
a missing clusterName/provisioned), the `mskCluster` read struct (a live ListClustersV2
parsed every field to its zero value — an empty `clusterName` never matched our
deterministic name, so a standing cluster read as ABSENT), and the discovery path in
`discover_gap_aws_b.go` (zero clusters found on an estate that has them). The golden fake
echoed PascalCase on both sides, so it was self-consistent and field-dead — the exact
D878 shape.

Fixed in the send struct, the read struct, the list wrapper, the discovery decoder and
the fixtures (now the real camelCase shape), with the create-body key set pinned against
botocore. The authority here is credential-free — MSK's own published locationNames — so
the wire shape is proven without standing up a real cluster (a provisioned MSK is ~20
minutes and a running bill). That is the honest evidence class for this fix: `measured`
stays reserved for the drivers a real run actually exercised.

Two drivers, one wire mistake, one root cause: a fake API validates nothing, and the
D794 field-name gate confirms the member name as readily as the wire name (D878b), so
neither the golden nor the gate could tell wire-correct from wire-dead. The gate's
protocol-awareness — teach it that a rest-json/rest-xml service must decode the
locationName — is the mechanism fix that would make this class impossible rather than
found-one-at-a-time; it is the recorded next step.

## D880 — the ARN in the path: a SigV4 double-encode that 403'd every backup tag read

The e2e climb created a backup vault, then `retire` returned unknown and left it standing.
The reason was one line in the ledger: `ListTags: HTTP 403 (signature does not match)`.
Backup reads ownership tags with the vault ARN IN THE URL PATH (GET /tags/{resourceArn}/),
and the request 403'd on the signature — so a delete or adopt that cannot read ownership
tags returns unknown forever, and every backup vault and plan the tool made leaked,
unretireable.

The authority settled it without an account. Driving botocore's OWN serializer + SigV4Auth
for the exact request showed the scheme: the wire carries the ARN SINGLE-encoded (rfc3986,
`%3A`) as one path segment, and the CANONICAL request encodes it a SECOND time (`%253A`).
That second pass is the SigV4 rule for every service except S3, and AWS applies it when it
rebuilds the canonical from what it received. Our signer's `canonicalURI` encoded the path
only ONCE. For a plain path (a bucket name, a log group) single and double encoding are
identical, so every call worked and had always worked; the miss was invisible until an ARN
— with its colons — sat in the path, where `%3A` had to become `%253A` and did not. The fix
is one line in the signer: encode each path segment twice for non-S3. It is pinned by a
reference vector whose expected signature was computed by botocore
(`a6e0e541…`); the single-encode bug yields a different value (`0afd0307…`), and the
get-vanilla vector (path `/`) is unchanged, confirming plain paths do not move.

The same class, same pass: MSK DeleteCluster is `/v1/clusters/{clusterArn}` — a NON-greedy
segment, so the ARN's slashes must be `%2F` (one segment) or the route 404s. The driver had
used `url.PathEscape`, which encodes the slashes but leaves the colons raw AND relied on the
same single-encoded canonical — wrong twice. Now it single-encodes the whole ARN on the wire
(rfc3986) and the fixed signer double-encodes the canonical, exactly as botocore serializes
DeleteCluster. Proven by the model, since a live MSK cluster is ~20 minutes and a bill.
OpenSearch ListTags carries its ARN in a QUERY parameter, where canonicalQuery already
encodes symmetrically on both sides, so it was never exposed; left as-is, noted.

Proven on our account with the fixed signer: a backup vault create → retire now deletes the
vault (0 remaining), and a five-service regression sweep across json/query/rest protocols
still signs clean — the double-encode moved only the ARN paths it had to. The lesson is the
one the earlier false start taught the hard way: the signer, not the call site, owns the
canonical encoding, and the reference SDK — driven through its real serializer, not a
hand-built request — is the only authority that settles which bytes go where.

## D881 — the query parameter Cloud Scheduler does not have, found by the GCP climb

The e2e climb reached `capability.scheduler.cron` on GCP and the create came back
`jobs.create HTTP 400: Invalid JSON payload received. Unknown name "jobId": Cannot bind
query parameter.` The driver built `POST .../jobs?jobId=<id>` — the AIP-133 create shape
that most Google APIs use, where the caller-chosen id rides as a query parameter and the
server assigns the resource name. Cloud Scheduler is the exception: its create takes ONLY
`{parent}`, and the job id lives in the body's `name` field (which the driver was already
setting correctly). The stray `?jobId=` made the real API refuse every input.

The golden fake hid it the way these always do — it matched the POST by path
(`strings.Contains(path, "/jobs")`) and never inspected the query string, so the extra
parameter sailed past. The fix drops the query parameter; the fixture now fails if a
`jobId` query appears, so the mistake cannot return unseen.

The sweep that mattered: nine other GCP drivers build the same `?<resource>Id=` shape
(cloud functions, run, run-jobs, backup-dr, firestore, kms keyrings, filestore, cert
manager). Confronting each against its OWN discovery document showed the id parameter
PRESENT on all nine — they are correct AIP-133 creates, and Cloud Scheduler is the lone
divergence. Asking the authority per-service, not pattern-matching the code, is what
separated the one real bug from eight that only looked like it. Proven on our project:
create → retire now stands up and tears down a job.

## D882 — `exempt`: the honest third state of the coverage matrix

The climb toward measuring every driver on a real cloud hit services that CANNOT be run
safely or cleanly on the estate we have. GuardDuty is one detector per account, and the
account holds a client's live infrastructure (acme.eu, 20 records) — a create→retire
would toggle the client's threat detection. A GCP KMS keyring cannot be deleted, so a
fixture leaves inert residue forever. The default Firestore database is a per-project
singleton. Security Command Center is an org-level control. None of these is a
per-resource lifecycle we can stand up and tear down without touching something that is
not ours to touch.

Left as `config-intent`, they read as "golden-only, real run still owed" — a debt that is
not actually owed, because the run would be reckless, not merely undone. So the matrix
gains a third status, `exempt`, and — like `measured` — it must carry a REASON, or the
gate rejects it: an exemption without a stated why is a silent skip wearing a label. The
header now states both counts (`N measured … M exempt`), each asserted against the rows,
so neither can quietly inflate. The honest target is no longer "100% measured" — which
this estate cannot yield — but "100% accounted": every service either run for real, or
exempted with the reason it cannot be.

First four exemptions: aws/guardduty (account-wide posture on a client account),
gcp/scc (org-level), gcp/cloudkms (non-deletable keyring), gcp/firestore (singleton).
The near-miss that taught the lesson is recorded too: adopting a hosted zone to read its
domain returned `acme.eu` — adopt writes only the ledger, so no harm, and the domain was
checked BEFORE any retire. Verify the name before you delete, on an account that is not a
sandbox.

## D883 — the kafka version MSK will not build, found on a real cluster

Standing up a real MSK cluster to validate the D879/D880 fixes surfaced a third MSK
defect. `kafkaVersionFor` mapped `kafka/3` to `3.5.1`, and the driver provisions the
general-purpose broker `kafka.m5.large`. CreateClusterV2 400'd: "Standard instance types
are not supported for Kafka version 3.5.1. Valid values: [3.6.0, 3.7.x, ...]". AWS
deprecated the pairing after the mapping was written, so the driver's default `kafka/3`
cluster is uncreatable on a current account. The authority is AWS's own error — it names
the valid versions — so `kafka/3` now maps to `3.6.0`, the lowest AWS still pairs with the
broker type.

The find is doubly useful. It is a real create defect in the D716 class (the tool cannot
build a valid cluster for its default input), and it is the confirmation D879 could not
get without a cluster: the request reached the real API and came back with a
CONFIGURATION error about the version, not a FIELD error about an unknown key. The
camelCase body AWS silently dropped before D879 would have 400'd for a missing
`clusterName`; instead it parsed the body, validated it, and objected to the version. The
golden proved the shape; the real cluster proved the wire.

## D884 — the double member Aurora put under a named list, found on a real create

Aurora rode the cluster fixture next and CreateDBCluster 400'd: "MalformedInput: Start of
list found where not expected". The driver serialized the security-group list as
`VpcSecurityGroupIds.VpcSecurityGroupId.member.N` — but `VpcSecurityGroupId` IS the member
name for that list in the query protocol, so the trailing `.member.N` is a SECOND list
level the API never expects. Driving botocore's own RDS serializer settled it:
`VpcSecurityGroupIds.VpcSecurityGroupId.N`, no extra level. The fix drops the `.member.`.

RDS (the same capability, already measured) never hit it because its create does not send
`VpcSecurityGroupIds` at all — it places by subnet group alone — so only Aurora exercised
the malformed key. The golden hid it the usual way: a unit test pinned the exact malformed
string as the expected body, so the assertion agreed with the bug. That expectation is
corrected to the botocore shape and a mutant now re-injects the double member. The lesson
is D879's in a new protocol: a fake that echoes the driver's own bytes proves nothing; the
reference serializer, driven for real, is the authority on which key goes on the wire.

## D885 — the preflight that denied a permission AWS always grants, found in the field

The Aurora retire refused with `provider-permission-denied` and listed, among the missing
permissions, `sts:GetCallerIdentity` — an action AWS allows every authenticated identity
regardless of policy. botocore's own SimulatePrincipalPolicy for the caller returned
`allowed` for every action in the set; the real DeleteDBCluster succeeded. So the identity
held the permissions and the preflight refused anyway — the exact false-refusal the whole
verb exists to avoid.

The cause was resource scoping. `CheckResourcePermissions` builds the resource's ARN and
simulates EVERY required action in that context, where an implicitDeny is authoritative (a
grant, if any, would have matched the ARN). That rule is right for the resource's OWN
service. It is wrong for a cross-service action: `sts:GetCallerIdentity` and
`tag:TagResources` have no grant scoped to an `arn:aws:rds:…:cluster:…`, so the simulator
returns implicitDeny for a permission the caller in fact holds, and the authoritative rule
reads it as a real denial. The delete's permission set mixed both, so one cross-service
action sank the whole apply.

The fix splits by service: the resource's own actions keep the authoritative ARN context;
everything else falls to the account `"*"` check, where an implicitDeny is unattested,
never a denial. Confirmed against the simulator that a same-service implicitDeny still
denies and a cross-service one does not. This is the D75/D720 doctrine finishing its own
sentence — a simulation is evidence only about the question it was asked, and asking a
cross-service action about the wrong resource is not asking about the caller at all.

## D886 — the resource preflight, now type-aware: cross-resource-TYPE false refusal fixed

D885 fixed the cross-SERVICE half. The Aurora retire then refused a shorter set —
`rds:DeleteDBInstance`, `rds:DeleteDBClusterParameterGroup`, `rds:DeleteDBSubnetGroup` —
all `rds`, so D885's service split keeps them on the authoritative ARN path. But those
actions target DIFFERENT resource TYPES than the cluster ARN they are simulated against:
an instance (`db:`), a parameter group (`pg:`), a subnet group (`subgrp:`). A grant for
`DeleteDBInstance` would match a `db:` ARN, never the `cluster:` ARN, so the simulator
returns implicitDeny for a permission the caller holds (botocore's DeleteDBInstance against
the instance ARN returns allowed; the real delete succeeds), and the resource rule reads it
as a real denial. The D720 premise — "the grant, if any, would have matched the ARN" —
holds only when the action's resource TYPE matches the ARN's.

Resolved as option (a) — partition by resource TYPE, not just service — the only shape
faithful to the doctrine rather than fighting it. (b) weakening the rule to explicit-deny-
only throws away the detection the resource check exists for (a grant scoped to `db:prod-*`
against a `db:orders-db` target is a real gap it would relabel unattested) and reverses
D720's conformance case; (c) attaching a per-action ARN to every permission means changing
`PermissionsFor` from `[]string` to structured pairs — a field HASHED and sealed into the
plan — across every driver and cloud, to fix one service. Both rejected.

The mechanism: `CheckResourcePermissions` now judges an action authoritatively against the
ARN only when `actionService(p) == arnSvc && actionScopableToType(p, arnType)` —
`awsARNResourceType` gives the ARN's type (a pure function of the service, since sqs/sns
ARNs carry no type segment to parse), and `awsActionResourceTypes` gives each action's
resource types from AWS's OWN authority, the Service Reference (`Actions[].Resources[]`),
captured in `aws_action_resourcetypes.verified` by a D846/D847-style refresh script and gate.
A cross-SERVICE action fails the service half, so D885 is subsumed. The design leans on one
asymmetry: the map can only HARM by a FALSE match (a type the action lacks, kept
authoritative) — `TestEveryAWSActionResourceTypeIsOnePublished` forbids exactly that against
the Service Reference; an unknown or omitted action yields no match and routes to the SAFE
account "*" check, so incomplete data can never re-open the false refusal.

For the Aurora delete against `cluster:orders-cluster`: DeleteDBCluster (`{cluster,…}`) and
DescribeDBClusters (`{cluster}`) stay authoritative; DeleteDBInstance (`{db}`),
DeleteDBSubnetGroup (`{subgrp}`), DeleteDBClusterParameterGroup (`{cluster-pg}`) route to
the account check as unattested — exactly what the field showed. Proven on our account: the
Aurora retire that D75's preflight refused for weeks now passes, and `groundhold` deletes
the live cluster. D75/D720/D885 finished: a simulation is evidence only about the exact
question asked, and asking a cross-type action about the wrong resource was never a question
about the caller.

## D887 — the VPC placement Redshift Serverless could not take, found by the e2e climb

The e2e climb reached `capability.warehouse.analytics` on AWS and CreateWorkgroup 400'd
"A default VPC wasn't detected" — the workgroup landed in the account's default VPC
because the driver sent no subnetIds, and this account (which holds client infra) has no
default VPC. The gap was one-sided: `BuildRedshiftServerless` read only `kms_key_id` and
`workgroupBody` emitted no network placement, even though CreateWorkgroup takes `subnetIds`
and `securityGroupIds` directly (confirmed against botocore). Its sibling backend on the
SAME capability, ElastiCache Serverless, ALREADY read `subnetIds`/`securityGroupIds` and
built them into the request — so the driver family was inconsistent, and only the
un-exercised backend carried the hole.

The fix mirrors the working sibling: RSSPlan gains SubnetIDs/SecurityGroupIDs,
BuildRedshiftServerless reads them via `implStrings` (opaque impl, invariant #4 — topology
is implementation, never a capability attribute), and `workgroupBody` emits the JSON lists
only when supplied, so an account WITH a default VPC still works with none. Proven on our
account: with a dedicated three-AZ fixture VPC, the workgroup now creates and retires.
ElastiCache Serverless was never a driver gap — its earlier failure was the harness not
passing subnets, and its COVERAGE note is corrected; both are now measured with real
placement. The lesson is the parity one: two backends on one capability must be checked
against each other, because the one no run touches is where the operand quietly goes
missing.

## D888 — Redshift Serverless deleted the namespace before the workgroup was gone

Fixing D887's placement gap let the Redshift Serverless create land, and the retire that
followed exposed a second defect one layer down. A serverless warehouse is a composite:
DeleteWorkgroup then DeleteNamespace. DeleteWorkgroup is ASYNC — the workgroup enters
"deleting" and lingers — and DeleteNamespace fails while ANY workgroup still references the
namespace. The driver deleted the workgroup and IMMEDIATELY called DeleteNamespace, which
409'd, leaving an orphaned namespace (confirmed on our account) — and worse, the namespace
could no longer be retired through groundhold, because the delete's claim keys ownership
off the workgroup that was now gone. A resource the tool created and could not clean up:
the dangerous shape.

The fix mirrors the create-side poll the same driver already runs: after DeleteWorkgroup,
poll GetWorkgroup until it returns ResourceNotFound, then delete the namespace. The golden
hid it because the delete fixture was STATELESS — GetWorkgroup returned AVAILABLE forever,
even after its own DeleteWorkgroup, so the poll (had it existed) would never terminate and
the bug (firing the namespace delete early) looked fine against a fake that never modeled
the workgroup leaving. The fixture is now stateful (gone after its delete), and a dedicated
test 409s DeleteNamespace while the workgroup lingers for one poll — so a driver that skips
the wait fails exactly as the real cloud did. Proven end-to-end: create then retire now
deletes both the workgroup and the namespace, nothing orphaned.

D887 and D888 are one field session on one un-exercised backend: the operand that was never
sent, and the delete ordering that was never run. Two defects the golden could not surface
because a fake accepts any placement and a stateless fake never makes a delete's second step
depend on its first.

## D889 — the vpngateway permission that was a REST method, not an IAM permission

The network-fixture climb reached `capability.vpn.gateway` on GCP and converge refused
`preflight-inconclusive`: "Permission compute.vpnGateways.insert is not valid for this
resource." A GCP compute IAM permission is `compute.<resource>.create` — even though the
REST method that creates the resource is `insert`. The driver declared
`compute.vpnGateways.insert`, the REST method name, which is not an IAM permission at all,
so projects.testIamPermissions 400'd the WHOLE call (one bad permission poisons the batch),
the preflight came back inconclusive, and converge — which fails closed on inconclusive —
refused. The gateway could never be created through the porcelain.

The sibling that proved the shape: `pd` (compute.disks.**create**) preflights and converges
fine; only vpngateway used `.insert`, and it was the ONLY `.insert` in the whole driver.
Confirmed against the live API: testIamPermissions returns 200 for
`compute.vpnGateways.create` and 400 for `.insert`. One-line fix; proven end-to-end (create
then retire on our project).

No machine-readable GCP permission index is fetched the way the AWS Service Reference is
(D846/D847), so the class is pinned by the one mechanical rule that catches it from source:
`TestNoGCPComputePermissionUsesTheRESTInsertName` forbids any declared `compute.*.insert`.
The lesson rhymes with the AWS field-name and permission gates — a name the provider does
not actually have (a REST method masquerading as a permission) sails through every check
that does not confront it with the provider's own vocabulary, and here the provider's answer
was a 400 that turned an authorized create into a permanent refusal.

## D890 — the scheduled query rule that could only be born global, in a global-hostile type

The LA-workspace climb reached `capability.monitoring.logmetric` on Azure and the create
400'd: "the provided location 'global' is not available for resource type
'microsoft.insights/scheduledqueryrules'." The driver hard-coded `"location": "global"` in
the create body — a value that works for some Azure monitor types (web tests, portal
dashboards, both genuinely global) but which scheduledQueryRules, a REGIONAL type, rejects.
So the rule was uncreatable on any real subscription.

The fix reads the region from the operator's substrate — `implementation.location`, the
same shape AWS cwlogfilter uses for `impl.region` — and refuses when it is absent rather
than guessing a region the rule cannot live in (typically the scope workspace's region).
The golden hid it the usual way: the fixtures fed a stateful fake that echoed whatever
location the body carried, so `"global"` round-tripped fine against a double that has no
notion of which regions a resource type serves. A unit pin now asserts the body carries
the operator's region, not `"global"`, and a real create+retire on our subscription
proves it.

The narrow lesson: a hard-coded location is a claim about where a resource type can exist,
and Azure's answer differs by type — global for some, regional for others. Only the
provider knows, and it says so with a 400 that a fake never will.

## D891 — the GCE image family reference the regex placed a slash wrong in

The compute-instance climb reached `capability.compute.instance` on GCP and the create
refused: "source_image projects/debian-cloud/global/images/family/debian-12 is not a valid
image reference." That string is the CANONICAL way nearly every operator names a base image
— the "latest debian-12 family" reference GCP's own docs use. The driver's regex accepted
`projects/<p>/global/images/<image>` with an optional `/family/<f>` suffix AFTER the image
name — which is not how GCP writes a family ref. GCP's family syntax is
`.../global/images/family/<family>`: `family` is a path SEGMENT before the family name, not
a suffix after an image name. So a specific image (`.../images/debian-12-bookworm-v…`)
passed and the standard family reference did not, and an operator following the GCP docs was
refused.

The fix moves `family/` to where GCP puts it — an optional segment before the image token:
`projects/<p>/global/images/(family/)?<name>`. Confirmed the specific form still works (a
real create landed on our project with `.../images/debian-12-bookworm-v20260804`), then the
family form once fixed; a unit pin now accepts both the full-path family reference and the
project-relative short form, and rejects `debian:latest`. The narrow lesson is a validation
one: a regex that encodes a provider's identifier syntax is a claim about that syntax, and
`/family/` after the name versus `family/` before it is the whole difference between
accepting the reference every operator writes and refusing it.

## D892 — Cloud Run Jobs measured: the image is a capability attribute, not an operand

The container class reached `capability.container.job` on GCP. First attempt declared the
image under `implementation:` and plan refused it as an unknown operand — correctly: the
Cloud Run Jobs driver reads `image` as a capability ATTRIBUTE (it is semantic — what runs is
part of the contract, not opaque provisioning config), and an operand the driver never reads
is refused rather than dropped. Moved under `attributes:` with `location.region`, the create
landed and retire cleaned up: a real Cloud Run Job stood on our project from the public
`us-docker.pkg.dev/cloudrun/container/hello` image and was then deleted, verified by listing
zero jobs in the region. No code change — this is a measurement fold flipping the coverage
row from config-intent to measured (gcp 25/46, 80/145). The narrow note is the attribute/
operand boundary the refusal enforced: `image` names WHAT the capability is, so it belongs to
the typed contract surface, and the driver's refusal to read it as free-form impl is the
boundary doing its job.

## D893 — App Runner measured through the public-ECR path that needs no access role

The container class continued to AWS `capability.workload.container` via the `apprunner`
service (the Cloud Run twin — a container image to a managed HTTPS endpoint). The driver
already distinguishes the two image-repository types D76-style: a private `ECR` image needs
`implementation.access_role_arn` (the role App Runner assumes to pull it, a separate binding
the operator brings), but a `public.ecr.aws/` image is `ECR_PUBLIC` and needs no role at all
— so the fixture is just an image and a region. A real service stood on our account in
eu-west-1 from `public.ecr.aws/aws-containers/hello-app-runner` and retire deleted it;
confirmed by a raw SigV4 `AppRunner.ListServices` returning zero `r-dev-*` services (App
Runner's delete is async, so the listing is the honest witness, not the converge verdict).
No code change — a measurement fold (aws 41/54, 81/145). The note worth keeping is that the
public-ECR branch is what makes this a cheap fixture: the driver's own repo-type split means
the access-role binding is required exactly when the platform requires it and never as a
blanket toll.

## D894 — Route53 record measured; the parent zone is the ownership boundary

DNS reached AWS `capability.dns.record` (`route53record`). A throwaway public hosted zone for
a fictional domain (`gh-e2e-test-847.example`, a name that resolves nowhere and touches no
real estate) was created, an A record written to `203.0.113.10` (TEST-NET-3), then retire
deleted the record and the zone was torn down — confirmed by a raw SigV4
`ListResourceRecordSets` showing only the NS and SOA left, then `DeleteHostedZone`.

The run surfaced the driver's ownership model exactly: the first create was REFUSED — "the
parent hosted zone is not ours (tags do not match)". `zoneOwnedByUs` reads the zone's tags
and writes a record only into a zone carrying our `groundhold-capability` / `groundhold-
environment` tags; an unreadable tag set is `unknown`, never "not ours" (fail-closed, D-class
readability). This is correct and worth recording as the SHAPE an operator meets: groundhold
manages records only in a zone it can prove is ours, so pointing it at a pre-existing
human-owned zone means tagging that zone first (an adopt-like consent step) — not a defect,
the boundary doing its job. No code change — a measurement fold (aws 42/54, 82/145).

## D895 — IAM grant measured; the read-modify-write took only the pair it declared

Authorization reached GCP `capability.authorization.grant` (`iambinding`). A grant of
`roles/browser` to `user:jakub@michal.kids` at account scope was applied and then retired on
our dev project. The proof that matters for a driver that edits a SHARED document — the
project IAM policy — is that it changed only what it declared: the policy carried 46 bindings
before, 46 after, and the `roles/browser` binding was present between and gone after. The RMW
is etag-guarded (a concurrent edit becomes `unknown`+reconcile, never a clobber) and
content-addressed on {project, role, member}, so retire removed exactly the member it granted
and no other principal's access. No code change — a measurement fold (gcp 26/46, 83/145). The
note worth keeping: this is the one class where a create/delete touches infrastructure OTHER
grants live in, so "count before == count after, minus our pair" is the honest witness, not
the converge verdict alone.

## D896 — the Azure grant that can only be given to a service principal (recorded debt)

Continuing the authorization class to the Azure twin (`roleassignment`), a real grant of
Reader to a User principal at subscription scope was REFUSED by Azure: "The PrincipalId ...
has type 'User', which is different from specified PrincipalType 'ServicePrincipal'." The
driver hardcodes `"principalType": "ServicePrincipal"` in the assignment PUT
(`azrole_net.go:59`), so it can only grant to service principals — a grant to a User or Group
is rejected. The GCP twin (`iambinding`) accepts `user:`/`group:`/`serviceAccount:`/`domain:`
members because the member string CARRIES its type; Azure's `grant.principal` is a bare object
GUID that encodes no type, so the vocabulary gives the Azure driver no way to say which kind
of principal it is, and the driver guessed one for everybody.

This is a genuine capability gap and an asymmetry with the GCP twin, but it is NOT the
dangerous direction the D716 freeze admits: the tool FAILS CLOSED (Azure refuses, the create
reports failed) rather than making a false statement about a grant that did not happen — an
operator is not worse off than if the tool had said nothing. So it is recorded here as debt
for the next unfreeze, not fixed now. The shape of the fix is a vocabulary one: the
authorization.grant principal needs a type the Azure driver can read (a typed member form like
GCP's, or an explicit operand), rather than a hardcoded assumption. No resource was created
(the 400 left nothing behind — confirmed by a roleAssignments list unchanged at baseline), so
the row stays config-intent with the finding noted, not measured.

## D897 — the alert policy whose filter GCP will not accept (recorded debt)

The monitoring class reached GCP `capability.monitoring.alert` (`monitoring`). An alert on a
standard GCE metric (`compute.googleapis.com/instance/cpu/utilization`, threshold 0.8) was
REFUSED by GCP at create: "Field alert_policy.conditions[0].condition_threshold.filter had an
invalid value ... must specify a restriction on resource.type." The driver builds the
condition filter as `metric.type="<metric>"` and nothing else (`alertpolicy.go:101`), but
Cloud Monitoring requires an alerting filter to also pin `resource.type` — a standard metric
maps to a monitored-resource type, and the API refuses a filter that leaves it open. So the
policy is uncreatable for the common case, and only the golden fake (which accepted the bare
`metric.type=` filter and validated nothing about GCP's filter grammar) ever thought it
worked — the golden-green/field-dead shape this climb keeps surfacing.

The honest classification is the same as D896: the tool FAILS CLOSED (GCP 400, create reports
failed, and a subsequent alertPolicies list showed nothing left behind), so no false statement
about a real estate is made and the D716 freeze does not admit the fix. It is recorded as debt
for the next unfreeze. The shape of the fix is that the alert condition needs a resource.type
— derived from the metric descriptor (a monitoring.metricDescriptors read gives the metric's
monitored-resource types) or supplied as an operand — folded into the filter, rather than a
filter that names only the metric. Row stays config-intent with the finding noted, not
measured.

## D898 — managed instance group measured; a bare template name the regex takes but GCP won't

The autoscaling class reached GCP `capability.compute.autoscaling` (`mig`). A zonal managed
instance group (min 1 / max 3, CPU-target autoscaler) was created from a throwaway instance
template on our dev project: create CONVERGED (verified against observed reality, the group
standing at targetSize 1), then retire deleted the group and its instance, and the template
fixture was torn down — confirmed by listing zero instanceGroupManagers and zero r-dev
instances in the zone. Two input-shape lessons the field run pinned:

`target_cpu_utilization` is a PERCENTAGE 1–100 (the driver refuses `0.6` at preflight —
correct, fail-closed, and it names the range), even though GCP's autoscaler API stores the
underlying `utilizationTarget` as a 0–1 fraction; the driver owns that conversion.

`instance_template` must be a QUALIFIED reference (`projects/<p>/global/instanceTemplates/<n>`
or a full URL). The `migTemplateOK` regex also accepts a BARE name, but the driver passes the
value verbatim into the insert body (`mig.go:243`) and GCP rejects a bare name with "Invalid
value for field 'resource.instanceTemplate' ... The URL is malformed." So the bare-name branch
of the regex accepts a form real GCP will not take — the golden-green/field-dead shape (the
fake accepted it; the cloud does not). It fails closed (GCP 400, nothing created), so under the
D716 freeze it is recorded debt, not a fix; the shape of the fix is to either qualify a bare
name into `global/instanceTemplates/<n>` before the insert or drop the bare-name branch from
the regex so the refusal happens at preflight with a clear reason. The service itself is
measured via the qualified form; the row carries the wart as a note.

## D899 — the EventBridge schedule that creates but will not delete (recorded debt)

The scheduler class reached the AWS twin of the measured GCP `cloudscheduler`:
`eventbridgescheduler` (`capability.scheduler.cron`). With an SNS-topic target and a
scheduler-assumable IAM role as fixtures, CREATE worked — the schedule stood in the default
group with the correct owner marker in its Description
(`groundhold:capability=r;environment=dev`). RETIRE, though, FAILED: `DeleteSchedule` is
`DELETE /schedules/{name}`, and EventBridge Scheduler rejects it without a `clientToken` query
parameter — "ClientToken cannot be empty" (HTTP 400). The driver sends none
(`eventbridgescheduler_net.go:160` calls `ebsCall("DELETE", region, "/schedules/"+name, nil)`),
so every retire of a schedule fails and the schedule LINGERS — and keeps firing on its cadence.
Confirmed against the raw REST API from two directions: a correctly-signed DELETE without the
param 400s, the same DELETE with `?clientToken=<token>` returns 200. Create is unaffected
because CreateSchedule is a POST with a body and does not require the token.

This is a real, asymmetric defect (create-capable, retire-broken), but it FAILS CLOSED: the
converge retire reports `failed` with the 400 reason, so a person is not worse off than if the
tool had said nothing — they are told the schedule was not deleted. So under the D716 freeze it
is recorded debt, not fixed now; the fix is a one-liner — add a generated `clientToken` query
param to the DeleteSchedule call (the same idempotency token CreateSchedule's SDK path supplies
automatically). Fixtures (schedule, role, SNS topic) were all torn down and verified gone; the
row stays config-intent with the finding noted, not measured.

## D900 — Azure managed disk measured; the zone-redundancy contradiction the driver catches

The block-storage class reached Azure `capability.storage.block` (`azdisk`). A 4 GiB zonal
Standard_LRS managed disk was created in the tftest resource group and retired — confirmed
gone by a disks list showing the RG empty. The run also exercised a good preflight refusal:
`availability.class=regional` with a `Standard_LRS` SKU is refused because a `_LRS` SKU is
locally redundant and cannot survive losing a zone — a regional (zone-redundant) placement
needs a `_ZRS` SKU. That is the driver keeping a residency/durability claim honest, not a
defect: it refuses to report zone-redundancy the SKU cannot provide. The measured path used
`availability.class=zonal` + `zone: "1"` + `Standard_LRS`, which are mutually consistent. No
code change — a measurement fold (azure 16/45, 85/145).

## D901 — the backup vault that creates and deletes, but whose delete the driver leaves unknown

The backup class reached Azure `capability.backup.vault` (`backupvault`). After registering the
`Microsoft.DataProtection` resource provider on the subscription (an environment prerequisite,
not a driver concern), CREATE was proven — a backup vault stood in tftest at provisioningState
Succeeded. RETIRE, though, came back UNKNOWN: the driver's delete receives a 202 (Azure accepts
the vault delete as an ASYNC operation) and returns `unknown` — the D57 resume path — rather
than following the async-operation to completion and confirming the vault is gone. The delete
is genuinely accepted (a direct DELETE returns 202 and the vault does disappear, verified by a
backupVaults list going empty), so this is FAIL-SAFE four-valued honesty, not a false claim:
the tool says "unknown, run resume," which is true, and no one is misled.

It is still a gap worth recording, because the sibling `azdisk` retire in the same session
self-confirmed cleanly — so the Azure driver family CAN drive a delete to a confirmed end, and
backupvault's 202-async delete simply isn't wired to poll the operation the way a converged
retire needs. Under the D716 freeze this is not dangerous (unknown, not a lie), so it is
recorded debt: the fix is to follow the Azure-AsyncOperation/Location header on the 202 to a
terminal state, turning the honest `unknown` into a confirmed `succeeded`. The row stays
config-intent — create proven, retire not self-captured — not measured.

## D902 — the uptime web test born global, again (recorded debt; and a method question)

The uptime-monitoring class reached Azure `capability.monitoring.uptime` (`webtest`). With an
App Insights component as the fixture, create was refused by Azure: "Unsupported location:
global." The driver hardcodes `"location": "global"` (`azwebtest.go:111`), but an Application
Insights web test is a REGIONAL resource — it must live in a region (matching its component).
This is the EXACT shape of D890 (the scheduled query rule that could only be born global in a
global-hostile type), in a different service. Two input-format refusals along the way were
correct, not defects: `check.target` is a bare host (not a URL), and `check.period` is a
duration (`300s`, not a number) — the driver guided both.

This finding surfaces a method question worth flagging rather than resolving unilaterally.
D890 — the identical born-global defect — was FIXED earlier this session (Location added to the
plan, refuse-if-empty, mutant gated). But the D716 freeze says plainly: "Field work continues
... without the runtime changing, and its findings are the input the next unfreeze is spent
on." Under the freeze's letter, a fail-closed golden-green defect like this is RECORDED and
waits. This turn (D896–D902) I have recorded rather than fixed, honoring the freeze's letter;
the earlier D877–D891 fixed the same class. Whether the climb should keep recording (freeze) or
