resume fixing (spend the unfreeze, as D877–D891 did) is a call for the human, so this row stays
config-intent with the finding noted, and the question goes to the user.

## D903 — the web test driver made to actually create a web test (fixes D902)

The user's call on the D902 method question was to RESUME FIXING (spend the unfreeze on this
golden-green class, as D877–D891 did), rather than keep recording. So the climb turns from
recording to fixing, and `azure/webtest` is the first fix. Field work surfaced not one but
THREE defects stacked in the same driver, each hidden behind the one before it — the signature
of a driver whose golden test never touched Azure:

1. **Born global** (the D902 finding): `createBody` hardcoded `"location": "global"`; an
   Application Insights web test is regional and Azure 400s "Unsupported location: global". Fix:
   a `Location` on the plan read from `implementation.location`, refuse-if-empty, used in the
   body — the exact D890 shape.
2. **No WebTest XML**: with the location fixed, Azure next rejected the create — "Value cannot
   be null. Parameter name: 'properties.Configuration.WebTest' must be specified." A ping test
   is created from a WebTest XML blob, which the body omitted entirely. Fix: generate the XML
   (deterministic GUIDs so a re-create is byte-identical) under `Configuration.WebTest`, and
   drop the structured `Request`/`ValidationRules` pair that Azure rejects ("Parameter name:
   format") — the XML is the authority.
3. **Observe read a field Azure never fills**: `observe` reverse-mapped the URL from
   `properties.Request.RequestUrl`, but a real web test GET returns `Request: null` and carries
   the URL only inside the WebTest XML. So observe would have found nothing on real Azure (the
   fake had echoed back the Request we sent — the golden green). Fix: parse the URL out of
   `Configuration.WebTest` with a small regex, XML-unescaped.

Proven end to end on our subscription: create CONVERGED (verified against observed reality, the
test standing in westeurope), retire deleted it, confirmed gone. A failing unit test pins the
regional location and the presence of the XML; two mutation-gate mutants (hardcode global;
empty the XML) were hand-verified to bite. Row flips config-intent → measured (azure 17/45,
86/145). The lesson is the stacking: a golden-green driver can hide several field-fatal gaps
behind each other, and only a real create walks through them one 400 at a time.

## D904 — the EventBridge schedule delete given its missing idempotency token (fixes D899)

Second fix of the resumed climb. `aws/eventbridgescheduler` created fine but its retire
FAILED (D899): DeleteSchedule is `DELETE /schedules/{name}`, and EventBridge Scheduler rejects
it without a `clientToken` query parameter — "ClientToken cannot be empty" (HTTP 400) — so every
retire failed and the schedule lingered, still firing on its cadence. The asymmetry that hid it:
CreateSchedule already computed a deterministic `ebsClientToken(name)` and put it in the request
BODY, but the delete path sent none. The fix adds the same deterministic token as a query
parameter on the delete (`?clientToken=`+ebsClientToken(name)); the request signer already
canonicalizes `u.Query()`, so the token is signed correctly. Determinism keeps a retried delete
idempotent rather than minting a new request each time.

Proven end to end: create then retire on our account with a real SNS-target schedule, then a
ListSchedules returning empty. The test double now rejects a token-less DELETE the way AWS does
("ClientToken cannot be empty") so a driver that forgets it fails the delete test rather than
passing against a shrug; a mutation-gate mutant (drop the token) was hand-verified to bite. Row
flips config-intent → measured (aws 43/54, 87/145).

## D905 — the MIG template reference the driver now qualifies (fixes D898)

Third fix of the resumed climb. `gcp/mig`'s `migTemplateOK` regex accepted a BARE instance-
template name, but the driver passed it verbatim into `instanceGroupManagers.insert`, which
GCP rejects — "Invalid value for field 'resource.instanceTemplate' ... The URL is malformed"
(D898). The golden test even asserted the bare name, so the fake blessed a value the platform
refuses. The fix qualifies a bare name to the project-relative partial URL GCP accepts —
`global/instanceTemplates/<name>` — and leaves an already-qualified reference (a full URL or a
`projects/.../` path) untouched. Proven on real GCP: a MIG created from a BARE template name
CONVERGED (verified against observed reality) and retired cleanly, confirming GCP accepts the
qualified partial form. The golden test now expects the qualified value, a table test covers
bare/partial/project/full inputs, and a mutation-gate mutant (drop the qualification) was
hand-verified to bite. mig stays measured; the note loses its wart.

## D906 — the role grant given a principal type it can read (fixes D896)

Fourth fix of the resumed climb. `azure/roleassignment` hardcoded `"principalType":
"ServicePrincipal"` in the assignment body, so a grant to a User or Group was rejected by Azure
("has type 'User', which is different from specified PrincipalType 'ServicePrincipal'") and only
service-principal grants could be created (D896). The root is that `grant.principal` is a bare
object GUID that carries no type — unlike the GCP twin's `user:`/`serviceAccount:` member
prefixes — so the driver had nothing to read and guessed one for everyone. The fix adds a
`principal_type` operand (User | Group | ServicePrincipal), defaulting to ServicePrincipal (the
workload-grant common case, so existing candidates are unchanged) and refusing an unknown value
rather than sending it to a 400; the body carries the operand. Proven on our subscription: a
Reader grant to a real USER at subscription scope created and retired, the principal's
assignment count 1 before and after. A unit test pins the default/honored/refused cases, a body
test pins that the PUT carries the operand type, and a mutation-gate mutant (re-hardcode
ServicePrincipal) was hand-verified to bite. Row flips config-intent → measured (azure 18/45,
88/145).

## D907 — the alert filter given its resource.type restriction (fixes D897)

Fifth fix of the resumed climb. `gcp/monitoring` built the alert condition filter as
`metric.type="X"` and nothing else, but Cloud Monitoring refuses an alerting filter that does
not also restrict `resource.type` ("must specify a restriction on resource.type") — a metric
maps to a monitored-resource type, so the policy was uncreatable for the standard case (D897),
and only the golden fake (which validated nothing about the filter grammar) thought it worked.
The type is not derivable from the metric string, so the fix adds a `resource_type` operand
(e.g. `gce_instance`), requires it, and folds it into the filter as
`metric.type="X" AND resource.type="Y"`. Proven on real GCP: an alert on the GCE CPU metric
with `resource_type=gce_instance` created and retired, zero policies left. A unit test pins the
resource.type clause in the filter and a missing-resource_type refusal, and a mutation-gate
mutant (drop the clause) was hand-verified to bite. Row flips config-intent → measured
(gcp 28/46, 89/145).

## D908 — the backup vault whose retention field was typed int, and the misdiagnosis it corrects

Sixth fix of the resumed climb, and a correction. D901 recorded backupvault as "async delete
returns unknown" — a plausible story from the outside (the retire did report unknown), but
WRONG. Tracing the driver on a real vault showed the pre-delete GET returned HTTP 200 and then
`json.Unmarshal` FAILED: "cannot unmarshal number 14.0 into Go struct field ...
softDeleteSettings.retentionDurationInDays of type int". Azure returns
`retentionDurationInDays` as a JSON number WITH a fraction (`14.0`), which cannot decode into a
Go `int`, so the WHOLE vault document failed to parse, the delete's ownership read returned
"unparseable — reconcile" (unknown), and `deleteAndConfirm` was never reached — every retire
died unknown and the vault was never deleted. The delete was never the problem; the read was.

The fix types the field `float64` (which accepts `14.0`) and casts to int where the hours are
computed. Proven end to end on our subscription: create then retire, the vault actually gone
this time. The fake now emits the retention as `30.0` (a `json.RawMessage`, since `json.Marshal`
of `float64(30)` drops the fraction), so the whole document carries the real Azure shape and a
struct that types the field `int` fails to parse it — a mutation-gate mutant (retype int) was
hand-verified to bite. Row flips config-intent → measured (azure 19/45, 90/145).

The lesson is about the D901 note itself: a field observation ("retire returns unknown") is a
symptom, and naming a mechanism from the symptom without tracing the code produced a confident,
wrong cause. The honest record now says so. It also flags a class worth a sweep at the next
unfreeze: any Azure struct field typed `int` that the service may return with a fraction is the
same latent parse failure waiting on a different resource.

## D909 — the D908 sweep: confirm per field, do not assume the class is blanket

The D908 fix (a `retentionDurationInDays` typed int that Azure returns as `14.0`) prompted a
sweep for the same shape: Azure struct fields typed `int` that decode a response and could come
back with a fraction. The scan surfaced four candidates; the two sharing D908's exact
"retention days" shape were `MessageRetentionInDays` (eventhubs) and `BackupRetentionDays`
(flexpostgres). Rather than assume they were broken — the very error D908's lesson warns against
— eventhubs was exercised end to end on our subscription (Standard namespace + hub, create then
retire, namespace gone). It PASSED with no parse failure: Azure returns `messageRetentionInDays`
as an int for event hubs, so the field is fine and the D908 shape is NOT blanket. eventhubs
flips config-intent → measured (azure 20/45, 91/145) as a side effect of the confirmation.

The remaining candidate, `flexpostgres.BackupRetentionDays`, is unconfirmed — a flexible server
is a ~5–10 min async create and none stands to GET — so it stays a NOTED candidate, not a
claimed defect. This is the D908 lesson applied to itself: the class is real but not universal,
and each member is confirmed by a real read before it is called a bug or fixed. The honest
record: eventhubs checked and clean; flexpostgres retention-days field awaits a field read.

## D910 — the D908 sweep, closed: both retention-days candidates return ints

Closes the open thread D909 left. The last unconfirmed D908 candidate,
`flexpostgres.BackupRetentionDays`, was checked by standing up a real PostgreSQL flexible
server (Standard_B1ms, tftest) and reading its raw JSON: `"backupRetentionDays":7` — an int, not
a fraction. So the flex server's create CONVERGED and its retire deleted it with no parse
failure (the pre-delete read the D908 bug lived in stayed clean), and flexpostgres flips
config-intent → measured (azure 21/45, 92/145) as a side effect of the confirmation.

Both "retention days" fields that shared backupvault's exact shape — `MessageRetentionInDays`
(eventhubs, D909) and `BackupRetentionDays` (flexpostgres, here) — come back as ints from
Azure. Only backupvault's `retentionDurationInDays` is serialized with a fraction (14.0). So
D908 was a SINGLE-FIELD defect, not a class across the retention-days fields, and the sweep's
value was proving that by reading each one rather than typing them all float64 on suspicion —
the D908 lesson (confirm per field, do not assume) applied to its own follow-up and coming back
clean. The int/float sweep is now closed for the retention-days shape; if a future field is
found to serialize with a fraction, it is the same one-line float64 fix, confirmed the same way.

## D911 — Azure Files measured; the driver stands up its own storage account

The filesystem class reached Azure `capability.storage.filesystem` (`azurefiles`). A file share
needs a parent storage account, and the driver creates BOTH — a StorageV2 account plus the SMB
share — so the fixture is just a resource group and a quota. Proven on our subscription: an SMB
share with a 100 GiB quota on a driver-created account in tftest, create then retire, the whole
account gone afterward (verified by a storageAccounts list going empty). No code change — a
measurement fold (azure 22/45, 93/145). The one input note: `protocol` is a typed scalar written
`engine/version` (e.g. `smb/3.1.1`), not a bare `SMB` string — the driver reads the engine half
and maps smb→StorageV2, nfs→Premium FileStorage.

## D912 — Azure Kafka measured (the Event Hubs Kafka endpoint)

The messaging class reached Azure `capability.messaging.kafka` (`azkafka`) — on Azure a Kafka
endpoint is a Standard-tier Event Hubs namespace, the same substrate as `eventhubs` (D909) with

`engine.protocol` `kafka/3.0`, create then retire, the namespace gone afterward. No code change

## D913 — the CDN the platform retired underneath the driver (recorded, not a quick fix)

The CDN class reached Azure `capability.cdn.distribution` (`azurecdn`). The create was refused
by Azure itself: "Azure CDN from Microsoft (classic) no longer support new profile creation."
The driver targets the classic Microsoft CDN profile, which Azure has since RETIRED for new
resources — the successor is Azure Front Door Standard/Premium, a different resource type on a
different API surface. This is not the golden-green shape the other fixes addressed: the driver
was CORRECT when written, and the platform moved out from under it. It fails closed (a clear 400,
nothing created — verified by an empty profiles list), so no false claim is made.

Unlike D905–D912, this is not a one-line fix: making the capability creatable again means
porting the driver from classic CDN to Front Door (afdProfiles/afdEndpoints/originGroups —
a materially different create body and capability model). That is a real piece of work, recorded
here rather than attempted at the tail of a fixing pass. Row stays config-intent with the
platform-retirement noted; the value of the field run is knowing the classic target is dead, so
the port is the actual next step for this capability rather than a debugging hunt.

## D914 — Azure change feed measured (an Event Grid subscription to a queue)

The observability class reached Azure `capability.observability.changefeed` (`changefeed`). On
Azure this is an Event Grid subscription that routes a storage account's blob events to a
storage QUEUE, so `feed.target` is the full queue resource id
(`<accountId>/queueServices/default/queues/<q>`) and the fixture is a StorageV2 account with a
queue (plus the Microsoft.EventGrid RP registered). Proven on our subscription: create then
retire, the subscription gone and the storage-account fixture deleted afterward. No code change
— a measurement fold (azure 24/45, 95/145).

## D915 — Activity Log measured; the custom-name operand that fights the ownership marker (design tension, not resolved)

The audit class reached Azure `capability.audit.trail` (`activitylog`) — a subscription
diagnostic setting delivering the Activity Log to a durable destination (a storage account
fixture here). With the DETERMINISTIC name it measured cleanly: create then retire, the setting
gone. But the run surfaced a real inconsistency in the driver, not a fix I should make alone.

The driver documents its ownership model explicitly (activitylog.go:124): diagnostic settings
carry NO tags, so the content-addressed deterministic NAME *is* the ownership marker —
"groundhold only ever mutates a setting at its own deterministic name." Yet the
`implementation.diagnosticSettingName` operand (activitylog.go:315) lets a create use an
ARBITRARY name verbatim. Such a setting is created fine, but the delete's ownership check
(correctly, per the invariant) refuses it — "does not carry our ownership marker" — so it can be
created and never retired: it leaks. I hit exactly this (a `gh-activitylog` setting the driver
would not delete; cleaned up by hand).

The two ways out pull against each other: (a) REFUSE a custom name that isn't the deterministic
marker — closes the footgun but removes the "pin the name" feature the operand advertises; or
(b) let the delete trust the ledger-bound providerId as ours rather than the name pattern —
restores custom names but weakens the tagless "ours by construction" safety the name-as-marker
model was chosen for (D-class brownfield reasoning). That is a deliberate ownership-model
decision with a security dimension, so per the the instructions file open-questions discipline it is FLAGGED
here rather than resolved at the tail of a fixing pass. activitylog flips config-intent →
measured on the deterministic-name path (azure 25/45, 96/145); the custom-name operand's
contradiction with the ownership marker is recorded for a deliberate decision.

## D916 — Azure Key Vault key measured; purgeable where GCP's keyring is not

The encryption class reached Azure `capability.key.encryption` (`keyvaultkey`) — the driver
stands up a Key Vault and a software-protected key inside it (the key builder accepts
location.region, protection.level software/hsm, rotation.period; it refuses vault-level attrs
like network.publicExposure because a key's material is never exported). Proven on our
subscription: create then retire, then the soft-deleted vault PURGED to fully clean —
confirmed gone from both the active and the deleted-vaults lists, with the resource group's
other (pre-existing, not ours) vaults untouched.

The contrast with the exempt GCP twin is the point. GCP `cloudkms` is EXEMPT because a KMS
keyring cannot be deleted at all — an e2e fixture would leave inert residue forever. An Azure
Key Vault soft-deletes (mandatory, 90-day) but is PURGEABLE when purge protection is off — and
the driver's create sets `enableSoftDelete: true` without `enablePurgeProtection`, so a test
vault can be purged to nothing. So the same capability is exempt on one cloud and measured on the
other, honestly, because the platforms genuinely differ on whether the key substrate can be
removed. keyvaultkey flips config-intent → measured (azure 26/45, 97/145).

## D917 — the preflight that over-blocked on a permission scoped off the project

Field work on `gcp/billingbudget` (`capability.cost.budget`) surfaced a real preflight defect,
fixed here. `capability.cost.budget` needs `billing.budgets.create`, which is a BILLING-ACCOUNT
permission — and GCP's `projects.testIamPermissions` rejects the WHOLE request with 400 if it
contains even one permission that is not valid for a project resource ("Permission
billing.budgets.create is not valid for this resource"). The old CheckPermissions turned that
400 into a hard "check could not run" → preflight-inconclusive → the service was uncreatable,
even though the acting identity HELD `billing.budgets.create` (confirmed by a
billingAccounts.testIamPermissions returning it granted). One cross-scope permission poisoned
the whole project-scoped check.

The fix peels off each permission the 400 names, marks it UNATTESTED — the project surface
genuinely cannot vouch for a permission scoped to the billing account, and that is the honest
four-valued answer (D75: unattested is never a denial and does not block), and retries with the
rest so the project-scoped permissions are still attested. A unit test stages a 400 on a
`billing.*` permission and asserts it comes back unattested (not a failure), including the
all-billing case where nothing is attestable and nothing blocks; a mutation-gate mutant (stop
peeling) was hand-verified to bite.

This unblocks the preflight for every billing/org-scoped capability, not just budgets. The
budget itself still does not fully MEASURE: past the preflight, the create 403s "billingbudgets
API requires a quota project" — the ADC-without-quota-project limitation (the same one assetfeed
hit), an auth-environment issue rather than a driver defect, so billingbudget stays config-intent
with the preflight fix landed and the environment blocker noted.

## D918 — AWS Backup plan measured (a rule + a selection over a vault and a role)

The backup class reached AWS `capability.backup.plan` (`backupplan`). A plan is a rule (a
schedule + a retention) plus a SELECTION of what to protect, over a target Backup vault, run by
a service role AWS Backup assumes. Fixtures: a `gh-e2e-bpvault` Backup vault and an IAM role
trusting `backup.amazonaws.com` with the managed backup policy. Proven on our account: a 24h-rule
/ 720h-retention plan with a tag selection, create then retire, the plan gone and the vault +
role torn down afterward. Three input notes the run pinned: `schedule.frequency` is a DURATION
(`24h`, not "daily"); `selectionTags` is a tag MAP, not a string, and a plan with no selection is
refused ("backs up nothing"); and `availability.class` is refused because a backup plan has no
availability-zone concept — placement is a property of the resource being protected, not of the
schedule. No code change — a measurement fold (aws 44/54, 98/145).

## D919 — OpenSearch Serverless measured; the driver brings its own policy triad

The search class reached AWS `capability.search.index` (`opensearch-serverless`). An AOSS
collection cannot stand alone — it needs an encryption policy, a network policy and a
data-access policy — and the driver creates all three itself, so the capability is
self-contained (no external fixture, unlike backupplan's vault+role or changefeed's account).
Proven on our account: a public regional collection, create then retire, the collection and all
three policy types gone afterward — confirmed via AOSS ListCollections / ListSecurityPolicies /
ListAccessPolicies. The create is async (the collection takes a few minutes to go ACTIVE), which
the converge polls to a terminal state. No code change — a measurement fold (aws 45/54, 99/145).

## D920 — Azure VM measured (100 of 145); the OS disk the retire leaves behind

The compute class reached Azure `capability.compute.instance` (`azvm`), the 100th service field-
tested. A VM needs a pre-existing NIC (the driver does not stand up the network), so the fixture
was a VNet + subnet + NIC; the driver takes `network_interface_id`, `image_reference`,
`vm_size`, `ssh_public_key` and an admin user. Proven on our subscription: a Standard_B1s Ubuntu
VM, create then retire, the VM gone.

The run surfaced a cleanup residue worth recording (D920): retire deletes the VM but leaves the
OS DISK the create implicitly provisioned — Azure does not cascade-delete a managed OS disk on
VM delete unless the disk carries `deleteOption: Delete`, which the create body does not set. So
a retired VM leaks its OS disk (a billable managed disk), which I deleted by hand. This is not a
false claim — the VM is genuinely gone — but it is an incomplete teardown: the driver created
the disk (as part of the VM create) and should arguably delete it on retire. The fix is small
(set `deleteOption: Delete` on the OS disk in the create body, or delete the disk in the VM's
retire), but it touches what "retiring a VM" is defined to remove, so it is recorded here rather
than changed at the tail of a long pass. azvm flips config-intent → measured (azure 27/45,
100/145).

## D921 — Azure VM scale set measured; a cleaner teardown than the single VM

The autoscaling class reached Azure `capability.compute.autoscaling` (`azvmss`). A scale set
takes a `subnet_id` (not a NIC — it manages its own NICs internally), so the fixture is just a
VNet + subnet, lighter than azvm's VNet+subnet+NIC. Proven on our subscription: a zonal Ubuntu
scale set (min 1 / max 3, CPU autoscaler) over the subnet, create then retire, the scale set
gone — and, unlike the single VM (D920), its disks cleaned up with it, so no residue. Two input
notes: `zones` is a LIST, and `resource_group` is required (groundhold does not create resource
groups). No code change — a measurement fold (azure 28/45, 101/145). The contrast with D920 is
worth keeping: a scale set owns its instances' disks and deletes them on teardown, while a
stand-alone VM leaves its OS disk unless the create pinned deleteOption — same platform, two
teardown behaviours the field runs distinguished.

## D922 — Container Apps measured; the managed environment the retire leaves (same shape as D920)

The container class reached Azure `capability.workload.container` (`containerapps`). A container
app runs on a managed ENVIRONMENT, and the driver creates both — so with `availability.class
zonal` it stands up a consumption environment (no subnet) and the app on a public image
(`mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/containerapps-helloworld`); `infrastructure_subnet_id` is needed
only for the zone-redundant `regional` class. Proven on our subscription: create then retire,
the app gone.

The retire left the managed ENVIRONMENT behind (D922) — the exact teardown-residue shape as D920
(azvm's OS disk): the create implicitly provisioned the environment, and retire deletes only the
app, so the environment lingers (billable, with its own Log Analytics workspace) until deleted
by hand, which I did. Not a false claim — the app is gone — but an incomplete teardown of what
the create made. This is now the SECOND instance of the pattern (azvm OS disk, containerapps
environment): a driver that stands up a parent/companion resource as part of a create should
decide whether retire tears the companion down too. Both are recorded, not fixed at the tail of
the pass, because both turn on what "retire" is defined to remove. containerapps flips
config-intent → measured (azure 29/45, 102/145).

## D923 — Container Apps job measured; the operand-fixture model retires clean

The container-job class reached Azure `capability.container.job` (`containerappsjob`). Unlike
its sibling `containerapps` (D922), the job takes the managed environment as an OPERAND
(`environment_id`) rather than creating it — so the fixture was a pre-created consumption
environment, and the job ran a manual-trigger public mcr image on it. Proven on our
subscription: create then retire, the job gone — and BECAUSE the environment is the operator's
fixture rather than something the driver made, retire deletes only the job and leaves no
residue. That is the clean counterpoint to D920/D922: when the companion resource is an operand
the driver never owned, teardown is unambiguous; the residue question only arises where a create
implicitly stands a companion up. No code change — a measurement fold (azure 30/45, 103/145).

## D925 — the Cloud Function whose create body named it wrong (fixes it in both builders)

Field work on `gcp/cloudfunctions-fn` (`capability.function.serverless`) surfaced a golden-green
defect, fixed here. The create is `POST .../functions?functionId=<name>` with a Function body,
and the body set `"name": <bare deterministic name>` — but Cloud Functions v2 validates that
name against the FULL resource pattern and rejects the short form: "Invalid resource name
'r-dev-...' for pattern 'projects/{project}/locations/{location}/functions/{function}'." The
golden fake accepted the bare name (it validated nothing about the name grammar), so the driver
could never create a real function. The fix sets the body name to the full path
`projects/{p}/locations/{l}/functions/{f}`; the functionId in the URL still names it.

The catch that made this take two passes: there are TWO builders — `BuildCloudFunctionCreateRequest`
(the `cloudfunctions` service, workload.container) and `BuildCloudFunctionFnRequest` (the
`cloudfunctions-fn` service, function.serverless) — and `capability.function.serverless` routes
to the SECOND. Fixing only the first left the field create still failing; both carried the same
bug and both are now fixed, each with a golden assertion on the full-path name and a
mutation-gate mutant (revert to the bare name) hand-verified to bite. Proven end to end: a Python
HTTP function built from a GCS source zip created (build + deploy) and retired on our project,
the function gone and the source bucket torn down. cloudfunctions-fn flips config-intent →
measured (gcp 29/46, 104/145); the `cloudfunctions` twin carries the same fix but is not itself
field-run here.

## D926 — the cloud-functions twin measured on the same D925 fix

`gcp/cloudfunctions` (`capability.workload.container`) is the other mapping of the same Cloud
Function resource fixed in D925 — the workload.container framing where cloudfunctions-fn is the
function.serverless one. With the full-path name fix already in its builder
(`BuildCloudFunctionCreateRequest`), it now creates: a Python HTTP function built from a GCS
source zip, create (build+deploy) then retire on our project, the function gone and the source
bucket torn down. No new code — this closes the loop on D925 by field-running the twin the fix
also repaired. cloudfunctions flips config-intent → measured (gcp 30/46, 105/145).

## D927 — the GKE operand whitelist that refused what the driver requires (fixes the greenfield create)

Field work on `gcp/gke` (`capability.cluster.kubernetes`) surfaced a golden-green defect. The
GKE driver READS the operands `network`, `subnetwork`, `zone` and `clusterName` (a greenfield
create needs a VPC network/subnet and — for a zonal cluster — a zone; `clusterName` is the
adopt-by-name handle), but the operand whitelist declared only
`{kmsKeyName, masterAuthorizedCidrs, nodePool}`. So the unknown-operand gate REFUSED `zone`,
`network` and `subnetwork` before the driver could read them — "r.zone is not an operand the
gcp/gke driver reads" — and a greenfield cluster was uncreatable: supply the network the driver
demands and the gate rejects it; omit it and the driver refuses. The whitelist and the builder
disagreed, and nothing cross-checked them (the D329 registry-drift class, here between
`ConsumedOperands` and the impl[...] reads — no gate proves every operand a driver reads is
declared).

The fix declares the operands the driver actually consumes:
`{clusterName, kmsKeyName, masterAuthorizedCidrs, network, nodePool, subnetwork, zone}`. Proven
end to end: after the fix a zonal 1-node e2-small cluster on the default VPC created (CONVERGED,
cluster RUNNING) and retired on our project. The operands golden (`TestConsumedOperandsExactSets`)
pins the set and a mutation-gate mutant (drop `network` again) was hand-verified to bite. gke
flips config-intent → measured (gcp 31/46, 106/145).

Two siblings that ride on a cluster were field-checked but stay config-intent, honestly:
gke-addon's create APPLIES (it triggered a real UPDATE_CLUSTER) but each addon toggle is a
~3-5 min async reconcile, so the full cycle outruns the poll (async-outruns-poll, create-proven);
gke-workloadidentity's GSA→KSA binding needs the project's Workload Identity pool, which exists
only once a WI-enabled cluster does ("Identity Pool does not exist") — an environment
prerequisite, not a driver defect.

## D928 — EC2 measured; and the D927 change that moved an existing mutant's anchor

`aws/ec2` (`capability.compute.instance`) measured on our account: a t3.micro Amazon Linux 2023
instance (image_id from the AL2023 SSM parameter) in a pre-existing subnet with an encrypted root
volume, create then retire — the instance terminated and its root volume gone (delete-on-
termination). The subnet was used, never created or deleted, since the account's VPC is shared.
aws 46/54, 107/145.

The slice also carried a mutation-gate repair the D927 gke fix forced. D927 rewrote the gke
operand line from `{kmsKeyName, masterAuthorizedCidrs, nodePool}` to the full seven-operand set,
which MOVED the anchor an existing mutant (D763) pinned — the meter caught it as a NO-OP ("the
substitution changed nothing — the anchor moved") and failed the whole gate rather than
silently passing a toothless mutant. The fix re-points D763's perl at the new line; hand-verified
to bite again. This is the shared-tree discipline the memory names: a change to a registry line
can strand a mutant that quoted the old line verbatim, and the meter's no-op backstop is what
surfaces it.

## D929 — the top-level ARM error the mutation-detail read swallowed

Debugging an AKS create failure surfaced a recurring diagnostics gap (the D306/D309 class). The
create failed with "managedClusters PUT HTTP 400: (the response carried no error code or
message)" — but the body carried a full explanation: `{"code":"K8sVersionNotSupported",
"message":"version 1.29.15 which is not supported in this region"}`. The reason it vanished is
that `azErrMessage`/`azErrCode` (and so `mutDetailAz`) parse ONLY the wrapped
`{"error":{"code","message"}}` shape, but a managedClusters 400 — and other ARM errors — put
`{"code","message"}` at the TOP LEVEL, with no "error" wrapper. So the wrapped-only read returned
"", and an operator (and the author) debugging a failed Azure create got nothing where the
service had said exactly what was wrong. Cosmos hit the same swallow earlier (recorded then as
debt); this is the fix.

The fix teaches both readers the top-level shape as a fallback: try `error.message`/`error.code`,
then the top-level `message`/`code`. A unit test pins both shapes (wrapped still works, top-level
now read, and `mutDetailAz` no longer says "no error code or message" for a top-level error), and
two mutation-gate mutants (drop each fallback) were hand-verified to bite. This is cross-cutting
— every Azure driver's mutation-failure Reason and every armread diagnosis gets the real error
now, not just AKS. No coverage row moves; it is a diagnostics repair, and it is what let the AKS
version problem be seen at all.

## D930 — AKS and its two riders measured; three services from one cluster

The Azure cluster class closed the parity with GKE. One AKS cluster (1-node Standard_B2s,
system-assigned identity, k8s 1.35) carried three measurements: `aks` (cluster.kubernetes),
`aks-addon` (cluster.addon — the azure-policy addon enabled then retired), and
`aks-workloadidentity` (identity.podidentity — a federated identity credential binding a
Kubernetes SA to a user-assigned managed identity over the cluster's OIDC issuer). All three
create+retire cleanly; the cluster and the UAMI fixture were torn down after.

Three field notes the run pinned. `identity` is an operand, not an attribute (the cluster.kubernetes
vocab governs version/exposure/secrets/topology, not the identity backend). `cluster.version` must
be a version the region supports — 1.29 failed with K8sVersionNotSupported, and that reason was
readable ONLY because D929 had just taught the ARM error-read the top-level shape; before it, the
same 400 was "no error code or message". And the two riders diverge from their GKE twins in a way
that is the platform's, not the driver's: aks-addon's toggle completes within the poll where
gke-addon's is a long async reconcile, and aks-workloadidentity WORKS where gke-workloadidentity
could not — AKS enables the OIDC issuer that the federated binding needs, so the identity pool
exists. One casing gotcha: Azure returns a UAMI id with lowercase `resourcegroups` but the driver
validates the canonical `resourceGroups`. aks/aks-addon/aks-workloadidentity flip config-intent →
measured (azure 33/45, 110/145).

## D931 — ACS email measured; the teardown-residue pattern's third instance

`azure/acsemail` (`capability.email.sending`) measured on our subscription: an Azure-managed
sending domain on an Email Communication Service, DKIM posture on, Europe data location, create
then retire — the domain gone. Two input notes: `location.region` is an ACS data-residency
(Europe / United States / UK / Australia, not "global"), and a sending domain requires
`authentication.dkim=true` (the domain attaches to the DKIM posture).

The retire left the parent Email Communication Service behind (D931) — the domain is the
capability resource and it was deleted, but the SERVICE the create implicitly stood up as its
parent lingers until deleted by hand. This is now the THIRD instance of the same teardown-residue
shape: azvm's OS disk (D920), containerapps' managed environment (D922), and here the email
service. Three drivers, one pattern — a create that provisions a companion/parent resource, and a
retire that removes only the leaf. It is not a false claim (the capability resource is gone) but
an incomplete teardown, and at three instances it is a class, not an accident: the drivers that
stand up companion resources on create should decide, uniformly, whether retire cascades to what
the create made. That is a design decision about what "retire" removes, still flagged rather than
resolved unilaterally. acsemail flips config-intent → measured (azure 34/45, 111/145).

## D932 — Azure Application Gateway measured (network.loadbalancer)

`azure/loadbalancer` (`capability.network.loadbalancer`) is an Application Gateway on Azure —
the driver builds the gateway; the operator brings a DEDICATED subnet (App Gateway will not
share one), a Standard static public IP, and a backend (backendFqdns / backendIps). Proven on

the gateway gone and the subnet/VNet/public-IP fixtures torn down. location.region is required

## D933 — Azure AI Search measured via resume; async-outruns-poll IS measurable (search.index)

The "async-outruns-poll" services were parked config-intent on the belief that a slow
provision means the full lifecycle can't be captured. It can. Proven end-to-end on our
subscription (tftest RG) for `azure/aisearch` (`capability.search.index`):

1. converge create — the service provisioned for ~20 min, longer than the driver's own
   bounded 20-min poll, so converge returned `unknown` with the create receipt still pending
   (exit 4, "run resume before retrying");
2. `resume` (D57) — asked ARM what actually happened; the receipt resolved to
   `provisioningState: succeeded` (exit 0). The create is confirmed against the provider,
   not inferred;
3. retire — converge APPLIED the delete; a direct ARM GET of the RG's searchServices returns
   zero. Teardown confirmed.

No driver change. The correction is to the earlier note (which blamed "ARM token lifetime"):
the mechanism is the poll BUDGET elapsing, and the designed remedy is exactly `resume`. The
first resume attempt returned still-unknown only because I passed an empty `--project`; with
the subscription scope the driver could query and conclude. This reclassifies the whole
async-outruns-poll set from "not capturable" to "measurable via create→resume→retire" — the
verb was built for this (D57: "concludes pending receipts read-only"). azure 36/45, 113/145.

## D934 — Cosmos default backup policy was field-dead: bare Periodic (database.nosql)

`azure/cosmos` built the databaseAccounts PUT body with `backupPolicy: {"type":"Periodic"}`
for the default (non-PITR) account. Azure rejects that with a 400:
"PeriodicModeProperties must be specified when BackupPolicyType is Periodic." So the COMMON
path — an account without point-in-time recovery — was uncreatable, while the fake accepted
the bare shape (golden-green / field-dead). The earlier "cosmos create proven 200" (D-note in
COVERAGE) exercised only the CMK path, which the operator drove with PITR on, and the
Continuous branch already carries its own `continuousModeProperties` — so the defect hid
behind the one path that happened to be tested.

Fix: the Periodic branch now carries `periodicModeProperties` with the mode's own defaults
(240-min interval, 8-hour retention). Proven end-to-end on our subscription (tftest RG): create
APPLIED, retire APPLIED, a direct ARM GET of the RG's databaseAccounts returns zero. Failing
test `TestBuildCosmosPeriodicCarriesModeProperties` (deletes CMK + sets PITR false to land on
the default path, asserts the mode properties are present); mutation-gate mutant strips them
back to the bare type. azure 37/45, 114/145.

Diagnostic footnote: the run that first surfaced this reported "the response carried no error
code or message" — that was a STALE test binary (built before D929), not a second D929
instance; the current binary parses the top-level `{code,message}` and names the reason in
full. The fresh binary was rebuilt before the measured fold.

## D935 — converge claimed "converged" over an unresolved unknown receipt (fail-open)

Admitted under the D716 freeze: the tool told the operator the world was clean while an
owned resource was live. Found in the field (Azure Cache for Redis, which provisions ~24 min —
past the driver's 20-min poll): a `converge` CREATE returned exit 4 with the create receipt
`unknown` (the resource may exist); a later `converge` RETIRE then reported exit 0,
outcome **converged**, while the cache was still running and billing.

Mechanism (confirmed by tracing, not from the symptom):
- an `unknown` create writes NO binding — `binding.updated` is on apply's success path only
  (apply.go), so `BoundProviderIDs()` has nothing for the capability; the deterministic
  providerId survives solely inside the pending receipt body;
- the retire compiler diffs desired-state against bound providerIds; with no binding it emits
  no delete → the plan is empty → `NothingToChange`;
- converge maps `NothingToChange` to "converged" (three sites: plan-phase, apply-returned,
  and converged-during-backoff) — none consulted the ledger's pending set;
- apply's pending-receipt guard ("must be reconciled first (D29)") DOES exist, but it iterates
  only the plan's write set (capabilities that carry an action), so an EMPTY plan bypasses it
  entirely. The guard's own prose — "apply keeps refusing until they conclude" — was only true
  when there was an action on the pending capability.

Fix: before converge declares "converged", `pendingBlocker` replays the ledger and, if any
in-scope capability still has `PendingCount > 0`, `refuseIfPending` turns the verdict into a
`reconcile-required` refusal (exit 3) that points at `resume` — the same code apply uses, now
reachable for the empty-plan path. Scoped to `o.Caps`, so a pending receipt on an out-of-scope
capability does not block an unrelated converge. Three tests (behavioral refusal, resolved-
receipt still converges, scope), a mutant that blinds the guard. Runtime change, spent under
the freeze because it is exactly the admitted shape: acting on "converged" here leaves a live,
billing resource the operator believes is gone.

## D936 — ElastiCache Serverless was create-only-blind: wrong list element (cache.keyvalue)

`aws/elasticache-serverless` read `DescribeServerlessCaches` under the XML path
`...ServerlessCaches>ServerlessCache`, but AWS wraps each list member in `<member>`. The wrong
element matched nothing, so `describeServerlessCache` always returned `len==0` → an unreadable
error, never a cache. The driver could POST a `CreateServerlessCache` (which lands), but every
read-dependent step then failed:

- create polled the observable state to AVAILABLE — but the read never parsed the cache, so it
  polled the full 20-min budget and returned `unknown` ("still creating at poll timeout") on a
  cache that had been AVAILABLE for ~15 minutes;
- observe/resume could never conclude the create → a pending receipt that never resolves;
- delete's pre-read returned the same unreadable error → `unknown`, so the porcelain never even
  issued the DeleteServerlessCache — a created cache was **undeletable through the tool** and
  kept billing.

The golden fixture emitted the same fake `<ServerlessCache>` shape, so the test agreed with the
bug — it was never validated against a real describe. The field exposed it: a create that timed
out to `unknown` while the AWS API plainly showed the cache `available`.

Fix: read `ServerlessCaches>member`. Proven end to end on our account (eu-central-1): create
CONVERGED (poll read AVAILABLE → succeeded), retire CONVERGED (pre-read found it, tags matched,
DeleteServerlessCache, poll to gone), a live DescribeServerlessCaches confirms zero.

Not-a-fix, recorded: AWS is internally inconsistent — the newer serverless `DescribeServerlessCaches`
uses `<member>`, but the older `ListTagsForResource` on the SAME service uses `<TagList><Tag>`.
A first "fix" changed BOTH to `<member>` on the Query-protocol convention; the field retire then
failed "tags do not match", proving the tags element was already correct. The convention was not
proof — only the real API was (the [[scrape-cannot-prove]] lesson, in the reverse direction).
Test + mutant on the describe element. aws 47/54.

## D937 — the D936 blind-read had a second copy in discovery (cache.keyvalue)

The D936 fix corrected the LIFECYCLE read (`describeServerlessCache`) but the driver has a
SECOND `DescribeServerlessCaches` parse in `discoverElastiCacheServerless` (the brownfield
enumeration path), and it carried the same wrong element — `ServerlessCaches>ServerlessCache`
instead of `>member`. So while create/observe/delete now read a cache, DISCOVERY still parsed
zero: `groundhold discover` would report a live serverless cache as ABSENT.

That is the more dangerous half. The lifecycle read failing is fail-safe (unknown/unreadable);
a discovery that returns EMPTY reads as "there is no serverless cache here" — an authoritative
false-absence. An operator onboarding an existing estate would miss it, and a later create
under the deterministic name would make a duplicate.

Found by the audit the D936 lesson prompted: grep every AWS driver's list-element XML tag,
keep the ones whose service is `measured` (their reads were field-validated), and look hard at
the rest — the second copy was in the same file. Fix: `>member` here too, plus
`TestDiscoverElastiCacheServerlessSeesTheCache` (asserts discovery finds the cache, fails on
the old element) and a distinct mutant. The lesson for the fixer: when a parse bug has a
sibling call site, grep the WHOLE file (and the discovery path) before calling it fixed — one
struct tag is rarely the only copy.

## D938 — redis measured via the resume path, correctly timed (cache.keyvalue)

`azure/rediscache` folds to measured by the same mechanism as aisearch (D933): a Basic C0 cache
provisions ~24 min, past the driver's 20-min poll, so converge returns `unknown`; once the cache
reaches `Succeeded`, `resume` concludes the create receipt (resolved: succeeded) and retire tears
it down (ARM confirms zero). The earlier config-intent note was a timing artifact — resume had
been run immediately after the poll timeout, while the cache was still `Creating`, so it stayed
unknown. The rule the two cases teach: `resume` concludes an async create only once the provider
has reached a terminal state; run it after, not at, the poll deadline. This same run validated
D935 in the field — the retire over the still-unknown create REFUSED (reconcile-required) instead
of the false "converged" the pre-fix binary produced. azure 38/45, 116/145.

## D939 — the D935 fail-open had a fourth emitter: the post-apply "verified" path

D935 guarded the three whole-empty-plan "converged" emitters, but an adversarial audit found a
fourth green exit it does not cover: the POST-APPLY exit-0 `Status:"applied" / Convergence:"verified"`
result (converge.go), which `finish()` paints CONVERGED. It shares D935's exact root cause and
dangerous direction.

The reach is a MIXED plan. Capability A carries a real action; capability B is `state: retired`
and UNBOUND with a pending `unknown` create receipt (the D935 precondition — an unknown create
writes no binding). The compiler drops B from the plan (`Bindings[capID] == "" → continue`), so:
- the plan is NON-EMPTY (A's action), so the three whole-empty-plan guards never fire;
- apply's pending guard iterates only the write set `{A}`, so B's pending receipt is not caught
  (the identical write-set-gated bypass);
- post-apply, observe (read-only, concludes nothing) then the convergence-check plan sees A
  reconciled and B gone → whole plan empty → "verified" → exit 0 CONVERGED, while B's resource
  may be live and billing.

Fix: call `refuseIfPending(phases)` before building the post-apply exit-0 result too — refuse
(reconcile-required) if any in-scope capability still holds an unresolved receipt. Behavioral
test drives the mixed plan through apply to the "verified" path and asserts exit 3; a mutant
blinds only this fourth site (the three D935 guards stay live). The lesson: when you close a
fail-open at N emitters, enumerate ALL emitters of the same verdict — a green banner has more
than one code path, and the audit that assumes "three is all" is how the fourth survives.

The same audit confirmed the read-path blind-read class (D936/D937) has no further instances,
and that resume/adopt/audit/direct-apply and the driver "already-gone → succeeded" delete paths
are sound (a blind/failing read there routes to `unknown`, never a false success). Recorded, not
fixed: `posture.Classify` omits a retired-unbound pending capability from its rows — an omission
(no false claim), so it waits rather than spends the freeze.

## D940 — retire reported succeeded while billable companions orphaned: a dead-code guard

Admitted under the D716 freeze (the tool says "succeeded"/clean while a billable resource
silently remains). `deleteAndConfirm` (vnet_net.go) NEVER returns nil — it returns
`{Status:"succeeded"}` on a clean delete. But the codebase's dominant idiom is
`if r := helper(...); r != nil { return *r }`, which is correct for `putAndPoll` (nil = success)
and WRONG for `deleteAndConfirm` (never nil). Two composite deletes used the wrong idiom for the
LEAF, so the leaf delete returned unconditionally and the companion cleanup after it was
UNREACHABLE DEAD CODE:

- **vnet** (vnet_net.go:429): create provisions a Standard public IP + a NAT gateway (both
  billable, driver-created) on the `egress.internet: nat` road, plus an NSG on restricted egress.
  The vnet delete returned first; the child cleanup loop (NSG → NAT gateway → public IP) never ran.
- **containerapps** (containerapps_net.go:222): create provisions a managed environment (billable);
  the app delete returned first; the environment cleanup never ran.

Both reported `succeeded`. Field-proven on our subscription with a two-binary A/B: the pre-fix
binary's vnet retire returned APPLIED yet left `…-nat` (NAT gateway) and `…-natip` (public IP)
standing; the fixed binary's retire left the resource group CLEAN of all four (vnet, NSG, NAT
gateway, public IP). Fix: the leaf guard becomes `r != nil && r.Status != "succeeded"` — the
idiom the WORKING companion-cleanup lines already used — so a succeeded leaf falls through to
reclaim its companions. Two tests assert the companion DELETEs are issued; two mutants restore
each dead-code guard.

Making the loop reachable then surfaced a SECOND, latent honesty bug that the D237 harness caught
immediately: when a companion delete hit a transient fault (5xx/429/timeout → `unknown`), the loop
set an "inconclusive" flag but STILL returned `Status:"succeeded"` (with a "…cleanup inconclusive
— reconcile" reason). An unconfirmed companion delete is UNRESOLVED — the resource may still exist
and bill — so the outcome must be `unknown` (keep the pid, reconcile), never a dressed-up
succeeded. Fixed to propagate the companion's own non-success result (`return *r`); the leaf is
already gone, so a retry re-runs the delete idempotently (an absent companion DELETEs to 404 =
succeeded, so no false unknown on a plain vnet). Two more mutants, gated by the honesty harness.
Lesson: dead code hides not just the work it fails to do but the bugs IN that work — reachability
is a prerequisite for the invariants to even be tested.

The D939 "enumerate all emitters" discipline found the scope: every `deleteAndConfirm` caller
was classified; the bare `r != nil` form is correct only for a FINAL single delete (loadbalancer,
managedidentity, backuppolicy, servicebus namespace cascade, etc.), and exactly two callers had
live companion cleanup behind it. This is the D920/D922 memory pattern's TRUE root cause: not a
design choice about "what retire removes", but a control-flow bug that made the cleanup the
authors DID write unreachable. (azvm's OS-disk residue, D920, is a separate mechanism — a missing
`deleteOption:Delete` on the osDisk, not dead code — and remains open.)

## D941 — the VM OS disk orphaned: Azure's Detach default (network.compute)

The sibling of D940 with a different mechanism (a missing field, not dead code). `azure/azvm`'s
create builds the OS disk with `createOption:FromImage` but no `deleteOption`, and Azure's default
is Detach — so deleting the VM left the Premium_LRS managed OS disk standing and billing, while
`observeAzureVM` reads only the VM's 404 and reports the estate "gone". The NIC is an operator
operand (`network_interface_id`), so the disk is the ONLY driver-created companion. Fix:
`deleteOption:Delete` on the osDisk, so it cascades with the VM. Test asserts the create body
carries it; mutant drops it. This closes the last of the three teardown-residue instances the
memory recorded (azvm/containerapps/acsemail): D940 fixed containerapps (dead code) and confirmed
acsemail's delete does reach its parent, D941 fixes azvm here. The residue pattern is retired as
a class — each instance had a concrete, different cause, none a genuine "design decision about
what retire removes".

## D942 — the flex-server tier was a constant, so GeneralPurpose/MemoryOptimized sizes were uncreatable (database.relational)

`azure/flexpostgres` sent `sku: {name: <sku>, tier: "Burstable"}` with the tier HARDCODED, never
derived from the sku. A GeneralPurpose (`Standard_D*`) or MemoryOptimized (`Standard_E*`) sku was
therefore sent with `tier:Burstable`, which Azure does not honor. Field-proven on our
subscription (isolating the tier as the ONLY variable): `Standard_D2s_v3` with the correct
`tier:GeneralPurpose` reached `Ready`, but the byte-identical body with `tier:Burstable` was
accepted (202) then ROLLED BACK during provisioning — so any non-Burstable size was uncreatable.
Azure's async acceptance-then-rollback is exactly why the golden fake (which accepts the body)
never caught it. Fix: `flexServerTier` derives the tier from the sku family (B→Burstable,
D→GeneralPurpose, E→MemoryOptimized); an unrecognized family refuses rather than guess. One
mutant (wrong-tier). No cloud claim beyond the field-proven derivation.

**Correction the field forced (the value of validating before committing):** an adversarial
audit ALSO claimed `availability.class: regional` (zone-redundant HA) is refused-by-Azure on the
Burstable tier, and a first cut of this fix REFUSED HA-on-Burstable and directed operators to a
GeneralPurpose sku. The field refuted both halves. The Flexible Server capabilities API for our
region shows every edition — Burstable INCLUDED — supports only `SameZone` HA, and zone-redundant
HA is `Disabled` region-wide for the subscription. So Burstable does support HA (SameZone), and
GeneralPurpose + zone-redundant HA fails for the SAME region reason Burstable does — the failure
is REGIONAL, not tier-based. The HA refusal was dropped as built on a false premise. What remains
open (recorded, not fixed): the driver maps `availability.class: regional` → `ZoneRedundant`
unconditionally, so in a region/subscription where `zoneRedundantHaSupported` is Disabled the
create rolls back (fail-closed unknown, not a false success). A correct preflight would query the
capabilities API for `zoneRedundantHaSupported` before emitting a ZoneRedundant server — larger
than this slice.

## D943 — the D940 companion cleanup could delete a FOREIGN resource (brownfield foreign-delete)

D940 made the Azure companion cleanup reachable — and an ownership audit immediately found that
reachability introduced a foreign-delete risk (the most dangerous direction: destroying a resource
we do not own). The companion deletes remove SEPARATE top-level ARM resources by DERIVED NAME
(vnet → `<name>-nsg`/`-nat`/`-natip`; containerapps → `<app>-env`) with NO ownership check of their
own, relying entirely on the parent's tag check. That parent check does not cover them: they are
SIBLINGS in the resource group, not children nested under the parent's URL.

- Greenfield: the parent name is content-addressed (`pv-<type>-<slug>-<sha8>`), so `<name>-nsg` is
  unguessable and can only be ours — safe.
- Brownfield: a vnet/app ADOPTED from an existing estate has an arbitrary operator name, and
  `<vnet>-nsg` / `<app>-env` is an extremely common Azure convention — so retire could `DELETE` a
  foreign NSG/managed-environment groundhold never created and never tagged. Both services are
  brownfield-adoptable.

Fix: `deleteCompanionIfOurs` reads each companion's tags before deleting — absent (404) → nothing
to do; foreign (tags absent or different) → LEAVE it untouched and surface a diagnostic; ours →
delete; read error → unknown. This is the Azure equivalent of GCP `deleteVPC`'s per-companion
`markerOurs` skip (the correct pattern already in the tree). Test: a foreign sibling standing at the
derived name is never DELETEd while the owned parent is; mutant drops the foreign-skip. Greenfield
cleanup is unchanged (companions are ours → still reclaimed, field-re-proven).

The lesson compounds D940's: making dead code reachable exposes not just the honesty bug IN it
(D940's succeeded-not-unknown) but a whole authorization surface the dead code had kept dormant.
A fix that changes what executes must re-ask every invariant — ownership included — of the newly
live path. (vmss's `<name>-cpu` autoscale companion is the same class but pre-existing, not made
reachable by D940; recorded for a follow-up — its autoscale-setting taggability needs confirming.)

## D944 — the vmss autoscale companion had the same foreign-delete gap (network.compute-fleet)

The ownership audit that found D943 flagged one sibling it did not cover: `azvmss`'s autoscale
setting, deleted by derived name `<name>-cpu` (`Microsoft.Insights/autoscalesettings/`) with no
ownership check — the same class as D943's vnet/containerapps companions, and vmss IS
brownfield-adoptable (`discoverAzureVMSS` + `TestAdoptsExistingAzureVMSS`), so a fleet adopted as
`web-fleet` would `DELETE web-fleet-cpu` on retire, potentially a foreign autoscale setting. Unlike
D943's companions this one is deleted BEFORE the fleet and its outcome must RESOLVE first (D29 — an
orphaned setting keeps evaluating against a gone target), so the fix threads `deleteCompanionIfOurs`
through that constraint: foreign => leave it and proceed; absent => proceed; ours-but-unresolved
(transient/failed/read-error) => return that and leave the FLEET in place. The create already tags
the setting, so ownership is confirmable; the test fixture was corrected to carry those tags (the
real shape). Test: a foreign autoscale setting is never DELETEd while the owned fleet is retired;
mutant (shared foreign-skip, pointed at the vmss test). Closes the last companion the audit found.

## D945 — two security changes applied without exposure consent (silent exposure / protection lift)

Admitted under the D716 freeze: `converge --yes` would apply a security-WEAKENING change with no
exposure consent, because the compiler under-declared the risk so the `--allow-exposure` gate
(D194) never fired. The gate reads `securityExposure == "certain"`, which for updates comes from
`weakensSecurity` — a bool-only allow-list of attribute prefixes (D628). Two weakening changes
slipped through it, found by a consent audit:

- **Silent exposure (highest):** `network.apiExposure` is a STRING enum (`public|private|mixed`)
  that decides whether a cluster's API/control-plane endpoint is internet-reachable. It is
  classified `mutable` and patched in place on all three clouds (EKS `endpointPublicAccess`, GKE,
  AKS). Because its path is not under `network.public*` AND its value is not a bool, `weakensSecurity`
  returned false → `securityExposure: possible` → no gate. A `private→public` flip opened the K8s
  control plane to `0.0.0.0/0` under plain `--yes`. Fixed: `apiExposureLevel` ranks
  private(0) < mixed(1) < public(2); a move up the rank is exposing.
- **Silent protection lift (high):** the threat-detection toggles `detection.enabled` /
  `protection.kubernetes` / `protection.malware` are bools, but their paths were outside the
  allow-list, so turning GuardDuty/SCC/Defender OFF via an in-place update rode through with
  `possible`. The protection-lift gate (D698) only binds on delete, so the update path was
  ungated by BOTH. Fixed: `detection.`/`protection.` added to `securityPaths` (they weaken on
  `true→false`, the existing "everything else weakens when it goes FALSE" branch; the string
  `protection.level` is filtered by the bool check, unchanged).

Tests extend the D628 gate test (apiExposure up/down the rank, threat-detection on/off). No cloud
e2e — this is a pure compiler classification and the driver harm (the PUT that opens the endpoint /
disables the detector) is established; the fix is that the plan a human consents to now says
`securityExposure: certain`, so the gate stops the apply. Continuation of D628's lesson: an
allow-list of "what counts as weakening" is a denial surface — every security attribute NOT on it
is a silent bypass, so enum-valued and posture-toggle attributes must be enumerated too.

## D946 — Azure Redis reported zone redundancy it did not have (false availability observation)

Admitted under the D716 freeze: observe reported a durability guarantee the live resource did not
provide, so a hard `availability.class == regional` constraint (a DR/HA requirement) read
`satisfied` against a cache that loses data on an availability-zone outage. Found by a derivation
audit. `observeRedisAzure` derived `availability.class` from the SKU TIER — `Standard`/`Premium` →
`regional` — but the Standard tier is a single-zone primary/replica (hardware failover only); zone
survival on Azure Cache for Redis exists ONLY when the top-level `zones` array is populated
(Premium/Enterprise), which the driver never read. The create compounded it: `regional` mapped to
`Standard` with NO `zones`, so it provisioned a non-zone-redundant cache and read it back
`regional` — an internally consistent, semantically false round-trip (pinned by tests that encoded
the lie). Field-verified: a Standard cache PUT with no zones array reports `zones: absent`.

Fix, mirroring the sibling drivers (`flexserver` reads `HighAvailability.Mode==ZoneRedundant`,
`azfiles` reads the `_ZRS` SKU, eventhubs/kafka read `zoneRedundant`): observe derives
`availability.class` from the actual `zones` array (regional iff populated, else zonal). That alone
closes the danger — a Standard cache now reads `zonal`, so a `availability.class == regional`
contract reads VIOLATED against it, never the old false `satisfied`. Tests: a cache WITH zones reads
regional, a Standard cache reads zonal; the tests that pinned the tier→regional lie were corrected.

Deliberately NOT done (and why): a first cut also REFUSED `availability.class: regional` at create.
The dead-enum ratchet (`TestNoVocabularyEnumValueIsDeadEverywhere`, D682 — "the count may only
fall") caught it: redis was the sole cache driver accepting `regional`, so refusing it made
`capability.cache.keyvalue availability.class = regional` unsatisfiable by every driver — a value
the vocabulary offers and nothing can keep. So the create keeps mapping `regional`→Standard (the
value stays accepted), but the mapping is now HONEST about its limit: it is hardware failover in one
zone, observed as `zonal`, so a regional contract does not converge rather than converging on a lie.
Genuine zone redundancy needs the Premium/Enterprise tier with an explicit, region-AZ-dependent
`zones` array — a larger slice, recorded not wired. The D938 measured status is unaffected (it used
`availability.class: zonal`). This is the D761/D753 shape — a default or a proxy (the tier) is not
the guarantee (zone redundancy); read the field that actually carries it.

## D947 — refuse an un-appliable zone-redundant flex server up front (the D942 recorded gap)

D942 recorded that `azure/flexpostgres` maps `availability.class: regional` to ZoneRedundant HA
unconditionally, so in a region/subscription where zone-redundant HA is Disabled the create is
ACCEPTED (202) and then ROLLED BACK ~20 minutes later — the operator gets a converge that returns
`unknown` and no server, with no idea why. This wires the preflight D942 flagged: before issuing a
ZoneRedundant create, `flexZoneRedundantSupported` GETs the region's Flexible Server capabilities
and reads the top-level `zoneRedundantHaSupported` flag; if Disabled, the create refuses UP FRONT
with a reason that names the cause and the remedy (pick a supporting region, or `zonal`).

Skip-loudly (the D75 stance): a capabilities read that does not CONCLUDE — transport/HTTP/parse
failure, or the flag absent — returns `known=false` and the create PROCEEDS rather than blocking on
an inconclusive check. So the preflight only ever ADDS an early refusal for a definitively-Disabled
region; it never turns a readable-elsewhere config into a failure, and it does not touch
`BuildFlexServer` (the pure builder still accepts `regional`, so the dead-enum ratchet is
untouched). Field-proven: `availability.class: regional` in westeurope (where the capabilities API
reports Disabled for this subscription) now refuses immediately instead of the 20-minute rollback.
Test drives Disabled→refuse and Enabled→proceed; mutant neuters the guard. This is the honest
completion of D942 — refuse an un-appliable config at plan-adjacent time rather than let the cloud
discover it slowly.

## D948 — wire genuine zone-redundant Redis (availability.class: regional now satisfiable)

D946 made observe read Redis zone redundancy from the real `zones` array, and honestly left
`regional`→Standard as a mapping that observe would then report `zonal` (violated, not a lie) —
because the dead-enum ratchet forbade refusing the value and true zone redundancy was a larger
slice. This is that slice. `regional` now maps to the Premium tier with a top-level `zones` array
spanning the region's availability zones, so it round-trips: create Premium+zones → observe
`regional` → satisfied.

The zones come from the region, not a guess: the net shell reads the subscription's per-region
availability-zone mapping (`Microsoft.Resources` locations API, `availabilityZoneMappings[].logicalZone`)
and (a) REFUSES up front if the region exposes fewer than two AZs — a Premium cache that cannot
survive a zone loss is not `regional`, so refusing beats provisioning a lie; (b) fills `zones` from
the actual logical zones when it can. Skip-loudly (D75): an inconclusive AZ read falls back to the
common `[1,2,3]` set rather than blocking. `BuildRedisAzure` still ACCEPTS `regional` (Premium), so
the dead-enum ratchet is untouched; the AZ refusal is a runtime check, not a Validate one. The sku
family also had to move — Premium is family `P`, not the `C` the body hardcoded (a wrong family is
a 400). Field-verified: westeurope exposes 3 AZs and a Premium cache with `zones:[1,2,3]` provisions
there (whereas flexpostgres zone-redundant HA is Disabled for this subscription — the two services
differ, which is why each reads its OWN capability rather than assuming). Tests: regional→Premium+
ZoneRedundant with a top-level zones body, and a single-AZ region refuses; new API field names
(availabilityZoneMappings/logicalZone) registered, the locations list read through listAllARMPages.
Authorized cost change: `regional` Redis is now a Premium cache, materially pricier than the Standard
it used to (falsely) map to — the operator asking for zone survival now pays for the tier that
provides it.

## D949 — the backup policy's default store/type was uncreatable for both documented datasources (golden-green)

A DataProtection backup policy's `dataStoreType` and `backupType` are not free defaults: the
accepted pair is DATASOURCE-specific, and Azure 400s (`BMSUserErrorInvalidInput`) a mismatch. The
driver hardcoded `VaultStore` + `Incremental` for every datasource — and a golden test (D934's
shape one cloud over) asserted that pair was correct for `Microsoft.Compute/disks`, the driver's own
primary example. Field 2026-08-08 against a live DataProtection vault: a disk policy with
`VaultStore` → 400; with `OperationalStore`+`Incremental` → 200. A Postgres flexible-server policy
with `Incremental` → 400; with `VaultStore`+`Full` → 200. So the driver's default body was
uncreatable for BOTH workloads it documents, and the test blessed it — the tool's own suite claiming
a shape works that the cloud rejects.

The fix derives the (store, backupType) pair from the datasource when the operator did not pin them
(`backupDefaultsFor`, field-verified: disks and AKS managed clusters → OperationalStore+Incremental;
Postgres flexible servers → VaultStore+Full), and REFUSES a datasource it has not confronted with the
real API rather than emit a guess — an explicit operand still overrides, and `backupType` is now
validated (Incremental|Full) the way dataStoreType already was. Blobs are DataProtection too but use a
distinct operational-backup rule shape (no schedule rule), not built here — the package doc and the
datasource example text drop the blob claim rather than imply the disk shape covers it. Field-proven:
the EXACT fixed driver body for a disk datasource (`createBody` dumped and PUT to the live `pv-bvault`
vault) returns 200 where the old default returned 400. Test `TestBackupPolicyDatasourceDefaults` pins
the derivation, the refusal, and the operand override; mutation restoring the VaultStore disk default
is caught.

## D950 — Cloud SQL sent the Postgres-only PITR flag for every engine, uncreatable for MySQL (golden-green)

`recovery.rpo` maps to Cloud SQL point-in-time recovery, and the driver set
`backupConfiguration.pointInTimeRecoveryEnabled: true` for EVERY engine. But the PITR spelling is
engine-specific and the two spellings are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE at the API — a fact the field
(a real GCP project, 2026-08-08) stated in its own error messages:

  - MySQL + `pointInTimeRecoveryEnabled` → 400 *"Point-in-time recovery can only be enabled for
    Postgres and SQL Server instances."* MySQL PITR is `binaryLogEnabled: true`.
  - Postgres + `binaryLogEnabled` → 400 *"Binary log can only be enabled for MySQL instances."*

So the driver's `recovery.rpo` body was uncreatable for MySQL — the flagship engine, the subject of
the first real-cloud run (the instructions file D15) — while the create golden test only exercised Postgres and
stayed green (the D934/D949 golden-green shape, engine-conditioned rather than datasource-conditioned).
This was found by an audit that hypothesised the wrong mechanism (MySQL needs binlog *as a companion
to* PITR); the field corrected the premise to *instead of* — the campaign's field-first rule
([[scrape-cannot-prove]]) earning its keep again. Both probes were synchronous-reject (400 before any
operation), so nothing was provisioned.

The fix assembles `backupConfiguration` from the engine: MySQL → `binaryLogEnabled`, Postgres/SQL
Server → `pointInTimeRecoveryEnabled`, across all three sites — create (`cloudsql.go`, deferred to
after `databaseVersion` is known), update (`update.go`, engine read from the current instance), and
observe (`observe.go`, which now reads EITHER spelling as PITR so a MySQL instance is not mis-reported
as a plain 24h window). The two spellings being mutually exclusive per engine is what lets observe
stay engine-agnostic. New tests exercise the MySQL path on all three (create/update/observe); the
existing Postgres goldens are unchanged because the Postgres body is identical. Mutation sending the
Postgres flag on the MySQL create path is caught.

## D951 — the D950 fix missed the tfstate importer path (the camelCase grep's blind spot)

D950 fixed four PITR sites, but a follow-up cross-path audit found a fifth: the state importer has TWO
independent readers — a pulumi path reading camelCase `binaryLogEnabled` (fixed in D950) and a
terraform-state path reading snake_case `binary_log_enabled` (`importer.go`, the tfstate mapping). The
D950 grep searched the camelCase spelling and found the pulumi sibling; the snake_case tfstate reader
never matched, so it still read only `point_in_time_recovery_enabled`. A MySQL
`google_sql_database_instance` in terraform state with `binary_log_enabled = true` and PITR therefore
fell through to the `recovery.rpo = 24h` hint — asserting a 24-hour data-loss window for an instance
with sub-minute recovery, the same false statement D950 closed, reachable through `groundhold hints`.
The fix reads both snake_case spellings, exactly as the pulumi path reads both camelCase ones. This is
the D950 lesson made concrete: an engine/mode-conditioned mapping must be swept in EVERY spelling the
codebase uses for it — a camelCase grep is not a whole-repo grep. Test exercises the MySQL tfstate
path; mutation reading a key the state never carries is caught.

## D952 — plain RDS observed MySQL/MariaDB TLS enforcement with the Postgres-only parameter (the D288 shape uncorrected)

`encryption.inTransit` on an RDS instance is measured by reading the attached DB parameter group for the
parameter that ENFORCES TLS — and that parameter is engine-specific. D288 fixed exactly this for Aurora
(`auroraTLSParam`: `rds.force_ssl` for PostgreSQL, `require_secure_transport` for MySQL), but the plain
RDS driver — which creates postgres, mysql AND mariadb — still scanned only `rds.force_ssl` in observe
(`dbForceSSL`). Field-confirmed on our account via `DescribeEngineDefaultParameters` (no instance
created): the mysql8.0 and mariadb10.11 families expose `require_secure_transport` and NOT `rds.force_ssl`;
postgres16 exposes `rds.force_ssl` and NOT `require_secure_transport`. So a MySQL or MariaDB instance
whose parameter group ENFORCES TLS via `require_secure_transport` was read as `encryption.inTransit=false`
(derivation `measured`) — a security control mis-stated as OFF, which reports a contract requiring
in-transit encryption as violated and churns converge against a resource that is in fact compliant. The
dangerous direction: the tool understates a security posture, and someone acting on it would "fix" an
already-secure instance or distrust a correct one.

The fix mirrors Aurora: `rdsTLSParam(engine)` names the enforcement parameter (postgres/sqlserver →
`rds.force_ssl`, mysql/mariadb → `require_secure_transport`, unknown → refuse with a diagnostic rather
than read the wrong parameter), and observe's reader (`dbTLSEnforced`, renamed from `dbForceSSL`, now
engine-aware and accepting the 1/ON/true spellings enforcement uses across engines) picks it from
`inst.Engine`. SQL Server keeps `rds.force_ssl` to preserve the correct reading it already had for adopted
instances. The create-side guidance string, which had told every engine to bring a group with
`rds.force_ssl=1`, now names both parameters. Test parametrises observe by engine — the MySQL/MariaDB
cases are the regression guard the old Postgres-only test lacked; mutation reading the Postgres parameter
for MySQL is caught. cloudsql-style note: RDS is already measured (Postgres cycle); the parameter names
were field-confirmed rather than re-running a full MySQL create.

## D953 — RDS/Aurora update reported succeeded on the async accept, not the applied state (user-directed)

An update-semantics audit found the one place in the whole update surface where the tool prints
`succeeded` for a change the cloud has merely ACCEPTED, not applied: `updateRDS` and `updateAurora`
returned `succeeded` on the 2xx from `ModifyDBInstance`/`ModifyDBCluster`. RDS/Aurora modifies are
asynchronous — the 2xx leaves the resource in `modifying`, and the change is not yet applied and can
still fail async. This was documented as intentional ("the accepted request is success; a later
observe/converge confirms", mirroring `deleteRDS`), but it is inconsistent with every sibling async
updater — EKS, GKE, AKS, Lambda, CloudSQL all poll to a terminal applied state before reporting
success. For a security-closing change (`network.publicExposure=false`), a bare `apply` reported
succeeded while the instance was still publicly reachable, and if the modify failed async it stayed
public — the operator, told it was done, stops watching. That is the dangerous direction (the freeze's
admitted class), so the presented trade-off was taken to the user, who chose to poll to terminal and
match the siblings.

The applied signal is `DBInstanceStatus`/cluster `Status == "available"` AND an EMPTY
`PendingModifiedValues` — AWS populates that element with the accepted-but-unapplied fields immediately
(before the resource even enters `modifying`) and empties it once they land. Reading its inner body is
field-agnostic (no per-field or engine-version comparison — it works for `PubliclyAccessible`,
`MultiAZ`, `BackupRetentionPeriod`, `EngineVersion` alike) and race-safe (non-empty from the instant the
modify is accepted). `updateRDS` polls the instance; `updateAurora` polls the cluster (for
ModifyDBCluster changes) and every member (for the per-member `PubliclyAccessible` patch). A change
still applying at `PollTimeout` is `unknown` (reconcile) WITH the providerId — never a false succeeded;
a `failed`/`incompatible-*` status is `failed`. Tests prove the poll waits (pending → applied →
succeeded) and times out honestly (pending forever → unknown); mutation reading an unapplied modify as
applied is caught on both the RDS and Aurora paths. The poll reuses the field-proven create-poll
mechanism; a full live modify cycle was not re-run.

## D954 — ECR reported a customer key off the encryption TYPE, not the key (false BYOK, the D800 shape)

A derivation-honesty audit found ECR observe emitting `encryption.customerManagedKeys` as
`repo.EncryptionConfiguration.EncryptionType == "KMS"`, tagged `measured` — and the decode struct did
not even read the `kmsKey` field. But `encryptionType=KMS` is true for BOTH a real customer key AND the
AWS-managed `aws/ecr` key: a repository created with `encryptionType=KMS` and no customer key resolves
to the managed key. Field-confirmed on our account (2026-08-08): a `CreateRepository` with
`encryptionConfiguration.encryptionType=KMS` and no `kmsKey` comes back with a resolved `kmsKey` whose
`DescribeKey` reports `KeyManager=AWS` ("Default key that protects my ECR data when no other key is
defined"). So observe reported `customerManagedKeys=true` measured for a repo with NO customer key, and
a hard BYOK constraint (`encryption.customerManagedKeys == true`) read satisfied against it — the exact
D800 lesson (a key id present is not a customer key), worse because ECR inspected nothing at all. It
bites the adoption/brownfield path (groundhold's own create requires a `kms_key` when CMEK, so
self-created repos happened to be correct — any externally-created `encryptionType=KMS` repo was a false
positive).

The fix decodes `kmsKey` and traces it to KMS `DescribeKey` (`kmsKeyIsCustomerManaged`, `KeyManager ==
"CUSTOMER"`) — the same reader RDS and elasticache use — so `customerManagedKeys` is measured from who
manages the key, not from the type. `AES256` (the AWS-owned key) and an unresolvable key are `false`; an
unreadable trace is a diagnostic, never a false. Tests: a customer-key repo reads true (via the trace),
and — the regression guard the type-only test lacked — an AWS-managed-key repo reads false. Mutation
inferring BYOK without the trace is caught, matching the D800 mutant family.

## D955 — ElastiCache reported regional off AutomaticFailover, but zone survival is MultiAZ (the D946 sibling)

A completeness-critic pass found the clean unfixed sibling of D946: ElastiCache observe derived
`availability.class=regional` from `AutomaticFailover=enabled`, tagged `measured` — but the field that
