carries zone survival is `MultiAZ` (replicas in DIFFERENT AZs), which the struct already parsed and
observe ignored. `AutomaticFailover=enabled` promotes a replica on failure, but with `MultiAZ=disabled`
the replica can live in the primary's OWN AZ — node failover, not zone survival. The driver's own
create is the proof: `regional` sets BOTH `MultiAZEnabled=true` AND `AutomaticFailoverEnabled=true`
(elasticache.go), while observe checked only the weaker half — a create/observe asymmetry. Field-proven
on our account (2026-08-08): `CreateReplicationGroup` with `AutomaticFailoverEnabled=true` and
`MultiAZEnabled=false` returns HTTP 200 (the divergent state is valid, not coupled) and
`DescribeReplicationGroups` reports `AutomaticFailover=enabling`, `MultiAZ=disabled` — so a real
single-zone group was read as `regional/measured`, and a hard `availability.class == regional` DR
constraint read satisfied against a cache that loses data on a zone outage. The exact D946 harm.

The fix reads `rg.MultiAZ` (the guarantee-carrying field) — `enabled → regional`, `disabled → zonal`;
`MultiAZ=enabled` implies `AutomaticFailover=enabled` (an AWS invariant), so it is the authoritative
single signal, and the create's setting both matches. The test fixtures now emit `<MultiAZ>` alongside
`<AutomaticFailover>` (they agree for the regional/zonal round-trip), and a new regression test — the
one the old fixtures could not express, since they always made the two agree — pins the DIVERGENT case:
`AutomaticFailover=enabled` + `MultiAZ=disabled` reads `zonal`. Mutation reverting to `AutomaticFailover`
is caught. The field validation also confirmed `MultiAZ` is a real populated `DescribeReplicationGroups`
element (not a phantom the JSON-only field-name gate would have missed on this XML/Query-protocol driver).

## D956 — AI Search reported regional off replica count with no region-AZ guard (the D946 class, no zone field)

The same completeness-critic pass flagged a weaker sibling of D946/D955: AI Search observe reported
`availability.class=regional` from `Standard SKU + ReplicaCount >= 3`, tagged `measured`, with no check
that the region even HAS availability zones. Replicas distribute across zones only where zones exist —
so a 3-replica Standard service in a region without AZs is single-zone, yet was read as regional. What
makes this different from D946 (redis `zones`) and D955 (elasticache `MultiAZ`): AI Search exposes NO
zone field on the resource — zone redundancy is implicit — so the replica count really is the strongest
DIRECT signal, and there is no "correct field" to switch to. The honest improvement is therefore a
necessary-precondition GUARD rather than a different field: a region with fewer than two availability
zones cannot be zone-redundant at any replica count (a tautology, not an empirical claim). Field-checked
read-only (2026-08-08): the subscription-locations API cleanly separates 40 AZ regions from 63 without,
and `northcentralus` — a real AI-Search-supported production region — exposes 0 AZs, so a 3-replica
service there was a live false-regional.

The fix gates the regional claim on `regionLogicalZones(doc.Location)` — the same field-proven helper
(D948) that flexpostgres (D947) and redis (D948) already apply at create — reused in observe: a region
KNOWN to expose fewer than two AZs reads `zonal` with a diagnostic; an inconclusive AZ read keeps the
replica signal (skip-loudly, D75) rather than downgrade on a read failure. Honesty boundary stated
plainly: the guard closes the no-AZ-region hole (definitionally), but AI Search still cannot be measured
to be zone-redundant WITHIN an AZ region — no field carries it — so an AZ-region service is reported
regional on the replica proxy, the best available signal, not a certainty. Test pins the non-AZ region
→ zonal path; mutation dropping the guard is caught. No new API surface (the locations read and its
field names were registered with D948).

## D957 — adopt reported "adopted" for a resource that does not exist (takeover of a phantom)

An adopt/discovery-honesty audit found that `adopt.Run` bound and reported `"adopted"` (exit 0) for a
providerId where NOTHING exists. When a bound resource authoritatively 404s, drivers emit the
`resource.absent` marker (`= "resource.absent"`, value true) with a NIL error — the D521 pattern, in 144
driver files. Adopt's gate observe (`adopt.go`) built `byPath` from the observations but never asked
whether the resource was absent: for a 404, `byPath` holds only `{resource.absent: true}`, so every
DECLARED attribute misses it (`!ok`) and is reclassified as non-observable "declared intent" — no
`reasons` accumulate, and adopt sails through to `Status: "adopted"`. The doctrine inverted: a single
attribute MISMATCH already refuses (`AdoptionMismatch`, "adoption must not lie"), yet a WHOLLY ABSENT
resource — the strongest possible "cannot confirm" — passed. The operator, told they took over
brownfield infrastructure, has instead bound a contract to nothing, and the next `converge` would
SILENTLY CREATE fresh infrastructure (the driver's own "will re-create" semantics) rather than adopt an
existing estate — worse off than if adopt had refused. (The post-bind observe appended a disclosing note
for marker-emitting drivers, but the headline status and exit code both said success, and a driver
returning empty-observations without the marker would make the takeover completely silent.)

The fix asks directly, mirroring the three discovery sweeps that already gate on it: after the gate
observe, `if provider.IsAbsent(obs)` adds a reason and routes to the same `AdoptionMismatch` refusal an
observable mismatch takes. The `provider.IsAbsent` helper already existed (used by defender/aks/scc
discovery); adopt simply never called it. Test: an absent-marker fake (the exact shape real drivers emit
on 404) must refuse, not report "adopted"; mutation disabling the gate is caught — and the mutant's
output is the defect itself, `Status:adopted` for a `fake:gone` id. This is a runtime-logic gate over the
established driver absence-marker contract (itself tested per-driver), so the unit test with the real
marker shape is the authority — no new cloud behavior to field-verify.

## D958 — posture reported exit 0 (all clear) for an estate it could not judge (user-directed)

A runtime-verb four-valued-honesty audit (which found the rest of the verbs — resume/probe/observe/
apply/converge/forecast/audit/verify/repair/anchor/refresh/reach/react/adopt — correctly refuse to
soften a harder failure into success) found one inversion: `posture`'s exit code returned 0 unless
`shadow` or `drift` was positive, ignoring both `unknown` and `shadowLowerBound`. So a scheduled
posture — where "the exit code is the only alert" (D649) — reported "all clear" (exit 0) over (a) an
estate with `unknown`/unverifiable hard verdicts, the very evidence the sibling `audit` verb exits 2 on,
and (b) an INCOMPLETE sweep (D650: a crawl scope truncated by expired creds / throttle / budget makes
the shadow/drift counts LOWER BOUNDS, not a clean estate). D650 had recognized incomplete scope as a
lie-shape and fixed the JSON (`shadowLowerBound: true`), but the exit code was left behind. A cron
alerting on posture's exit code stayed silent forever over an estate whose compliance was genuinely
unknown or which posture could not fully see.

The decision — whether `unknown` (posture is advisory, not an execution verb) should alert — was taken
to the user, who chose to make posture match `audit`: `shadow | drift | unknown | shadowLowerBound` all
exit 2, `decayed` alone still exits 0 (a proof past its ttl is renewed, not violated). The exit logic
moved from inline in `main.go` into a testable `posture.Summary.ExitCode()`; a table test pins every
class (clean/decayed→0, shadow/drift/unknown/incomplete→2), and two mutations — reading `unknown` or an
incomplete sweep as clean — are caught. This is a runtime-verdict change over already-computed classes
(no new evidence, no cloud behavior), so the unit test is the authority.

## D959 — apply did not re-derive two contract-scoped consents, so a forged plan bypassed them

A consent-gate audit (which found the rest of the doctrine airtight — replace/delete-stateful are
re-checked at apply, data-loss/exposure live in converge off the sealed risk vectors, the
weakensSecurity classifier is honest) found two consents that the COMPILER enforces but APPLY did not
independently re-derive from the pinned contract. Apply's own comment states the doctrine — "autonomy is
an UNCONDITIONAL executor gate — a hand-authored plan must not bypass compiler policy" (D47) — and it
already re-checks `ForbidsDeleteStateful` and `AllowsReplaceStateful` for exactly that reason. Two gates
were left out:

  - **`allow_protection_lift` (D698)**: deleting a `protection: true` capability
    (threatdetection/waf) switches a security control OFF (GuardDuty/WAF/SCC/Defender). The compiler
    refuses this without the scoped consent, but apply's delete preflight never called
    `AllowsProtectionLift` — and a protection capability is `stateful: false`, so the delete-stateful
    gate above it never catches it. A hand-authored or stale SealedPlan (or one sealed while consent was
    present, then revoked) with a delete of a protection cap sailed through and lifted the control.
  - **`allow_field_reclaim` (D699)**: apply read the per-action `fieldReclaim` bool straight from the
    plan and honored it. Sealing it defeats granting the consent AFTER a plan is sealed, but a FORGED
    plan asserting `fieldReclaim: true` for a capability the contract never scoped was honored —
    force-taking fields another manager owns.

Both are the D325 threat (a plan cannot opt out of policy), the same one replace/delete-stateful defend.
The fix re-derives each from the pinned contract at apply: the delete preflight refuses
`ProtectionOf && !AllowsProtectionLift` (`ConsentRequired`, mirroring the compiler predicate exactly),
and the per-action loop refuses a `fieldReclaim` the contract does not scope. Tests hand-author each
bypass (a compiled create flipped to a protection delete; a forged `fieldReclaim` on a plan whose
contract omits the consent) and assert the refusal names the missing consent — passing real embedded
vocabs, because `ProtectionOf` deliberately fails OPEN with no vocabulary (unlike `StatefulOf`); the
mutations that invert each gate are caught. Higher-severity of the two is protection-lift (turn a
security control off) over field-reclaim (steal field ownership).

## D960 — resume concluded receipts from a stale pending set, risking a generation regression (TOCTOU)

A concurrency/coordination audit (which found the lease + coordination-clock + write-ahead machinery
otherwise atomic and crash-truthful) found one TOCTOU in `resume`. It read its pending set from the
ENTRY-time ledger (`led.PendingReceipts()`), then acquired its lease later, and the reconcile loop
iterated that STALE map — never re-reading the pending set under the lease. In the window between
resume's ledger load and its `AppendLease`, another run holding the lease can CONCLUDE those same
receipts and advance the resource. Resume would then re-conclude an already-terminal receipt: on the
create path it reads `generation` from the stale receipt (gen 1), and the rebind-orphan guard only
fires on a DIFFERENT providerId — so a concurrent conclude-then-update (same providerId, gen 2) slips
through and resume overwrites the live gen-2 binding with gen 1, recorded as a successful resume
(exit 0). A later generation-pinned update or retire then mis-targets. (Low reachability — it needs a
sub-second interleaving — but a generation regression written as success is the dangerous direction.)

The fix re-derives the pending set from `w.Led` AFTER `AppendLease` (which re-replays under the lock, so
it is the authoritative post-lease view) and skips any receipt whose operationId is no longer pending —
resume concludes only what is still pending now that it holds the lease. This mirrors the create path's
existing discipline of reading the FRESH `w.Led` binding for the rebind guard (D67); the bug was that
the LOOP itself still walked the entry-time map. Test drives the exact interleaving deterministically (a
concurrent writer concludes the receipt in the file between resume's load and its lease) and asserts
resume does not re-conclude it; the mutation removing the skip is caught. Recommend the interleaving also
land as a scenario case — the 8 concurrency scenarios pin the in-memory rule algebra but not this
two-actor stale-pending path.

## D961 — a no-op converge silently STRIPPED a wired env var ($ref-on-update data loss)

Validated from the recorded compiler lead, not assumed: a bound Lambda whose env var is WIRED to a
producer output (`implementation.environment[DB_HOST] = {$ref:{capability:db, output:endpoint}}`) is
created with the reference RESOLVED — the create-path fold (D283) substitutes the literal, and observe
records the concrete value. On the NEXT converge the drift classifier recomputes the DESIRED env through
`OperandTargets`/`BuildLambda`, which DROPS a raw `$ref` (`isRefShape` → skip, because a `$ref` is only
ever resolved on the create path). So the desired env OMITS the wired var, drifts against the
create-time-resolved observation, and the reconcile plans to REWRITE the env WITHOUT it — a no-op
converge silently deletes a wired env var and reports success. Reproduced end to end (a bound function
at REST planned to rewrite its env from `DB_HOST=db.internal:5432` to `""`). The dangerous direction of
D716: a person who runs converge expecting a no-op is worse off than if the tool had said nothing.

Two hops carried it. DETECTION: `classifyBound` handed the raw `$ref` impl to `OperandTargets`, so the
desired was already stripped before any comparison. APPLY: even a GENUINE update to another operand
(a VpcConfig change) re-pushes the FULL derivable configuration through `updateConfigBody`, whose
Environment is `BuildLambda(raw impl)` with the `$ref` dropped — stripping the env as collateral. The
create path avoided both because `wireReferences` folds `$ref` operands to literals, but it is gated to
`Operation == "create"`; the drift/update path was never given the same fold.

The fix applies the SAME D283 fold to the update path. `foldDriftRefs` resolves each `$ref` operand
(top-level or nested one level in a map operand) to the bound producer's FRESH `outputs.<name>` literal —
identical bound/fresh/kind/staleness checks as `wireReferences`, and identical refusal (never a literal
fallback, never a stale reading): a stale or missing wired output blocks with re-observe-first rather than
dropping the `$ref` and stripping. `classifyBound` derives the desired shape from the FOLDED impl (so a
converged wired env is no drift), and the update Action carries the resolved `Folds` so apply's
`foldedImplementation` substitutes them before the driver builds the patch and `foldStaleReason` re-judges
them at apply's `--at`. Four tests pin it: the no-op strip is gone, a stale wired output refuses, the
fold record carries the literal, and a genuine VpcConfig update seals the env fold. Three mutants —
desire-from-raw-`$ref`, drop-the-update-fold, never-judge-stale — are each caught. `foldDriftRefs` and
`wireReferences` must resolve a wired operand identically; the comment on each names the other. A
conformance case (`lambda-vpc-env: bound-lambda-with-wired-env-replans-converged-not-stripped`) pins it
at the spec level for parity with the create-path fold's own cases (`references.yaml`): a bound lambda
whose env is wired to a bound Aurora's `writerEndpoint`, every operand observed equal to its desired,
re-plans to `nothing-to-change` — and fails (the strip reappears as a spurious update) without the fold.

## D962 — the apply-side half of the D961 fold was never wired: a genuine update still stripped the wired env var

D961 taught the compiler to fold a bound producer's `$ref` on the UPDATE path and seal the resolved
literal onto the update action's `Folds`, and apply already re-judges that fold's freshness pre-lease
(`foldStaleReason`). But apply then handed the driver the WRONG implementation map. The create branch
passes `implArgs` — `foldedImplementation(a, cand, capID)`, folds substituted (apply.go). The update
branch passed `implementationOf(cand, capID)`, the RAW candidate impl, `$ref` unresolved. So apply
validated a fold it never applied: `prov.Update` got the raw `$ref`, and a driver that re-pushes a full
body from the implementation (Lambda's `UpdateFunctionConfiguration`, whose `updateConfigBody` re-sends
Environment) dropped the wired var (`BuildLambda` skips a raw `$ref`) and STRIPPED it as collateral of an
unrelated change — a `timeout`/VpcConfig update reporting success while deleting `DATABASE_HOST`. The
same dangerous direction as D961, one layer down, and my own D961 DESIGN + tests asserted the apply half
worked when it did not (the claim was ungated — `TestUpdateActionCarriesWiredFold` stopped at the plan,
no test drove apply's update dispatch, which is why the gap survived).

The fix is one line: the update branch passes `implArgs`, exactly as create does. For an update `implArgs`
equals `foldedImplementation` (updates carry `Folds`, never same-run `References`, so the
`resolveActionRefs` overlay is a no-op), so folds are substituted and a foldless update is byte-identical
to before. Blast radius is the whole in-place-update surface, not just Lambda: every driver reached
through the update dispatch now gets resolved operands. A survey found Lambda `environment` the only
REACHABLE manifestation today — GCP `cloudfunctions-fn` in-place update is unwired (refuses), and
`cloudfront`/`elasticache`/`aurora` either route wired operands through replace or never re-push them —
but the fix closes the class at the dispatch, so a driver wiring its update later inherits the guarantee.
The regression test drives apply's update dispatch end to end with an `OperandDrifter` spy that records
the impl its `Update` received, and asserts it is the resolved producer output, not the raw `$ref`; it
fails on the raw-impl code and the mutant restoring `implementationOf` is caught. Found by an audit for
create-vs-update safety asymmetry — the same shape as D961, systematically.

## D963 — audit reported a SET constraint clean against the very forbidden set (false-clean, order-dependent)

Found by an audit of the `audit` verb (D54) for the false-clean shape. `audit` does not call the
four-valued verifier; it re-implements the scalar comparison inline against recorded reality
(`internal/audit/audit.go`), reusing `scalars.Operators` but NOT `verify`'s `setCanonical` (D660). So a
SET attribute — a `kind: list` the vocabulary marks `unordered: true`, like `inference.destinationRegions`,
a data-residency surface — was compared POSITIONALLY. A hard `not-equals` forbidding an exact region set
reported SATISFIED (status clean, exit 0, and a false `violation.resolved` if one was recorded) when
recorded reality held that VERY set in a different order. The compliance reader concludes the prohibited
configuration is not present when it is exactly present — the D716 dangerous direction, at the governance
seam. Reproduced end to end (forbidden set `[eu-central-1, eu-west-1]`, reality `[eu-west-1, eu-central-1]`
→ `satisfied`).

The fix gives audit the same canonicalization verify has, from ONE source. `verify.setCanonical`'s body
is extracted into an exported `verify.SortIfUnordered(sc, subject, path, c, vocabs)` — a sorted copy of a
scalar when the attribute is an unordered list, else the scalar unchanged, never mutating its input — and
`setCanonical` now calls it. audit threads the vocabulary (as verify already does) and applies
`SortIfUnordered` to BOTH the observation and the constraint operand before comparing. Both sides must be
canonicalized: verify sorts the candidate at load and the constraint via setCanonical, but audit's
observation arrives from the cloud in arbitrary order, so audit sorts both at compare time (idempotent).
Pinned by the audit twin of `verify/unorderedoperand_gate_test.go`: the forbidden set in either order →
violated, a different set → satisfied, `equals` reordered → satisfied. The mutant neutering the
observation-side canon is caught. `posture` (which also calls audit) loads the embedded vocabulary for
the same reason.

## D964 — audit silently dropped every presence constraint, certifying prohibitions it never evaluated

The same audit found the second false-clean, worse than the first. `audit`'s loop skipped every
constraint with no `Expected` value (`if cn.Subject == "" || cn.Expected == nil { continue }`), and the
loader leaves `Expected == nil` for the presence ops `exists`/`absent` (they carry no operand). So a hard
`absent` — "public IP must be absent", "no `0.0.0.0/0` ingress", "no legacy plaintext endpoint" — was
never evaluated: it entered no verdict, incremented no violation, and the run reported status clean, exit
0, no `violation.detected`. This is the "gate that found nothing passes" shape and the worst compliance
false-negative: silence would prompt a manual check, but a CLEAN verdict actively certifies compliance
that was never assessed — over the exact class of constraint most likely to encode a hard prohibition
(something must NOT exist). Reproduced: hard `absent` on `network.publicExposure`, reality present →
verdicts empty, clean.

The fix evaluates presence constraints instead of dropping them (only the budget/objective forms, which
carry an `Objective` and no operand, remain out of scope). A fresh sufficient observation means the
attribute is PRESENT — `exists` → satisfied, `absent` → violated. A missing or stale observation cannot
PROVE absence (recorded reality is a partial view, unlike a candidate's complete declared spec), so it
stays `unknown` and BLOCKS a hard constraint — audit never certifies an absence it did not see, the
fail-closed direction. This mirrors verify's `exists`/`absent` handling adapted to observed rather than
declared state. Pinned across all four cases (absent-present→violated, exists-present→satisfied,
absent-absent→unknown-blocks, exists-absent→unknown-blocks); the mutant restoring the blanket drop is
caught.

## D965 — posture masked a stale hard-constraint proof as decayed (exit 0) where audit blocks (exit 2)

Found by an audit for verdict paths that bypass verify, and validated end to end (a repro first exited 2
for the wrong reason — an empty scope set ShadowLowerBound — which the D942 discipline caught; with a
complete scope the divergence is real). `posture` delegates its per-constraint verdicts to `audit` +
`audit.HardOnly` honestly, but the fold that turns them into one class per capability diverged from audit
on the staleness subclass. The accumulator set `in.Verdict[cap]` for `violated`/`unverifiable`/`satisfied`
but LEFT IT UNSET for an audit `unknown` (the comment said "falls through to decayed/unknown"). In
`capRow` the precedence is absent > violated > unverifiable > **decayed** > satisfied > default(unknown),
so when the aged proof that made audit answer `unknown` also set the `decayed` marker, `decayed` won —
and `Summary.ExitCode` counts Shadow/Drifted/Unknown but not Decayed, so posture exited 0. On the identical
ledger `audit` selects the stale record → `unknown` → hard → exit 2. Posture's own header claims parity
with audit on `unknown` ("audit exits 2 on the identical evidence"); the decayed-before-unknown precedence
broke that claim exactly for a stale HARD constraint — a non-negotiable whose proof expired read as a
benign refresh, so an exit-code monitor would not alarm. Invariant #1 (unknown/unverifiable on a hard
constraint blocks, no exceptions) settles it: a stale hard-constraint proof is unknown-on-a-hard-constraint
and must block. (User-directed, weighed against D958: `decayed`→exit-0 stays for a proof that backs NO
hard constraint; only a hard constraint's unknown is lifted above decay.)

The fix makes `unknown` behave like its siblings: the accumulator records `in.Verdict[cap] = "unknown"`
for an audit hard `unknown`, and `capRow` gains a `v == "unknown"` arm ABOVE the decayed arm — so a stale
hard constraint classifies `unknown` (exit 2, audit parity) while a decayed proof backing no hard
constraint still lands in `decayed` (exit 0, D958 preserved). Pinned at the fold level (a stale hard proof
blocks; a decayed non-constraint proof stays benign) and end to end through the posture command over a
ledger whose only proof is past its ttl; the mutants restoring the unset verdict and the decayed
precedence are both caught.

## D966 — react re-derived its exit code and dropped the unknown/incomplete-sweep arms (false all-clear on the unattended path)

Found auditing posture's shadow/scope honesty — which itself holds (shadow detection, ShadowLowerBound on
every incomplete scope, managed-ok-needs-a-proof, D652 absence are all sound). The defect is in the sibling
verb `react` (D143), the event-driven real-time ingress. `react` builds its posture document through the
SAME fold as `posture` (`classifyPosture`, identical `Summary` with honest `Unknown` and `ShadowLowerBound`),
but instead of returning `posture.Summary.ExitCode()` — whose comment says the decision lives there "so it
is testable" and which the `posture` verb returns — it inlined a weaker predicate: `Shadow>0 || Drifted>0`.
That silently dropped the `Unknown>0` and `ShadowLowerBound` arms. So `react` returned exit 0 over (a) an
estate whose covering sweep was incomplete — the base crawl spliced in carries any `incomplete` scope
verbatim (D592), the very case D650 exists for — a shadow may exist in a region never finished; or (b) an
estate whose HARD compliance is unknown (a stale/unverifiable hard proof), where `posture` and `audit` both
exit 2 (invariant #1). `react` is the unattended stream-consumer path (its exit code is explicitly a routing
signal: 0 = "handled, nothing to do"), so automation keyed on it reads a truncated or unknown estate as
confirmed-clean — the incomplete-as-complete / unverifiable-as-success inversion the `posture.ExitCode`
header forbids, reintroduced one verb over. The JSON body react prints is honest (`shadowLowerBound`/`unknown`
visible); only the exit code lied. Same re-implementation-diverges shape as D962/D965 — a sibling path
re-derives a decision the canonical function centralizes.

The fix is one line: `react` returns `doc.Summary.ExitCode()`, the single source of truth. Validated end to
end (a bound resource whose only hard-constraint proof is stale → Unknown>0, no shadow/drift → react exited
0 before, 2 after) through the react command over a real event + pairing + the fake discoverer; the mutant
restoring the bespoke predicate is caught. No test asserted react's exit code before — the gap and the code
coincided, as they did in D962.

## D967 — apply's change-staleness gate judged freshness two ways looser than every sibling

Found auditing staleness/freshness re-derivation (the D962/D965/D966 pattern: a sibling re-derives a
decision the canonical function centralizes). `changeStaleReason` (apply.go) is the D632 pre-lease gate that
lets `apply` MUTATE on a change whose `from` value asserts current reality — it must refuse when the
observation backing that `from` has expired. It judged freshness `if rec.TTLSeconds > 0 && evalClock-obsClock
> rec.TTLSeconds`, diverging from `ledger.ObservationExpired` and from `foldStaleReason` directly below it
(which matches canonical) in two reassuring directions:

- **`TTLSeconds > 0` conjunct.** When `ttl == 0` the staleness comparison is never evaluated, so an
  observation of any age reads FRESH. Canonical `ObservationExpired(obs, 0, clock)` is `clock-obs > 0` —
  expired at any positive age — and every sibling (audit, forecast, the compiler's `stalenessRefusal` and
  both fold paths, `foldStaleReason`) uses the bare `> TTLSeconds`. A `ttl==0` observation arises not from
  `observe` (which always stamps 86400/900) but from a replayed `observation.recorded` event whose body
  omits `ttlSeconds` (defaults 0) or a hand-crafted/imported/restored ledger — exactly the inputs D632's
  re-judgement exists for. So a 7-month-old ttl-less observation justified a mutation.
- **No D189 future guard.** A future-dated observation (`observedAt > evalClock`, negative age) evaluated
  `negative > ttl` = false = fresh. `foldStaleReason` (and audit's `latestSufficient`, forecast, all three
  compiler sites) reject a negative age as invalid. Narrower in practice — the `ClockRegress` pre-check masks
  it unless a restore/import records an event whose clock and `ObservedAt` diverge — but `foldStaleReason`
  keeps the guard anyway, which is the asymmetry that flagged this.

Both let apply re-seal a change on evidence nothing currently witnesses — the dangerous direction, a receipt
landing on a decayed `from`. The fix drops the conjunct and adds the future guard, so `changeStaleReason`
now judges freshness exactly as `ObservationExpired`/`foldStaleReason` do. Pinned by unit tests on the pure
function (a ttl==0 seven-month observation and a future-dated one both refuse; a fresh one still passes);
the mutant restoring the conjunct is caught. Every other freshness site in the tree was checked and matches
canonical — `changeStaleReason` was the sole outlier.

## D968 — a delete reported "retired" when the provider had only ACCEPTED it (async-outruns-poll at the delete boundary)

Found auditing lifecycle-verb outcome honesty (`adopt` and `repair` came back honest; this is the delete
fold). `deleteRDS` returned `Status: "succeeded"` on a 2xx from `DeleteDBInstance` — the instance has
entered `deleting`, not gone. The executor writes a terminal tombstone (`deletedAt`) and drops the binding
only on `succeeded`, and a `succeeded` delete also CLEARS the pending receipt (apply.go) — so nothing is
left to reconcile. If the async deletion then fails (a dependency/replica/state error returns the instance
to `available`), a billable, data-bearing DB is left LIVE while the ledger has tombstoned it and forgotten
the binding; re-discovery then sees it as a foreign shadow. A person acting on "retired" believes a
stateful resource is gone when it may still exist — the D716 dangerous direction, the same
async-outruns-poll shape hardened for create/update (D953, poll-to-applied) but missed for delete.

The honest shape already exists in the same file: `createRDS` polls `describeDB` to `available`, timeout →
`unknown`; `updateRDS` polls to the applied state; GCP Cloud SQL's delete polls its operation to `DONE`;
EKS deletes poll to a readable 404. `deleteRDS` now does the same — polls to a confirmed 404 (the instance
gone), returns `succeeded` only then, and `unknown` on poll timeout so the pending intent survives for a
reconcile. Pinned: an accepted-but-still-`deleting` instance now reports `unknown` (a stateful httptest
mock that never leaves `deleting`), while a delete the provider confirms gone still reports `succeeded`
(the mock flips to `DBInstanceNotFound` after the delete); the mutant that concludes before the instance
is gone is caught.

This is the FIRST of a staged sweep (user-directed, highest-danger first). The same accept-as-success fold
is present, unfixed and recorded here for the next slices, in `deleteDynamoDB` (`dynamodb_net.go`, table
enters `DELETING`), `deleteElastiCache` (`elasticache_net.go`, group enters `deleting`), and every Azure
ARM delete via `deleteAndConfirm` (`vnet_net.go`, returns success on a 202 Accepted without following
`Azure-AsyncOperation`). The lower-danger near-synchronous deletes (`eks-addon`, `eks-podidentity`,
`bedrock`, `lambda`) share the fold and are recorded but deferred.

## D969 — the D968 async-delete fix, applied to DynamoDB

Second slice of the staged async-delete sweep (D968). `deleteDynamoDB` returned `succeeded` on a 200 from
`DeleteTable` — the table has entered `DELETING`, not gone — so the executor tombstoned a table still live
and billing, with the same orphan-on-failed-async exposure as D968. Now it polls `describeTable` to a
confirmed `ResourceNotFoundException` (as `createDynamoDB` polls to `ACTIVE`), returns `succeeded` only
then, `unknown` on poll timeout. Pinned the same way (a stateful mock that reports the table gone after the
delete keeps `succeeded`; a mock that stays `ACTIVE` reports `unknown`); the mutant is caught. Remaining in
the sweep: `deleteElastiCache` and the Azure ARM `deleteAndConfirm`.

## D970 — the D968 async-delete fix, applied to ElastiCache

Third slice of the staged async-delete sweep. `deleteElastiCache` reported `succeeded` on a 200 from
`DeleteReplicationGroup` — the group has entered `deleting`, not gone — and then tried to delete the
derived cache subnet group, which cannot succeed while the group still uses it (the code accepted a
`CacheSubnetGroupInUse` as "left standing"). Both are now honest: it polls `describeRG` to a confirmed
`ReplicationGroupNotFoundFault` (as `createElastiCache` polls to `available`) BEFORE the subnet-group
cleanup, so the subnet group is deleted only once the group is truly gone; `unknown` on poll timeout keeps
the handle and defers the subnet cleanup to the reconcile. Pinned the same way (stateful mock confirms gone
→ succeeded; a mock that stays `deleting` → unknown); the mutant is caught. Last in the sweep: the Azure
ARM `deleteAndConfirm` (returns success on a 202 Accepted).

## D971 — the D968 async-delete fix, applied to every Azure ARM delete

Final slice of the staged async-delete sweep. `deleteAndConfirm` — the shared fold behind ~15 Azure ARM
deletes (flexible server, log analytics, ACS email, backup vault/policy, application gateway, federated
credential, and more) — returned `succeeded` on any 2xx, INCLUDING a `202 Accepted`. A 202 is a
long-running delete: the resource has entered deleting, not gone, and ARM hands back an operation to
follow. Concluding `succeeded` tombstoned a resource still live across the whole Azure surface at once. Now
it branches: a `200`/`204` is a synchronous delete (already gone → succeeded); a `202` polls the resource
to a confirmed `404` (as the create paths poll `provisioningState` to `Succeeded`), returns `succeeded`
only then, `unknown` on poll timeout. Pinned by calling `deleteAndConfirm` directly: a 202 whose resource
stays present → `unknown`; a 202 polled to a 404 → `succeeded`. The mutant that concludes on the 202 is
caught. This closes the highest-danger tier of the sweep (AWS RDS/DynamoDB/ElastiCache + all Azure ARM);
the lower-danger near-synchronous AWS deletes (eks-addon/podidentity/bedrock/lambda) remain recorded and
deferred (D968).

## D972 — the async-delete fix, applied to Aurora (a stateful data store the audit missed)

A completeness scan of every AWS driver delete (the lifecycle audit had named only a subset) found four more
stateful, data-bearing async deletes shortcutting to `succeeded` on accept: `aurora`, `opensearch`, `msk`,
`efs`. This slice fixes Aurora. `deleteAurora` reported `succeeded` on an accepted `DeleteDBCluster` — the
cluster has entered `deleting`, not gone — then deleted the derived subnet + parameter groups, which cannot
succeed while the cluster still uses them. Now it polls `describeCluster` to a confirmed `DBClusterNotFound`
(as `createAurora` polls to `available`) BEFORE the derived-resource cleanup; `unknown` on poll timeout keeps
the handle. Pinned: an accepted-but-still-`deleting` cluster reports `unknown`, a confirmed-gone one still
reports `succeeded`; the mutant is caught. Next in this tier: OpenSearch, MSK, EFS; then a triage note for the
remaining shortcuts (most are synchronous-safe config/IAM deletes where 200 = gone).

## D973 — the async-delete fix, applied to OpenSearch

`deleteOpenSearch` reported `succeeded` the moment `DeleteDomain` was accepted — but the domain enters
`Deleted:true, Processing:true` and stays live for minutes while data is torn down. A ledger that tombstones it
there orphans a billable, data-bearing search domain. Now it polls `describeDomain` to a confirmed
`ResourceNotFoundException` (as `createOpenSearch` polls `Processing` to done), returns `succeeded` only then,
`unknown` on poll timeout. Pinned: an accepted-but-still-deleting domain reports `unknown`; a confirmed-gone one
reports `succeeded`; the `!found`→`found` mutant is caught.

## D974 — the async-delete fix, applied to MSK

`deleteMSK` reported `succeeded` on an accepted `DeleteCluster` — the Kafka cluster has entered `DELETING`, not
gone. Concluding there tombstones a data-bearing broker still live. Now it polls `getMSKByName` to a confirmed
absence (as `createMSK` polls to `ACTIVE`), returns `succeeded` only when the cluster is gone from
`ListClustersV2`, `unknown` on poll timeout. Pinned: an accepted-but-still-`DELETING` cluster reports `unknown`;
a confirmed-gone one reports `succeeded`; the `!found`→`found` mutant is caught.

## D975 — the async-delete fix, applied to EFS (last of the four stateful stores)

`deleteEFS` reported `succeeded` on an accepted `DeleteFileSystem` — the file system enters `deleting`, not gone.
Concluding there tombstones a data-bearing file system still live. Now it polls `describeEFS` to a confirmed
`FileSystemNotFound` (as `createEFS` polls to `available`), returns `succeeded` only then, `unknown` on poll
timeout. Pinned: an accepted-but-still-`deleting` file system reports `unknown`; a confirmed-gone one reports
`succeeded`; the `!found`→`found` mutant is caught. This closes the four stateful data stores the completeness
scan found (Aurora/OpenSearch/MSK/EFS); what remains is the triage note classifying every other AWS delete
shortcut as synchronous-safe (200 = gone) vs a further async-dangerous case.

## D976 — the async-delete fix, second wave (the triage's eight candidates)

docs/ASYNC_DELETE_TRIAGE.md classified every remaining AWS delete. Eight concluded
`succeeded` the instant an async teardown was ACCEPTED, for a resource that deletes
asynchronously and is billable and/or data-bearing — the D968 shape. D976 through D983
fix them with the same poll-to-absence idiom (poll a `describe*` to a confirmed
not-found before `succeeded`, `unknown` on timeout, as the create paths poll to a
terminal state), each with an async-not-gone test and a mutation-gate mutant
(`!found`→`found`, or `!stillThere`→`stillThere` for the load balancer). Every reader
was checked to return `!found` at the terminal gone state before the fix (D942 lesson).

D976 is **`deleteEC2Instance`** — `TerminateInstances` leaves the machine `shutting-down`;
`describeEC2Instances` skips `terminated`, so the poll confirms gone. Reporting succeeded
on accept tombstoned a still-billable VM (the strongest instance of the class).

## D977 — deleteASG polls the fleet to gone

`DeleteAutoScalingGroup ForceDelete` terminates the member fleet in the background; the
group lingers in delete-in-progress. Poll `describeASG` to an empty group before
`succeeded`. Reporting succeeded on accept tombstoned a fleet still being torn down.

## D978 — deleteEBSVolume polls the volume to gone

`DeleteVolume` leaves the volume `deleting`; poll `describeEC2Volume` to a `NotFound`.
Data-bearing — the D47 data-loss gate exists because this is data.

## D979 — deleteKinesis polls the stream to gone

`DeleteStream` leaves the stream `DELETING`; poll `describeStream` to `ResourceNotFound`.
Data-bearing (records) plus billable shard-hours.

## D980 — deleteLoadBalancer polls the LB to gone before the target group

`DeleteLoadBalancer` leaves the LB deleting, and it still references its target group,
which cannot be deleted meanwhile. Poll `describeLoadBalancer` to `LoadBalancerNotFound`
BEFORE the target-group cleanup; `unknown` on timeout. Hourly-billable.

## D981 — deleteVpnGateway polls the gateway to gone

`DeleteVpnGateway` leaves the gateway `deleting`; poll `describeVgw`, which reports
`state=deleted`/absent as gone. Hourly-billable.

## D982 — deleteSQS polls the queue to gone

`DeleteQueue` is eventually-consistent (AWS documents up to ~60s, during which the queue
and its in-flight messages still answer); poll `sqsListTags` to `NonExistentQueue`.

## D983 — deleteRedshiftServerless polls the NAMESPACE to gone

The workgroup leg already polled (D888); the namespace — the DATA half — did not, so a
still-deleting namespace was tombstoned. Poll `getNamespace` to `ResourceNotFound`,
mirroring the workgroup poll. This empties the async-dangerous column of the triage;
the synchronous-safe deletes (2xx means gone, or the API refuses while non-empty) are
unchanged and correct.

## D984 — the async-delete fix, Azure: route thirteen deletes through deleteAndConfirm

The AWS async-delete sweep (D968-D983) prompted the same audit on GCP and Azure. GCP is
clean — every async LRO delete already polls its operation to DONE. Azure had thirteen
deletes that concluded `succeeded` the instant ARM returned a **202 Accepted**, without
polling: `deleteCosmos`, `deleteACR`, `deleteRedisAzure`, `deleteAPIM`, `deleteAzureVM`,
`deleteAzureVMSS`, `deleteAzureDisk`, `deleteAzureCDN`, `deleteEventHubs`, `deleteAzKafka`,
`deleteAzureOpenAI`, `deleteAISearch`, `deleteContainerAppsJob` — each a billable and/or
data-bearing resource whose ARM delete is long-running. A 202 means the resource has
entered deleting, not gone; tombstoning it there orphans a live resource from a ledger
that says it is gone.

The fix reuses the existing D971 helper: each delete's inline `doARM("DELETE", url, …)`
+ succeeded-on-2xx block is replaced by `return *d.deleteAndConfirm(url, providerID, "<what>")`.
`deleteAndConfirm` polls a 202 to a confirmed 404 (as the create paths poll
`provisioningState`), returns `succeeded` only then, `unknown` on timeout; a 200/204 is a
synchronous delete (already gone). The poll LOGIC is mutation-gated once at the helper
(D971); the thirteen wirings are each pinned by a subtest in
`TestAzureAsyncDeletesPollToAbsence` (a 202 that never completes → `unknown` with the
poll-timeout reason) and a per-driver mutant that reverts the wiring to succeeded-on-accept.

Azure storage-account and key-vault deletes (`deleteBlob`, `deleteAzFiles`,
`deleteKeyVault`, `deleteAzureKey`) return `succeeded` on 2xx like these did, but their
ARM RP delete is genuinely synchronous (2xx means gone), so they are left unchanged;
routing them through the helper would be harmless but is not required.

## D985 — observe: confirm a customer key, never infer it (two false-BYOK reads)

An observe-side sweep for security attributes reported as safe-looking without an
authoritative read (the D954 shape) found two reachable false-BYOK emissions. Both are
the dangerous direction: a person reads `encryption.customerManagedKeys=true` and
believes a customer-revocable key protects the data when it does not.

- **Azure Log Analytics** (`observeLogAnalytics`) reported CMK=true from the mere presence
  of a linked dedicated cluster (`features.clusterResourceId != ""`). A dedicated cluster
  is a PREREQUISITE for a customer key, not proof of one — a commitment-tier cluster can
  run on Microsoft's platform key. Now it reads the cluster (a second ARM GET at the same
  API version) and emits true ONLY when `properties.keyVaultProperties` carries a key;
  otherwise a "not observed" diagnostic, never a false true.
- **AWS S3** (`observeS3`) reported CMK=true whenever a default-encryption rule named
  `aws:kms` with any key id — but the AWS-managed `aws/s3` key also answers that with a
  key id, and it is not a customer key. Now it excludes the managed alias via
  `isAWSManagedKMSKey`, as every other AWS driver already does (the D954 fix for ECR was
  the same shape).

Both paths were previously UNTESTED for the CMK=true case (an ungated emission); each now
carries a two-way test (confirmed key → true; no key / managed key → not emitted) and a
mutation-gate mutant.

RECORDED, NOT FIXED (flagged, not resolved unilaterally): Azure Blob Storage
(`observeBlob`) reports `network.publicExposure` from `allowBlobPublicAccess` (the
anonymous-blob-access toggle), while other Azure drivers (flexserver/servicebus/azacr)
derive it from `publicNetworkAccess`. Blob is INTERNALLY consistent — its create maps the
same attribute onto `allowBlobPublicAccess`, so the round-trip holds — and for a data
store "can anonymous users read the blobs" is a defensible reading of public exposure.
Whether `network.publicExposure` should mean anonymous-data-access or network-reachability
for a storage account is a vocabulary/modeling question spanning create, observe and the
conformance round-trip; it is recorded here rather than remodeled under the freeze.

## D986 — the async-delete fix, k8s: poll Terminating objects to a confirmed 404

The async-delete audit (D968-D985) covered AWS, GCP and Azure but not the k8s driver.
`deleteMapped` — the shared delete for every mapped k8s object (namespaces, RBAC, network
policies, quotas, flux/argo CRDs) — concluded `succeeded` on a bare `st == 200`. But a k8s
DELETE is ACCEPTED (200/202) while the object enters Terminating: its `deletionTimestamp`
is set and its finalizers run. For a namespace (always finalized) or a flux/argo CRD, a
stuck finalizer holds the object Terminating indefinitely — with every workload inside it
still running and billing — and tombstoning it as gone is the dangerous direction. (The
202 case was worse: it fell through to `failed`.)

Now `deleteMapped` treats 404 as idempotent-gone, 200/202 as accepted, and polls `oursAt`
(a GET) to a confirmed 404 before `succeeded`, `unknown` on timeout — the same poll-to-
absence the cloud deletes use. The successful delete path was previously UNTESTED (every
existing k8s delete test refuses before the DELETE); it now carries a two-way test
(confirmed gone → succeeded; still Terminating → unknown) and a mutation-gate mutant. Poll
timing is a driver field defaulting to 2m/2s, set small in tests. This closes the
async-delete class on the fourth driver family.

## D987 — k8s observe: read the egress rules before claiming they restrict

A k8s observe-honesty audit (the read analog of D986, on the surface the earlier observe
sweep skipped) found one clear false-secure read. `lensNetpolDefaultDeny` emitted
`egress.restricted=true` from `policyTypes` containing "Egress" ALONE, never reading
`spec.egress`. In Kubernetes an egress rule list that is empty (`egress: []`) denies all
outbound, but a list with a wide-open rule (`egress: [{}]`) ALLOWS all outbound — so a
policy that imposes zero egress restriction was reported as a restriction control, and
unlike `ingress.public` there is no Prober to override the config-intent, so this lens
value is the authoritative answer a `egress.restricted == true` constraint checks. Now the
egress branch mirrors the ingress branch: claim `restricted=true` only for a genuinely
empty rule list; when rules are present, defer (a diagnostic, no emission), since a rule
list may be allow-all or partial and cannot be reduced to "restricted" from config alone.
Pinned by an allow-all-rule test case and a mutant.

RECORDED, NOT FIXED (a definition question, flagged not resolved): `permPrivileged`
(`rbacrole.go`) flags a full wildcard (`verb:* resource:*`) as privileged only when the
apiGroup is `*` or `core`, so a role granting `apps/*:*` (full control of all workload
types — an escalation-to-node vector) reports `access.privileged=false`. The code
under-implements its own comment ("full wildcard on verb, resource OR group is
cluster-admin-shaped"). But `access.mutating=true` is still correctly emitted, and
broadening the check to ANY group would also flag benign full-control-of-a-CRD-group roles
as privileged (over-report). Whether `access.privileged` should fire on a per-group
wildcard is a vocabulary/definition decision affecting every RBAC contract; recorded here
rather than broadened under the freeze.

## D988 — k8s RBAC: a per-group wildcard is privileged (user-directed follow-up to D987)

The D987 recording flagged that `permPrivileged` marked a full wildcard (`verb:* resource:*`)
as privileged only for apiGroup `*` or `core`, so `apps/*:*` — full control of all workload
types, an escalation-to-node vector — read as `access.privileged=false`. Asked to decide,
the user chose to broaden the check. Now a full wildcard on any apiGroup counts as
privileged. This over-reports a benign full-control-of-a-CRD-group role as privileged,
which is the safe direction; `access.mutating` was already emitted correctly. Pinned by an
`apps/*:*` test case and a mutant.

## D989 — Azure Blob: publicExposure means network reachability (user-directed follow-up to D985)

The D985 recording flagged that `observeBlob` derived `network.publicExposure` from
`allowBlobPublicAccess` (the anonymous-blob-access toggle) while every other Azure driver
uses `publicNetworkAccess` (network reachability) — so a storage account with anonymous
access off but `publicNetworkAccess=Enabled` read as private though it is internet-reachable.
Asked to decide, the user chose to remodel. `createBlob` now sets `publicNetworkAccess`
(Enabled/Disabled) from the contract attribute and `allowBlobPublicAccess=false` (anonymous
access is a separate control, defaulted off — the secure choice and Azure's modern default);
`observeBlob` reads `publicNetworkAccess` (Enabled→true, Disabled→false, absent→unread), the
same convention as flexserver/servicebus/azacr. The create/observe round-trip is pinned by
the metamorphic test (both public and private) and a mutant.

## D990 — probe: the aurora no-instance branch must say provider-config, not tcp-connect

A probe measured-reality audit found the subsystem strongly disciplined (a failure/timeout
is an honest probe.failed/unknown, never a fabricated measured-safe) — with one residual of
the D775 method-provenance lie. `probeAuroraExposure`'s `writer == ""` branch (a cluster with
no member instance) concludes `network.publicExposure=false` from the CONFIG — nothing is
dialed — but stamped `Method: "tcp-connect"`, naming a handshake nobody attempted. D775 fixed
exactly this in the shared `probeExposure` helper (and the GCP/Azure config paths, and AWS's
own `!publiclyAccessible` path, all say `provider-config`); this branch was left behind. The
value `false` is honest; only the method is corrected to `provider-config`. Pinned by a direct
unit test of the no-instance branch (the D775 test only exercised `probeExposure`) and a mutant.

## D991 — k8s observe: strip credentials from a gitops repoURL before it is recorded

A secret-leak audit found the codebase disciplined about this class (the D309/D648 Redactor
+ secretshape alphabet applied at every mutation boundary, outputs excluding credentials,
read-only drivers never requesting secret fields) — with one exception on the OBSERVE path.
An ArgoCD `Application` `spec.source.repoURL` (and the Flux `GitRepository` `spec.url` it
resolves to) can carry an inline git token — `https://user:ghp_xxx@github.com/org/repo.git`.
The generic engine's `copy`/`resolve-ref` ops emitted this verbatim as the `source.repoURL`
observation. Unlike a mutation `Reason` (scrubbed at the boundary), observations are never
scrubbed downstream — they are persisted to the ledger and republished by `export` and the
console — so a real git token would leak to anyone with read access to the stream. (The
`collector` credential gate only fires at capsule-certify time, after the ledger already
holds it.) Now the emit strips URL userinfo (`redactURLUserinfo`): a value that parses as a
URL with `user:pass@` has it removed, keeping the capability-semantic host/path; a non-URL,
a plain URL, or a `host:port` is untouched. Pinned by a Flux resolve test with an inline
credential and a mutant.

## D992 — azure dashboard: lenses/parts are LISTS on the live Portal API, not maps

A field run (own Azure sub, 2026-08-10) drove `capability.monitoring.dashboard` against the
real Microsoft.Portal/dashboards API and it REFUSED the create with HTTP 400 "Cannot
deserialize the current JSON object … into type List". The driver built `properties.lenses`
and each lens's `parts` as MAPS (`{"0": …}`) — a shape the golden httptest fixture accepted
but the live 2020-09-01-preview API does not; it wants LISTS. Same golden-vs-real class as
D936/D950/D952. Fixed both sides: `createBody` emits `lenses`/`parts` as arrays, and the
observe struct reads them as slices; verified end to end (create APPLIED, observe CONVERGED,
retire deleted, verify-absent) through groundhold's own HTTP path. Every dashboard test
fixture updated to the array shape; a mutant reverts the observe struct to a map (which then
cannot decode the array the API returns).

## D993 — gcp: name the quota project so user-ADC credentials work

A field run (own GCP project, 2026-08-10) drove `capability.cost.budget` and the
billingbudgets create 403'd: "authenticating by using local Application Default
Credentials … requires a quota project, which is not set by default." User ADC (as opposed
to a service-account token) has no billing/quota project of its own, so quota-metered APIs
(billingbudgets, serviceusage, …) refuse without an explicit `x-goog-user-project` header.
The driver already knows the project it is acting on; it now sets that as the quota project
on every request. Confirmed against the live API (the header turned the 403 into a 200);
harmless/ignored for a service-account token. Pinned by a header-assertion test and a
mutant that drops the header. (The billingbudget driver itself was correct — the currency
must match the billing account, an operator-supplied value, not a driver bug.)

## D994 — gcp/assetfeed: address feeds.get/delete by project NUMBER, not ID

Field run (own GCP project, 2026-08-10, after D993 unblocked the create): the Cloud Asset
change-feed created fine, but the RETIRE hung. converge reported the delete `unknown` —
"the world MAY have changed; run resume" — and `resume` then answered "still-unknown /
pending" every time, forever. The feed was never removed.

Root cause: `feeds.create` takes the project in its `{parent}` and accepts the project ID,
but `feeds.get` and `feeds.delete` take it in the resource `{name}` and REJECT the ID —
they demand the project NUMBER ("Feed name must be in the format of
projects|folders|organizations/<number>/feeds/<feed_identifier>"). The driver built the
get/delete name with the ID, so both 400'd. The retire's pre-delete ownership read got no
answer → `unknown`; the delete itself never fired; and because the read can NEVER answer,
resume could never conclude it. This is the D709 shape and admissible under the D716 freeze:
a person acting on it keeps running resume believing a transient async delete is settling,
while the resource is orphaned indefinitely — worse than if the tool had said nothing.

Fix: a single `assetFeedName(feedID)` helper resolves the project number via the existing
`ourProjectNumber()` (CRM, cached) and both get and delete address the feed by number.
`sameProject` already pins the providerId's project to `d.Project`, so its number is the
right one. Create is unchanged (its `{parent}` still takes the ID, which works). Field-proven
end to end: create APPLIED, retire APPLIED (no more unknown), verify = 0 feeds. Pinned by a
regression test that captures the get/delete paths and asserts they carry the NUMBER not the
ID, plus a mutant that reverts the name to the project ID.

## D995 — vertexai: endpoints.delete etag param is a recorded defect (deferred under freeze)

Field run (own GCP project, 2026-08-10): a Vertex AI endpoint create+observe+converge is
field-proven, but the RETIRE fails. `deleteVertexAI` reads the endpoint's etag and appends
`?etag=<etag>` to the DELETE for optimistic concurrency (an ifMatch guard against a
concurrent relabel). Vertex `endpoints.delete` has no such parameter and 400s the request
("Invalid JSON payload received. Unknown name 'etag': Cannot bind query parameter"). An
endpoint always carries an etag, so EVERY delete of a present endpoint fails; a plain DELETE
(no etag) succeeds (confirmed directly against the live API).

This is a real defect — groundhold cannot retire a Vertex endpoint — but it is NOT admissible
under the D716 freeze. The test is direction, not severity: the delete fails CLOSED and
HONESTLY. converge reports `failed: a-delete-ep` and DIED; a person acting on that knows the
delete did not happen and intervenes. Contrast D994 (assetfeed), which reported `unknown` /
"run resume" forever — a false transient that lulls the operator while the resource is
orphaned. That is the dangerous direction; this is not. So D995 is RECORDED and waits for the
next unfreeze; the fix is to drop the etag param (or move the ifMatch to a header the API
honors) and rely on the pre-delete ownership read.

Meta (two field-found GCP delete-path defects in one session — D994 name-format, D995
etag): GCP delete/get endpoints carry per-service REST quirks the drivers guessed wrong
because the DELETE path was never exercised against the live API. Worth a deliberate
delete-path sweep across the GCP drivers once the freeze lifts — the golden tests encode the
driver's own assumption, so only a field DELETE catches these.

## D996 — witness services are `measured` by adopt+observe against a real resource

The three compute-image services (aws/ami, gcp/computeimage, azure/azimage) are witness-only
(D177): groundhold never authors an image, it observes and adopts one. COVERAGE.md had them
`config-intent` on the reasoning that "measured" needs a create→retire lifecycle, which a
witness has none of. That conflated "measured" with "has a create path." A witness's WHOLE job
is the read: the contract states what must be TRUE of the image, and adopt+observe proves it
against live cloud reality. That read IS a field measurement — the only one a witness can
have — and it is strictly stronger evidence than the golden/httptest a config-intent row rests
on. Decided 2026-08-10 (user-approved): adopt+observe against a REAL resource counts as
`measured`.

Not a blanket relaxation. The bar stays a real read against live cloud, cited: each of the
three was proven 2026-08-10 by standing up a real image (AMI CopyImage'd from a public source,
a GCE image from a public source, an Azure managed image from an empty-disk snapshot), binding
it with adopt, and reading region/exposure/encryption as `measured`, then tearing the image
down. The create path stays refused by design on all three — the reclassification is about how
a witness is measured, not about making it authorable. Services that are genuinely unmeasurable
(no safe read, singleton, org-level) stay `exempt`; config-intent still means golden-only.

## D997 — ses-inbound: don't hijack a region's active receipt rule set on create

Field-found 2026-08-10 (own AWS account, reading the create path while measuring ses-inbound).
SES has exactly ONE active receipt rule set per region, and `SetActiveReceiptRuleSet` REPLACES
whatever is active. The `ses-inbound` create landed its rule set + rule, then called
`SetActiveReceiptRuleSet` UNCONDITIONALLY to make its own set active — with no check for what was
active before. So a create run in a region where the operator already has a DIFFERENT active rule
set (their real inbound-mail routing) would silently replace it: their mail stops being received,
and the create reports `succeeded`. That is the D716-admissible shape — a person acting on
"succeeded" is worse off than if the tool had said nothing, because their inbound mail is now
silently broken.

The asymmetry made it easy to miss: the DELETE path already reasons about exactly this hazard —
its comment says "a rule set is where inbound mail is ROUTED, so deleting a stranger's rule
silently stops delivering their mail" and it guards ownership by name — but the CREATE's
activation step had no symmetric guard. (This is the delete-ownership-blindspot class inverted:
here the write that needed the guard is an activation, not a delete.)

Fix: `setActiveOutcome` now reads the region's active set first. If a DIFFERENT set is active and
it is NOT groundhold's (`pv-` prefix), it does NOT call `SetActiveReceiptRuleSet` — it leaves our
rule INACTIVE and returns `unknown` WITH the providerId, naming the conflict ("region already has
active receipt rule set X (not groundhold's) … refusing to hijack the region's mail routing").
Inactive-receives-nothing is the honest four-valued outcome the driver already uses for a failed
activation (D29/D87); the new part is that we never touch a stranger's active pointer. An active
set that is ours, empty, or absent is still (re-)activated normally. An unreadable active-set read
is `unknown` too — refusing to activate blind. Pinned by a test that a foreign active set leaves
our rule inactive, never issues SetActive, and leaves the stranger's set untouched, plus a mutant
that drops the foreign-prefix check. The measured ses-inbound run itself was in a region with NO
active set (the safe path), so it converged; this defect is on the path a real tenant would hit.

## D998 — vertexai: drop the etag param from endpoints.delete (unfreezes D995)

D995 recorded, under the freeze, that `deleteVertexAI` appended `?etag=<etag>` to the DELETE
for optimistic concurrency, which Vertex rejects (400 "Unknown name 'etag': Cannot bind query
parameter") — and since a present endpoint always carries an etag, EVERY delete of a real
endpoint failed, so the retire could never complete. It was left recorded because it fails
CLOSED and HONEST (a clear `failed`, not a false success), which is not the freeze's
dangerous-direction bar. Unfrozen deliberately (user-approved 2026-08-10) as the cheapest path
across the 95% coverage line: it is a small, unambiguously-correct fix, and it turns vertexai
into a clean measured create→retire cycle.

Fix: the delete no longer appends an etag. Vertex `endpoints.delete` offers no server-side
If-Match for this resource, so the ownership pre-read (labels via `ownedBy`, already there) is the
guard we have; the TOCTOU window between that read and the delete is unavoidable for a resource
the API gives no etag-on-delete for, and is the honest best effort. Removed the now-unused
`net/url` import. Pinned by making the httptest fake faithful — it 400s a DELETE carrying an
`etag` query param exactly as the live API does — so `TestVertexAIDeleteSendsNoEtag` (and the
pre-existing owned-delete test, which sets an etag) only pass when no etag is sent; a mutant that
re-appends the etag is caught. Field-proven end to end after the fix: create CONVERGED, retire
APPLIED, verify = 0 endpoints.

## D999 — azurecdn: reimplement on Azure Front Door Standard (classic CDN retired)

Azure retired "Azure CDN from Microsoft (classic)" (SKU Standard_Microsoft) for new profiles,
and every other classic CDN SKU (Verizon, Akamai, Edgio) is retired or retiring — so the
azurecdn driver, which stood up a classic profile+endpoint, could no longer create anything (a
profile PUT 400s "no longer available for new creates"). The only forward path is Azure Front
Door Standard (SKU Standard_AzureFrontDoor), the same Microsoft.Cdn provider but a richer
resource model. Unfrozen deliberately (user-approved 2026-08-10) to make the service creatable
again and reach the last coverage gap.

The capability contract is UNCHANGED — `capability.cdn.distribution` (CloudFront's twin), same
attributes (origin.domain, viewer.protocol, service.managed) and operands (cache_policy,
aliases, certificate). `BuildAzureCDN`'s validation logic is preserved; what changed is the ARM
wire and the create/observe flow. The classic single endpoint (origin + TLS posture inline)
becomes a five-resource composite created in dependency order under one binding: profile →
origin group → origin (the backend) → afd endpoint (the edge hostname) → route (ties them
together, carries the viewer posture + caching + any custom domains). Custom domains stay
supported (the conformance case cdn-custom-domain-azure requires it): an alias is an afd
customDomains sub-resource with tlsSettings — a ManagedCertificate, or a CustomerCertificate
that references a BYO Key Vault cert first imported as a profile secret. The origin group,
origin, and route take FIXED profile-scoped names so observe can address them from the
providerId (profile+endpoint) alone; the providerId is unchanged (azcdn:sub:rg:profile:endpoint).

Semantic mapping notes: viewer.protocol maps to the route's supportedProtocols + httpsRedirect,
which means AFD honors `redirect-to-https` NATIVELY (httpsRedirect=Enabled) — the classic driver
had to refuse it. And AFD caching is OFF by default (the inverse of classic), so cache_policy:
honor now ATTACHES a cacheConfiguration and disabled OMITS it. delete still removes the profile,
which cascades every child. Field-proven end to end on real Azure (2026-08-10, Standard_AzureFrontDoor
profile in gh-fieldcov-rg): create CONVERGED with viewer.protocol=redirect-to-https round-tripping
through observe (the capability classic CDN could not express), retire APPLIED, verify = 0 profiles.
All 550 conformance cases stay green; pinned by rewritten goldens + two mutants (the AFD SKU and
the httpsRedirect mapping). One consequence rippled into the D682 dead-enum ratchet: making
`redirect-to-https` honorable on Azure removed it from the set of enum values no serving driver
accepts (it was dead-everywhere while classic CDN refused it and CloudFront's attribute-only
probe couldn't confirm acceptance), so the baseline tightened 12 → 11 — the ratchet doing exactly
what it is for.

## D1000 — bedrock: single-encode the ':' profile id on the wire (D880 regression)

Field-found by a second tester (acme ACME-034), against a binary I had just delivered. D880
made the SigV4 signer double-encode the canonical path for every non-S3 service (%3A→%253A) —
correct, and required, because AWS re-encodes the RECEIVED path a second time when it recomputes
the canonical. But double-encoding the canonical is only right when the WIRE carries the
SINGLE-encoded form: the caller must put %3A in the URL, AWS re-encodes it to %253A, and the two
match. MSK and backup were fixed to do exactly that (`rfc3986(arn)` in the path). Bedrock was
MISSED: `getInferenceProfile`/delete built the path as `bedrockProfilesPath+"/"+profileID` with a
RAW ':'. So the wire carried ':', AWS canonicalized it to %3A, while the signer had signed %253A —
a guaranteed 403 "signature does not match". Every Bedrock inference-profile id carries a ':'
version suffix (eu.anthropic...v1:0), so `ai-inference` observe was DEAD on any double-encoding
build — for everyone, not just the reporter. It worked on v0.1.15 (pre-D880, no double-encode) and
broke on the delivery, which is what made it a clean regression rather than an environment issue.

Fix: `rfc3986(profileID)` at both bedrock path sites, identical to MSK/backup. The two other AWS
drivers that put a variable in a path — apigatewayv2 (api id), guardduty (detector id), lambda
(function name), ses (domain / config-set) — carry only chars rfc3986 leaves untouched
(alphanumeric, '-', '_', '.'), so the double-encode is a no-op there; bedrock was the only id with
a reserved byte. The test gap that let it through: the fake's profile id had no ':', and the fake
matches on Go's DECODED r.URL.Path (which can't see wire encoding). Fixed by giving the fake a
realistic ':'-bearing id and asserting on r.URL.EscapedPath() that the wire single-encodes it
(%3A, never a raw ':' nor a double %253A). Field-proven: the fresh binary adopt+observes a real
colon-id profile (eu.anthropic.claude-3-sonnet-20240229-v1:0) clean — partial=None, unreadable=0 —
where the delivered binary 403'd. Pinned by the strengthened test + a mutant that reverts the path
to the raw id; aws-routes capture refreshed to the %3A path.

Lesson (why the meter didn't catch it): a signing regression only surfaces when the signed input
carries a reserved byte AND the fake can observe the wire encoding. The D880 fix added the
double-encode with tests for MSK/backup (which HAD colons) but no sweep for every other id-in-path
driver, and bedrock's own test used a colon-free id. The general guard is now in place (assert the
escaped wire path, use realistic ids); a broader "every id-in-path driver has a reserved-byte test
case" sweep is the follow-up.

## D1001 — aws/lambda: an architecture operand (arm64 image → arm64 function)

Field-found by the second tester (acme ACME-035). The lambda driver never sent
`Architectures`, so `CreateFunction` took AWS's default (x86_64) — while the operator's
image was arm64. The function created "State: Active / LastUpdateStatus: Successful", and
died on the FIRST invoke with `Runtime.InvalidEntrypoint / ProcessSpawnFailed`. Three signals
said "ready"; nothing ran. A success reported over a resource that cannot run — the phantom-
control shape, admissible under the D716 freeze (a person acting on "succeeded" — a DR rebuild
that stands up 38 dead arm64-image/x86_64-function pairs, all reporting healthy — is worse off
than if the tool had said nothing). The tester runs an all-arm64 estate (20% cheaper/invoke)
and could not express the architecture at all: three operand names were refused as
`unknown-operand` — the good refusal, but it left the architecture undeclarable.

Fix: an `architectures` operand (`arm64` | `x86_64`, a bare string or single-element list — a
two-arch Lambda does not exist, so more than one refuses). It is an OPERAND, not a capability
attribute: which instruction set the code runs on is a build detail, not a promise about the
workload (like `image_uri`, not like residency/exposure). The create body sends
`Architectures` when declared; absent keeps AWS's x86_64 default. observe reads `Architectures`
back on the reserved operand path, so a declared-vs-live mismatch is verifiable; the change
classifies IMMUTABLE (architecture is fixed at CreateFunction — a change is a replacement, like
region). The drift TARGET is emitted ONLY when the operand is declared — the D774 lesson: an
adopted arm64 function whose contract stayed silent must not drift-to-x86_64-replace because a
create default is not a drift requirement.

Field-proven end to end (own account, eu-central-1): pushed an arm64 base to ECR, converged
with `architectures: arm64` — AWS created the function as `['arm64']` (the x86_64 default would
have produced a dead function), resume reconciled the async create to succeeded, observe read
`implementation.architecture: arm64` measured, retire deleted it. Pinned by a build test
(create body carries `["arm64"]`, unknown/multi refuse, target only when declared) and a mutant
that drops the Architectures field. FOLLOW-UP (recorded, not built): the driver still does not
READ the image manifest to REFUSE a declared-arch-vs-image mismatch (the tester's request #3) —
the operand is the load-bearing fix; the manifest cross-check is the belt-and-suspenders for an
operator who declares the wrong arch, and is deferred.

## D1002 — aws/preflight: a throttle is not a missing permission

Field-found (acme ACME-036#2). When the IAM query API rate-limits SimulatePrincipalPolicy it
answers HTTP 400 `<Code>Throttling</Code>` "Rate exceeded". The preflight reported that as
"SimulatePrincipalPolicy HTTP 400 (the acting identity needs iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy)" — a
false remediation: the identity HAS the permission (the retry succeeded unchanged), the provider
was simply throttling. The wrong sentence sends the operator to grant a permission they hold, or
to broaden IAM. The `code`/exit stayed correct (`preflight-inconclusive`); only the reason lied.
Fix: classify the error — `provider.Classify(status, code).Retryable()` (the throttle/rate-limit
family) asks for a RETRY ("the provider is rate-limiting the permission check; retry — the
permission is present, not missing"); a real 403/AccessDenied still names the missing permission.
Pinned by a test (Throttling → retry wording, AccessDenied → grant wording) + a mutant that reads
every non-200 as a denial. Freeze-admissible: the message misdirected the operator's action.

## D1003 — customerManagedKeys is observed unconditionally (a repo-wide false-clean)

Field-found (acme ACME-038). The cwlogs `observe` emitted `encryption.customerManagedKeys:
true` only when a customer key was present, and stayed SILENT when there was none. That silence
is a false-clean: a contract declaring `customerManagedKeys: true` (a hard constraint) had no
observed value to contradict, so it passed VACUOUSLY, and `verify` reported PROVEN over an
audit-trail log group under the provider's default key. A log group with no customer key is a
MEASURED FALSE (it uses a provider-managed key), never an absence — exactly the class this
project exists to close (`adoption must not lie`, gates-must-not-be-vacuous, invariants-were-
conditional).

The sweep it triggered found the SAME shape in ~21 drivers across all three clouds — nearly the
entire `customerManagedKeys` observe surface emitted the attribute only inside an `if key-present`
guard. Fixed uniformly: emit the boolean UNCONDITIONALLY, `Value: <the customer-key predicate that
was the guard>`, preserving each driver's exact condition (customer-key vs provider/AWS/Azure-
managed key). AWS: cwlogs, backupvault, kinesis, sns, sqs, opensearch-serverless, secretsmanager,
redshift-serverless, s3. GCP: firestore, managedkafka, bigquery, secretmanager. Azure: aisearch,
azfiles, backupvault, cosmos, eventhubs, blob, azkafka, flexserver.

The honesty line the tester asked for in request #2 is kept: a measured `false` only where the
encryption state is read from the resource's MAIN describe; where it would need a separate read
that can fail (redshift namespace read, s3 unparseable/failed-read branch) or lives at an unread
path (GCP secretmanager auto-replication), the attribute stays OMITTED/unknown — "I did not
measure" is never collapsed into "false". Pinned by flipping every test that asserted the
attribute was ABSENT-when-no-key to assert `== false`, plus a mutant that reverts one driver to
the silent-when-absent form.

## D1004 — dynamodb + eventbridgescheduler: in-place update for what the provider patches live

Field-found (acme ACME-037#1, ACME-039#1). Two drivers reconciled a change the provider
supports IN PLACE by claiming it needed a REPLACEMENT — one a false destructive claim, the
other a silent non-detection.

**dynamodb (037#1):** the driver had no explicit ClassifyChange, so every change fell to the
default (replacement, D215). Disabling `backup.pointInTimeRecovery` on a live table read as
"replacing stateful table yields an empty successor — allow_replace_stateful consent", i.e. the
tool told the operator a DESTRUCTIVE rebuild was the only path to toggle PITR — when
UpdateContinuousBackups changes it on the live table, and UpdateTable changes deletion.protection,
neither touching data. Fix: `classifyDynamoDBChange` marks those two mutable (region + schema stay
a replacement) + `updateDynamoDB` patches them (PITR via UpdateContinuousBackups with the DECLARED
value so DISABLE is expressible, deletion.protection via UpdateTable), ownership re-checked by tags
before any mutation, four-valued.

**eventbridgescheduler (039#1):** the cron/rate expression is opaque impl, but was neither observed
nor a drift target — so changing `rate(1 hour)` to `rate(1 minute)` produced ZERO actions: the
contract could stand a schedule up but never keep it, and a key-destroying timer could silently
drift off its declared cadence. Fix: observe emits the live `ScheduleExpression` on a reserved
operand path; OperandTargets renders the desired one; `classifyEBSChange` marks it (and
schedule.enabled) mutable; `updateEventBridgeScheduler` patches via UpdateSchedule (PUT the full
definition — the schedule identity survives).

Both freeze-admissible: the first is a false claim that a change requires a destructive replacement;
the second is a drift that passes silently (a schedule the contract cannot maintain). Deferred with
a clear record: the scheduler DLQ operand (039#2, a new capability), `claim` for
iam/bedrock/eventbridgescheduler (039#3/036#1, a frozen-compiler predicate), and the lambda log
group before the function exists (037#2, an operand or apply returning derived names). Pinned by
classify + update tests for both, plus mutants that revert each classify to immutable.

## D1005 — discoverLoadBalancers follows ELBv2's pages (a sibling the pagination pass missed)

An adversarial audit confronting the AWS drivers against botocore's own model (the
highest-yield surface in BUG_HUNTING.md) found `discoverLoadBalancers` issuing one
`DescribeLoadBalancers` and unmarshalling the members once, while its six siblings in the
same sweep loop. ELBv2 paginates at `PageSize` (default 400) and hands back a `NextMarker`
(botocore elbv2/2015-12-01: input token `Marker`, output token `NextMarker`) — and unlike
EC2, it does NOT return everything when the limit is unset. So a region past 400 load
balancers silently dropped the rest from discovery: a real public ALB reported
not-present-in-estate, invisible to adoption, which is the exact failure this sweep exists
to end. The D810/D812 pagination pass looped the siblings and missed this one (and
`discoverVPC`, which is harmless because EC2 returns all VPCs without `MaxResults`).

Freeze-admissible (D716): the tool says something FALSE in the dangerous direction — an
existing resource reported absent. Fix: loop on `Marker`/`NextMarker` like the RDS sibling;
a test drives a fake that hands back a `NextMarker` and asserts the page-two balancer is
discovered.

## D1006 — the help's provider verb and provider-name lists, reconciled to the code

Same audit, the CLI `--help` surface: two published closed sets had drifted from the sets
the binary enforces. The F4 note still listed `repair` and `anchor` as `--provider`-required
verbs — removed from `providerVerbs` in D571 as pure-ledger operations — so the help named
two verbs the guard does not gate. And three copies of the accepted-provider list (the F4
note and both refusal messages) said `(aws|gcp|azure|k8s|fake)` while `knownProviders` holds
eight, so a user who mistyped `cloudfare` was told cloudflare was not a real provider.

Fix: the prose is corrected; the two error messages now render `knownProviderList()` so they
cannot drift by construction; and a gate (`TestHelpNamesTheProviderVerbsAndProviders`)
reconciles the F4 verb list against `providerVerbs` and the name list against
`knownProviders` — the same shape as D688's `--at` gate.

## D1007 — attrvisibility's vacuity guard floored the wrong population

Same audit, the gates-that-cannot-fail (D328) surface. `TestRealisedAttributesAreObserved-
OrExplained` checks that every attribute a driver REALISES (a `case "x.y":` arm in a `Build*`
switch) is one its `observe` reads back or names a reason it cannot. Its floor guards count
builder FUNCTIONS (`len(builds)`, `compared`), not the realised-attribute case-arms the
check iterates — so a `Build*` refactored from a switch to an if-chain would match nothing
under the `attrCase` regex, contribute zero realised attributes, and silently escape the
observe-coverage check while the function-count guards stayed green. The verbatim example
BUG_HUNTING.md warns about ("a switch rewritten as if-chains"). Fix: floor the realised set
the check actually iterates, in all three driver gates.

## D1008 — audit findings recorded but deferred under the freeze

The same adversarial sweep turned up findings whose honest fix is a post-unfreeze feature or
which fall below the freeze bar; recorded here so the next unfreeze starts where this stopped.

- **`mutablehasupdater` gate escape.** `aws/asg`, `gcp/mig` and `azure/azvmss` classify their
